question_text: A 28-year-old man presented with dysphasia, dysarthria, descending symmetric flaccid paralysis of voluntary muscles, diplopia, decreased deep tendon reflexes, constipation. The probable diagnosis of botulism is made. Which membrane transport is affected?
explanation:
Option C: Diagnosis: Botulism, caused by botulinum toxin.

  • Affected Process: Exocytosis, necessary for neurotransmitter release.
  • Mechanism:
    • SNARE proteins (e.g., Synaptobrevin) are crucial for exocytosis of acetylcholine.
    • Botulinum toxin degrades SNARE proteins, inhibiting neurotransmitter release and leading to paralysis.

Why not others:

Option A: Facilitated diffusion is not primarily involved in neurotransmitter release.

Option B: Primary active transport is related to ion movement, not exocytosis.

Option D: Simple diffusion does not apply to neurotransmitter release mechanisms.

Key takeaways:

Botulism inhibits exocytosis by degrading SNARE proteins, leading to paralysis.

question_text: Neurological examination of a patient revealed the following Diplopia and suspected involvement of other cranial nerves, tingling and numbness in the lower extremities. Symptoms were getting worse upon taking hot bath. Defect of which of the following cells is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Oligodendrocytes are responsible for producing and maintaining myelin in the central nervous system (CNS). The patient's diplopia (cranial nerve involvement), sensory symptoms (tingling, numbness), and worsening with heat (Uhthoff's phenomenon) strongly suggest demyelination, commonly seen in Multiple Sclerosis (MS). MS is an autoimmune disorder characterized by loss of oligodendrocytes, leading to impaired nerve conduction.

Incorrect Options:

Option B: Ependymal Cells: These line the ventricles and produce cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Damage to these cells is associated with hydrocephalus or CSF flow obstruction, not demyelinating diseases.

Option C: Astrocytes: Provide support, maintain the blood-brain barrier, and regulate ion balance. They are involved in reactive gliosis (scar formation) in MS but are not the primary cells affected.

Option D: Microglia: These are the immune cells of the CNS, responsible for phagocytosis and inflammatory responses. While they play a role in MS-related neuroinflammation, the primary defect in MS is oligodendrocyte destruction.

Key Takeaways:

  • Oligodendrocytes produce CNS myelin; their loss causes MS.
  • MS presents with diplopia, sensory deficits, and worsening with heat (Uhthoff's phenomenon).
  • Other glial cells (ependymal, astrocytes, microglia) have different CNS functions and are not the primary cause of demyelination.

question_text: A 35-year-old female presented with difficulty in walking, fatigue and reduced reflexes. She was diagnosed to be the case of Lambert Eaton syndrome. Antibodies are produced against which channels?
explanation:
Option A: In Lambert Eaton syndrome, antibodies are produced against the voltage gated calcium channels present on the presynaptic membrane, which destroy the channels leading to muscular weakness.

Option B: Potassium channel.

Potassium channels are responsible for repolarizing the membrane after depolarization by allowing potassium ions (K+) to flow out of the cell.

Disease: Potassium channel autoimmune syndromes (e.g., Hypokalemic periodic paralysis).

Option C: Sodium channel:

Sodium channels play a crucial role in initiating action potentials by allowing sodium ions (Na+) to flow into cells during depolarization.

  • Disease: Na+ channelopathies (e.g., Sodium channel myotonia or periodic paralysis).

Option D: Chloride channel:

  • Disease: Cystic fibrosis Mucoviscidosis(due to mutations in the CFTR chloride channel located on chromosome 6). Most common mutation is ΔF508 deletion which codes for phenylalanine.

Key take aways:

In Lambert-Eaton syndrome, antibodies are produced against calcium channels leading to impaired release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction and resulting in muscle weakness.

Reference: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, 26th Edition, Page no. 328

question_text: 34-year-old man was not able to recognize the face of his college friend although he was able to recognize his friend by his voice. Where could be the site of lesion in this case scenario?
explanation:
Option C: In humans, storage and recognition of faces are more strongly represented in the inferior temporal lobe. Damage to this area can cause prosopagnosia, the inability to recognize faces. Patients with this abnormality can recognize people by their voices, body language, etc. However, they cannot identify the familiar people by seeing their faces.

  • Many of them show autonomic responses when they see familiar as opposed to unfamiliar face. The presence of an autonomic response to a familiar face in the absence of recognition has been explained by postulating the existence of a separate dorsal pathway for processing information about faces that leads to recognition at only a subconscious level.

Option A: Parietal lobe - Involved in spatial awareness and sensory integration, but not specifically in facial recognition.

Option B: Occipital lobe - Primarily responsible for visual processing, but damage here affects basic vision rather than the specific ability to recognize faces.

Option D: Frontal lobe - Involved in decision-making, problem-solving, and social behavior but not directly responsible for facial recognition.

Key takeaways :

Damage to the inferior temporal lobe can lead to prosopagnosia, which is the inability to recognize faces while retaining the ability to recognize individuals through other cues, such as voice. This area is crucial for facial recognition.

question_text:
A 55-year-old male presents to the clinic with progressive weakness in the right leg and altered sensation on the left side of his body. The patient reports difficulty walking, stumbling frequently, and feeling an unusual numbness in his left leg. These symptoms have been progressively worsening over the past few months. He also reports intermittent episodes of back pain, radiating down his right leg.
Upon further inquiry, the patient reveals that he has noticed a decrease in his ability to feel light touch and temperature on the left side of his body, below his waist. Conversely, he feels an unusual tightness and increased muscle tone in his right leg. Additionally, there have been urinary hesitancy and occasional constipation, but no significant bladder incontinence or bowel leakage.
The patient has no history of recent trauma, and his medical history is significant for hypertension and a recent unintentional weight loss of 5 kg over three months. No family history of neurological disorders was reported.
After advising MRI of the thoracic spine a spinal cord tumor compressing the right side of the spinal cord at T10 level is suspected.
What could be the probable clinical diagnosis based on above investigations?
explanation:
• Right-Sided Symptoms:
    • Motor Weakness: Indicates damage to the corticospinal tract, causing weakness in the right leg.
    • Spasticity: Increased muscle tone in the right leg points to upper motor neuron involvement.
    • Loss of Proprioception and Fine Touch: Dorsal column impairment due to right-sided spinal cord compression.
  • Left-Sided Symptoms:
    • Loss of Pain and Temperature Sensation: Affects the spinothalamic tract, which decussates, explaining the contralateral sensory loss.
  • Overall Pattern:
    • Unilateral Weakness with Contralateral Sensory Loss: This specific neurological deficit pattern is characteristic of Brown-Sequard Syndrome, resulting from compression on one side of the spinal cord.

Why Not Other Options:

  • A (ALS):
    • Incorrect because ALS does not present with sensory changes; it primarily affects motor neurons, leading to muscle weakness without sensory loss. ALS include both UMN+LMN symptoms.
    • UMN findings: hyperreflexia, spasticity.
    • LMN findings: muscle atophy, fasciculations and weakness.
  • B (MS):
    • Incorrect as MS typically presents with multiple lesions affecting different CNS regions over time, rather than the unilateral, progressive symptoms observed here. It is a demyelinating disorder, in spinal cord it affects short segment.
    • CHARCOATS TRIAD: Scanning speech, Intentional tremors, Nystagmus(SIN)
    • OTHER FINDINGS; Lhermette sign, Uthoff sign, U/L asymmetrical optic neuritis.
  • D (Transverse Myelitis):
    • Incorrect because transverse myelitis usually results in bilateral motor and sensory deficits below the level of the lesion. This patient has unilateral symptoms, more indicative of Brown-Sequard syndrome.

Key Takeaways:

  • Brown-Sequard Syndrome is characterized by ipsilateral motor weakness and contralateral sensory loss (pain and temperature), commonly due to a unilateral spinal cord lesion.
  • The patient's MRI findings and symptomatology support this diagnosis, distinguishing it from other neurological conditions.

question_text: A man suffered from road traffic accident that lead to trauma to the spinal cord. On investigation, a complete transection of one side of the spinal cord is suspected. For below the level of injury Which of the following statement is incorrect regarding this case?
option_a: Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature
option_b: High dose of corticosteroids have been shown to be of value if administered soon after the onset of spinal cord injury
option_d: Weakness and spasticity in certain muscle groups on same side of body
explanation:
• Contralateral loss of pain and temperature occurs because the spinothalamic tract crosses to the opposite side at the spinal cord level. This means damage on one side results in loss of these sensations on the opposite side of the body, below the lesion.
  • Corticosteroids are effective in reducing inflammation if administered early, as they suppress immune cells and reduce capillary permeability, preventing further damage from swelling and inflammation.
  • Ipsilateral loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception occurs due to damage to the fasciculus gracilis or fasciculus cuneatus (dorsal column), which ascends without crossing until it reaches the medulla. This leads to loss of stereognosis on the same side of the lesion.
  • Ipsilateral weakness and spasticity arise from damage to the corticospinal tract (a motor pathway) that affects the same side of the body. Since corticospinal fibers cross at the medulla, any damage below this level affects motor control ipsilaterally.

Why not others:

  • Contralateral pain and temperature loss happens due to spinothalamic tract involvement.
  • Corticosteroids prevent secondary damage from inflammation and swelling.
  • Ipsilateral stereognosis loss is due to the dorsal column damage, and ipsilateral motor weakness is caused by corticospinal tract disruption.

Key Takeaways:

  • Spinal cord hemisection results in contralateral loss of pain/temperature and ipsilateral loss of fine touch, proprioception, and motor control.
  • Early corticosteroid therapy can reduce secondary damage in spinal cord injuries.

question_text: A patient who had a stroke 2 days ago now presents with uncontrollable, violent, and jerking movements of the limbs on one side of the body. What is the most likely site of the lesion?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's presentation is consistent with hemiballismus, a hyperkinetic movement disorder marked by involuntary, forceful, flinging movements of the extremities on one side. This condition typically follows a vascular insult (stroke) that damages the subthalamic nucleus.

Basal Ganglia and Movement Disorders:

  • Hypokinetic Disorders
    • Parkinsonism: Caused by dopamine deficiency in the substantia nigra pars compacta.
    • Clinical features: Akinesia, bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, resting tremor, shuffling gait, stooped posture, micrographia, reduced facial expression, and mood/cognitive changes.
  • Hyperkinetic Disorders
    • Hemiballismus: Lesion of the subthalamic nucleus → decreased inhibition of the thalamus → excessive, uncontrolled movements.
    • Huntington’s Disease: Degeneration of striatal neurons in the indirect pathway → choreiform, dance-like movements.
    • Dystonia: Dysregulation of the direct pathway → sustained, twisting, and abnormal postures.

Anatomical Role of Basal Ganglia Structures:

  • Striatum (Caudate + Putamen): Major input center receiving cortical signals. (Options C & D ruled out)
  • Globus Pallidus (GPe, GPi): Processes inhibitory and excitatory motor signals. GPi exerts tonic inhibition on the thalamus.
  • Substantia Nigra:
    • Pars compacta: Dopamine production (degenerates in Parkinsonism).
    • Pars reticulata: Inhibitory output to the thalamus via GABA. (Option B ruled out)
  • Subthalamic Nucleus: Provides excitatory glutamatergic input to GPi and SNr. Damage → loss of inhibition → hyperkinetic state → hemiballismus. (Correct Answer)

Key Neurotransmitters:

  • Dopamine: From substantia nigra (pars compacta), modulates direct & indirect pathways.
  • GABA: Major inhibitory transmitter (striatum, GPi, GPe, SNr).
  • Glutamate: Major excitatory transmitter (cortex → striatum; subthalamic nucleus → GPi/SNr).

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Substantia nigra (Option B): Lesions here reduce dopamine and produce Parkinsonism (hypokinetic features: rigidity, tremor, bradykinesia), not violent flinging movements.

Putamen (Option C): As part of the striatum, it primarily influences voluntary motor control, but isolated lesions here are not associated with hemiballismus.

Caudate nucleus (Option D): Involved in cognitive and limbic aspects of motor control; its degeneration is classic in Huntington's disease, producing chorea rather than hemiballismus.

question_text: A 40 year old man presents to the clinic with a sudden onset of facial weakness on the right side. He is unable to close his eye, and his mouth droops on the same side. He reports no other symptoms, and there is no history of trauma. On examination, he can't raise his right eyebrow or smile symmetrically, the most likely diagnosis is?
explanation:
• Bell's palsy is characterized by unilateral facial paralysis involving both the upper and lower face. It results from damage or inflammation of the facial nerve (CN VII), affecting the ability to close the eye, raise the eyebrow, and smile.

Characteristics features of Bell's palsy

  • Inability to raise the eyebrow or close the eye on the affected side.
  • Drooping of the mouth on the affected side.
  • Upper and lower face are both affected (distinguishing it from a stroke).
  • The onset is usually rapid, occurring over hours to days.
  • No other neurological deficits or history of trauma.
  • Bell's phenomenon is a normal reflex that occurs when the eyes roll upward and outward when a person tries to close their eyelids

Why Not Other Options

  • B (Stroke): A stroke typically spares the forehead due to bilateral cortical innervation of the upper facial muscles, so the patient would be able to raise their eyebrow.
  • C (Trigeminal neuralgia): Causes severe facial pain but does not result in facial weakness or paralysis.
  • D (Myasthenia gravis): Causes fluctuating muscle weakness but would not typically cause sudden, complete facial paralysis on one side.

Key Takeaways

  • Bell's palsy involves complete unilateral facial paralysis affecting both the upper and lower face, unlike stroke which spares the forehead.

question_text: A 32-year-old man presents with progressive weakness in both lower limbs that started 5 days ago and has now ascended to involve the upper limbs. He reports a history of diarrheal illness 2 weeks earlier. On examination, there is flaccid quadriparesis, areflexia, and bilateral facial weakness. Nerve conduction studies show demyelinating polyneuropathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Guillain-Barré syndrome is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP) that often follows infections such as Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis.
  • It is characterised by rapidly progressive, symmetrical, ascending muscle weakness, areflexia, and sometimes cranial nerve involvement (commonly facial palsy).
  • Autonomic dysfunction may also occur. Nerve conduction studies typically show slowed conduction velocities due to demyelination. This clinical presentation is classic for GBS.

Explanation of other options:

Myasthenia gravis (Option A): Causes fluctuating muscle weakness with diurnal variation, but reflexes are preserved, and it is not preceded by infection in most cases.

Poliomyelitis (Option C): Presents with asymmetrical flaccid paralysis and preserved sensation, unlike GBS, which is symmetrical.

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (Option D): Associated with paraneoplastic syndromes (especially small-cell lung carcinoma), shows proximal weakness that improves with activity, not ascending paralysis.

question_text: Which of the following statements is correct concerning a 50-year-old male who was diagnosed with a submandibular gland tumor, underwent surgical removal, and subsequently suffered lingual nerve damage?
option_a: The taste sensation of the posterior one-third of the tongue is lost
option_b: The taste sensation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is lost
option_c: A general sensation of the posterior one-third of the tongue is lost
option_d: A general sensation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is lost
explanation:
Explanation :

The lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3), is responsible for providing general sensation (touch, pain, and temperature) to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Additionally, it carries taste fibers from the chorda tympani (a branch of the facial nerve, CN VII), which are involved in taste perception in the same region.

Damage to the lingual nerve primarily affects general sensory input from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. This is the most consistent and reliable symptom following lingual nerve injury.

Clinical Insight:

During submandibular gland surgery, the lingual nerve is particularly vulnerable due to its close anatomical relationship with the gland. Postoperative complications commonly include:

  • Loss of general sensation in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
  • Occasional loss of taste in the same area if the chorda tympani is also damaged.

Explanation for other options:

The taste sensation of the posterior one-third of the tongue is lost (Option A):
Incorrect. This region is innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) for both taste and general sensation, and is not affected by lingual nerve injury.

The taste sensation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is lost (Option B):
incorrect. The lingual nerve does carry chorda tympani fibers for taste, but taste loss only occurs if the chorda tympani is also injured. However, general sensation loss is the more reliable and consistent symptom of lingual nerve damage.

General sensation of the posterior one-third of the tongue is lost (Option C):
Incorrect. This area is also innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), and is not impacted by damage to the lingual nerve.

question_text: A patient who recently had a leg amputation reports feeling pain in the missing limb, a phenomenon known as phantom limb pain. This phenomenon is based on which of the following mechanism.
explanation:
• Phantom limb pain arises due to cortical plasticity, which refers to the brain's ability to reorganize itself after injury or amputation.
  • After the loss of a limb, the cortical representation of that limb is taken over by adjacent areas in the brain. This can lead to misinterpretation of signals, resulting in sensations like pain, itching, or tingling in the missing limb.
  • Rewiring of neural circuits occurs, and neurons that were previously connected to the amputated limb now respond to stimuli from other parts of the body, but the brain may still perceive these signals as coming from the missing limb.
  • This process is an example of the brain's adaptability but can cause discomfort as the brain attempts to process signals without proper input from the absent limb.

Why Not Other Options

  • B (Weber French Law): Deals with the relationship between stimulus magnitude and perception, irrelevant to cortical reorganization.
  • C (Principle of Labeled Time): Involves temporal coding of sensory information, not applicable to phantom limb pain.
  • D (Muller's Specific Nerve Energy): Relates to how specific nerves produce distinct sensations, regardless of stimulus, which doesn't explain cortical reorganization.

Key Takeaways

  • Cortical plasticity leads to phantom limb pain, where the brain reorganizes and adjacent regions take over the area once representing the amputated limb.
  • This reorganization may cause sensory confusion, leading to the perception of pain or sensations in the missing limb.

question_text:
During a pulmonary function test, a patient first generated Curve #1. Subsequent to administration of a bronchodilator, she generated Curve #2.

The increased flow in Curve #2 versus Curve #1 is a result of which of the following?
option_a: Stimulation of beta 2-adrenergic receptors in bronchial smooth muscle
option_b: Stimulation of alpha-adrenergic receptors in bronchial smooth muscle
option_c: Stimulation of parasympathetic nerves to airway smooth muscle
option_d: Stimulation of irritant airway receptors in airway epithelium
explanation:
Reversibility of airway obstruction is assessed by the change in expiratory flow rate before and after administration of a bronchodilator.

Stimulation of b2-adrenergic receptors mediates dilation of bronchial smooth muscle.

Mast cell degranulation or stimulation of alpha-adrenergic receptors, parasympathetic nerves to bronchial smooth muscle, or irritant airway receptors all cause bronchoconstriction, which would decrease expiratory flow rates.

question_text: A 45-year-old male presents with double vision and difficulty swallowing. He has a history of autoimmune disease and notices that his symptoms worsen as the day progresses. Neurological examination shows ptosis and muscle weakness, which improve after a brief period of rest. There are no sensory deficits, and deep tendon reflexes are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Myasthenia gravis (MG) presents with fluctuating muscle weakness that worsens with activity and improves with rest.
  • Common symptoms include ptosis, diplopia, and difficulty swallowing.
  • MG is caused by autoantibodies against acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
  • No sensory deficits or reflex abnormalities, which aligns with MG.

Presentation

  • weak neck muscles give cause the head to fall forward or backward
  • Drooping eyelids (ptosis)
  • Inability to move eyes side to side
  • double vision (diplopia)
  • difficulty speaking (dysarthria)
  • difficulty swallowing (dysphagia)
  • Worsening of symptoms as the day progresses is typical in MG.

Why not othchroers:

  • A) Guillain-Barre Syndrome (GBS): It is is a rare autoimmune disorder in which the body's immune system mistakenly attacks the peripheral nervous system. It often follows an infection, surgery, or vaccination. It Causes ascending weakness with areflexia, not the fluctuating weakness seen in MG. Symptoms do not improve with rest.
  • B) Multiple Sclerosis (MS): It is a chronic autoimmune disease of the central nervous system (CNS), primarily affecting the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerves. It is demyelinating disorder causing sensory disturbances and varied neurological deficits, not pure muscle fatigability seen in MG.
  • D) Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS): In LEMS, the immune system attacks voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) on nerve terminals, reducing the release of acetylcholine. It Causes proximal muscle weakness, improving with exercise. Unlike MG, ptosis and diplopia are uncommon early in LEMS.

Key Takeaways:

  • Myasthenia gravis presents with fluctuating muscle weakness, worsens with activity, and improves with rest, affecting the ocular and bulbar muscles.
  • Other conditions (GBS, MS, LEMS) show different patterns of weakness and involve distinct neurological signs.

question_text:
A 45-year-old woman comes to the office due to a 4-month history of headaches and blurred vision. She takes no medications and has no other medical conditions. After the initial laboratory work-up, a CT scan of the abdomen is performed that reveals a 2-cm left-sided adrenal mass. The patient undergoes an uncomplicated left-sided adrenalectomy. Gross examination of the adrenal gland demonstrates a well-defined yellowish tumor within the cortex. Further evaluation reveals that the tumor cells are functionally similar to cells from the outermost hormone-producing layer of the adrenal cortex.
This patient would most likely have had which of the following additional symptoms?
explanation:
• Primary Hyperaldosteronism:(CONN~
    • The well-defined yellowish tumor in the adrenal cortex suggests excess aldosterone production, characteristic of primary hyperaldosteronism.
  • Symptoms Related to Hyperaldosteronism:
    • High sodium levels lead to hypertension.
    • Low potassium levels cause muscle weakness and paresthesia.
    • Additionally, metabolic alkalosis may occur due to hydrogen ion loss.

Why not other options:

  • Excessive hair growth:
    • Incorrect: This symptom is associated with excess androgen production, not aldosterone.
  • Weight gain and bruising:
    • Incorrect: These symptoms are indicative of Cushing's syndrome, which involves excess cortisol, not aldosterone.
  • Diarrhea and flushing:
    • Incorrect: These symptoms are more typical of carcinoid syndrome, which is unrelated to aldosterone excess.

Key Takeaways:

  • The patient's symptoms of muscle weakness and paresthesia are consistent with hyperaldosteronism due to low potassium levels.
  • Identifying the correct hormonal dysfunction is essential for understanding the clinical presentation and management of adrenal tumors.

question_text: 49-year-old male developed chest pain, nausea and uneasiness. On investigation, ECG shows ST segment elevation. The probable diagnosis is Myocardial infarction. The best cardiac marker marker is:
explanation:
Option C: Troponin I is the best cardiac marker for diagnosing myocardial infarction.

  • Timing: Troponin I rises in 2-4 hours after injury and remains elevated for 7-10 days.
  • Specificity: It is highly specific for cardiac injury.
  • Other Markers:
    • LDH: Normally, LDH2 > LDH1, but in myocardial infarction, this reverses (LDH Flip).
    • CK-MB: Good for detecting re-infarction, rising in 2-4 hours and falling in 2-3 days.
    • Myoglobin: One of the earliest markers to rise (within 1 hour) but lacks specificity, falling within 24 hours.

Why Not Others:

Option A: LDH: Not specific for myocardial infarction and has a delayed rise compared to troponin.

Option B: CK-MB: Good for re-infarction but less sensitive and specific than troponin I for initial diagnosis.

Option D: Myoglobin: Rises early but lacks specificity for myocardial infarction, as it can be elevated in other conditions.

Key takeaways:

The best cardiac marker for diagnosing myocardial infarction is Troponin I, as it rises within 2-4 hours and remains elevated for 7-10 days.

question_text: A 28-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigable weakness, particularly involving her eyelids and extraocular muscles. By the evening, she develops ptosis and diplopia, which improve after rest. Reflexes and sensation are normal. The ice pack test on the eyelid improves ptosis. Which of the following best describes the underlying mechanism of her condition?
option_a: Autoantibodies blocking acetylcholine receptors at the presynaptic terminal
option_b: Autoantibodies blocking acetylcholine receptors at the postsynaptic terminal
option_c: Autoimmune destruction of voltage-gated calcium channels at the presynaptic terminal
option_d: Autoimmune destruction of voltage-gated calcium channels at the postsynaptic terminal
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation is classic for myasthenia gravis (MG), an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction.
  • In MG, autoantibodies target nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the postsynaptic membrane, reducing the number of functional receptors.
  • This leads to impaired neuromuscular transmission and fatigable weakness, which improves with rest (as acetylcholine accumulates) and with the ice pack test (cold reduces acetylcholinesterase activity, increasing acetylcholine availability).

Explanation of other options:

Presynaptic receptor block (Option A): MG is not a presynaptic disorder; presynaptic pathologies include botulism.

Presynaptic Ca2+ channel destruction (Option C): This describes Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), where impaired calcium influx reduces acetylcholine release.

Postsynaptic Ca2+ channel destruction (Option D): No such mechanism exists in neuromuscular junction diseases.

question_text: A man presents to the hospital with complaints of drooping of eyelids and increasing eye irritation. He reports his symptoms to be worsening as the day goes on, particularly during outdoor activities. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation of ptosis and fatiguability is suggestive of myasthenia gravis.

Myasthenia gravis

  • Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder with antibodies directed against acetylcholine receptors at the postsynaptic neuromuscular junction.
  • Primarily leads to weakness of the voluntary muscles, particularly the ocular and facial muscles.
  • Clinical features
    • Fatiguability: Symptoms worsen with activity and improve with rest.
    • Ptosis
    • Diplopia
    • Generalised muscle weakness.

Disorders related to Neuromuscular junction:

Explanation:

Botulism Toxicity (Option C): Botulinum toxin inhibits acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. It results in muscle weakness, but symptoms typically include descending paralysis and can affect multiple muscle groups. While ptosis may occur, botulism generally presents with more widespread weakness and not specifically with worsening symptoms throughout the day.

Tetanus Toxicity (Option D): Tetanus caused by Clostridium tetani leads to severe muscle spasms and rigidity. Symptoms often include lockjaw, muscle stiffness, and generalised spasms, rather than ptosis or symptoms that worsen with the day.

question_text: A 45-year-old man presents with muscle cramps, which are worse at the night. Fasciculations are frequent and multiple. The probable diagnosis of amyotropic lateral sclerosis is made. In this disease due to overactivity of NMDA receptors (shown in figure) there will be?
explanation:
Option B: In Amyotropic lateral sclerosis due to overactivity of NMDA receptors there will be enhanced calcium ion influx. NMDA receptor is a receptor of glutamate.

Riluzole is a NMDA receptor blocker used in the treatment of amyotropic lateral sclerosis.

Option A: Decreased chloride ions influx: Chloride influx is typically associated with inhibitory neurotransmission (e.g., GABA receptors), not NMDA receptors, which are excitatory. GABA receptor stimulation leads to increased Cl- influx.

Option C: Enhanced potassium ions influx: Potassium typically moves out of neurons during repolarization, not into the cell via NMDA receptors, though NMDA receptors are permeable to K+.

Option D: Decreased sodium ion influx: NMDA receptors also allow sodium influx, but the primary issue in ALS is excessive calcium influx, not reduced sodium influx.

Key takeaways :

In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), overactivity of NMDA receptors leads to enhanced calcium ion influx , which contributes to neuronal damage and excitotoxicity.

question_text: A 42-year-old male presented with convulsions, awful taste, dilated pupil and increased reflex. The probable?
explanation:
Option C: Strychnine is a competitive antagonist of glycine receptors. Glycine is an inhibitory neurotransmitter, particularly in the spinal cord and brainstem. It normally prevents excessive neuronal firing by inhibiting motor neurons. Strychnine toxin acts by blocking the action of glycine at the post-synaptic receptors in the motor neurons of the anterior horn of the spinal cord.

Option A: Agonist of Dopamine: Dopamine is a neurotransmitter involved in various functions such as movement control, reward, and motivation. Strychnine does not interact with dopamine receptors.

Option B: Agonist of Serotonin: It is involved in mood regulation, sleep, and more. Serotonin agonists enhance serotonin activity. Strychnine does not stimulate serotonin receptors.

Option D: Antagonist of Acetylcholine: Antagonists of ACh receptors block cholinergic transmission, which could lead to paralysis or reduced muscle activity. Strychnine primarily affects glycine receptors, not acetylcholine receptors.

Key takeaways :

In strychnine poisoning, the toxin acts as an antagonist of glycine leading to increased neuronal excitability and convulsions.

question_text: A 35-year-old man presented with ptosis, dysarthria and descending flaccid paralysis 5 days after consumption of canned beverage. On examination, there is decreased deep tendon reflexes. The probable diagnosis is botulism. The botulinum toxin degrades SNARE proteins like synaptobrevin (shown in the figure). Which of the following neurotransmitter will not be released?
explanation:
Option D: Botulinum toxin inhibits Ach release by cleaving SNARE proteins, which are necessary for vesicles containing acetylcholine to fuse with the presynaptic membrane. It  binds to acetylcholine receptors on the nerve terminals at neuromuscular junction, which results in blockage of release of the acetylcholine, leading to flaccid paralysis.

A. GABA: Inhibitory neurotransmitter released in the CNS, not affected by botulinum toxin. GABA is not typically involved in neuromuscular transmission, and its inhibition does not directly lead to flaccid paralysis.

B. Serotonin: Primarily involved in mood and cognition, not impacted by botulinum toxin. Its dysfunction does not explain the motor symptoms observed in this patient.

C. Glycine: Inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord, not directly affected by the toxin. Glycine is more implicated in diseases like tetanus, where glycine release is inhibited, leading to spastic paralysis (in contrast to the flaccid paralysis seen in botulism).

Key Takeaways:

In botulism, botulinum toxin blocks the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, causing flaccid paralysis.

question_text: A 32-year-old female presents with sudden, severe right-sided facial pain that is sharp and lasts for a few seconds. The pain is triggered by chewing and touching her face. She reports multiple episodes per day, but no motor or sensory deficits on examination. Her neurological examination is otherwise unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Trigeminal neuralgia presents with sudden, sharp facial pain in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve.
  • Pain is brief (lasting a few seconds) and can be triggered by chewing, touching the face, or other stimuli.
  • Patients typically have no motor or sensory deficits, and the neurological examination is often unremarkable.
  • Cluster headaches and migraines involve longer-lasting, more diffuse pain and may include other symptoms (e.g., nausea, autonomic signs).

Why not others:

  • B) Temporal Arteritis: Typically affects individuals over 50; presents with symptoms like jaw claudication and visual disturbances, not the sharp, brief pain seen in this case.
  • C) Cluster Headache: Causes severe, unilateral pain usually around the eye, accompanied by autonomic symptoms (e.g., tearing, nasal congestion), lasting longer than the few seconds described here.
  • D) Migraine: Involves throbbing, unilateral pain with nausea and light sensitivity; pain is generally longer-lasting and not triggered by light touch or chewing.

Key Takeaways:

  • Trigeminal nerve carries general sense from the face and supplies the muscle of mastication.
  • Trigeminal neuralgia is characterized by brief, sharp facial pain triggered by simple activities like chewing or touching.
  • Other conditions (temporal arteritis, cluster headache, migraine) have distinct presentations and symptoms that do not align with the patient's description.

question_text: A patient experiences phantom limb pain following the amputation of the right limb. What would a PET scan most likely reveal in such a case?
option_a: Expansion of right somatosensory fibres for the hand into neighbouring areas
option_b: Neighbouring fibres of the right somatosensory area extending into the right-hand area
option_c: Expansion of the right sensory cortex
option_d: Expansion of the left sensory cortex
explanation:
Explanation:

  • After amputation, the brain undergoes cortical reorganisation.
  • In this case, the neighbouring somatosensory fibres that previously represented adjacent body parts extend into the region that formerly represented the right hand.
  • This reorganisation is associated with the perception of phantom limb pain.

Explanation for other options:

Expansion of right somatosensory fibres for the hand into Neighbouring areas (Option A):

  • Somatosensory fibres specifically responsible for the right hand expand into neighbouring regions.
  • However, it is not the fibres themselves that expand; rather, it is the cortical representation that changes.

Expansion of right sensory cortex (Option C):

  • Implies a general enlargement of the right sensory cortex.
  • However, the expansion is not global; rather, it involves the Neighbouring cortical areas invading the region corresponding to the amputated limb.

Expansion of left sensory cortex (Option D):

  • The left sensory cortex is responsible for processing sensory input from the right side of the body.
  • The reorganisation occurs in the sensory cortex corresponding to the amputated limb (in this case, the right cortex, which processes left-sided sensations).

Learning objective:

Phantom Limb Pain

  • Perceived due to cortical plasticity
  • In the phantom limb phenomenon, the limb does not exist (amputated), but the patient complains that he feels pain or itch in the limb.
  • Based on the evidence, brain reorganisation occurs when sensory input is cut off. For example, in leg amputees, the ventral posterior thalamic nucleus can perceive the signal that once received input from the leg and foot, now responds to stump (thigh) stimulation.

Management :

  1. Epidural Anaesthesia: Used during amputation surgery to reduce acute pain and subsequent need for opioids, lowering phantom pain incidence.
  2. Spinal Cord Stimulation: Electric current stimulates spinal pathways, reducing phantom limb pain and causing a tingling sensation instead in the phantom limb

question_text: A military after amputation tells the doctor that he still feels the pain in the amputated part. Which is incorrect statement regarding this case?
option_a: Reduced incidence of phantom pain following epidural anaesthesia during surgery is reported
option_c: Lateral dorsal thalamic nucleus is one example where this change can occur
option_d: Spinal cord stimulation has been shown to be effective therapy for phantom pain
explanation:
• Reduced incidence of phantom pain has been reported after epidural anesthesia during amputation surgery, as it may prevent acute surgical pain.
  • Phantom pain is based on cortical plasticity, where adjacent areas take over the cortical representation of the amputated limb.
  • The ventral posterior thalamic nucleus, not the lateral dorsal thalamic nucleus, is one example where cortical changes can occur.
  • Spinal cord stimulation has been shown to effectively reduce phantom pain. Electric current passed next to spinal cord interferes with the impulses ascending to the brain and lessens the pain felt in the phantom limb.

Why Not Others

  • A: Correct, as evidence supports the reduction of phantom pain with epidural anesthesia.
  • B: Correct, phantom pain is associated with cortical plasticity.
  • C: Incorrect, the ventral posterior thalamic nucleus is involved, not the lateral dorsal.
  • D: Correct, spinal cord stimulation is an effective therapy for phantom pain.

Key Takeaways

  • Phantom pain is due to cortical plasticity and can be managed with spinal cord stimulation.
  • The ventral posterior thalamic nucleus is involved in phantom pain, not the lateral dorsal nucleus.

question_text:
Mr. A.K. with the Age of 45 a pure vegetarian businessman having multiple sexual partners over the last two decades is presented to a neurophysician with complaints of difficulty walking, vision disturbances, and severe stabbing pains in the lower limbs for the past few months.

History:
No any trauma or accident
No any signs of tumor of nervous system (also confirmed by further radiological investigations)
No previous neurological or cardiovascular issues before the recent symptoms
Habit of having few pegs of alcohol every night after dinner.
On detailed history taking it was found that about 12 years ago, he had suffered from a painless ulcer on his penis (likely chancre) and swelling of lymph nodes in the inguinal region as well as he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous papules on his genitals and around the anus after 3 months of the healing of the chancre, which was adequately treated by a local dermatologist.
Over the last three weeks, he had experienced progressively worsening difficulty in maintaining his balance, especially in the dark, alongside a loss of fine touch and vibration sensations in his lower limbs. He also complains of sharp, shooting pains in the legs and a sense of numbness. Additionally, Mr. A.K. mentions episodes of blurred vision and difficulty focusing. There is also urinary incontinence and constipation

Physical examination reveals:
Ataxic gait with foot slapping, particularly during walking in low-light conditions.
Positive Romberg's Test.
Diminished deep Tendon Reflexes
Sensory disturbances like loss of proprioception, especially in the lower limbs, diminished vibration sense bilaterally.
Loss of two-point discrimination in the feet.

Cardiovascular Examination reveals abnormal Heart sounds: Early diastolic murmur suggestive of aortic regurgitation.

Lab investigations

Lumbar Puncture (CSF Analysis):
-Elevated protein levels
-Positive VDRL in cerebrospinal fluid.
-Lymphocytic pleocytosis (increased white blood cells in CSF).
-FTA-ABS positive in CSF.

CVS Examination:
-Echocardiogram: Confirms aortic regurgitation, showing regurgitate flow in the aortic valve.

Imaging:
-MRI Brain and Spinal Cord:
Shows signs of degeneration in the dorsal columns of the spinal cord.

Ophthalmological Examination:
-Argyll Robertson pupils (pupils accommodate but do not react to light).

What is the probable diagnosis?
option_d: B12 deficiency leading to subacute combined degeneration
explanation:
Tabes Dorsalis:

  • Late Complication of Syphilis: Tabes dorsalis is a chronic complication of untreated syphilis, typically developing 10-30 years post-infection.
  • Dorsal Columns and Roots Affected: It primarily affects the dorsal columns and dorsal roots of the spinal cord, leading to:
    • Ataxia: Unsteady gait due to loss of proprioception.
    • Sensory Loss: Diminished deep tendon reflexes and loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception in lower limbs.
    • Severe Pain: Sharp, shooting pains (neurogenic pain) in the legs.
    • Argyll Robertson Pupils: Pupils that accommodate but do not react to light are characteristic.
  • Lab Findings: Confirmation through positive syphilis serological tests (VDRL and FTA-ABS) in CSF.
  • MRI Findings: Degeneration in the dorsal columns of the spinal cord aligns with the expected pathology.

Why Not Other Options:

A (Wernicke's Encephalopathy):

  • Incorrect as it is caused by thiamine deficiency, typically associated with alcohol abuse, and presents with confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia, rather than the specific sensory loss and pupil abnormalities seen here.

C (Ataxia Telangiectasia):

  • Incorrect because this is a genetic disorder characterized by ataxia, telangiectasia, and immune deficiencies, not related to syphilis or the specific neurological findings in this case.

D (B12 deficiency leading to subacute combined degeneration):

  • Incorrect as this condition presents with both motor and sensory deficits affecting both the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, and would not typically include Argyll Robertson pupils or the specific history of syphilis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Tabes Dorsalis is a severe complication of untreated syphilis, manifesting with ataxia, sensory loss, and pupil abnormalities.
  • Diagnosis is supported by positive serological tests and characteristic MRI findings, emphasizing the importance of recognizing historical context in neurological symptoms.

question_text:
A 32-year-old male presents after a penetrating spinal cord injury. Examination reveals:
1.Ipsilateral loss of proprioception, vibration sense, and fine touch below the level of the lesion.
2.Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation starting one or two segments below the lesion.
Which of the following syndromes best explains these findings?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Brown-Séquard syndromeresults from hemisection of the spinal cord (lateral half).
  • Key features:
    • Ipsilateral (same side) deficits:Loss of proprioception, vibration, and fine touch due to dorsal column-medial lemniscal tract injury (fibers cross in the medulla).
    • Contralateral (opposite side) deficits:Loss of pain and temperature starting 1-2 segments below lesion due to spinothalamic tract damage (fibers cross within 1-2 spinal segments).
  • Motor deficits may also occur on the ipsilateral sidedue to corticospinal tract involvement.

Explanation of Other Options:

Weber's syndrome (Option A):

Midbrain lesion involving corticospinal tract + oculomotor nerve (CN III).

Clinical features: Contralateral hemiparesis + ipsilateral oculomotor palsy.

Does not involve the spinal sensory cross-pattern.

Dejerine syndrome (Option B):

Medial medullary syndrome (medulla infarct).

Features: Contralateral hemiparesis + ipsilateral tongue weakness + medial lemniscus involvement.

Wallenberg syndrome (Option D):

Lateral medullary syndrome (posterior inferior cerebellar artery infarct).

Features: Ipsilateral facial pain/temp loss + contralateral body pain/temp loss, ataxia, dysphagia.

Key Takeaway Points:

  1. Spinal Cord Syndromes Comparison
  2. Clinical Pearls:
    • Spinothalamic fibers:cross 1-2 segments above entry → contralateral pain/temp loss.
    • Dorsal columns:cross at medulla → ipsilateral proprioception/vibration loss below lesion.
    • Motor fibers (corticospinal):cross at pyramidal decussation → ipsilateral weakness if lesion is below medulla.
  3. Common Causes of Brown-Séquard:
    • Penetrating trauma (knife/gunshot)
    • Multiple sclerosis (rare hemisection)
    • Tumors causing lateral cord compression

question_text: A 38-year-old woman was rushed to the emergency department after getting stabbed with a sharp weapon. On MRI, complete transection of one side of spinal cord is suspected. Which of the following is least likely to be seen in this patient?
explanation:
Option C: Brown-Sequard Syndrome results from hemisection of the spinal cord, causing:

  • Ipsilateral Loss of Proprioception: Due to damage to dorsal columns.
  • Contralateral Loss of Pain and Temperature: Due to damage to the spinothalamic tract.
  • Ipsilateral Flaccid Paralysis: At the level of the lesion due to lower motor neuron damage.
  • Contralateral Spastic Paralysis: Below the level of the lesion due to upper motor neuron damage.

Why not other options:

Option A: Ipsilateral loss of proprioception: This is expected in Brown-Sequard syndrome due to damage to the dorsal columns on the same side as the lesion.

Option B: Contralateral loss of pain: This occurs because the spinothalamic tract, responsible for pain and temperature sensation, crosses over to the opposite side before ascending.

Option D: Contralateral loss of temperature: Similar to pain, the loss of temperature sensation occurs contralaterally due to the crossing of the spinothalamic tract.

Key Takeaways: In a patient with suspected complete transection of one side of the spinal cord, the least likely finding would be contralateral flaccid and spastic paralysis, as paralysis is typically ipsilateral due to damage to the corticospinal tract on the same side as the injury (Brown-Sequard syndrome).

question_text:
A 68-year-old male with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia is brought to the emergency department after his wife noticed that he suddenly developed weakness in his right arm and leg and has difficulty speaking.
Upon examination, the patient is found to have right-sided hemiparesis, with increased muscle tone and hyperreflexia in the right arm and leg.
He has a positive Babinski sign on the right side. A CT scan reveals an ischemic stroke in the left hemisphere of the brain, specifically affecting the regions involved in motor control.
Based on the above findings, which of the following symptoms would most likely be observed in this patient due to damage to the corticospinal tract?
option_a: Loss of proprioception and fine touch sensation on the right side of the body.
option_b: Ipsilateral facial weakness with contralateral hemiparesis.
option_c: Bilateral weakness of the lower limbs.
explanation:
Corticospinal Tract Damage:

  • Contralateral Hemiparesis: Damage to the left hemisphere results in weakness on the right side of the body, consistent with the patient's presentation.
  • Hyperreflexia: Increased reflexes indicate upper motor neuron (UMN) involvement, typical in corticospinal tract lesions.
  • Positive Babinski Sign: Also a sign of UMN lesion, further supporting the diagnosis.

Why Not Other Options:

A (Loss of proprioception and fine touch sensation on the right side of the body):

  • Incorrect because this indicates damage to the dorsal columns, not the corticospinal tract, which primarily affects motor functions.

B (Ipsilateral facial weakness with contralateral hemiparesis):

  • Incorrect as facial weakness due to UMN lesions affects the contralateral side. The corticobulbar tract would cause left facial weakness with right hemiparesis.

C (Bilateral weakness of the lower limbs):

  • Incorrect because the weakness is unilateral and specific to the right side, not bilateral.

Key Takeaways:

  • Corticospinal tract damage leads to contralateral hemiparesis and hyperreflexia, reflecting the effects of upper motor neuron lesions.
  • Recognizing the location of the stroke and associated symptoms is crucial in diagnosing motor pathway involvement.

question_text: A 55 y of came to emergency department after suffering a stroke. She has difficulty maintaining balance and posture, and upon neurological examination, it is noted that she has proximal limb weakness, especially when trying to stand or walk. His fine motor control in his hand remains intact. There are no signs of sensory loss or cranial nerve involvement. So, which pathway is most responsible for this?
explanation:
• The reticulospinal tract is primarily involved in controlling balance and posture by influencing the muscles of the trunk and proximal limbs. It plays a significant role in maintaining muscle tone and helps coordinate movements necessary for standing and walking.

Why Not Other Options

  • A (Lateral Corticospinal tract): Responsible for fine motor control, particularly of distal muscles, such as those in the hands. Since fine motor skills are intact, this pathway is not the primary issue.
  • B (Rubrospinal tract): Involved in the control of distal limb movements, particularly the upper limbs. It doesn't have a major role in posture and balance.
  • D (Vestibulospinal tract): Contributes to balance by coordinating head and eye movements, but the reticulospinal tract is more involved in trunk and limb stability.

Key Takeaways

  • Reticulospinal tract is most responsible for postural control and proximal muscle tone in this scenario, differentiating it from pathways involved in fine motor skills.

question_text: A 60 year old female is brought to the clinic after experiencing sudden weakness in her right arm and leg. On examination, she is found to have increased muscle tone (spasticity) and hyperactive reflexes in the affected limbs. She also has a positive Babinski sign on the right side, where her big toe moves upward when the sole of her foot is stimulated. Fine motor control is particularly affected in her right hand, but sensation remains intact. Which of the following neural pathways is most likely damaged in this patient?
explanation:
The corticospinal tract is crucial for controlling voluntary movements, particularly fine motor tasks, especially in the limbs. Damage to this tract, often due to stroke or lesions, results in upper motor neuron paralysis

  • Spasticity and hyperreflexia: Loss of inhibition leads to increased muscle tone and exaggerated reflexes.
  • Positive Babinski sign: An upward movement of the big toe indicates upper motor neuron damage, specific to corticospinal tract involvement.
  • Fine motor impairment: Particularly evident in tasks requiring precision, such as hand movements, while sensation remains intact.

Why not others:

  • Rubrospinal tract (A) affects motor control of upper limbs but does not cause spasticity or Babinski sign.
  • Reticulospinal tract (C) assists with posture and balance, not fine motor skills.
  • Spinothalamic tract (D) primarily deals with pain and temperature sensation, not motor control.

Key takeaway: The corticospinal tract is responsible for precise motor control, and its damage leads to spasticity, hyperreflexia, and a positive Babinski sign.

question_text:
A 75-year-old male presents to the neurology clinic with complaints of a progressive tremor in his hands, which has worsened over the past year. He also reports increasing stiffness in his arms and legs, difficulty initiating movements (bradykinesia), and episodes of shuffling when he walks. His wife mentions that he seems less expressive and has developed a tendency to fall over the past few months.
Based on the patient's symptoms, which part of the extrapyramidal nervous system is most likely affected, and what is the underlying mechanism?
option_a: Subthalamic nucleus; decreased inhibition of the thalamus
option_c: Globus pallidus interna; excessive excitation of the motor cortex
option_d: Substantia nigra; reduced dopamine release to the striatum
explanation:
• Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by:
    • Resting tremors: Shaking that occurs when the muscles are at rest.
    • Bradykinesia: Difficulty in initiating movements.
    • Rigidity: Stiffness in the limbs and trunk.
    • Postural instability: Tendency to fall, indicating balance issues.
  • The pathophysiology of PD involves:
    • Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra.
    • Dopamine deficiency leads to impaired communication within the basal ganglia, disrupting normal motor control.
  • Clinical diagnosis is primarily based on:
    • Neurological assessment and characteristic symptoms.
  • Treatment options include:
    • Medications like levodopa and dopamine agonists.
    • Surgical interventions such as deep brain stimulation, for advanced cases.

Why not the other options?

  • A) Subthalamic nucleus; decreased inhibition of the thalamus: While the subthalamic nucleus plays a role in the basal ganglia circuitry, it is not primarily affected in Parkinson's disease; rather, it's the substantia nigra that shows degeneration.
    Damage to subthalamic nucleus causes intense flailing movement of proximal parts of limbs leading to hemiballismus
  • B) Caudate nucleus; increased dopamine release: This is incorrect because, in Parkinson's disease, dopamine levels are reduced, not increased. Damage to caudate nucleus produces chorea that is rapid involuntary dancing like movement of distal parts of limb.
  • C) Globus pallidus interna; excessive excitation of the motor cortex: While the globus pallidus is involved in the indirect pathway and can contribute to motor dysfunction, the primary issue in PD is the loss of dopamine from the substantia nigra affecting overall basal ganglia function.

Key Takeaways:

  • In Parkinson's disease, the substantia nigra is affected, leading to reduced dopamine release.
  • This results in a disruption of motor control manifesting as tremors, stiffness, and bradykinesia. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for effective diagnosis and treatment.
  • Direct pathway in relation to dopamine (DA)
    • DA stimulates D1 receptors on the striatum
    • leads to inhibition of the globus pallidus internus (GPi)
    • thalamus becomes disinhibited
    • sends excitatory input into the cortex
  • Indirect pathway in relation to dopamine
  • DA stimulates D2 receptors on STN
  • STN stimulates GPi
  • Thalamus is inhibited
  • No excitatory input into cortex.

question_text:
A 60-year-old man presents with tremors that occur when he is using her hands, such as when writing or drinking from a cup, or doing fine motor movements. Tremors do not occur on resting. Her mother had similar symptoms, and her condition improves with alcohol consumption. Neurological exam shows no signs of rigidity or bradykinesia.
What is the most likely diagnosis and what part of the nervous system is primarily affected?
explanation:
Essential tremor is characterized by:

  • Action tremors: These occur during voluntary movements, such as writing or holding objects, distinguishing them from resting tremors.
  • Familial pattern: The presence of similar symptoms in the patient's mother suggests a genetic component.
  • Improvement with alcohol: Essential tremor often temporarily improves with alcohol consumption, which is a classic feature.

The pathophysiology involves:

  • Cerebellar dysfunction: The cerebellum and its connections are primarily involved, affecting coordination and fine motor control.

Why not the other options?

  • A) Parkinson's disease; Substantia nigra: This condition is characterized by resting tremors, rigidity, and bradykinesia. The patient's action tremors and absence of resting tremors make this diagnosis unlikely.
  • C) Dystonia; Putamen: Dystonia involves sustained muscle contractions causing abnormal postures or movements, which are not present in this patient. The lack of rigidity or abnormal posturing further rules this out.
  • D) Huntington's disease; Caudate nucleus: Huntington's disease presents with chorea, cognitive decline, and psychiatric symptoms. The absence of these symptoms in this case makes this diagnosis inappropriate.

Key Takeaways:

  • The diagnosis of Essential tremor aligns with the presence of action tremors and familial history, with cerebellar involvement being key.
  • Differentiating features like the absence of resting tremors and improvement with alcohol help clarify the condition. Understanding these nuances is essential for accurate diagnosis and management.

question_text:
A 60-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a fall resulting in a traumatic brain injury. Upon examination, he is found to have an abnormal posturing response. His arms are flexed at the elbows and wrists, and his legs are extended. The medical team notes that he does not respond appropriately to verbal commands but exhibits some spontaneous movements.
The patient is found in below given position.
explanation:
• Decorticate Rigidity:
    • Characterization: Flexion of the arms at the elbows and wrists while the legs are extended.
    • Indicates Damage: Suggests injury to the corticospinal tract, typically above the level of the red nucleus.
    • Significance: Reflects loss of higher inhibitory control over spinal reflexes, leading to increased flexor tone. Involves overactivity of vestibulospinal and rubrospinal tracts.

Why not the other options?

  • A) Decerebrate Rigidity:(e-extended)
    • Characterization: Extension of arms and legs, with arms adducted and extended at the elbows. The head may be extended backward.
    • Indicates Damage: Suggests severe brainstem injury, especially in the upper brainstem or midbrain. Indicates disruption of both corticospinal and rubrospinal pathways, leading to unopposed extensor tone.
  • C) Opisthotonos:
    • Characterization: Spasm of back muscles leading to hyperextension of the back and neck, resulting in an arched body posture.
    • Indicates Damage: Often suggests severe central nervous system irritation, such as meningitis or significant brain injury.
  • D) Flaccid Posturing:
    • Characterization: Lack of muscle tone, with limbs hanging loosely and without movement.
    • Indicates Damage: Indicates severe neurological damage, often associated with conditions like brain death or extensive brain injury, where no motor responses are observed.

Key Takeaways:

  • Decorticate rigidity indicates damage to the corticospinal tract and reflects the brain's inability to exert inhibitory control over motor responses.
  • Understanding these postures helps assess the level of neurological impairment and the location of brain injury.

question_text: A 62-year-old patient is brought to the emergency department following a suspected stroke. On evaluation, he can speak fluently, but the words uttered lack coherent meaning and understanding. Which type of aphasia is most likely present in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

As the patient speaks fluently but the speech is nonsensical, lacks meaningful content, and comprehension is poor, the findings are characteristic of Wernicke's aphasia.

Aphasia

  • Aphasias are disorders of language function that occur independently of visual, auditory, or motor deficits.
  • They result from lesions in the dominant (categorical) cerebral hemisphere, most commonly due to embolism or thrombosis of a cerebral artery.
  • Based on speech characteristics, aphasias are broadly classified into nonfluent, fluent, conduction and anomic types.

question_text: A 55-year-old man presents with gradually worsening weakness and spasticity in his right leg. On examination, there is increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, and a positive Babinski sign, all confined to the right lower limb. His left leg and both upper limbs show no abnormalities. An MRI of the brain shows a lesion affecting the left motor cortex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's symptoms-progressive weakness, spasticity, increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, and a positive Babinski sign in the right leg-are classic indicators of an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion. These signs are typical of damage to motor pathways above the level of the spinal cord.

The MRI reveals a lesion in the left motor cortex, which is responsible for controlling voluntary movement on the contralateral (right) side of the body due to the decussation (crossing over) of motor fibers in the medulla. This correlates well with the patient's right-sided motor findings and confirms the presence of a left-sided UMN lesion.

Explanation for other options:

Parkinson's disease (Option A): This condition primarily involves the basal ganglia and is characterized by bradykinesia, resting tremor, and rigidity-not by spasticity, hyperreflexia, or a Babinski sign. It does not typically present with isolated UMN signs.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Option B): ALS affects both upper and lower motor neurons. While UMN signs can be seen, patients usually also show lower motor neuron features such as muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and flaccid weakness-none of which are present in this case. Thus, isolated UMN involvement makes ALS less likely.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) (Option C): MS commonly presents with relapsing-remitting neurological deficits and multiple demyelinating lesions throughout the central nervous system. The patient's symptoms are progressive and localized, with imaging showing a focal cortical lesion, which is not typical for MS.

question_text:
A 62-year-old man presents with progressive involuntary movements, dementia, aggression, cognitive decline, He has a family history of a similar condition that affected his father at age of 68. Upon examination, you observe jerky, rapid, and irregular movements of the limbs (chorea).
No history of substance abuse.
What is the primary underlying mechanism leading to the symptoms in this patient?
option_a: Overstimulation of the cerebral cortex due to loss of GABAergic neurons in the basal ganglia
option_b: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra
option_c: Accumulation of misfolded tau protein in the neurons
explanation:
Huntington's Disease (HD):

  • Primary Mechanism: In HD, there is degeneration of GABAergic neurons (inhibitory neurons) in the basal ganglia, especially affecting the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen).
  • Outcome: This loss of inhibitory control leads to overstimulation of the cerebral cortex, resulting in the characteristic hyperkinetic movements, particularly chorea (involuntary, jerky movements).
  • Additional Symptoms: Cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms like aggression are also linked to the disruption of basal ganglia circuits.

Why not the other options?

  • B) Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra:
    • This is typical of Parkinson's disease, where loss of dopamine leads to bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting tremor, not chorea.
  • C) Accumulation of misfolded tau protein in the neurons:
    • This is associated with tauopathies, such as Alzheimer's disease and does not explain the hyperkinetic movements seen in HD.
  • D) Demyelination of neurons:
    • Demyelination is characteristic of conditions like multiple sclerosis, leading to varied neurological symptoms, but not specifically the involuntary movements seen in Huntington's disease.

Key Takeaways:

  • In Huntington's disease, the loss of GABAergic neurons leads to cerebral cortex overstimulation, causing chorea and associated cognitive and psychiatric symptoms.
  • Differentiating the mechanisms behind neurodegenerative disorders is critical for accurate diagnosis and management.

question_text:
A 45-year-old woman presents with involuntary, jerky movements of her limbs and face, which have progressively worsened over the past year. She also reports mood changes and memory difficulties. Her father had similar symptoms in his mid-40s. A brain MRI is performed, revealing atrophy of the nucleus in the basal ganglia, resulting in enlarged lateral ventricles.

Which brain structure is most likely to be atrophied in this patient?
explanation:
Caudate Nucleus:

  • Primary Affection: Atrophy of the caudate nucleus is characteristic of Huntington's disease.
  • Imaging Findings: This atrophy leads to enlargement of the lateral ventricles, known as hydrocephalus ex vacuo.
  • Function: The caudate nucleus is crucial for movement control, and its degeneration results in the choreiform movements seen in this condition.

Why not the other options?

  • B) Putamen:
    • Explanation: While the putamen is involved in basal ganglia circuits, it is not the primary site of degeneration in Huntington's disease. It is more associated with conditions like dystonia or Parkinson's disease.
  • C) Substantia Nigra:
    • Explanation: This structure is predominantly affected in Parkinson's disease, leading to loss of dopaminergic neurons and symptoms such as resting tremor and bradykinesia. It is not primarily involved in Huntington's disease.
  • D) Hippocampus:
    • Explanation: The hippocampus is critical for memory formation and is primarily affected in Alzheimer's disease. Although cognitive decline occurs in Huntington's disease, the hippocampus is not the main area of atrophy; the caudate nucleus is.

Key Takeaways:

  • Atrophy of the caudate nucleus is a hallmark of Huntington's disease, leading to characteristic movement disorders and cognitive changes.
  • Understanding the specific brain structures affected in different movement disorders aids in accurate diagnosis and management.

question_text:
A 68-year-old male is brought to the emergency department following a fall. He is unconscious and exhibits abnormal posturing. Neurological examination reveals extension of the limbs when stimulus is applied. There is no response to verbal commands, and the patient shows signs of severe brain injury on imaging studies.

What is the primary mechanism underlying the posturing observed in this patient?
option_a: Damage to the corticospinal tract, cerebral cortex
option_b: Disruption of the basal ganglia, above brainstem
option_c: Loss of inhibition from the brainstem, between red nucleus and vestibular nuclei
option_d: Dysfunction of the cerebellum, dentate lobe of cerebellum
explanation:
Loss of inhibition from the brainstem:

  • Correct Mechanism: The observed decerebrate rigidity results from unopposed activity of the extensor muscles due to the loss of inhibitory control from the brainstem following severe brain injury.

Why not the other options?

  • A) Damage to the corticospinal tract:
    • Explanation: While damage to the corticospinal tract can cause abnormal posturing, decerebrate rigidity is specifically linked to brainstem inhibition loss.
  • B) Disruption of the basal ganglia:
    • Explanation: Although basal ganglia disruption is associated with various movement disorders, it is not the primary cause of decerebrate rigidity.
  • D) Dysfunction of the cerebellum:
    • Explanation: Cerebellar dysfunction mainly affects coordination and balance but does not primarily lead to decerebrate rigidity.

Key Takeaways:

  • Decerebrate rigidity arises from a loss of inhibitory control from the brainstem, leading to unopposed extensor muscle activity.
  • Recognizing the mechanisms behind abnormal posturing is crucial for understanding the extent and nature of brain injuries.

question_text: A 42-year-old man presented with complaints of abnormal, sudden involuntary writhing movements (shown in the figure). What is the probable diagnosis and loss of which of the following is responsible for the hyperkinetic features seen in this case scenario?
option_b: Rheumatic chorea, Glutamate and cholinergic pathway
explanation:
Option A: Huntington's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder that primarily affects the intrastriatal GABAergic pathway. This pathway involves gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) neurons within the striatum. The loss of GABAergic pathway to the globus pallidus external segment releases inhibition, permitting the hyperkinetic features of the disease to develop.

Option B: Rheumatic chorea, Glutamate and cholinergic pathway: Rheumatic chorea is linked to streptococcal infection, not Huntington's. The pathophysiology of rheumatic chorea involves immune-mediated inflammation in the basal ganglia, particularly affecting the glutamate and cholinergic neurotransmitter pathways.

Option C: Huntington's disease, Nigrostriatal dopaminergic pathway: Dopaminergic pathways are more relevant to Parkinson's, not Huntington's. There is degeneration of the dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, leading to hypokinetic symptoms

Option D: Rheumatic chorea, Intrastriatal cholinergic pathway: ·Rheumatic chorea is associated with disruption of various neurotransmitter systems in the basal ganglia, including the intrastriatal cholinergic pathway.

Huntington's disease involves GABAergic loss, not cholinergic.

Key takeaways :

Huntington's disease characterized by involuntary movements (chorea). This is due to the loss of the intrastriatal GABAergic pathway which leads to hyperkinetic symptoms.

question_text: A 32-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. Following the accident, he exhibits significant behavioral changes, including increased appetite and overeating. Neurological examination reveals that he has difficulty regulating his body weight, and he reports feeling excessively hungry. MRI scans show's lesion in which part of hypothalamus?
explanation:
• The patient’s symptoms of increased appetite and overeating indicate a dysfunction in the hypothalamus, specifically in the ventromedial nucleus (VMN).
  • Function of the VMN:
    • Known as the satiety center, the VMN inhibits hunger and regulates energy balance.
    • Lesions in this nucleus lead to hyperphagia (increased eating) and obesity due to the loss of inhibitory signals for hunger, consistent with the patient's condition.
  • Mechanism:
    • The VMN receives input from various hormonal signals (like leptin) that inform the body about energy reserves.
    • When functioning properly, it signals the cessation of eating. However, lesions disrupt this signaling pathway, resulting in uncontrolled eating.
  • Behavioral Changes: The patient’s difficulty regulating body weight and excessive hunger post-accident may reflect both the direct effects of the lesion and possible compensatory mechanisms activated in response to perceived energy deficiency.

Why Not Other Options

  • A (Lateral hypothalamic area): Known as the "hunger center," lesions here typically cause decreased appetite and weight loss, contradicting the patient’s increased appetite.
  • C (Paraventricular nucleus): While involved in hormone production, lesions here do not primarily lead to increased appetite or hyperphagia.
  • D (Suprachiasmatic nucleus): Responsible for regulating circadian rhythms, it does not influence appetite or eating behaviors.

Key Takeaways

  • The ventromedial nucleus (VMN) lesion leads to hyperphagia and obesity due to the loss of inhibitory signals for hunger.
  • Recognizing the specific roles of different hypothalamic nuclei can aid in effective diagnosis and treatment of eating disorders and obesity-related conditions!
  • Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for managing behavioral changes following hypothalamic injuries.
  • HYPOTHALAMIC NUCLEI
    Lateral-hunger
    Ventromedial-satiety
    Anterior-cooling in response to heat
    Posterior-heating in response to cold
    Suprachiasmatic-circadian rhythm
    Supraoptic-ADH(SAD)
    Paraventricular-oxytocin(POX)
    Preoptic-sexual response, determines GNRH release.
    Lateral and posterior nucleus controls sympathetic system. Preoptic nucleus controls parasympathetic system.

question_text: Kluver bucy syndrome is due to the lesion in which of the following structure
explanation:
Kluver-Bucy Syndrome

  • Occurs due to Bilateral Ablation of the Amygdala
  • Characterized by,
    • Not able to recognize objects by sight - Visual agnosia
    • Tendency to examine objects excessively by mouth
    • Hyperorality
    • Compulsion to intensively explore the immediate environment - Hypermetamorphosis
