question_text: You review a 28-year-old girl who has been referred with amenorrhoea. She is noted on routine screening to have a raised prolactin level. Patient is keen to know about prolactin physiology. Thinking of hormones in general, which of the following hormones is under continuous inhibition?
explanation:
• Prolactin is under predominantly inhibitory control, by levels of dopamine. Prolactin levels are known to rise during pregnancy, lactation, severe stress, sleep and coitus. Mildly increased prolactin levels in the range of 400-600 mU/litre may be physiological, but higher levels require a diagnosis. Levels above 1000 imply the possibility of microprolactinoma, and levels above 5000 imply the presence of macroprolactinoma.
  • Drug causes of Hyperprolactinaemia are, not surprisingly, the dopamine antagonists, which include metoclopramide, domperidone and the phenothiazines.
  • Features of Hyperprolactinaemia in women include amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, loss of libido, subfertility and features of androgen deficiency.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20th edition Chapter:371, Page number:2660-61

question_text: The presence of galactorrhoea is MOST suggestive of which one of the following conditions?
explanation:
• Galactorrhoea is nonpuerperial expression of milk. Hyperprolactinaemia causes galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea, which may result from a prolactin secreting pituitary tumour or hyperplasia.
  • Hypothyroidism is a cause of raised prolactin levels. In acromegaly one-third of patients have mild elevation of prolactin levels resulting in galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea and decreased libido. Similar elevation of prolactin levels occurs in a small percentage of patients with primary hypothyroidism.
  • Low T4 and T3 levels associated with primary hypothyroidism is associated with increase in TSH and TRH levels. TRH would stimulate prolactin production from the pituitary.
  • Sheehan's syndrome is a primary hypopituitarism due to ischaemic necrosis of the pituitary gland caused by postpartum haemorrhage; it is characterised by failure of postpartum lactation and failure to resume normal cyclic menstruation.
  • Turner's syndrome (ovarian dysgenesis) causes primary amenorrhoea with poor development of the breast. Galactorrhoea and raised prolactin levels may also be seen in PCOS.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:2935

question_text:
A 55-year-old man presents with a new diagnosis of Type 2 diabetes. He is also concerned that his fingers seem a little swollen and he is unable to wear his wedding ring anymore. He attends with some pictures from his youth, which appear to show that his jaw has acquired increasing prominence over the past few years. On examination his BP is 152/90 mmHg.
Investigations;
Hb 14.0 g/dl
WBC 5.1 x 10^9/L
PLT 302 x 10^9/L
Na+ 140 mmol/l
K+ 5.0 mmol/l
Creatinine 1.0 mg/dl
Glucose 165 mg/dlWhich of the following would be the most appropriate initial screening test for the likely underlying condition?
option_b: Oral glucose tolerance test with growth hormone measurement
explanation:
• Growth hormone stimulates the production of IGF-1, and IGF-1 has a long half-life, as such it is the ideal measure of growth hormone secretion.
  • The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) using 75g is a sensitive test for acromegaly, with failure of growth hormone to suppress suggesting the diagnosis, it should be noted however that 15-20% of patients with acromegaly have a paradoxical rise in growth hormone secretion post OGTT.
  • IGFBP-3 is the main circulating binding protein for IGF and may of utility in the future as a screening test for acromegaly.
  • Random growth hormone measurements are not useful as a screening test for acromegaly because of the episodic nature of secretion.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:2912

question_text: A 29-year-old man presents with coarse facial features and progressive enlargement of his hands and feet over the past 10 years. Acromegaly is confirmed by raised IGF-1 levels and failure of growth hormone suppression after a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. Which medication is advised for his treatment?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The presentation is consistent with acromegaly, and lanreotide, a somatostatin analogue, is effective in suppressing GH and IGF-1 levels while offering the benefit of prolonged action.
  • Lanreotide, given as a long-acting depot injection, is the preferred first-line medical treatment for acromegaly, acting by binding to somatostatin receptors on the pituitary tumour to suppress GH release and restore IGF-1 levels to normal.

Explanation of other options:

Terlipressin (Option B): Terlipressin, a synthetic analogue of vasopressin, is mainly used in managing hepatorenal syndrome and oesophageal variceal bleeding. It is not useful in acromegaly since it does not influence growth hormone secretion or activity.

Ketoconazole (Option C): Ketoconazole is an antifungal drug that, although sometimes used off-label for endocrine issues like adrenal hypercortisolism, is not used in treating acromegaly since it has no impact on GH or IGF-1 levels.

Leuprolide (Option D): Leuprolide, a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist, is mainly prescribed for conditions like prostate cancer and endometriosis, but since it does not influence GH secretion, it is not useful in managing acromegaly.

question_text: A 15-year-old boy presents with progressive enlargement of hands and feet, coarse facial features, prominent enlarged jaw, and frontal bossing. On examination, he is noted to have bitemporal hemianopia. Which of the following is the most definitive test to confirm the diagnosis?
option_c: Increased IGF-1 levels with oral glucose challenge test
option_d: Increased GH with oral glucose challenge test
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical scenario points towards Acromegaly, characterized by progressive enlargement of hands and feet, coarse facial features, prominent jaw, frontal bossing, and bitemporal hemianopia due to pituitary adenoma. The definitive test for acromegaly/gigantism is failure of growth hormone (GH) suppression after an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Normally, glucose ingestion suppresses GH, but in acromegaly due to a pituitary adenoma, GH levels remain elevated after the glucose load.

  • Acromegaly results from hypersecretion of growth hormone either due to a somatotrope adenoma or extra-pituitary lesions.
  • More common in males.
  • Both growth hormone and IGF-1 levels are increased.

Investigations:

  • Elevated GH levels increase IGF-1 blood levels, and elevated IGF-1 levels almost always indicate acromegaly.
  • GH has a pulsatile release, so a random assessment would not be helpful. Because IGF-1 levels are much more stable for the day, they are often a more practical and reliable measure than GH levels.
  • The oral glucose tolerance testis the confirmatory test for Ingestion of 75 g of the sugar glucose lowers blood GH levels less than 0.4 ng/ml in healthy people. In patients with acromegaly, this reduction does not occur.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Increased IGF-1 levels (Option A): Sensitive screening test but not definitive; IGF-1 may be elevated in other conditions.

Increased GH levels (Option B): GH secretion is pulsatile and may be elevated in normal individuals at random times, limiting diagnostic value.

Increased IGF-1 levels with oral glucose challenge test (Option C): Only GH suppression during OGTT is diagnostic; IGF-1 is not measured during the test.

question_text: A 12-year-old girl presents with short stature, webbed neck and primary amenorrhoea.Given the likely clinical diagnosis, which hormone would be most appropriate to treat this condition?
explanation:
• This girl most probably has Turner's syndrome, which is most commonly associated with absence of one X chromosome (XO pattern).
  • Characteristic features in this condition include streak ovaries and absent internal genitalia.
  • Estrogen administration will develop female secondary sex characters and life-long therapy will be required.
  • Growth hormone may be useful for a limited period to increase her height.
  • As the ovaries are absent, pulsatile GnRH and luteinising hormone would be of no use.
  • Progesterone would be useful for inducing withdrawal bleed in females sufficiently treated with estrogen.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 3000

explanation:
• Prolactin is under predominantly inhibitory control, by levels of dopamine. Prolactin levels are known to rise during pregnancy, lactation, severe stress, sleep and coitus.

question_text: A 23-year-old student presents for review. She is distressed by the fact that she is overweight and is embarrassed of excessive facial hair. She also notices that she appears to have more generalized body hair than other women. On further history, she can sometimes miss a couple of menses, but pregnancy testing is consistently negative. Her mother apparently had similar problems in her youth, took a while to conceive and now has type-2 diabetes. Testosterone is just above the upper limit of normal range, her LH:FSH ratio is increased and prolactin is normal. Which diagnosis fits best with this woman's clinical picture?
explanation:
• PCOS is said to occur in 3% of adult women.
  • Symptoms usually begin around the time of menarche and the diagnosis is often made in adolescence. Obesity is present in around 40% of sufferers and there is an increased association with type-2 diabetes due to insulin resistance.
  • Biochemical abnormalities characteristically include a mildly raised testosterone level and an increased LH: FSH ratio.
  • The cornerstone of management is life style modifications to achieve weigh reduction.
  • The use of OCPs can reduce the androgen levels and help achieve regular menstrual cycles.
  • The anovulation associated with PCOS is treated with ovulation induction agents like Clomiphene citrate and Letrozole

Hyperprolactinemia is unlikely as her prolactin is normal.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 3036

question_text:
A 51-year-old woman presents with increasing lower back pain for the last six months. The pain is increased by working as a floor-layer, and is worse in the evening.
There is no weight loss, night pain, or fever. Her back is stiff for 15 minutes in morning.
Over the last few months she has developed firm to hard swelling on several distal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and has anterior knee pain worsened by climbing stairs. A full blood count, ESR, and CRP done by the GP have been normal.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient has generalised osteoarthritis (GOA), as there are OA related symptoms in at least three joint areas, namely

Bony swellings at distal and proximal IPJs termed Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes respectively

Anterior knee pain, worse on climbing stairs, suggesting patella-femoral joint OA, and Low back pain, suggesting spinal degenerative changes.

Ankylosing spondylitis typically occurs in young men, and associates with pronounced early morning stiffness and buttock pain.

Osteoporosis is not symptomatic, unless accompanied by a spinal fracture. Osteoporotic spinal fractures present with acute pain which improves over a period of few weeks to a couple of months.

There are no red-flag symptoms to raise the possibility of discitis or malignancy.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 371 Pg: 2858-2859

question_text:
A 56-year-old man with a history of smoking and hypertension presents to the emergency room with central crushing chest pain, nausea and sweating. On examination his BP is 104/70 mmHg, his pulse 105/min regular and he looks pale, grey and sweaty.
ECG: ST elevation V1-V4, ST depression II, III and aVL
Which of the following is the most likely finding on angiography?
option_b: 70% stenosis of left anterior descending artery
option_c: Total occlusion of left anterior descending artery
explanation:
This man is suffering from an ST elevation anterior myocardial infarction and most likely has an occlusion of his left anterior descending artery due to plaque rupture.

Left circumflex or right coronary artery occlusions would be expected to result in either lateral or inferior ECG changes.

Management of choice is primary PCI, as early as possible after the onset of chest pain.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 21st edition Page 2044

question_text:
A 62-year-old smoker is admitted with nausea, sweating and central crushing chest pain. A 12 lead ECG reveals ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF.
Which coronary artery is most likely to have been affected in this case?
explanation:
• Right coronary artery supplies the right ventricle, the posterior third of the interventricular septum, the inferior wall of the left ventricle and a portion of the posterior wall of the left ventricle. (leads II, III, aVF corresponds to inferior wall)
  • Occasionally the posterior interventricular septum may be supplied by a branch of the of the left circumflex artery, called left dominant circulation.
  • The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries arise at the left main coronary artery bifurcation and supply the anterior left ventricle, the bulk of the interventricular septum (anterior two thirds), the apex, and the lateral and posterior left ventricular walls.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page no: 2035
subject: Medicine

question_text:
A 52-year-old man presents with central crushing chest pain. Examination is normal.
The 12-lead ECG shows ST segment elevation in leads II, III, aVF, and ST depression in V1, V2 and V3.
Which coronary artery is occluded?
explanation:
The ECG describes an inferior-posterior myocardial infarction (MI). This territory is supplied by a dominant right coronary artery. The concept of coronary dominance refers to which coronary artery supplies the posterior descending coronary artery.

In the case of approximately 85% of patients this is the right coronary artery with about 15% of patients having a dominant left circumflex.

The territories supplied by the arteries are as follows:

  • Circumflex: Lateral
  • Left anterior descending: Anterior and septum
  • Left main stem: Branches into the left anterior descending artery and circumflex and supplies most of the left ventricle. Complete left main stem occlusion is invariably fatal
  • Obtuse marginal: One of the branches of the circumflex and supplies the 'high lateral' region of the left ventricle (ECG leads I and aVL).

Basic understanding of coronary anatomy is important as this is predictive of problems following MI.

  • Right coronary artery supplies the AV node, so heart block following inferior MI is common. However, heart block following anterior MI is a grave prognostic marker as this indicates a large anterior wall infarct.
  • The right coronary system also supplies the right ventricle, hence problems relating to a right ventricular infarct are commonly associated with an inferior MI.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page no: 2058
subject: Medicine

question_text: Which of the following is the most commonly affected coronary artery in a patient with myocardial infarction?
explanation:
• The frequency of involvement of coronaries in MI is left anterior descending artery > right coronary artery > left circumflex artery
  • Left anterior descending artery is also referred to as 'widow's artery'.

question_text: What is the diagnosis if the axis is on the mark '?'from the diagram shown below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The QRS axis falls within the range of +90° to +180°, which is diagnostic for Right Axis Deviation (RAD). This is determined using the hexaxial reference system, where the quadrant between +90° and +180° represents RAD.

  • QRS Axis Interpretation:
    • Normal:-30° to +100°, positive QRS in leads I and aVF. (Option B ruled out)
    • Left Axis Deviation (< -30°):Tall R in I, deep S in III, biphasic RS in II; causes → LVH, left anterior fascicular block, inferior MI, normal variant. (Option C ruled out)
    • Right Axis Deviation (> +90° to +100°):Tall R in III > II, deep S in I, tall R in II/III/aVF; causes → RV overload, lateral MI, left posterior fascicular block, dextrocardia, left pneumothorax, electrode misplacement, normal in children/young adults.

Explanation of other options:

Extreme axis deviation (Option D ruled out): This occurs when the axis lies between -90° and ±180°, which is a more extreme range than the marked location.

Key Takeaways:

  • The hexaxial system is used to determine the electrical axis of the heart.
  • Right Axis Deviation is defined as a QRS axis greater than +90°.

question_text: A 48-year-old man presents with persistent headaches and progressive visual disturbance. On examination, he has prominent frontal bossing, thickened palms and soles, spaced central incisors, and coarse facial features. He is hypertensive and diabetic. What is the most appropriate screening test to evaluate his condition?
option_a: GH levels <0.4 µg/L after 1 hour of 75 g oral glucose load
option_b: Single early morning fasting GH level to establish the diagnosis
option_c: Age-specific IGF-1 levels are useful for screening
option_d: GH levels are used to assess disease severity
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Serum IGF-1, which reflects integrated GH secretion, is the most sensitive and reliable screening test for acromegaly.

  • The patient's features-frontal bossing, acral enlargement, coarse facies, visual symptoms, and associated hypertension and diabetes-are classical signs of acromegaly, a disorder resulting from chronic growth hormone (GH) excess, usually due to a GH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma.
  • The first-line screening test is serum Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1), measured against age-specific reference ranges.
  • IGF-1 is more stable and reflects long-term GH exposure, unlike GH which has pulsatile secretion and fluctuating levels throughout the day.

Acromegaly - Summary and Clinical Essentials

  • Acromegaly is primarily due to excess growth hormone (GH) secretion, most commonly from a pituitary somatotroph macroadenoma (>1 cm).
  • Cause:
    • Mixed mammosomatotroph tumors (secreting GH and PRL)
    • Acidophilic stem cell adenomas (PRL co-secretion → hypogonadism, galactorrhea)
    • Ectopic GH/GHRH secretion from carcinoid tumors, pancreas, lungs, or ovaries
  • Clinical Features
    • Acral Changes:
      • Frontal bossing, enlarged hands and feet
      • Mandibular overgrowth (prognathism), interdental spacing
    • Soft Tissue Features:
      • Coarse facial features, macroglossia
      • Increased heel pad (>25 mm), larger ring/shoe/glove size
    • Visceromegaly:
      • Cardiomegaly, thyroid enlargement
    • Other Signs:
      • Hyperhidrosis, oily skin, deep voice
      • Arthropathy, kyphosis, carpal tunnel syndrome
      • Acanthosis nigricans, skin tags, muscle weakness
  • Complications
    • Metabolic: Diabetes mellitus, hypertension
    • Cardiac/Respiratory: Cardiomyopathy, sleep apnea
    • Neoplastic: Colon polyps and malignancy
    • Mass effect: Visual disturbances, hypopituitarism
  • Investigations
    • Screening test: Age-adjusted serum IGF-1 levels (stable marker of GH excess)
    • Diagnostic test: 75 g Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT)
      • GH suppression to <0.4 µg/L confirms diagnosis
      • 20% may show paradoxical GH rise
    • GH levels: Not reliable for diagnosis or severity due to pulsatile secretion
    • MRI Brain with contrast: Investigation of choice for tumor localization
    • Other labs: Elevated PRL (25% cases), assess other pituitary hormones
  • Management
    • First-line: Transsphenoidal surgery (especially for GH-secreting adenomas)
    • Medical therapy:
      • Somatostatin receptor ligands (SRLs): Octreotide, Lanreotide
      • GH receptor antagonist: Pegvisomant (normalizes IGF-1 in ~70%)
      • Dopamine agonists: High-dose cabergoline (modest effect)
    • Radiotherapy: For non-responders or surgical failures

Explanation of other options:

GH levels <0.4 µg/L after 1 hour of 75 g oral glucose load (Option A): This is a confirmatory test, not a screening test. It is used after IGF-1 is found to be elevated.

Single early morning fasting GH level to establish the diagnosis (Option B): Incorrect. GH secretion is pulsatile and highly variable, making a single random or fasting level unreliable for diagnosis.

GH levels are used to assess disease severity (Option D): Incorrect. GH levels may correlate poorly with clinical severity due to fluctuations. IGF-1 is more reliable for both screening and monitoring.

Reference:

https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1155/2024/5085905

question_text:
A 52-year-old patient who has had chemotherapy for metastatic breast cancer 6 months earlier comes to the clinic complaining of shortness of breath on exertion. Her BP is 125/78 mmHg, her pulse is 94/min and her apex beat is displaced to the anterior axillary line.
CXR - Cardiomegaly, increased shadowing consistent with mild pulmonary oedema at both bases
Which chemotherapeutic agent is most likely to be responsible for this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Doxorubicin can be associated with cardiac failure, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction and tachyarrhythmias. Platinum based chemotherapies are associated with peripheral neuropathy, and bleomycin with interstitial pneumonitis and a specific skin lesion called 'flagellate dermatitis'.

Drugs causing dilated cardiomyopathy

  • Trastuzumab (Herceptin)
  • Tacrolimus
  • Zidovudine

Drugs like NSAIDs, Thiazolidinediones can cause fluid retention and thus worsen heart failure in patients with underlying disease.

question_text: A 52-year-old man suffers an extensive anterior myocardial infarction but recovers well in hospital. His pre-discharge ECHO shows him to have an ejection fraction 35%. He is otherwise asymptomatic. His medications on discharge should include which of the following?
option_a: Aspirin, metoprolol, ramipril and a statin
option_b: Aspirin, atenolol, ramipril, furosemide and a statin
option_c: Aspirin, isosorbide mononitrate, ramipril and a statin
option_d: Aspirin, nitrate, losartan and a statin
explanation:
Following a myocardial infarction, patients with LV dysfunction benefit from taking β-Blockers and RAAS blockers. There is strong evidence supporting the use of aspirin and a statin post-MI. In the absence of anginal pain, prophylactic use of nitrates is not mandatory. Diuretics is indicated for patients with symptomatic heart failure and those with fluid overload.

question_text: What is the most likely diagnosis for a 30-year-old woman presenting with headache, vomiting, amenorrhea, spontaneous lactation, reduced libido, acromegaly, infertility, and bitemporal hemianopia found on physical examination?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation of a 30-year-old female with headache, vomiting, amenorrhea, galactorrhea (lactation without pregnancy), decreased libido, acromegaly, infertility, and bitemporal hemianopia strongly suggests a pituitary adenoma affecting multiple hormone-producing cells.

Mammosomatotroph adenoma is the most probable diagnosis because:

  • It secretes both prolactin and growth hormone (GH).
  • Excess prolactin explains the amenorrhea, galactorrhea, infertility, and decreased sexual desire.
  • Excess GH leads to acromegaly, causing characteristic physical changes.
  • The headache, vomiting, and bitemporal hemianopia are due to the mass effect of the tumor compressing the optic chiasm.

Explanation for other options:

Corticotroph adenoma (Option A): produces ACTH, leading to Cushing's disease, which is not consistent with the described symptoms.

Gonadotroph adenoma (Option B): typically presents with hypogonadism but rarely causes hypersecretion symptoms like galactorrhea or acromegaly.

Glioma (Option D): is a brain tumor that does not explain the endocrine symptoms described.

question_text:
A 52 year old lady complains of gradual onset of blurred vision in her left eye. Examination reveals a left sided relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy reveals left sided optic atrophy. Visual fields show a left sided central scotoma and an upper quadrantic visual field defect in the right eye.
Where is the lesion?
explanation:

question_text:
A 43- year-old gentleman develops chest pain 7 minutes after fibreoptic bronchoscopy. The procedure had been performed without sedation following an intratracheal injection of 5 ml 2.5% cocaine solution and xylocaine spray to the pharynx for topical anaesthesia. ECG showed an evolving anterior myocardial infarction.
Which of the following would you prefer for his management?
explanation:
The underlying mechanism here is vasoconstriction, not thrombosis.

Cocaine is cardiotoxic and its use has been linked to coronary artery spasm, angina, myocardial infarction, arrhythmias, sudden cardiac death, and myocardial contraction bands, which might act as a substrate for arrhythmias.

It is important to avoid β-blockers in treating cocaine induced chest pains or acute myocardial infarctions as this may result in unopposed α1 adrenergic action with worsening coronary spasm.

Calcium channel antagonists or nitrates should be administered as early as possible.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:447 pg:3289,3290

question_text:
A 19-year-old man is referred to the endocrine clinic by his GP because he had poorly developed secondary sexual characteristics. He describes anosmia. On examination, he has lack of axillary or pubertal hair, small sexual organs (testicular volumes of approximately 5 ml). Investigations reveal:
Testosterone 3.5 nmol/L (10-30)
Prolactin 350 mU/L (<450)
FSH 2.2 iu/L (1-7)
LH 1.8 iu/L (1-10)
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• X-linked Kallmann's syndrome (KS) is a genetic disease characterized by anosmia and hypogonadism due to impairment in the development of olfactory axons and in the migration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)-producing neurons. 50% of the patients also have unilateral renal agenesis.
  • Abnormalities of the sexual organs, mainly cryptorchidism and testicular atrophy are common.

question_text: A 24-year-old woman visits her doctor complaining of feeling tired all the time for the last few months. She has amenorrhea for 6 months, and has been feeling dizzy while getting up in the morning. Which of the following clinical signs would the family doctor most likely find if the diagnosis was thought to be Addison's disease?
option_d: Hypertension in supine position with postural hypotension
explanation:
• Hypoadrenalism has many causes including Addison's disease, granulomatous disorders, TB, tumour (particularly lung) or infections (meningococcal septicaemia).
  • Secondary hypoadrenalism is caused by hypopituitarism or hypothalamic disorders.
  • Pallor is present in hypopituitarism due to normochromic, normocytic anemia and a lack of melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH; cleaved from the precursor of ACTH).
  • Secondary AI differs from Addison disease in that it lacks the hyperpigmentation, and aldosterone production is spared as it is regulated by RAAS rather than ACTH.
  • Buccal pigmentation is also associated with glucocorticoid deficiency, most commonly from Addison's disease. ACTH is elevated in Addison's disease and results in higher levels of MSH, which causes the skin and buccal pigmentation found in this condition.
  • Lack of body hair and amenorrhoea are features of hypogonadism in hypopituitarism.
  • Postural hypotension is related to glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency and is more common in primary than secondary AI.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page Number-2971.

question_text: Which of the following is least associated with mitral valve prolapse?
explanation:
Whilst some patients with acromegaly have mitral valve prolapse (MVP) it is not a common association.

It should be remembered that the prevalence of MVP in a standard population is around 5-10%

Mitral valve prolapse

Mitral valve prolapse is common, occurring in around 5-10 % of the population. It is usually idiopathic but may be associated with a wide variety of cardiovascular disease and other conditions

Associations

  • Congenital heart disease: PDA, ASD
  • Cardiomyopathy
  • Turner's syndrome
  • Marfan's syndrome, Fragile X
  • Osteogenesis imperfecta
  • Pseudoxanthoma elasticum
  • Wolff-Parkinson White syndrome
  • Long-QT syndrome
  • Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome
  • Polycystic kidney disease

Features

  • Patients may complain of atypical chest pain or palpitations
  • Mid-systolic click (occurs later if patient squatting)
  • Late systolic murmur (longer if patient standing)
  • Complications: mitral regurgitation, arrhythmias (including long QT), emboli, sudden death.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2000

question_text: A 70-year-old female is being reviewed in a clinic after having had an anterior wall MI. Her Echocardiogram showed an EF of 36%. Patient is already on diuretics, ramipril, aspirin and rosuvastatin. Which of the following beta blockers should be avoided in this patient?
explanation:
• Sotalol may prolong the QT interval and leads to an increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias.
  • This risk is increased in individuals with hypokalemia, which can occur due to co-administration of diuretics
  • Conversely, beta blockers are the main stay of medical management in patients with congenital long QT syndrome to reduce ventricular arrythmias. Nadolol and Propranolol are the preferred agents for prophylaxis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1925

question_text: What is the name of the device shown in the image below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The device shown in the x-ray is a cardiac pacemaker.

Cardiac Conduction Devices (CCDs)

Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillators (ICDs)

Purpose:

ICDs are designed to detect and correct life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias by delivering electrical shocks to restore normal sinus rhythm.

Types of ICDs:

  • Transvenous ICD (T-ICD):
    • Leads are inserted via veins and positioned at the junction of the brachiocephalic vein/superior vena cava and the right ventricle (RV).
    • May be combined with biventricular pacemakers in Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy (CRT).
  • Subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD):
    • No transvenous leads are used.
    • The pulse generator is placed beneath the skin, and a subcutaneous lead is positioned along the left parasternal border to deliver shocks

Main Components of CCDs:

  • Pulse Generator:
    • Produces electrical impulses to regulate heart rhythm.
  • Electrodes:
    • Conduct impulses directly to heart tissue.
  • Lead Wires:
    • Connect the pulse generator to the heart; may have different fixation mechanisms:
      • Active Fixation: Uses helical (screw-like) tips to anchor directly into the myocardium.
      • Passive Fixation: Relies on fibrosis to secure the lead within the trabeculae of the heart.

Chest X-Ray in CCD Assessment

Preferred modality for evaluating:

  • Device placement
  • Lead positioning
  • Detection of complications (e.g., lead fracture, dislodgement)

Two Standard Radiographic Views:

  • Posterior-Anterior (PA) View:
    • Useful for assessing lead continuity and device placement.
  • Lateral (LAT) View:
    • Crucial for identifying lead tip location and distinguishing between right and left ventricular lead positions.

Explanation for other options:

Chemoport Device (Option B): Implantable ports also known as chemoports, Port-A-Caths, or totally implantable venous access devices (TIVADs) are a type of central venous catheter specifically designed for patients who require long-term intravenous access.

These ports offer a durable and reliable option for extended venous access, commonly used in patients undergoing chemotherapy. Compared to peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs), chemoports provide several benefits, including a lower risk of infection and improved patient comfort over prolonged use.

Options C and D are incorrect.

Reference:

  1. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4286824/
  2. https://radiopaedia.org/articles/implantable-port

question_text: What is the probable diagnosis for an overweight elderly man who arrived at the emergency department with intense chest pain lasting for two hours? He also experienced excessive sweating, pain in the left arm, nausea, and one instance of vomiting. During examination, his pulse rate was recorded as 58 beats per minute and his blood pressure was 90/60 mm of Hg. An electrocardiogram (ECG) was conducted and revealed the following results. Additionally, the patient's cardiac biomarkers indicated increased troponin levels.
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation is classic for an acute Inferior Wall Myocardial Infarction (MI). Key indicators include:

  • Symptoms:Typical ischemic chest pain with autonomic features (sweating, nausea, vomiting).
  • ECG:ST-segment elevation in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF).
  • Hemodynamics:Bradycardia and hypotension can occur due to vagal stimulation or right ventricular involvement, which is common in inferior MIs.
  • Biomarkers:Elevated troponin confirms myocardial necrosis.

Explanation of other options:

Anterior wall MI (Option A): Presents with ST-elevation in precordial leads V1-V4.

Posterior wall MI (Option C): Typically shows ST-depression in V1-V4 with a tall R wave; it is often associated with an inferior or lateral MI.

Pericarditis (Option D): Causes diffuse ST-elevation (often concave up) in multiple leads not following a vascular territory, and PR segment depression is common.

Key Takeaways:

  • ST-elevation in leads II, III, and aVF is diagnostic for an inferior wall MI.
  • Inferior wall MIs are most commonly due to occlusion of the Right Coronary Artery (RCA).

question_text: A 33-year-old man is brought to ER in a collapsed state having sustained a precordial stab wound.Which of the following cardiac valves is most likely to have been injured?
explanation:

question_text: A 28-year-old woman who is 3 months' postpartum comes to the OPD complaining of tiredness, she has had no periods since the baby was born and she has been unable to breast-feed because of a lack of milk production. You notice in her case sheet that she required a blood transfusion after delivery for postpartum hemorrhage. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Sheehan's syndrome is hypopituitarism following pregnancy complicated by hemorrhage at the time of delivery. The hemorrhage and associated hypotension is thought to cause pituitary infarction. Patients fail to lactate and remain amenorrhoeic post delivery, and also develop other pituitary hormone deficiencies of the thyroid and adrenal axis.
  • Nelson's syndrome is seen in patients with pituitary-driven Cushing's syndrome many years after bilateral adrenalectomy. Such patients are deeply pigmented.
  • Empty sella syndrome is associated with hypopituitarism, imaging of the pituitary fossa shows no obvious pituitary tissue. It is idiopathic.
  • Lymphocytic hypophysitis is an inflammation of pituitary gland occurring in the 3rd trimester or postpartum females. They tend to present with mass effects and features of anterior pituitary hormone deficiency commonly ACTH and TSH.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2897

question_text: A 34-year-old woman presents with extreme lethargy a couple of weeks after the birth of her third child by emergency cesarean section. She complained to the health visitor of increasing problems some 7 days earlier, but was told that this was to be expected after the birth of her child. Her lactation was normal. On admission via casualty she was noted to have a sodium concentration of 127 mmol/l, a potassium concentration of 6.8 mmol/l and a urea of 70 mg/dl. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• One should always think of the possibility of Sheehan syndrome when a postpartum female presents with fatigue and hyponatremia. This is attributed to secondary adrenal insufficiency. Hyperkalemia is not seen in Sheehan syndrome as low ACTH doesn't impact aldosterone production from adrenal gland.
  • However, absence of lactation is the most specific feature associated with Sheehan syndrome. The presence of normal lactation along with presence of hyperkalemia in the patient makes the diagnosis of Sheehan syndrome unlikely.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2971

question_text: A 55-year-old man has a pituitary adenoma on imaging that has extended directly superiorly and is compressing his optic chiasm. Which of the following visual field deficits is most likely present?
explanation:
Because optic tracts may be contiguous to an expanding pituitary mass, reproducible visual field assessment using perimetry techniques should be performed on all patients with sellar mass lesions that impinge the optic chiasm.

Bitemporal hemianopia, often more pronounced superiorly, is observed classically. It occurs because nasal ganglion cell fibers, which cross in the optic chiasm, are especially vulnerable to compression of the ventral optic chiasm.

Occasionally, homonymous hemianopia occurs as a result of post chiasmal compression, or monocular temporal field loss occurs as a result of pre chiasmal compression.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2902

question_text: What is the likely diagnosis for a 53-year-old woman presenting with dysphagia, burning tongue, worsening exertional dyspnoea, palpitations, and mucosal webs in the upper third of the oesophagus on barium swallow?
explanation:
Explanation

  • Plummer-Vinson Syndrome (PVS) is classically seen in middle-aged women and is associated with iron deficiency anaemia.
  • It is characterized by the triad:
    • Dysphagia → due to esophageal webs (typically in the upper oesophagus).
    • Iron deficiency anaemia → manifests as fatigue, exertional dyspnoea, palpitations.
    • Glossitis & angular cheilitis → cause burning tongue and oral discomfort.

Barium swallow in PVS demonstrates thin mucosal webs in the proximal esophagus, consistent with the finding in this patient.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Achalasia (Option B):

  • Involves failure of relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter due to loss of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus.
  • Presents with progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation, and weight loss.
  • Barium swallow shows bird-beak appearance in the distal esophagus, not mucosal webs in the upper esophagus.

Esophageal adenocarcinoma (Option C):

  • Usually arises in the lower third of the esophagus, commonly associated with Barrett's esophagus (longstanding GERD).
  • Symptoms include progressive dysphagia (first solids, then liquids), weight loss, anemia.
  • Barium swallow would reveal an irregular mass/narrowing, not thin mucosal webs.

Zenker diverticulum (Option D):

  • A pharyngoesophageal false diverticulum, located just above the upper esophageal sphincter (Killian's triangle).
  • Presents with regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, gurgling in neck, chronic cough, and sometimes aspiration.
  • Barium swallow shows an outpouching, not mucosal webs.

question_text: A patient presents to the OPD with a history of diarrhoea after consuming a salad. What is the most likely organism responsible for this illness?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Staphylococcus aureus causes food poisoning due to ingestion of preformed enterotoxin, often found in improperly stored salads, dairy products, and bakery foods.
  • The illness is characterised by a rapid onset (1-6 hours) of vomiting, abdominal cramps, and sometimes diarrhoea.
  • Because the toxin is preformed, antibiotics are not useful; management is supportive.

Explanation of other options:

Bacillus cereus (Option B): Classically linked to reheated rice ("fried rice syndrome"), not fresh salads.

Vibrio cholerae (Option C): Causes profuse watery diarrhoea (rice-water stools) due to contaminated water/seafood, not typically linked to salads.

Salmonella enteritidis (Option D): Causes invasive gastroenteritis with fever, abdominal cramps, and diarrhoea after contaminated poultry/eggs; onset is slower (12-72 hours).

question_text: Which of the following investigations is most useful for the diagnosis of carcinoid tumors?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most useful diagnostic test for carcinoid tumors is a 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA measurement. These tumors are neuroendocrine in origin and secrete serotonin, which is metabolized to 5-HIAA and excreted in urine.

Carcinoid Syndrome

  • Results from hormone secretion (mainly serotonin) from neuroendocrine tumors (NETs), usually in the small intestine or appendix.
  • Syndrome occurs when tumors metastasize to the liver or retroperitoneum, allowing hormones to reach systemic circulation. Histamine and tachykinins (e.g., substance P) may also contribute.

Clinical features

  • Flushing: Sudden, intense red/purple color on face, neck, upper body, often with warmth.
  • Diarrhea: Frequent watery stools (>10/day), affecting quality of life.
  • Wheezing/asthma-like symptoms
  • Cognitive impairment (advanced cases)
  • Pellagra-like skin lesions (niacin deficiency due to tryptophan diversion to serotonin)

Diagnosis of Carcinoid Syndrome

Management:

  • Somatostatin analogues: First-line therapy; inhibit hormone secretion. ~90% of NETs express somatostatin receptors.
  • Telotristat ethyl: Inhibits serotonin synthesis; adjunct for refractory diarrhea.
  • Surgery: For localized tumors; often not feasible in metastatic disease.

Explanation of other options:

24-hour urinary catecholamines (Option A): 24-hour urinary catecholamines is used to diagnose pheochromocytoma and other catecholamine-secreting tumors, not carcinoid tumors.

Serum calcitonin levels (Option B): Calcitonin levels are used in the diagnosis of medullary thyroid carcinoma, a type of neuroendocrine tumour. Calcitonin is unlikely to be elevated in carcinoid syndrome.

question_text: With respect to gastric carcinoma, which of the following statements is true?
option_a: Aspirin use is a risk factor for gastric carcinoma
option_b: Early diagnosis of gastric carcinoma results in a five year survival rate of 20%
option_c: Endoscopic ultrasonography is superior to conventional CT scanning for local tumour staging
option_d: Helicobacter pylori infection is not associated with gastric carcinoma
explanation:
Incidence of distal stomach tumors is actually decreasing while the incidence of tumors in the proximal stomach is increasing.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use is associated with decreased risk of certain gastric tumors.

  1. pylori infection has been associated in a number of studies with increased risk of gastric carcinoma.

Screening for gastric carcinoma in Japan detects up to 40% of gastric carcinomas at an early stage and in skilled hands five year survival can be upwards of 90%.

Computed tomography (CT) with gastric dilatation is a useful complementary investigation in the staging of gastric carcinoma, but endoscopic ultrasonography is superior to conventional CT scanning as it is able to assess depth of infiltration and lymphatic dissemination of tumor.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 80, Pg: 629-632

question_text: Which of the following pharmacological agents is most likely to benefit a patient with angina due to cardiac syndrome X?
explanation:
Nitrates are often effective in patients with syndrome X, which is currently termed 'microvascular angina'.

Cardiac syndrome X consists of angina-like chest pain during exertion, characteristic ECG changes during exercise testing, normal coronary arteries on cardiac catheterisation and no inducible coronary artery spasm during catheterisation. It should not be confused with the metabolic syndrome X, which comprises central obesity, glucose intolerance, dyslipidemia, and high blood pressure.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page no: 2031, 2034

question_text: A patient is diagnosed with an ileal tumor, with elevated urinary 5-HIAA levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Carcinoid tumors arise from enterochromaffin (neuroendocrine) cells of the GI tract. They produce serotonin, metabolized to 5-HIAA in urine. Elevated urinary 5-HIAA is a diagnostic marker.

  • Common sites: GI tract (small intestine, appendix, rectum), lungs.
  • Clinical features:
    • Local symptoms: obstruction, bleeding.
    • Carcinoid syndrome (with metastasis): flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm, right-sided valvular heart disease.
  • Diagnosis: Urinary 5-HIAA, chromogranin A, imaging with PET/Octreoscan, histopathology (synaptophysin+, chromogranin+).
  • Management: Surgery; medical control with somatostatin analogs (octreotide). Liver metastasis → embolization, RFA.

Explanation of other options:

Neuroblastoma (Option B): Pediatric tumor, presents with abdominal mass and systemic features.

Leiomyoma (Option C): Benign smooth muscle tumor, no 5-HIAA secretion.

Chromaffinoma (Option D): Pheochromocytoma, secretes catecholamines, not serotonin.

Key Takeaways:

  • Carcinoid tumors → serotonin → urinary 5-HIAA.
  • Classic carcinoid syndrome occurs after hepatic metastasis.

question_text: A patient comes to you with history of head ache for the last one week. It is a dull aching occipitofrontal head ache. He has noticed that it becomes worse after he gets up and is relieved when he lies down for a while. What will be the imaging finding most likely to be seen in this patient?
option_a: Diffuse meningeal enhancement after Gd contrast
option_c: Space occupying lesion in the brain parenchyma
option_d: Blood in the sub arachnoid space
explanation:
The question deals with a low CSF volume headache. It is due to CSF leak either spontaneous or associated a Lumbar puncture. The characteristic feature is head ache that worsens on assuming an upright posture and improves on lying down.

The characteristic imaging finding is a diffuse meningeal enhancement. The site of CSF leak can be visualised by a spinal MRI.

The main treatment is bed rest. If a leak is identified, it can be closed by a blood patch. IV Caffeine is often curative in patients with persistent pain.

Empty sella is seen in head ache due to Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension.

Blood in the sub arachnoid space is seen in SAH, which presents with thunderclap head ache.

We should remember that meningeal enhancement can be seen in head ache due to meningitis as well, but here the history will be typical, with systemic symptoms.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 16, Pg:115-116

question_text: A patient presents with headache and confusion and is diagnosed with a brain tumor. Family history reveals the presence of both brain and kidney tumors in close relatives. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

The combination of brain tumors, kidney tumors, and a positive family history strongly suggests Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome.

  • VHL syndrome is a rare, inherited autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the VHL tumor suppressor gene, predisposing affected individuals to a variety of benign and malignant tumors across multiple organ systems.
  • This includes brain and kidney tumors, which are central to the case described.
  • Common manifestations include:
    • CNS hemangioblastomas: especially in the cerebellum, leading to headache, ataxia, and vomiting.
    • Retinal hemangioblastomas: which may impair vision and may be an early sign.
    • Renal cell carcinoma (clear cell type): Occurs in ~70% of patients and is a leading cause of mortality in VHL.
    • Pheochromocytomas: Can cause hypertension, palpitations, and sweating.
    • Pancreatic cysts and neuroendocrine tumors
    • Endolymphatic sac tumors: May lead to hearing loss.
  • Diagnostic criteria (Dutch and Danish):
    • With a family history: One VHL-associated tumor and a first-degree relative with VHL.
    • Without family history: At least two distinct VHL-related manifestations (e.g., cerebellar hemangioblastoma and renal cell carcinoma). Genetic testing confirming a pathogenic variant in the VHL gene is definitive.
  • Management is multidisciplinary:
    • Surgical removal of CNS hemangioblastomas, retinal tumors, pheochromocytomas, and renal tumors.
    • Targeted therapies such as Pazopanib for advanced renal cancers and Belzutifan for VHL-associated tumors.
    • Kidney transplant may be needed after bilateral nephrectomy in cases with extensive renal involvement.

Explanation of other options:

Neurofibromatosis (Option A): NF1 and NF2 can involve brain tumors (optic gliomas or vestibular schwannomas), but kidney tumors are not typical features.

Li-Fraumeni syndrome (Option B): Associated with brain tumors, breast cancer, sarcomas, and adrenocortical carcinomas, but not classically with kidney tumors.

Churg-Strauss syndrome (Option D): A vasculitic disorder with asthma and eosinophilia; tumors are not part of its clinical spectrum, ruling it out in this context.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1463/#
