question_text: Which of the following is caused by a lesion of the parietal lobe?
explanation:
• Lesions of the frontal lobe include:

Difficulties with task sequencing and executive skills

Expressive aphasia (receptive aphasia, a temporal lobe lesion)

Primitive reflexes

Perseveration (repeatedly asking the same question or performing the same task)

Anosmia

Changes in personality.

  • Lesions of the parietal lobe include

Apraxias

Neglect

Astereognosis (unable to recognise an object by feeling it)

Visual field defects (typically homonymous inferior quadrantanopia).

They may also cause acalculia (inability to perform mental arithmetic).

  • Lesions of the temporal lobe cause

Visual field defects (typically homonymous superior quadrantanopia)

Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia

Auditory agnosia

Memory impairment.

Occipital lobe lesions include

Cortical blindness (blindness due to damage to the visual cortex and may present as Anton syndrome where there is blindness but the patient is unaware or denies blindness)

Homonymous hemianopia

Visual agnosia (seeing but not perceiving objects - it is different to neglect since in agnosia the objects are seen and followed but cannot be named).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3326-3328

question_text: Which of the following is not seen in pituitary apoplexy?
explanation:
Pituitary apoplexy is an endocrine emergency characterized by hypotension, hypoglycemia, head ache, bilateral visual symptoms, ophthalmoplegia and coma and death in severe cases.

It occurs in a pre existing adenoma of the pituitary or spontaneously in post partum, sickle cell anemia, diabetes, hypertension or shock.

question_text: Hamman crunch sign is seen in?
explanation:
The three main causes are

  1. Alveolar rupture with dissection of air into the mediastinum;
  2. Perforation or rupture of the esophagus, trachea, or main bronchi; and
  3. Dissection of air from the neck or the abdomen into the mediastinum.

There is severe substernal chest pain with or without radiation into the neck and arms. The physical examination usually reveals subcutaneous emphysema in the suprasternal notch and Hamman's sign, which is a crunching or clicking noise synchronous with the heartbeat and is best heard in the left lateral decubitus position.

The diagnosis is confirmed with the chest radiograph.

Usually no treatment is required, but the mediastinal air will be absorbed faster if the patient inspires high concentrations of oxygen. If mediastinal structures are compressed, the compression can be relieved with needle aspiration.

question_text: A 41 year old woman presents with a history of headaches. She also reports menstrual irregularities. On examination, she was noted to be obese. Fundoscopy revealed bilateral papilloedema. Tone, power and reflexes in the limbs were normal. Investigations show a normal CT scan and MRI. EEG normal. Lumbar puncture reveals elevated CSF pressure but the constituents of CSF are normal. In this particular patient, which of the Following would suggest that a complication has arisen?
explanation:
• The diagnosis is idiopathic intracranial hypertension (benign intracranial hypertension).
  • In this condition papilloedema may result in an enlarged blind spot.
  • Unilocular visual loss would suggest infarction of the optic nerve consequent on severe and long standing papilloedema.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 16Pg: 116

question_text: What is the most probable diagnosis in an adult presenting with a pulsatile swelling in the neck, located below the angle of the jaw, showing an outward expansile impulse on examination, as confirmed by MRI angiography findings?
explanation:
Explanation:

In this case, the presence of a pulsatile neck swelling along with the MRI angiography finding of Lyre's sign-which is the splaying of the internal and external carotid arteries-is diagnostic of a carotid body tumor.

Carotid Body Tumor (CBT):

Also known as paraganglioma or chemodectoma, CBT is a rare benign tumor arising from neural crest cells located in the adventitia at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery.

CBTs typically grow slowly, have a low malignancy rate, and show no strong predilection for age or sex, although some studies suggest a slight female predominance. The exact cause is unclear but has been linked to chronic hypoxia and mutations in mitochondrial oxygen-sensing genes.

Diagnosis:

  • B-mode Ultrasonography: Reveals solid, hypoechoic masses adjacent to blood vessels.
  • Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA): Demonstrates the tumor's blood supply and arterial displacement with nearly 100% diagnostic accuracy.
  • Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI): Shows a mass at the carotid artery bifurcation compressing and displacing the arteries. Tumors typically appear round or oval with heterogeneous or high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. The classic Lyre sign, representing the arterial splaying, is commonly seen on angiographic studies and can also be identified on CT angiography.

Treatment:

  • Surgical Removal: The primary and most effective treatment for carotid body tumors.
  • Other Options: Radiotherapy, embolization, or a combination of therapies may be considered depending on the case.

Explanation for other options:

Grave's disease (Option A): is a hyperthyroid disorder characterized by protruding eyes, but the neck swelling in this condition is not pulsatile.

Branchial cysts (Option B): are small, fluid-filled sacs that appear as lumps on the side of the neck and are more frequently seen in children than in adults.

A thymic cyst (Option C): is a benign condition affecting the mediastinum and typically presents with symptoms such as shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, hoarseness, and difficulty swallowing.

Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8748146/

https://radiopaedia.org/articles/lyre-sign-carotid-artery

question_text: A 45-year-old chronic smoker with a 15-year history presents with hemoptysis. Imaging reveals a 3 cm mass in the upper lobe near the lung apex. What should be the next appropriate step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation suggests a potentially malignant lung lesion that necessitates histological confirmation. Since the mass is peripheral and located near the lung apex, the best next step is a CT-guided biopsy.

  • In a CT-guided biopsy, a radiologist employs CT imaging to precisely direct a needle into the lung lesion to collect a tissue sample.
  • This method yields reliable histopathological details about the mass, helping determine if it is malignant or benign, an essential step in a patient with a notable smoking history and hemoptysis.

Explanations of other options:

Bronchoscopy (Option A): Although bronchoscopy is valuable for assessing central or endobronchial tumors, it is less effective for peripheral lung lesions, particularly those situated near the lung apex.

Sputum cytology (Option C): Sputum cytology is a low-cost, noninvasive test, but its sensitivity is lower than that of a biopsy, particularly when imaging already suggests a lung mass. It is most effective in detecting larger, centrally located tumors such as squamous cell carcinoma and small-cell carcinoma.

Sputum for AFB (Option D): Although tuberculosis may present with hemoptysis, a 3 cm apical mass in the upper lobe on chest X-ray is not the usual finding for TB and instead suggests a possible malignancy, making tissue diagnosis a priority.

question_text: Oral thrush is most commonly seen in which part of the oral cavity?
explanation:
Oral thrush (due to Candida infection appears as a white, cheesy exudate, often on an erythematous mucosa in the posterior oropharynx. While most commonly seen on the soft palate, early lesions are often found along the gingival border

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 216, Pg: 1672

question_text: A 46-year-old diabetic man on oral hypoglycemic drugs is found to have hyponatremia. Which of the following drugs is most likely to cause this complication?
explanation:
• Up to 5% of patients taking chlorpropamide may develop inappropriate ADH-like syndrome resulting in dilutional hyponatremia.

Drugs causing SIADH: (5C + SVOT)

  • Cyclophosphamide
  • Chlorpropamide
  • Carbamazepine
  • Chlorpromazine
  • Clofibrate
  • SSRI
  • Vincristine
  • Oxytocin
  • Tricyclic antidepressants

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2924

question_text: A patient presents with a five-day history of nausea and vomiting and watery diarrhea after eating crabs. He appears ill and is orthostatic. Serum Na is 129 mmol/L. Which of the following statements is true?
option_a: Urine Na will be less than 20 mEq/U
option_d: Serum osmolality is likely to be high
explanation:
This patient has developed hypovolemia from fluid losses from vomiting and diarrhea. There is no evidence that other osmotically active compounds have been ingested, thus serum osmolality is likely to be low. Because of hypovolemia, ADH (and aldosterone) will be stimulated, and serum ADH levels will be high. The kidney will be resorbing water and Na, and urine Na concentration will be low. Intravenous volume repletion with normal saline is advisable.

Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 342

question_text:
A 19-year-old woman sustains severe head injuries in a road traffic accident.
The following day her investigations show:
Sodium 160 mmol/l (137-144)
Potassium 3.7 mmol/l (3.5-4.9)
Chloride 120 mmol/l (95-107)
Urea and Creatinine are Normal
Which one of the following statements is correct?
option_a: Rapid rehydration with 5% dextrose is indicated
option_b: She should be treated with sodium restriction
option_c: She has the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
explanation:
• There is a marked hypernatremia with elevated chloride but normal potassium and urea in a patient with severe head injuries.
  • The likely cause of this presentation is diabetes insipidus. Urine osmolality is therefore likely to be low.
  • You cannot say that she has a hyperchloraemic acidosis as you do not have her bicarbonate concentration but if you assume that the anion gap would be normal, that is 10-12, then this would suggest that the bicarbonate is elevated, suggesting either a metabolic alkalosis or respiratory acidosis with compensation.
  • Although restoration of normal volume and osmolality is required, giving 5% dextrose may exacerbate any cerebral oedema and so correction should be gradual.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 53, Pg: 345

question_text: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is most commonly associated with which of the following paraneoplastic syndromes?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a highly aggressive neuroendocrine tumour strongly associated with paraneoplastic syndromes.
  • The most common is SIADH, where ectopic secretion of ADH leads to hyponatremia, low serum osmolality, and high urine osmolality.
  • Other associations include ectopic ACTH production (Cushing syndrome) and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, but SIADH is the most frequent.

Explanation of other options:

Hypercalcemia (Option A): Hypercalcemia is classically associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung due to secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP). It is not a common feature of small-cell lung cancer.

Cushing syndrome (Option B): SCLC may produce ectopic ACTH, leading to Cushing syndrome with hypertension, hyperglycemia, and muscle weakness. However, this is less frequent compared to SIADH.

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (Option C): This paraneoplastic syndrome in SCLC occurs due to autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, causing proximal muscle weakness. Still, its incidence is lower than SIADH in SCLC patients.

question_text: A patient has marked dizziness and unsteadiness during walking. On examination, he has a left sided Horner's syndrome and left sided ataxia. There is loss of sensation to pinprick on the right side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
option_b: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion
explanation:
The question describes the typical presentation of Lateral Medullary Syndrome

  • Embolic occlusion or thrombosis of a V4 segment causes ischemia of the lateral medulla. The constellation of vertigo, numbness of the ipsilateral face and contralateral limbs, diplopia, hoarseness, dysarthria, dysphagia, and ipsilateral Horner's syndrome is called the lateral medullary (or Wallenberg's) syndrome. Ipsilateral upper motor neuron facial weakness can also occur.
  • Most cases result from ipsilateral vertebral artery occlusion; in the remainder, PICA occlusion is responsible. Occlusion of the medullary penetrating branches of the vertebral artery or PICA results in partial syndromes. Hemiparesis is not a typical feature of vertebral artery occlusion; however, quadriparesis may result from occlusion of the anterior spinal artery.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3330

question_text: Infarctions secondary to low flow in the "watershed" between the distal PCA and MCA territories, as occurs after cardiac arrest is seen in which of the following?
explanation:
• Bilateral visual association area lesions may result in Balint’s syndrome, a disorder of the orderly visual scanning of the environment, usually resulting from infarctions secondary to low flow in the “watershed” between the distal PCA and MCA territories, as occurs after cardiac arrest. Patients may experience persistence of a visual image for several minutes despite gazing at another scene (palinopsia) or an inability to synthesize the whole of an image (asimultagnosia).
  • Anton’s syndrome occurs due to bilateral occlusion of distal posterior cerebral arteries. It produces cortical blindness (blindness with preserved pupillary light reaction). The patient is often unaware of the blindness or may even deny it.
  • Wallenberg’s syndrome is lateral medullary syndrome which occurs due to occlusion of vertebral arteries. It results in acute onset ataxia, dizziness, Horner's syndrome and contralateral sensory loss.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Chapter:426 page number:3329

question_text:
A 22-year-old is noted to have persistent polyuria in excess of 6 liters per day. She mentions recently being involved in an accident and sustained head injury which she thinks she has recovered from. Investigations reveal:
potassium 4.2 mmol/l
calcium 8.6 mg/dl
glucose 106 mg/dl
Serum osmolality : 290 mOsm/kg (280-295)
Urine osmolality : 192 mOsm/kg
Which one of the following is the best way of confirming the diagnosis?
option_d: Therapeutic trial of low dose DDAVP
explanation:
• The diagnosis is likely to be diabetes insipidus.
  • The causes for polyuria in a patient include primary polydipsia, central DI and Nephrogenic DI
  • Diagnosis of DI in a patient with polyuria (urine output more than 50 ml/kg) is suggested by high plasma osmolality (>295 mOsm/kg) in a patient passing dilute urine ( urine osmolality <300 mOsm/kg).
  • If the diagnostic thresholds of DI are not met, DI can be confirmed by a water deprivation test where failure of urine concentration would be expected. During this test a patient is not allowed to drink and plasma ADH, plasma osmolality and urine osmolality are measured.
  • A therapeutic trial of DDAVP is only appropriate if a diagnosis of DI is confirmed (On the water deprivation test) and helps to differentiate between cranial or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2921

question_text:
A 49-year male presents to the ER with complaints of polyuria. He mentions that he has been passing about 4 liters of urine per day. He has recently been prescribed a new drug. Investigations show:
Serum sodium 141 mmol/l
Serum potassium 4.2 mmol/l
Plasma osmolality 296 mosmol/l (280-295)
Urine osmolality 230 mosmol/l (300-1000)
What drug was likely to have been prescribed?
explanation:
• The patient has drug induced Diabetes Insipidus based upon increased urine output, low urine osmolality, high plasma osmolality. This is most likely to be caused by lithium.

Drugs causing diabetes insipidus:

  • Lithium
  • Aminoglycosides
  • Methoxyflurane
  • Amphotericin B
  • Demeclocycline
  • Cisplatin
  • Rifampin
  • Foscarnet
  • Drugs like carbamazepine and chlorpropamide has been linked with SIADH resulting in hyponatremia

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2920

question_text:
A 66-year-old man presents with seizures. Past medical history includes a smoking history of 30 cigarettes a day for many years. His family report a weight loss over the past 8 months.Serum electrolytes show:
Sodium 109 mmol/L (135-145)
Potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0)
Glucose 126 mg/dL
Urea 3.0 mmol/L (3.2-8.1)
Urine sodium : 68 mmol/ L
These findings are most likely to be due to:
explanation:
• The biochemistry points to a syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion, with a low serum osmolality [2(Na + K) + urea + glucose].
  • The clinical picture is consistent with small cell carcinoma of the lung, which is often associated with SIADH.
  • SIADH should be diagnosed only after ruling out hypothyroidism and cortisol deficiency.
  • Diuretic use associated hyponatremia could be associated with low normal serum potassium.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2924

question_text: A 33-year-old woman is evaluated in the endocrinology clinic for increased urine output. She weighs 60 kg and has a 24-hour urine output of 3500 ml. Her basal urine osmolality is 210 mOsm/kg. She undergoes a fluid deprivation test and her urine osmolality after fluid deprivation (loss of weight 3 kg) is 350 mOsm/kg. A subsequent injection of subcutaneous DDAVP (desmopressin acetate) did not result in a further significant rise of urine osmolality after 2 hours (355 mOsm/kg). Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Diabetes insipidus (DI) is suspected when the urine output is > 50 ml/kg per day . If the basal urine osmolality is > 300 mOsm/kg, it suggests an osmotic diuresis (due to glucose / mannitol).
  • If fluid deprivation causes a urine osmolality > 300 mOsm/kg, it suggests psychogenic (primary) polydipsia as in this patient.
  • If not, it is either pituitary or nephrogenic DI. These are differentiated by the administration of subcutaneous DDAVP which causes an increased urine osmolality > 300 mOsm/kg in pituitary DI.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2921-22

question_text: A 28-year-old woman presenting with polyuria is found to have diabetes insipidus. Which part of the nephron is most affected in this condition?
explanation:
• Fine-tuning of salt and water balance is achieved in the distal and collecting tubules under the influence of aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone (ADH). ADH, however, plays a central role in urinary concentration by increasing the water permeability of the normally impermeable cortical and medullary collecting tubules. In the absence of ADH, little water is reabsorbed in the collecting tubules and dilute urine is excreted.
  • ADH mediated water reabsorption from the collecting tubules is facilitated via aquaporin 2 channels on the luminal surface.
  • Around 15-20% of renal water reabsorption is ADH mediated.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2919

question_text:
A 16-year-old boy is being treated with desmopressin for diabetes insipidus. His plasma glucose level (fasting) is 108 mg/dl, sodium 139 mmol/l (137-144), potassium 4.5 mmol/l (3.5-4.9) and calcium 10.9 mg/dl.
He still has complaints of polyuria, polydipsia and nocturia. What could be the most probable cause?
explanation:
• This boy most probably has nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. In this condition, renal tubules are resistant to antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which is due to a receptor defect of vasopressin-2 receptor or a post-receptor defect in an ADH-sensitive water channel called aquaporin-2.
  • The findings do not suggest diabetes mellitus, which is also associated with these symptoms. In patients with the syndrome of inappropriate secretion of ADH (SIADH), sodium levels are usually low.
  • Primary polydipsia is a psychiatric disturbance characterized by the excessive intake of water. It is unusual at this age. Sodium levels fall as a result and the urine produced is appropriately dilute.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2920

question_text: A 46-year-old patient with hypomania is referred for opinion. She is noted to have a sodium concentration of 142 mmol/l, with a urea of 72 mg/dl and a creatinine of 1.58 mg/dL. Urine osmolality is 250 mOsmol/l and serum osmolality was 297 mOsm/L. Fasting plasma glucose is normal. The nurses have monitored her urine output and found it to be 4.4 liters in 24 h. Which of the following statements best fits with her condition?
option_a: Psychiatric drugs are unlikely to have played a part in her condition
option_b: Symptoms are unlikely to improve with desmopressin
option_c: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus has a dominant pattern of inheritance
option_d: She is likely suffering from primary polydipsia as a part of psychiatric illness
explanation:
• This patient has diabetes insipidus, probably renal in origin related to the use of lithium as treatment for manic depression.
  • Diagnosis of diabetes insipidus in this case is established by the passage of dilute urine (<300 mOsm/kg) in the presence of high serum osmolality (>295 mOsm/kg)
  • Primary polydipsia would also have dilute urine but the serum osmolality will be lower / low normal with urine concentration during water deprivation.
  • Patients with nephrogenic DI won't respond to desmopressin
  • In this patient if possible, lithium should be withdrawn in consultation with a psychiatrist, and another drug such as lamotrigine substituted.
  • Amiloride has been used to control polyuria in lithium induced DI.
  • Inherited form of Nephrogenic DI is most commonly due to V2 receptor mutation inherited by X-linked recessive pattern, whereas cranial diabetes insipidus is inherited with an autosomal-dominant or recessive pattern.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2920

question_text: A 39-year-old psychiatric patient who is being treated for depression is admitted with increased confusion. His sodium is 122 mmol/l, with a plasma osmolality of 235 mOsmol/kg. Urine osmolality is 300mOsm/kg. There is no evidence on examination of cardiac, renal or hepatic failure. Random plasma cortisol and thyroid function are normal. Given the most likely diagnosis, which of the following statements best fits this condition?
option_a: This is a likely case of pseudo-hyponatremia
option_b: Treatment with IV saline will improve sodium levels
option_c: Renal sodium excretion is likely to be normal
option_d: Psychiatric drugs are very unlikely to be related to the underlying condition
explanation:
• This is the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) secretion.
  • Criteria for diagnosis are:
    • Hyponatraemia with an osmolality of < 270 mOsmol/kg.Inappropriately raised urine osmolality (> 100 mOsmol/l).
    • High urinary sodium of > 20 mmol/l (reflecting relative increased concentration due to reduced water loss)
    • Normal renal, adrenal and thyroid function.

Sodium handling by the kidney is not affected in SIADH.

  • A wide variety of medications including psychotropic medications have been implicated in SIADH.
  • Treatment is with fluid restriction, demeclocycline or V2 receptor antagonists like tolvaptan.
  • Another possible diagnostic consideration in a presentation of hyponatremia, especially given the psychiatric aspect here, is that of psychogenic polydipsia. However, in this condition urine is maximally dilute (urine osmolality < 100mOsm/kg), in contrast to SIADH.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2924

question_text: Hyperthermia results due to lesion in which part of the hypothalamus?
explanation:
Hemorrhage in anterior & preoptic hypothalamus may cause acute hyperthermia accompanied by paradoxical vasoconstriction & tachycardia.

Lesion in posterior hypothalamus could lead to hypothermia.

Hypothalamic nuclei and their functions

  1. Anterior - thermoregulation
  2. Preoptic - thermoregulation, sexual behavior
  3. Supraoptic - vasopressin and oxytocin secretion
  4. Paraventricular - oxytocin and vasopressin production
  5. Suprachiasmatic - circadian rhythm regulation
  6. Ventromedial - satiety centre
  7. Posterior - thermoregulation and arousal
  8. Arcuate - secretion of releasing hormones of hypothalamus
  9. Lateral hypothalamus - hunger centre

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2905

question_text: A patient presented with nystagmus, ataxia and dysdiadokinesia. Identify the artery involved
explanation:
The symptoms of nystagmus, ataxia, and dysdiadochokinesia suggest involvement of the cerebellum or its connections.

The blood supply to the cerebellum is primarily from the branches of the vertebrobasilar system, which includes the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and branches from the basilar artery, such as the superior cerebellar artery (SCA), anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA), and posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA).

Among the options given, the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) is part of this system and can be involved in cerebellar pathology.

question_text: Pituicytes are seen in ?
explanation: Ans. B. Posterior lobe Pituicytes are glial cells of posterior pituitary.

question_text: Lateral medullary syndrome is caused by thrombosis of:
explanation: Answer is C > B (Vertebral artery > Posterior inferior cerebellar artery): `Most cases result from ipsilateral vertebral artery occlusion; in the reminder occlusion of posterior inferior cerebellar artery is responsible' – Harrison Vessel occlusion that result in Lateral Medullary syndrome: - Vertebral (most common)  - Posterior inferior cerebellar (2nd most common)  - Superior, middle or Inferior lateral medullary arteries Vertebral artery The vertebral artery consists of four segments. The fourth segment courses upward to joint the other vertebral artery to form the basilar artery. Only this segment gives rise to branches that supply the brainstem and cerebellum. Embolic occlusion or thrombosis of the fourth segment is responsible for this syndrome Q Posterior inferior cerebellar artery Posterior inferior cerebellar artery in its proximal part supplies the lateral medulla and in its distal branches the inferior surface of cerebellum.

question_text: Which of the following is not true regarding SIADH?
option_b: Patient is euvolemic and at times hypervolemic
explanation: The syndrome of inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) is a disorder of impaired water excretion caused by the inability to suppress the secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). In SIADH, the urine sodium excretion is high. Hyponatremia (ie, serum Na+< 135 mmol/L) with concomitant hypo-osmolality (serum osmolality < 280 mOsm/kg) and high urine osmolality are the hallmark of SIADH.

question_text: A 16-year-old boy is being treated with desmopressin for diabetes insipidus. His plasma glucose level (fasting) is 108 mg/dl, sodium 139 mmol/l (137-144), potassium 4.5 mmol/l (3.5-4.9) and calcium 10.9 mg/dl. He still has complaints of polyuria, polydipsia and nocturia. What could be the most probable cause?
explanation:
• This boy most probably has nephrogenic diabetes insipidus due to hypercalcemia. In this condition, renal tubules are resistant to antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which is due to a receptor defect of vasopressin-2 receptor or a post-receptor defect in an ADH-sensitive water channel called aquaporin-2.
  • Central DI (ADH deficiency) show good response to desmopressin (V2 agonist) administration.
  • The findings do not suggest diabetes mellitus, which is also associated with these symptoms.
  • In patients with the syndrome of inappropriate secretion of ADH (SIADH), low sodium levels are the hallmark.

Metabolic causes of Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus:

  • Chronic Hypokalemia
  • Chronic Hypercalcemia

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2920

question_text: A 50-year-old male patient presents with polyuria and polydipsia of 2 months duration. He has been on a chronic medication for last 15 years. The urine is hypoosmolar. His blood sugars are normal. Which could be the drug?
explanation:
Polyuria, polydipsia with large volume of hypoosmolar urine suggest the diagnosis of Diabetes insipidus. Among the following, Lithium therapy causes nephrogenic diabetes.

Other drugs causing Diabetes Insipidus: Lithium, Demeclocycline, Methoxyflurane, Amphotericin B, Aminoglycosides, Cisplatin, Rifampin, Foscarnet.

Lithium causes DI by entering the Collecting Duct via the ENaC, where it down regulates the Aquaporin channels.

Lithium also causes Chronic Tubulointerstitial Disease.

Amiloride can be used to prevent and treat Lithium induced Diabetes Insipidus.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, Ch: 316, Pg: 2363.

question_text:
A 67-year-old woman sustained a stroke and is receiving enteral nutrition by nasoduodenal tube at a nursing home. She is transferred to the hospital with altered mental status. Nursing home staff reported that she had plentiful urine output 2 days before transfer. Laboratory data on hospital arrival reveal serum sodium of 165 mmol/l, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 60 mg/dl, and creatinine 1.6 mg/dl; all were normal 6 weeks earlier. Additional laboratory data include:
Serum osmolality of 341 mOsm/kg (NR: 275 to 295 mOsm/kg)
Urine osmolality 690 mOsm/kg (NR:500-850 mOsm/kg)
Urine sodium 7 mmol/l (NR:>20 mmol/L)
Urine potassium 32 mmol/l (NR: ~20 mEq/L)
The most likely explanation for this patient's polyuria and hyper-natremia and the most appropriate confirmatory test are:
option_a: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and measurement of ADH
option_b: Central diabetes insipidus and measurement of ADH
option_c: Lithium toxicity and measurement of serum lithium level
option_d: Increased solute load and measurement of electrolyte-free water clearance
explanation:
A calculation would reveal that this patient is excreting electrolyte- free water despite the urine osmolality being much greater than serum osmolality. In such a patient setting, the failure to replace electrolyte free water losses results in increased serum sodium concentration. The hyperosmolality of the urine is primarily caused by the extremely high excretion of urea in this patient receiving high-protein enteral feedings.

Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 346-347

question_text:
A 28-year-old female sustained a minor head injury, was seen in the emergency department with headache and was discharged following a normal computed tomography of the head, She presented again 2 months later with polyuria and polydipsia. She has a 2-year history of recurrent pyelonephritis and is under investigation by the urologists. A water deprivation test was performed:
Water deprivation phase: Plasma osmolality 295 mOsmol/kg (NR: 275 - 295 mOsmol/kg), Urine osmolality 220 mOsmol/kg
Desmopressin (DDAVP) phase (after administration of 2 pg desmopressin): Plasma osmolality 300 mOsmol/kg Urine osmolality 250 mOsmoL/kg. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, the water deprivation test after overnight fast shows the maximal osmolality of urine is abnormally low < 750 mOsmol/ kg, After administration of exogenous vasopressin (DDAVP), there is only slight increase in urine osmolality In cranial diabetes insipidus, DDAVP produces a rise in urine osmolality of about 50%. In psychogenic polydipsia, a low initial plasma and urine osmolality.

Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:381 Pg: 2920

question_text: Which of the following is seen in encephalitic rabies?
explanation:
Rabies encephalitis is distinguished by early brainstem involvement, which results in the classic features of hydrophobia (involuntary, painful contraction of the diaphragm and accessory respiratory, laryngeal, and pharyngeal muscles in response to swallowing liquids) and aerophobia (the same features causedby stimulation from a draft of air). These symptoms are probably due to dysfunction of infected brainstem neurons that normally inhibit inspiratory neurons near the nucleus ambiguus, resulting in exaggerated defense reflexes that protect the respiratory tract. The combination of hypersalivation and pharyngeal dysfunction is also responsible for the classic appearance of "foaming at the mouth".
Brainstem dysfunction progresses rapidly, and coma-followed within days by death-is the rule unless the course is prolonged by supportive measures. With such measures, late complications can include cardiac and/or respiratory failure, disturbances of water balance (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion or diabetes insipidus), noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Cardiac arrhythmias may be due to dysfunction affecting vital centers in the brainstem or to myocarditis. Multiple-organ failure is common in patients treated aggressively in critical care units.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 208, Pg: 1621

question_text: A patient came to medical OPD with complaints of polyuria. He has a history of undergoing total hypophysectomy. His Na+ levels were found to be 155 mEq/L, and his urine osmolarity was 200 mOsm/L. What is the definitive management in this patient?
option_a: DDAVP for 2 weeks and then discontinue
option_c: Upsetting of receptors, so no treatment required
explanation:
Explanation:

Lifelong desmopressin (DDAVP) is the definitive treatment for central diabetes insipidus following total hypophysectomy.

  • This patient has central diabetes insipidus (DI), a condition resulting from decreased vasopressin (ADH) secretion due to complete removal of the pituitary gland.
  • Clinical features include polyuria, hypernatremia (Na⁺ = 155 mEq/L), and low urine osmolality (200 mOsm/kg), all indicating impaired water reabsorption.
  • The definitive treatment is lifelong DDAVP (desmopressin), a synthetic ADH analog that restores water retention and corrects electrolyte imbalance.

Explanation of other options:

DDAVP for 2 weeks and then discontinue (Option A): Inappropriate, as hypophysectomy causes permanent ADH deficiency.

Upsetting of receptors, so no treatment required (Option C): Incorrect; central DI involves hormone deficiency, not receptor issues.

Thiazides for 2 weeks (Option D): Used in nephrogenic DI, not effective in central DI where ADH is lacking.

question_text: Which of the following is the vasopressor of choice in patients with septic shock?
explanation:
In patients with distributive shock, the primary action used to mitigate the shock is to increase the systemic vascular resistance. Norepinephrine is the first choice vasopressor. It has potent action at alpha1 and beta1 adrenergic receptors. The alpha1 causes vasoconstriction while beta1 has positive inotropic and chronotropic effects.

Option B: At high doses, epinephrine has a similar profile (at lower doses the β effects predominate), but is associated with tachyarrhythmia, myocardial ischemia, decreased splanchnic blood flow, pulmonary hypertension, and acidosis.

question_text: Which of the following best explains the development of hyponatremia in a hypovolemic patient with diarrhea?
option_a: Decreased reabsorption of sodium from kidney
option_d: Decreased sodium absorption from the intestine
explanation:
Explanation:

In a hypovolemic patient with diarrhea, significant loss of sodium and water occurs through the gastrointestinal tract. To maintain blood pressure and perfusion, the body triggers a non-osmotic release of ADH, which causes the kidneys to retain free water. This dilutes the serum sodium, leading to hyponatremia. The key mechanism here is water retention without equivalent sodium, resulting from volume depletion rather than hypo-osmolality.

Mechanism of Hyponatremia in Hypovolemia

Explanation for other Options:

Decreased reabsorption of sodium from kidney (Option A): volume depletion stimulates sodium reabsorption in the kidneys via activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). The kidneys conserve sodium, not waste it, in hypovolemia.

Decreased secretion of aldosterone (Option B): Hypovolemia causes increased aldosterone secretion, which enhances sodium and water reabsorption in the distal nephron to restore intravascular volume.

Decreased sodium absorption from the intestine (Option D): While diarrhea causes sodium loss, the resulting hyponatremia is not due to impaired absorption, but due to free water retention via ADH. Sodium loss alone does not explain the drop in serum sodium concentration unless accompanied by water retention.

Key takeaway:

Summary of Stimuli affecting Vasopressin Secretion

question_text: Below image shows Vasopressin and the regulation of water permeability in the renal collecting duct. AT which receptor vasopressin act?
explanation:
Vasopressin binds to the type 2 vasopressin receptor (V2R) on the basolateral membrane of principal cells, activates adenylyl cyclase (AC), increases intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphatase (cAMP), and stimulates protein kinase A (PKA) activity. Cytoplasmic vesicles carrying aquaporin-2 (AQP) water channel proteins are inserted into the luminal membrane in response to vasopressin, thereby increasing the water permeability of this membrane. When vasopressin stimulation ends, water channels are retrieved by an endocytic process and water permeability returns to its low basal rate. The AQP3 and AQP4 water channels are expressed on the basolateral membrane and complete the transcellular pathway for water reabsorption. pAQP2, phosphorylated aquaporin-2.

Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 339

question_text: A patient presented with acute chest pain radiating to the left shoulder. An ECG was performed which showed ST elevations in leads II, III, and aVF. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation

  • ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF is diagnostic of an Inferior wall Myocardial Infarction.
  • These leads correspond to the inferior wall of the left ventricle, which is usually supplied by the right coronary artery (RCA) (occasionally the left circumflex artery).
  • Clinical features often include chest pain, radiation to left shoulder/jaw, bradyarrhythmias, or hypotension due to RCA involvement affecting the SA/AV nodes.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Lateral wall MI (Option B):

  • ST elevation occurs in leads I, aVL, V5, and V6, not in II, III, aVF.
  • Usually supplied by the left circumflex artery.

Anterior wall MI (Option C):

  • ST elevation is seen in precordial leads V1-V4, indicating LAD artery involvement.
  • Not the pattern described in this case.

Posterior wall MI (Option D):

  • Characterized by ST depression in V1-V3 with tall R waves, or reciprocal ST elevation in posterior leads V7-V9.
  • Not consistent with ST elevation in II, III, aVF.

explanation:

question_text: All of the following are the cause of NDI (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), except?
explanation:
Hypercalcemia can also cause polyuria and NDI; calcium signals directly through the calcium-sensing receptor to downregulate Na+, K+, and Cl– transport by the TALH and water transport in principal cells, thus reducing renal concentrating ability in hypercalcemia.

Another common acquired cause of NDI is hypokalemia, which inhibits the renal response to AVP and downregulates aquaporin-2 expression. Several drugs can cause acquired NDI, in particular lithium, Ifosfamide , and several antiviral agents. Lithium causes NDI by multiple mechanisms, including direct inhibition of renal glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3), a kinase thought to be the pharmacologic target of lithium in bipolar disease; GSK3 is required for the response of principal cells to AVP

Thiazides may reduce polyuria due to NDI, ostensibly by inducing hypovolemia and increasing proximal tubular water reabsorption. Occasionally, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) have been used to treat polyuria associated with NDI, reducing the negative effect of intrarenal prostaglandins on urinary concentrating mechanisms; however, this assumes the risks of NSAID-associated gastric and/or renal toxicity.

Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:381 Pg: 2920

question_text: A 58-year-old diabetic man presents with septic shock. He is febrile, tachycardic, and has a blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg, despite adequate fluid resuscitation with crystalloids. His urine output is low and he is drowsy. What is the next best step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

Norepinephrine is the preferred first-line vasopressor for treating hypotension in septic shock, and should be initiated after fluid resuscitation if blood pressure remains low.Sepsis is defined as a life-threatening condition caused by a dysregulated immune response to infection, resulting in organ dysfunction.It is clinically diagnosed when there is suspected or confirmed infection along with an increase of 2 or more points in the SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) score.Septic shock is a more severe subset, characterized by:

  • The need for vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥ 65 mmHg
  • A serum lactate level > 2 mmol/L, despite adequate fluid resuscitation

Initial Management Approach:

  • Antibiotic Therapy:
    • Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be administered within the first hour of recognition.
    • Blood cultures must be obtained prior to antibiotic administration, if possible, but treatment should not be delayed.
  • Fluid Resuscitation:
    • Crystalloids (e.g., normal saline or lactated Ringer’s) should be administered at a dose of 30 mL/kg within the first 3 hours.
    • The goal is to restore tissue perfusion and prevent progression of organ dysfunction.
  • Vasopressors:
    • If hypotension persists despite fluids, norepinephrine is the vasopressor of choice.
    • The target MAP is 65 mmHg, and arterial line monitoring is recommended for accurate pressure measurement.

Additional Considerations in Sepsis Management:

  • Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS):
    • In sepsis-associated ARDS, mechanical ventilation with low tidal volume (6 mL/kg) and high PEEP settings is advised to minimize ventilator-induced lung injury.
  • Supportive Care Measures:
    • Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis unless contraindicated
    • Stress ulcer prevention using proton pump inhibitors or H2 blockers
    • Tight glucose control to avoid both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia
    • Renal replacement therapy (RRT) when indicated in patients with acute kidney injury (AKI)

Dopamine is no longer preferred in the management of septic shock because it has a higher risk of causing arrhythmias and provides less consistent effects on blood pressure compared to norepinephrine. It may be considered in rare cases with bradycardia, but it is not the best choice for this patient.

Explanations for other Options:

Administer dopamine (Option A): Dopamine is no longer preferred in the management of septic shock because it has a higher risk of causing arrhythmias and provides less consistent effects on blood pressure compared to norepinephrine. It may be considered in rare cases with bradycardia, but it is not the best choice for this patient.

Administer hydrocortisone (Option C): Hydrocortisone is used only in patients with septic shock who do not respond to both fluids and vasopressors, i.e., refractory shock. Since this patient has not yet received vasopressors, starting hydrocortisone at this point would be premature.

Administer vasopressin (Option D): Vasopressin is used as a second-line vasopressor and is usually added to norepinephrine when blood pressure is still not maintained with norepinephrine alone. It is not recommended as an initial vasopressor, so it is not the next best step in this case.

Key takeaway:

SOFA SCORE

question_text: An 80-year-old man with a long history of poor urinary stream and nocturia presented with malaise and vomiting. His plasma creatinine concentration was 10.5 mg/dl and his urea 220 mg/dl. Renal ultrasound showed gross bilateral hydronephrosis with thin cortices. A urinary catheter was placed and he passed 7.6 litres of urine over the next 24 hours, during which time he received no supplemental iv fluid. His blood pressure is now 80/50 mmHg, he has no oedema and his neck veins are flat. His serum Na+ is 150 mmol/l and urine osmolality is 198 mOsm/l. Which of the following most accurately describes the hormonal milieu?
option_a: High ADH, high aldosterone, high renin
option_b: High ADH, high aldosterone, low renin
option_c: High ADH, low aldosterone, low renin
option_d: Low ADH, high aldosterone, high renin
explanation:
In the setting of long-standing urinary tract obstruction, as evidenced by the severity of uraemia and thin cortices, the ability of the kidney to concentrate urine becomes severely impaired, resulting in partial nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Much of the polyuria that occurs after urinary tract obstruction is relieved is an appropriate attempt by the kidneys to deal with salt and water overload. However, a rise in serum osmolality to > 300 mOsm/l, as in this case, in the presence of a low urine osmolality indicates that the polyuria is pathological. The ability of the kidney to conserve Na+ is also impaired, as the patient becomes clinically volume-depleted. Therefore, one can infer that there is severe distal tubular damage with effective unresponsiveness to both ADH and aldosterone. Hypovolaemia is a potent stimulus for renin production from the juxtaglomerular apparatus and hypernatraemia is a potent stimulus for ADH production from the posterior pituitary. As there is nothing in this case to suggest adrenal disease, secondary hyperaldosteronism would be present. Obviously, this situation should never be allowed to occur in practice. A reasonable approach in postobstructive diuresis is to replace half the volume of urine with 0.45% saline or alternating dextrose 5% and normal saline, with frequent assessment of fluid status. Replacing urine ml for ml or even 'output minus 30 ml/h', prolongs the duration of diuresis.

Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 319, Pg: 2376.

question_text: A patient is admitted with acute gastroenteritis. Laboratory results show a serum potassium level of 2.8 mEq/L. Which of the following is not a recognized complication of this electrolyte abnormality?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • A serum potassium level of 8 mEq/L indicates hypokalemia, defined as potassium concentration below 3.5 mEq/L.
  • Hypokalemia affects neuromuscular, gastrointestinal, and cardiac systems, but does not cause cerebral edema.
  • Cerebral edema is typically associated with hyponatremia, not potassium disturbances.

Cerebral Edema

  • Pathophysiology: Occurs due to osmotic fluid shifts into brain cells when serum sodium is low, leading to neuronal swelling.
  • Clinical features: Headache, confusion, seizures, papilledema, and coma.
  • Causes: Rapid correction of hyponatremia, SIADH, or hypotonic fluid administration.

Hypokalemia - Serum potassium < 3.5 mEq/L

Complications of Hypokalemia:

  • Arrhythmias (e.g., ventricular tachycardia, atrial arrhythmias) (Option D ruled out)
  • Quadriparesis (Option C ruled out)
  • Hypokalemic polyuria (mimics nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) (Option A ruled out)
  • Ileus (constipation or bowel obstruction)
  • Respiratory muscle weakness
  • Metabolic alkalosis
  • Rhabdomyolysis
  • Impaired insulin secretion
  • Increased risk of digitalis toxicity
  • Psychiatric symptoms (e.g., confusion, delirium)
  • Tetanus

Management:

Potassium Replacement:

  • Oral potassium chloride for mild cases.
  • Intravenous potassium for severe or symptomatic cases (administer cautiously to avoid hyperkalemia).
  • Correct Underlying Cause

question_text: In a hypothyroid patient becoming pregnant, dose of levothyroxine should be?
explanation:

question_text: Calcitonin is a marker of which of the following malignancies?
explanation:
Explanation:

Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) originates from parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid, and calcitonin produced by these cells serves as a precise tumour marker for its diagnosis and follow-up.

Explanations of other options:

Papillary thyroid cancer (Option A): Papillary thyroid carcinoma develops from the thyroid's follicular epithelial cells rather than the parafollicular C-cells, and its follow-up is generally done with thyroglobulin measurement instead of calcitonin levels.

Follicular thyroid cancer (Option B): Like papillary thyroid carcinoma, follicular thyroid carcinoma originates from the thyroid follicular cells and typically does not cause raised calcitonin levels. Thyroglobulin serves as the preferred tumour marker for its follow-up.

Anaplastic thyroid cancer (Option D): Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is a rare, highly aggressive thyroid malignancy that does not cause an increase in calcitonin levels. It develops from thyroid follicular cells, much like papillary and follicular thyroid cancers.

question_text: A female patient presents with severe restlessness, palpitations, and tremors to the emergency department. She is a known case of bronchial asthma. On examination, the neck looks swollen. Blood pressure is elevated, and tachycardia is noted. ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Which of the following drugs is used for immediate management in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Diltiazem is preferred for rate control in atrial fibrillation in thyroid storm when beta-blockers are contraindicated, such as in bronchial asthma.

  • The patient's presentation-restlessness, palpitations, tremors, tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, and a swollen neck-suggests thyroid storm, a life-threatening complication of hyperthyroidism.
    • Clinical features:
    • Fever
    • Delirium, seizures, coma
    • Vomiting, diarrhea
    • Jaundice
    • Hyperthermia
    • Cardiac failure
    • Arrhythmias
  • Precipitating factors:
    • Stress:
      • Acute illnesses like stroke, trauma, diabetic ketoacidosis
      • Surgery, commonly of the thyroid
      • Infections
    • Acute iodine load:
      • Radioiodine treatment of a patient with partially or untreated hyperthyroidism
      • Iodinated contrast agents
      • Amiodarone administration
  • In thyroid storm, immediate management involves controlling the heart rate, especially in cases of atrial fibrillation.
  • Beta-blockers like propranolol and esmolol are commonly used to manage symptoms and block peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
  • However, they are contraindicated in bronchial asthma due to their bronchoconstrictive potential.
  • In asthmatic patients, diltiazem, a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, is used instead for rate control as it avoids bronchospasm.
  • After initial stabilization and rate control, antithyroid drugs like propylthiouracil are administered to block thyroid hormone synthesis.

Explanation of other options:

Propranolol (Option B): Beta-blocker used in thyroid storm, but contraindicated in asthma due to risk of bronchospasm.

Esmolol (Option C): Short-acting beta-blocker also used in thyroid storm; however, not preferred in asthmatics.

Propylthiouracil (Option D): Drug of choice to inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis in thyroid storm, but not used first in unstable patients with atrial fibrillation-rate control is the immediate priority.

question_text: Which anti-thyroid drug is preferred in pregnancy with Grave's disease in 1st trimester?
explanation:
Treatment of Hyperthyroidism during Pregnancy

  • Antithyroid drugs should be used to manage Grave's disease in pregnancy. Because transplacental passage of these drugs may produce fetal hypothyroidism and goiter if the maternal dose is excessive, maternal antithyroid dose titration should target serum free or total T4 levels at or just above the pregnancy reference range.
  • If available, propylthiouracil should be used until 14-16 week’s gestation because of the association of rare cases of methimazole/carbimazole embryopathy, including aplasia cutis and other defects, such as choanal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistulae.
  • Antithyroid drugs given to the mother can be used to treat the fetus and may be needed for 1-3 months after delivery, until the maternal antibodies disappear from the baby's circulation.
  • The postpartum period is a time of major risk for relapse of Grave's disease.
  • Breast-feeding is safe with low doses of antithyroid drugs.
  • Use of radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnant women

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition, Ch:377 Pg:2940-42

question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents with weight loss, palpitations, diarrhoea and irregular menstrual cycles. Examination reveals a single nodule on the left lobe of her thyroid gland, about 1.5 cm in diameter. Thyroid scanning with technetium shows increased uptake within the nodule with reduced activity throughout the rest of the gland. Thyroid function tests showed a free thyroxine of 30 pmol/l (9-25 pmol/l), TSH < 0.05 mU/l (0.5-5). Based upon these findings, what would be the definitive treatment?
explanation:
• Toxic thyroid nodules preferentially take up radioactive iodine. This makes them particularly amenable to radioactive iodine treatment.
  • A dose of 300-500 MBq is usually sufficient to cure the thyrotoxicosis.
  • Radioiodine therapy is contraindicated in children and women who are lactating or pregnant, and where the safety of cohabitants from the effects of radioactivity can't be guaranteed.
  • Surgery is the next best option for patients in whom radioiodine is contraindicated or refused.
  • Carbimazole alone or in combination with thyroxine replacement is used in the medical treatment of Grave's disease.
  • Propanolol is a useful symptom reliever for thyrotoxicosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:2942

question_text:
A 27-year-old woman with thyrotoxicosis presents with a 6-week history of amenorrhoea. Laboratory investigations confirm an early pregnancy.
Which of the following drugs would be most appropriate in this condition?
explanation:
• Propylthiouracil is the drug of choice in pregnancy as its greater protein binding reduces the risk of transplacental passage.
  • Methimazole is the active metabolite of carbimazole.
  • Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in pregnancy as it can destroy the fetal thyroid gland.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:2940

question_text: History of exposure to head and neck irradiation increases risk of:
explanation:

  • Other risk factors include female sex, family history of thyroid cancer and advanced age

question_text: What would be the most suitable course of action for managing a 65-year-old male who presented with symptoms of weakness, lethargy, excessive cold intolerance, and slow ankle jerk? His thyroid function test (TFT) revealed a TSH level of 16 Mu/L (normal range: 0.4 - 4.0 mu / l), T4 level of 0.3 ng/dl (normal range: 0.6 - 1.6 ng / dl), and T3 level of 70 pg /dl.
option_a: Start levothyroxine at 100 micrograms and decrease the dose gradually
option_b: Start levothyroxine at 25 micrograms and increase the dose gradually
option_c: Start levothyroxine at 25 micrograms and decrease the dose gradually
option_d: Give T3 and T4 drugs simultaneously
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient has overt primary hypothyroidism (high TSH, low T4/T3). In an older adult, it is crucial to start with a low dose of levothyroxine (e.g., 25 mcg/day) and titrate upwards gradually every 4-6 weeks based on TSH levels. This cautious approach prevents precipitating adverse cardiac effects like angina or arrhythmias, which can occur with rapid hormone replacement.

Thyroid Function Test :

  • TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone)
    • Normal range: 0.4-4.0 mIU/L
  • Interpretation of Results:

Treatment of hypothyroidism:

  • Levothyroxine -6 µg/kg to be started
  • Available as 25 µg / 50 µg / 88 µg / 100 µg
  • If the dose is >100µg, it increases O2 consumption resulting in angina. Hence, careful titration of dose increments should be done.

Explanation of other options:

Start levothyroxine at 100 micrograms and decrease the dose gradually (Option A): A full replacement dose is too aggressive for initial therapy in an elderly patient and carries a high risk of cardiac complications.

Start levothyroxine at 25 micrograms and decrease the dose gradually (Option C): The dose should be increased, not decreased, to reach a euthyroid state.

Give T3 and T4 drugs simultaneously (Option D): Combination therapy is not first-line and is generally reserved for special circumstances under specialist care.

Key Takeaways:

  • Levothyroxine is the treatment for hypothyroidism.
  • In elderly patients or those with known cardiac disease, "start low and go slow" is the guiding principle for initiation and titration.

question_text: T4 to T3 conversion may be impaired by?
explanation:
• T4 to T3 conversion is impaired by fasting, systemic illness or acute trauma, oral contrast agents, and medications like propylthiouracil, propranolol, amiodarone, glucocorticoids.
  • Phenytoin, salicylates, frusemide and free fatty acids can cause displacement of thyroid hormones from binding proteins.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 2930

question_text: A 37-year-old woman comes to you for consultation . She has experienced cold intolerance, weakness and constipation for 3 months. Her menses are regular but scanty. Her history is significant for hypertension and peptic ulcer disease. The patient is married but has never been pregnant and takes cimetidine 400 mg at bedtime, sustained-release nifedipine 60 mg daily and docusate sodium 100 mg three times a day. Her pulse is 58 beats/minute with a blood pressure of 135/90 mm Hg; Labs show a normal CBC, free thyroxine (T4) is 6.4 pmol/l (normal range, 10-22 pmol/l) and thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) is 1.5 mIU (normal range, 0.3-5.0 mIU). Which of the following is most likely to confirm the underlying cause?
explanation:
• This patient has central hypothyroidism and should be evaluated for pituitary and end organ function as well as the presence of a pituitary tumor. The prolactin level should be measured and the pituitary adrenal, gonadal and growth hormone axes assessed.
  • It is important to note that TSH may be either normal or low in central hypothyroidism
  • The presence of a pituitary tumor can be determined by imaging the pituitary gland with MRI or computed tomography (CT) scan.
  • Presence of pituitary tumor should also prompt evaluation for other anterior pituitary hormone status.
  • Where appropriate, this should be followed by evaluation of the visual fields.
  • Treatment of choice for most pituitary adenomas is trans sphenoidal resection, although microprolactinoma may be managed successfully with dopamine agonist therapy.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2898

question_text: A 32-year-old woman presents to her GP with a history of amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. She is keen to become pregnant and has been trying for 12 months to conceive without success. She is of normal weight and has no other constitutional symptoms. Which of the following is most likely to be the reason for her symptoms?
explanation:
• Her symptoms are consistent with hyper-prolactinaemia. Raised prolactin has many causes including pituitary tumors (micro- and macroadenomas), drug treatment (some antidepressants like tricyclic antidepressants, antiemetics and cimetidine), pregnancy, stress, hypothyroidism (because thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) stimulates TSH and prolactin in primary hypothyroidism) and renal failure (prolactin accumulates in renal failure but not in hepatic impairment).
  • While hyperprolactinemia can be present in hypothyroidism, it is usually associated with menorrhagia rather than amenorrhoea.
  • Polycystic ovarian syndrome may be associated with amenorrhea and mildly raised prolactin levels, but unlikely to result in galactorrhea.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2909

question_text: A 55-year-old man presents to the Emergency department with altered consciousness, his blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg, his skin is pigmented and he has a past history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. His family say he has been tired for several months and has been losing weight and complaining of abdominal pain. Which of the following results is most likely to be found on investigation?
explanation:
• The clinical picture is suggestive of Addison's disease with hypotension, pigmentation and a prodromal period with symptoms in keeping with glucocorticoid deficiency in a man with a history of another autoimmune endocrine disorder.
  • Addison's disease refers to adrenal insufficiency due to an adrenal ethology (primary adrenal insufficiency)
  • The most common cause for Addison disease worldwide is autoimmune adrenalitis while Tuberculosis is the most likely cause in India.
  • Hypoglycemia, hyponatraemia, hyperkalemia, hypotension and an elevated urea are all present during a hypoadrenal crisis due to steroid deficiency and subsequent salt and water loss.
  • Lymphocytosis along with eosinophilia are seen in acute adrenal insufficiency.

question_text:
A 19-year-old girl referred for evaluation of menstrual disturbances. She weighs only 38 kg and is 1.78 m tall. She is emaciated, her skin is dry and she has excessive growth of lanugo hair. She has been amenorrhoeic for 9 months. Her cortisol level is elevated, her Free T4 is normal. She has anemia and associated reduced white cell and platelet count.
Which of the following diagnoses is most likely to fit with this clinical picture?
explanation:
• Anorexia nervosa has a female to male preponderance of 9:1. It is estimated that around 0.5-1% of women between 15 and 30 years of age have anorexia. The aetiology of anorexia is unknown, but it is likely to be an interaction between environmental and genetic factors,
  • Patient may also have bradycardia and low / low-normal BP
  • Typical laboratory tests include decreased FSH, LH, estrogens and 17-OH steroids. Free T4 and TSH levels are usually normal.
  • Anemia with decreased white and platelet cell count may also occur. There may be metabolic alkalosis, hypocalcaemia, hypokalemia and hypomagnesaemia.
  • Treatment may involve complex psychotherapy for a number of years, and referral to a specialist in the field is recommended.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20th edition Chapter:444 Page number: 3274

question_text: An elderly woman came with a weight loss of 6 kg over 6 months and increased fatigue and prostration during febrile episodes. Investigation showed lowFree T3, low Free T4 and low TSH. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• The patient is likely to be suffering from multiple pituitary hormone deficieny.
  • Low T3 and T4 in the presence of low TSH suggests central hypothyroidism. Isolated secondary hypothyroidism would not usually be associated with weight loss.
  • Presence of significant weight loss and excessive fatigue during febrile episodes is suggestive of coexistent secondary adrenal insufficiency. Low cortisol and ACTH values would confirm the same.
  • The investigation of choice to elucidate the cause is MRI of the pituitary fossa to exclude a pituitary tumor.
  • Addison disease refers to primary AI and it may be associated with high TSH levels.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2898

question_text: A person living in an iodine deficient area developed hyperthyroidism after taking iodine supplementation. Which phenomenon explains this?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Jod-Basedow phenomenon describes the occurrence of iodine-induced hyperthyroidism, particularly in individuals with preexisting thyroid abnormalities such as multinodular goitre. When a person who has been iodine-deficient is suddenly exposed to high levels of iodine-either through dietary supplements or iodinated contrast media-the thyroid may begin producing excessive amounts of hormones, leading to thyrotoxicosis.

This happens because autonomous thyroid tissue or nodules in these individuals function independently of pituitary feedback regulation. In contrast, individuals with a healthy thyroid typically do not experience this effect.

Explanations for other Options:

Wolff-Chaikoff effect (Option A): The Wolff-Chaikoff effect is the opposite of the Jod-Basedow effect. It describes a temporary suppression of thyroid hormone production in response to excess iodine. This is a protective autoregulatory mechanism to prevent hyperthyroidism, especially in people with a normal thyroid. However, this effect can "escape" after a few days, allowing hormone synthesis to resume.

Goitre (Option C): A goitre is an enlargement of the thyroid gland, commonly caused by iodine deficiency, autoimmune disease, or nodular disease. While goitre can be seen in iodine deficiency, it does not explain the development of hyperthyroidism after iodine supplementation. It is more of a structural change, not a functional effect like the Jod-Basedow phenomenon.

Medullary thyroid cancer (Option D): Medullary thyroid cancer (MTC) is a neuroendocrine tumor arising from parafollicular C cells of the thyroid that produce calcitonin, not thyroid hormones. It does not cause hyperthyroidism, and it is not related to iodine intake.

question_text: A female presented with increased TSH and very low T4. What could be the diagnosis?
explanation:
A low T4 and a high TSH suggest the diagnosis of primary hypothyroidism.

The commonest cause of primary hypothyroidism is Autoimmune.

question_text: A patient presents with lethargy, increased sleep, and weight gain. Lab values show low plasma TSH, low T3, and low T4. After TRH administration, TSH levels increase. Which condition is likely?
option_a: Hyperthyroidism due to disease in the pituitary
option_b: Hypothyroidism due to disease in the pituitary
option_c: Hypothyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus
option_d: Hyperthyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus
explanation:
Explanation:

The lab profile (low T3, T4) confirms hypothyroidism (Option A and D ruled out). The key to localization is the TSH response to TRH.

  • Low TSH with Low T4: Indicates a problem at the pituitary or hypothalamus (secondary/tertiary hypothyroidism), not the thyroid itself (which would have high TSH).
  • Positive TRH Stimulation Test (Increase in TSH): This demonstrates that the pituitary gland is intact and capable of producing TSH when stimulated. Therefore, the defect lies "upstream" in the hypothalamus, which is failing to produce adequate TRH to stimulate the pituitary under normal conditions.

This pattern is diagnostic of Tertiary Hypothyroidism due to hypothalamic disease.

Clinical Features of Hypothyroidism:

  • Fatigue, weakness and increased sleep
  • Cold intolerance, Weight gain
  • Dry, coarse skin, Hair loss
  • Constipation
  • Depression and cognitive impairment
  • Menstrual irregularities and infertility
  • Bradycardia
  • Myxedema Hoarse voice
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome, Slow reflexes
  • Goiter, Anemia, Hypercholesterolemia

Primary hypothyroidism is due to thyroid gland dysfunction causing low thyroid hormones, commonly from Hashimoto's thyroiditis, surgery, radiation, iodine deficiency, medications, or infiltrative diseases.

Secondary hypothyroidism results from pituitary or hypothalamic dysfunction leading to insufficient TSH, caused by tumors, surgery, Sheehan's syndrome, trauma, or genetic/hypothalamic defects. Labs show high TSH in primary and low/normal TSH in secondary, with low free T3/T4 in both. (Option B ruled out)

Clinically, both present with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, hair loss, bradycardia, constipation, and myxedema, while secondary may have other pituitary hormone deficiencies. Treatment is levothyroxine, guided by TSH in primary and by free T4 in secondary hypothyroidism.

Interpretation of thyroid function tests:


Key Takeaways:

  • Low T4 + Low/Normal TSH + Positive TRH test = Hypothalamic (Tertiary) Hypothyroidism.
  • Low T4 + Low/Normal TSH + Blunted TRH test = Pituitary (Secondary) Hypothyroidism.

question_text: Titration of doses of anti-thyroid drugs is best based on?
explanation:
• Thyroid function tests and clinical manifestations are reviewed 4-6 weeks after starting treatment, and the dose is titrated based on unbound T4 levels.
  • Most patients do not achieve euthyroidism until 6-8 weeks after treatment is initiated.
  • TSH levels often remain suppressed for several months and therefore do not provide a sensitive index of treatment response.
  • When TSH suppression is alleviated, TSH levels can also be used to monitor therapy.
  • Though total T3 and T4 can also be used, free hormones would be the better option.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:2931

question_text:
You are asked to review a 58-year-old woman who presents with a slowly enlarging hard mass in the anterior neck. Thyroid ultrasound reveals infiltration of the mass to adjacent structures,and biopsy reveal dense fibrous change and no atypical cells. Free T4 is low and her TSH is markedly raised, consistent with hypothyroidism. Thyroid autoantibodies are negative.
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis given this clinical picture?
explanation:
• By the nature of its presentation, Riedel's thyroiditis is often confused with thyroid carcinoma especially the anaplastic variant.
  • It is characterised by marked fibrous infiltration of the thyroid gland, the aetiology of this being as yet unidentified.
  • Treatment is with thyroxine replacement.
  • Hashimoto's thyroiditis is autoimmune in aetiology and is characterised by lymphocytic infiltration and the presence of antimicrosomal antibodies(anti TPO). Grave's disease is associated with thyroid-stimulating autoantibodies and hyperthyroidism.
  • Thyroid ultrasound reveals infiltration but no discrete mass is identified, and biopsy reveal dense fibrous infiltration of the gland.
  • If the patient presents with severe compressive symptoms like dysphagia and dyspnea, then glucocorticoid therapy is useful.
  • Other immunomodulators like mycophenolate and tamoxifen have also been tried.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:2944

question_text:
A 44-year-old woman presents to the Emergency department with palpitations and shortness of breath. Recent thyroid function tests on the hospital computer reveal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) of <0.05 mU/l and a markedly elevated T4. You advise for blood gas testing.
Which of the following findings would be most consistent with Grave's disease?
explanation:
• Compared with normal subjects, hyperthyroid patients show significantly lower resting arterial CO2 tension, tidal volume and significantly higher mean inspiratory flow and pa(O2).
  • This may of course lead to misdiagnosis of patients with hyperthyroidism as having hyperventilation syndrome.
  • Patients with hyperthyroidism also show a greater ventilatory response to hypoxia than normal patients. These ventilatory changes are significantly correlated with T3 levels.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:2939

question_text:
A 42-year-old female complains of feeling tired all the time. The following laboratory results have been obtained: Cholesterol 324 mg/dl Low-density
lipoprotein (LDL) 212 mg/dl
Thyroid-stimulating
hormone (TSH) 92.5 mu/l
What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
• In hypothyroidism, serum low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol and, less frequently, serum triglycerides are raised.
  • Levels of high-density lipoprotein (HDL) tend to be increased. There is decreased receptor-mediated LDL catabolism, and lipoprotein lipase activity may be decreased.
  • Hypothyroidism should always be considered in the diagnosis of hyperlipidaemia, and it is particularly important to exclude it when marked hyperlipidaemia occurs in women and in diabetic patients.
  • Treatment with levothyroxine most often normalises lipid profile avoiding the need of lipid lowering drugs.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:2935

question_text:
A 26-year-old woman is referred by her family doctor. She is 10 week's pregnant and complaining of anxiety and an inability to sleep. Total thyroxine (T4) is noted to be 160 nmol/l (normal 70-140)
Free T4 is noted to be 27 pmol/l (normal 9-25) thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) 0.4 mU/l.
Which of the following is the management of choice in this patient?
option_c: Observe and repeat thyroid function tests in 1 month
option_d: Start high dose carbimazole and thyroxine concomitantly
explanation:
• Suppression of TSH is seen in the first trimester in around 10% women, small but transient rises in T3 and T4 are also seen, this is physiological and due to the thyroid-stimulating action of b-human chorionic gonadotrophin (b-HCG).
  • Total T4 rises due to increases in thyroid-binding globulin and again is physiological.
  • A 10-20% increase in thyroid mass also occurs. Physiological suppression of TSH is also seen in 4-5% of women in the second trimester.
  • Maternal hyperthyroidism has an incidence of 0.2%, in women who are in remission from Grave's disease, exacerbation occurs most commonly in the first trimester.

question_text: A 62-year-old, non-smoking woman with no previous cardiac history presents for cardiac risk-factor evaluation. Her total cholesterol is 350 mg/dl. She is overweight and has sleep apnoea. On examination you notice her skin is particularly dry and there appears to be some evidence of hair loss. What is the next step in her management?

explanation:

  • Frank hypothyroidism is said to occur in 4% of patients with dyslipidaemias, and a further 10% of patients with dyslipidaemia have a raised TSH level, but with a free T4 still within the normal range.
  • Total cholesterol often improves with thyroxine therapy, but statins may be required in addition.

question_text: Wolff–Chaikoff effect is due to?
explanation: Ans. D. Iodine intake Iodine is the fastest acting thyroid inhibitor. The most important action is inhibition of hormone release (thyroid constipation), but all facets of thyroid synthesis may be affected. Excess iodide inhibits its own transport in thyroid cells and may alter the redox potential of cells, thus interfering iodination reduced T3/T4 synthesis (Wolff–Chaikoff effect).

question_text: Which of the following statements about TPP (thyrotoxic periodic paralysis) is true?
option_a: It is caused by missense mutations of voltage sensor domains within the α1 subunit of L- type potassium channels
option_b: B TPP develops more frequently in patients of Asian or Hispanic origin
option_c: TPP typically present with weakness of the respiratory muscles with paralytic episodes that occur most frequently between 1 and 6 p.m
option_d: Hypokalemia is usually accompanied by hyperphosphatemia and hypermagnesemia
explanation:
Redistributive hypokalemia can also occur in the setting of hyperthyroidism, with periodic attacks of hypokalemic paralysis (thyrotoxic periodic paralysis [TPP]).

Similar episodes of hypokalemic weakness in the absence of thyroid abnormalities occur in familial hypokalemic periodic paralysis, usually caused by missense mutations of voltage sensor domains within the α1 subunit of L-type calcium channels or the skeletal Na+ channel; these mutations generate an abnormal gating pore current activated by hyperpolarization.

Thyrotoxic Periodic Paralysis

  • Develops more frequently in patients of Asian or Hispanic origin
  • linked to genetic variation in6, a muscle-specific, thyroid hormone-responsive K+ channel.
  • Patients typically present with weakness of the extremities and limb girdles, with paralytic episodes that occur most frequently between 1 and 6 a.m.
  • Signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism are not invariably present.
  • Hypokalemia is usually profound and almost invariably accompanied by hypophosphatemia and hypomagnesemia.
  • The hypokalemia in TPP is also attributed to both direct and indirect activation of the Na+/K+-ATPase, resulting in increased uptake of K+ by muscle and other tissues.
  • Increases in β-adrenergic activity play an important role in that high-dose propranolol (3 mg/kg) rapidly reverses the associated hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, and paralysis.

References: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 348
