question_text: Which of the following blood glucose readings is diagnostic of gestational diabetes according to IADPSG criteria?
explanation:
• The screening for Diabetes mellitus should be performed in women at the first prenatal visit
  • First trimester screening is performed for high risk women according to ADA while ACOG advocates universal screening for all women
  • The diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes mellitus is made if either one of the following is satisfied:
    • Fasting blood glucose > 92 mg/dl
    • 1 hr post OGTT > 180 mg/dl
    • 2 hr post OGTT > 153 mg/dl
  • If fasting blood glucose is more than 126 mg/dl or 2-hour post glucose load value is > 200 mg/dl, the diagnosis of overt diabetes mellitus is made

Reference: ADA Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes 2023

question_text: Which of the following is part of diagnostic criteria for Diabetes mellitus?
option_a: FBS more than 100 mg/dl with osmotic symptoms
option_b: FBS more than 140 mg/dl without osmotic symptoms
option_c: PPBS more than 140 mg/dl without osmotic symptoms
option_d: RBS more than 200 mg/dl with osmotic symptoms
explanation:
• WHO criteria for the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus:
    • Fasting Blood glucose > 126 mg/dl
    • Post-prandial Blood glucose > 200 mg/dl
    • Random blood glucose > 200 mg/dl with symptoms
    • HBA1C > 6.5

If any of the above is satisfied, then the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus is made.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 3095

question_text: A 38-year-old woman has been prescribed a sulphonylurea for type-2 maturity-onset  diabetes mellitus. She complains of severe facial flushing and sweating when she drinks alcohol.  Which of the following is most probably responsible for this reaction?
explanation:
• Of the sulphonylureas, chlorpropamide is the main one associated with facial flushing following alcohol intake, although a lesser reaction may be seen with other SUs.
  • This disulfiram-like reaction is also seen in those who are on treatment with metronidazole.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:3110

question_text: A 42-year-old man is suffering from type-2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Which of the following antihypertensive drugs is most likely to cause hyperglycaemia if  prescribed for this patient?
explanation:
• Thiazide diuretics are associated with impaired glucose tolerance.
  • They are usually not recommended for the treatment of hypertension in patients with diabetes mellitus.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:3095

question_text: The dual GLP-1 and GIP agonist used in the management of Diabetes mellitus is:
explanation:
• Tirzepatide is the dual GLP1 and GIP agonist (SURPASS clinical trial)
  • Teduglutide is the GLP2 inhibitor used in short bowel syndrome
  • Imeglimin is the oxidative phosphorylation inhibitor used in Diabetes
  • Dorzagliatin is the glucokinase activator for the management of DM

Reference: SURPASS Trial - NEJM 2021

question_text: In glucagonoma the MOST likely associated skin lesion is?
explanation:
• Glucagonoma syndrome (diabetes mellitus, weight loss and anaemia) is associated with a characteristic skin rash (necrolytic migratory erythema) in 75% of cases.
  • The lesion starts as an indurated erythema at the perineum, face and nose.
  • Within a few days blisters will cover the surface of the skin which then crust and heal leaving hyperpigmented skin.
  • This process takes 7-14 days with lesions developing in one area while others are resolving.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20th edition Pg:597,599,609,2749

question_text: What is the standard amount of glucose used for testing when diagnosing diabetes mellitus?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In adults, the standard OGTT for diagnosing diabetes mellitus uses 75 grams of anhydrous glucose dissolved in water, administered orally after an overnight fast.
  • Blood glucose levels are measured fasting and 2 hours after ingestion to assess glucose tolerance.
  • In pregnancy, Gestational DM is screened with a 50 g glucose challenge test and diagnosed with a 100 g OGTT.

question_text: A 45-year man with hypertension has currently developed diabetes mellitus. Lipid profile shows low HDL with high TG and high LDL. Which drug would be recommended?
explanation:
Elevated LDL cholesterol with or without Triglycerides in patients with ASCVD risk, statins are the drug of choice.

Among the given options, Rosuvastatin 10mg is the correct option. The dose of Atorvastatin is 20-40 mg/day to begin with.

question_text: Renal papillary necrosis is almost always associated with one of the following conditions: March 2004
explanation: Ans. A i.e. Diabetes mellitus `Renal papillary necrosis, an accompaniment of acute pyelonephritis is most often seen in diabetics and is characterised by necrosis of renal papillae of one or both kidneys with sharped demarcation between necrotic and living tissue' — Dorlands Thus while papillary necrosis is a feature of more than one conditions mentioned in the question, it is most commonly seen with diabetes mellitus.

question_text: A 57-year-old man, newly diagnosed with type-2 diabetes mellitus, presents to the clinic for his first assessment. He is found to have changes in his eyes on fundoscopy. Which of the following is most likely to need immediate referral to the ophthalmologist?
option_a: A few dot and blot haemorrhages
option_b: Some hard exudates > 1 disc diameter from the fovea
explanation:
• Background diabetic retinopathy consists of dot and blot haemorrhages and hard exudates. Patients do not need to be referred to the ophthalmologist unless these are within 1 disc diameter of the fovea.
  • This can be monitored annually at the routine clinic.
  • Cataracts appear about 10 years earlier in type-2 diabetes than in non-diabetic patients.
  • If the vision is significantly affected the patients warrant routine and not urgent referral to the ophthalmologist.
  • Soft exudates suggest retinal ischaemia, which would require routine referral to the ophthalmologist.
  • New vessels anywhere in the fundus are a feature of proliferative retinopathy and, as new vessels have a risk of haemorrhage and can threaten sight, they should be referred urgently to the ophthalmologist.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 20th edition Ch:398 Pg:2877

question_text: A 25-year-old woman with type-1 diabetes mellitus came for her routine review and says she is keen on becoming pregnant. Which of the following is the factor most likely to make you ask her to defer pregnancy at this stage?
option_c: She hasn't been taking folic acid
option_d: Microalbumin level of 6-mg excretion in 24 hours
explanation:
• Pregnancy in type-1 diabetes is still associated with a two- to threefold increase in congenital abnormalities when compared with the background population.
  • It is also associated with higher neonatal morbidity and mortality and higher operative delivery rates.
  • Prepregnancy counselling with the aim of bringing the Hb A1c to near-normal levels are associated with better pregnancy outcomes.
  • Diabetic retinopathy can progress during pregnancy and the eyes must be checked at least once each trimester; if there is progression that is sight-threatening then the patient should be referred to an ophthalmologist. Background retinopathy would not be a contraindication to pregnancy.
  • The microalbumin level is within normal limits.
  • Nephropathy can also progress during pregnancy, but microalbuminuria would not be a contraindication to pregnancy and nor would sensory neuropathy.
  • It is important that patients with diabetes take 5 mg folic acid daily prepregnancy (this reduces neural tube defects) and this can be started when the patient starts trying to conceive, although it should ideally be taken for 3 months before hand.
  • The most important thing this woman can do is to improve her glycaemic control before trying to conceive.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 3096

question_text: A 64-year-old man presents to the diabetes clinic for review. He  complains of difficulty in maintaining penile erection despite having normal libido. Which of the following is true regarding his condition?
option_a: Diabetes mellitus is less likely to cause these conditions
option_b: Penile pain is a common association
option_c: Autonomic neuropathy is unlikely to be present
option_d: β-blockers and thiazide diuretics may exacerbate the problem
explanation:
• Libido is rarely affected, which makes the condition all the more frustrating for affected men. Between 30 and 50% of men with diabetes of more than 6 years' duration are affected.
  • There is an association with other autonomic neuropathies such as postural hypotension and gastroparesis.
  • The condition is not usually associated with pain, and may be exacerbated by both β-blockers and thiazide diuretics. PDE-5 inhibitors are available as oral therapies for impotence, but these are often required at high dose.
  • Alprostadil and vacuum devices are alternative methods. Estimates put successful treatment at only around 70%.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 3058

question_text: A 40 year old man with type 1 diabetes attends a follow up appointment in the diabetic clinic. He has a blood pressure of 145/86 mmHg. There is no evidence of diabetic retinopathy or neuropathy. He has an elevated albumin: creatinine ratio in his urine. Creatinine is 1.01 mg/dl. Which of the following should be done?
option_b: Commence on an Angiotensin Receptor Blocker
explanation:
The patient has a raised albumin: creatinine ratio in the urine.

Early morning Albumin: Creatinine ratio is a substitute to 24 hour protein estimation in urine. AC ratio in grams is roughly equivalent to proteinuria in grams. 

The given patient is a Type I diabetic. It has not been mentioned if his blood sugars are controlled or not. His BP is 145/86mmHg, which is above the target recommended for diabetics by JNC8 guidelines(Goal is <140/90 mm Hg). Also he  has high AC ratio, indicative of proteinuria.

Presence of proteinuria indicates that the patient will develop decline in GFR. So our aim is to retard the progression of the disease. In Type I diabetes, strict control of blood sugars has shown to prevent the development or retard progression of proteinuria. Such a control has not been shown with Type II diabetes. Also when significant proteinuria has set in, there is no role for strict glycemic control.

In our patient it has not been mentioned about his glycemic status. But his blood pressure is not controlled.

ACEI or ARBS and SGLT 2 inhibitors are drugs that retard the progression of nephropathy. Here adding ACEI or ARB will have the additional advantage of lowering his BP as well.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Ch:314, Pg:2344

question_text:
A 50-year-old male with an 8 year history of type 2 diabetes is being treated with Metformin 1g bd and gliclazide 80 mg daily. He is obese, has gained weight over the last year and his HbA1c has deteriorated from 7.5 to 7.9%. His physician wishes to stop the gliclazide and treat him with Pioglitazone
Which of the following would be regarded as a typical side effect of Pioglitazone therapy?
explanation:
Pioglitazone like other PPAR gamma agonists such as rosiglitazone may cause fluid retention (about 10%) and this can be minimized by avoiding agents that may exacerbate fluid retention such as calcium antagonists.

Due to this effect, it is contraindicated in patients with advanced heart failure and also in severe diabetic retinopathy where it may precipitate macular edema.

Other notable side effects include reduction of bone density, reduction of haematocrit due to hemodilution and a doubtful increase in risk of bladder cancer.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1936

question_text:
A 50-year-old male with diabetes mellitus presents with shortness of breath, esecially on exertion and while lying flat.Investigations show:
1. Ejection fraction (EF): 40%
2. Fasting glucose: 135 mg/dL
3. HbA1c: 7.8%
4. BP: 164/93 mmHg
5. Hb: 13 g/dL
Which of the following anti-diabetic medications is most appropriate for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

This patient has type 2 diabetes mellitus with an elevated HbA1c and fasting glucose, and evidence of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), given his dyspnea, orthopnea, and EF = 40%.

  • Dapagliflozin, an SGLT-2 inhibitor, is the best option for this patient because it is not only effective in managing diabetes but also has proven cardioprotective effects, especially in patients with heart failure.
  • It works by inhibiting the Sodium-Glucose Co-Transporter 2 (SGLT-2) in the kidneys, which reduces the reabsorption of glucose, leading to increased urinary glucose excretion and lowering of blood glucose levels.
  • Additionally, dapagliflozin offers cardiovascular benefits.

Explanation of Other Options:

Liraglutide (Option B):

  • Mechanism: Mimics incretin (GLP-1), enhancing insulin secretion and inhibiting glucagon release.
  • Benefits: Weight loss, cardiovascular benefit in atherosclerotic heart disease (ASCVD).
  • Limitation: No direct benefit in heart failure; may cause mild tachycardia.
  • Use: Best suited for diabetic patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, not those with HFrEF.
  • Adverse Effects: Nausea, vomiting, pancreatitis risk.

Glimepiride (Option C):

  • Mechanism: Stimulates insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells (independent of glucose levels).
  • Drawbacks:
    • No cardiovascular or renal benefit.
    • Can cause hypoglycemia and weight gain, both undesirable in HF.
    • May increase risk of mortality in patients with advanced cardiac disease.
  • Clinical Note: Should be avoided in patients with heart failure or elderly diabetics.

Pramlintide (Option D):

  • Mechanism: Slows gastric emptying, suppresses postprandial glucagon, and promotes satiety.
  • Indication: Adjunct to insulin therapy in type 1 or type 2 diabetes.
  • Limitations:
    • No evidence of cardiovascular or renal benefit.
    • Requires multiple daily injections.
    • Risk of hypoglycemia when combined with insulin.
  • Not indicated in heart failure or as first-line therapy in type 2 diabetes.

question_text: A 70 year female who is a known case of type2 diabetes mellitus was admitted with complaints of excessive thirst and frequent urination. Laboratory investigations showed blood sugar was 700 mg/dl and serum sodium of 115 meq. Insulin infusion was started. Which of the following events will occur after insulin administration?
explanation:
In hyperosmolar coma noted with diabetes mellitus, serum sodium concentration is often decreased due to the osmotic flux of water from the intracellular to extracellular space in the presence of hyperglycemia.

Therefore, sodium and blood sugar follow inverse relation in DM.

Diagnostic criteria for HHS

  • Profound dehydration
  • Neuronal symptoms
  • Plasma sugar level>600 mg/dl
  • Normal anion gap <14mEq/L
  • Arterial pH >7.3
  • Plasma bicarbonate levels >15 mmol/L
  • Absence of ketones

Reference: Harrison 20th chap. 387 pg. 2872

question_text:
A 72 year old woman with a history of hypertension and insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus presented with new onset of uncontrolled violent movements of the left extremities accompanied by headaches. Neurological examination was normal except for the constant, relentless, violent movement of her left arm and leg. Although she was fully awake, alert, and oriented, she could not stop the abnormal movements except for a short period of time.
This presentation is likely to be due to a lesion in the:
explanation:
Hemiballismus is a rare disorder characterised by involuntary wild flinging movements of the limbs. It is usually unilateral (hence hemiballismus) and is caused by lesions in the contralateral subthalamic nucleus.



Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 436, Pg: 3406

question_text: A 74-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and multiple transient ischaemic attacks (TIAs) comes to the hospital complaining of visual field loss. He says this happened suddenly and he woke up with problems with his vision the morning before coming to the Emergency department. Medications include clopidogrel, ramipril, atorvastatin, and metformin. On examination his BP is 165/100 mmHg, his pulse is 76 and regular. Visual field examination reveals a right homonymous upper quadrantanopia. Where is the most likely site for the underlying lesion?
explanation:
Lesions beyond the optic chiasma produces homonymous hemianopia. Hence optic chiasm and optic nerve are ruled out. Optic chiasmal lesions cause bitemporal hemianopia and optic nerve lesions cause complete blindness in the affected eye.

Involvement of the optic radiation that loop inferiorly into the temporal lobe, called the Meyer’s loop, cause superior quadrantanopia which will be homonymous.

Lesions of the occipital cortex causes homonymous hemianopia.

Optic radiation that loops superiorly into the parietal lobe causes inferior qudrantanopia.

Hence among the given options the one that unequivocally causes a quadantanopia superiorly on the right side is a temporal lobe lesion on the left side

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st h edition Chapter:32, page number:219

question_text: In a patient with type 1 diabetes with 3rd stage of beta cell damage, which of the following situations is associated with the same?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Stage 2 of type 1 diabetes is defined by the presence of islet autoimmunity along with dysglycemia but without overt symptoms.

  • Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) is an autoimmune disease characterized by T-cell-mediated destruction of pancreatic β-cells, leading to absolute insulin deficiency.
  • It progresses through three defined stages before becoming symptomatic.

Stages of T1DM Development:

  • Stage 1:
    • Positive for ≥2 islet autoantibodies (e.g., GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8, ICA)
    • Normoglycemia on glucose testing (Option A ruled out)
    • Clinically asymptomatic
  • Stage 2:
    • Positive islet autoantibodies (same as stage 1)
    • Dysglycemia (abnormal glucose tolerance, elevated fasting glucose or postprandial glucose)
    • Still asymptomatic
  • Stage 3:
    • Islet autoantibody positive
    • Hyperglycemia exceeding diagnostic threshold for diabetes
    • Clinically symptomatic (e.g., polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, possible DKA)
  • The patient is autoantibody positive and has dysglycemia but no overt symptoms yet, making this Stage 2 of T1DM.
  • This staging allows for early identification of individuals at risk for T1DM, which is especially important for clinical trials and preventive strategies.

Explanation of other options:

Autoimmune negative with normoglycemia (Option C): This individual does not have autoimmune T1DM and shows no biochemical evidence of dysglycemia-unlikely to progress.

Autoimmune negative with dysglycemia (Option D): May suggest Type 2 diabetes or another form of non-autoimmune dysglycemia, not T1DM.

question_text: A patient with type 2 diabetes experiences hypoglycemia and falls, resulting in incoherent speech. A CT scan reveals a large subdural hematoma >30 cc. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
option_d: Stabilize the patient and urgently seek a neurosurgical consultation
explanation:
Explanation:

  • This case represents an acute subdural hematoma (SDH) with significant volume (>30 cc) requiring urgent surgical management.
  • On CT, acute SDH appears hyperdense (white), and large hematomas pose a high risk of brain compression and herniation.
  • Emergency craniotomy is the definitive treatment, allowing prompt evacuation of the hematoma to prevent further neurological deterioration and potentially fatal complications.

Fig: CT brain showing subdural hematoma, seen as hyperdense clot that has an irregular border with the brain with mass effect

Acute SDH vs Chronic SDH:

Explanation of other options:

Administer Mannitol (Option A): Mannitol is used to manage elevated intracranial pressure, but it is not the definitive treatment for a large subdural hematoma. While mannitol can temporarily reduce intracranial pressure, it does not address the underlying compression from the hematoma, which requires surgical evacuation.

Administer Aspirin and Clopidogrel (Option B): Antiplatelets and anticoagulants like aspirin and clopidogrel are contraindicated in acute SDH, as these antiplatelet agents could worsen the bleeding.

Stabilize the patient and urgently seek a neurosurgical consultation (Option D): While important, delays the definitive treatment needed in this case. Given the large volume of the hematoma and altered mental status, immediate surgical intervention through craniotomy is required rather than waiting for further consultation.

question_text:
A 43 year old man is being investigated for a 3 year history of arthralgia. On examination, his skin color was normal and there was no evidence of jaundice or hepatomegaly. He has the following results:
Alanine aminotransferase 35 U/L
Aspartate aminotransferase 40 U/L
Fasting plasma glucose 126 mg/dl
Ferritin 500 ug/L, (15-300)
Which one of the following is an appropriate investigation?
explanation:
In hemochromatosis, the serum Fe is elevated (> 300 mg/dL). The serum transferrin saturation is a sensitive parameter of increased Fe and merits evaluation when > 50%. The serum ferritin is increased. Urinary Fe excretion is markedly increased (> 2 mg/24 h) by the chelating drug deferoxamine (500 to 1000 mg IM based on the size of the patient), and this has been used as a diagnostic test.

In addition, when the Fe content in the liver is significantly increased, an MRI may reflect this change.

Liver biopsy had been the gold standard in diagnosis; it now serves only to provide evidence of fibrosis (cirrhosis). It is considered only when genetic testing is negative along with ferritin >1000 μg/L or abnormal LFT

Gene assay (Homozygosity C282Y mutations) is also an excellent diagnostic test.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 414, Pg: 3232-3234

question_text: A 70-year-old male with a 5-year history of type II diabetes mellitus presents for annual review with a blood pressure of 188/88 mmHg. Clinical examination was normal. An ECG reveals evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy. Which one of the following drugs is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's hypertension?
explanation:
This elderly male diabetic has isolated systolic hypertension associated with left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH being defined as a complication of hypertension).

Evidence would support the use of a calcium channel blocker and/or ACE inhibitor as first line.

In a diabetic patient with evidence of nephropathy or any patient with LVH there is compelling evidence to suggest that ACE inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor blockers should be first line treatment for hypertension.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:271 pg:1901,1902

question_text:
A 24 year old woman has type 1 diabetes. She has weight loss over the past 3 months, and irregular menstrual cycles. Her bowel habit has been unchanged. On examination her BMI was 24 kg/m2.
Investigations show:
haemoglobin of 8.1 g/dl
with a MCV of 69 fl.
Which is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient has type 1 diabetes – an autoimmune condition.

She now presents with iron deficiency anemia along with weight loss. So the possibility of celiac disease should be ruled out as people with type 1 diabetes are at up to six times greater risk of having celiac disease.

Dietary deficiency of iron and heavy menstrual loss will not cause weight loss there is no abdominal pain or blood in stools to suggest a Chron's Disease.

Antibodies to gliadin should be sent and the diagnosis of celiac disease can be confirmed by a biopsy of small intestine which will show villous atrophy.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 325, Pg: 2463

question_text: A 65 year old woman has a diagnosis of insulin dependent diabetes mellitus (poorly controlled) for 25 years. She complains of repeated episodes of abdominal pain following meals. These episodes have become more frequent over the past 3 months. There is no abdominal tenderness on palpation. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Abdominal angina is postprandial pain that occurs in mesenteric vascular occlusive disease when blood flow to the colon is unable to meet visceral demands. Atherosclerotic disease is the most common cause of abdominal angina. It frequently involves ostia of the mesenteric vessels. In most people, it is occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery that is responsible for the abdominal symptoms.

Diabetes, especially Type 2 diabetes, is associated with macrovascular disease.

Differential Diagnosis

  • Chronic pancreatitis
  • Intra abdominal malignancy
  • Chronic cholecystitis
  • Peptic ulcer disease

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed Ch:329 Pg: 2507

question_text: In which of the following situations urinary Na+ level is more than 20 mM?
explanation:
Non renal causes of hypovolemic hyponatremia include GI loss (e.g., vomiting, diarrhoea, tube drainage) and insensible loss (sweating, burns) of Na+-Cl- and water, in the absence of adequate oral replacement; urine Na+ concentration is typically < 20.

In renal causes like Diuretic use, salt wasting syndromes and ketonuria sodium is retained in the urine due to poor reabsorption and osmotic drag, hence UNa is > 20

Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 342

question_text: Which of the following is seen in a patient with Right ventricular myocardial infarction?
option_a: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF
option_b: Occlusion of the left circumflex artery
explanation:
• Right ventricular myocardial infarction (RVMI) usually occurs in association with an inferior-wall left ventricular infarction, as revealed by the ECG.
  • In ECG, along with ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF which suggests an inferior wall MI, a patient with RVMI may also have ST elevation in V1 and in right sided chest leads V3R-V6R.
  • The typical clinical findings in RVMI include bradycardia (due to AV node involvement), hypotension, raised JVP with positive Kussmaul sign (inspiratory rise of JVP).
  • Hypotension is typically treated with IV fluids (0.9% saline)
  • There is usually a right coronary occlusion. Characteristic clinical features include a low cardiac output syndrome with jugular venous distension but no pulmonary vascular congestion.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page no: 2062

question_text: A 53 year old man has type 2 diabetes. He complains of difficulty walking. On examination, he is unable to evert his right foot. He has intact knee reflexes. There is also sensory loss in the lateral aspect of the foot to pin prick. Which nerve root is involved?
explanation:
• The common peroneal nerve is involved. Nerve roots L5 and S1 supply the nerve for foot eversion. L5 supplies the lateral border of the foot except the little toe which is supplied by S1
  • Intact knee reflex indicates normal L3 and L4
  • L1 & L2 are required for hip flexion

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine , 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

question_text: Which of the following is not a treatment goal of Type 2 DM according to ADA?
explanation:
The glycemic targets set by American Diabetic Association are:

  • Pre-prandial plasma glucose between 80 - 130 mg/dl
  • Peak post-prandial plasma glucose less than 180 mg/dl
  • HBA1C < 7%

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 3104

question_text: A 30 year old man has a blood pressure of 200/90. His serum potassium is 2.8 mmol/l, creatinine is 0.9 mg/dl. Urine dipstick shows protein trace. Which of the following diagnoses is likely?
explanation:
This patient is having hypertension with hypokalemia. The answer is Conn's syndrome. Another associated finding would be metabolic alkalosis.

Other conditions that can present with the same findings will be Liddle Syndrome, Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess, Cushing syndrome, renal artery stenosis and renin secreting tumors. They can be distinguished by the Renin and aldosterone levels.

Option B: Pheochromocytoma presents with episodic headache, sweating and palpitations. Hypokalemia is not an associated feature

Option C: Diabetic nephropathy will cause a rise in serum creatinine and hyperkalemia. Proteinuria is a cardinal feature.

Option D: Hypertensive nephropathy will cause a rise of serum creatinine with hyperkalemia.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 53, Pg: 354.

question_text: A 77-year-old male presented with a quadrantic hemianopia. Which of the following conditions is most likely to cause such a presentation?
option_b: A lesion of the optic chiasma
explanation:
Superior quadrantanopia is seen in temporal lobe lesion . inferior quadrantanopia is seen in parietal lobe lesion.

  • Unilateral occipital lobe lesions (left or right) cause contralateral hemianopia or quadrantanopia, visual agnosia, visual illusions and elementary visual hallucinations.
  • Left occipital lobe lesions cause these symptoms and alexia and colour agnosia.
  • Right occipital lobe lesions cause impaired visual orientation and topographical memory in addition.
  • Bioccipital lesions are rare, but cause cortical blindness, altitudinal hemianopia, impaired colour perception, Anton syndrome and prosopagnosia.
  • A lesion of the optic chiasm would cause a Bitemporal hemianopia.
  • Diabetic retinopathy can rarely cause an 'apparent quadrantic hemianopia' because the distribution of the retinal changes may just correspond to quadrantic hemianopia - but this is not the most likely.
  • Tobacco amblyopia causes symmetric central or centrocecal scotomas.
  • Chloroquine poisoning causes symmetric bilateral scotomas.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 219

question_text: A 56-year-old woman presents to the diabetes clinic for review. She has suffered from diabetes mellitus for many years and has now progressed from sulphonylurea treatment to insulin therapy. A past history of gallstones is noted and she failed to tolerate metformin due to chronic diarrhea. She has been slowly losing weight over the past few months and has mild anemia. Ultrasound scan of her liver reveals a suggestion of a number of small metastases within the liver. When considering that this woman has a primary pancreatic tumor, which of the following statements best fits the condition?
option_a: Somatostatin, ACTH and calcitonin may all be raised
option_b: Contrast spiral-CT scanning is effective in demonstrating the primary tumor in 90% of cases
option_c: Curative surgery is possible in the majority of cases
option_d: There is almost always an association with MEN-1
explanation:
• The history is suggestive of a somatostatinoma, the annual incidence of which is estimated at 1 in 40 million.
  • There is a 95% association with impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) or diabetes mellitus, 68% with gallstones, weight loss (25%) and anemia (14%)
  • There is also an association with diarrhea.
  • The tumors are often multi secretory and ACTH and calcitonin levels may be raised in addition to that of somatostatin. There is an association with MEN-1 in some (7%). Many tumors may occur undetected, and not causing the somatostatinoma syndrome.
  • Contrast spiral-CT scanning is effective in detecting the primary tumor in only 50% of cases; DOTATATE PET scan or endoscopic ultrasound scanning may often be required.
  • Although surgical cure is rarely possible due to the presence of metastases, hepatic embolisation may be helpful for symptom control.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20th edition Page number:264, 597, 599, 601, 609

question_text: What is the most reliable method to confirm that a central line is correctly placed in the jugular vein?
explanation:
Explanation:

Role of Chest X-ray in Central Line Placement

  • Initial Assessment: A chest X-ray should be obtained immediately after placing a central line in the internal jugular or subclavian vein to confirm proper catheter position and to exclude complications such as iatrogenic pneumothorax.
  • Post-Procedure Verification: It is essential to verify the catheter's placement and ensure there are no complications like pneumothorax following the procedure.
  • Ipsilateral Side Approach: If insertion into the internal jugular vein fails, the next step is to attempt placement in the ipsilateral subclavian vein. Before attempting catheterization on the opposite side, a chest X-ray or ultrasound must be performed to avoid the risk of bilateral pneumothoraces.

Options B, C, and D are incorrect.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470286/

question_text:
You see a 16-year-old girl with Type 1 diabetes. She is currently managed with 18U of 30/70 mixed insulin BD. Her parents tell you that she does not eat properly, and they occasionally hear her dreaming in the night and go in to find her suffering a hypoglycaemic attack.
Investigations;
Hb 13.9 g/dl
WBC 5.4 x 10^9/L
PLT 234 x 10^9/L
Na+ 140 mmol/l
K+ 5.0 mmol/l
Creatinine 1.0 mg/dl
HbA1c 9.4%
You decide to make a change to an insulin glargine/ aspart insulin basal bolus regime.Which of the following best represents the main advantage of insulin glargine?
option_d: Increased ability to undertake exercise more easily
explanation:
• Insulin glargine is an insulin analogue produced by substitution of glycine for Asparagines at A21 and by adding two arginines to the B chain.
  • It is formulated at pH 4, but, when injected, the transformation to pH 7 causes the insulin crystals to precipitate leading to a slowly released, "peak less" profile.
  • The main advantage of insulin glargine is in reduction of nocturnal hypoglycaemia.
  • Short acting analogues are useful in reducing post-prandial hypoglycaemia, as their profile is more in keeping with physiological insulin release.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:3108

question_text: A 58-year-old man with type-2 diabetes presents with background diabetic retinopathy. His HB A1c has been consistently above 9% for the past 5 years. Which of the following factors may impact most negatively on the prognosis for his retinopathy?
option_a: Rapid improvement in blood glucose levels
explanation:
• Rapid improvement in blood glucose levels may be associated with worsening of diabetic eye disease.
  • Both the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) in type-1 diabetes and the UKPDS (United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study) in type-2 diabetes have demonstrated the long-term benefits of reducing blood sugar levels in controlling future microvascular complications.
  • All diabetic patients should be offered yearly eye screening, preferably with a digital retinal camera.
  • Rapidly deteriorating visual acuity, hard exudates encroaching on the macula, preproliferative changes or new-vessel formation are all reasons for early referral to an ophthalmologist.
  • Diabetic retinopathy has been known for many years to be the leading cause of blindness in people of working age.
  • Smoking has no effect on the prognosis of retinopathy.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20th edition Ch:398 Pg:2877

question_text: A 56-year-old woman, diagnosed with type-2 diabetes mellitus and losing weight, is referred for an opinion; her doctor is thinking about insulin therapy. A normochromic, normocytic anemia is noted. On examination she has angular stomatitis and a well-demarcated erythematous rash in her groin, which extends to her lower limbs, buttocks and perineum. What is the next step in her management?
option_c: Observe and see again in 6 months
explanation:
• There is a suggestion that this patient has a glucagonoma, 90% of which are associated with the characteristic skin rash - necrolytic migratory erythema.
  • The annual incidence of glucagonoma is estimated at 1 in 20 million.
  • Over 70% of glucagonomas are malignant, but, because of their indolent presentation, the diagnosis is often overlooked for many years.
  • Due to insulin antagonism over 90% are associated with impaired glucose tolerance, and eventually weight loss due to protein catabolism.
  • Surgical cure rate is as low as 5%, due to metastases many years prior to presentation.
  • Octreotide improves the skin rash but may have a detrimental effect on glucose control; combination chemotherapy with streptazocin and 5-fluoruracil (5-FU) gives good palliative results, as does hepatic embolisation.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:384,665

question_text: A 56-year-old man came to the clinic following a myocardial infarction one year previously. During his admission he was found to be hypertensive and diabetic. He complains that he has put on 5kg in weight in the past 6 months. Which of his medications may be contributing to his weight gain?
explanation:
Sulfonylureas

Sulfonylureas are oral hypoglycaemic drugs used in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus. They work by increasing pancreatic insulin secretion and hence are only effective if functional B-cells are present.

Common adverse effects

  • Hypoglycaemic episodes (more common with long-acting preparations such as chlorpropamide)
  • Weight gain

Rarer adverse effects

  • Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion
  • Bone marrow suppression
  • Liver damage (cholestatic)
  • Photosensitivity
  • Peripheral neuropathy

Sulfonylureas should be avoided in breast feeding and pregnancy

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:3110-3112

question_text: A 48-year-old man presents for review at the type-2 diabetes clinic. He is on maximal metformin and his Hb A1c is still 7.8%. You decided to add the drug pioglitazone. Which of the following best describes the mode of action of the drug?
option_a: They act at the PPAR-g receptor site, promoting binding as a heterodimer with the retinoid X-receptor to DNA
option_c: They act by reducing peripheral insulin sensitivity
explanation:
• Pioglitazone is a PPAR-g agonist that act by binding to the PPAR-gamma receptor, which binds to a promoter region of DNA in tandem with the retinoid X-receptor.
  • This then leads to the upregulation of a number of enzymes concerned with lipid metabolism, bringing about a fall in free fatty acids.
  • The fall in free fatty acids promotes a reduction in hepatic insulin resistance, a rise in adiponectin and improved peripheral insulin sensitivity.
  • Imeglimin is an oxidative phosphorylation inhibitor while Dorzagliatin inhibits the hepatic and pancreatic isoforms of glucokinase enzyme.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 3112

question_text: Which of the following is a pharmacological action of metformin?
explanation:
• Metformin decreases hepatic gluconeogenesis there by reducing insulin levels and also increases insulin sensitivity by enhancing glucose uptake into muscle
  • The actions of Metformin is mediated via activation of AMP kinase enzyme
  • Decreased insulin levels lead to reduction in insulin mediated androgen production from the ovary thereby improving signs and symptoms of polycystic ovarian disease

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 3110

question_text: The risk of which of the following is increased by Empagliflozin?
explanation:
• Empagliflozin belongs the class of SGLT2 inhibitors
  • SGLT2 transporter is concerned with reabsorption of glucose from proximal tubules of kidneys
  • Inhibition of SGLT2 results in glucosuria and decrease in renal threshold for glucose excretion
  • An important side effect of these class of drugs is increased risk of Diabetic ketoacidosis which may occur at normal or slightly elevated blood glucose (Euglycemic DKA)
  • Recurrent genitourinary infections is also a feature
  • Other specific warnings issued by FDA regarding the use of individual drugs are:
    • Canagliflozin - lower limb amputation, upper extremity fractures, hyperkalemia
    • Dapagliflozin - Bladder cancer

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 3110-3111

question_text: The oral anti-hyperglycemic drug associated with osteoporosis is:
explanation:
• Pioglitazone belongs to thiazolidinediones group of OHAs
  • Acts as an agonist in PPAR gamma receptor thereby improving insulin sensitivity
  • Important adverse effects include:
    • Weight gain and fluid retention
    • Decrease in hematocrit (dilution effect)
    • Osteoporosis (increased risk of fractures - not preferred in post-menopausal females)
    • Risk of bladder cancer
  • Contraindicated in cardiac and hepatic failure

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 3110

question_text:
A 60-year-old type 2 diabetes patient who is fasting for religious rituals. He has background diabetic retinopathy, and currently takes metformin 500mg TDS as well as ramipril 10mg and aspirin 75mg.
Investigations
Hb 12.1 g/dl
WCC 5.0 x 10^9/L
PLT 212 x 10^9/L
Na+ 139 mmol/l
K+ 4.9 mmol/l
Creatinine 1.0 mg/dl
HbA1c 7.8% What advice would you give him regarding his medication while fasting?
option_b: Give short acting insulin for the evening meal
option_d: Give metformin 500mg in morning, 1000mg in evening
explanation:
• Metformin is not associated with hypoglycaemia when used as monotherapy.
  • It reduces hepatic glucose output and has its predominant effects on fasting plasma glucose.
  • Even so, it would seem sensible to divide the dose with the larger portion taken in the evening after the fast is broken.
  • Giving short acting insulin or switching to insulin is likely to increase the risk of hypoglycaemia.
  • Whilst diabetes patients are exempted from the need to fast, if this patient wishes to do so in this case it would seem unfair to prevent him fasting, as metformin should not preclude it altogether.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 20th edition Ch:397 Pg:2865-66,2868-69

question_text:
The adverse reaction of Metformin include:
1. B12 deficiency anemia
2. Lactic acidosis
3. Pedal edema
4. Flatulence and diarrhea
explanation:
• Pedal edema is a common side effect of Thiazolidinediones
  • Adverse reactions of Metformin include gastric upset, flatulence and diarrhea, B12 deficiency anemia and lactic acidosis
  • Metformin dose should be reduced in subjects with eGFR between 30-45 ml/min/1.73m2 and should not be used in those with eGFR of < 30 ml/min/1.73m2
  • Incidence of B12 deficiency anemia increases on use of Metformin doses above 1 gm for a duration of > 4 years

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 3110

question_text: Majority of patients with Type 2 Diabetes are obese. Which of the following medications would aid in weight loss for these patients?
explanation:
• The class of oral hypoglycemic drugs that aid in weight loss include GLP-1 analogues (Dulaglutide), SGLT-2 inhibitors (Empagliflozin) in addition to Metformin
  • DPP-4 inhibitors (Linagliptin, Sitagliptin) are weight neutral
  • Insulin and insulin secretagogues (sulfonyl ureas, meglitinide analogues) and thiazolidinediones (due to fluid retention) promote weight gain

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 3110

question_text: Which of the following is not an action of Liraglutide?
explanation:
• Liraglutide is a GLP-1 analogue administered as once-daily subcutaneous injection
  • The actions of Liraglutide include:
    • Increases glucose dependent insulin secretion
    • Promotes weight loss
    • Improves satiety
    • Mild reduction in blood pressure
    • Decreases cardiovascular mortality
    • Improves liver enzymes in NASH
  • Liraglutide has been approved for treatment of obesity for subjects aged > 12 years
  • Liraglutide is used at a dose of 3 mg for weight reduction while the dose range for diabetes treatment is 0.6-1.8 mg

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 3110-3112

question_text: Which of the following antidiabetic drugs can cause glucosuria?
explanation:
Explanation:

Empagliflozin which belongs to the class of SGLT-2 inhibitors causes glucosuria.

Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) Inhibitors

  • Acts by blocking the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 in the proximal convoluted tubules of the nephron.
  • This inhibits the reabsorption of glucose in the proximal convoluted tubule, promoting the excretion of sodium and glucose in urine
  • Commonly used SGLT-2 inhibitors
    • Canagliflozin
    • Dapagliflozin
    • Empagliflozin

Indications

  • Reduce progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD)
  • Diuretic effect, leading to sodium loss
  • Reduces systolic blood pressure (SBP) by 3-6 mmHg
  • Cardiorenal advantage
  • CHF to decrease mortality with or without DM

Side Effects

  • Increased risk of urinary tract infections (UTIs)
  • Glucosuria (leading to UTIs and vulvovaginal candidiasis)
  • Dehydration (orthostatic hypotension)
  • Weight loss

Contraindications

  • Not recommended if estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 45 ml/min
  • Use with caution in renal insufficiency (decreased efficacy with decreased GFR)

Explanation of other options:

Glimepiride (Option A): Glimepiride belongs to the sulfonylurea class of OHA. It works by stimulating insulin release from pancreatic beta cells, causing hypoglycemia and weight gain; does not cause glucosuria.

Exenatide (Option B): A GLP-1 receptor agonist that binds pancreatic beta-cell GLP-1 receptors, enhancing insulin secretion and suppressing glucagon. It also delays gastric emptying, promotes early satiety (weight loss), and stabilizes atherosclerotic plaques. It does not affect renal glucose reabsorption, so it does not cause glucosuria.

Acarbose (Option C): This alpha-glucosidase inhibitor works by controlling post-prandial glucose spikes through reduced carbohydrate absorption in the intestine. It may cause abdominal bloating and diarrhea but does not affect renal glucose handling or cause glucosuria.

question_text: A 50-year diabetic patient is on the following medication: Metformin 1g tds Gliclazide 80 mg bd Ramipril 5 mg daily Atenolol 50 mg. Her blood results show: urea 78 mg/dl creatinine 2.15 mg/dl sodium 138 mmol/ l potassium 4.0 mmol/l. Which of the following medications should be withdrawn?
explanation:
The drugs that should be avoided in renal failure are Metformin, Mepiridin, NSAIDs and OHAs that are eliminated by the kidneys.

Sulfonyl ureas should be avoided only in advanced renal failure. ACEI or ARBs are not contraindicated in CKD. If there is a >30 rise in creatinine within 2 weeks of initiation or increase in dose or if there is hyperkalemia, they should be stopped.

Beta blockers don’t need any dose modification.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 311, 404, Pg: 2320, 3111

question_text: A 72-year-old diabetic man being treated with amiloride for congestive heart failure is admitted in a comatose state. Blood tests: sodium 152 mmol/l (137-144), potassium 5.0 mmol/l (3.5-4.9), chloride 115 mmol/l (95-107), bicarbonate 30 mmol/l (20-28), glucose 520 mg/dl and pH 7.35 (7.36-7.44). Creatinine is raised at 1.9 mg/dl. He is taking metformin for his diabetes. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• The investigations suggest that this patient has non-ketotic hyperosmolar coma.
  • The bicarbonate level and blood pH would both be low in patients with diabetic ketoacidosis.
  • The raised anion gap is almost certainly contributed to by metformin and his degree of renal impairment.
  • Ventricular arrhythmia is unlikely at potassium levels of 5 mmol/l.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:3116

question_text: A patient requires the management of oral blood glucose lowering agents  in patients post myocardial infarction.  Looking at a synthesis of the available evidence, which of the following pieces of advice would you give?
option_a: Pioglitazone should be started in patients post myocardial infarction
option_b: Metformin should be stopped in all patients post myocardial infarction
option_c: Metformin should be stopped in patients in those patients who have an unstable circulation post infarct
option_d: Insulin should be given IV for the first 48hrs
explanation:
• Glitazones are generally not used in patients at risk of fluid retention due to the risk of heart failure, which includes some of those patients who have suffered a myocardial infarction.
  • Metformin was originally ruled out in all patients who suffered an MI, but is continued by many clinicians now unless there is evidence of significant circulatory impairment or raised creatinine.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:3110

question_text: A 50-year-old lady has been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, a year ago. Since the diagnosis was made, she was found to have pre-proliferative diabetic retinopathy. She has a history of rheumatoid arthritis and has been taking ibuprofen regularly for 6 years. She was referred for investigation of renal impairment. The HbA1C is 9% urea 35 mg/dl creatinine 2.0 mg/dl, Urine dipstick shows blood +, protein ++ What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Diabetic nephropathy, amyloidosis and chronic interstitial nephritis are all possible answers.

Ours is a middle aged female with diabetes detected 1 year back. Most probably it is a Type II Diabetes. She has evidence of diabetic retinopathy. How ever in Type II diabetes, the correlation between retinopathy and nephropathy is poor. Only 60% of patients with nephropathy have retinopathy co-existing.

Hence the presence of retinopathy should not prompt us to write the answer as diabetic nephropathy. But the correlation between the presence of retinopathy in patients with nephropathy is >90% in Type I diabetes.

Also, diabetic nephropathy rarely presents with hematuria.

Indications for biopsy in Diabetic Kidney disease is:

  1. No retinopathy in Type I diabetes.
  2. Kidney disease in Type 1 DM <10 years duration.
  3. Sudden appearance of nephrotic range proteinuria
  4. Active urinary sediments.

So, presence of blood makes the diagnosis of Diabetic kidney disease unlikely.

Renal calculi is unlikely as there is no history of pain or gross hematuria.

Chronic interstitial nephritis causes mild proteinuria. RBC is not seen in urine.

Renal amyloidosis can explain proteinuria and hematuria. The cause of amyloidosis being AA amyloid secondary to rheumatoid arthritis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 314, Pg: 2344

question_text: A 68-year-old man with diet controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and a creatinine of 3.0 mg/dl. Which of the following drugs should be avoided?
explanation:
• Metformin is a biguanide which acts by improving insulin sensitivity through mechanisms involving hepatic gluconeogenesis and improved muscle glucose utilization.
  • Thus, some insulin must be produced for it to have an effect.
  • It is associated hypoglycaemia although this side effect is unusual.
  • It is contraindicated in subjects with renal failure, hepatic failure and heart failure due to an association with lactic acidosis.
  • Linagliptin can be used without dose modification in renal dysfunction
  • Glimepiride is a sulphonyl urea which requires dose reduction in renal failure due to increased risk of hypoglycemia but is not contraindicated.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:3111

question_text: A 52-year-old obese female with a 10-year duration of Type 2 Diabetes mellitus was admitted for evaluation of exertional dyspnea and orthopnea. Echocardiogram revealed heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. She is currently on Metformin 1.5 gm/day and Glimepiride 2 mg BD with an HBA1C of 8.1%. What additional medication would you add for glycemic control in this patient?
explanation:
• DAPA-HF trial has demonstrated that the use of Dapagliflozin in patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction irrespective of the presence of Diabetes mellitus had reduced worsening of heart failure and decreased mortality from cardiovascular causes
  • The weight loss and diuretic effect provided by SGLT2 inhibitor addition would also benefit the patient
  • Saxagliptin has been shown to worsen the cardiovascular outcomes in patients with heart failure (SAVOR-TIMI trial)
  • Insulin glargine would benefit in obtaining glycemic control but has no added benefit in heart failure improvement
  • Liraglutide (GLP-1 analogue) has been shown to decrease progression of coronary artery disease, new incident MI and cardiovascular mortality but is inferior to SGLT2 inhibitor in patients with heart failure

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 3110

question_text: Which is an intermediate acting insulin?
explanation: Ans. is 'c' i.e., NPH insulin om

question_text:
The oral hypoglycemic agents not contraindicated in renal failure:
1. Acarbose
2. Repaglinide
3. Linagliptin
4. Glimepiride
explanation:
• Acarbose is an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor which decrease post-prandial blood glucose by inhibiting absorption of monosaccharides
  • Acarbose is contraindicated in inflammatory bowel disease, renal failure and decompensated hepatic failure
  • Linagliptin is the only DPP-4 inhibitor approved for use in renal failure
  • Repaglinide is meglitinide analogue which is short acting and used for control of post-prandial blood glucose
  • Repaglinide is cleared entirely by liver
  • Rosiglitazone is also not affected by renal failure, however due to risk of fluid retention, it is not preferred in renal failure

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 3110-3112

question_text: A 54-year-old obese woman presents to the casualty department with worsening dyspnoea and ankle swelling due to NYHA 3 heart failure. Her renal functions are within normal limits and her potassium is 4.4 mmol/l. Which of the following combinations of drugs is best suited for her in terms of mortality benefit?
explanation:
Diuretics are useful in patients with heart failure and features of fluid overload though they don't confer mortality benefit. Beta blockers shown to have mortality benefit include carvedilol, metoprolol, bisoprolol. While administering ACE inhibitor and spironolactone, we need to be cautious about the risk of hyperkalemia.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1945-47

question_text:
A 54-year-old diabetic man presents with malaise and loss of libido. On examination there is evidence of hepatomegaly. Blood tests show Hb 14.1 g/dl (13-18), fasting glucose 144 mg/dl, serum iron 45 mmol/l (14-29) and serum ferritin 250,000 mmol/l (15-200). 
What would be the most appropriate treatment for his symptoms?
explanation:
• This patient most probably has hereditary haemochromatosis which causes hypo gonadotrophic hypogonadism or rarely hyper gonadotropin hypogonadism due to iron deposition in pituitary and testis respectively.
  • Although venesection is the treatment of choice for reducing the iron load, this will not correct testicular atrophy or hypopituitarism, either or both of which may contribute to a loss of libido.
  • Testosterone replacement is used for improvement of symptoms in these patients.
  • Desferrioxamine is indicated in rare cases who cannot tolerate venesection (because of severe cardiac disease or anemia). Insulin therapy would not be helpful in restoring libido.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20th edition Chapter:407 Page number:2890-82

question_text: A patient with a history of recurrent retrosternal chest pain, each episode lasting 3-5 min and subsiding with sublingual nitrate. Now presented in emergency with chest pain. He is a k/c/o HTN, DM, hypercholesterolemia. On losartan, aspirin, atenolol, metformin. ECG shows LVH with an inversion of the T wave. What is the next step in management
option_d: Increase the dose of the beta blocker
explanation:
In the question, the patient's pain is subsiding with sublingual nitrates, but has recurrent angina and multiple risk factors, the ideal treatment would be an early invasive treatment. But since that is not there LMWH or heparin is the next best.

The patient in the question is suffering from an acute coronary syndrome, given the T inversions, it could either be an Unstable angina or an Non St elevation MI.

The initial treatment of these consist of providing pain relief. The main anti ischemic treatments given are nitrates, Beta blockers and bed rest.

Antithrombotic treatment remains the cornerstone of treatment. Thus includes antiplatelets and anticoagulants.

Antiplatelets: in patients with NSTEMI or UA two antiplatelets should be used.

  • Cyclooxygenase inhibitor aspirin should be given in a dose of at least 162 mg followed by 75-100mg/day.
  • A P2Y12 inhibitor should be added, if there is no high risk for bleeding.
  • Clopidogrel 600 mg loading followed by 75mg/day. Other P2Y12 inhibitors are Prasugrel, 60mg loading followed by 10 mg per day. It is preferred for those in whom an invasive strategy is planned. It is contraindicated in the previous stroke, TIA. It is associated with a high bleeding risk.
  • Ticagrelor is reversible. 180 mg loading dose followed by 90 mg twice daily is used. Beneficial for both invasive as well as conservative management.
  • Cangrelor is an IV P2Y12 inhibitor which is rapid and IV. It is recommended as an adjunct in patients undergoing PCI to reduce post-procedure MI, recurrent revascularization and stent thrombosis.

Anti coagulants: unfractionated heparin, LMWH, fondaparinux and Bivaluridin are the anticoagulants used.

After giving the initial treatment, the patient has to be risk stratified to determine if the patient has to be taken up for an early PCI VS conservative management.

In high risk patients, those with multiple risk factors, ECG changes and positive troponin, an early invasive strategy should be followed which is definitely beneficial than a conservative strategy.

In low risk patients, early invasive or conservative approaches have similar outcomes. In a low risk patient, a PCI is carried out if the CT Coronary angio shows occlusion, positive stress test or raising biomarkers.

question_text: A 45-year-old diabetic gentleman had a renal biopsy during investigation of worsening renal failure. Which of the following is typical of diabetic nephropathy?
option_d: Basement membrane thickening and mesangial widening
explanation:
The earliest morphologic abnormality in diabetic nephropathy is the thickening of the glomerular basement membrane(GBM) and expansion of the mesangium due to accumulation of extracellular matrix. Light microscopy findings show an increase in the solid spaces of the tuft material(diffuse diabetic glomerulopathy).

Large acellular accumulations also may be observed within these areas. These are circular sections and are known as the Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules which are PAS positive, eosinophilic material. Immunofluorescence microscopy may reveal deposition of immunoglobulin G along the GBM in a linear pattern, but this is not diagnostic. In advanced disease, the mesangial regions occupy a large proportion of the tuft, with prominent matrix content. Further, the basement membrane in the capillary walls(i.e., the peripheral basement membrane) is thicker than normal.

Diabetic glomerulopathy of Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease

Option A: Hyaline changes in blood vessel is seen in hypertension and is non specific.

Option B:Mesangeal hypercellularity is seen in glomerular diseases like Ig A nephropathy, Lupus Nephritis, post streptococcal glomerulonephritis etc.

Option C: Basement membrane spikes are seen in membranous nephropathy.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 314, Pg: 2344.

question_text: A 78-year-old man with type-2 diabetes and a creatinine level of 1.85 mg/dl presents to radiology for a contrast angiography. He has had a mild episode of gastroenteritis but is keen to go ahead with the investigation. He is discharged the following morning but presents to ER 48 h later feeling acutely unwell. His serum creatinine level is now 2.85 mg/dl.What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
In patients who have impaired renal function, the use of iodine-containing contrast media may be directly nephrotoxic.

Contrast nephropathy mechanisms include:

  1. Hypoxia in the renal outer medulla due to perturbations in renal microcirculation and occlusion of small vessels
  2. Cytotoxic damage to the tubules directly or via the generation of oxygen-free radicals, especially because the concentration of the agent within the tubule is markedly increased
  3. Transient tubule obstruction with precipitated contrast material.

The toxic effects appear to be dose-dependent and therefore where large amounts of contrast are used, such as in angiography, there is an increased incidence of contrast nephropathy.

The most common clinical course of contrast nephropathy is characterized by a rise in S.Cr beginning 24-48 h following exposure, peaking within 3-5 days, and resolving within 1 week.

Dialysis requiring renal impairement is seen in the setting of severe pre existing renal failure, congestive cardiac failure etc.

Risk factors for Contrast induced Nephropathy:

  • Diabetic nephropathy
  • Coexistent hypovolaemia
  • Multiple myeloma
  • Pre-existing CKD

Low fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) and relatively benign urinary sediment without features of tubular necrosis (see below) are common findings

Prehydration with normal saline and acetylcysteine may reduce the incidence of contrast nephropathy, although care must be taken not to precipitate volume overload.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, chp:310, pg: 2300

question_text: A 70-year-old man with type-2 diabetes is found to have an elevated plasma creatinine of 1.6 mg/dl. His blood pressure is 180/100 mmHg and fundoscopy reveals mild hypertensive changes and background diabetic retinopathy. He has an ischaemic ulcer on his right foot and no palpable pedal pulses. Urine dipstick is negative and renal ultrasound shows a 9-cm left kidney and 7.0-cm right kidney, with reduced cortical thickness. What is the most likely cause of the renal impairment?
explanation:
An elderly man with atherosclerotic risk factors with asymmetric kidneys point to atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis.

There is no correlation between the presence of retinopathy and nephropathy in type II diabetes as in Type I.

Membranous nephropathy causes nephrotic range proteinuria.

Cholesterol emboli syndrome is seen where the aorta is manipulated and results in livido reticularis, discolouration of toe and hematuria, with retinal plaques.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition, Ch:314, Pg:2347, 2348.

question_text: A 75-year-old man visits his GP for a new-patient screen. His only previous complaints have been type-2 diabetes and mild long-standing back pain. Screening tests reveal an elevated serum creatinine of 2.15 mg/dl and anaemia with Hb of 10.1 g/dl. A back X-ray shows collapse of the lumbar spine and there is a monoclonal band on serum protein electrophoresis. What is the most likely cause of his deteriorated renal function?
explanation:
This patient is suffering from Myeloma as evidenced by the presence of anemia, renal impairment and bone involvement. Myeloma can affect the kidney in several ways - the filtered light chains are toxic to the tubules and can cause acute obstruction:

  • Cast nephropathy
  • The light chain impairs the proximal tubular function and cause RTA
  • Hypercalcemia can cause tubulointerstitial disease
  • Amyloidosis
  • LCDD

All forms of renal involvement is reversible to a certain extend with treatment of myeloma.

Among the given options Amyloidosis is the best pick

Amyloidosis presents predominantly between the ages of 60 and 70 years.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Ch:111, Pg:870.

question_text: A type-2 diabetic patient with chronic renal failure is started on metformin. What is the most likely serious complication?
explanation:
Metformin accumulates in renal failure. Metformin inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis - a process that constantly consumes the lactate produced by glycolysis. Blood lactate levels are modestly raised in patients receiving biguanides and can escalate rapidly and cause life-threatening acidosis if lactate is overproduced.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Ch:404, Pg:3110-3111

question_text: Kallmann's syndrome is due congenital synthesis defect of?
explanation:
Kallmann's syndrome is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia.

It is due to defective hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)synthesis. KAL gene defect on chromosome Xp22.3 is the culprit. Embryonic migration of GnRH neurons from hypothalamic olfactory placode to hypothalamus is prevented due to this genetic defect.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 3013

question_text: Which is the most common congenital heart defect in Turner syndrome?
explanation:
Bicuspid aortic valve is the most common congenital heart defect in patients with Turner syndrome followed by Coarctation of aorta.


Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:264 pg:1831,1832

question_text: A 39-year-old woman presents to the clinic with difficult to treat hypertension. She is on two anti-hypertensives  and currently has a BP of 155/95 mmHg. She has noted that her face has become more rounded over the years and she is having increasing trouble with both acne and hirsutism. Fasting blood glucose testing has revealed impaired glucose tolerance. There has also been increasing trouble with abdominal obesity and she has noticed some purple stretch marks appearing around her abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis
explanation:
• Cushing's syndrome is associated with a round, plethoric, facial appearance and weight gain - in particular truncal obesity, buffalo hump and supraclavicular fat pads, skin fragility, proximal muscle weakness, mood disturbance, menstrual disturbance and reduced libido.
  • Hypertension is present in more than 50% of patients, impaired glucose tolerance in 30%. Osteopenia and osteoporosis, and premature vascular disease are an inevitable consequence in untreated Cushing's.

Phaeochromocytoma presents with episodic headaches, sweating and palpitation along with refractory hypertension.

Primary aldosteronism is characterised by resistant hypertension with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2961

question_text: What condition is illustrated in the image provided below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image displays characteristic features of Cushing's syndrome, a condition caused by prolonged exposure to elevated levels of glucocorticoids.

Cushing's Syndrome Overview

Cushing's syndrome refers to a group of clinical signs and symptoms resulting from chronic glucocorticoid excess.

When the cause is specifically a pituitary adenoma producing ACTH, the condition is termed Cushing's disease.

Though rare, subtle or early forms of the syndrome may be more common, especially in patients presenting with central obesity, type 2 diabetes, or osteoporosis.

Clinical Features of Cushing's Syndrome

Physical Appearance

  • Weight gain with central (truncal) obesity
  • Moon face: Rounded, full face
  • Buffalo hump: Fat pad over the upper back/neck
  • Skin changes:
    • Thin, fragile skin prone to easy bruising
    • Wide, purple striae (stretch marks), especially on the abdomen
    • Acne and hirsutism

Musculoskeletal

  • Osteoporosis, especially spinal fractures (see Option B)
  • Proximal muscle weakness, particularly in the thighs and upper arms
  • Reduced deep tendon reflexes

Metabolic

  • Hyperglycemia or overt type 2 diabetes
  • Dyslipidemia (elevated cholesterol/triglycerides)

Cardiovascular

  • Hypertension
  • Hypokalemia
  • Peripheral edema

Reproductive & Hormonal

  • Amenorrhea and reduced libido
  • Menstrual irregularities in women, often due to gonadotropin suppression

Neuropsychiatric

  • Mood disturbances: Irritability, depression, emotional lability
  • Cognitive issues, sometimes progressing to psychosis in severe cases

Immune & Hematologic

  • Immunosuppression: Higher risk of infections
  • Elevated WBC count, eosinopenia
  • Hypercoagulable state: Risk of DVT or pulmonary embolism

Explanation for other options:

Acromegaly (option A): incorrect because Features include enlarged hands/feet, coarse facial features, jaw protrusion are not seen here.

PCOS (Polycystic Ovary Syndrome) (option B): Typically presents with menstrual irregularities, acne, and hirsutism, but lacks the specific Cushingoid features like striae and buffalo hump.

Advanced Obesity (option D): While obesity is present, the hallmark signs of glucocorticoid excess (e.g., moon face, striae, muscle wasting) differentiate it from simple obesity.

question_text: A 35 year old male presents with history of weakness of both the lower limbs of insidious onset, for the past 2 years. He has mild difficulty in swallowing liquids too. There are no sensory symptoms. On examination, he has fasciculations and areflexia. You also notice gynecomastia. He is also undergoing investigation for infertility. What is the likely molecular abnormality be seen in this patient?
explanation:
The given patient has an LMN type of weakness without any sensory symptoms and with associated androgen insensitivity as evidenced by the gynecomastia and the sub fertility. This is classical of the Spinobulbar muscular atrophy or the Kennedy syndrome.

It is an X linked disorder and is associated with CAG trinucleotide repeats on the androgen receptor gene on the X chromosome.

CGG trinucleotide repeats is seen in Fragile X syndrome. It is associated with mental retardation. There may be ataxia and ovarian failure associated with it.

GAA trinucleotide repeats are seen in Friedrich's Ataxia.

CTG trinucleotides are seen in Myotonic dystrophy.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 347, Pg: 3415

question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct regarding hypogonadal hypogonadism in males?
1. Kallmann syndrome is a form of primary hypogonadism.
2. In secondary hypogonadism, serum LH and FSH are low or inappropriately normal.
3. Low testosterone with elevated LH and FSH indicates secondary hypogonadism.
4. Clinical features may include decreased libido and infertility.
explanation:
Explanation:

If the hypothalamic-pituitary axis fails to produce adequate GnRH or gonadotropins, the testes do not receive stimulation, so testosterone falls. The expected pituitary response to low testosterone would be increased LH/FSH; if LH/FSH are low or are within the normal range despite low testosterone, that is inappropriate and indicates a central (secondary) cause. Causes include: Kallmann syndrome, pituitary adenomas, infiltrative disease, head trauma, hyperprolactinemia, systemic illness, certain medications (e.g., opioids), and functional hypogonadism (obesity, chronic illness).

Low testosterone commonly causes reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, decreased spontaneous erections, loss of morning erections, decreased muscle mass and strength, increased fat mass, low energy, depressed mood, and reduced bone density. Fertility is affected because impaired spermatogenesis may accompany hypogonadism-this is particularly important in secondary hypogonadism where gonadotropin therapy can stimulate spermatogenesis, whereas in primary hypogonadism the testes often cannot respond.

Key takeaway:

Kallmann syndrome is a congenital hypogonadotropic (secondary) hypogonadism caused by deficient GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus (often due to migration failure of GnRH neurons). Clinically it presents with delayed/absent puberty and anosmia or hyposmia. Since the defect is at the level of the hypothalamus, LH and FSH are low (or inappropriately normal), not elevated as in primary testicular failure.

Low testosterone with high LH and FSH reflects primary hypogonadism, because the pituitary is responding to failed testes by increasing gonadotropin output.

question_text:
A 12-year-old boy with bilateral gynaecomastia is being investigated. 
Which one of the features points towards hypogonadotropic hypogonadism being a  likely cause?
explanation:
• Hypospadias, micropenis and cryptorchidism point towards reduced androgen exposure in utero
  • Kallmann syndrome is characterised by hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia. Although hypogonadotropic hypogonadism can be caused by pituitary disorders, a common presentation in childhood is with anosmia (Kallman's syndrome).
  • Causes of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism:.

Genetic:

Mutations in following genes:

  • KAL1
  • FGFR1
  • GNRHR
  • PC1

Acquired:(more common)

  • Stress
  • Athletes
  • Chronic illness
  • Obesity
  • Hyperprolactinemia
  • Sellar lesions

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 3014

question_text: A 19-year-old young woman is referred to the endocrinologist with primary amenorrhoea. She is of normal height and weight. She has moderate hirsutism. A male cousin was seen in the clinic at the age of 8 years with precocious puberty. What is the most likely cause for her primary amenorrhoea?
explanation:
• Turner's syndrome (genotype XO) is associated with primary amenorrhoea and short stature while the risk of of hyperandrogenism is extremely less
  • Hyperprolactinaemia and PCOS are more commonly associated with secondary amenorrhoea and the association of precocious puberty in a family member cannot be explained
  • Testicular feminisation causes primary amenorrhoea and is caused by either a partial or complete androgen-receptor defect. Affected patients are genotypically male (XY) but phenotypically female.
  • Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is most commonly caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Severe forms present in infancy with salt-losing crises and females can have ambiguous genitalia.
  • Milder forms cause precocious puberty in boys and virilism, hirsutism and primary amenorrhoea in girls.
  • Diagnosis is by finding raised serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone. Treatment is with glucocorticoids.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 3032

question_text: Most common cause of anovulation in females is:
explanation:
Five most important causes for anovulation in females include PCOS and other hyperandrogenic disorders, hypothalamic anovulation, hyperprolactinemia, POI and chronic illnesses

Reference: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 14th edition Page 601

question_text: According to the International Consensus PCOS guidelines, the number of follicles per ovary (2-9 mm) required to make a ultrasonographic diagnosis of PCO pattern is:
