question_text:
A 47-year old alcoholic man presents with gradually increasing confusion and drowsiness over the past two weeks.
He had previously attended the Emergency department having fallen over drunk, but had discharged himself before being reviewed by a doctor.
On examination he has multiple old bruises including one to his right arm and to the right side of his face above his eye. His BP is 150/82 mmHg, his pulse is 67 and irregular. There is 3/5 power weakness of his left arm, he is drowsy and confused.
Investigations show:
Haemoglobin 10.2 g/dl(13.5-17.7)
White cell count 12.3 x 10^9/L (D-11)
Platelets 121 x 10^9/L (150-400)
Sodium 133 mmol/l (135-146)
Potassium 3.9 mmol/l (3.5-5)
ALT 190 U/l (5-40)
Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
• The suspicion is that this patient has a subdural haematoma. In patients with alcoholism who are more likely to have abnormal clotting, what seems like a very minor, innocuous injury may lead to a potentially serious bleed. CT head is the initial investigation of choice.
  • Whilst sepsis is possible, we have no indication on initial findings of a source of infection, therefore antibiotics are not appropriate.
  • A lumbar puncture should also be avoided until after CT head.
  • An ultrasound, whilst it would confirm liver changes, is unlikely to be helpful in the acute stage, and the anaemia is likely to be chronic, rather than due to an acute bleed.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 443 Pg: 3457

question_text: An alcoholic patient presented to the emergency in an unconscious state. Relatives stated that he had a similar episode of binge drinking one week back. On examination, his glucose was 49 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate treatment?
option_a: IV thiamine followed by dextrose infusion
option_b: Injection vitamin K followed by dextrose infusion
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

In an unconscious alcoholic with hypoglycemia, IV thiamine must be given before glucose to prevent precipitation or worsening of Wernicke's encephalopathy.

Wernicke Encephalopathy: "The Emergency Neurological Manifestation of Thiamine Deficiency"

  • This case is a classic presentation of Wernicke encephalopathy due to chronic alcohol use and malnutrition, worsened by hypoglycemia.
  • Key Triad of Wernicke Encephalopathy:
    • Confusion
    • Ataxia
    • Ophthalmoplegia (or nystagmus)
  • Though all three may not be present initially, altered mental status in an alcoholic with hypoglycemia is Wernicke encephalopathy until proven otherwise.
  • Thiamine (Vitamin B1) is a cofactor in glucose metabolism, particularly for the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
  • In thiamine deficiency, giving glucose without prior thiamine results in accumulation of lactate and pyruvate, worsening neuronal energy failure → leading to irreversible neurological damage or coma.
  • Treatment Protocol:
    • IV Thiamine: 100-500 mg IV over 30 min (depending on severity)
    • Then: Give IV dextrose (e.g., 25% or 50%)
    • Follow with maintenance fluids and supportive care
    • Note: IM or oral thiamine may be used later but IV is essential in emergency settings for rapid CNS availability.
  • MRI Findings (if done):
    • Symmetric hyperintensities on T2/FLAIR in:
      • Mammillary bodies
      • Medial thalami
      • Periaqueductal gray matter
      • Tectal plate
      • Around the 3rd and 4th ventricles

Explanation of other options:

Injection vitamin K followed by dextrose infusion (Option B): Vitamin K is used for coagulopathy in liver disease or anticoagulant overdose; it has no role in reversing altered sensorium due to thiamine deficiency.

IV 25% dextrose (Option C): Administering dextrose before thiamine in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate acute Wernicke encephalopathy, making this dangerous without thiamine priming.

NS infusion (Option D): While normal saline may help with volume resuscitation, it does not correct hypoglycemia or treat underlying vitamin B1 deficiency, hence is inadequate in this scenario.

Reference:

Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome | National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (nih.gov)

Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome: Practice Essentials, Background, Etiology (medscape.com)

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482360/

question_text:
A 51 year old male presents with general weakness. He drinks approximately 20 units of alcohol each week and smokes 10 cigarettes daily. Examination reveals jaundice, numerous spider naevi and he has a temperature of 37.5°C. Abdominal examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly. Investigations show :
Bilirubin 12 mg/dl
Alkaline phosphatase 525 iu/l (45-105)
AST 178 iu/l (1-31)Albumin 28 g/L (37-49)
Hepatitis B virus surface antigen - negative
Hepatitis B virus e antigen - negative
Hepatitis B virus e Antibody- positive
IgG Hepatitis B core Antigen (anti-HBc) - positive
Hepatitis B virus DNA - undetectable
What is the likely diagnosis?
option_b: Remote Hep B infection from which he has recovered
explanation:
In a patient with acute hepatitis B, HBsAg will be positive, HBe will be positive as the patient will be highly infective, shortly after the HBsAg appears, IgM anti HBc antibody also appears.

Subsequent serological changes depends upon the immune response of the patient.

In those in whom the immune system is able to contain the infection, the HBsAg will disappear followed by the appearance of Anti HBs, the IgM Anti HBc being replaced by IgG variety and anti HBe also appears. This serological pattern indicates an infection from which the patient has recovered completely.

In those where the body is unable to contain the infection, the patient goes for chronicity. Here the HBs Ag will be positive, there will be IgG Anti HBc. The HBe can be positive or negative, just indicating the level of infectivity.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:339 Pg:2565

question_text: A chronic alcoholic male patient presents to the emergency department with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. On examination, his abdomen is tender in the epigastric region, and there is no palpable mass. Which of the following is the most specific and reliable marker for diagnosing acute pancreatitis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Serum lipase is the most specific and reliable marker for diagnosing acute pancreatitis in the scenario described.

  • Elevation Duration:Serum lipase remains elevated for a longer duration (7-14 days) compared to serum amylase, which tends to return toward normal after 3-7 days even if evidence of pancreatitis persists. This makes lipase a more reliable marker during the later stages of the presentation.
  • Specificity:Serum lipase is more specific than amylase for pancreatitis. While both amylase and lipase can be elevated in acute pancreatitis, lipase is less likely to be elevated in other conditions.
  • Diagnostic Utility:Serum lipase helps differentiate pancreatic from non-pancreatic causes of hyperamylasemia, offering a clearer diagnostic pathway in clinical settings where the cause of symptoms might be ambiguous.

Diagnosis of Pancreatitis

Amylase and Lipase Elevation: Both serum amylase and lipase levels threefold or more above normal strongly support the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis, assuming other conditions like gut perforation, ischemia, and infarction are excluded.

  • Severity Correlation:There is no direct correlation between the severity of pancreatitis and the levels or trends of serum amylase and lipase.
  • Duration of Elevation:While serum amylase levels may normalize within 3-7 days despite ongoing pancreatitis, serum lipase levels may remain elevated for a longer period, 7-14 days.
  • Conditions Affecting Amylase Levels:
    • Amylase can be spuriously elevated in conditions such as diabetic ketoacidosis due to academia (arterial pH ≤7.32).
    • Amylase levels can be misleadingly low in cases of severe hypertriglyceridemia.
  • Specificity of Lipase:Lipase is more specific than amylase and is thus the preferred test, especially for distinguishing between pancreatic and non-pancreatic causes of hyperamylasemia.

Explanation of other options:

Serum Amylase (Option A): Although amylase is elevated in pancreatitis, it is not specific to pancreatic pathology. Can be elevated in various conditions (e.g., salivary gland disorders, perforated peptic ulcers, and mesenteric ischemia). Shorter duration of elevation (normalizes in 3-7 days).

Serum Bilirubin (Option C): Serum bilirubin may be elevated in gallstone-induced pancreatitis, but it is not a specific marker for acute pancreatitis itself.

Serum Creatinine (Option D): Serum creatinine is useful in assessing kidney function and may be elevated in severe pancreatitis with organ failure but is not a diagnostic marker for pancreatitis.

Key Takeaways:

Serum lipase is the most specific and reliable marker for acute pancreatitis, as it remains elevated longer and is more specific to pancreatic injury compared to amylase.

question_text: What is the likely diagnosis for a 37-year-old chronic alcoholic male who recently stopped drinking and, after three days, presents to the emergency department with disorientation, tremors, hallucinations, and high blood pressure?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation following sudden cessation of alcohol, characterized by disorientation, tremors, hallucinations, and hypertension, suggests delirium tremens because of alcohol withdrawal.

Alcohol Use Disorder and Alcohol Withdrawal Delirium (DT):

Pathophysiology:

    Explanation of other options:

  • Alcohol acts as a central nervous system (CNS) depressant by enhancing GABA activity and inhibiting NMDA receptors.
  • Chronic alcohol use leads to decreased GABA activity and increased NMDA receptor activity, causing CNS excitability when alcohol intake stops abruptly.
  • This results in withdrawal symptoms such as agitation, tremors, and increased heart rate.

Risk Factors for Withdrawal:

  • History of delirium tremens, concurrent illnesses, older age, low potassium levels, and previous withdrawal episodes increase risk.

History and Examination:

  • Important to assess alcohol use details, timing of last drink, prior withdrawal history, and any comorbidities.
  • Physical exam should check for electrolyte imbalances, liver function abnormalities, infections, and other medical issues.

Withdrawal Symptom Timeline:

  • 6-12 hours: Mild symptoms like anxiety, palpitations, and gastrointestinal upset.
  • 12-48 hours: Alcohol hallucinosis involving visual, auditory, or tactile hallucinations.
  • 6+ hours: Alcohol withdrawal seizures, potentially progressing to delirium tremens.
  • Delirium tremens manifests with visual hallucinations, confusion, rapid heart rate, high blood pressure, agitation, and fever.

Evaluation:

  • Assess for dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, low blood sugar, and nutritional deficiencies.

Management:

  • Aim to control agitation, prevent seizures, and reduce morbidity and mortality.
  • Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, diazepam, chlordiazepoxide) are first-line treatments, administered either symptom-triggered or on a fixed schedule.
  • Symptom-triggered regimens use less medication overall.
  • In severe or unresponsive cases, barbiturates (phenobarbital) or propofol with benzodiazepines may be needed, often requiring ICU care.
  • Alpha-2 agonists (clonidine, dexmedetomidine) can be adjuncts but are not effective alone.
  • Avoid alcohol, antipsychotics, anticonvulsants, beta-blockers, and baclofen due to lack of proven safety in withdrawal management.

Alcoholic hallucinosis (Option A): is a rare condition associated with chronic alcohol use, mainly characterized by auditory hallucinations. These hallucinations usually occur during or shortly after heavy drinking episodes.

Korsakoff syndrome (Option B): is a chronic neuropsychiatric disorder caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency. It results in brain damage that leads to symptoms like memory loss and confusion.

Marchiafava-Bignami disease (MBD) (Option D): is a very rare disorder involving demyelination and necrosis of the corpus callosum and adjacent subcortical white matter. It most often occurs in individuals with chronic alcohol use disorder, especially those who are malnourished.

Reference:

  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK539854/
  3. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK526007/
  4. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3830167/

question_text: Which of the following is not a cause of necrotizing myopathy?
explanation:
• IMNM, or autoimmune necrotizing myopathy, is characterized by the acute or insidious onset of symmetric, proximal more than distal weakness.
  • Specific autoantibodies associated are: (anti-3-hydroxy-3methyl-glutaryl-coenzyme reductase [HMGCR] and anti-signal recognition particle [SRP]).
  • Anti-HMGCR myopathy can be seen in patients receiving statins, inhibitors of HMGCR, particularly in patients aged >50 years. However, anti-HMGCR myopathy can develop in children and young adults without a history of statin use and can mimic a limb girdle muscular dystrophy.

question_text:
A 64 year old woman presents with a history of worsening dysphagia over many years. A barium swallow performed shows narrowing at the level of the gastroesophageal junction. 
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a case of achalasia cardia caused by loss of ganglion cells within the esophageal myenteric plexus.

It is thought to be an autoimmune process linked to latent HSV infecton in genetically susceptible individuals.

Barium swallow a Narrowing at the level of the LES (Bird beak appearance) and various degrees of megaesophagus (esophageal dilation) as the esophagus is gradually stretched by retained food.

Manometry can also be done for establishing the diagnosis. The diagnostic criteria for achalasia with esophageal manometry are impaired LES relaxation and absent peristalsis.

Esophageal carcinoma can also cause dysphagia, but it will be more shorter in duration compared to achalasia and there will be constitutional symptoms.

Barrett's Esophagus is gastric metaplasia seen in long standing GERD.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2427

question_text: A 70 year old male comes with history of severe epigastric pain for the  second time. His serum lipase levels are ten fold elevated. A CT scan of the abdomen reveals a diffusely  swollen pancreas, with a hypoechoic rim around it. Which of the following statement might not hold true for this patient?

The response of both type of AIP to steroids is 100%.

Intraepithelial granulocytic lesion may be seen in Tpe 2 AIP

Risk of relapse is there for Type 1 AIP

Chance of other organ involvement is more for type 1 AIP

The image on the left shows a bulky pancreas with a hypoechoic rim called the capsule sign. The figure on the left shows the response to steroids.

question_text:
A 26 years old woman has acne and is taking oral medication. She develops polyarthritis and has raised liver enzyme tests.
Investigations show:
AST 95 U/l (A-3D-
ALT 170 U/l (5-35)
Bilirubin 0.6 mg/dl
Antinuclear antibodiesStrongly positive at 1/20
Negative at 1/640
Which of the following drugs is she most likely to have been prescribed?
explanation:
All other drugs listed above are used in the treatment of acne.

Among the given options,

  • ANA positivity with autoimmune hepatitis is seen with Minocycline. Other drugs which produce the same profile are Alpha methyl dopa, Hydralazine, and nitrofurantoin. These agents cause autoimmune hepatitis with anti LKM2 positivity.
  • Erythromycin causes cholestatic jaundice and not hepatitis and is not associated with ANA.
  • Oxytetracycline causes fatty liver and photosensitivity.
  • Isotretinoin is associated with neutropenia and headaches as the common side effects, but hepatitis and arthritis are very rare and ANA positivity has not been described.

Usually Drug induced lupus is anti ds DNA negative. But anti ds DNA is positive with DIL caused by Minocycline and TNF inhibitors.

Anti histone is not specific for DIL as it may be positive in 85% of idiopathic SLE.

question_text: A 32 year old psychology lecturer has deranged liver function tests. She also has jaundice, pruritus and xanthelasmata .Blood tests reveal elevated levels of conjugated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase and positive anti-mitochondrial antibody. She seeks advice about the associations of the disease.Which one of the following is likely to be associated?
explanation:
The diagnosis is primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC):

  • Presents in middle aged females with chronic fatigue, jaundice and pruritis (worse in evenings).
  • Hyperpigmentation and xanthelesma are seen due to altered cholesterol metabolism.
  • Associated with autoimmune conditions such as hashimoto's thyroiditis, celiac disease, systemic sclerosis. Osteomalacia is seen due to impaired vitamin D absorption.

Investigations:

  • Cholestatic liver pattern (ALP >> AST). Elevated bilirubin, ϒ - glutamyl - transpeptidase.
  • Anti- mitochondrial antibody (AMA) positive
  • Liver biopsy - Inflammation and necrosis small- and medium sized bile ducts.
  • IgM is raised.

Treatment:

  • Ursodeoxycholic acid
  • Liver transplantation

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch:344 , Pg: 2627

question_text: A 38 year old lady has noticed mild jaundice, worsening joint pains and is complaining of itching on her skin for the past 8 months. On examination, she has palpable hepatomegaly and a bronze pigmentation on her skin.Her liver function tests show a bilirubin of 1.5 mg/dl, ALT 100 U/l, ALP 480 U/l. ANA is negative, anti-mitochondrial antibody is positive at 1:320.Which of the following medications is helpful?
explanation:
Primary biliary cirrhosis is described. Liver transplantation does not cure the condition. Histology shows white cell damage to the biliary epithelium with non necrotising granuloma formation in the portal triad.Ursodeoxycholic acid lowers serum bilirubin and symptoms of itching, and prolongs the progression towards requirement for liver transplantation. IgM levels are particularly high in PBC.

Desferrioxamine is used to treat hemochromatosis

Prednisolone is used to treat autoimmune hepatitis

Propranolol is for prophylaxis of upper GI bleed in patients of portal hypertension.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 244, Pg: 2627

question_text: A 32 year old psychology lecturer has deranged liver function tests. She also has jaundice, pruritus and xanthelasma.Blood tests reveal elevated levels of conjugated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase and positive anti-mitochondrial antibody. She seeks advice about the associations of the disease.Which one of the following is likely to be associated?
explanation:
The diagnosis is primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC).

It is based on a combination of findings including cholestatic liver enzymes, a positive antimitochondrial antibody (AMA), and characteristic liver biopsy findings. Elevated serum alkaline phosphatase of liver origin is the most common laboratory finding. Fatigue, jaundice, pruritus and xanthelasma are other features of primary biliary cirrhosis.In the disease, IgM is raised. Primary biliary cirrhosis is associated with autoimmune conditions such as scleroderma and Sjogren's syndrome. These conditions are also associated with distal RTA (type 1). There is xanthelasma formation due to impaired cholesterol excretion and also osteomalacia due to impaired Vitamin D absorption.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 244, Pg: 2627

question_text: Which one of the following statements is true of autoimmune hepatitis?
option_b: It may be associated with keratoconjunctivitis sicca
option_c: It rarely interferes with menstruation except in later stages
option_d: It rarely presents before 20 years of age
explanation:
It occurs frequently in young (10-20 years) and middle-aged women.

Twenty five per cent present as acute hepatitis, but usually the onset is insidious.Some may be asymptomatic for years and then are found to have signs of chronic liver disease. Amenorrhoea is common. It is associated with hyperglobulinemia and other autoimmune diseases.

Sixty per cent are associated with HLA-B8, DR3 and Dw3.

Extrahepatic features include:

  • arthritis
  • Sjögren syndrome
  • thyroiditis
  • nephritis
  • ulcerative colitis
  • Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia.

question_text: A 46 year old man presents with lethargy and pruritus. He has lost one stone in weight over the past two years.He does not smoke. There is no family history of bowel malignancy.On examination he looks pale but is not jaundiced. There is no hepatomegaly and there are no signs of chronic liver disease. Liver ultrasound shows small gallstones. The gallbladder is not inflamed. There is no biliary duct dilatation. Bilirubin is 1.2 mg/dl, ALT is 180 U/l, ALP is 800 U/l. ANA and AMA are negative but pANCA is positive.What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis presents at this age, there is cholestatic picture on the liver function tests, but not necessarily high bilirubin. pANCA is positive in about 90% of patients with PSC. A small proportion of patients (3%) will progress to cholangiocarcinoma at a later age.

question_text:
A 45 year old lady has a two month history of nausea, jaundice and dark urine. She also has a history of arthralgia and autoimmune thyroid disease.On examination, her abdomen was nontender with 4 cm hepatosplenomegaly.Investigations reveal AST 1675 U/L (5 - 40), ALT 3900 U/L (5 -40), GGT 179 U/L (10 - 60), bilirubin 6.8 mg/dl, increase in total globulin and smooth muscle antibodies are positive. Serum immunoglobulins were elevated Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) were positive at 1:320 titer in a homogenous speckled pattern.Anti-smooth muscle and liver-kidney microsomal antibodies were positive.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Presentation of autoimmune hepatitis

  • onset: usually insidious
  • 1/3rd patients: asymptomatic
  • 20% cases present with acute hepatitis (and occasionally acute liver failure), and some cases follow a viral illness (such as hepatitis A, Epstein-Barr infection, or measles) or exposure to a drug or toxin (such as nitrofurantoin, minocycline, hydralazine, methyldopa, or infliximab).
  • Exacerbations may occur postpartum.
  • Amenorrhea may be a presenting feature, and the frequency of depression appears to be increased.
  • Examination may reveal a healthy-appearing young woman with multiple spider telangiectasias, cutaneous striae, acne, hirsutism, and hepatomegaly.
  • Extrahepatic features include arthritis, Sjögren syndrome, thyroiditis, nephritis, ulcerative colitis, and Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia.
  • Patients, especially elderly are at increased risk for cirrhosis, which, in turn, increases the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (at a rate of about 1% per year).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch:341 , Pg: 2613-2615

question_text: A patient with hemolytic anemia presents with dactylitis and chest pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Symptoms of dactylitis and chest pain in a patient with hemolytic anemia are characteristic of a sickling crisis, seen in sickle cell disease due to vaso-occlusion by sickled RBCs.

  • Sickle cell disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a point mutation on chromosome 11, where glutamic acid is replaced by valine at position 6 of the β-globin chain.
  • This mutation produces abnormal hemoglobin (HbS), which polymerizes under low oxygen tension, causing red blood cells to become sickle-shaped, rigid, and fragile.
  • These deformed cells lead to vaso-occlusion, tissue ischemia, and hemolysis, resulting in the characteristic acute painful crises.
  • The term "sickle cell crisis" includes several acute manifestations such as vaso-occlusive crisis, aplastic crisis, splenic sequestration crisis, hyperhaemolysis crisis, hepatic crisis, dactylitis, and acute chest syndrome.

Types of Sickle Cell Crises

Explanation of other options:

Microangiopathic anaemia (Option A): Occurs due to mechanical destruction of RBCs as they pass through damaged small vessels, as in DIC, HSP. Schistocytes (fragmented RBCs) are seen on peripheral smear. It does not cause dactylitis or chest pain.

Intravascular haemolysis (Option C): Refers to the destruction of RBCs within blood vessels, releasing free haemoglobin, causing haemoglobinemia, haemoglobinuria, and jaundice. It is a mechanism of anaemia, not a specific disease causing vaso-occlusion or dactylitis.

Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (Option D): Caused by autoantibodies against RBCs, leading to extravascular destruction in the spleen. Patients present with jaundice, pallor, and splenomegaly, but not with dactylitis or chest pain.

question_text: The most common type of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is:
explanation:
• Autoimmune processes account for 90% of adult cases of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, usually caused by GM-CSF autoantibodies. It also can be congenital or secondary to dust exposure or hematologic malignancy and is the most common form overall.
  • Most patients (72%) are smokers. Patients present with the insidious onset of dyspnoea and cough, which may be dry or occasionally productive of grayish material.


  • Bilateral alveolar opacities with “crazy paving” and diffuse areas of ground-glass attenuation on CT scan are characteristic of PAP.
  • Mild cases can be managed with smoking cessation; severe cases require whole lung lavage.

Reference: Goldman Cecil Medicine 26th edition chapter 85 page number. 554

question_text: A 32 year old woman who has been previously well presents with apparent loss of consciousness. You suspect a diagnosis of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Which of the following observations would be least common in fitting with that diagnosis?
explanation:
Purpura is rare in TTP despite the name of the disorder. In conditions where prothrombotic states are associated with thrombocytopenia, it is often the case that there is a lack of purpura: e.g. in haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

Like DIC and also heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is a disorder in which thrombosis is accompanied by paradoxical thrombocytopenia.

Pathogenesis: It is an acute autoimmune disorder mediated by antibodies against ADAMTS-13 (a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with a thrombospondin type 1 motif). This enzyme normally cleaves vWF multimers to produce normal functional units, and its deficiency results in large vWF multimers that cross-link platelets. It may occur alone or in association with drugs (ticlopidine, ciclosporin), HIV, shiga toxins, and malignancy

TTP is characterized by a pentad of findings, although few patients have all five components:

  • thrombocytopenia
  • microangiopathic haemolytic anemia
  • neurological sequelae
  • fever
  • Renal impairment

Treatment: emergency plasma exchange

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 317, Pg: 2365

question_text: A 35 year old woman has abdominal pain, jaundice and worsening ascites. She drinks 20 units of alcohol each week, and takes the oral contraceptive pill. Which of the following findings would make a diagnosis of Budd Chiari syndrome likely?
explanation:
Budd-Chiari syndrome is an uncommon condition induced by thrombotic or nonthrombotic obstruction to hepatic venous outflow.The classic triad of abdominal pain,ascites, and hepatomegaly is observed in the vast majority of patients but is nonspecific.

Ascetic fluid protein may be high or low in Budd Chiari syndrome.

Tender hepatomegaly on examination is one of the hallmark signs.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch:50, Pg: 323

question_text: A 37 year old lady has sudden onset right upper quadrant pain and abdominal distension. She was well until 5 weeks ago, when over several days she rapidly developed abdominal distension and pain. She was also nauseous and vomiting.On examination, temperature was 37.1°C, her JVP was not raised and breath sounds were clear. Abdominal examination revealed tender hepatomegaly, jaundice and gross ascites. There was also bilateral ankle oedema.What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Budd-Chiari syndrome is a condition induced by thrombotic or nonthrombotic obstruction to hepatic venous outflow. The classic clinical triad of abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, and ascites is seen in BCS

The syndrome most often occurs in patients with underlying thrombotic diathesis, including

  • myeloproliferative disorders such as polycythemia vera
  • paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
  • pregnancy
  • tumors
  • chronic inflammatory diseases
  • clotting disorders
  • infections.

Doppler ultrasonography, as was used in this case, is the most effective primary initial screening method. CT and magnetic resonance angiography are both more sensitive than ultrasonography. The gold standard for diagnosis is hepatic venography, which should be performed when there is a high index of clinical suspicion and the results of noninvasive testing are either equivocal or negative.

Dubin Johnson syndrome is a disorder of bilirubin excretion which results in isolated conjugated hyperbilirubinemia

Constrictive pericarditis presents with ascites followed by lower limb edema; however or is insidious in onset and gradually progressive. JVP is elevated due to increased right side filling pressures

Lymphoma is likely to present with constitutional features like fever, night sweats and weight loss that develop gradually.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 343, Pg: 2615

question_text: A 25-year-old woman is referred from the Emergency department with a paracetamol overdose.Which of the following is an indication for liver transplantation in acute liver failure as a result of paracetamol overdose?
explanation:
Prothrombin time > 100 seconds in acute liver failure with paracetamol poisoning is one of the selection criteria for liver transplantation.

The remainder of the selection criteria for liver transplantation in acute liver failure with paracetamol overdose are as follows:

  • Arterial pH < 7.3 (this needs to be interpreted with caution as pH may improve with N-acetylcysteine and rehydration)
  • Creatinine > 2.5 mg/dL
  • Grade III or grade IV encephalopathy.

Serum bilirubin > 15 mg/dl is part of the selection criteria for liver transplantation in non-paracetamol induced acute liver failure.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 340, Pg: 2589

question_text: A 37 year old man has chronic liver disease secondary to hepatitis. He comes on having had a depressive episode but also feels tired and unwell. He reveals that he has had a bottle of wine a day for a week.On examination he has gross abdominal distension. A peritoneal tap is done. Results from the tap show that it has albumin of 2.5g/dl, LDH of 320 U/l, RBS of 70 mg/dl and a white cell count of 700 per mm3 (90% neutrophils).What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
A white cell count of > 250/mm3 is diagnostic of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. There is underlying cirrhotic liver disease and this should always be considered related to decompensation.

Tuberculous peritonitis will cause lymphocyte predominant ascites with high protein and low glucose.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 344 Pg:  2632

question_text: A 56 year old chronic alcoholic is found on the street with a low conscious level. His GCS is 3/15 on arrival in casualty. On examination, his BP is 110/65 and he is jaundiced. There is marked ascites and he has 7 spider naevi. ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 120. Which is the most practical test to elucidate why he is unconscious?
explanation:
In a patient with liver disease, it is important to exclude hypoglycemia as a cause of unconsciousness. Following confirming that baseline observations and BM is normal, the next best step is to perform a CT of his head to exclude a central neurological cause of decreased conscious level.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 28, Pg: 187

question_text: A 54 year old man has a long history of alcohol use. On the average he drinks two bottles of wine a day. He presents with tremors, hallucinations and has signs of chronic liver disease as well as ascites. A senior resident doctor assesses the status of chronic liver disease with the Child Pugh Classification. Which of the following is one of the criteria used to assess severity?
explanation:
Child Pugh classification includes: (Mnemonic: A BEAP)

  • Albumin
  • Bilirubin level
  • Encephalopathy
  • Ascites
  • Prothrombin time

AST is not used to assess severity of liver disease.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch:345 Pg: 2635

question_text: Which of the following genotypes is associated with the lowest levels of alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT)?
explanation:
α-1antitrypsin deficiency is due to the insufficient plasma activity of the enzyme that degrades several proteins like neutrophil elastase, cathepsin G and proteinase 3. It is an AR disease and is characterized by emphysema and cirrhosis.

The wild genotytpe is PiMM seen in > 90% of individuals. The clinically significant mutation is PiZZ, which is associated with < 10% levels of the enzyme.

The null phenotype (not in the list of options) is the least common but the most severe form of the disease where there is no detectable AAT in the serum.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 341, Pg: 2615

question_text: A 22 year old man presents with a 6 month history of depression and painful sensory disturbance in both legs. He has also become very confused. There are myoclonic jerks observed in his legs. His MRI scan reveals thalamic hyperintensity and EEG is normal. The most likely diagnosis is:
explanation:
• New variant CJD commonly presents in young adults painful sensory symptoms in the lower limbs and also psychiatric symptoms.
  • Cognitive impairment, pyramidal signs, myoclonus and primitive reflexes eventually
  • MRI commonly shows high signal on T2-weighted images in the pulvinar (posterior aspect of thalamus). EEG is often normal, unlike sporadic CJD, in which triphasic waves are observed.
  • Option B: Huntington disease (HD) is an inherited progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by choreiform movements, psychiatric problems, and dementia. Chorea is a key feature of HD, and the defining sign at the time of diagnosis
  • Option C:Clinical manifestations of Wilson disease are predominantly hepatic (acute liver failure, acute hepatitis, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis) neurologic (dysarthria, tremors) and psychiatric (depression, personality changes)
  • Option D: PML typically presents with subacute neurologic deficits, including altered mental status, visual symptoms such as hemianopia and diplopia, hemiparesis or monoparesis, and appendicular or gait ataxia

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 438, Pg: 3420

question_text: What is the Most common clinical manifestation of gonorrhea in males?
explanation:
Acute urethritis is the most common clinical manifestation of gonorrhea in males. The usual incubation period after exposure is 2-7 days, although the interval can be longer and some men remain asymptomatic

Epididymitis is now an uncommon complication, and gonococcal prostatitis occurs rarely, if at all.

question_text: Which of the following hepatic porphyrias present during adult life?
explanation:
Four of the five hepatic porphyrias present during adult life:

  • acute intermittent porphyria (AIP)
  • hereditary coproporphyria(HCP)
  • variegate porphyria (VP)
  • ALA-dehydratase porphyria (ADP)

acute attacks of neurologic manifestations and elevated levels of one or both of the porphyrin precursors, ALA and PBG, and are thus classified as acute porphyrias. Patients with ADP have also presented in infancy and adolescence.

Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 20th Edition, chapter. 409, page number.2989

question_text: Which of the following is recommended for a newborn born to a mother suffering from acute viral hepatitis B infection?
explanation:
HBIG is indicated for newborn infants of HBsAg-positive mothers, with initiation of the vaccine series at the same time, both within 12 hours of birth (administered at different injection sites).

Infection at birth is associated with clinically silent acute infection but a 90% chance of chronic infection, whereas infection in young adulthood in immunocompetent persons is typically associated with clinically apparent acute hepatitis but a risk of chronicity of only ~1%

Tenofovir is indicated in the management of chronic hepatitis B infection

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 341 pg. 2592

question_text: A 30 year old male presented to the emergency department with features suggestive of acute pancreatitis. Which one of the following would you consider for his fluid management?
explanation:
• Lactated Ringer's solution has been shown to decrease systemic inflammation (lower C-reactive protein levels from admission) and may be a better crystalloid than normal saline.
  • Intravenous fluids of lactated Ringer's or normal saline are initially bolused at 15-20 mL/kg (1050-1400 mL), followed by 2-3 mL/kg per hour (200-250 mL/h), to maintain urine output >0.5 mL/kg per hour.
  • Serial bedside evaluations are required every 6-8 h to assess vital signs, oxygen saturation, and change in physical examination to optimize fluid resuscitation
  • A decrease in hematocrit and BUN during the first 12-24 h is strong evidence that sufficient fluids are being administered
  • A rise in hematocrit or BUN during serial measurement should be treated with a repeat volume challenge with a 2-L crystalloid bolus followed by increasing the fluid rate by 1.5 mg/kg per hour

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 348, pg. 2663

question_text: A patient was asked to replicate the face of a clock, and the drawing is shown below. What is the appropriate term to describe this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image depicts a patient with hemispatial neglect, as evidenced by missing details on the left side of the clock drawing.

Hemispatial Neglect:

Hemispatial neglect is a condition where the patient is unable to perceive or respond to stimuli on one side of space, usually the side opposite to a brain lesion, despite having no sensory or motor impairments.

Lesion Location and Types:

  • Often caused by damage to cortical or subcortical areas involved in spatial attention.
  • It is not always due to parietal lobe damage alone, as previously thought.
  • The right hemisphere typically directs attention to the entire surrounding space, while the left hemisphere primarily attends to the right side.
  • Lesions in the left hemisphere tend to cause mild neglect because the right hemisphere compensates.
  • Lesions in the right hemisphere cause more severe neglect of the left side due to the left hemisphere's limited attentional capacity to compensate.

Clinical Features:

  • Patients may ignore or neglect grooming, eating, and reading on the left side.
  • Drawings and writing commonly show omissions on the left side.
  • Neglect tests include:
    • Simultaneous Bilateral Stimulation: Patients ignore stimuli on the neglected side when both sides are stimulated.
    • Target Detection Task: Difficulty spotting targets on the neglected side, indicating attentional rather than sensory deficits.
  • Some patients may deny paralysis or hemiparesis on the affected side (anosognosia).

Explanation for other options:

Confabulation (Option A): refers to when a patient unknowingly fills gaps in their memory with fabricated or distorted information.

Kinetic apraxia (Option C): is the inability to carry out precise, purposeful movements despite having the physical ability and desire to do so. This condition is associated with lesions in the paracentral cortex.

Asterixis (Option D): is a form of negative myoclonus characterized by irregular, brief lapses in the maintenance of posture in certain body parts.

question_text:
Which of the following are features of Korsakoff's psychosis?
1. Amnesia
2. Confabulation
3. Ophthalmoplegia
4. Polyneuropathy
explanation:
Explanation:

Ophthalmoplegia (Statement 3) is characteristic feature of Wernicke's encephalopathy, not Korsakoff's psychosis.

Wernicke's encephalopathy is the acute phase of thiamine deficiency, presenting with ophthalmoplegia (eye muscle paralysis), ataxia, and confusion. If untreated, it can progress to Korsakoff's psychosis.

question_text: A 49-year-old man presents with confusion and drowsiness. A diagnosis of hepatic encephalopathy is suspected and treatment with lactulose is begun. Which of the following concerning lactulose is true?
option_d: Inhibits proliferation of ammonia-forming organisms in the gut
explanation:
Lactulose, an osmotic laxative which causes hypomagnesaemia associated with diarrhea, is not absorbed, does not affect the absorption of spironolactone and may be used in diabetics.

In the management of hepatic encephalopathy lactulose has a number of actions to help reduce gut ammonia 'production' and absorption, production of a more acidic colonic pH is key in this. These mechanisms are:

  1. Conversion of lactulose of lactic acid acidifies the gut the lumen, this favors oxidation of NH4+ to NH3 and the passage of NH3 from tissues into the lumen
  2. The acidic pH inhibits the proliferation of ammonia producing microbes and promotes colonization by non-ammonia producing bacteria such as lactobacilli;
  3. The laxative effect leads to an overall reduction in colonic bacterial load and reduction in the protein load absorbed from the gut.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 344, Pg: 2633

Predictors of survival in liver transplant patients.

question_text: A 46 year old man is known to have alcoholic liver cirrhosis. He drinks 60 units of alcohol per week. He presents unwell and confused. Temperature is 38°C and blood pressure is 96/50 mmHg. Abdominal palpation reveals hepatomegaly and ascites. What should be done next?
explanation:
There is a high chance of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in this patient with cirrhotic liver disease. When analysis of ascitic fluid reveals a white blood cell count of more than 250 cells/cc, SBP is likely. Cefotaxime should be commenced after a tap is done and blood cultures are sent.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 344 Pg: 2632

question_text:
A 45 year old man has had long standing jaundice, malaise and poor appetite. Over the past 6 months he has lost 2 stones in weight. On examination he has palmar erythema, jaundiced sclera, spider naevi, hepatomegaly and ascites. His bloods reveal:
Bilirubin 2.5 mg/dl
ALT: 150 U/l
ALP: 240 U/l
Hep C core antibody Positive
HBsAg: Negative
Hep A antibody Negative
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient has features of chronic liver disease, as evidenced by the presence of ascites and spider angiomas. The patient also gives history of jaundice with deranged SGPT , which indicates an active hepatitis.

Acute infection with Hepatitis E or C will cause SGPT elevation of the order of 1000.  So from among the options the most probable option is HCC.

The risk of HCC is increased as well in patients with chronic hepatitis C almost exclusively in patients with cirrhosis, and almost after at least several decades, usually after three decades of disease. Among such cirrhotic patients with chronic hepatitis C, the annual risk of HCC is ~1-4%.

30% of patients with hepatitis C develop hepatocellular carcinoma over 30 years. 20% develop cirrhosis over 20 years.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 82, Pg: 643

question_text: A 52 year old alcoholic patient presents with confusion and severe derangement of liver function. On examination, his MMSE score is 22 / 30. He has signs of spider naevi, jaundice and gross ascites.Which one of the following features defines fulminant acute hepatic failure?
explanation:
Acute liver failure may be fulminant or subfulminant.

  • Fulminant hepatic failure is characterized by the development of hepatic encephalopathy within 8 weeks after the onset of acute liver injury. Coagulopathy (INR 1.5 or higher) is invariably present.
  • Subfulminant hepatic failure occurs when these findings appear between 8 weeks and 6 months after the onset of acute liver injury and carries an equally poor prognosis.
  • Acute-on-chronic liver failure refers to acute deterioration in liver function (often caused by infection) in a person with preexisting chronic liver disease.

Commonest causes are paracetamol overdose and viral hepatitis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 339, Pg: 2877

question_text: Which one of the following is the most important manifestation of acute hepatic failure?
explanation:
Hepatic encephalopathy is the cardinal manifestation of acute hepatic failure.

It is characterized by various neurologic symptoms including changes in reflexes, changes in consciousness, and behavior changes that can range from mild to severe. The exact cause is unknown, but one substance believed to be particularly toxic to the central nervous system is ammonia which is normally detoxified by the liver.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 339, Pg: 2877

question_text: A 68-year-old man is referred with abnormal liver function and undergoes a liver biopsy. Which of the following count against hepatic cirrhosis?

In the micronodular form, the nodules are less than 3 mm across with uniform liver involvement-seen in alcohol or biliary disease.

In the macronodular form, there are larger nodules, classically seen in chronic viral hepatitis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 344, Pg: 2624

question_text: Milan criteria is used for:

In transplantation medicine, the Milan criteria are applied as a basis for selecting patients with cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma for liver transplantation.

question_text: Which of the following regions of the abdomen is preferred for abdominal paracentesis?
explanation:
The lower quadrants are the most frequent sites for paracentesis. The left lower quadrant is preferred because of the greater depth of ascites and the thinner abdominal wall.

Paracentesis is a safe procedure even in patients with coagulopathy; complications, including abdominal wall hematomas, hypotension, hepatorenal syndrome, and infection, are infrequent.

Cirrhosis accounts for 84% of cases of ascites. Cardiac ascites, peritoneal carcinomatosis, and 'mixed' ascites resulting from cirrhosis and a second disease account for 10-15% of cases

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 50 pg. 323

question_text: Which of the following is not a parameter used to calculate MELD score?
explanation:
AASLD guidelines

Parameters used to assess MELD score (Model for End stage Liver Disease) (CBI)

  • Creatinine
  • Bilirubin
  • INR

Utility: A prognostic tool which predicts 6 month mortality; MELD score has been shown to reduce waiting list mortality, to reduce waiting time prior to transplantation, to be the best predictor of pretransplantation mortality

Patients with cirrhosis are typically candidates for liver transplantation once their biologic Model for End-stage Liver Disease (MELD) score is ≥15

In 2016, the MELD score was modified to incorporate serum sodium, another important predictor of survival in liver transplantation candidates (the MELD-Na score).

Pediatric End-Stage Liver Disease (PELD) score, is used for children (<12 years old)

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 345 pg. 2635

question_text: Which of the following is not included in the Child-Pugh score assessment?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Child-Pugh score is utilized to evaluate the extent of liver disease, estimate prognosis in cirrhosis, and guide decisions regarding suitability for liver transplantation. Liver function enzymes such as ALT (alanine aminotransferase) and AST (aspartate aminotransferase) are not included in the Child-Pugh scoring system.

The Child-Pugh classification uses a scoring method based on the following factors:

  • Bilirubin
  • INR
  • Albumin
  • Presence of ascites
  • Degree of hepatic encephalopathy
  • The Child-Turcotte-Pugh (CTP) classification is calculated by adding up the points assigned to each parameter.
  • However, the Child-Pugh score has limitations, as ascites and encephalopathy may not always be graded with precision. This drawback is addressed more effectively by the MELD scoring system

question_text: Which one of the following hepatitis viruses is primarily transmitted via contaminated water?
explanation:
Explanation:

Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is a waterborne viral infection. It spreads predominantly through the fecal- oral route, especially in areas where sanitation and hygiene are inadequate. Contaminated drinking water or food prepared with infected water serves as the main source of transmission.

Outbreaks commonly occur in developing regions, particularly during monsoon seasons or in overcrowded communities with poor sewage disposal. HAV infection is typically acute and self-limiting, and it does not progress to chronic hepatitis.

Transmission of Other Hepatitis Viruses: Hepatitis B, C, and D are transmitted through parenteral routes (i.e., through blood, semen, or other bodily fluids). This includes modes such as blood transfusions, sharing needles, or sexual contact.

question_text: A 47-year-old male with a long history of alcohol abuse presents with a two day history of deteriorating confusion.On examination he is drowsy, has a temperature of 39&deg:C, a pulse of 110 beats per minute, a small amount of ascites and has features of a left side hemiparesis.What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This man with chronic alcohol abuse now presents with a fever and left hemiparesis. The most likely diagnosis would therefore be cerebral abscess. The fever would not itself be explained by a subdural haematoma nor would a simple CVA explain this. Similarly, delirium tremens or encephalopathy would not be associated with the hemiparesis since they cause global cerebral dysfunction.

In patient with CLD, there is a high risk of infections. And also, there will be pulmonary shunting in patients with CLD, called the Hepatopulmonary syndrome, which predisposes the patient to brain abscess.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 345, Pg: 2633

question_text: A patient with chronic liver disease presents with abdominal distension, jaundice, and pruritus. Ascitic fluid analysis reveals a neutrophil count of 650/mm³ . What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of ascites, abdominal distension, jaundice, pruritus, and an ascitic fluid neutrophil count >250/mm³ confirms the diagnosis of Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP).

Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP):

Explanation of Other Options:

Malignant Ascites (Option B): Usually due to cancers (intra- or extra-abdominal); fluid typically shows high VEGF or tumor markers and may be bloody or milky, unlike SBP.

Tubercular Ascites (Option C): Seen with tuberculous peritonitis; ascitic fluid is exudative, protein-rich, and lymphocyte-predominant, not neutrophil-predominant.

Intestinal Obstruction (Option D): Presents with abdominal pain, vomiting, and cessation of bowel movements, which are absent in this case.

question_text: Which of the following conditions will cause an ascites with a serum ascites albumin gradient > 1.1g/dL with a high ascitic protein concentration?
explanation:
• The SAAG is useful for distinguishing ascites caused by portal hypertension from non portal hypertensive ascites. The SAAG reflects the pressure within the hepatic sinusoids and correlates with the hepatic venous pressure gradient. The SAAG is calculated by subtracting the ascitic albumin concentration from the serum albumin.
  • A SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL reflects the presence of portal hypertension and indicates that the ascites is due to increased pressure in the hepatic sinusoids.
  • An ascitic protein level of ≥2.5 g/dL indicates that the hepatic sinusoids are normal and are allowing passage of protein into the ascites, as occurs in cardiac ascites, early Budd-Chiari syndrome, or sinusoidal obstruction syndrome.
  • An ascitic protein level <2.5 g/dL indicates that the hepatic sinusoids have been damaged and scarred and no longer allow passage of protein, as occurs with cirrhosis, late Budd-Chiari syndrome, or massive liver metastases.

Option A: Cirrhosis will cause a low protein high SAAG ratio ascites

Option B: Nephrotic syndrome causes loss of protein through kidneys hence causes a low SAAG ratio ascites

Option C: Tuberculous peritonitis will cause an exudative ascites which will result in loss of protein from the serum into the peritoneum; hence low SAAG ratio ascites level and does not change with diuresis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 50 pg. 323

question_text: Which one of the following is least expected to precipitate hepatic encephalopathy in a liver cirrhosis patient:
explanation:
Factors precipitating hepatic encephalopathy:

  • nitrogen load (GI bleed, protein load from food intake, renal failure, constipation)
  • drugs (narcotics, CNS depressants)
  • electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia, alkalosis, hypoxia, hypovolemia)
  • infection (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis)
  • deterioration in hepatic function or superimposed liver disease
  • spontaneous portosystemic shunts (e.g. splenorenal shunts) or intentional portosystemic shunts (e.g. TIPS)

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 344 pg. 2632

question_text: A 49-year-old man with a history of alcohol abuse was admitted for treatment of alcoholic hepatitis. He has jaundice, tense ascites, severe leg edema, and mild to moderate encephalopathy. His blood tests revealed: urea 192 mg/dl, creatinine 5 mg/dl, ALT 140(5-35) U/l, AST 180 (A-31) U/l, ALP 360 (20-120) U/l, Bilirubin total 2.2 mg/dl, Albumin 3 g/dl. Which of the following should he be treated with?
explanation:
The diagnosis is hepatorenal syndrome.

The patient is in acute hepatic failure, as evidenced by jaundice and encephalopathy. Renal failure that arises in the setting of a hepatic dysfunction is called Hepato R enal syndrome(HRS).

There are two types of HRS.


Treatment :

Volume replacement

Stopping diuretics

Albumin+ vasopressors (Terlipressin/ Nor epinephrine/ vasopressin/ Octreotide with midodrine) is the approved treatment.

Liver transplantation is the definitive management.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 344 Pg: 2632.

question_text: A 55-year-old male with chronic alcoholism presents with vomiting, altered sensorium, and hypotension. His last binge was 7 days ago. Ultrasound shows small coarse liver and mild portal vein dilatation. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
option_a: Administer lactulose and wait for stool passage
option_b: Perform endoscopy to assess for varices
option_c: Initiate treatment with thiamine and chlordiazepoxide
option_d: Conduct a CT scan of the brain
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture is consistent with alcohol withdrawal syndrome (AWS) specifically delirium tremens (DTs), which usually occurs 3-10 days after last drink.
Symptoms: confusion, agitation, tremors, hallucinations, sweating, and autonomic instability.

Key Principles of Management:

  • Prevent Wernicke's Encephalopathy:
    • Administer Thiamine (100 mg IV) before any glucose-containing fluids to prevent precipitation of Wernicke's (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion).
  • Control Withdrawal Symptoms:
    • Use benzodiazepines (Chlordiazepoxide or Lorazepam) to manage agitation and prevent seizures.
  • Supportive Measures:
    • Correct fluids, electrolytes, and monitor for hepatic encephalopathy.

Explanation of Other Options:

Administer lactulose and wait for stool passage (Option A):

  • Lactulose is used in hepatic encephalopathy, not alcohol withdrawal.
  • Works by reducing intestinal ammonia absorption.
  • Here, altered sensorium is from withdrawal, not ammonia accumulation.
  • Giving lactulose delays life-saving benzodiazepine therapy.

Perform endoscopy to assess for varices (Option B):

  • Used for portal hypertension screening in stable patients.
  • Not indicated in acute alcohol withdrawal.
  • Performing endoscopy in a delirious patient is unsafe.
  • Priority is stabilization, not endoscopic evaluation.

Conduct a CT scan of the brain (Option D):

  • Not the first step andindicated only if neurological deficits persist after stabilization.
  • Altered mental status in AWS is metabolic, not structural.
  • Early imaging can delay critical intervention.
  • Focus should be on supportive and sedative therapy.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Small coarse liver → chronic liver disease
  • Last drink 7 days ago + altered sensorium → delirium tremens (not hepatic encephalopathy, which occurs later with hyperammonemia).

question_text: Which of the following criteria is used for the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?
explanation:
The revised Atlanta classification requires that two or more of the following criteria be met for the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis:

  1. Abdominal pain consistent with acute pancreatitis (acute onset of a persistent, severe, epigastric pain often radiating to the back);
  2. serum lipase activity (or amylase activity) at least three times greater than the upper limit of normal;
  3. characteristic findings of acute pancreatitis on contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) and less commonly magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or transabdominal ultrasonography.

The Revised Atlanta Criteria define

  1. Phases of acute pancreatitis,
  2. severity of acute pancreatitis, and
  3. radiographic definitions

Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 348, pg. 2661

question_text: A 44 year old man has drunk 50 units a week of alcohol for 20 years. During investigations, she has :Haemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, MCV 110 fL (80-96), white cell count 2.1 x 10^9/L (4-11), platelet count 75 x 10^9/L (150-400). What might explain these results?
explanation:
The haematological picture is that of macrocytic anemia (most commonly due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency).

Folate deficiency occurs in the majority of binge-drinking alcoholics and is a common cause of anemia. Inadequate dietary intake, intestinal malabsorption, and impaired folate storage in the liver all contribute to folate deficiency.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine21st ed, ch: 99, Pg: 773

question_text: A 34 year old lady has developed worsening pruritus and jaundice over the past year. Investigations revealed a positive antimitochondrial antibody and a liver biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of primary biliary cirrhosis. Which of the following is associated with the condition?
explanation:
Primary biliary cirrhosis is more common in females and is usually associated with raised IgM levels. Xanthelasma are present due to cholestasis. Connective tissue disorders such as Sjogren's syndrome are associated. A positive antimitochondrial antibody and liver biopsy are the best ways to confirm the diagnosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine , 21st Ed, Ch: 344 Pg: 2627

question_text: The patient is exhibiting these specific hand movements. Which condition is most likely associated with this presentation?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The typical hand movements shown in the image are known as asterixis or flapping tremors. These can be seen in

Asterixis

  • The hand movements shown in the image are called asterixis, also referred to as flapping tremors.
  • These movements are characteristic of toxic-metabolic encephalopathy.
  • Common causes include:
    • Hepatic encephalopathy
    • Due to elevated ammonia levels.
    • Uremic encephalopathy - due to elevated urea levels.
    • Hypercapnia (chronic CO retention)
      • Often seen in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), especially those receiving supplemental oxygen.
  • Asterixis is elicited by having the patient extend their arms, dorsiflex the wrists, and spread the fingers.
  • The involuntary flapping movement of the hands indicates impaired motor control associated with metabolic derangements.

Explanation of other options:

Thyrotoxicosis (Option A): Thyrotoxicosis presents with fine tremors. The tremor pattern is distinctly different from the coarse flapping movements seen in asterixis.

Hemiballismus (Option C): Manifests with wild, flinging movements at the shoulder joint. These movements are abrupt and unilateral compared to the bilateral wrist movements seen in asterixis.

Hypoxia (Option D): Hypoxia typically causes disorientation and mental status changes with O2 saturation <90%. While it can cause neurological symptoms, it does not specifically produce the characteristic flapping tremor seen in this case.

Reference:

  1. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK535445/#:~:text=Definition%2FIntroduction,lapses%20during%20a%20sustained%20posture.

question_text: Which drug should be preferred for treating a 45-year-old individual with a history of chronic alcoholism, who has been admitted to the hospital with symptoms of fever and abdominal pain, and was previously diagnosed with liver cirrhosis two years ago, as indicated by a neutrophil count of 360 cells/microliter in the ascitic fluid?
explanation:
Explanation:

An ascitic fluid neutrophil count >250 cells/µL in a cirrhotic patient with symptoms confirms Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP). Empiric antibiotic therapy must cover the most common gram-negative enteric organisms (e.g., E. coli, Klebsiella) and gram-positive organisms (e.g., Streptococcus species). Intravenous third-generation cephalosporins, like cefotaxime, are the first-line empiric treatment due to their broad coverage and excellent ascitic fluid penetration.

Explanation of other options:

Metronidazole (Option B): Covers anaerobic bacteria, which are not common pathogens in SBP.

Amoxicillin (Option C): Lacks sufficient spectrum and is not recommended for empiric SBP treatment.

Vancomycin (Option D): Reserved for suspected or proven methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections, not for initial empiric coverage.

Key Takeaways:

  • Ascitic fluid neutrophil count >250 cells/µL is diagnostic for SBP.
  • IV cefotaxime (or ceftriaxone) is the empiric antibiotic of choice.

question_text: A 45-year-old patient with chronic hepatitis C has now developed hypotension and oliguria. His liver and renal function tests suggest hepatorenal syndrome. Which of the following measures is likely to improve his prognosis?
explanation:
Hepatorenal syndrome is due to reduced renal cortical perfusion, caused by accumulation of toxins which would normally be cleared by the liver. Liver transplantation is the only option which would provide a resolution of this problem.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 310, Pg: 2306.

question_text: Which among the following indicates characteristic bilateral asterixis sign in a drowsy & confused patient?
explanation:
Characteristic bilateral asterixis sign is s/o metabolic encephalopathy or drug intoxication in a drowsy and confused patient.

Reference: Harrison 20th chap 300 pg. 2071

question_text: All of the following are true about NLPHL except
option_d: Poor prognosis compared to classical Hl
explanation: NLPHL is now considered to be a distinct entity from HL. The neoplastic cells in NLPHL are called the HRS like cells or L&H cells or popcorn cells. They lack CD15 and CD 30 unlike RS cells. They are positive for CD19, 20, 45, 79a and BCL2. They run a chronic indolent course. EBV is implicated in HL and not NLPHL.

question_text:
A 35-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C is admitted with general deterioration, he has no specific symptoms.He has missed many of his previous outpatient appointments and currently is not receiving any treatment.On examination he is generally unwell with a temperature of 37.4°C, blood pressure of 130/72 mmHg and appears jaundiced with the presence of ascites.His investigations reveal:
Serum Sodium 133 mmol/L (137-144)
Serum Potassium 4.3 mmol/L (3.5-4.9)
Serum Urea 100 mg/dl (18-44 mg/dL)
Serum Creatinine 3 mg/dL (0.6-1.4 mg/dL)
Bilirubin 4.8 mg/dl (0.2-1.2 mg/dL)
AST 92 U/L (5-35)
Alk Phosphatase 267 U/L (45-105)
Albumin 3.0 g/dL (3.7-4.9)
Urine sodium 60 mmol/L
Urine dipstick - + blood, +++ protein, leukocytes trace, nitrites negative
Ascitic fluid analysis - RBCs 1,231/mm3, WBCs 190/ mm3 (60% lymphocytes), albumin 12 g/L
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This gentleman has renal failure with evidence of a primary renal pathology - significant proteinuria, relative hypertension. Hepatitis C infection is strongly associated with mixed essential cryoglobulinemia which may produce mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis. This condition is associated with renal impairment, systemic vasculitic manifestations (including neuropathy, skin manifestations) and arterial thrombosis.

Hepatorenal syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion and requires correction of hypovolaemia, withdrawal of any diuretics, treatment of sepsis and exclusion of a primary renal pathology prior to diagnosis. In hepatorenal syndrome the kidneys are functionally normal and biopsy is normal, where patients in this situation receive liver transplantation the kidneys will almost always resume normal function. The urinary sodium and urine dipstick results given here indicate a primary renal pathology.

The ascitic tap results indicate that ascites is due to portal hypertension (serum albumin ascites gradient >11 g/L) and do not support the presence of infection within the ascitic fluid, counting against both abdominal tuberculosis and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

In the absence of symptoms, a urine dipstick indicating a trace of leukocytes and negative nitrite is poorly predictive of the presence of a urinary tract infection, additionally this diagnosis does not adequately explain the degree of proteinuria or renal impairment.

question_text:
A 42 year man with chronic hepatitis C has nonspecific general deterioration.On examination he has a temperature of 37.8 C, pressure of 100/70 mmHg and is jaundiced. His investigations reveal:

bilirubin 3.2 mg/dl

Alk Phosphatase 250 (50-120) U/l
Albumin 3.0 (3.3-4.2) g/dl
Urine sodium 15 mmol/l
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is the development of renal dysfunction in patients with severe liver disease (acute or chronic) in the absence of any other identifiable causes of renal pathology.

Two types of HRS have been described:

Type 1 is mainly associated with acute liver failure or alcoholic cirrhosis, but it can develop in any other form of liver failure. It is characterized by rapid deterioration of renal function, with marked increase in serum creatinine and urea. Hyponatremia and hyperkalemia are usual findings.

Type 2 is a more stable form. Peritoneal dialysis, hemodialysis, and hemofiltration remain controversial because of their limited benefit. However, they are still employed by certain centers in patients awaiting liver transplantation.

question_text: A patient comes with a blood pressure of 160/100 mmHg and left-sided facial paralysis and weakness for the last 8 hrs, there are no significant findings in her CT brain. What would be your next step of management?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient presents with an acute ischemic stroke outside the 4.5-hour therapeutic window for IV thrombolysis. A non-contrast CT brain is typically normal in the early hours of an ischemic stroke. Therefore, the cornerstone of management at this stage is supportive care, which includes close observation and monitoring for neurological changes, managing complications, and initiating secondary prevention (e.g., antiplatelets, statins).

Explanation of other options:

Intravenous labetalol and Oral Nifedipine (Option B and D): Blood pressure should not be aggressively lowered in acute ischemic stroke unless it is very high (>220/120 mmHg) or the patient is eligible for thrombolysis (requiring BP <185/110 mmHg). Aggressive reduction can worsen perfusion in the ischemic penumbra.

Intravenous thrombolysis (Option C): This is contraindicated as the symptom onset was 8 hours ago, which is beyond the standard 4.5-hour window for alteplase.

Key Takeaways:

  • IV thrombolysis is only indicated within 4.5 hours of symptom onset.
  • For patients presenting outside the window, management focuses on supportive care, rehabilitation, and secondary prevention.

question_text: The patient presents to the clinic with pedal oedema, elevated JVP up to the mandible, and ascites. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of pedal oedema, markedly raised JVP to the mandible, and ascites indicates severe systemic venous congestion, a hallmark of right-sided heart failure.

  • When the heart's pumping function is impaired, it causes venous backpressure, leading to fluid buildup in dependent regions (pedal oedema), distension of the jugular veins (raised JVP), and fluid collection in the abdomen (ascites).
  • The Framingham criteria are used to establish the diagnosis of congestive heart failure (CHF).

Explanations of other options:

Renal failure (Option B): Although renal failure can result in fluid overload and oedema, it usually does not produce the characteristic combination of elevated JVP and ascites seen here. While kidney failure may cause swelling, this pattern of findings is more strongly linked to heart failure.

Liver failure (Option C): Liver failure may cause ascites because of impaired fluid regulation and reduced synthesis of proteins that help retain fluid within blood vessels. However, the marked rise in JVP up to the mandible is unlikely in liver failure and is more typical of systemic venous congestion seen in cardiac failure.

Brain injury (Option D): Brain injury is unlikely to account for the symptoms described unless it directly affects regions regulating fluid balance. While it may produce neurological deficits, it does not explain the triad of pedal oedema, elevated JVP, and ascites observed in this patient.

Reference:

question_text:
Which of the following findings from a pleural fluid aspirate will suggest an exudative pleural effusion?
*Normal Values: Serum Protein: 6-8 gm%; Serum LDH: 140-280 IU; Serum Glucose: 140-200 mg%*
option_a: Pleural:Serum protein ratio > 0.5, Pleural:Serum LDH ratio > 0.6, or Pleural LDH > ⅔ of the upper limit of normal serum LDH
option_b: Pleural fluid protein = 4.5 gm% and glucose = 30 mg%
option_c: Pleural fluid LDH = 90 IU and glucose = 30 mg%
option_d: Pleural fluid protein = 3.5 gm% and glucose = 90 mg%
explanation:
Explanation:

The definitive method to classify a pleural effusion as exudative is by applying Light's Criteria. An effusion is an exudate if it meets at least one of the following three conditions:

  1. Pleural fluid protein / Serum protein ratio > 0.5
  2. Pleural fluid LDH / Serum LDH ratio > 0.6
  3. Pleural fluid LDH level > 2/3 the upper limit of normal serum LDH

These ratios and absolute value effectively differentiate effusions caused by increased capillary permeability (exudates, e.g., due to pneumonia, cancer, TB) from those due to imbalances in hydrostatic or oncotic pressure (transudates, e.g., due to heart failure, cirrhosis).

In pleural effusion on X-ray, about 200 mL of fluid is required for detection on the PA view, while as little as 50 mL can cause blunting of the costophrenic angle on the lateral view.

Pleural effusion typically appears as a homogeneous opacity with obliteration of the costophrenic and sometimes cardiophrenic angles, often showing a curved upper border called the Ellis S-shaped curve. Ultrasound is more sensitive, revealing a hypoechoic space in transudates and moving internal echoes in exudates.

Explanation of other options:

Pleural fluid protein = 4.5 gm% and glucose = 30 mg% (Option B): While a low glucose suggests an exudate, the protein level is intermediate. Without the serum protein for ratio calculation, it cannot be definitively classified using Light's Criteria.

Pleural fluid LDH = 90IU and glucose = 30 mg% (Option C): The LDH value is too low to meet the exudative threshold. The low glucose is not a primary criterion.

Pleural fluid protein = 3.5gm% and glucose = 90 mg% (Option D): This combination (low protein, normal glucose) is classic for a transudative effusion.

Key Takeaways:

  • Light's Criteria are the gold standard for differentiating exudative from transudative pleural effusions.
  • An effusion must meet at least one of the three criteria to be classified as an exudate.
  • Findings like low glucose or specific cell counts help narrow the cause of an exudate but are not used for the initial classification.

A 77-year-old male is admitted with acute confusion and is agitated and aggressive to staff.

explanation:
The patient in this question is suffering from Delirium.

From among the options Quetiapine is the drug used in delirium, though with limited proven benefits. Chlorpromazine is another antipsychotic, but its use is associated with significant adverse effects and should be avoided in elderly.

Management of delirium:

  • Treating the underlying cause.
  • Sensory aids to promote wakefulness at day time. Like keeping the windows open, using glasses and hearing aids, engaging in walking. Attempting to mimic home environment.
  • Maintaining dark environment at night.
  • Minimizing restrains.
  • Drugs to calm the patient should be avoided, and should be given only if there is a risk of self harm or harm to the care givers. Typical or atypical antipsychotics should be given, in a very low dose, on an as needed basis. But they don't have a proven benefit in treating delirium.
  • Benzodiazepines should not be used as it worsens confusion.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 27, Pg: 182

question_text: CFTR gene mutation involves which ion and which mutation?
option_a: Chloride ion and deletion of phenylalanine at 508 positions
option_b: Chloride ion and deletion of tryptophan at 508 positions
option_c: Chloride ion and deletion of phenylalanine at 708 positions
option_d: Chloride ion and deletion of tryptophan at 708 positions
explanation:
The gene product responsible for CF is CFTR, which serves as an anion channel in the luminal surfaces of epithelial cells, where it regulates the volume and consistency of exocrine secretions.

CFTR mutations lead to abnormally thick secretions. In the lung it leads to recurrent infections.

In the pancreas, it leads to the obstruction of the pancreatic duct leading to malabsorption and steatorrhoea.

Obstruction of intrahepatic bile duct leads to cirrhosis, in males it leads to involution of vas deferens and infertility.

CFTR mutations:

Class I mutation: Absence of synthesis of CFTR. CFTR nonsense mutations like G542X, R553X, or W1282X are examples.

Class II mutation: Defective protein maturation and premature degradation. F508 deletion. Most common mutation. Lumacaftor and Tezacaftor repair CFTR misfolding and promote cell surface localization of F508 CFTR. Elexacaftor, is a third generation molecule effective for F508 as well as a variety of other CFTR mutations.

Class III: Disordered gating, ATP binding or hydrolysis. G551D, leads to inability to transport Cl or HCO3. Ivacaftor overcomes the defect. Approved for 96 other variants apart from G551D.

Class IV: Defective conductance through the pore.

Class V: A reduced number of CFTR transcripts.

Class VI: Accelerated turnover from the cell surface.

Ivacaftor tezacaftor and Elixacaftor are approved as triple combination therapy for CF. it benefits >90% cases with the disease. Improvements in FEV1, fewer infections, improvement in QOL and diminished sweat chloride levels. Designated as Highly Effective Modulator Treatment.

question_text: A 65 year old male patient visited the ER for chest pain and his BP was measured as SBP 190 mmHg, DBP 70 mmHg, Pulse pressure 90 mmHg. Which of the following parameters should decrease for the high pulse pressure?
explanation:
Pulse pressure = Systolic BP-Diastolic BP

The diastolic BP is determined by the arterial compliance.

The diastolic BP falls as the arterial compliance decreases as in old age.

The systolic BP is dependent on the stroke volume.

So for pulse pressure to increase, either the stroke volume has to increase or the arterial compliance has to decrease.

question_text: A 30-year-old woman presents with symptoms of an unsteady gait, memory loss, and mood swings. During the neurological examination, the findings shown in the image below are observed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image displays fine pigmented, granular deposits characteristic of Kayser-Fleischer rings, which result from copper buildup in the Descemet's membrane of the cornea. This finding is highly suggestive of Wilson's disease.

Wilson's Disease

Also called hepatolenticular degeneration, Wilson's disease is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by abnormal copper accumulation in the liver, brain, eyes, and other organs. This leads to elevated free copper levels, increased copper in the liver and urine, and decreased serum ceruloplasmin.

Genetic Cause:

The disease is caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene on chromosome 13. This gene encodes a copper-transporting ATPase responsible for removing copper from the liver into bile.

Pathogenesis:

  • Mutation in the ATP7B gene
  • Impaired biliary copper excretion
  • Copper accumulates in liver cells (hepatocytes)
  • Excess copper causes oxidative damage, promoting inflammation and fibrosis in the liver
  • When liver storage capacity is exceeded, copper is released into the bloodstream
  • Copper then accumulates in other tissues:
    • Brain: Particularly basal ganglia, causing neurological symptoms
    • Cornea: Forms Kayser-Fleischer rings
    • Kidneys: Can lead to renal dysfunction
    • Joints: Causes arthritic changes
  • Copper accumulation causes tissue damage through oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and enzyme inhibition

Explanation of Other Options:

Neurofibromatosis 2 (Option A): typically presents with juvenile cataracts in children, retinal hamartomas, and similar features.

Neurofibromatosis 1 (Option C): is characterized by Lisch nodules, which are small, raised brown spots on the iris.

Cataracts (Option D): usually appear as wedge-shaped opacities (cortical cataracts) or darkened lenses (nuclear cataracts) with distinct clinical signs. The scenario described here does not align with cataract presentations.
