question_text: Congo red positivity and apple green bifringence is seen in which among the conditions?
explanation:
Explanation:

The diagnostic hallmark of amyloidosis is the detection of amyloid protein deposits in tissues. The most widely used method is Congo red staining, which shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy.

  • Amyloid is formed from misfolded proteins that aggregate into β-pleated sheet structures, giving them a unique staining pattern.
  • On routine histology, amyloid appears as amorphous, eosinophilic deposits. When stained with Congo red dye, these deposits display apple-green birefringence under polarized light - a pathognomonic feature of amyloidosis.
  • This is in contrast to other protein deposits such as collagen, which appear white under polarized light.
  • The deposits can be detected in tissues like abdominal fat (via fat pad biopsy), kidney, heart, liver, rectal mucosa, or gingiva.

Multiple myeloma (Option A): While AL amyloidosis can occur secondary to multiple myeloma, the staining pattern itself is not a feature of myeloma but specifically of amyloid.

Sarcoidosis (Option B): Characterized by non-caseating granulomas, not amyloid deposits, and does not show Congo red positivity.

Hemochromatosis (Option C): Involves iron overload in tissues, demonstrated by Prussian blue staining, not Congo red.

He also has a history of hypertension, for which he takes Ramipril. Which of the following drug classes is most well known as a cause of impaired glucose tolerance?
explanation:
• Older atypical antipsychotic agents have been implicated as a cause of impaired glucose tolerance, and are thought to put those taking them at increased risk of type-2 diabetes.
  • Thiazides and β-blockers may also impact negatively on the incidence of new diabetes, and this combination of antihypertensives is no longer a first choice for patients with a high type-2 diabetes risk.
  • Ramipril was shown in the HOPE (Healthcare Options Plan Entitlement) study to reduce progression to type-2 diabetes; this is thought to be mediated by a reduction in insulin resistance.
  • The LIFE (Longitudinal Interval Follow-up Evaluation) study using losartan has demonstrated that angiotensin-receptor blockers also probably reduce the incidence of new cases of type-2 diabetes.
  • Thiazolidinediones and biguanides work by primarily reducing insulin resistance, sulphonylureas stimulate insulin release; all three are used as treatments for type-2 diabetes.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Pg:3095

question_text: A 43-year-old woman is diagnosed with pheochromocytoma. Screening with pentagastrin testing suggests that she has medullary thyroid carcinoma, and you plan a thyroidectomy. What anti-hypertensive medication should be started before surgery for a patient with pheochromocytoma?
explanation:
• Phenoxybenzamine is a more potent alpha-blocker than doxazosin and is the recommended choice for initial anti-hypertensive medication in pheochromocytoma where surgery is contemplated. It should be given in divided doses, at 20 mg initially, increasing to 80 mg.
  • Patients should then be considered for additional b -blockade with propranolol, again in divided doses up to 240 mg/day. Always start with a -blockade first, as initial use of β-blockers may worsen hypertension. Labetalol is not recommended.


Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 20th edition Chapter:380 Page number:2743

question_text: A 52-year-old patient on metformin and gliclazide for his type-2 diabetes presents for review. He has a BMI of 31 and his blood pressure is 158/92 mmHg. When considering hypertension in type-2 diabetes, which of the following statements best fits the condition?
option_a: Development of hypertension is strongly linked to a genetically inherited variant of red cell sodium-lithium counter-transport activity
option_b: Good hypertensive control has a weaker effect on macrovascular outcomes than good tight glucose control
option_c: Hypertension in type-2 diabetes is primarily associated with hyperinsulinaemia and insulin resistance
option_d: Thiazide diuretics are the treatment of choice in patients with hypertension and microalbuminuria
explanation:
• Hyperinsulinaemia directly stimulates sympathetic nervous system activity, increasing renal sodium reabsorption and promoting vascular smooth muscle proliferation.
  • Insulin resistance is also associated with the reduced activity of nitric oxide synthase, leading to reduced vasodilatation in response to vascular stress.
  • Red cell sodium-lithium counter-transport activity abnormalities are associated with the early development of hypertension in type-1 diabetes.
  • Between 30 and 50% of Caucasians with type-2 diabetes have a systolic blood pressure above 160 mmHg.
  • ACE inhibitors are the treatment of choice for diabetic hypertension, particularly where micro-albuminuria coexists.
  • Thiazide diuretics and β-blockers may worsen glycaemic control.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:3096

question_text: All of the following increase risk of Alzheimer's disease except?
explanation:
• A history of head trauma with concussion increases the risk for AD.
  • AD is more common in groups with low educational attainment, but education influences test-taking ability, and it is clear that AD can affect persons of all intellectual levels.
  • Diabetes increases the risk of AD threefold.
  • Elevated homocysteine and cholesterol levels; hypertension; diminished serum levels of folic acid; low dietary intake of fruits, vegetables, and red wine; and low levels of exercise are all being explored as potential risk factors for AD.

Several retrospective studies suggest that nonsteroidal antiinflammatory agents and 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase inhibitors (statins) may have a protective effect on dementia if used prior to the onset of disease but do not influence clinically symptomatic AD.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 431, Pg: 3372

question_text: A 30-year-old woman presents with vomiting, malaise and weakness 5 weeks after delivering a healthy male infant. The pregnancy had been uncomplicated with no hypertension evident. Her blood pressure is now 210/110 mmHg, plasma creatinine is 5.5 mg/dl and potassium: 6.9 mmol/l. Haemoglobin: 7.6 g/dl, platelet count of 65000/&microl, reticulocytes of 7%, normal clotting indices and lactate dehydrogenase levels of 800 IU/l. Which of the following most accurately describes the pathological process?
explanation:
The history is typical of postpartum haemolytic-uraemic syndrome(HUS), which usually occurs 4-6 week's postpartum and is characterised by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, severe irreversible renal failure and hypertension. Schistocytes are evident on the blood film but the clotting indices are normal, the latter helping to distinguish it from the DIC. The differential diagnosis of acute renal failure in the setting of pregnancy includes postpartum HUS, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura(which occurs invariably antepartum and usually before 24 weeks and is associated with relatively mild renal failure) and the HELLP syndrome(which is usually preceded by a history of pre-eclampsia and is characterised by evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation). All may be complicated by acute cortical necrosis, resulting in oliguria, haematuria and flank pain. In cases of postpartum HUS, it is important to consider the possibility of retained products of conception.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2348.

question_text: A 39 year old man who has a history of heavy alcohol intake presents with hematemesis and melena. On admission, he was in a pre-shock state with severe anemia and was resuscitated with blood and fresh frozen plasma. Endoscopic examination identified bleeding from the varices in the lower esophagus. Which one of the following drugs should be used for treatment?
explanation:
Octreotide and terlipressin are widely used in acute variceal hemorrhage to reduce the bleeding rate octreotide is often used for emergency treatment of bleeding oesophageal varices in patients with cirrhosis of the liver. It is given intravenously.It acts by causing splanchnic vasoconstriction and should be given for a minimum 48 hours.

Propranolol and Nadolol are used for prophylaxis of bleeding in a patient known to have esophageal varices. They should not be used in an acute condition as they can cause hypotension.

Vitamin K is used to treat hepatic coagulopathy in acute liver failure, warfarin overdose and vit K deficiency of the newborn.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine , 21st Ed, Ch: 344 Pg: 2630

question_text: A 60-year-old male with a history of cirrhosis presents with worsening ascites. The physician decides to calculate the Serum-Ascitic Albumin Gradient(SAAG). Based on the SAAG value, the physician can classify the likely cause of the ascites. Which of the following statements regarding the SAAG score is incorrect?
option_a: SAAG score < 1.1 is typically associated with ascites due to peritoneal carcinomatosis, tuberculous peritonitis, or nephrotic syndrome.
option_b: SAAG score > 1.1 suggests ascites is most likely caused by portal hypertension due to conditions such as cirrhosis, heart failure, or Budd-Chiari syndrome.
option_c: SAAG score > 2.5 is often associated with ascites caused by cirrhosis and heart failure, where there is high protein content in the ascitic fluid.
option_d: SAAG score < 2.5 typically suggests that ascites is due to non-portal hypertensive conditions, which generally result in low protein content in the ascitic fluid.
explanation:
Explanation:

A high serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL) combined with a high ascitic fluid protein level (≥2.5 g/dL) suggests preserved hepatic sinusoidal integrity. This pattern is characteristic of conditions such as cardiac ascites or early Budd-Chiari syndrome, rather than cirrhosis or advanced heart failure, where sinusoidal damage typically leads to a low protein content in the ascitic fluid despite a high SAAG.

  • Serum-Ascitic Albumin Gradient (SAAG): Calculated by subtracting the ascitic albumin concentration from the serum albumin level.
  • SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL: Indicates portal hypertension, with possible causes including cirrhosis, cardiac ascites, Budd-Chiari syndrome, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, or massive liver metastases.
  • SAAG < 1.1 g/dL: Suggests non-portal hypertensive conditions like tuberculous peritonitis or peritoneal carcinomatosis.
  • Ascitic Protein Level: Additional diagnostic marker with a high protein level (≥2.5 g/dL) indicating conditions like cardiac ascites and a low level (<2.5 g/dL) typical of cirrhosis or late Budd-Chiari syndrome.
  • Additional Testing: Depending on clinical suspicions, tests like ascitic glucose, LDH, amylase, cytology, and cultures may be required to further identify the cause of ascites.

Explanation of other options:

SAAG score < 1.1 is typically associated with ascites due to peritoneal carcinomatosis, tuberculous peritonitis, or nephrotic syndrome. (Option A): A SAAG value less than 1.1 g/dL suggests that the ascites is not related to portal hypertension. This score points to causes like peritoneal carcinomatosis, tuberculous peritonitis, and nephrotic syndrome, where portal hypertension is not a factor.

SAAG score > 1.1 suggests ascites is most likely caused by portal hypertension due to conditions such as cirrhosis, heart failure, or Budd-Chiari syndrome. (Option B): A SAAG greater than 1.1 g/dL indicates the presence of portal hypertension, which could be due to conditions such as cirrhosis, heart failure, or Budd-Chiari syndrome. This is the usual threshold to indicate that the ascites is due to increased pressure within the hepatic sinusoids.

SAAG score < 2.5 typically suggests that ascites is due to non-portal hypertensive conditions, which generally result in low protein content in the ascitic fluid. (Option D): This statement is misleading as it seems to conflate the protein content with the SAAG score. SAAG is calculated solely based on the difference between serum and ascitic albumin levels and does not directly measure protein content. A low protein content (<2.5 g/dL) with a high SAAG (≥1.1 g/dL) indicates damaged hepatic sinusoids, typical of cirrhosis.

Key Takeaways:

A high SAAG (>1.1 g/dL) with a high ascitic protein (>2.5 g/dL) is more typical of cardiac ascites or early Budd-Chiari syndrome, not cirrhosis. The incorrect statement in this question is Choice C.

question_text:
A 37-year-old female presents with headaches. Examination reveals papilloedema.
Which of the following would make the diagnosis of benign intracranial hypertension (BIH) unlikely?
option_c: Normal ventricles on CT or MRI scan
explanation:
• BIH is typically associated with papilloedema, reduced venous pulsation and normal appearances of the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
  • A VIth nerve palsy is a recognised association.
  • Reflexes are preserved and plantars are flexor.
  • Extensor plantars suggest an alternative diagnosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 16Pg: 116

question_text:
A 60-year-old man takes atenolol for hypertension. 
Which of the following side effects is he most likely to be aware of two hours after taking atenolol?
explanation:
Atenolol is a water soluble beta blocker, taken once daily and is not associated with drowsiness/sleep disturbance like the lipid-soluble β-blockers. It is not associated with nausea or hesitancy of micturition and would be unlikely to produce significant postural hypotension in a hypertensive subject.

However, fatigue is a frequent side effect which typically is felt two hours and beyond after taking the drug.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:271 pg:1903

question_text: A 44-year-old woman is referred to the clinic with difficult to manage hypertension. She is currently taking indapamide, Ramipril, amlodipine and doxazosin, yet her blood pressure is still 155/95 mmHg. On examination she has a BMI of 25. Ophthalmoscopy reveals evidence of Stage 3 hypertensive retinopathy. Blood reports reveal;Hb 14.0g/dl, WCC 5800/mm³, PLT 184000/mm³, Na+ 139mmol/l, K+ 3.1mmol/l and Creatinine 1 mg/dl. Her USG abdomen and Renal artery Doppler testing was normal. What would be your next step in evaluation?
explanation:
• This patient has hypertension not controlled even on 4 antihypertensive agents with target organ damage and hypokalemia
  • Aldosterone-renin ratio is the screening investigation of choice for primary aldosteronism
  • Whilst CT/ MRI abdomen is useful in differentiating the underlying cause of primary hyperaldosteronism (bilateral adrenal hyperplasia vs adenoma, aldosterone: renin ratio is still needed to make the primary diagnosis.
  • Antihypertensives can affect interpretation of the result and ideally the test should be done following a period off medication.
  • History is not suggestive of Pheochromocytoma to warrant plasma metanephrine testing
  • There is no indication of Cushing's, so a morning cortisol is not likely to be useful in this case.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2965

question_text: A 38-year-old laborer is admitted to the Emergency room after falling off his ladder. Past history of note includes hypertension which is managed with nifedipine 10 mg daily. The Emergency scan reveals a 4 cm right sided adrenal mass. His blood pressure in the Emergency room is 145/90 mmHg. Blood results: Hb 12.1 g/dl, WCC 6200/mm³, PLT 232000/mm³, Na+ 138 mmol/l, K+ 2.6 mmol/l, Creatinine 0.8 mg/dl. Which of the following would be most likely to reveal the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
• Hypertension in a patient with adrenal mass suggest the possibility of either aldosterone producing adenoma or Pheochromocytoma. Presence of hypokalemia favours the diagnosis of primary aldosteronism.
  • Primary hyperaldosteronism is more common than was first believed, and may be responsible for 10-15% of cases of what is thought to be essential hypertension.
  • Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia is more common than aldosterone producing adenoma (Conn syndrome)

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2965

question_text: Pontine hemorrhage most common cause is
explanation: Answer- A. Hypertension Most common cause of pontine hemorrhage is hypertension.

question_text: Which among the following are false statements regarding pheochromocytoma?
option_a: Diagnosed by urine VMA and catecholamines
option_b: Treatment of choice is surgical excision
option_c: Propranolol is given initially to treat hypertension
option_d: Can present as hypertension alone, sometimes with abdominal pain and vomiting
explanation:
In the medical management of pheochromocytoma, the initial drug given is alpha adrenergic blockers, usually oral Phentolamine 0.5-4 mg/kg body weight.

While adequate alpha blockade is being achieved, any paroxysms of hypertension should be managed by either oral Prazosin or IV phentolamine.

Beta blockers are added later on.

If therapy is initiated with beta blocker alone, the catecholamines will act on the alpha receptors and will result in acute hypertensive crisis.

question_text: In a 35 year female patient with grade 2 primary pulmonary hypertension the vasoreactivity test was negative. Which of the following is the next step in management?
explanation: Negative vasoreactive test in young patients without any high risk factors, treatment with combination oral agents is considered. This includes Endothelin receptor antagonists and Phosphodiesterase inhibitors.

question_text:
A 14-year-old boy presents with hypertension. 
Which of the following statements concerning hypertension in the young is true?
option_a: Sodium nitroprusside is useful for the long-term treatment of severe cases.
option_b: It is defined as systolic blood pressure above the 99th centile for age.
option_c: Abnormalities are frequently seen on DMSA scan.
option_d: Aortic coarctation is the commonest secondary cause.
explanation:
Secondary causes are usually due to renal abnormalities, with reflux associated scarring being the commonest renal disease. This will cause abnormalities on DMSA scan.

Coarctation of the aorta is the commonest non-renal cause, with pheochromocytoma / neuroblastoma, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing Syndrome and steroid therapy being rarer causes.

Sodium nitroprusside is useful only in the short term, as cyanide levels accumulate with time.

Hypertension is usually diagnosed incidentally, and is defined as systolic blood pressure >95th centile for age.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:271 pg:1896,1897

question_text: A patient with hypertension is taking thiazide diuretics and reports fatigue with laboratory evidence of hypokalemia. Which of the following drugs can help prevent potassium loss?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic that acts by inhibiting the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in the distal nephron.
  • When used in combination with thiazide diuretics, it helps prevent hypokalemia while maintaining Thiazide's antihypertensive efficacy.
  • This combination approach is particularly useful in patients experiencing thiazide-induced hypokalemia.
  • Amiloride works as a weak antihypertensive but is valuable for its potassium-sparing properties, though it should be used cautiously in patients with renal failure or hyperkalemia.

question_text: Portal hypertension is defined as hepatic venous pressure gradient above __mm Hg?
explanation:
Portal hypertension is defined as the elevation of the hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) to >5 mm Hg.

clinically significant portal hypertension is defined as a HVPG ≥10 mmHg, when there is substantial risk of decompensation with variceal bleeding.

Cirrhosis is the most common cause of portal hypertension

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 344 pg. 2629

question_text: Which of the following leads to postsinusoidal hepatic portal hypertension?
explanation:
Veno occlusive syndrome leads to Hepatic sinusoidal obstruction and causes portal hypertension

Options A and C: BCS and constrictive pericarditis are posthepatic causes of portal hypertension

Option D: Alcoholic hepatitis is a sinusoidal hepatic cause

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 344 pg. 2629

question_text: In a patient with pheochromocytoma, what is the drug of choice for controlling high blood pressure?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In pheochromocytoma, catecholamine excess causes paroxysmal or sustained hypertension.
  • The drug of choice for preoperative blood pressure control is phenoxybenzamine, an irreversible non-selective α-adrenergic blocker.
  • It prevents catecholamine-induced vasoconstriction, reduces blood pressure, and helps expand intravascular volume before surgical resection.

Explanation of other options:

Labetalol (Option B): Although it blocks both α and β receptors, it is not preferred initially because β-blockade without adequate α-blockade can precipitate hypertensive crisis.

Propranolol (Option C): A pure β-blocker; contraindicated before α-blockade since unopposed α-adrenergic activity can worsen hypertension.

Prazosin (Option D): A selective α1-blocker that may be used, but phenoxybenzamine remains the preferred drug due to its irreversible action and long duration.

question_text: A patient who is a known case of hypertension on multiple antihypertensive medications came to the OPD. His ECG finding is given below. Which of the following drugs is responsible for the ECG finding?
explanation:
Explanation:

Spironolactone can cause hyperkalemia, which presents on ECG as tall, peaked T waves.

  • The ECG finding of tall, peaked T waves is a classic sign of hyperkalemia.
  • Among the given options, spironolactone is the most likely culprit because it is a potassium-sparing diuretic.
  • It acts by blocking aldosterone receptors in the distal tubule and collecting duct, thereby inhibiting sodium reabsorption and reducing potassium excretion.
  • This leads to potassium retention, raising serum potassium levels and causing hyperkalemia.
  • ECG changes in hyperkalemia progress with severity:

Explanation of other options:

Prazosin (Option A): Alpha-1 blocker used in hypertension; not associated with hyperkalemia.

Metoprolol (Option B): Beta-blocker; does not usually cause hyperkalemia, though rare cases exist in renal dysfunction.

Hydrochlorothiazide (Option C): Thiazide diuretic that promotes potassium loss, leading to hypokalemia rather than hyperkalemia.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6205312/

question_text: Correct about presentation of neurogenic shock is?
explanation: Neurogenic shock is associated with bradycardia and hypotension. It is a type of distributive shock.

question_text: Resistant hypertension is defined as when BP control is not occurring with use of 3 drugs. Among these, which of the following drug patients has to be on to meet the definition?
explanation: The term resistant hypertension refers to patients with blood pressures persistently >140/90 mmHg despite taking three or more antihypertensive agents, including a diuretic.

question_text: 'Obstruction of Inferior vena cava' presents :
explanation: :B A. Paraumbilicus vein dilation and B i.e. Thoraco-epigastric dilation The thoracoepigastric vein is unique in that it drains to both the Superior Vena Cava (SVC) and to the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC). Hence, it serves as an anastomotic caval-caval link between the two. Furthermore, the thoracoepigastric vein is connected to the portal vein via the paraumbilical vein and thereby serves as a portocaval anastomosis as well. When a patient experiences portal hypertension, there can be congestion (backup) of blood that enters into the caval system via the thoracoepigastric vein. When this occurs, there can be an externally visible dilation of the paraumbilical (and perhaps even the thoracoepigastric veins) which leads to the appearance of "Caput Medusae"

question_text: The predominant symptom/sign of pheochromocytoma is:
explanation: Answer is D (Episodic Hypertension): The predominant manifestation of Pheochromocytoma is Hypertension which classically presents as Episodic Hypertension (Sustained Hypertension and Orthostatic Hypotension may also be seen). 'The dominant sign is Hypertension. Classically patients have episodic hypertension, but sustained hypertension is also common' - Harrison

question_text: A 37 year old man presents with 2 bowls full of haematemesis. He drinks 10 pints of beer a day and has done so for 10 years. Upper GI endoscopy reveals esophageal varices. Which of the following is effective in reducing the rates of rebleeding in the future?
explanation:
Beta blockers (propanolol, nadolol), nitrates, vasopressin analogues and somatostatin analogues can be used for reducing rebleeding in oesophageal varices.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 344 Pg: 2630

question_text: Which animal is most likely to have bitten a 10-year-old child who now presents with tachycardia, hypertension, tongue fasciculations, excessive salivation, dilated pupils, and mild redness around the wound? The child remembers that the animal had a curved tail pointing upwards.
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical symptoms and the description of the animal with a curved tail pointing upwards strongly suggest a scorpion sting.

Less dangerous scorpions:

  • Cause local pain, swelling, and burning sensations.
  • Symptoms usually resolve within a few hours.
  • Allergic reactions to venom are possible.

Bark scorpions (e.g., Centruroides species):

  • Cause intense pain, tingling, and heightened sensitivity, worsened by tapping.
  • Symptoms include restlessness, blurred vision, abnormal eye movements.
  • Excessive salivation, sweating, and difficulty managing secretions.
  • Nausea, vomiting, slurred speech.
  • Muscle twitching, jerking, and shaking that may mimic seizures.
  • Tachycardia, arrhythmias, hypertension, hyperthermia, and rhabdomyolysis.
  • Risk of respiratory arrest, especially in children and elderly patients.

Venomous scorpions (e.g., Tityus serrulatus, Leiurus quinquestriatus):

  • May cause hypertensive crises, arrhythmias, and myocardial damage.
  • Pulmonary edema and central nervous system toxicity are possible.

Other species (e.g., Hemiscorpius lepturus):

  • Pain, hemolysis, and tissue necrosis with delayed onset.
  • Systemic effects can include hemoglobinuria and acute kidney injury.

General symptoms of scorpion envenomation:

  • Immediate sharp local pain.
  • Swelling, bruising, and burning sensation.
  • Most symptoms resolve within hours for less dangerous species.

Treatment:

  • Identifying the scorpion species is crucial to guide treatment. Non-lethal stings typically require only basic care.
  • For mild stings, home management with ice packs, pain relief, and antihistamines is often sufficient. Patients should seek emergency care if neurological symptoms develop.
  • Severe envenomations require aggressive supportive care and may need antivenom to prevent fatalities.
  • Initial measures include keeping the patient calm, applying pressure dressings, and using cold packs to reduce venom spread.
  • Midazolam IV infusion can help control agitation and muscle spasms, but patients must be monitored closely due to the risk of respiratory arrest, especially when sedatives or narcotics are used.
  • Hypertension and pulmonary edema can be treated with medications such as nifedipine, nitroprusside, hydralazine, or prazosin.
  • Bradycardia is managed with atropine.
  • FDA-approved antivenin (e.g., sculpturatus IgG F(ab')2) is available in some countries and can quickly reverse neurological and muscular symptoms when given intravenously.

Options A, B, and D are incorrect.

question_text: A patient with uncontrolled hypertension on amlodipine losartan and hydrochlorothiazide medications taken regularly. What is the next best step for the management of hypertension
explanation:
Explanation:

The next best step in this patient, already on a CCB (amlodipine), an ARB (losartan), and a thiazide diuretic (HCTZ), is spironolactone.

  • Spironolactone is highly effective because resistant hypertension is often driven by excess aldosterone activity.
  • When a patient remains hypertensive despite being on three antihypertensive agents (including a diuretic), the condition is termed resistant hypertension.
  • In resistant hypertension, the first step is to rule out pseudo-resistance (improper BP measurement, white coat effect, poor adherence) and secondary causes (OSA, renal artery stenosis, drugs raising BP, etc.).
  • Once true resistant hypertension is confirmed, guidelines recommend adding a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) such as spironolactone as the fourth-line therapy.

Increase dose of Losartan (Option B): Simply increasing ARB dose rarely controls resistant hypertension and is less effective than adding a new class (MRA).

Start Clonidine (Option C): Centrally acting drugs like clonidine are not the first choice due to side effects (sedation, rebound HTN). Used only in refractory cases.

Add Atenolol (Option D): Beta-blockers are not preferred unless there is a compelling indication (e.g., CAD, HF). They are not first choice in resistant hypertension.

question_text: Patient presented with massive abdominal swelling. Paracentesis fluid was sent for lab analysis and came out to be having serum protein to be 3g/dl and ascitic fluid protein to be 1g/dl. What could be the possible diagnosis?
explanation:
This question deals with the concept of SAAG. If the SAAG is <1.1, portal hypertension can be easily ruled out.

The causes are TB peritonitis, Carcinomatous peritonitis, pancreatitis and nephrotic syndrome.

A high SAAG with low ascitic fluid protein means the sinusoids are scarred and cant secrete protein and is seen in Cirrhosis, Late Budd chiari and massive liver mets.

High SAAG with high protein in ascitic fluid is seen in cardiac failure, early budd chiari, sinusoidal obstruction, IVC obstruction

Ascitic fluid LDH is measured if a secondary peritonitis is suspected. Secondary peritonitis is characterized by ascitic fluid glucose of < 50mg/dl, ascitic fluid LDH > serum LDH and poly bacterial culture of ascitic fluid.

Ascitic fluid amylase >1000 indicates pancreatitis.

With a cut off of 35-40u/L, ADA has a > 90% sensitivity in diagnosis of TB peritonitis.

question_text: Metabolic syndrome criteria include all. except?
explanation:
Metabolic syndrome constitutes a constellation of metabolic abnormalities that increases the risk of cardiovascular disease and diabetes.

The main components of metabolic syndrome are

  • central obesity,
  • hypertriglyceridemia,
  • low HDL,
  • hyperglycemia and
  • hypertension

CONDITIONS ASSOCIATED WITH METABOLIC SYNDOME X:

Cardiovascular diseases, Diabetes mellitus, non alcoholic steatohepatitis, hyperuricemia, PCOS, obstructive sleep apnoea.

Other metabolic alterations that occur secondary to or accompany insulin resistance include increases in apoB and apoC-III, uric acid, prothrombotic factors (fibrinogen, plasminogen activator inhibitor 1), serum viscosity, asymmetric dimethylarginine, homocysteine, white blood cell count, proinflammatory cytokines, C-reactive protein, urine albumin/creatinine ratio.

KEY TAKE AWAY

question_text: Which of the following is true regarding laboratory findings of  Zieve's Syndrome?
explanation:
A unique form of hemolytic anemia (with spur cells and acanthocytes) called Zieve's syndrome can occur in patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis. Platelet counts are often reduced early in the disease, reflective of portal hypertension with hypersplenism. Serum total bilirubin can be normal or elevated with advanced disease. Prothrombin times are often prolonged and usually do not respond to administration of parenteral vitamin K. Serum sodium levels are usually normal unless patients have ascites and then can be depressed, largely due to ingestion of excess free water. Transient hyperlipidemia may also be seen.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 344 pg. 2625

question_text: A 29-year-old man presents to casualty with a sudden loss of vision in his right eye. His only past history of note is a previous cerebellar hemorrhage. On examination he has Blood pressure of 130/86 mmhg, evidence of bilateral retinal angiomas, and a partial retinal detachment in his right eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Von Hippel-Lindau disease is characterized by:

  • CNS and retinal hemangioblastomas (presenting feature in 40% of patients)
  • Renal cysts and carcinomas (most common variant of RCC is clear cell carcinoma)
  • Pheochromocytoma (20% of affected families, bilateral in 40% of patients) and
  • Pancreatic tumours (30% non-functioning).

mean age at presentation :27 years.

Most common site of CNS hemangioblastoma is cerebellum.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20th edition Page number:2754, 2151

question_text: A 74-year-old male presents with sudden loss of vision in his right eye, associated with a relative afferent pupillary defect. He has poorly controlled systemic hypertension and raised cholesterol.What is the most likely aetiology of his presentation?
explanation:
• The history of acute loss of vision affecting one eye suggests an acute vascular occlusion, especially given the associated vascular risks. The others cause a more chronic visual loss.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 222

question_text: A 66-year-old patient with a history of chronic hypertension presents to the emergency room with altered mental status and severely elevated blood pressure of 210/110 mm Hg. A brain CT scan reveals bleeding within the brain tissue. What is the most common site of such hemorrhage in similar cases?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation indicates intraparenchymal hemorrhage caused by hypertension, which typically occurs in the deep regions of the brain, with the putamen being the most common site.

A sudden spike in blood pressure can overwhelm cerebral autoregulation, most often affecting the small penetrating arteries known as lenticulostriate arteries.

Common causes of intracerebral hemorrhage include:

  • Hypertension (the most frequent cause, affecting areas such as the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, and cerebellum)
  • Drug use (e.g., cocaine, methamphetamine), especially in younger patients
  • Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (usually in the elderly, causing lobar hemorrhages)
  • Coagulopathies
  • Vascular malformations
  • Head trauma
  • Hemorrhagic transformation of ischemic stroke

Regarding vessel wall damage:

  • Chronic cocaine use can lead to endothelial dysfunction and vessel damage, but acute hemorrhage is mainly caused by pressure effects rather than direct injury.
  • Vasculitis, sometimes linked to chronic cocaine use, usually affects multiple vascular territories, often causing ischemic events rather than acute hemorrhage, and develops over time.

Amyloid deposition:

  • Seen mainly in elderly patients (over 60 years)
  • Associated with lobar hemorrhages
  • Results from β-amyloid buildup in vessel walls

Although intraparenchymal hemorrhage can also affect other brain areas like the thalamus (Option B), pons (Option C), or cerebellum (Option D), the putamen remains the most frequently involved site in hemorrhages related to chronic hypertension.

question_text: Which of the following diseases presents with Thrombotic microangiopathy without Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia?
explanation:
Thrombotic microangiopathy(TMA) is a pathological lesion characterized by the presence of endothelial injury in the terminal arteriole and capillaries of organs, causing hyaline platelet thrombi, resulting in partial or complete occlusion of vessels.

In kidneys it leads to a membranoproliferative pattern in glomerulus.

Usually TMA is associated with Micro angiopathic hemolytic anemia(MAHA) characterized by schistocytes and thrombocytopenia.

Typical examples of TMA include:

  • Hemolytic uremic syndrome
  • Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura
  • Malignant hypertension
  • Scleroderma renal crisis
  • APLa syndrome
  • HELLP syndrome
  • HIV infection
  • Radiation nephropathy

TMA without MAHA is seen in

  • POEMS Syndrome
  • TMA associated with Myeloproliferative neoplasias

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 217, Pg: 2364.

question_text: Which one of the following features is characteristic of Bartter's syndrome?
option_b: Reduced urinary excretion of potassium and chloride
explanation:
Bartter's syndrome is a childhood disease inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. Pathophysiology impaired loop sodium NaK2Cl reabsorption leads to increased renin and aldosterone secretion with juxtaglomerular hyperplasia. Enhanced sodium-chloride delivery to the collecting duct stimulates potassium secretion leading to hypokalemia. It also causes hydrogen ion secretion resulting in metabolic alkalosis. Accelerated kinin and prostaglandins secretion may account for the vascular unresponsiveness to the pressor effect. This explains the absence of increase in blood pressure and oedema despite the elevated levels of renin and aldosterone. Indomethacin inhibits prostaglandin and restores normal physiological vascular response.

Hypokalemia with hypertension is seen with disorders that are related to the ENaC Conn's Syndrome, Liddle syndrome.

Bartter's syndrome is associated with increased urinary excretion of potassium and chloride.

IN Bartter's syndrome, the addition of Spironolactone, Amiloride or ACE inhibitors improves hypokalemia, but worsens the hypovolemia. NSAIDS may be useful in Bartter's syndrome, as they inhibit the tubuloglomerular feedback. Potassium supplementation and liberal salt intake should be given.

Gitelman syndrome also should be treated similarly, but NSAIDS have no role.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 53, Pg:353.

question_text: What is not seen on chest X-ray in pulmonary artery hypertension
explanation: Answer- C. Narrowing of central arteries Characteristic radiological feature of pulmonary hypertension is enlargement of central arteries with peripheral prunning. Increased pulmonary artery pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance characterize pulmonary hypertension. PAH is defined as systolic pressure in the pulmonary artery exceeding 30 mm Hg.

question_text: Graham steel murmur is seen in?
explanation:
Explanation for answer:

Graham Steell Murmur

  • Definition: High-pitched, decrescendo diastolic murmur heard along the left sternal border.
  • Cause: Pulmonary regurgitation (PR) due to pulmonary valve ring dilation from long-standing severe pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH).
  • Mechanism: Backflow of blood from pulmonary artery (PA) to right ventricle (RV) during diastole.

Pathophysiology of Pulmonary Regurgitation (PR)

  • RV Changes: Causes RV chamber enlargement and eccentric hypertrophy (similar to aortic regurgitation).
  • Hemodynamics:
    • ↑ Preload and afterload.
    • Reverse pressure gradient (PA → RV) in diastole → decrescendo murmur.
    • Murmur duration shortens as RV diastolic pressure rises.
  • Cardiac Output: Initially maintained; declines with progression, especially on exertion.

Symptoms of PR

  • Mild to Moderate PR: Often asymptomatic.
  • Severe PR/RV Dysfunction:
    • Fatigue
    • Exertional dyspnea
    • Abdominal fullness
    • Lower extremity edema

Physical Findings

  • Graham Steell Murmur: Louder with inspiration; may mimic aortic regurgitation.
  • Additional Signs:
    • Loud/palpable P2
    • Right ventricular lift → suggests significant PAH

Laboratory & Imaging Evaluation

  • ECG: RV hypertrophy (RVH), right atrial (RA) enlargement.
  • Chest X-ray: RV and RA enlargement.
  • Echocardiography:
    • Primary tool for assessing pulmonary valve and RV systolic pressure (via tricuspid regurgitation jet).
  • Cardiac MRI (CMR):
    • Detailed valve anatomy; accurate RV volume/function assessment.
  • Cardiac Catheterization:
    • Used when planning transcatheter pulmonary valve procedures.

Explanation of other options:

Pulmonary Hypertension (Option A): Pulmonary hypertension is a cause of Graham Steell murmur but not the murmur itself. The murmur results from pulmonary regurgitation secondary to PAH.

Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) (Option C): VSD causes a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, not a diastolic murmur. Large VSDs can lead to pulmonary hypertension, but the Graham Steell murmur is specifically due to PR.

Pulmonary Stenosis (PS) (Option D): Pulmonary stenosis produces a harsh, systolic ejection murmur, typically heard best at the left upper sternal border with an ejection click. It does not cause a diastolic murmur.

Key Takeaways:

Graham Steell murmur is a high-pitched, early diastolic murmur caused by pulmonary regurgitation, most commonly due to pulmonary hypertension. It is best heard at the left upper sternal border and intensifies with inspiration.

question_text: A 65-year-old man has renal bruits, renal impairment and hypertension. Which one of the following tests is most appropriate?
option_d: Magnetic resonance angiography(MRA) of renal arteries
explanation:
From the options above, For renal artery stenosis, MRA remains the best investigation with high sensitivities and specificities. MRI is not effective for detecting stent thrombosis.

CT angiography provides excellent imaging of the vessels and is less affected by stents. Risk of contrast nephropathy in renal impairment.

Though Intra Arterial angiography remains Gold standard for diagnosis of Large vessel diseases.

Doppler is very less expensive but is operator dependent and not useful for distal renal arteries and Fibromuscular dysplasia.

Captopril renography has strong negative predictive value.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 278, Pg: 2088-2089.

question_text: A 55-year-old man with a history of hypertension has renal impairment. His creatinine is 2.8 mg/dl. Urine dipstick shows blood ++ and protein +. What is the most useful investigation?
explanation:
A urinalysis of 2+ blood and 1+ protein are strong pointers towards glomerular disease. Hence among the options, biopsy is the most useful investigation.

Renal ultrasound may be useful in assessing the kidney size and echoes, but it may not help us arrive at a diagnosis.

IV urogram is used in the investigation of Obstruction to urinary tract and DTPA nucleide scan is used to asses the functional status of kidneys. 

Indications of Renal biopsy(when suspected):

  • Glomerulonephritis
  • Nephrotic Syndrome
  • Vasculitis
  • Interstitial nephritis
  • Myeloma kidney
  • HUS and TTP
  • Allograft rejection

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 21st edition, Ch: 310, Pg: 2305.

question_text: A 1 year old boy presents with renal insufficiency. Upon evaluation he has evidence of portal hypertension and dilation of intra hepatic bile ducts. Which protein mutation is he likely suffering from?
explanation:
The history of renal insufficiency in a young infant with portal hypertension and dilation of intrahepatic bile duct points towards the diagnosis of Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease. The gene responsible is PKHD1 gene on chromosome 6, which encodes for protein Fibrocystin/polyductin.

The classical form presents with fetal oligamnios and pulmonary hypoplasia with neonatal death due to pulmonary insufficiency(not renal).

The older forms is seen in infants in association with congenital hepatic fibrosis and intra hepatic bile duct dilation(Caroli's Disease). Renal impairment is slowly progressive and is due to fibrosis rather than formation of cysts.

Polycystin gene is mutated in ADPKD

Hamartin and tuberin are the proteins involved in Tuberous sclerosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 315, Pg: 2353-2354.

question_text: A 44-year-old man presents with haematemesis and melaena. He admits to high alcohol intake. On examination, his heart rate is 110 beats per minute and blood pressure is 92/74 mmHg. There is evidence of leukonychia and abdominal examination reveals tenderness in the epigastrium. What is the most likely underlying cause of the gastrointestinal haemorrhage?
explanation:
Peptic ulceration is the most common cause of acute upper gastrointestinal (GI) haemorrhage.

Epigastric tenderness also points towards peptic ulcer disease. The history of high alcohol intake can be misleading the candidate towards varices.

In this case the answer is the most common cause of an acute upper GI bleed which is peptic ulceration.

Gastric antral vascular ectasia is a relatively uncommon condition. It typically presents as a cause of iron-deficiency anaemia as a result of chronic GI blood loss. Overt symptoms of upper GI haemorrhage may be precipitated by administration of anti-platelet agents or anti-coagulants. The mean age of diagnosis is around 70 and there is an association with scleroderma.

Portal hypertensive gastropathy is a poorly understood complication of portal hypertension (usually as a result of chronic liver disease). There is a typical mosaic or snake skin like appearance to the gastric mucosa.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 48 Pg: 331

question_text: A 50 year old man with a history of hypertension was investigated for renal impairment. Renal angiography confirms renal artery stenosis. Which one of the following features is an indication for stenting in renal artery stenosis?
explanation:
Revascularization is considered when:

  • Progressive decline in GFR during treatment of systemic hypertension
  • Failure to achieve adequate blood pressure control with optimal medical therapy(medical failure)
  • Rapid or recurrent decline in the GFR in association with a reduction in systemic pressure
  • Decline in the GFR during therapy with ACE inhibitors or ARBs
  • Recurrent congestive heart failure in a patient in whom the adequacy of left ventricular function does not explain a cause

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch:278, Pg: 2090.

question_text: What is the most probable diagnosis for a 45-year-old man presenting with chest pain and shortness of breath that worsen when lying down but improve when sitting up, along with muffled heart sounds on examination?
explanation:
Explanation:

The symptoms of breathlessness worsening when lying down and improving when sitting up, along with the enlarged cardiac silhouette seen on the X-ray, strongly suggest a diagnosis of pericardial effusion.

Pericardial effusion:

This condition involves the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac, which can lead to cardiac tamponade if the fluid builds up rapidly. Clinical signs include muffled or faint heart sounds and an enlarged cardiac silhouette on chest X-ray.

Chest X-ray showing waterbottle configuration in Pericardial effusion

Electrical alternans is a classic ECG feature seen in pericardial effusion, especially when it progresses to cardiac tamponade. It appears as a beat-to-beat variation in the QRS complex amplitude, caused by the swinging motion of the heart within the fluid-filled pericardial sac. This finding indicates a substantial buildup of fluid and increased pressure inside the pericardium, which hinders proper heart filling during diastole.

ECG showing Electrical alternans

Explanation for other options:

Tetralogy of Fallot (Option B): typically presents with a boot-shaped heart on an X-ray.

Transposition of the great arteries (Option C): is characterized by an egg-on-string appearance on the X-ray.

Pulmonary hypertension (Option D): displays a pruned tree appearance of the pulmonary vasculature on imaging.

question_text: A young male presents to the clinic with a persistent high-grade fever lasting 5 days. On examination, he has painless lesions on his hands and a newly detected regurgitant heart murmur. Echocardiography reveals a mass on the mitral valve. Considering these findings, which of the following abdominal signs is most likely to be observed in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of persistent high-grade fever, painless lesions on the hands (likely Janeway lesions), and a newly developed regurgitant heart murmur is strongly indicative of infective endocarditis. In such cases, splenomegaly is a common abdominal finding due to immune system activation and potential embolic phenomena.

Acute Bacterial Endocarditis

  • Course: Rapid and more severe than subacute endocarditis.
  • Common Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (most frequent, including MRSA), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Listeria monocytogenes, Haemophilus species, and group A, B, or G streptococci.
  • Risk Factors: Underlying conditions such as cancer, diabetes, intravenous drug use, or chronic alcohol use.
  • Clinical Presentation:
    • Rapid onset of symptoms, typically within 2 weeks.
    • Fever, general fatigue, and malaise.
    • New or changing heart murmur; possible progression to heart failure.
  • Physical Findings:
    • Janeway lesions (painless hemorrhagic spots on palms and soles)
    • Petechiae
    • Roth's spots (retinal hemorrhages)
    • Splinter hemorrhages (under fingernails)
    • Splenomegaly may occasionally be present (Option B)

Options A, C, and D are incorrect.

Reference:

  1. Subacute
  2. SBE
  3. Peripheral signs

question_text: What is the most common presentation of visceral leishmaniasis?
explanation:
The most common presentation of visceral leishmaniasis (VL) is an abrupt onset of moderate to high-grade fever associated with rigor and chills. Fever may continue for several weeks with decreasing intensity, and the patient may become febrile for a short period before experiencing another bout of fever.

Other features:

  • Splenomegaly may be palpable by the second week of illness (may be massive)
  • Hepatomegaly (usually moderate in degree) soon follows.
  • Lymphadenopathy; common in most endemic regions of the world except the Indian subcontinent, where it is rare.
  • Weight loss
  • Skin hyperpigmentation that is most easily seen in brown-skinned individuals.
  • In advanced illness, hypoalbuminemia may manifest as pedal edema and ascites.
  • Anemia appears early and may become severe enough to cause congestive heart failure.
  • Epistaxis, retinal hemorrhages, and gastrointestinal bleeding are associated with thrombocytopenia.
  • Secondary infections such as measles, pneumonia, tuberculosis, bacillary or amebic dysentery, and gastroenteritis are common.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 226Pg 1744

question_text:
A 65-year-old man with a known history of hypertension presents with ankle oedema after taking an antihypertensive prescribed by his General Practitioner. He is now found to have a Blood Pressure of 160/100 mmHg.
Which of the following would be the preferred drug for this patient?
explanation:
The patient has ankle oedema which is usually due to vasodilatation by calcium channel blockers.

The preferred initial antihypertensive therapy for the elderly patient will be hydrochlorthiazide.

ACE inhibitors are preferred for those patients with heart failure or diabetic nephropathy.

β-blockers are preferred for post-myocardial infarction and ischemic heart disease.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:271 pg:1901,1903

question_text: Which of the following is not true regarding the cardiac biomarkers in myocardial infarction?
option_a: Myoglobin is the earliest to rise following MI
option_b: CK-MB is useful in assessment of reinfarction as it returns to baseline following 48-72 hours
option_c: Troponins are more specific for MI diagnosis than Creatine kinase
option_d: The order of rise of biomarkers is CK-MB, LDH followed by troponins
explanation:
• The order of rise of cardiac biomarkers is Myoglobin (2-3 hours) → CK-MB (3-6 hours) → Troponins (3-12 hours) → LDH (24 hours)
  • CK-MB levels rise by 3-6 hours, reaches its peak by 12-24 hours and return to baseline by 48-72 hours. Hence it is useful for evaluation of a suspected reinfarction.
  • In myocardial infarction, levels of LDH 1 > 2 in plasma which is called 'flipped LDH' pattern.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page no: 2055

question_text: A 45 year old male who presented with sudden onset severe chest pain was detected to have bradycardia and hypotension on evaluation. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Inferior wall MI can lead to bradycardia and hypotension by 2 mechanisms:

Ischemia of the AV node: The AV nodal artery, which arises from the right coronary artery (RCA) 80% of the time, supplies blood to the AV node. In an inferior wall MI, if the RCA is occluded, it can lead to ischemia of the AV node, resulting in significant bradycardia.

Bezold-Jarisch reflex: This reflex is characterized by increased vagal tone secondary to ischemia. The heightened vagal activity can slow the heart rate and cause vasodilation, leading to hypotension

  • Anterior wall MI may be associated with features of sympathetic overactivity like tachycardia and hypertension, while extensive anterior wall MI can lead to reduced cardiac output and hypotension.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page no: 2054

question_text: Defects in which of the following proteins is responsible for the pathogenesis of Dubin Johnson Syndrome?
explanation:
Defects in Inheritable Disorders of Bile Canalicular Function

PFIC: Progressive Familial Intrahepatic Cholestasis

BRIC: Benign Recurrent Intrahepatic cholestasis

Defective UDP glucuronyl transferase activity is a feature of Gilbert and crigler Najjar syndromes.

question_text: A 18 year old boy with a mild learning disability presents for assessment. He was apparently well 5 years ago, when he developed jaundice which persisted for 4 months. He was found to have difficulty speaking, walking up the stairs and he also had choreoathetoid movements of the arms. On examination, there was jaundice, but no clubbing, cyanosis or peripheral lymphadenopathy. A neurological examination showed weakness and wasting of muscles acting on the shoulder and hip joints and brisk deep reflexes. The plantar responses were flexor. There were no extrapyramidal signs. The patient had Kayser Fleisher rings confirmed by slit-lamp examination. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Wilson disease is a rare autosomal recessive inherited disorder of copper metabolism. The condition is characterized by excessive deposition of copper in the liver, brain, and other tissues.
  • Wilson's disease usually presents at ages less than 40. Hepatic dysfunction is the presenting feature in more than half of patients. Apart from hepatitis, neuropsychiatric presentation and movement disorders are common presentations. Kayser-Fleischer rings are observed in up to 90% of individuals with symptomatic Wilson disease.
  • Manifestations include dystonia, choreoathetoid movements, spasticity, grand mal seizures, rigidity, and flexion contractures.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 415 Pg: 3235-3237

question_text: A 40 year old man has symptoms of lethargy, joint pains and jaundice which have occurred over the past 8 months. Four years later he became diabetic and was referred to our hospital clinic. He was noted to be pigmented.Haemochromatosis was confirmed by an iron saturation of 93.4%, a ferritin concentration of 1050 µg/l, and typical pre-cirrhotic changes in a liver biopsy specimen. What is the recommended management?
explanation:
The aim of treatment in hemochromatosis is to remove the excess iron to prevent organ damage associated with it

This can be achieved by 2 ways:

  1. Phlebotomy: first line treatment; 500 ml weekly or twice weekly continued till ferritin drops to <100 μg/L.
  2. Chelation: using desferrioxamine when the patient has severe anemia or hypoproteinemia which precludes phlebotomy

Liver transplant is done for end stage liver disease.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine , 21st Ed, Ch: 414, Pg: 3234

question_text: A 42 year old man has worsening jaundice and has deranged liver function tests which have worsened over the last 3 months. He has positive IgG to hepatitis C. Which of the following investigations is most useful for management of the condition?
explanation:
Liver biopsy is useful to determine the severity of the disease and for monitory progression when treatment with ribavirin and interferon is instigated. Cirrhosis develops in 20-25 percent of patients with chronic hepatitis C after 10 years.

It is also important to rule out liver carcinoma which may be a complication of long standing hepatitis C infection

Hepatitis C is an RNA virus and hence option C is incorrect. ERCP is done in cases of obstructive jaundice. CT abdomen is not going to help in this patient

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 341, Pg: 2592

question_text:
A 34 year old patient has had a hepatitis test for investigation of jaundice. He has a positive Hep BsAg (HBsAg) and has IgM antibodies to Hep B Core (anti-HBc).
What is he likely to have?
explanation:
The positive anti-HBc (IgM) and HBsAg suggests acute infection. When the infection resolves, HBsAg becomes negative and anti-HBc (IgG) is positive. In patients who have been vaccinated, HBsAg is negative and anti-HBs is positive.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 339, Pg: 3577

question_text: The following are examples of severity scoring systems in the intensive care unit except:
option_a: Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation III (APACHE III).
explanation:
Following assess severity and predict mortality to pt admitting to ICU APACHE, SOFA, MDM, Simplified Acute Physiology Score (SAPS) and Multiple Organ Dysfunction Score (MODS).
The Glasgow-Blatchford Score is used to risk stratify patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding at first presentation and has little applicability to those who are critically ill.

Reference: Harrison 20th pg. 2023

question_text: Vitamin K is given to a patient of jaundice but PT remains unchanged. The probable cause is?
explanation:
• Vitamin K requires biliary excretion for its subsequent absorption; thus, in patients with chronic cholestatic syndromes, vitamin K absorption is frequently diminished.
  • Intravenous or intramuscular vitamin K can quickly correct this abnormality. More commonly, the synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors is diminished because of a decrease in hepatic mass, and, under these circumstances, administration of parenteral vitamin K does not improve the clotting factors or the prothrombin time.
  • Marked prolongation of the prothrombin time, >5 s above control and not corrected by parenteral vitamin K administration, is a poor prognostic sign in acute viral hepatitis and other acute and chronic liver diseases

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 337 pg. 2556

question_text: Which of the following investigations is not useful in assessment of acute liver injury?
explanation:
Serum albumin has a long half-life: 18-20 days, with ~4% degraded per day. Because of this slow turnover, the serum albumin is not a good indicator of acute or mild hepatic dysfunction; only minimal changes in the serum albumin are seen in acute liver conditions such as viral hepatitis, drug-related hepatotoxicity, and obstructive jaundice.

Hypoalbuminemia is more common in chronic liver disorders such as cirrhosis and usually reflects severe liver damage and decreased albumin synthesis.

Option A: The aminotransferases (transaminases) are sensitive indicators of liver cell injury and are most helpful in recognizing acute hepatocellular diseases such as hepatitis. They include aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT). AST is found in the liver, cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle, kidneys, brain, pancreas, lungs, leukocytes, and erythrocytes in decreasing order of concentration. ALT is found primarily in the liver and is therefore a more specific indicator of liver injury

Option B: The prothrombin time may be elevated in hepatitis and cirrhosis as well as in disorders that lead to vitamin K deficiency such as obstructive jaundice or fat malabsorption.

Option C: The activities of three enzymes-alkaline phosphatase, 5′-nucleotidase, and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT)-are usually elevated in cholestasis. Alkaline phosphatase and 5′-nucleotidase are found in or near the bile canalicular membrane of hepatocytes, whereas GGT is located in the endoplasmic reticulum and in bile duct epithelial cells. Reflecting its more diffuse localization in the liver, GGT elevation in serum is less specific for cholestasis than are elevations of alkaline phosphatase or 5′nucleotidase.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 337 pg. 2555

question_text: A patient is being evaluated for jaundice and liver fibrosis. His AST-57 and ALT-81 IU/mL serological tests are given below. Which of the following is the next step in the diagnosis?
explanation:
• The serological status of this patient shows HCV infection since anti-HCV antibody is reactive.
  • Hepatitis B surface antigen is negative and IgG Anti- HBcAg is reactive indicating remote infection with hepatitis B.
  • Recovery is the rule in hepatitis B. In contrast hepatitis C results in development of cirrhosis. Even if transaminases are normal. hepatitis C results in long term damage to the liver.
  • Hence the reason for elevated liver enzymes with development of liver fibrosis points to HCV being the culprit. The next step shall be to perform a PCR-HCV RNA and initiate treatment based on prevalent genotype in the area.
  • Approximately one-third of patients with chronic hepatitis C have normal or near-normal aminotransferase activity; although one-third to one-half of these patients have chronic hepatitis on liver biopsy
  • Liver biopsy is ruled out as the question says the patient is already having fibrosis.

Standard indications of therapy in

Standard Indications for Therapy in HCV

  1. All patients with chronic HCV infection (detectable HCV RNA, with or without elevated ALT) except for those with short life expectancies owing to comorbid conditions.
  2. Any stage of fibrosis; pretreatment biopsy is no longer embraced and has been supplanted by noninvasive measures of fibrosis, e.g., imaging to determine liver elasticity.
  3. Responsiveness in groups previously refractory to interferon-based therapy (HIV-HCV co-infection, renal insufficiency, African-American and Latino ethnicity, IL28B non-C haplotype, obesity, insulin resistance, hepatic decompensation, etc.) is not diminished to contemporary direct-acting oral combination regimens.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 341 pg. 2604, 2608

question_text: A HIV positive man presented with nonproductive cough, fever and dyspnea. Chest examination is normal. He had a history of TB contact. Which of the following test would be helpful in evaluation of this patient?
explanation:
TB is the m/c opportunistic infection in HIV patients.And in the absence of typical clinical scenario,to detect pulmonary TB or pleural TB HRCT should be done which is the most sensitive for the same.Plus it can give more information about other etiologies.And sputum culture can detect non-tuberculous infection. So A is better option than B and C.

question_text:
A 72 year old man is admitted with pruritus, lethargy and jaundice. He has not drank any alcohol for five years.One month ago, he completed a course of Co-Amoxiclav which was prescribed by his GP. He also takes diclofenac for osteoarthritis. Investigations reveal:
