question_text: Laboratory investigations of a patient with jaundice reveal elevated bilirubin and markedly raised alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels. Other liver enzymes (AST, ALT) are within normal limits. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of elevated bilirubin and ALP with normal transaminases (AST, ALT) is characteristic of obstructive jaundice. This pattern indicates impaired bile flow due to blockage, leading to accumulation of conjugated bilirubin in the bloodstream.

Comparison of Different Types of Jaundice

Explanation of other options:

Haemolytic jaundice (Option B): Results from increased RBC breakdown. Causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia; ALP and transaminases remain normal.

Hepatic jaundice (Option C): Due to intrinsic liver disease. Shows both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin elevation with marked rise in AST/ALT.

Prehepatic jaundice (Option D): Essentially overlaps with haemolytic jaundice; unconjugated bilirubin rises with normal ALP.

Key Takeaways:

  • Obstructive jaundice: Raised bilirubin + ALP with normal AST/ALT.
  • Haemolytic jaundice: Unconjugated bilirubin ↑ with normal ALP.
  • Hepatic jaundice: Mixed bilirubin pattern with markedly raised AST/ALT.

question_text: Which of the following enzyme elevation is/are less specific for the cholestasis jaundice?
explanation:
ENZYMES THAT REFLECT CHOLESTASIS

The activities of three enzymes-alkaline phosphatase, 5′-nucleotidase, and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT)-are usually elevated in cholestasis. Alkaline phosphatase and 5′-nucleotidase are found in or near the bile canalicular membrane of hepatocytes, whereas GGT is located in the endoplasmic reticulum and in bile duct epithelial cells.

Reflecting its more diffuse localization in the liver, GGT elevation in serum is less specific for cholestasis than are elevations of alkaline phosphatase or 5′- nucleotidase. Some have advocated the use of GGT to identify patients with occult alcohol use.

question_text: A 33 year old lady presents with intense pruritus in her third trimester of pregnancy. Clinically there are no abnormalities apart from scratch marks.Investigations reveal: ALT 150 U/L, Alkaline phosphatase 320 U/L, bilirubin 6 mg/dl. CBC is normal.What should be the next management step?
explanation:
The patient has intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy.

Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy usually presents during the third trimester, at a mean 30 weeks of gestation. The characteristic symptom is itching (pruritus gravidarum), which involves the trunk, extremities, palms, and soles. The itching may be severe, and it is often worse at night.

Jaundice develops in 20 to 60 percent of women one to four weeks after the onset of itching. The features of obstructive jaundice, including pale stools and dark urine, may be present, but patients do not have constitutional symptoms. Intrahepatic Cholestasis is associated with an increased risk of prematurity and stillbirth. Women with intrahepatic cholestasis should be treated at centers capable of caring for premature infants.

Treatment is symptomatic with ursodeoxycholic acid (cholestyramine and high dose steroids can also be used).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 479, Pg: 3767

question_text: A 47 year old man has painless jaundice. He has pale stools and dark urine. On examination he is deeply jaundiced and has scratch marks all over his body. On palpation of the abdomen Courvoisier's sign is positive. Where is the level of biliary obstruction?
explanation:
Courvoisier's sign is a palpable distended gallbladder on examination of the abdomen. Obstruction below the level of the cystic duct causes this, probably due to carcinoma of the pancreas.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine Ch:83, Pg: 659,

question_text: A 33 year old man presents with jaundice. He has been on a drug which was prescribed by his GP for several weeks. His blood tests show a bilirubin of 2.6 mg/dl, ALP of 450 U/l and AST 50 U/l. Which one of the following drugs is likely to cause cholestatic jaundice?
explanation:
Drugs causing Cholestasis:

  • anabolic steroids containing an alkyl or ethinyl group at carbon 17
  • azathioprine
  • cetirizine
  • cyclosporine
  • Chlorpromazine
  • Co amoxiclav
  • Erythromycin estolate
  • diclofenac
  • estrogen
  • febuxostat
  • indinavir
  • mercaptopurine
  • methyltestosterone
  • tamoxifen
  • ticlopidine.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine , 21st Ed, Ch: 340 Pg: 2587

question_text: A young man had a history of jaundice and raised HBsAg levels a year back. On follow-up now, he has normal levels of liver enzymes. His current profile is shown in the image. What is the diagnosis for his current condition?
option_a: Chronic Hepatitis B with HBeAg negative
option_c: Chronic Hepatitis B with HBeAg positive
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Persistent HBsAg positivity >6 months, HBeAg positivity, and anti-HBc IgG indicate chronic active Hepatitis B with ongoing viral replication.

  • The key diagnostic criteria for chronic Hepatitis B infection are:
    • Persistence of HBsAg for >6 months
    • Presence of anti-HBc IgG
    • Absence of anti-HBs
  • In this case, the patient continues to have HBsAg positivity after 1 year, indicating chronic infection.
  • The presence of HBeAg implies active viral replication and high infectivity.
  • Since anti-HBc IgG is positive and IgM is negative, the acute phase is over, confirming the chronic stage.
  • There are two main types of chronic Hepatitis B:
    • HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B: High infectivity, active replication
    • HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B (precore mutant): Lower replication, often inactive phase or fluctuating activity
  • The current serology fits the HBeAg-positive type, with active replication and potential for liver damage even if enzymes are temporarily normal.

Acute HBV infection with recovery

Chronic HBV infection

Reference:

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/354997816_Hepatitis_B_Vaccines

question_text:
A patient comes with fever, jaundice, and malaise. Based on the following serology findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
Serology Reports:
1. HBsAg: Positive
2. Anti-HBc: Positive
3. Anti-HCV: Negative
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of clinical presentation (fever, jaundice, malaise) along with the serological profile is most consistent with acute hepatitis B.

  • HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen): Its positivity indicates an ongoing hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, essential for diagnosing both acute and chronic HBV.
  • Anti-HBc (IgM anti-Hepatitis B core antibody): The detection of IgM anti-HBc denotes a recent exposure and acute infection with HBV, as IgM antibodies are produced in the early phase.
  • Anti-HCV: Negative result excludes hepatitis C, thereby ruling out acute or chronic hepatitis C (Option D excluded).

Table: Clinical Phases of HBV Infection and Serology

Additional Diagrams:

  • Acute HBV infection with recovery
  • Chronic HBV infection

Explanation of Other Options:

Acute hepatitis D (Option A): Hepatitis D virus requires the presence of hepatitis B infection to replicate. In this case, although anti-HBc is positive, no additional hepatitis D markers (e.g., HDV RNA) are present, hence this option is not correct.

Chronic hepatitis B (Option C): Chronic infection would typically show persistent HBsAg for >6 months, with anti-HBc usually being IgG rather than IgM. Since IgM anti-HBc is positive here, chronic HBV is excluded.

Chronic hepatitis C (Option D): Ruled out due to negative anti-HCV in the serology profile.

Reference:

Hepatitis B Vaccines - ResearchGate

question_text: A 23-year-old woman was referred for investigation of iron deficiency anemia.Her mother died aged 28 years from colonic carcinoma complicating Peutz-Jegher syndrome.Which is the most likely mode of inheritance of Peutz-Jegher syndrome?
explanation:
Peutz-Jegher syndrome is a condition characterized by perioral pigmentation and numerous hamartomas of the bowel.Originally it was assumed that these did not predispose to malignancy but studies now suggest the contrary.The condition is autosomal dominant.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 81, Pg: 638

question_text:
A 32 year old lady has altered bowel habit. At the gastroenterology clinic, her symptoms are reviewed. She has a 2 year history of bloating and abdominal pains which get better after defecation. Some weeks she is constipated and during others she has diarrhoea.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a case of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

IBS is a functional bowel disorder occurring in the absence of detectable structural abnormalities.



Weight loss, fevers and blood in the stool are features which suggest a different organic cause other than irritable bowel syndrome.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 327 pg: 2490

question_text: A 29 year old lady presents with abdominal pain to the GP who suspects irritable bowel syndrome. Which of the following is a recognized feature of irritable bowel syndrome?
explanation:
Irritable bowel syndrome is a clinical diagnosis characterized by-

  • Abdominal pain relieved by defecation
  • Bloating
  • Alternating bowel habits - constipation, diarrhoea - alone or alternating with each other.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 327 pg: 2490

question_text: A 66-year-old lady presents with symptoms suggestive of irritable bowel syndrome. Which of the following would represent a 'red flag' indicator and prompt further investigation?
option_c: Change in bowel habit for last two years
option_d: More frequent stools last two months
explanation:
The 'red flag' indicators listed in the NICE guidelines as:

  • Unintentional and unintended weight loss
  • Rectal bleeding
  • A family history of bowel or ovarian cancer
  • A change in bowel habit to loose and / or more frequent stools persisting for more than six weeks in a person aged over 60 years.

Also, on clinical examination the other 'red flag' indicators are:

  • Anaemia
  • Abdominal mass
  • Rectal mass
  • Inflammatory markers for inflammatory bowel disease.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 327 Pg: 2493

question_text:
A 64-year-old lady has a six month history of abdominal discomfort, bloating and altered frequency in stools. Her symptoms seem to be worse following a large meal where she also feels nausea. Clinical examination is normal. She is suspected of fulfilling the criteria for irritable bowel syndrome.
Which of the following investigations should be undertaken to exclude other diagnoses?
explanation:
Patients who fulfil the diagnostic criteria for irritable bowel syndrome should be screened for other conditions with-

  • Complete blood count to rule out anemia
  • Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C reactive protein to rule out inflammatory etiology
  • Anti-endomysial antibodies, Tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibodies to rule out celiac disease. Some patients with IBS-D may have undiagnosed celiac sprue. Because the symptoms of celiac sprue respond to a gluten-free diet, testing for celiac sprue in IBS may prevent years of morbidity and attendant expense

Other tests can be done to rule out any other suspected pathology depending on the presenting symptoms.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 327 Pg: 2493

question_text:
A 56-year-old man presents with a history of abdominal discomfort that is relieved by passing stool. In the past month his stools have been looser in nature and he has had a feeling of urgency and incomplete evacuation. His symptoms seem to be worse with eating. He has also noticed that he has passed mucus per rectum. He is overweight with a BMI of 28 kg/m2. His weight has fallen. He says that he has adjusted his diet in the last six months.
Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?
explanation:
Weight loss, tenesmus and a recent change in bowel habit all point towards an underlying diagnosis of colorectal cancer. Onset of symptoms in later life and a relatively short duration (that is, weeks rather than years) also point towards a 'biological' cause rather than irritable bowel syndrome.

The passage of mucus per rectum is a normal physiological function and not indicative of underlying pathology.

The symptoms are not suggestive of malabsorption.

Diverticulitis and inflammatory bowel disease are both potential diagnoses but given the duration of symptoms less likely than a colonic neoplasm.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, CH: 81, Pg: 639

question_text: What is the differentiating feature between IBS and organic GI disease?
explanation:
Irritable bowel syndrome is a functional bowel disorder which is non inflammatory. The unifying feature of inflammatory diarrhea due to any cause is the presence of leukocytes or leukocyte derived protein Calprotectin in stools.

  • Another inflammatory marker in stool is Fecal Lactoferrin, which is also present in activated neutrophils.
  • Both of them can be used in diagnosis of relapses of inflammatory bowel disease from IBS or bacterial overgrowth.
  • Fecal calprotectin is also having the advantage of being a sensitive marker of Colonic or ileocolonic inflammation rather than isolated ileal inflammation.

Abdominal pain, diarrhea and presence of mucous in stools can be seen in IBS as well as inflammatory diarrhea. Blood in stools, nocturnal symptoms and weight loss is uncommon in IBS.

question_text:
A 42 year old man presented with a 5 day history of bloody diarrhea. On examination, he was apyrexial, jaundiced and pale. There was no organomegaly but there was mild lower abdominal tenderness.Investigations reveal:
Hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL
White cell count 17500/μL
Platelets 70000/μL
urea 54 mg/dl
creatinine 2.0 mg/dl
aspartate aminotransferase 110 IU/L
Prothrombin time 12s (11.5-15.5)
Blood film shows fragmented red cells
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The combination of haemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia in the setting of a normal coagulation profile is consistent with haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS - TTP). The fragmented cells are schistocytes which are a consequence of small vessel thrombosis which cause intravascular hemolysis

The most likely cause of diarrhea is E coli O157.

Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is characterized by the triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure.

Diarrhea and upper respiratory infection are the most common precipitating factors. Other bacterial agents include Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, and Campylobacter species.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 317 Pg: 2365

question_text:
A 55-year-old man on no current treatment for his quiescent ulcerative colitis (UC) is found to have an ESR of 95 mm/hr (0-20mm/1st hour).
Investigations show:
Haemoglobin 13.2g/dL (13.0-18.0)
WCC 4.5 x 10^9/L (4-11)
Platelets 160 x 10^9/L (150-400)
Corrected Calcium 8.8 mg/dl
IgG 25g/L(6-13)
IgA 1.8g/L(0.8-3.0)
IgM 1.6g/L(0.4-2.2)
What is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation:
The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is not raised in quiescent UC. Hence there must be another reason in this case.

The only abnormal result given is a raised IgG.

This suggests that myeloma is a possible diagnosis.

Plasma immunoelectrophoresis to look for an M band is the most appropriate next investigation.

A bone marrow trephine is the definitive investigation but is traumatic and painful to the patient and so is not the next investigation of choice.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st d, Ch:111 Pg: 867

question_text:
A 44 year old man has a diagnosis of Ulcerative Colitis. He was incidentally found to have positive anti smooth muscle antibodies by the GP who sent an autoimmune screen.
Which is the next recommended test for this patient?
explanation:
A positive anti smooth muscle antibody test is suggestive of autoimmune hepatitis. Liver function tests may demonstrate elevated levels of bilirubin, AST and ALT. A liver biopsy may then be warranted.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg: 2482

question_text:
A 44 year old man has a diagnosis of Ulcerative Colitis. He was incidentally found to have positive anti smooth muscle antibodies by the family doctor who sent an autoimmune screen.
Which is the next recommended test for this patient?
explanation:
The features are suggestive of autoimmune hepatitis. Liver function tests may demonstrated elevated levels of bilirubin, AST and ALT. A liver biopsy may then be warranted.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch:341 , Pg: 2613-2615

question_text: A 43 year old man has recurrent episodes of bloody diarrhea and lower abdominal cramping. Histologic evaluation of a biopsy from flexible sigmoidoscopy reveals acute inflammation without architectural distortion consistent with ulcerative colitis.Which of the following conditions is associated with the condition?
explanation:
75% of patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis have inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic cholestatic liver disease of unknown etiology. In the absence of underlying bile duct abnormalities, a generalized beading and stenosis of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary tree characterize PSC.

PSC is usually progressive, leading to cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and liver failure.Typically, a cholestatic jaundice picture is seen with the liver function tests.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, ch: 344, Pg: 2627-2628

question_text:
A 42-year-old man with a history of ulcerative colitis (UC) comes to the gastroenterology clinic. He currently takes mesalazine and has quiescent disease. He has had three episodes of severe disease, the last one some two years ago. On examination he looks well, his BP is 115/72 mmHg, his pulse is 75 and regular, and his BMI is 23. His abdomen is soft and non-tender.
Investigations show:
Haemoglobin 13.0 g/dl(13.5-17.7)
White cells 7.8 x 10^9/L (4-11)
Platelets 189 x 10^9/L (150-400)
Sodium 138 mmol/l (135-146)
Potassium 4.4 mmol/l (3.5-5)
Creatinine 0.8 mg/dl
Albumin 4.0 g/dl (3.5-5.0)
Alanine aminotransferase35 U/l (5-40)
He asks questions about his UC and risk of colonic malignancy with respect to his UC.
Which of the following features would give you most cause for concern?
option_a: Disease confined to the rectum only
option_d: No signs of primary sclerosing cholangitis
explanation:
Out of these factors, pancolitis would give most cause for concern with respect to risk of colonic malignancy.

Other features of concern for malignancy in patients with UC include:

  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis
  • Presence of dysplastic lesions within the colon
  • Prolonged disease (8-10 years after diagnosis or more).

High-grade dysplasia or carcinoma necessitates colectomy, while many also recommend colectomy in patients with low-grade dysplasia.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:326 Pg: 2489

question_text: A male patient presents with recurrent oral ulcers and painful ulcers in the anal canal. He is diagnosed with Behçet's disease. Which of the following findings is not characteristic of this condition?
option_a: Ulcer over the dorsum of the penis
option_b: It is more similar to Crohn's disease than ulcerative colitis
option_d: Pathergy test positive is a criterion of ISG diagnostic criteria
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Ulcers on the dorsum of the penis are not typical of Behçet's disease.
  • In males, genital ulcers in Behçet's disease most commonly occur on the scrotum or glans penis and usually heal with scarring.

In contrast, ulcers on the dorsal aspect of the penis are atypical and should prompt evaluation for other causes such as sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or traumatic ulcers.


Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470257/

question_text:
A 24 year old man presents with a 10 month history of weight loss, oral ulceration and diarrhoea. A flexible sigmoidoscopy is performed and a colonic biopsy was taken.
Which of the following histological features would favour a diagnosis of Crohn's disease over ulcerative colitis?
explanation:
Crohn's disease is characterized by transmural inflammation (inflammation of all layers of the gut), fissures, preservation of crypt architecture and non caseating granulomata.

Ulcerative colitis is typified by mucosal inflammation, general inflammatory cell infiltration, goblet cell mucus depletion and crypt abscesses.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg:2474-2475

question_text:
A 19-year-old woman returns from her gap year travels with chronic low grade fever, intermittent abdominal pain and diarrhoea. She has been feeling unwell for the past few months and has returned to the UK because she has begun to lose weight. Her only medication is the combined oral contraceptive pill. On examination she looks pale, her BP is 110/60 mmHg, pulse is 75, and her BMI is 18 kg/m2. Her abdomen is soft, but she does complain of some right-sided abdominal pain.
Investigations show
Hb 11.0 g/dl(11.5-16.5)
WCC 9.8 x 10^9/L (4-11)
PLT 187 x 10^9/L (150-400)
CRP 67 mg/l (<10)
Na 139 mmol/l (135-146)
K 4.8 mmol/l (3.5-5)
Cr 1.3 mg/dl
Colonoscopy reveals areas of discrete ulceration identified, punctuated by normal mucosa. The biopsy reveals transmural noncaseating granulomata.
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The presence of skip lesions and full thickness inflammation with granuloma formation is typical of Crohn's disease.

Corticosteroids and 5-ASA compounds are the mainstay of therapy for Crohn's.

Whilst an infectious agent is a possibility, it is less likely than inflammatory bowel disease here.

We are not given a history of significant oral or genital ulceration, which makes Behcet's less likely.

Ulcerative colitis does not have granulomas. Only mucosal inflammation is seen in UC.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg:2474-2475

question_text: A child with fever with ABCs & pus in stools, causative organism is ?
explanation: Ans. is 'b' i.e., EHEC [Ref Harrison 18thle p. 1084] Fever with RBC and pus in stools suggest inflammatory diarrhea. Amongst the given options EHEC causes invasion.

question_text:
A 33 year old man had previous bowel resection for acute abdomen. He continues to have frequent episodes of bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain.
Which one of the following is an X-ray change which suggests Ulcerative Colitis?
explanation:
Loss of haustral pattern (lead pipe appearance) is seen in ulcerative colitis.



Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg:2474-2475

question_text: A 36 year old woman presents with abdominal pain, weight loss, diarrhoea and mouth ulcers. Full blood count reveals normocytic normochromic anaemia, inflammatory markers are raised, and biochemical investigation reveals a raised alkaline phosphatase. Barium follow through shows terminal ileal inflammatory disease. Long term remission may be maintained by the use of which of the following drugs?
explanation:
This is a case of Crohn’s disease.

Remission of Crohn's disease may be achieved by the use of steroids, elemental diet, surgery or infliximab.

Mesalazine may maintain remission if induction has been achieved by surgery and if an 8-week course of metronidazole is administered. It has many side effects.

In other scenarios, the most useful drug to maintain long term remission is azathioprine.

Steroids (prednisolone) are only used for induction of remission. They are not appropriate for long term maintenance therapy.

Cyclosporine is used in severe cases of ulcerative colitis refractory to steroid therapy.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg: 2488

question_text:
A 38 year old presents with a 10-day history of loose stools and mild abdominal discomfort, and recent onset of blood in stool. Ulcerative colitis was suspected by the gastroenterologist.
Which one of the following is the investigation of choice?
explanation:
Colonoscopy is the investigation of choice to evaluate ulcerative colitis (UC).

Colonoscopy in UC shows continous involvement of mucosa with no skip lesions.

Features such as loss of haustral pattern, erythema, oedema, granular mucosa, blood, pseudopolyps, erosion, ulceration are seen.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:326 Pg: 2475

question_text: Which of the following features seen on barium studies is typical of both ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease?
explanation:
Pseudopolyps are seen in both ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease.

The remainder of options listed are features of Crohn's disease rather than ulcerative colitis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg: 2475-2477

question_text:
A 26-year-old woman had ulcerative colitis (UC) for seven years and was prescribed mesalazine 1.5 g per day. She smokes upto 20 cigarettes per day and is 10 weeks pregnant. She complaines of worsening symptoms with six bloody stools per day.
Which one of the following statements is correct?
option_b: Initiation of an elemental diet risks fetal malnutrition.
option_d: Oral mesalazine therapy should be withdrawn.
explanation:
The effect of pregnancy on ulcerative colitis is variable.

In general, the health of a mother with UC is the best predictor of the outcome of the pregnancy. Hence drug treatment is preferred to leaving active disease untreated.

Azathioprine should not generally be started during pregnancy, but it is only relatively contraindicated. However, azathioprine is concentrated in breastfeeding.

In the context of pregnancy, an elemental diet does not risk maternal and/or fetal malnutrition.

Oral corticosteroids and mesalazine are not contraindicated in pregnancy. Additional folate supplementation should be given. Topical 5- ASA is also not contraindicated.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 326, Pg: 2488

question_text: A 72 year old woman with longstanding hip osteoarthritis presents complaints of constipation and loose stool. She undergoes a sigmoidoscopy. A rectal biopsy shows pigment-laden macrophages in the lamina propria. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
The pigment laden macrophages suggest that there is melanosis coli. The most common association is with laxatives. To a lesser extent, melanosis coli is also associated with ulcerative colitis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 46 Pg: 307

question_text: A 25-year-old man has been admitted with severe ulcerative colitis. He has been on high-dose steroids intravenously for three days but there have been no signs of improvement. The gastroenterology team have decided to commence cyclosporine. Which of the following is a recognized adverse effect of cyclosporine?
explanation:
The side effects of cyclosporine include -

  • Hypertension
  • Nephrotoxicity
  • Gum hypertrophy
  • Hirsutism
  • Convulsions

The indications for cyclosporine use include - Eczema, psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, IBD.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 313 Pg: 2328

question_text: A 68 year old man is admitted with a history of sudden onset abdominal pain, followed by watery diarrhea and subsequent profuse rectal bleeding. He has been a smoker for 40 years and had a myocardial infarction 5 years ago. He has a family history of colon carcinoma. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The history of pain, diarrhea and bleeding per rectum in a patient with vascular risk factors suggest large bowel infarction. Ischaemic bowel disease may be acute or chronic. Most cases result from arterial occlusion, usually of the superior mesenteric artery. The small bowel is not commonly involved.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:329 pg: 2507

question_text: What is the likely eye manifestation seen in a patient diagnosed with ulcerative colitis?
explanation:
Explanation:

In a patient with ulcerative colitis, the most likely eye manifestation is anterior uveitis.

  • Ocular involvement occurs in 1-10% of patients with Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), including ulcerative colitis (UC).
  • The most common ocular complications are:
    • Conjunctivitis
    • Episcleritis (benign, with mild burning, often linked to Crohn's colitis)
    • Anterior uveitis (iritis)
  • Anterior uveitis is particularly important because it can occur in both UC and Crohn's colitis, sometimes even during remission or after bowel resection.
  • It presents with:
    • Ocular pain
    • Photophobia
    • Blurred vision
    • Headache
  • Prompt treatment, often with systemic corticosteroids, is essential to prevent scarring and long-term visual impairment.

Extra-intestinal manifestations of Inflammatory Bowel Disease:

Corneal ulcer (Option A): Usually due to trauma, infections, or vitamin A deficiency; not a classic IBD association.

Cataract (Option B): May occur as a side effect of long-term steroid therapy, but not a direct ocular manifestation of UC.

Trachoma (Option D): A chronic infectious disease caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, unrelated to IBD.

question_text:
A 56 year old woman presents with a 2 month history of diarrhoea with no blood or mucous, colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and 1 stone weight loss. She has a history of arthritis for which she takes diclofenac regularly. On examination she was afebrile and looked pale. The abdomen was diffusely tender but soft. Bowel sounds were normal and rectal examination was normal.
Investigations showed: Hb 8.5 g/dL, MCV 68 fl, CRP 160, celiac antibodies were negative.
Colonoscopy revealed several areas of superficial ulceration in the ascending colon.
Biopsies from these areas showed non-specific inflammation.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient with a history of regular diclofenac use most likely has NSAID colopathy.

NSAID-colopathy can mimic Crohn's and ulcerative colitis.

Presenting symptoms and signs include iron-deficiency anaemia and crampy abdominal pain. Endoscopy reveals superficial ulcerations.

Symptoms usually resolve with discontinuation of the drugs.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg:2479

question_text:
A 44 year old man has 5 year history of bloody diarrhoea mixed with mucus. He had lost 2 stones in weight over this time. Flexible sigmoidoscopy showed loss of vascular appearance, erythema, and superficial ulceration consistent with ulcerative colitis.
Which one of the following features is associated with the condition?
explanation:
The extraintestinal manifestations of Inflammatory Bowel Disease include-

  • Ocular - Episcleritis, uveitis
  • Rheumatological - Ankylosing spondylitis, peripheral migratory arthritis
  • Dermatological - Erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis – most common in ulcerative colitis
  • Nephrolithiasis (calcium oxalate stones - most common)- most common in crohn's disease (CD)

Terminal ileum is the most commonly involved site in CD. Megaloblastic anaemia occurs in CD as vitamin B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 326, Pg: 2480-2482

question_text:
A 72 year old man presents with a six month history of diarrhea and pale stools. He has lost 1 stone in weight over the past 6 months.Investigations show :
Calcium 6.8 mg/dl
Phosphate 1.4 mg/dl
Alkaline phosphatase 360 U/L (45-105)
Stool for occult blood: negative
Fecal calprotectin: negative
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pancreatic carcinoma is the most probable diagnosis in view of his presenting symptoms and age.

Option A: Amoebiasis presents as colitis (fever, bloody diarrhea, blood loss anemia) or may complicate to present as liver abscess (RUQ pain, vomiting, fever)

Option B: Whipple's disease presents with features of malabsorption along with arthritis, neurological features like confusion, opsoclonus, dementia

Option C: Crohn's disease would present most commonly with ileocolitis (Right lower quadrant pain, blood in stools, fever). Fecal calprotectin is a sensitive noninvasive test used to screen for inflammatory bowel disease.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 83, Pg: 657

question_text: A patient with known ulcerative colitis (UC) who has failed to respond to anti-TNF-α therapy requires an alternative drug for moderate to severe disease. Which of the following Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors is most appropriate in this setting?
explanation:
Explanation:

Tofacitinib is an orally active JAK inhibitor approved for the management of moderate to severe ulcerative colitis, particularly in patients who are refractory or intolerant to anti-TNF-α therapy.

It acts by inhibiting Janus kinases (JAK1 and JAK3), thereby blocking the JAK-STAT intracellular signaling pathway, which mediates the action of multiple proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21, and interferons.

This suppression of cytokine-driven immune activation helps reduce intestinal inflammation, promote mucosal healing, and maintain remission in ulcerative colitis.

Mechanism of Action

  • Normal Pathway: Cytokine → JAK receptor activation → STAT phosphorylation → Gene transcription → Inflammation
  • Tofacitinib action: Inhibits JAK1 and JAK3 → prevents STAT activation → reduces transcription of proinflammatory cytokines → controls mucosal inflammation

Side effects include an increased risk of infections, venous thromboembolism, and lipid elevation, requiring careful patient selection and monitoring.

Explanation of Other Options:

Vedolizumab (Option A):

Class:

  • Gut-selective anti-integrin monoclonal antibody.

Mechanism of Action:

  • Targets α4β7 integrin, a cell adhesion molecule present on the surface of gut-homing T lymphocytes.
  • Prevents these activated T cells from binding to MAdCAM-1 (mucosal addressin cell adhesion molecule-1) on intestinal endothelial cells.
  • This selectively blocks lymphocyte trafficking into the gastrointestinal mucosa, thereby reducing inflammation in the colon.
  • Acts primarily in the gut, with minimal systemic immunosuppression.

Clinical Use:

  • Approved for moderate to severe ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease, especially when conventional therapies (steroids, azathioprine, 5-ASA) or anti-TNF agents fail.
  • Effective for induction and maintenance of remission.
  • Often preferred in patients who are at higher risk of systemic infections, given its gut-selective mechanism.

Adverse Effects:

  • Infusion reactions (headache, arthralgia, nausea).
  • Risk of upper respiratory tract infections.
  • Rarely, hypersensitivity reactions.
  • No association with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), unlike natalizumab.

Ozanimod (Option C):

Class:

  • Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) receptor modulator.

Mechanism of Action:

  • Selectively binds to S1P1 and S1P5 receptors on lymphocytes.
  • Causes functional sequestration of lymphocytes in lymph nodes → prevents them from entering systemic circulation and reaching inflamed intestinal tissue.
  • Reduces local intestinal inflammation by decreasing immune cell infiltration.

Clinical Use:

  • Approved by the FDA (2021) for moderate to severe ulcerative colitis.
  • Also indicated for multiple sclerosis (MS).
  • Used when patients are refractory to anti-TNF agents or cannot tolerate JAK inhibitors.

Dosing and Route:

  • Oral, once daily - convenient compared to injectable biologics.
  • Dose titration is required initially to minimize cardiac side effects.

Adverse Effects:

  • Cardiac: Bradycardia and atrioventricular (AV) block, especially with the first dose (due to S1P1 receptor modulation on cardiac tissue).
  • Hepatic: Elevated liver enzymes.
  • Respiratory: Mild reduction in FEV��� in some patients.
  • Infectious: Risk of reactivation of viral infections such as VZV.
  • Ophthalmologic: Rare macular edema (requires baseline eye exam).

Leflunomide (Option D):

Class:

  • Disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD); pyrimidine synthesis inhibitor.

Mechanism of Action:

  • Inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, an enzyme essential for de novo pyrimidine synthesis in rapidly dividing lymphocytes.
  • Decreases proliferation and activation of T and B cells → immunomodulatory effect.

Clinical Use:

  • Primarily used in rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis.
  • Sometimes used as an alternative to methotrexate in patients with intolerance or contraindications.
  • Not used in ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease.

Adverse Effects:

  • Hepatotoxicity (requires regular liver function monitoring).
  • Teratogenicity - contraindicated in pregnancy.
  • Gastrointestinal upset, diarrhea.
  • Hypertension, weight loss, rash, and alopecia.

question_text: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with complaints of fever for 1 week. He also has cracked lips, which are painful. On examination, his eyes are red and he has a lymph node in the cervical region. Kawasaki syndrome is suspected. Which of the following is the best treatment choice?
explanation:
This is a case of Kawasaki's syndrome, which is also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome and occurs mainly in children under 10 years of age. It is a form of vasculitis, which affects coronary arteries and is associated with the development of coronary aneurysms. Aspirin and IV immunoglobulin at high doses is the treatment of choice. Corticosteroids used to be contraindicated, but recently trials have shown that it reduced the risk of heart damage caused by coronary vessel vasculitis. Infliximab is also being used in trials. Warfarin is used if coronary aneurysms develop as a complication.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch: 363 Pg: 2816

question_text: A 64-year-old man presents with palpitations and syncope. He has a history of an inferior-wall myocardial infarction one year ago. A 24-hour Holter study was performed, and the ECG strip obtained is given below. What is the long-term treatment for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation of syncope and palpitations in a patient with a prior MI, combined with a Holter monitor showing sinus pauses or arrests, is diagnostic of sick sinus syndrome (sinus node dysfunction).

Rationale for Permanent Pacemaker

  • Symptomatic Bradycardia: The syncope is directly attributable to the arrhythmia, making it a Class I indication for permanent pacing. The goal is to prevent life-threatening pauses and alleviate symptoms.
  • Irreversible Cause: Sinus node dysfunction following a myocardial infarction is often permanent due to irreversible damage to the heart's conduction system. Pharmacological agents like atropine or isoproterenol are only temporary measures.
  • Standard of Care: According to ACC/AHA/HRS guidelines, permanent pacemaker implantation is the definitive long-term therapy for symptomatic sinus node dysfunction.

Sick Sinus Syndrome

This syndrome encompasses various sinus node abnormalities, including severe sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses >3 seconds, and sinoatrial exit block. The history of inferior MI is highly relevant, as the sinus node artery often originates from the right coronary artery, which is commonly involved in inferior wall infarctions.

In hemodynamically unstable patients, bradycardia is managed with intravenous atropine 0.5 mg every 3-5 minutes to a maximum dose of 3 mg, and if there is no improvement, a temporary pacemaker should be considered.

In stable patients, long-term management involves treating underlying causes, withdrawing bradycardia-inducing medications, and inserting a permanent pacemaker when indicated.

Explanation of other options:

Amiodarone (Option A): This is a Class III antiarrhythmic drug. It can itself cause or exacerbate bradycardia and is contraindicated in this scenario. It is used for tachyarrhythmias, not symptomatic bradycardia.

Atropine only (Option B): Atropine is an anticholinergic agent used for acute, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia in an emergency setting. It is not a sustainable or appropriate long-term treatment.

Atropine and isoproterenol (Option D): Isoproterenol is a beta-agonist used as a temporary chronotropic agent. Combining these drugs is a short-term bridge to pacing in an acute care setting and is not a long-term solution.

Key Takeaways:

  • Symptomatic bradycardia due to sick sinus syndrome requires a permanent pacemaker.
  • Drugs like atropine are for acute management only.
  • A history of myocardial infarction, especially inferior, is a common cause of acquired sinus node dysfunction.

question_text: A patient arrives at the emergency department after consuming ten paracetamol tablets. He now has oliguria, and his liver function tests are abnormal. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's presentation with a history of paracetamol overdose, oliguria, and deranged liver function strongly suggests paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity. The specific antidote in this situation is N-acetylcysteine (NAC).

Acetaminophen (Paracetamol) Toxicity:

  • Most common cause of acute liver failure worldwide.
  • Toxic dose: Ingesting ≥25 g may be fatal.
  • Clinical features: Oliguria, elevated liver enzymes, signs of hepatic injury.

Mechanism of Toxicity:

  • Normally, paracetamol is metabolized in the liver.
  • A fraction is converted via CYP2E1 into a toxic metabolite, NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine).
  • In overdose, glutathione stores become depleted, leading to accumulation of NAPQI, which causes hepatocellular necrosis.

Management:

  • Antidote: N-acetylcysteine (NAC).
    • Mechanism: Restores glutathione reserves, thereby detoxifying NAPQI.
    • Timing: Most effective when administered within 8 hours of overdose; benefit persists up to 36 hours.
  • Severe cases: Liver transplantation may be required if fulminant hepatic failure develops despite NAC therapy.

Explanation of other options:

Dopamine (Option B): Used in cardiogenic or septic shock; has no role in paracetamol toxicity.

Ursodeoxycholic acid (Option C): Utilized in cholestatic liver diseases such as primary biliary cholangitis, not in drug-induced hepatic injury.

Furosemide (Option D): A loop diuretic for fluid overload; does not treat paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity.

Key Takeaways:

  • N-acetylcysteine is the drug of choice in paracetamol overdose.
  • Works best within 8 hours but still beneficial later.
  • In refractory cases, liver transplantation is the definitive treatment.

References:

https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.107.728840

question_text: A 45 year old man presents with  acute, profuse, watery diarrhea some days after returning from a holiday. Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

Most secretory forms of traveler's diarrhea (usually due to enterotoxigenic or enteroaggregative E. coli or to Campylobacter) can be treated effectively with rehydration, bismuth subsalicylate, or antiperistaltic agents. Antimicrobial agents can shorten the duration of illness from 3-4 days to 24-36 h but may be associated with the acquisition of multidrug-resistant organisms; their use should therefore be reserved for severe cases

question_text: Which of the following is false about acute intermittent porphyria (AIP)?
option_b: Due to half-normal level of HMB-synthase activity
explanation:
• Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is an autosomal dominant hepatic porphyria resulting from half-normal level of HMB-synthase activity. AIP is especially common in Scandinavia & Great Britain.
  • AIP is almost always latent before puberty.
  • Porphyria is a group of diseases characterised by excess production and excretion of porphyrins and their precursors.
  • They are caused by enzyme defects within the haem metabolic pathway.
  • Stress, infection, pregnancy, menstruation, starvation, and certain drugs may precipitate acute attacks.
  • Definite precipitants include sulphonamides, barbiturates, and phenytoin.
  • may be acute or non-acute
  • The most common presenting sign of PCT is fragility of sun exposed skin after mechanical trauma, leading to erosions and bullae, worst on dorsal hands, forearms, and face.

Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP)

  • autosomal dominant
  • defect in porphobilinogen deaminase
  • caused by a defect in porphobilinogen deaminase, an enzyme involved in the biosynthesis of haem.
  • 20–40-year-olds more likely to be affected (only rarely presents before puberty)
  • AIP is more common in females (5:1)
  • 90% of affected individuals remain asymptomatic throughout their lives.
  • typically present with abdominal symptoms, neuropsychiatric symptoms
  • Seizures occur in 10-20% of patients with acute intermittent porphyria (AIP).
  • A range of psychiatric symptoms, including hypomania and delirium may be seen.
  • hypertension and tachycardia common
  • urine turns deep red on standing
  • Patients excrete urinary porphobilinogen (PBG) between and during acute attacks.
  • Faecal porphyrin excretion is usually normal or slightly increased.
  • Photosensitivity is unusual in AIP
  • All attacks of porphyria increase the activity of hepatic 5-aminolevulinate (ALA) synthase.

Lab features

hyponatraemia, mild leukocytosis.

Treatment of seizures in AIP = Gabapentin



Diagnosis

Urinary porphobilinogen assay is the optimal way to establish the diagnosis.

Treatment:

Glucose and heme, which inhibit delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase, thereby decreasing heme precursor synthesis.

Two procedures have been shown to decrease the activity of ALA synthase in animals:

  1. carbohydrate loading and
  2. parenteral infusion of haem arginate.
  • The treatment of choice in acute porphyria is intravenous haem arginate
  • High-glucose diets or infusions have been used for mild attacks of pain without neurological Symptoms.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 20th edition Chapter:409 Page number:2990-2993

question_text: A patient who was on antihistamine therapy was feeling drowsy and sleepy. What is the alternative treatment for the same?
explanation:
Explanation:

Fexofenadine is specifically highlighted as a nonsedating antihistamine and is the most suitable alternative for a patient who develops drowsiness and sleepiness on older sedating antihistamines.

  • First-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine are effective but are sedating and cause psychomotor impairment due to their ability to cross the blood-brain barrier.
  • They also have anticholinergic side effects like blurred vision, urinary retention, and constipation.
  • To avoid these adverse effects, second-generation H1 antihistamines are preferred.
  • Agents such as loratadine, desloratadine, cetirizine, bilastine, and fexofenadine are long-acting, nonsedating (or low-sedating) and thus improve compliance and quality of life in patients with chronic urticaria.

Bilastine (Option A): It is also a nonsedating second-generation antihistamine, but fexofenadine is more established and widely used in clinical guidelines.

Prednisolone (Option B): A systemic glucocorticoid, not indicated for routine treatment due to long-term toxicity.

Desloratadine (Option C): Another second-generation nonsedating antihistamine, but fexofenadine is the standard recommended switch when sedation is problematic.

question_text:
A 27 year old man presents with sudden onset left sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. On examination he is distressed, tachypnoeic and has tracheal displacement to the right together with a hyper-resonant percussion note on the left side. There were no breath sounds on the left. Chest x ray shows a < 2 cm left sided pneumothorax.
What is the best management procedure?
explanation:
The history of a young male without any prior lung disease with a pneumothorax suggests the possibility of a Primary Spontaneous Pneumothorax due to rupture of sub pleural blebs.

  • Treatment of a pneumothorax of < 2 cm margin would be initial aspiration.
  • This is less painful, leads to a shorter duration of admission, reduces the need for pleurectomy.
  • If the lung does not expand with aspiration or if the patient has a recurrent pneumothorax, thoracoscopy with stapling of blebs and pleural abrasion is indicated. Thoracoscopy or thoracotomy with pleural abrasion is almost 100% successful in preventing recurrences.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 294Pg 2200

question_text: A 50-year-old man is evaluated for hyperaldosteronism because of difficult to-control hypertension. He is otherwise healthy. Evaluation was done during treatment with agents that do not affect aldosterone or renin levels and include an aldosterone-to-renin ratio of more than 40 and lack of aldosterone suppression to oral salt loading. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the adrenal glands shows a 1-cm mass on the right with a density of 10 HU. What is the next best step?
option_d: Review of CT scan to exclude hyperplasia of the left adrenal gland
explanation:
• Adrenal venous sampling should be performed to identify the source of excess aldosterone. It is possible that the visualized mass is a non functioning tumor.

  • This man is a good surgical candidate, and laparoscopic adrenalectomy would be recommended if venous sampling is consistent with unilateral disease. The CT scan is not helpful in identifying bilateral disease.
  • Treatment with eplerenone or spironolactone would be done if he were not a surgical candidate; eplerenone would be an appropriate treatment for bilateral disease.

question_text:
A 15 year old female who is diagnosed with SLE has come to your OP for review. Which of the following statements is true?
1. Permanent remission is seen only in <5% individuals.
2. Aim of treatment is disease remission on treatment or Low Lupus Disease Activity.
3. Anti ds DNA or C3 levels are used as markers of disease flare
4. SLEDAI 2k score of >3 indicates active disease.
explanation:
The question deals with treatment endpoints in SLE.

  1. Complete permanent remission(no disease activity without any treatment) is seen in <5% only.
  2. Aim of treatment in SLE is disease remission on treatment or low level disease activity.
  3. Disease activity is measured using SLEDAI 2k score and a score of > 4 indicates an active disease.
  4. Anti ds DNA titres and C3 complement levels are used as markers of disease flare.

From among the given options, SLEDAI2K score of > 3 does not indicate active disease. Hence it is wrong.

So statements 1,2 and 3 are correct.

Latest treatment is POEM.

CDC recommends the use of pretomanid 200 mg daily for 26 weeks in the treatment of adults with pulmonary extensively drug-resistant (XDR), pre-extensively drug-resistant (pre-XDR) (i.e., resistant to isoniazid, rifampin, and at least one fluoroquinolone or injectable medications (i.e., amikacin, kanamycin, capreomycin)) or treatment-intolerant (TI)/nonresponsive (NR) multidrug-resistant TB when a safe and effective treatment regimen cannot otherwise be provided and when administered in combination with bedaquiline and linezolid as the BPaL regimen.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 178 Pg: 1377

question_text: Drug of choice for treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is
explanation:
• Nitrofurantoin, ampicillin, and cephalosporins are considered relatively safe in early pregnancy.
  • One retrospective case-control study suggesting an association between nitrofurantoin and birth defects has not been confirmed.
  • Sulfonamides should clearly be avoided both in the first trimester (because of possible teratogenic effects) and near term (because of a possible role in the development of kernicterus).
  • Fluoroquinolones are avoided because of possible adverse effects on fetal cartilage
  • Ampicillin and the cephalosporins have been used extensively in pregnancy and are the drugs of choice for the treatment of asymptomatic or symptomatic UTI in this group of patients. Generally, pregnant women with ASB are treated for 4-7 days in the absence of evidence to support single-dose therapy.
  • For pregnant women with overt pyelonephritis, parenteral ß-lactam therapy with or without aminoglycosides is the standard of care.

question_text: A 63-year-old diabetic woman presents with fever, flank pain, dysuria, and elevated WBC count. Imaging reveals mild hydronephrosis. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. She is diagnosed with a complicated urinary tract infection (UTI). Which of the following is the best initial treatment?
explanation:
Explanation:

She is diagnosed with a complicated urinary tract infection (UTI) and hence the patient should be treated with Meropenem.

Meropenem is the best initial treatment in this case because:

  • The patient has a complicated UTI (due to diabetes, systemic signs, and possible urinary tract obstruction).
  • There is a high risk of infection with resistant organisms, particularly ESBL-producing Gram-negative bacilli like E. coli.
  • Meropenem, a carbapenem, offers broad-spectrum coverage including Gram-negative organisms, anaerobes, and ESBL producers.
  • It is effective when oral agents or narrower-spectrum antibiotics are likely to fail or when systemic illness is present.

Explanations for other Options:

Ceftriaxone (Option A): Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin that is commonly used for UTIs, but it may not be effective against ESBL-producing organisms, which are often found in complicated infections, especially in diabetic or hospitalized patients. While it can be used in some uncomplicated cases, it is not the preferred choice for severe or high-risk infections like the one described.

Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Option C): Amoxicillin-clavulanate is an oral antibiotic with some activity against common urinary pathogens, but it has limited effectiveness against resistant Gram-negative bacteria, including ESBL-producing strains. It is not suitable for treating complicated UTIs, especially when there are systemic signs such as fever or flank pain, or imaging findings like hydronephrosis.

Nitrofurantoin (Option D): Nitrofurantoin is only effective for lower urinary tract infections (cystitis) because it does not reach adequate concentrations in the renal tissue. Therefore, it is ineffective for pyelonephritis or complicated infections involving the kidneys or upper urinary tract, such as in this case with flank pain and hydronephrosis.

question_text: What is the drug of choice for Legionnaire's disease?
explanation:
Explanation:

Azithromycin is the preferred agent for treating Legionnaire's disease due to its superior efficacy, better tolerability, and lower potential for drug interactions compared to erythromycin.

Legionella Features:

  • Thin, Gram-negative, non-capsulated bacilli.
  • Poor Gram staining; best visualized by Direct Fluorescent Antibody (DFA) staining.
  • Requires Buffered Charcoal Yeast Extract (BCYE) agar for growth.

Mode of Infection: Microaspiration and aerosol inhalation; no human-to-human transmission.

Epidemiology: Associated with air conditioners, showers, coolers; commonly seen in smokers, immunocompromised, and elderly patients.

Treatment:

  • First-line: Macrolides [Azithromycin preferred over Erythromycin], ciprofloxacin, tetracyclines.
  • Severe cases: Rifampicin may be added.
  • Ineffective: Beta-lactams and aminoglycosides.

Explanation of other options:

Vancomycin (Option A): Active against Gram-positive bacteria like Staphylococcus and Enterococcus; ineffective for Legionella.

Streptomycin (Option C): Aminoglycoside used in TB and plague; lacks efficacy against Legionella.

Erythromycin (Option D): Previously first-line, now replaced by Azithromycin due to better tolerability.

References:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK7619/

question_text: What is the treatment of Grade I Meningioma?
explanation:
Explanation:

The standard treatment for a symptomatic or growing Grade I (benign) meningioma is surgical excision. The goal is complete resection, which is often curative for this slow-growing tumor.

Meningioma is the most common primary CNS tumor arising from the dura mater, usually slow-growing but with higher-grade variants being rare. It is linked to genetic mutations, radiation exposure (especially in childhood), neurofibromatosis type 2, and older age.

Grading:

  • Grade 1 (low grade):Most common, slow-growing, more frequent in females.
  • Grade 2 (atypical):Higher recurrence risk; includes chordoid and clear cell types; may invade bone.
  • Grade 3 (anaplastic/malignant):Aggressive, fast-growing; includes papillary and rhabdoid types; can spread to brain and other organs.

Clinical features depend on location and may include seizures, morning headaches, vision or hearing loss, altered smell, and confusion. MRI typically shows an enhancing extra-axial mass, with Grade 2/3 lesions appearing brighter with contrast.

Treatment: Grade 1 is managed primarily with surgical excision. Grades 2 and 3 require surgery followed by adjuvant radiotherapy, chemotherapy, or clinical trials (e.g., targeted or immunotherapy).

Explanation of other options:

Reassurance (Option A): Asymptomatic, small, incidentally discovered Grade I meningiomas may be managed with observation and serial imaging.

Chemotherapy (Option C): Has a very limited role and is generally reserved for recurrent or higher-grade (Grade II/III) meningiomas that are not amenable to surgery or radiation.

Radiotherapy (Option D): Used as adjuvant therapy for subtotally resected or higher-grade meningiomas, or as primary treatment for surgically inaccessible tumors.

Key Takeaways:

  • Grade I meningiomas are benign and surgical resection is the primary curative treatment.
  • Management strategy depends on the tumor's size, location, associated symptoms, and growth rate.

Reference: https://www.cancer.gov/rare-brain-spine-tumor/tumors/meningioma

question_text: A retro-positive patient has been started on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Which of the following is the best parameter to monitor treatment efficacy?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Viral load (HIV RNA levels) is the most reliable marker for assessing the efficacy of HAART.
  • It reflects the degree of viral replication and treatment response.
  • A significant drop (≥10-fold) is expected within 1-2 months of therapy, with the target being <50 copies/mL within 6 months of treatment initiation.

Explanation of other options:

CD4+ T cell count (Option A): Indicates immune reconstitution and helps stage disease but is less sensitive for early response compared to viral load.

p24 antigen (Option C): A structural core protein used in early diagnosis before antibody formation; not used for treatment monitoring.

Viral serotype (Option D): Identifies viral subtype (commonly HIV-1) but has no role in monitoring therapeutic efficacy.

Key Takeaways:

  • Viral load monitoring is the gold standard for assessing HAART response.
  • CD4+ count is useful for staging and prognosis but not the primary efficacy marker.

Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4872286/

question_text: The preferred test for confirming H. pylori eradication is:
explanation: Answer is A (Urease Breath Test) The test of choice for documenting eradication is urease breath test. Assessment of success of Treatment with Eradication of H. Pylori should be done at least 4 weeks after completion of anti H. Pylori therapy. Non-invasive tests are typically preferred for assessment of Eradication. The test of choice for documenting eradication is urease breath test. Urease breath test detects H. pylori infection by 'bacterial urease activity' and remains positive till the bacteria has not been eradicated with treatment. Thus urease breath test becomes negative only aftereradication of organism following treatment and not with chronic infection.

question_text: A 50 year old man presents with a history of intermittent, but slowly progressive dysphagia for both solids and liquids. He has pain on swallowing and has regurgitation of food swallowed several hours earlier. He has not lost weight. Barium swallow demonstrates proximal dilatation of the oesophagus and failure of relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter. Which treatment option is best in the long term?
explanation:
The diagnosis is achalasia cardia. This is a functional obstruction at the lower oesophageal sphincter caused by a failure of relaxation.

Heller's oesophageal myotomy (surgical division of the lower oesophageal sphincter) is the best treatment option. It can be done via an abdominal incision or laparoscopically. It is often combined with fundoplication for reflux.

Pneumatic dilation is another procedure done for achalasia.

Per Oral Esophageal Myotomy(POEM) is the latest treatment for Achalasia and is as effective as Heller's Myotomy with few complications and early recovery.

Botulinum toxin injection can be used to treat achalasia. But it is a temporary measure.

Sengstaken Blakemore tube is used in the management of esophageal varices via balloon tamponade.

Amyl nitrite is an arterial vasodilator. It has no role in management of achalasia.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 23,Pg: 2427-2428

question_text: A 15-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhoea. She represents her school in athletics and is now training for the national championships. Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment for her?
explanation:
• Menarche may be delayed in girls who are involved in strenuous physical activity.
  • This is termed as"Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea" in which strenuous physical activity, caloric restriction and extreme stress can lead to reduced GnRH and gonadotropins production from hypothalamus and pituitary.
  • Treatment with GnRH or gonadotropins are not required as the reversal of these risk factors would lead to resumption of normal menstrual cycles.
  • Provision of an adequate diet and the relief of stress would be the most appropriate treatment in this case.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 3035

question_text: What is the treatment of a patient diagnosed with H.pylori?
option_a: A combination of a proton pump inhibitor and an antibiotic
explanation:
Explanation:

The treatment regimen for a patient with H.pylori is a combination of a proton pump inhibitor and antibiotics.

  • Although pylori is sensitive to many antibiotics in vitro, monotherapy is generally ineffective due to insufficient antibiotic delivery to its colonization site.
  • The failure of single-drug therapy led to the development of multidrug regimens.
  • At present, standard treatment consists of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) combined with two or three antimicrobial agents for 10-14 days.

Common Treatment Regimens for H.pylori

question_text: A 25-year-old male presents with fever, chills, and malaise, and is diagnosed with malaria caused by Plasmodium vivax. He has a history of hemolytic anemia among males in his family. Before initiating treatment, which of the following should be checked to ensure the safety of antimalarial therapy
explanation:
Explanation:

Primaquine is used for the radical treatment of Plasmodium vivax malaria to eradicate persistent liver stages and prevent relapse. However, primaquine can cause hemolysis in individuals with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. This genetic condition is more prevalent in certain populations and can lead to severe hemolytic anemia if drugs like primaquine are administered. Since the patient has a history of hemolytic anemia among males in his family, which is suggestive of a possible G6PD deficiency, it is crucial to check G6PD levels before initiating treatment with primaquine.

  • Primaquine Use in Malaria Treatment:
    • Used to eradicate persistent liver stages and prevent relapse in Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale infections.
    • Recommended dose is 0.5 mg/kg in East Asia and Oceania and 0.25 mg/kg elsewhere, daily for 14 days.
  • G6PD Testing:
    • Essential to test for G6PD deficiency before administering primaquine due to the risk of hemolysis in deficient individuals.
    • In mild variants of G6PD deficiency, primaquine is administered weekly for 8 weeks at 0.75 mg/kg.
  • Alternative Treatment Strategies:
    • Pregnant women should not receive primaquine but rather suppressive prophylaxis with chloroquine until they can undergo radical treatment post-delivery.
  • Tafenoquine:
    • A slowly eliminated 8-aminoquinoline that can be administered as a single dose for radical cure.
    • Requires a quantitative G6PD test before administration; only patients with >70% of normal G6PD activity should receive it.
    • Its radical curative efficacy is noted to be lower than primaquine in Southeast Asia.
  • Implications for Patients:
    • The need for quantitative testing of G6PD activity is underscored due to the severe potential complications associated with hemolysis, particularly in those with unrecognized or borderline G6PD deficiency.

Explanation of other option:

Liver function tests (LFTs) (Option B): Although antimalarials like quinine or chloroquine can affect liver function, primaquine-related hemolysis is the primary concern. LFTs are not necessary before treatment unless there is a known hepatic disease.

Complete blood count (CBC) (Option C): A CBC can help monitor anemia or thrombocytopenia in malaria, but it does not predict hemolytic risk. Checking G6PD status is the priority before primaquine use.

Reticulocyte count (Option D): A high reticulocyte count may indicate ongoing hemolysis, but it does not determine whether the patient has G6PD deficiency. Testing G6PD directly is necessary.

Key Takeaways:

Before prescribing primaquine or tafenoquine for Plasmodium vivax malaria, G6PD levels must be checked to prevent life-threatening hemolysis.

question_text:
A 36-year-old man who is known to drink three bottles of wine per day presents to the Emergency department with dull abdominal pain. He tells you that he has suffered from increasing abdominal swelling over the past month.On examination his BP is 105/72 mmHg, his pulse is 92 and regular. He is pyrexic with T: 37.9°C. His abdomen is generally tender but there are bowel sounds on auscultation. He is penicillin allergic.
Investigations show:
Hemoglobin 10.5 g/dl(13.5-17.7)
White cell count 11.5 x 10^9/L (4-11)
Platelets 125 x 10^9/L (150-400)
Sodium 134 mmol/l (135-146)
Potassium 3.6 mmol/l (3.5-5)
Creatinine 0.9 mg/dl
280 neutrophils / ml in ascitic fluid(<250)
Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
The diagnosis here is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis - note the history of alcohol excess, gradually increasing abdominal girth and elevated neutrophil count in the ascitic fluid.

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis should be managed aggressively, and whilst piperacillin and tazobactam or a third generation cephalosporin are an appropriate choice in those who are not penicillin allergic, in this case ciprofloxacin and vancomycin are the default choice due to the presence of penicillin allergy.

Oral continuation therapy is with ciprofloxacin alone or co-trimoxazole.

Co-amoxiclav is not appropriate due to the presence of penicillin allergy, nor is the piperacillin and tazobactam combination.

The two erythromycin combinations do not provide an adequate breadth of coverage.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 344, Pg: 2632

question_text: Which among the following is not a component of initial treatment of orthostatic hypotension?
option_d: Elevate head end of BED 10cm to minimize supine hypertension.

Initial treatment of orthostatic hypotension (OH) includes:

  • Patient education: Mechanisms and stresses of OH
  • High salt diet (10-20 gm/day)
