question_text: A patient presents with flaccid bullous lesions as shown in the image below, involving the entire trunk and oral cavity. Acantholytic cells are seen on Tzanck smear. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation is classic for Pemphigus Vulgaris (PV), it is the most common chronic autoimmune blistering disease caused by antibodies against desmosomal adhesion proteins.

. The key diagnostic clues are:

  1. Flaccid Bullae: Very fragile blisters that rupture easily, leading to painful erosions.
  2. Mucosal Involvement: Oral lesions are present and are often the initial sign.
  3. Tzanck Smear Finding: The presence of acantholytic cells (rounded-up keratinocytes) is characteristic of pemphigus, indicating loss of adhesion between epidermal cells (acantholysis).

Pathophysiology

In pemphigus vulgaris, histopathology shows intraepidermal cleavage with acantholysis, where keratinocytes detach mainly in the suprabasal region. This leads to separation of basal keratinocytes along the basement membrane zone, producing the classic "row of tombstones" appearance. The principal target antigen is Desmoglein 3, and in some cases Desmoglein 1, both of which are implicated in intraepidermal immunobullous disorders.





Explanation of other options:

Pemphigus foliaceus (Option A): This variant also shows flaccid bullae and acantholysis, but it typically spares the mucous membranes. Lesions are more superficial, often appearing as scaly, crusted erosions on the face and trunk.

Dermatitis herpetiformis(Option C): This is associated with celiac disease and presents with intensely pruritic papules and vesicles on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks), not flaccid bullae.

Bullous pemphigoid (Option D): This disorder features tense, robust bullae on an erythematous base that do not rupture easily. Mucosal involvement is rare. The split occurs below the epidermis (subepidermal), so acantholytic cells are not seen on Tzanck smear.

Key Takeaways:

  • Pemphigus Vulgaris = Flaccid bullae + Oral lesions + Acantholysis on Tzanck smear.
  • The target antigen is primarily Desmoglein 3.

Reference: Pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, and diagnosis of pemphigus - UpToDate

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC

question_text: Which of the following is most commonly associated with the development of pseudomembranous colitis?
explanation:
Clostridium difficile a Gram positive anaerobic bacterium is the cause of pseudomembranous colitis.

Studies show that when C. difficile colonise the gut they release two potent toxins, toxin A and toxin B, which bind to certain receptors in the lining of the colon and ultimately cause diarrhoea and inflammation of the large intestine or colon (colitis).

Commonly the disease is caused by broad spectrum antibiotics most commonly cephalosporins, broad spectrum penicillins and clindamycin. Less commonly, macrolides and quinolones have been reported to cause the disorder.

Oral Vancomycin and Fidaxomycin are the agents used for mild infections.

Metronidazole is reserved for fulminant cases.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 138, Pg: 1069

question_text: Endemic goiter is said to exist when more than ___ % of children aged 6-12 years have enlarged thyroid glands
explanation:
• Endemic goiter is characterized by enlargement of the thyroid gland in a significantly large fraction of a population group, and is generally considered to be due to insufficient iodine in the daily diet.
  • Endemic goiter exists in a population when >5% of 6-12-year-old children have enlarged thyroid glands
  • Most mountainous districts in the world have been or still are endemic goiter regions

Reference: Eastman CJ, Zimmermann MB. The Iodine Deficiency Disorders. [Updated 2018 Feb 6]. In: Feingold KR, Anawalt B, Boyce A, et al., editors. Endotext

question_text: A 20 year old male was brought for psychiatric evaluation for intellectual disability. On examination, his IQ was 45. He has a long face, large ears, large testis and a cardiac murmur and history of poor intellectual function is present in the paternal family. What is his diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation is classic for Fragile X syndrome, an X-linked dominant disorder caused by CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion (>200 repeats) in the FMR1 gene, with premutation carriers having 55-200 repeats and the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability. Key features include:

  • Intellectual disability(IQ ~45)
  • Characteristic facial features: Long face, large prominent ears.
  • Macroorchidism(large testicles)
  • Mitral valve prolapse(causing murmur)
  • Positive family historyon the paternal side (X-linked inheritance)

It is more common in males, while females are usually carriers.Female carriers may present with premature ovarian failure, and about 10% can show low IQ or intellectual impairment.

Explanation of other options:

Cushing's syndrome (Option A): Characterized by centripetal obesity, moon facies, hypertension, and hyperglycemia, not intellectual disability or the described dysmorphic features.

Rett syndrome (Option B): An X-linked dominant disorder almost exclusively affecting females, characterized by developmental regression, loss of purposeful hand skills, and stereotypic hand movements.

Williams syndrome (Option D): Characterized by "elfin" facies, supravalvular aortic stenosis, and a highly sociable personality, not macroorchidism or a strong X-linked family history.

Key Takeaways:

  • Fragile X syndrome should be suspected in males with intellectual disability, characteristic facies, and macroorchidism.
  • It is caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome.

question_text: Following are indications of aspiration of liver abscesses, Except:
option_c: Lack of a clinical response in 3-5 days.
option_d: To prevent rupture of left lobe abscesses into the pericardium.
explanation:
Indications for aspiration of liver abscesses are (1) the need to rule out a pyogenic abscess, particularly in patients with multiple lesions; (2) the lack of a clinical response in 3-5 days; (3) the threat of imminent rupture; and (4) the need to prevent rupture of left-lobe abscesses into the pericardium. There is no evidence that aspiration, even of large abscesses (up to 10 cm), accelerates healing.

Percutaneous drainage may be successful even if the liver abscess has already ruptured. Surgery should be reserved for instances of bowel perforation and rupture into the pericardium.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 223Pg 1718

question_text: You are called urgently to review a 52-year-old man who has developed acute onset pulmonary oedema around 36 hour after myocardial infarction. His blood pressure is 95/50 mmHg with a pulse of 100/min and auscultation revealed a pan-systolic murmur along with bibasilar crepitations. What is the likely diagnosis in this patient?
explanation:
Acute Mitral regurgitation due to papillary muscle dysfunction / rupture:

  • Mitral valve is supported by 2 papillary muscles - anterolateral and posteromedial. Posteromedial muscle has a single blood supply from either left circumflex or right coronary artery. This papillary muscle rupture can occur along with anterior or lateral MI
  • Acute MR due to papillary muscle dysfunction occurs 3-5 days following MI and present with pulmonary edema which progress to cardiogenic shock
  • Diagnosis is established by Echocardiography which shows eccentric jet of MR
  • Management involves the use of vasodilators such as sodium nitroprusside and the use of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibition if tolerated. Inotropic support with drugs such as dopamine or dobutamine may also be required.

Other mechanical complications of Acute MI

  • Ventricular septal defect
  • Rupture of ventricular free wall
  • Pseudoaneurysm

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2255

question_text: A 76-year-old woman presents with acute monocular visual loss. Fundoscopy reveals a swollen pale optic disc in the affected eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• The presence of a swollen optic disc suggests ischaemic optic neuropathy.
  • In elderly people giant cell arteritis is a common presentation of acute monocular visual loss.
  • Optic neuritis is very rare in people over the age of 50.
  • You would expect bilateral swollen optic discs in raised intracranial pressure.
  • In central retinal vein occlusion you would expect diffuse retinal haemorrhages.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3343

question_text: What is the Most common source of E. coli bacteremia?
explanation:
The urinary tract is the most common source of E. coli bacteremia, accounting for one-half to two-thirds of episodes

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 135, Pg: 1071

question_text: What is by far the Most common site of Proteus infection?
explanation:
Proteus species are part of the colonic flora

P. mirabilis causes 90% of Proteus infections, which occur in the community, LTCFs, and hospitals. By contrast, Proteus vulgaris and Proteus penneri are associated primarily with infections acquired in hospitals.

Adhesins, flagella, IgA protease, and urease representing the principal known urovirulence factors.

Clinical spectrum of Proteus infections:

  • Urinary tract infections (most common)
  • Pneumonia
  • Nosocomial sinusitis
  • Intra abdominal abscesses
  • Biliary tract infection
  • Surgical site infection
  • Soft tissue infection (especially decubitus and diabetic ulcers)
  • Osteomyelitis
  • Bacteremia

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 161 Pg: 1278

question_text:
A 29 year old man presents with a 4 week history of a painful swollen left knee. He has a past medical history of a treated sexually transmitted disease 6 months ago. On examination there was a large effusion in the left knee. Synovial fluid analysis shows a white cell count of 15 x 10^9/L but culture was negative.
Which one of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
explanation:
History of sexually transmitted disease, followed by a monoarthritis favors the diagnosis of Gonococcal Arthritis.

Gonococcal arthritis is caused by an infection with the gram-negative diplococcus N gonorrhoeae. Neisseria gonorrhoea occurs in young adults, often preceded by a migratory arthritis.

The bacteremic phase is a classic triad of migratory polyarthritis, tenosynovitis, and dermatitis. This patient was treated previously for a sexually acquired infection hence may be the reason for the culture to be negative. Also, gonococci are rarely recovered from joint effusions.

The initial treatment of choice for gonococcal arthritis is a third-generation beta-lactamase resistant cephalosporin (eg, ceftriaxone, ceftizoxime, cefotaxime) or a penicillin, if the organism is sensitive.



Multiple intracellular gram negative diplococci

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 156 Pg: 1239

question_text: A 36 year old lady who is asymptomatic has an ultrasound of her abdomen done privately. It showed several gallstones and no biliary duct dilatation. She has no other past medical history.What should be done?
explanation:
In carefully selected patients with a functioning gallbladder and with radiolucent stones<10 mm in diameter, complete dissolution can be achieved in nearly 50% of patients within 6 months to 2 years.

The natural history of asymptomatic gallstones (GS) suggests that a large number of affected individuals will remain asymptomatic throughout life; only 1-4% per year will develop symptoms or complications of GS disease. Therefore, the natural history of asymptomatic GS is so benign that surgery is generally not recommended and watchful waiting is the best course of management.

Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is recommended for asymptomatic patients with risks factors such as sickle cell disease and diabetes.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 346, Pg: 2645

question_text:
A 27-year-old man is noted to have cyanosis of the lower limbs and clubbing of the toes but not the fingers. The blood pressure in the arm and lower limb is the same.
Which of the following statements is true?
option_b: He has coarctation of the aorta.
option_c: He is likely to have a loud continuous 'machinery' murmur below the left clavicle.
option_d: He is likely to need urgent surgery.
explanation:
Differential cyanosis (cyanosis only in lower extremities) is seen in a patient with patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) when there is reversal of shunt. There is a right-left shunt from the pulmonary artery to the aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery. This is Eisenmenger's syndrome.

Coarctation causes radiofemoral delay and a lower blood pressure in the leg as compared to the arm. It may be associated with PDA but there is no suggestion in this patient.

Continuous machinery murmur is the classic murmur of PDA but when the shunt reverses (as in patients with a large PDA and/or pulmonary disease) the murmur becomes softer and shorter.

When Eisenmenger's syndrome has developed surgery is associated with a very high mortality.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:264 pg:1838,1839

question_text:
A 42 year old man who usually drinks only 2 units of alcohol a day went on an 
alcohol binge with his friends. On that day, he vomited 10 times and was brought to hospital feeling very unwell. He has not previously had any symptoms of dyspepsia or abdominal pains. During physical assessment, he vomits a large bowlful of blood.
What is the likely cause of his haemetemesis?
explanation:
This is a case of Mallory Weiss tear.

  • Longitudinal tear in the mucosa at the gastroesophageal junction.
  • Caused by forceful or prolonged vomiting or coughing.
  • They may also be caused by epileptic convulsions.
  • Usually seen in alcoholics, bulimia nervosa patients.
  • The tear may be followed by vomiting bright red blood or by passing blood in the stool.
  • Active bleed can be treated by endoscopy (band ligation or coaptive coagulation).

A transmural rupture at gastroesophageal junction is called Boerhaave's syndrome.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2433

question_text: Which of the following factors decrease large intestinal motility?
explanation:
Anticholinergic agents decrease large intestinal motility.

The other options and cholinergic agents increase large intestinal motility.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch:327, Pg: 2494

question_text: Which of the following statements is false?
option_a: Post obstructive diuresis is more common in unilateral than bilateral obstruction.
option_b: Large amount of hypotonic urine will be voided.
option_c: Electrolyte free water excretion may result in hypernatremia.
option_d: Urine output and urinary and serum electrolytes should guide the fluid replacement
explanation:
Post obstructive diuresis occurs when obstruction of urinary tract is relieved.

More common in bilateral obstruction

The fluid excreted will be massive and hypotonic.

But it contains large amount of sodium, potassium, phosphate and magnesium, because salt reabsorption will be impaired when urine flow is established.

When GFR improves, the retained urea will cause salt free osmotic diuresis, resulting in loss of electrolyte free water, causing hypernatremia. Hypernatremia also occurs due to suppression of ADH.

Salt free water is defined as urine where the amount of urinary sodium and potassium is less than serum sodium.

So fluid and electrolyte supplementation should be tailored by measuring the amount of solutes in urine and serum.

Replacement of fluid should be less than the urine output to prevent hypernatremia.

Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 319, Pg: 2376.

question_text: A 30-year-old male presents with the clinical sign shown in the image. What is the name of this physical finding?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image displays classic features of digital clubbing, which is often associated with various cardiopulmonary disorders. Although commonly considered a permanent change, clubbing can be reversible in some underlying conditions.

Explanation for other options:

Koilonychia (Option A): Also known as spoon-shaped nails, this condition features thin, brittle nails with a concave shape. The center of the nail appears sunken, while the edges curve outward, forming a spoon-like appearance.

Raynaud's Phenomenon (Option B): This condition involves recurrent episodes of blood vessel constriction in the fingers and toes, usually in response to cold exposure or emotional stress.

Pallor (Option C): Describes a noticeable lightening or loss of normal skin or mucosal coloration, commonly due to reduced blood flow, anemia, or other underlying causes.

question_text: Medial calcification is seen in -
explanation: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Monckebergs sclerosis First see types of arteries Based on their size and structural features, arteries are divided into three types. Large or Elastic arteries Aorta Its large branches, eg. - Innominate, Subclavian, common carotid, iliac. Pulmonary arteries. Medium sized or muscular arteries Small branches of aorta → Coronary, Renal Small arteries and arterioles Within substance of the tissue Now see their affection ? Arteriosclerosis Dont get confuse with atherosclerosis. Arteriosclerosis means hardening of arteries by thickening and loss of elasticity of arterial wall. o There are three patterns of arteriosclerosis. Atherosclerosis Characterized by intimal lesions, i.e. atheromas, which project into vascular lumen and may obstruct it. o This is the most common pattern of arteriosclerosis. It involves elastic arteries, and large & medium size muscular arteries. Arteriolosclerosis Seen in arterioles of patiens with hypertension and diabetes. Two anatomic variants are common —> hyaline and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis. Monkeberg medial calcific sclerosis It is seen in small and medium sized muscular arteries. It is a degenerative and apparently non-inflammatory disease. Media of these arteries becomes calcified. It occurs in patients older than 50 years.

question_text: What will you give to stop chyluria in diet?
explanation: Ans. is 'b' i.e.,Medium Chain FA [Ref Harrison's 18thie p. 294] Medium chain fatty acids directly enter the portal vein on absorption,bypassing the lymphatics.Hence,they are used in chyluria

question_text: Patients with Giant cell arteritis present with history of headache, jaw claudication, polymyalgia rheumatica and mononeuritis multiplex. What should be the first line treatment?
explanation:
The universally accepted treatment of giant cell arteritis (GCA) is high-dose corticosteroid therapy.

The major justification for the use of corticosteroids is the impending danger of blindness in untreated patients.

question_text: A 20 year old lady is short in stature for her age. She has a webbed neck andoligomenorrhoea. On physical examination, she a continuous murmur heard over bothfront of the chest as well as her back. A chest radiograph reveals a prominent left heartborder and rib notching.Which of the following lesions best explains these findings?
explanation:
Coarctation of the aorta is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with Turner's syndrome.

Rib notching on the chest X ray is a big clue. This occurs due to collateral vessel formation.

The underlying abnormality is a deformity of the aortic media that causes eccentric narrowing of the lumen.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:264 pg:1837

question_text: Which of the following medium vessel vasculitis is due to immune complex deposition?
explanation:
Among the given options, PAN and KAwazaki Disease are medium vessel vasculitis, of which PAN is due to immune compex deposition and Kawazaki disease is due to anti endothelial cell antibodies.

Giant Cell Arteritis and Takayasu are large vessel and not medium vessel vasculitis.

Lets summarise the different vasculitis and their pathogenic mechanisms together:

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 363, Pg 2803

question_text:
A 75 year man presents with right foot drop, hand numbness, fevers, malaise, weight loss, polymyalgia and diffuse joint pains for 2 months.
On examination, he appears unwell and has a temperature of 38°C.
Investigations reveal:Hb 8.5 g/dL
erythrocyte sedimentation rate 95 mm/hr
serum creatinine 2.0 mg/dL
urine analysis: blood ++
urine microscopy: white cells & red cell casts seen
Which one of the following is the LEAST likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient presents with multi system involvement as characterized by the presence of multiple peripheral nerve involvement, arthralgia and fever. His laboratory reports show features of inflammation characterized by anemia, high ESR. He also has renal impairment with hematuria and RBC cast which indicates glomerulonephritis. The entire constellation of symptoms points towards the diagnosis of a vasculitis.

PAN is a disease of medium sized vessels and it does not cause glomerulonephritis. Renal impairment and hypertension can be seen in PAN due to involvement of the renal artery or its branches.

All the other options are small vessel vasculitis and can cause glomerulonephritis.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:363 Pg:2810

question_text: A 46 year old woman presents with claudication in her lower limbs. She is noted to have absent left arm pulses. The previous year she had a small hemispheric cerebrovascular infarct. Her ESR is 100mm/hr. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This question deals with a young female who has a previous history of CVA, now presents with claudication pain in lower limbs. She has absent pulses in her upper limbs too.

Coarctation of Aorta can cause claudication pain. But high ESR is not seen.

Familial hypercholesterolemia may cause stroke in young, but absent pulses is not seen.

GCA and Takayasu Arteritis becomes the possibility in view of high ESR. GCA usually involves branches of the Carotid artery, but can involve other branches of Aorta. GCA is seen usually in patients > 50 years of age.

So in a young female, the cause of large vessel arteritis is Takayasu Arteritis.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch: 363 Pg: 2813

question_text: To which category of vasculitis does Behcet disease fall under?
explanation:
• According to the 2012 Revised Chapel Hill classification, Behcet and Cogan syndrome are classified under variable vessel vasculitis
  • BD is commonly known as a triad of oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, and ocular disease.
  • Cogan's syndrome (CS) is an uncommon autoimmune systemic disease classically described as a triad of non syphilitic interstitial keratitis, audio vestibular symptoms resembling Meniere's disease, and an interval between ophthalmologic and auditory manifestations of less than 2 years.

Reference: Harrison's principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 364, Pg: 2817

question_text: Takayasu arteritis most commonly involves:
explanation:
Explanation:

Takayasu arteritis, also known as "pulseless disease," is a large-vessel vasculitis that most frequently and characteristically involves the aortic arch and its major branches. The inflammation targets the vessel wall, leading to stenosis, occlusion, or aneurysm formation.

Site of Predilection

The classic initial presentation often involves the branches arising from the arch of the aorta, such as the subclavian, carotid, and brachiocephalic arteries. This results in the classic clinical findings of arm claudication, absent radial pulses, blood pressure discrepancies between arms, and vascular bruits. While the disease can affect the entire aorta (including the abdominal aorta) and pulmonary arteries, the arch and its branches are the primary and most commonly affected sites.

Key Disease Characteristics

  • Demographics: Predominantly affects young women, typically under 40 years of age.
  • Phases: The disease often has a systemic "pre-pulseless" phase with constitutional symptoms, followed by a vascular phase.
  • Diagnosis: MR angiography is the investigation of choice for visualizing the characteristic vascular lesions.

Explanation of other options:

Pulmonary artery (Option A): Pulmonary artery involvement can occur in Takayasu arteritis but is not the most common site. It is seen in a subset of patients.

Coronary arteries (Option B): Coronary ostia can be involved due to proximal inflammation, but this is a complication rather than the primary or most common site of disease.

Abdominal aorta (Option D): The abdominal aorta can be affected, often leading to renal artery stenosis and hypertension. However, the arch of the aorta and its branches are involved more frequently and characteristically.

Key Takeaways:

  • Takayasu arteritis is the leading cause of renal artery stenosis in young Indian females.
  • The arch of the aorta and its branches are the hallmark sites of involvement.
  • The classic clinical triad includes pulselessness, claudication, and blood pressure asymmetry.

question_text: A 35-year-old female presented with claudication in forearm, transient loss of vision and abdominal pain. She also had weak femoral pulses. Fundus also showed retinal haemorrhages. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
In this question, we have a young female with symptoms of upper limb claudication, visual loss, abdominal pain and weak femoral pulses.

  • The history points to the involvement of the branches of Aorta.
  • The retinal hemorrhage could be secondary to hypertension.
  • The involvement of large and medium vessels in a young female points towards the diagnosis of Takayasu Arteritis.

PAN typically involves renal and visceral vessels, ie, small and medium sized arteries. It does not produce absent peripheral pulses.

Microscopic polyangiitis is a small vessel vasculitis, mainly presenting as glomerulonephritis and pulmonary vasculitis.

Thromboangiitis obliterans(Buerger's disease) is an inflammatory occlusive vascular disorder of small and medium sized arteries of the distal upper and lower limb and is seen in men <40 years. Although the disease presents with claudication, larger pulses like brachial will be preserved and radial pulses will be absent.

question_text: A 50 year old female presents with history of palpable purpurae for the last 6 months. Now she has cough and hemoptysis and she presents with desaturation. Her investigations shows Hb of 9g/dL, ESR of 100mm/ 1st hour. A biopsy of her skin lesions shows fibrinoid necrosis without granulomas. Which of the following is the most likely disease?
explanation:
Patient here presents with cutaneous symptoms and pulmonary involvement and histologically shows fibrinoid necrosis without granulomas. Among the small vessel vasculitis, Microscopic polyangiitis presents lacks granulomas and presents with fibrinoid necrosis. Among the given potions PAN also presents with fibrinoid necrosis without granulomas. So PAN is also a possibility. But what makes PAN unlikely is the pulmonary involvement.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:363 Pg:2809

question_text: Large PDA leads to ?
explanation: Ans. is 'd' i.e., All of above Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) Small PDA may not cause any complication but large defect if untread may leads to : Pulmonary hypertension Left to Right shunt leads to too much circulation of blood in lung which leads to pulmonary hypertension. Eisenmenger's syndrome - Large standing pulmonary hypertension leads to permanent lung damage and causes Right to Left shunt. Endocarditis. Arrhythmia Enlargement of heart due to PDA increase risk of arrhythmias

question_text: A 45 year old male patient presents with history suggestive of vasculitis. A biopsy from the involved organ was sent to the pathologist who sees granulomas in the specimen. Which of the following diseases is least likely to be responsible for the same?
explanation:
Granuloma formation is the basic pathology seen in:

Giant cell arteritis

Takayasu arteritis

Wegerner’s Granulomatosis

Churg Strauss vasculitis

Microscopic Polyangitis causes necrotizing vasculitis without granuloma formation. It is associated with circulating ANCA.

Circulating ANCA is also seen in Wegener’s Granulomatosis and Churg Strauss Vasculitis.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 363, Pg: 2803

question_text: A 64-year-old man awakens with painless loss of vision of his left eye. Three years earlier he had suffered a similar episode involving the right eye. Visual loss in that eye has been stationary. He does not complain of any systemic symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Sudden onset of painless monocular visual loss in patients aged 50 or more is commonly due to ischaemic optic neuropathy.
  • Commonly the symptoms are first noticed upon awakening in the morning. The other eye may suffer a similar event within five years.
  • There are no systemic features (weight loss, lethargy, malaise, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness) to suggest arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy (giant cell arteritis). In giant cell arteritis, the other eye is usually affected within four weeks.
  • Optic neuritis is unlikely in a man of this age who had painless loss of vision.
  • In older persons it is due to ischemia, which can be arteritic or non-arteritic. Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy based on cardiovascular risk factors essentially. Arteritic AION is concern with temporal arteritis which has a typical prodrome of jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and headaches.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 223

question_text: A young boy presents with PAN like vasculitis. Which of the following diseases is he likely to harbor?
explanation:
PAN like vasculitis is seen with Hepatitis B, C, Adenosine deaminase deficiency Type 2 and Hairy cell leukemia.

PAN is a disease of middle aged, and is common in males. If a very young boy presents with PAN like symptoms Adenosine deaminase deficiency should be suspected.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 363, Pg 2810-2811

question_text: A 35 year old man whose condition has suddenly deteriorated is brought to ER. He had arrived 30 minutes earlier with a 2-hour history of central pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. He collapsed while awaiting CXR. He is cyanosed and has a pulse 130/min and BP of 85/45 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is reading 81%, despite high flow oxygen via a re-breathe mask. Respiratory examination reveals reduced breath sounds in the right lung field with deviation of the trachea towards the left. What immediate course of action should be taken?
option_a: Contact ITU to arrange for the patient to be ventilated
option_b: Insert large bore needle into right hemithorax
option_c: Arrange for urgent portable chest XR
option_d: Check arterial blood gases and commence BIPAP
explanation:
• The diagnosis is a right sided spontaneous pneumothorax, which has now developed into a tension pneumothorax.
  • As the patient is unstable, there is no time to arrange for a portable chest XR, insertion of a large bore needle would reduce the pressure in the right hemithorax.
  • Mechanical ventilation at this stage would be detrimental as additional positive pressure would be transmitted to the mediastinum causing a further reduction in venous return and cardiac output
  • Large right sided pneumothorax


Cardinal features of a Tension pneumothorax:

  • Enlarged hemithorax
  • Absent air entry
  • Deviation of mediastinum to the contralateral side
  • Hyper resonance
  • Hypotension
  • Raised JVP

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition, Ch:310, Pg-2226

question_text: The chest X-ray shows right-sided white-out lung and contralateral tracheal deviation. Based on the X-ray findings, which of the following conditions is most likely?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The X-ray shows tracheal deviation to the side opposite the white-out lung field, typically caused by a thoracic mass such as a massive pleural effusion.
  • This occurs when a space-occupying lesion resulting in pleural effusion for example from lung cancer, produces a mass effect that pushes the mediastinal structures away from the affected side.
  • The pleural fluid is seen as opacity (single large black arrow) with lateral upward sloping of a meniscus- shaped contour.
  • The right diaphragmatic contour is also completely obliterated, indicating presence of fluid in the right pleural space.
  • In spite of a moderately large right pleural effusion, the trachea appears to be slightly shifted to the right side (as depicted by small black arrows) indicating an underlying lung pathology on the right side.

Explanation of other options:

Pneumothorax (Option A): Pneumothorax typically presents with a hyperlucent lung field without vascular markings due to air collection in the pleural space.

Consolidation (Option B): In a chest xray, consolidation is seen as haziness or opacity on X-ray but maintains some visualization of underlying vascular markings. A complete white-out appearance is not typical. Furthermore, significant tracheal deviation is not a characteristic feature of simple consolidation.

Collapse of the lung (Option C) would show tracheal deviation toward the same side as the opacity, not away from it. This is because collapse creates negative pressure that pulls the mediastinal structures toward the affected side.

question_text: A 65 year old man has had 5 kg weight loss over 6 months. He is an ex-smoker of 25 cigarettes a day for 40 years and used to work in a coal mine.  A Chest X ray shows a large right sided pleural effusion and several pleural plaques in both lung peripheries.  Pleural aspiration reveals an exudate with 42 g of protein.  What investigation should be recommended?
explanation:
• This patient probably has a malignant effusion as demonstrated by the exudate from the pleural effusion. As he is symptomatic, the best option would be to drain the fluid as well as confirm a diagnosis simultaneously.
  • A video assisted thoracoscopy would help to do this. In this procedure, an illuminated tube is inserted through a small incision made between the ribs. It allows the operator to visualize structures inside the chest and to perform simple procedures such as biopsy and nodule excision.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 286 Pg 2140

question_text: A 30-year-old asymptomatic woman, as part of her routine health checkup, underwent ECG testing which is shown below. Which of the following drugs should be started on her?
explanation:
The ECG shows bradycardia. The QT interval, ie, from the beginning of the Q wave to the end of the T wave here is 5 large squares. One large square is 0.2 seconds. So, here the QT interval is 1 second. The QT interval varies with the heart rate and hence it has to be corrected for the heart rate, which is called the corrected QT interval or QTc.

QTc=QT/square root of RR interval

So here the RR interval is 9 large squares. Which is 1.8 seconds.

So, the corrected QT will be 1/square root of 1.8= 0.74

The normal QTc is 0.42 seconds.

So here the QT is prolonged.

So, in an asymptomatic patient we should think of congenital long QT syndromes.

QT prolongation is associated with risk of ventricular arrhythmias.

Non selective beta blockers should be started in such patients to prevent ventricular arrhythmias. Hence the answer is propranolol

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page Number-1925.

question_text: A 40-year-old man presents with a history of dyspnoea and palpitations. On examination he has a jerky carotid pulse, an ejection systolic murmur is audible at the base of the heart which enhances on standing and Valsalva and a pan systolic murmur at the apex. Echocardiography shows asymmetric left ventricular hypertrophy and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. The patient's symptoms may be treated with:
explanation:
The diagnosis is hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HCM) as suggested by the signs of jerky pulse, ejection systolic murmur which intensifies on standing and on performing valsava manoeuvre and echocardiographic findings. Other notable findings which may be seen on clinical examination include pulsus bsiferiens and double apex beat.

HCM should be suspected in a young previously well individual presenting with sudden onset arrythmia especially VT or VF.

Medical therapy of choice in such patients are β-blockers and verapamil (non-dihydropyridine CCB) either alone or in combination. Disopyramide is also used as second line treatment with persistent symptoms

Drugs to be avoided in management include ACE inhibitors / ARBs, nitrates, dihydropyridine CCBs, digoxin, diuretics etc.

Patients at high risk of sudden cardiac death like those with sustained ventricular tachycardia, syncope, LV septal thickness more than 3 cm, family history of sudden cardiac death etc should be treated with Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator (ICD) implantation.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1970

question_text: A 62-year-old man has complained of a pain in the temples, fevers, sweats and malaise for 4 weeks. The right side of the face was mildly swollen and he experienced visual loss in the right eye. On examination, he had prominent and tender temporal arteries on the right. Blood tests revealed: Hb 12.5 g/dl MCV 86 fl WCC 12 x 10^9/L platelets 212 x 10^9/LESR of 90 mm/hr. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Tender temporal artery with visual loss and constitutional symptoms with high ESR suggests the diagnosis of Giant Cell Arteritis.

Although it is termed as Temporal arteritis, it can involve any branches of the Aorta

The cause of blindness is Anterior Ischemic optic Neuritis, due to involvement of the Posterior Ciliary artery that supplies the optic disc.

The treatment is to start glucocorticoids immediately, where GCA is suspected, to prevent blindness in the opposite eye. Methylprednisolone 1g for 3 days should be commenced if vision is involved. Otherwise Prednisolone 1mg/kg body weight should be started. Tocilizumab is an alternative.

Aspirin should be started in all patients with GCA, without any contraindications, as it is proven to prevent the incidence of Cranial ischemic events.

The diagnosis should be confirmed with a Temporal Artery biopsy. Biopsy may show the changes of inflammation even up to 14 days of steroid therapy. Since the disease is patchy, 3-5 Cm segment has to be taken. Ultra sound can also be used in arriving at the diagnosis.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:363 Pg: 2811-2812

question_text: Atheromatous changes of blood vessels affects early in -
explanation: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Heart Sites of Atherosclerosis Atherosclerotic plaques develop primarily in elastic arteries (e.g., aorta, carotid and iliac arteries), and large & medium sized muscular arteries (e.g., coronary artery and poplitial arteries). In descending order, the vessels most commonly involved are - Abdominal aorta (most common) → Causing aneurysm Coronary arteries (heart) → Causing MI Popliteal arteries → Causing ischemic gangrene of lower limbs. Internal carotid arteries → Causing stroke a Circle of willis Vessels usually spared are Vessels of upper extremities Mesentric and renal vessels, except at their ostia.

question_text: Which of the following features is not associated with patent ductus arteriosus?
explanation:
PDA is associated with a collapsing pulse

Patent ductus arteriosus

Overview

  • Acyanotic congenital heart defect
  • Connection between the pulmonary trunk and descending aorta
  • More common in premature babies, born at high altitude or maternal rubella infection in the first trimester

Features

  • Left subclavicular thrill
  • Continuous 'machinery' murmur
  • Large volume, bounding, collapsing pulse
  • Wide pulse pressure
  • Heaving apex beat

Management

  • Indomethacin closes the connection in the majority of cases
  • If associated with another congenital heart defect amenable to surgery then prostaglandin E1 isuseful to keep the duct open until after surgical repair.

Reference: Braunwald's heart disease 12th edition, page no.1559

question_text: A 67 year old woman has neck pains and occipital headaches for 2 years. She is referred to the neurology outpatients for assessment. Investigations showed a normal CT of the brain. Cervical X ray showed degenerative changes of narrowed disc spaces and loss of cervical lordosis. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• In cervical spondylosis, several overlapping syndromes are seen: neck and shoulder pain, suboccipital pain and headache, radicular symptoms, and cervical spondylotic myelopathy.
  • Examination findings include neck pain, radicular signs, and myelopathic signs. Cervical spine films can demonstrate disk space narrowing, osteophytosis, loss of cervical lordosis, uncovertebral joint hypertrophy, apophyseal joint osteoarthritis, and vertebral canal diameter.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 442, Pg: 3452

question_text: Most sensitive test for the diagnosis of enteric fever?
explanation:
• The definitive diagnosis of enteric fever requires the isolation of S. Typhi or S. Paratyphi from blood, bone marrow, other sterile sites, rose spots, stool, or intestinal secretions.
  • The sensitivity of blood culture is only 40-80%, probably because of high rates of antibiotic use in endemic areas and the small number of S. Typhi organisms (i.e., <15/mL) typically present in the blood. Because almost all S. Typhi organisms in blood is associated with the mononuclear cell/platelet fraction, centrifugation of blood and culture of the buffy coat can substantially reduce the time to isolation of the organism but do not increase sensitivity.
  • Bone marrow culture is >80% sensitive, and, unlike that of blood culture, its yield is not reduced by up to 5 days of prior antibiotic therapy.
  • Culture of intestinal secretions (best obtained by a noninvasive duodenal string test) can be positive despite a negative bone marrow culture.
  • If blood, bone marrow, and intestinal secretions are all cultured, the yield is >90%. Stool cultures, although negative in 60-70% of cases during the first week, can become positive during the third week of infection in untreated patients

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 165 Pg: 1294

question_text: Which of the following is the commonest cause of ectopic ACTH secretion leading to Cushing's syndrome?
explanation:
• Ectopic ACTH is predominantly caused by occult carcinoid tumors, most frequently in the lung, but also in thymus or pancreas. Because of their small size, these tumors are often difficult to locate.
  • Historically, small cell carcinoma lung was considered as the most common cause for the same.
  • Advanced small-cell lung cancer can cause ectopic ACTH production. In rare cases, ectopic CRH and/or ACTH production has been found to originate from medullary thyroid carcinoma or pheochromocytoma, the latter co-secreting catecholamines and ACTH.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition,page number 2960

question_text: A 32-year old man presents to the diabetes clinic with a history of thirst, polyuria, and a recent 3.2 kg weight loss. His urine contains a small number of ketones. Which of the following would suggest that he is most likely to have type-2 rather than type-1 diabetes?
explanation:
• Type-1 diabetes mellitus is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the presence (in many patients) of autoantibodies to the islet cell (ICA), insulin (IAA) or glutamic acid dehydrogenase (GAD).
  • It is associated with HLA DR-3 or DR-4.
  • Patients with type-2 diabetes more commonly have a high BMI > 25, as this form of diabetes is associated with insulin resistance and high insulin levels rather than low insulin levels.
  • Presence of ketosis/ketoacidosis is extremely rare in Type 2 DM, while around 30% patients with Type 1 DM may present with DKA.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page Number 3099-3101.

question_text: A 63-year-old diabetic presents with pyrexia, productive cough, and shortness of breath for 5 days. She has RLL consolidation and a small unilateral pleural effusion on CXR. Which is a marker of poor prognosis?
explanation:
Indicators of poor prognosis in pneumonia include:

  • Age >65
  • Co-existing morbidity including diabetes mellitus, chronic renal failure, stroke, coronary artery disease.
  • Respiratory rate>30
  • Mental impairment
  • Biochemical/haematological markers which include white blood count < 4000/µL or > 30,000/µL; hypoxia needing CPAP or FiO2>60%, positive blood culture and blood urea>7 mmol/L.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:126Pg 1015

question_text: Identify the causative organism for rash shown below
explanation:
Molluscum contagiosum virus is likely the most common poxvirus infection that will be seen by practitioners in the United States.Disease is transmitted through contact, usually through no intact skin. Children are affected, likely transmitting disease through play activities. In HIV or AIDS patients, disease can be severe. Genital involvement can be seen in adults. Clinical disease is usually recognized by the development of flesh-colored papules, sometimes umbilicated as they mature aka Dimple rash.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 196 Pg:1493

question_text: Dystrophin absent and presence of small muscle fibrils cause?
explanation:
Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy are the Dystrophinopaties.

DMD is characterized by absent dystrophin and Becker's muscular dystrophy is characterized by either decreased level or size of dystrophin.

Total absence of dystrophin points to the diagnosis of DMD.

Biopsy is not diagnostic in myopathies. So the microscopy will be almost the same for DMD and BMD.  Muscle biopsy in young ages will show degeneration and regeneration of muscle fibres with preserved architecture. There is no active inflammation except for myophagocytosis.

 As the disease progresses, the muscle fibers are replaced by fatty infiltration. The remaining muscle fibers show varying size from atrophic to hypertrophic.

Immunohistochemical staining shows absence of sarcolemmal staining in DMD and reduced staining in BMD.

They are both XL recessive inheritance. Dystrophin provides stability to the muscle fibre by acting as a bridge between the cytoskeleton inside the muscle fibre and the basement membrane outside the cell. DMD results from deletions or frameshift mutations in the dystrophin gene, leading to total absence of the protein, whereas BMD results in the formation of truncated variant of dystrophin that leads to partially functional protein.

question_text:
A 25-year-old female presents with red crusted lesions around the mouth and finger pulps, three months after having had small bowel resection for Crohn's disease.
What is the most likely cause of her skin condition?
explanation:
The features of this patient who had bowel resection suggest zinc deficiency.

Zinc deficiency can lead to a condition called acrodermatitis enteropathica which presents with diarrhea, alopecia, muscle wasting, depression, irritability, and a rash involving the extremities, face (perioral), and perineum. The rash is characterized by vesicular and pustular crusting with scaling and erythema.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:333 Pg: 2532

question_text: Which of the following is an indication to start corticosteroids in a patient with IgA vasculitis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Indication for Corticosteroid Use in IgA Vasculitis

  • Gastrointestinal Bleeds: Severe GI involvement causing bleeding, leading to significant morbidity and mortality.
  • Intractable Abdominal Pain: Persistent, severe abdominal pain alleviated by corticosteroids to reduce inflammation.

question_text: A 67 year old man presents with dysphagia of solids for the past three months. There is a history of 10 kg weight loss in 4 months following loss of appetite. He has had symptoms of indigestion and heartburn for 10 years. He regularly takes Gaviscon and milk of magnesia. He is a heavy smoker. He undergoes endoscopy, which reveals a small tumour at the lower part of the oesophagus. What is the likely aetiological cause?
explanation:
The history is suggestive of gastro oesophageal reflux for the past 10 years.

Continuous acid reflux causes metaplasia of the stratified squamous epithelium (which normally lines the distal oesophagus) to an abnormal columnar epithelium. This is known as Barrett's oesophagus.

Barrett's oesophagus increases the risk of development of adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 323 Pg: 2430

question_text: Which joints are Most frequently involved in reactive arthritis?
explanation:
The knees are most frequently involved in reactive arthritis, next most commonly affected are the ankles and small joints of the feet

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 362, Pg: 2797

question_text: Which of the following is NOT fitting criteria for APLA?
option_b: Death of normal fetus at 12th week of gestation
option_c: Premature birth at 35th week of gestation
explanation:
Clinical criteria include

  1. vascular thrombosis, defined as one or more clinical episodes of arterial, venous, or small vessel thrombosis in any tissue or organ; and
  2. pregnancy morbidity, defined as
    1. one or more unexplained deaths of a morphologically normal fetus at or beyond the 10th week of gestation;
    2. one or more premature births of a morphologically normal neonate before the 34th week of gestation because of eclampsia, severe preeclampsia, or placental insufficiency; or
    3. three or more unexplained consecutive spontaneous abortions before the 10th week of gestation.
  3. Laboratory criteria include
    1. LA,
    2. anticardiolipin (aCL), and/or
    3. anti-β2 GPI antibodies, at intermediate or high titres on two occasions 12 weeks apart.

Reference: HARRISON'S PRINCIPLES OF INTERNAL MEDICIENE, ED 21st , CHAPTER 357 pg 2749

question_text: A 45-year-old man presents with fatigue and hemoptysis. His hemoglobin has dropped from 12 g/dL to 8 g/dL in one week. Bronchoalveolar lavage reveals a reddish fluid, and his serum creatinine is elevated at 1.7 mg/dL. He tests ANCA-positive, and a renal biopsy shows pauci-immune glomerulonephritis without granulomatous inflammation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Microscopic polyangiitis presents with ANCA-positive pauci-immune glomerulonephritis and pulmonary-renal syndrome, without granulomas.

  • Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) is a pauci-immune small vessel vasculitis characterized by necrotizing glomerulonephritis and pulmonary capillaritis.
  • The hallmark features include:
    • Hemoptysis (due to alveolar hemorrhage)
    • Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (causing a drop in hemoglobin, elevated creatinine)
    • ANCA positivity - typically p-ANCA (anti-MPO antibodies)
    • Pauci-immune pattern on renal biopsy (minimal immune complex deposition)
    • Absence of granulomatous inflammation (unlike GPA or Churg-Strauss)
  • This clinical presentation of pulmonary-renal syndrome, especially with no granulomas, strongly favors MPA.

Microvascular Vasculitis:

Explanation of other options:

Systemic lupus erythematosus (Option C): SLE causes immune complex-mediated (not pauci-immune) nephritis and is typically ANA positive. It does not usually present with ANCA-positive vasculitis or isolated pulmonary-renal syndrome.

Henoch-Schonlein purpura (Option D): HSP is an IgA-mediated vasculitis seen mainly in children, with purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal involvement. Pulmonary hemorrhage and ANCA positivity are uncommon.

question_text: A 38-year-old male patient complains of paranasal sinus pain and bloody nasal discharge over the past few days. He has a history of previous hemoptysis and hematuria. Imaging studies reveal multiple bilateral nodular cavitary infiltrates. Which of the following antibodies is likely to be positive in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), formerly called Wegener's granulomatosis, is characterized by upper respiratory symptoms (sinus pain, bloody nasal discharge), lung findings (hemoptysis, cavitary nodules), and kidney involvement (hematuria), with c-ANCA serving as its specific marker.


Explanations of other options:

ANA (antinuclear antibodies) (Option B): These antibodies are mainly linked to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and other connective tissue disorders. The current presentation with granulomatous inflammation and vasculitis does not fit SLE, which more commonly manifests with malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, joint involvement, and serositis.

Anti-histone antibodies (Option C): These antibodies are most often linked to drug-induced lupus, which usually presents with milder features such as joint pain, muscle aches, and serositis, and seldom affects the kidneys or leads to serious organ injury.

Anti-Jo 1 antibodies (Option D): These antibodies are linked to polymyositis and dermatomyositis, conditions that typically manifest with proximal muscle weakness along with features such as Gottron's papules, heliotrope rash, and mechanic's hands.

question_text:
A 34-year-old man presented for a routine check-up from company. He was symptom free, but clinical examination suggested a small ventricular septal defect.
Which one of the following findings was most likely to have been present?
option_b: A short systolic murmur at the right sternal edge
option_c: A systolic murmur maximal at the apex
option_d: A systolic murmur with thrill at the left sternal edge
explanation:
Typically, a small VSD generates a pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border(LSB) accompanied by a thrill.

The murmur may be heard at the apex but is usually loudest at the LSB. Very small defects may generate an early/late systolic murmur.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:234,264 pg:1673,1833

question_text: A 61-year-old male presents with a six month history of a gradually increasing burning sensation in his feet. Examination revealed normal cranial nerves and higher mental function. He has normal bulk, tone, power, light touch and pinprick sensation, co-ordination and reflexes in upper and lower limbs. With which of the following are these clinical findings consistent?
explanation:
The burning sensation described is typical of a small fibre sensory neuropathy.

  • The small unmyelinated and thinly myelinated nerve fibres are affected.
  • General neurological examination and reflexes are usually normal in this type of neuropathy.
  • Treatment - Symptomatic therapy with local Lidoderm patch or oral amitriptyline, gabapentin or duloxetine.

Conditions in which the small fibres are preferentially affected in the early stages include diabetes and amyloidosis. In the later stages however the neuropathy in these conditions also affects large fibres.The neuropathy associated with Sjogren's syndrome is a pure sensory neuropathy (ganglionopathy). Neuropathy affecting the large myelinated sensory fibres generally causes glove and socking sensory loss and loss of reflexes.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3482

question_text: Causes of a small pupil include which of the following?
explanation:
Causes of small pupils include:

  • Horner's syndrome
  • Old age
  • Pontine haemorrhage
  • Argyll Robertson pupil
  • Drugs and poisons (opiates, organophosphates).
  • Causes of dilated pupils include:
  • Holmes-Adie (myotonic) pupil
  • Third nerve palsy
  • Drugs and poisons (atropine, cobalt [CO], ethylene glycol).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 216

question_text: A 15-year-old boy presents with a non-blanching rash over his shins and a swollen knee. He has noticed haematuria. Blood tests show a urea of 72 mg/dl and Creatinine 3 mg/dl. Urine dipstick shows: blood +++, protein +. What is the renal biopsy likely to show?
explanation:
The clinical presentation fits Henoch Schoenlein purpura renamed as IgA vasculitis.

This is an autoimmune disorder which is related to multisystemic IgA deposition. It is usually a self-limited disease.

It is the most common form of childhood vasculitis and results in Inflammatory changes in small vessels.

Male:female = 1.5:1

It presents acutely with

  • Headache
  • Fever
  • GI symptoms: loss of appetite, cramping abdominal pain
  • Joint pain
  • Red or purple spots typically appear on the skin(petechial purpura). Palpable purpurae is seen in almost all patients.

Inflammatory changes associated with Henoch-Schönlein Purpura can also develop in the joints, kidneys, digestive system, and in rare cases, the brain and spinal cord.

Mesangial Ig A deposits are typical features of HSP on the renal biopsy.

IgA nephropathy is clinically similar to HSP, except that it lacks the systemic features, slightly older age of development, absence of abdominal pain and preceding infection.

Serum complement levels are normal. Serum IgA levels May be elevated.

Glucocorticoids have been proven to be beneficial in abdominal pain, arthralgias. Not in skin and renal disease, except in RPGN.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 363, Pg: 2813-2815.

question_text: A 50 year old asthmatic treated with a high dose of inhaled corticosteroids develops a skin rash. His routine blood tests show mild renal dysfunction and blood eosinophilia. His chest radiograph is normal. Which blood test should be done next?
explanation:
• Skin rash and renal dysfunction in an asthmatic suggests Churg- Strauss syndrome.
  • Churg-Strauss syndrome, or allergic granulomatous angiitis, is a rare syndrome that affects small- to medium-sized arteries.

The presence of 4 or more criteria indicates a high likelihood of Churg-Strauss syndrome.

These criteria are:

  1. asthma
  2. eosinophilia of more than 10% in peripheral blood
  3. paranasal sinusitis
  4. pulmonary infiltrates (may be transient)
  5. histological proof of vasculitis with extravascular eosinophils
  6. mononeuritis multiplex or polyneuropathy.

Hypergammaglobulinemia, increased immunoglobulin E (IgE) levels, rheumatoid factor, and positive ANCA are usually present.

Pulmonary Infiltrates in Churg Strauss


Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:293 Pg: 2196

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding SSc is false?
option_a: ESR is usually normal in SSc, and an elevated ESR indicates coexisting myositis or malignancy
option_b: Sicca Syndrome can occur with SSC and is due to lymphocytic infiltration
option_c: Trigeminal neuropathy may occur with SSc
option_d: SSc may represent a paraneoplastic manifestation in those with malignancies of breast, lung or ovarian carcinoma and is associated with RNA polymerase III
explanation:
Sicca symptoms are common in SSc, but unlike in Sjogren's Syndrome, it is due to fibrosis of the glands rather than lymphocytic infiltration.

ESR is usually normal in SSc, since there is no active inflammation of vessel walls. A high ESR indicates myositis or malignancy. The CNS is usually spared in SSc, the only CNS manifestation could be unilateral or bilateral trigeminal neuropathy.

Breast, lung, ovarian malignancy and lymphoma may occur in temporal association with SSc, where SSc may represent a paraneoplastic manifestation and is associated with antibodies to RNA polymerase III

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 360, Pg: 2783

question_text: Which of the following is false regarding Systemic Sclerosis?
option_a: Calcinosis cutis is more seen with long standing SSc, with anti SCl-70 positivity
option_b: The calcium and phosphate levels are normal
option_c: Crystals are composed of calcium hydroxypetite
option_d: Paraspinal sheet calcifications may occur with neurological complications
explanation:
Calcinosis cutis is more seen with long standing systemic sclerosis, especially the anti centromere positive limited SSc. The serum calcium and phosphate levels are normal and the deposits are composed of calcium hydroxyapatite. The calcifications usually occur in finger pads, palms, extensor aspects of forearm. Large deposits can cause local nerve compression. Paraspinal sheet calcification can be seen with neurological complications. The lesions can ulcerate the overlying skin too.

Reference: Harrison's principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 360, Pg: 2779

question_text: What are the parameters that you use in a patient with SLE for assessing the disease activity?
option_a: Anti ds DNA and serum Complement levels
explanation:
The disease activity in SLE can be assessed by measuring the Serum ds DNA activity and a decrease in Serum complement levels(C3 or C4).

ESR and CRP can be raised in disease flare or during infections and hence cant be used to differentiate them.

Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed Ch: 356, Pg:2745

question_text: A 21-year-old woman with no underlying health conditions presents with numbness and tingling in the fingers of both hands. The image below shows a characteristic finding. She reports that these episodes typically occur during periods of high stress or exposure to cold weather. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

This patient is most likely experiencing Primary Raynaud's phenomenon because:

  • She is a young female (age 20-40 years; female-to-male ratio 5:1)
  • There is no underlying disease
  • Symptoms are symmetrical
  • Episodes are triggered by cold

Raynaud's Phenomenon Overview:

Primary Raynaud's:

  • Typically affects young women
  • No associated underlying illness
  • Normal nail fold capillaries with regular hairpin loops
  • Accounts for over 50% of cases
  • Has a better prognosis-improves in 15%, worsens in 30%
  • Characterized by classic triphasic color changes (white, blue, red)

Secondary Raynaud's (Option B ruled out):

  • Commonly caused by connective tissue diseases, especially scleroderma (Option D ruled out)
  • Other causes include arterial occlusive diseases, blood disorders, certain drugs (ergot, beta-blockers, bleomycin), and occupational exposures (vibrating tools)

Clinical Features:

  • Sequential color changes: White (ischemia) → Blue (deoxygenation) → Red (reperfusion)
  • Triggered by cold or emotional stress
  • Can involve fingers, toes, nose, ears
  • May be accompanied by pain, numbness, or tingling

Treatment:

  • Conservative: Warm clothing, avoiding cold, smoking cessation
  • Medications for severe cases: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, alpha-1 blockers (prazosin), phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, topical nitroglycerin
  • Digital sympathectomy for refractory cases

Explanation of other options:

Cold sores (Option C): are caused by the herpes virus and present as small fluid-filled blisters on the lips, mouth, nose, or cheeks, which does not fit this patient's symptoms or presentation.

question_text: A 26 year old patient who is a known case of SLE is coming to you with a positive UPT. She is on 5mg prednisolone and 200 mg HCQ daily and her disease is well controlled. What advice will you give her?
option_a: It is safe to continue both prednisolone and HCQs
option_b: Prednisolone has to be changed to Dexamethasone, HCQS is safe and may be continued
option_c: Prednisolone is safe and can be continued, but HCQS has to be stopped
option_d: No need to continue treatment as the disease is well controlled
explanation:
SLE and Pregnancy:

  • Rate of fetal loss is high in people with SLE than in general population and hence treatment has to be continued. So option D is incorrect.
  • Risk of fetal loss in SLE is associated with high disease activity, APLA, Lupus nephritis and Hypertension.
  • Prednisolone is the drug that can be given in pregnancy since 11β degydrogenase in placenta inactivates it and prevents fetal exposure.
  • 11β dehydrogenase cant inactivate fluorinated glucocorticoids like dexamethasone and hence it is contraindicated in pregnecy, except for neonatal lupus.
  • HCQS is also recommended by FDA for controlling disease activity in pregnancy.

Drugs used in treatment of SLE in pregnancy

First line agents: prednisone, prednisolone, HCQ

Second line agents: Azathioprine. (May cause fetal harm)

Breast feeding is contraindicated with immunosuppressants

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21th edition Ch:346 Pg:2747

question_text:
Which of the following is true regarding life threatening manifestations of SLE?
1. Cognitive dysfunction is the most common neurological manifestation.
2. Vaso occlusion in SLE is closely related to the presence of anti phospholipid antibodies.
3. Increased ALT and AST are seen during disease flares.
4. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea are common during disease flares.
5. Head ache and psychosis can occur due to complication of treatment for SLE
explanation:
NEUROLOGICAL 60%

May be due to vasoocclusion or primary neurological disease like cognitive dysfunction, head ache, seizure and psychosis. Head ache and psychosis can occur as a complication of treatment with steroids.

VASOOCCLUSIVE 15%: Risk of vaso occlusion is high in people with SLE and is not related to the presence of APLA

PULMONARY 60%:

MC is pleurisy

Life threatening is pulmonary hemorrhage and interstitial fibrosis

CARDIAC (60%)

Pericarditis is most common manifestation. Life threatening is myocarditis and endocarditis

GASTROINTESTINAL 40%: nausea, vominting and diarrhea and raised liver enzymes are common with lupus flare.

Life threatening complications include peritonitis and mesenteric ischemia

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:356 Pg:2740-3

question_text: What is the entry criteria in the new ACR/EULAR classification scheme for SLE?
explanation:
It is important to know that ANA is a highly sensitive test and thus a good screening test. In the new ACR/EULAR classification scheme, ANA positivity of more than 1:80 by ELISA is the entry criterion for classification to SLE.

SLICC does not have such entry criteria.

The old SLICC criteria did not have any such entry criterion.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:356 Pg:2741

question_text: Which of the following is an incorrect statement for SLE?
option_a: The most common symptom complex of SLE is musculoskeletal
option_b: Most arthritis in SLE is erosive on XRAY
option_c: The most common acute cutaneous lesion is a butterfly rash
option_d: The most frequent hematological manifestation is anemia

The clinical manifestations can be divided into life threatening and non life threatening

question_text: A 49 year old woman presents with breathlessness. She has a 2 year history of Raynaud's phenomenon. On examination, she had telangiectasia and tight skin around the mouth. She had no other systemic manifestations. Her investigations show an ESR of 70 mm/hr and positive anti-centromere antibodies. Which of the following is a typical late complication of this disorder?
explanation:
This patient has skin changes typical of Systemic Sclerosis. Apart from the skin changes, she is having Raynaud’s Phenomenon. The antibody profile indicates she has limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. One of the late complication is Pulmonary artery Hypertension.

question_text: A 40-year-old woman is found to have absent ankle jerks and gait disturbance.Which of the following investigations is not indicated?
explanation:
Absent ankle jerks may occur in conditions associated with neuropathy like

  • Vitamin B12 deficiency
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) - Elevated ANA titre present
  • Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis - High cholestanol levels present
  • Dorsal root disease (tabes dorsalis).

Gait disturbance may occur for a variety of reasons:

  • Sensory ataxia in B12 deficiency and tabes dorsalis
  • Pyramidal signs in B12 deficiency and SLE
  • Cerebellar ataxia in cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis.

To clarify option 3, cholestanol is a derivative of cholesterol.

In cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis there is a deficiency in sterol storage, and diagnosis is based on high serum (and tendon) cholesTANOL. Serum cholesterol may be normal or low. Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis is an inherited condition, associated with accumulation of cholesterol in tissues including brain, peripheral nerve and tendons.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3481

question_text: If a patient with Lupus nephritis class 1 has a kidney biopsy what would they find on a light microscopy and what is the most common class of lupus nephritis?
option_a: Focal, segmental or global endo- or extracapillary glomerulonephritis involving ≤50% of all glomeruli, class 4
explanation:
This question deals with the classification of Lupus Nephritis.

Here we will discuss about the classification of Lupus Nephritis

You have to be familiar with certain terms in the histological classification.

The microscopy may show activity in the form of proliferation or chronicity in the form of sclerosis denoted by A or C along with the class.

Focal : <50% of all the glomeruli are affected in the given specimen

Diffuse : >50% of the glomeruli are affected,

Segmental: <50% of individual glomeruli affected

Global: >50% of individual glomeruli is affected.

Mesangial proliferation may be seen in all classes of lupus nephritis. Proliferative means-either exo or endocapillary

Endocapillary proliferation is specific of SLE

CLASS IV IS THE MOST COMMON HISTOLOGY


Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:356 Pg:2739

question_text: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) presents with a platelet count of 5000/μL. Which of these is the most likely presenting symptom?
explanation:
Bleeding into muscle and joints, along with retroperitoneal and intracranial hemorrhage, indicates a likely defect in coagulation factors. Purpura, prolonged bleeding from superficial cuts, epistaxis, gastrointestinal hemorrhage or menorrhagia is more likely to be due to thrombocytopenia, a platelet function disorder or von Willebrand disease. Recurrent bleeds at a single site suggest a local structural abnormality rather than coagulopathic bleeding.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:65, Pg: 454

question_text: Which is not included in the pathologic triad for Systemic sclerosis?
explanation:
Three cardinal pathomechanistic processes underlie the protean clinical manifestations and pathologic changes of SSc:

  1. diffuse microangiopathy,
  2. inflammation and autoimmunity, and
  3. visceral and vascular fibrosis affecting multiple organs. In general, autoimmunity and reversible vascular reactivity are early features of SSc, whereas fibrosis and atrophy occur later in the disease.

Diffuse Microangiopathy is the first and primary pathogenic event and is responsible for most of the clinical symptoms, including, telangiectasis, Raynaud's Phenomenon, digital ulcers, renal crisis, myocardial involvement and PAH.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Chapter:360 Page number:2773

question_text: Most common manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is:
explanation:
Explanation:

The most frequent initial symptom of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is joint and muscle pain (arthralgia and myalgia). SLE can affect multiple organ systems, each presenting with distinct clinical features:

  • Skin: Photosensitivity is a common dermatologic manifestation.
  • Renal system: Proteinuria is often an early sign of kidney involvement.
  • Neurologic system: Patients may experience cognitive dysfunction, psychosis, depression, or seizures.
  • Cardiovascular system: Pericarditis is a typical cardiac complication.
  • Respiratory system: Pleuritis is commonly observed.
  • Hematologic system: Anaemia is a frequent finding.

The multi-system involvement highlights the diverse and systemic nature of SLE.

Characteristic Findings in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)

Explanations for other Options:

Photosensitivity (Option A): Photosensitivity is a common skin manifestation of SLE, where patients develop rashes or other skin reactions after exposure to sunlight. While it is a recognized feature of the disease and included in diagnostic criteria, it is not as common as musculoskeletal symptoms like joint and muscle pain.

Nephrotic syndrome (Option C): Nephrotic syndrome can occur in SLE due to lupus nephritis, a serious form of kidney involvement. However, kidney disease tends to appear later in the disease course and is not the most common presenting symptom. It is also less frequently seen compared to musculoskeletal and skin manifestations.

Seizures (Option D): Seizures are a possible neurological complication of SLE and are part of what is known as neuropsychiatric lupus. Although significant when present, seizures are relatively rare and certainly not among the most common initial or overall manifestations of the disease.

question_text:

2. Leucopenia in SLE predisposes to life threatening infections
3. Thrombocytopenia in SLE is a recurrent problem

explanation:

Most common ocular manifestation is SICCA syndrome and non specific conjunctivitis. Vision threatening diseases include retinal vasculitis and optic neuritis

question_text: A 49 year old female is having history of Raynaud's phenomenon for the last 6 years. She has noticed skin tightening for the last one year. On examination, you pinched the skin of her chest and found that it was normal.  Which of the following complication is she least likely to develop?

The associations of limited cutaneous scleroderma are:

CREST syndrome

Isolated PAH

Less frequent associations are:

Primary Biliary Cirrhosis

Sjogren's syndrome

Hypothyroidism

Renal involvement and renal crisis are very rare in limited cutaneous disease

The antibody associated is anti-centromere antibody

Difference between Limited Cutaneous and Diffuse cutaneous Systemic Sclerosis

question_text: Which of the following statements is false?
option_a: Localized scleroderma is more common in children
option_b: It spares fingers and Raynaud's phenomenon is rare
option_d: Linear scleroderma can cross joints leading to contractures and can cause growth retardation of long bones
explanation:
Localized scleroderma is more common in children.

Raynaud's phenomenon is rare.

There is no finger involvement. Internal organ involvement is rare. Linear scleroderma can cross joints causing contractures and growth retardation of long bones.

Eosinophilic fasciitis is a disorder of adults which presents as skin thickening, having the same features as above. There will not be auto antibodies in SSc. Fingers will be spared and there will be no internal organ involvement. It is often seen in association with myelodysplastic syndrome or multiple myeloma.

question_text:
A 25 year old female develops cyanosis of digits when hand is put in cold water followed by redness. Which of the following is responsible for this manifestation?
a. Scleroderma
b. Migraine
c. Cryoglobulinemia
d. Hyperthyroidism
explanation:
The question deals with Raynaud's phenomenon: Raynaud's phenomenon is episodic vasoconstriction affecting the tops of fingers and toes and sometimes of the tip of nose and earlobes. Attack typically begins with pallor(vasoconstriction), cyanosis(ischemia) and hyperemia(reperfusion).

Primary Raynaud's phenomenon: Raynaud's disease. Occurs in the absence of any underlying condition. It is just an exaggerated vasomotor response to cold.

Secondary Raynaud's phenomenon: occurs in association with Systemic sclerosis, Sjogren syndrome, PAN, Takayasu Arteritis, Antisynthetase syndrome, acromegaly, progressive diaphyseal dysplasia, drugs like beta blockers, cisplatin, bleiomycin, ergot alkaloids, bromocriptine, Clonidine, cocaine, Dextramphetamine, methylphenidate, phentermine, interferons
