question_text: Which antibody does not have Scleroderma as its phenotype?
explanation:
Anti-Ribosomal antibodies are not typically associated with Scleroderma as their phenotype.

  • Anti-Pm-Scl antibodies: These are often found in patients with overlap syndromes involving features of both Scleroderma and Polymyositis.
  • Anti-Ku antibodies: These are associated with some cases of Scleroderma, particularly the limited cutaneous form.
  • Anti-U1 RNP antibodies: These are more commonly associated with Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD), which can have overlapping features of Scleroderma among other autoimmune conditions.
  • Anti-Ribosomal antibodies: These antibodies are primarily associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and are not a typical feature of Scleroderma.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Chapter:360 Page number:2776

question_text: A 20 year old female comes with history of arthritis, butterfly rash and fever of one month duration. Up on testing, her ANA is positive with positive anti ds DNA and Anti histone antibody. What is your diagnosis?
explanation:
This question deals with the different types of auto antibodies associated with SLE and their clinical significance.

Antibodies in SLE:

ANA is highly sensitive test for SLE but is very non specific. Positive in 98% of patients with SLE.

Immunoflourescence(IF) is the gold standard technique for detecting ANA. Several Antinuclear antibodies have been identified based on the pattern of fluorescence in IF.

Seeing this question, we may tend to answer it as Drug induced lupus since she has anti histone antibodies.

Anti histone antibody is seen in drug induced lupus, but it is not specific for it. Anti ds DNA is specific for SLE. Hence drug induced lupus will be negative for ds DNA. Anti histone antibodies will be seen in 70% of SLE. So the answer is SLE.

Anti Ribosomal P antibody is seen in Neuropsychiatric lupus.

Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed Ch: 356, Pg: 2738

question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents with symptoms of dry mouth and eyes and tests positive for anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies. The image below demonstrates a positive test result, showing a score of less than 5 mm in 5 minutes without anesthesia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of dry eyes and dry mouth, along with a Schirmer's test result of ≤5 mm in 5 minutes and positive anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies, strongly suggests a diagnosis of Sjogren syndrome.

Sjogren Syndrome

Pathogenesis:

Sjogren syndrome is an autoimmune disease primarily targeting exocrine glands. It involves lymphocytic infiltration-mainly T and B cells-into the salivary and lacrimal glands. This immune attack is triggered by a combination of genetic susceptibility, environmental factors, and an abnormal immune response. Key features include:

  • B-cell hyperactivity causing hypergammaglobulinemia and autoantibody production (anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB).
  • Exocrine gland epithelial cells express autoantigens (Ro, La), secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines, and activate immune pathways via Toll-like receptors.
  • Genetic predisposition, such as specific HLA alleles (e.g., HLA-DQA1*0501) and immune regulatory genes (IRF5, STAT4), increase susceptibility.

Clinical Features:

  • Xerostomia (dry mouth) and keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) are hallmark symptoms.
  • Oral symptoms: difficulty swallowing, increased dental caries, and parotid gland enlargement.
  • Ocular symptoms: gritty sensation, burning, and decreased tear production.
  • Systemic signs: fatigue, joint pain, Raynaud's phenomenon, and increased risk of lymphoma (especially marginal zone B-cell lymphoma).

Diagnosis:

Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and supportive tests:

  • Unstimulated whole saliva flow rate ≤0.1 mL/min.
  • Schirmer's test ≤5 mm/5 min in at least one eye.
  • Ocular staining score ≥5 or van Bijsterveld's score ≥4 in at least one eye.
  • Presence of serum antibodies (anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB).
  • Minor salivary gland biopsy showing lymphocytic infiltration with a focus score ≥1.

Treatment:

Management focuses on symptom relief and controlling systemic disease:

  • For eye symptoms: artificial tears and topical cyclosporine for inflammation.
  • For dry mouth: frequent sips of water, pilocarpine, or cevimeline to stimulate saliva production.
  • For systemic involvement: hydroxychloroquine for mild symptoms, and immunosuppressants such as rituximab in severe cases.

Explanation for other options:

Scleroderma (Option A): is associated with anti-Scl-70 and anti-centromere antibodies, so it is unlikely to be the diagnosis in this case.

Dehydration and lacrimal duct stones (Options B and C): are also unlikely, as the presence of anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies is characteristic of Sjogren syndrome.

question_text: A female patient feels numb on the fingertip. Her facial skin was tightened. ANA was found to be positive. Immunofluorescence showed a nucleolar pattern. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: Tightening of skin, nucleolar pattern of ANA is suggestive of Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

question_text:
A 36 year old lady presents with myalgia and lethargy. Her blood tests show a positive ANA with a titre of 1:1024 and rheumatoid factor is negative.The CK is raised at 360 U/l. Extranuclear antigen tests show a negative Ro and negative La, negative Scl70 and positive ribonuclear protein antibody at 160 units.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
The presence of muscle pain, positive ANA and antibodies to RNP points to the diagnosis of Mixed Connective Tissue Disease

MCTD is a disorder where limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis is associated with features of RA, SLE and polymyositis.

The initial presentation is puffy fingers and Raynaud’s Phenomenon

The rash may be of SLE or dermatomyositis

The response to steroids is excellent

They have high titres of U1RNP antibody

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 360, Pg: 2787

question_text: A 24-year-old female patient presented with malar rash, recurrent oral ulcers, and multiple joint pains. She has no relevant past history and does not take any medication. On further investigations, thrombocytopenia was seen, and the anti-Sm antibody was positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:
In the given clinical scenario the patient's presentation is highly characteristic of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). The combination of clinical criteria (malar rash, oral ulcers, arthritis) with laboratory findings of thrombocytopenia and a positive anti-Smith (anti-Sm) antibody which is highly specific for SLE confirms the diagnosis.

  • SLE is a multisystem autoimmune disease most common in young women.
  • The anti-Sm antibodyis considered a specific serological marker for SLE, though it is not highly sensitive.
  • Thrombocytopenia is one of the hematological manifestations of SLE.

Explanation of other options:
Scleroderma (Option A): The patient presents with skin thickening (sclerodactyly), Raynaud's phenomenon, and internal organ fibrosis, not typically with malar rash or anti-Sm antibodies.


Sjogren's syndrome (Option B): Primarily characterized by sicca symptoms (dry eyes, dry mouth) and is associated with anti-Ro/SS-A and anti-La/SS-B antibodies.

Rheumatoid arthritis (Option C): Primarily causes a symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis and is associated with antibodies like RF and anti-CCP, not malar rash or anti-Sm.

Key Takeaways:

  • Anti-Sm antibody is highly specific for SLE and is included in the classification criteria.

question_text: Which is the wrong statement regarding Systemic Sclerosis?
option_a: Raynauds phenomenon is the most common extracutaneous complication of SSc
option_b: Raynauds phenomenon can preceed SSc by years
option_c: Renal and lung damage occurs late in the course of SSc
option_d: Pigment loss in SSc may lead to salt and pepper appearance
explanation:
• RAYNAUD'S PHENOMENON Raynaud's phenomenon, the most frequent extracutaneous complication of SSc, is characterized by episodic vasoconstriction in the fingers and toes, sometimes also affecting the tip of the nose and earlobes. Secondary Raynaud's phenomenon tends to occur at an older age, is more severe (episodes are more frequent, prolonged, and painful), and is frequently complicated by ischemic digital ulcers and loss of digits. Nail fold capillaroscopy can be helpful for both differentiating primary from secondary Raynaud's phenomenon and for establishing the early diagnosis of SSc.
  • While advancing skin involvement is the most visible manifestation of early dcSSc, important and clinically silent internal organ involvement can occur during this stage (within the first 4 years).
  • Bilateral symmetrical skin thickening is the hallmark that distinguishes SSc from other connective tissue diseases. Skin involvement starts in the fingers and characteristically advances from distal to proximal extremities in an ascending fashion. Pigment loss sparing the perifollicular areas gives rise to a "salt-and pepper" appearance of the skin, most prominently on the scalp, upper back, and chest (sparing the mid-back).

Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 360, Pg: 2778-2781

question_text: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibody is most strongly associated with which of the following complications?
explanation:
Explanation:

Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibodies are highly specific for systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), especially the diffuse cutaneous form. Their presence is strongly associated with an increased risk for developing interstitial lung disease (ILD), which is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in these patients.

question_text: A 54-year-old woman presents with finger swelling, heartburn, and intermittent joint pain. On examination, her hands show shiny, tight, thickened skin with non-pitting edema. She also has interstitial lung disease. Laboratory tests reveal positivity for ANA, anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70), and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient presents with skin thickening (shiny, tight skin with non-pitting edema), finger swelling, heartburn (suggestive of esophageal dysmotility), intermittent joint pain, and interstitial lung disease. These features point strongly toward systemic sclerosis (scleroderma).

Diffuse Scleroderma

  • Characterized by widespread skin thickening, involving the fingers, hands, arms, legs, anterior trunk, and face.
  • Carries a high risk of internal organ involvement, particularly affecting the gastrointestinal tract, kidneys, lungs, and heart.
  • Common symptoms include dry skin, pruritus (itching), and musculoskeletal discomfort.
  • Can become life-threatening, especially with severe pulmonary or cardiac complications.
  • May present with acute hypertensive episodes, potentially resulting in renal damage.

Cutaneous Features of Systemic Sclerosis (SSc)

Explanation for other options:

Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (Option A): is typically associated with the presence of anti-centromere antibodies (ACA).

Raynaud's phenomenon (Option C): is a common clinical feature seen in diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis, characterized by episodes of numbness and cold sensations in areas like the fingers and nose, often triggered by cold exposure or emotional stress.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (Option D): is a hereditary disorder that increases the likelihood of developing hamartomatous polyps in the gastrointestinal tract and various malignancies, including those of the breast, ovaries, and testes. Since the patient lacks gastrointestinal polyps, this diagnosis is less likely.

question_text:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the management of Lupus nephritis?
1. HCQS should be included as treatment for all classes since it reduces the accrual of tissue damage.
2. Management of class I and Class II should be guided by the extra renal manifestations.
3. Class III and IV requires aggressive immunosuppression.
4. Isolated Class V has got better prognosis than class IV.
5. Isolated class V without nephrotic range proteinuria requires only supportive management.
explanation:
The question deals with the management and prognosis of Lupus Nephritis. HCQ should be in the management of allclasses of lupus nephritis. Class I and II should be treated mainly based on the extra renal manifestations. Class III and IV are the proliferative and serious forms and require aggressive immunosuppression with high dose glucocorticoid with either MMF or Cyclophosphamide. Isolated Class V presents with proteinuria alone and has got better outcome than class IV. But class V often co exists with class III and IV. Class V with nephrotic range proteinuria should be treated with immunosuppression, usually steroid with calcinurin inhibitors.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:356 Pg:2739-2747

question_text: A woman presents with fever, joint pains, oral ulcers, and fatigue for six months, now associated with hematuria. Urine analysis reveals red blood cell casts and proteinuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of systemic features of SLE (fever, arthralgia, ulcers, fatigue) along with renal involvement (RBC casts, proteinuria, hematuria) strongly indicates lupus nephritis, a renal manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus caused by immune complex deposition in the glomeruli.

Lupus Nephritis:

  • Pathophysiology: Immune complex-mediated glomerular injury involving anti-dsDNA antibodies.
  • Clinical features:
    • Proteinuria (may reach nephrotic levels)
    • Hematuria with RBC casts
    • Systemic SLE manifestations: fever, arthralgia, oral/nasal ulcers, photosensitivity, fatigue
    • Risk of progression to hypertension and ESRD if untreated
  • Diagnosis:
    • Urinalysis: proteinuria, hematuria, RBC casts
    • Serology: ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm positivity
    • Renal biopsy: classification into six histological classes (I-VI)
  • Management:
    • Corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate mofetil
    • Hydroxychloroquine (for systemic SLE; safe in pregnancy)

Explanation of other options:

Acute interstitial nephritis (Option A): Typically drug-induced (e.g., NSAIDs, antibiotics) or due to infections. Presents with fever, rash, eosinophilia, and urine showing WBC casts-not RBC casts.

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (Option B): Seen in children post-streptococcal infection; presents with hematuria, edema, and hypertension, but lacks systemic lupus features such as ulcers or arthritis.

IgA nephropathy (Option D): Often presents with recurrent hematuria following an upper respiratory infection; shows mesangial IgA deposits on biopsy but does not include systemic SLE manifestations.

Key Takeaways:

  • RBC casts + systemic SLE features = lupus nephritis.
  • Always confirm with serology and renal biopsy for classification and prognosis.
  • Requires immunosuppressive therapy to prevent progression to renal failure.

question_text: A 28-year-old pregnant woman with known Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) undergoes a routine fetal ultrasound at 22 weeks. The scan reveals a persistent fetal heart rate of 55 bpm, consistent with complete heart block. The transplacental passage of which maternal autoantibody is the most likely cause of this fetal condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

This scenario describes Neonatal Lupus Erythematosus, with its most severe manifestation being Congenital Heart Block. This condition is caused by the passive transfer of maternal Anti-Ro (SSA) and/or Anti-La (SSB) antibodies across the placenta. These antibodies bind to components of the fetal cardiac conduction system (specifically the AV node), inducing an inflammatory response that leads to fibrosis and irreversible heart block.

Key Maternal Antibodies and Their Pregnancy Implications in SLE:

Explanation of Other Options:

Anti-dsDNA antibody (Option A): This antibody is a marker of maternal SLE disease activity, particularly lupus nephritis. It does not cross the placenta to cause heart block.

Anti-Smith (Sm) antibody (Option C): This antibody is highly specific for the diagnosis of SLE in the mother but is not associated with any specific fetal complications.

Antiphospholipid antibody (Option D): These antibodies (e.g., lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin) cause a hypercoagulable state, leading to placental thrombosis, recurrent pregnancy loss, and preeclampsia, but they do not cause congenital heart block.

question_text: A 35-year-old female patient with fever and malar rash was found to have vegetations on either side of the heart valves. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation of fever, malar rash, and cardiac vegetations is classic for Libman-Sacks endocarditis, which is a non-infectious complication of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).

Key Diagnostic Features

  • Malar Rash: A hallmark cutaneous manifestation of SLE.
  • Vegetations: Libman-Sacks lesions are characterized by sterile, verrucous (wart-like) vegetationsthat are unique because they can occur on both sides of the valve leaflets (mitral and tricuspid are most common).
  • Systemic Illness: Fever is a common systemic feature of active SLE.

Explanation of other options:

Infective endocarditis (Option A): This involves infective vegetations usually in a patient with predisposing factors (e.g., valvular disease, IV drug use). While fever is present, a malar rash is not a typical feature.

Rheumatic Heart Disease (Option C): This results from untreated Group A streptococcal infection, leading to valvular damage (e.g., mitral stenosis). It does not cause a malar rash or the specific bilateral vegetations seen in Libman-Sacks endocarditis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Libman-Sacks endocarditis is a diagnostic feature of SLE.
  • The vegetations are sterile and can be found on both sides of the valve leaflets.
  • The presence of a malar rash strongly points toward an underlying autoimmune etiology.

question_text: A 30-year-old woman with known SLE presents with ankle swelling. Her blood pressure is 170/100 mmHg and she has marked lower limb oedema. Urine dipstick discloses +3 protein with no haematuria. Plasma creatinine concentration is 1.1 mg/dl, albumin is 1.2 g/dl and urinary protein excretion rate is 6.9 g/24 h. What is the cause of this presentation?
explanation:
This patient is a young female with SLE who presents with massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia and hypertension without hematuria. This is typical of Nephrotic syndrome.

Amyloidosis is known to cause nephrotic syndrome. But the diseases that are known to be associated with AA amyloid are Rheumatoid Arthritis, Juvenile idiopathic arthritis, chronic infections and Familial Mediterranean Fever. And AL amyloidosis with monoclonal gammopathies.

Class II Lupus Nephritis typically presents as Nephritic syndrome and not pure nephrotic syndrome.

Class V Lupus nephritis is the one which may present as pure Nephrotic syndrome. The histology will be pure membranous nephropathy. It can precede the extra renal manifestations in SLE.

Fibrillary glomerulopathy is characterized by the accumulation of congo red negative fibrils in the glomerulus. It is found to be associated with malignancies, autoimmune diseases, monoclonal gammopathies. It presents with proteinuria and hematuria.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition, Ch:314, Pg:2345, 2338

question_text: A 19-year-old girl presents with a 6-week history of pain in multiple joints with early morning stiffness. Her symptoms responded well initially to Ibuprofen but then they worsened again. She has no other systemic symptoms. She had been taking Minocycline for her acne. Investigations show: ESR 140 mm/hr, CRP 110 mg/l, Rheumatoid Factor negative, ANA strongly positive (1:1600). What is the most probable diagnosis and which antibody are you most likely to find?
explanation:
The question deals with inflammatory arthritis(joint pain with stiffness) in a female of reproductive age group. A raised ESR, CRP also points towards an inflammatory cause. The most common cause of inflammatory arthritis in females of reproductive age group is SLE. If we look more into the details given, it is said that she is on Minocycline, which is implicated in drug induced lupus. So it is not simple SLE, but Drug induced lupus(DIL). It is associated with anti histone antibodies.

Drug induced Lupus(DIL):

  • Positive ANA
  • Fever, malaise, arthritis or intense arthralgias/myalgias, serositis, and/ or rash,
  • Rarely involving the kidney and brain.
  • Associated with anti-histone antibodies.
  • It resolves over weeks after discontinuation of medications.
  • Asymptomatic ANA positivity is also seen on exposure to the drugs.
  • SHIP Pnemonic may be used to remember a few. S- Sulfasalazine, H-Hydralazine, I-Isoniazid, P-Procainamide, P-Phenytoin
  • TNF alpha inhibitors can also cause this.
  • The incidence of Drug Induced Lupus is less in females and more in whites.

Common drugs that can cause lupus.

Hydrochlorthiazide, Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, beta blockers, Propylthiouracil, lithium, phenytoin, isoniazid, minocycline, and nitrofurantoin, sulfasalazine, lovastatin and simvastatin.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:356 Pg:2748-2749

question_text:

explanation:

Large tendon xanthomata.

It is eminently treatable by the oral administration of chenodeoxycholic acid.

To clarify option 3, cholestanol is a derivative of cholesterol. In cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis there is a deficiency in sterol storage, and diagnosis is based on high serum (and tendon) cholestanol Serum cholesterol may be normal or low.

question_text: A 52-year-old woman presents with hand changes as shown in the image, along with decreased mobility in the small joints and loss of wrinkle lines on her facial skin. Her chest X-ray reveals prominent bilateral infiltrates in the lower lobes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

A patient with diffuse systemic sclerosis is presented to you with complained of progressive dyspnea and cough.respiratory examination shows bilateral crepitation.X-ray suggest bibasilar reticular shadow.What is the next step of investigation?
explanation:
This case scenario suggests interstitial lung disease in patients with diffuse systemic sclerosis.

In a patient with diffuse systemic sclerosis who presents with progressive dyspnea and cough, along with bilateral crepitations on respiratory examination and bibasilar reticular shadowing on X-ray, the next step of investigation is High-Resolution CT (HRCT) of the thorax. This choice is supported because:

HRCT Thorax: It is the most sensitive and specific imaging modality for detecting interstitial lung disease (ILD), which is common in patients with systemic sclerosis. HRCT can provide detailed images of the lung parenchyma, allowing for the identification of the extent and pattern of fibrosis, ground-glass opacities, and other interstitial changes.

2D ECHO: While echocardiography can be useful to evaluate for pulmonary hypertension, which can occur in systemic sclerosis, it does not provide detailed information about lung parenchymal disease.

CT Pulmonary Angiography: This is typically used to assess for pulmonary embolism. While it can show large vessel involvement, it is not the best choice for evaluating diffuse parenchymal lung disease in the context of systemic sclerosis.

Bronchoscopy: This invasive procedure is more useful for evaluating airway lesions, infections, or malignancies. It is not the first-line investigation for interstitial lung disease.

question_text: An elderly female with a known history of scleroderma presents with shortness of breath. On clinical evaluation, her right ventricular systolic pressure is found to be 70-80 mmHg, and right heart catheterization reveals a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 35 mmHg. Which of the following statements is true regarding her condition?
option_a: Calcium channel blockers are given to all patients
option_b: Lung transplant is the best treatment if identified early
option_d: Lifestyle modification is the only possible approach
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Endothelin receptor antagonists are effective in improving symptoms and slowing disease progression in pulmonary hypertension, particularly in connective tissue disease-associated PH like in scleroderma.

  • This patient with scleroderma, dyspnea, elevated right ventricular pressure, and elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP = 35 mmHg) is likely suffering from pulmonary hypertension (PH)-specifically group 1 (pulmonary arterial hypertension) or group 2 PH (due to left heart disease) depending on underlying pathology.
  • Pulmonary Hypertension (PH):
    • Defined as mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) > 20 mmHg (updated threshold).
    • In scleroderma, pulmonary hypertension may result from:
      • Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) due to vascular remodeling (Group 1)
      • Interstitial lung disease with PH (Group 3)
      • Left heart involvement (diastolic dysfunction) leading to increased PCWP (Group 2)
    • Clinical Clues from the Question:
      • Elevated RV pressure (70-80 mmHg): Sign of significant pulmonary arterial pressure load.
      • PCWP = 35 mmHg (Normal = 6-12): Suggests post-capillary PH (Group 2) possibly from diastolic dysfunction or pulmonary venous hypertension in scleroderma.
    • Symptoms: Dyspnea, fatigue, and signs of right heart failure.
    • Therapeutic Approach:
      • Endothelin Receptor Antagonists (ERAs) (e.g., Bosentan, Ambrisentan) are approved for symptom relief and improved exercise tolerance in PAH, including scleroderma-associated PAH.
      • These block endothelin-1-mediated vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling.
      • Also used in combination therapy with PDE-5 inhibitors or prostanoids in advanced cases.

Explanation of other options:

Calcium channel blockers are given to all patients (Option A): CCBs are indicated only in patients with a positive vasoreactivity test (seen in ~10% of idiopathic PAH). They are not beneficial and may be harmful in connective tissue-associated PAH like in scleroderma.

Lung transplant is the best treatment if identified early (Option B): Transplant is reserved for advanced, treatment-refractory cases, not early-stage disease. Pharmacological therapy is preferred initially.

Lifestyle modification is the only possible approach (Option D): Lifestyle changes (e.g., sodium restriction, exercise, oxygen therapy) are supportive but not curative. Targeted pharmacologic therapies are essential for symptom control and survival benefit.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482463/

question_text: A 30-year-old heroine addict was found dead in his room. He was last seen alive by his neighbours around 4 weeks ago and he was presumed to be unwell over the past 4 weeks. question_text: A 44 year woman has Raynaud's phenomenon. She also has difficulty in swallowing and dyspnoea. Echocardiography shows right heart strain. Her BP was 150/100 and her renal functions were derranged. Which one of the following antibodies is specific to this lady's condition?

Anti RNA polymerase III will have rapidly progressive skin thickening and joint symptoms and renal crisis, like Scl-70, but instead of ILD, they are at risk of developing GAVE and contemporaneous cancers.

question_text: What is the appropriate treatment for a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presenting with wire loop lesions on renal biopsy?
explanation:
Explanation:

The appropriate treatment for a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presenting with wire loop lesions on renal biopsy is to give steroid and cyclophosphamide.Wire-loop lesions on renal biopsy are the hallmark of Class IV lupus nephritis (diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis), the most aggressive renal manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).This lesion reflects heavy subendothelial immune-complex deposition that can rapidly progress to end-stage kidney disease if not treated promptly.

Recommended therapy

  • Induction phase: High-dose corticosteroids (e.g., IV methylprednisolone pulses followed by oral prednisone) plus a potent cytotoxic agent-traditionally cyclophosphamide (NIH or Euro-Lupus regimen) or, in modern protocols, mycophenolate mofetil combined with steroids.
  • The classical regimen is steroid + cyclophosphamide.

Explanation for other Options:

Steroid alone (Option A): Corticosteroids reduce inflammation but monotherapy has a high relapse and progression rate in Class IV disease.Without an additional immunosuppressant, irreversible renal scarring and end-stage kidney disease are common.

Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) alone (Option C): MMF is an accepted alternative to cyclophosphamide when combined with steroids, but MMF by itself is not recommended for induction.Using it alone provides inadequate suppression of the intense proliferative activity seen with wire-loop lesions.

Hydroxychloroquine (Option D): Excellent for cutaneous and musculoskeletal SLE and for long-term maintenance to reduce flares. However, it is not potent enough to control severe proliferative nephritis, so it cannot be the sole treatment in this setting.

question_text:
A 42-year-old female with a recent diagnosis of systemic sclerosis, is referred to hospital with a complaint of headaches, blurred vision. On examination, her blood pressure is 230/120 mmHg and there is bilateral papilloedema. Her creatinine is 5.2. Her ECG is suggestive of hyperkalemia.
Which of the following should not be prescribed for this patient?
option_d: Renal transplant, as with creatinine derranged, damage is irreversible
explanation:
Accelerated hypertension in a patient with Systemic Sclerosis with renal impairment indicates Scleroderma Renal Crisis.

The mortality of scleroderma has come down drastically with the use of ACE Inhibitors.

Substantial renal recovery can occur following an episode of scleroderma renal crisis, and renal replacement therapy can be ultimately discontinued in 30-50% of patients in 6 months and renal transplant is rarely needed.

The pathogenesis is obliterative vasculopathy of the arcuate and interlobar vessels, with intra vascular hemolysis.

RAAS is upregulated due to reduced renal blood flow, further compromising the blood flow.

Risk factors:

  1. Male sex
  2. African-american race
  3. Rapidly progressive skin involvement
  4. Use of glucocorticoids.
  5. UIII RNP antibodies

Pericardial effusion, tendon friction rub and new unexplained anemia and thrombocytopenia are harbingers of a renal crisis.

BP should be reduced by 20/10mmHg each day using ACEI. ARBs are used only if ACEI is contraindicated. Once ACEI is in its maximum dose , other antihypertensives may be added. ACEI improves the renal recovery and should be continued during dialysis too.

Since there is intra renal complement activation, Eculizumab may also be used.

TTP is a close DD and ADAMTS 13 levels should be measured, as it will be normal in renal crisis.

Normotensive renal crisis has worse outcome than with hypertension.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Chapter:360 Page number:2782

question_text: A 71-year-old man develops weakness of the shoulders and around the hips over a 6-month period. He has also noticed weak finger flexors. He complained of difficulty swallowing liquids. There is no other significant past medical history. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and drinks a bottle of wine at the weekend. A creatinine kinase level comes back at 120 U/l.A muscle biopsy sample shows myopathic changes. There are also inflammatory. infiltrates and intracytoplasmic vacuoles present. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Clinical points towards diagnosis of IBM:

  • Age over 50 years
  • Weakness of finger flexors
  • This is an inflammatory condition affecting patients over the age of 50.
  • Proximal muscles in the upper and lower limbs, and finger flexors are predominantly involved.
  • The onset of muscle weakness in IBM is generally gradual (over months or years).
  • Dysphagia is common, occurring in 40-66% of patients. IBM occurs more frequently in men than women. CK may be normal.
  • A muscle biopsy usually shows intracytoplasmic inclusions and also inflammatory infiltrates.
  • Granular lymphocytic leukemia/ lymphocytosis, sarcoidosis, sicca or Sjögren’s syndrome are the conditions that may be associated.


Thigh atrophy seen in inclusion body myositis


Inclusion bodies and inflammatory infiltrates(arrows)

Reference: Harrison's principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 365, Pg: 2823

question_text: Pathognomonic sign seen in Juvenile dermatomyositis is?
explanation:
The most common clinical manifestations at disease onset are muscle weakness, easy fatigability, skin rash, malaise, and in some cases, fever. The CK levels tend to be mildly elevated, whereas other muscle enzymes such as aspartate aminotransaminase (AST), alanine aminotransaminase (ALT), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) might be more commonly elevated.

The skin rash is often pathognomonic and similar to that in adult DM: the most typical skin manifestations are heliotrope discoloration of the upper eyelids, Gottron's papules, periungual erythema, and capillary loop abnormalities (dilated and tortuous with decreased capillary density). Calcinosis, cutaneous ulceration, and lipodystrophy are more common in juvenile cases than in adults.

question_text: A 64 year old man presents with muscle weakness and difficulty swallowing. On examination, he has proximal and distal upper and lower limb weakness. There is wasting of the intrinsic muscles of the fingers and of his thigh muscles. CK is elevated and EMG findings are consistent with a myopathic process. Which condition is likely?
explanation:
• The distribution of the muscles involved are typical of inclusion body myositis, although the distribution is usually asymmetric. In this condition, dysphagia and respiratory involvement can also occur. Muscle biopsy shows intracellular inclusions (amyloid precursor protein, ubiquitins) and inflammatory infiltrates.


Inclusion body in IBM

Inclusion Body Myositis

  • IBM is a rare sporadic disorder in adults that causes muscle weakness with an insidious onset. The distribution of weakness can be either symmetric or asymmetric, and both proximal and distal muscle groups can be involved. Dysphagia occurs in about one-third of patients.
  • Muscle enzymes are typically normal or mildly elevated in IBM, with Creatine kinase (CK) levels generally being less than 10 times normal.
  • The diagnosis of sporadic IBM depends upon the presence of characteristic clinical and laboratory findings which include a slowly progressive muscle weakness with early involvement of the quadriceps muscles and wrist/finger flexors, and elevated muscle enzymes.
  • A muscle biopsy should be performed in patients with suspected IBM. However, histopathological confirmation is not always possible, and the diagnosis may still be made based on characteristic clinical findings.
  • Muscle biopsy findings that are highly specific for IBM include the presence of rimmed vacuoles, mononuclear cell inflammatory infiltrate of non-necrotic muscle fibers, and the presence of either amyloid deposits or tubulofilaments by electron microscopy

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 365, Pg: 2823

question_text: A 55-year-old woman presents with a history of progressive difficulty in climbing stairs and rising from chairs. She also complains of difficulty in swallowing. She complains that her hands discolor and become cold easily. On examination she has purple discoloration of her eyelids and periorbital oedema. There is weakness of the muscles of her limb girdles. What is the likely cause of the dysphagia?
explanation:
The diagnosis is dermatomyositis.

Characteristic features of DM:

  • Symmetric, proximal greater than distal weakness
  • Heliotrope rash (erythematous discoloration of eyelids with periorbital edema)
  • Gottron sign (erythematous rash over the extensor surfaces of joints such as the knuckles, elbows, knees, and ankles)
  • Gottron papules (raised erythematous rash over knuckles)
  • V-sign (rash on the sun-exposed anterior neck and chest)
  • Shawl sign over the back of the neck and shoulders

Dysphagia in dermatomyositis is primarily due to weakness of the striated musculature of the posterior pharynx. Dysphagia may also result from cricopharyngeal obstruction secondary to inflammation or fibrosis of the cricopharyngeus muscles.


Heliotrope rash in dermatomyositis

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:365 Pg:2820

question_text: A 50-year-old female reports trouble performing tasks such as climbing stairs, rising from a seated position, and combing her hair. On examination, a violaceous rash over the upper eyelids is observed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Proximal muscle weakness (problems climbing stairs, getting up from a chair, and combing hair) combined with the distinctive violaceous rash on the upper eyelids (heliotrope rash) points to a diagnosis of dermatomyositis.


Explanations of other options:

Inclusion body myositis (Option A): Inclusion body myositis mainly occurs in older individuals and is characterized by distal, often asymmetric muscle weakness. Unlike dermatomyositis, it lacks skin involvement and most commonly affects the quadriceps and finger flexors.

Polymyositis (Option C): Polymyositis is an autoimmune condition marked by inflammatory muscle involvement, presenting as symmetric proximal muscle weakness. Unlike dermatomyositis, it does not feature the distinctive skin signs such as the heliotrope rash or Gottron's papules.

Scleroderma (Option D): Scleroderma is a connective tissue disease that mainly involves the skin and internal organs. Although muscle weakness may occur, its defining features are skin thickening and fibrosis rather than the violaceous rash of dermatomyositis. It is also associated with Raynaud's phenomenon and multi-organ involvement.

question_text: A 36 year old man is admitted with acute right sided weakness and slurred speech. He does not have a history of hypertension, diabetes or high cholesterol. There is no family history of CVA. He does not smoke. He complains of headaches and generalised limb weakness infrequently. On examination, he has hypotonia and weakness in the proximal muscles more than the distal muscles. His laboratory tests show a high lactate to pyruvate ratio. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• This patient has MELAS (myopathy, encephalopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes).
  • Lactic acidosis is a very important feature of this disorder, as measured by a high lactate to pyruvate ratio.
  • However, in general, lactic acidosis does not lead to systemic metabolic acidosis, and it may be absent in patients with impressive involvement of the central nervous system.
  • Patients have a myopathy causing proximal muscle weakness and hypotonia, seizures and stroke-like episodes. It is a mitochondrial inherited disorder.
  • Polymyositis would present with a progressive limb girdle pattern of proximal muscle weakness; This weakness is typically bilateral and not associated with headache or slurred speech
  • IBM presents with a characteristic pattern of weakness that involves proximal lower limb and distal upper limb. It usually affects elderly males
  • PML usually affects AIDS patients; it is caused by reactivation of JC virus and presents with an insidious onset progressive focal weakness, slurring of speech and diplopia. UMN signs are seen rather than hypotonia.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 449, Pg: 3529

question_text: What is the investigation of choice for detecting enteric fever in the first week?
explanation:
Explanation:

Blood culture is the most sensitive diagnostic modality for early detection of enteric fever, as Salmonella typhi or Salmonella paratyphi are present in the bloodstream during the initial phase of infection.

Enteric Fever: Diagnosis

  • Definitive Diagnosis: Isolation of Typhi or S. Paratyphi from blood, bone marrow, sterile sites, rose spots, stool, or intestinal secretions.
  • Blood Culture: ~60% sensitive; lower with small volume, prior antibiotics, or early illness (<1 week) due to low bacteremia (<15/mL). Buffy coat culture reduces isolation time but not sensitivity.
  • Bone Marrow Culture: >80% sensitive; unaffected by up to 5 days of prior antibiotics.
  • Intestinal Secretions: Positive even if bone marrow culture is negative; duodenal string test is preferred noninvasive method.
  • Combined Cultures: Blood + bone marrow + intestinal secretions → >90% yield.
  • Stool Culture: Often negative in the first week (60-70%), may become positive by the third week in untreated cases.
  • Serology:
  • Widal Test: Rapid, simple, but limited sensitivity/specificity; cannot distinguish active vs. prior infection or vaccination.
  • IDL Tubex, Typhidot: More accurate but expensive, limiting use in low-resource settings.
  • Molecular Methods: Nucleic acid-based tests not yet commercially available.

question_text: A 25-year-old female presented with a sudden onset of left sided head and neck pain. 24 hours later she presents with sudden onset of right hemiparesis, facial weakness and homonymous hemianopia and left Horner's syndrome. A CT brain showed a left middle cerebral artery territory infarction. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The presence of neck pain on the left side, followed by a right sided weakness points to the diagnosis of carotid dissection.

  • The two commonest causes of young onset stroke (less than 40 years) are cardio-embolism and carotid artery dissection.
  • Carotid artery dissection is either spontaneous or traumatic. Facial/head/neck pain and Horner's syndrome are characteristic features.
  • Migrainous stroke usually affects the posterior circulation (posterior cerebral artery territory is the commonest).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3341

question_text: Presence of which of the following will help to determine HBV-HDV coinfection and exclude HBV-HDV superinfection
explanation:
When a patient presents with acute hepatitis and has HBsAg and anti-HDV in serum, determination of the class of anti-HBc is helpful in establishing the relationship between infection with HBV and HDV.

Although IgM anti-HBc does not distinguish absolutely between acute and chronic HBV infection, its presence is a reliable indicator of recent infection and its absence a reliable indicator of infection in the remote past.

In simultaneous acute HBV and HDV infections, IgM anti-HBc will be detectable, whereas in acute HDV infection superimposed on chronic HBV infection, anti-HBc will be of the IgG class.

question_text: A 38-year-old woman is referred to the gastroenterology clinic. The patient has persistent lethargy and blood results have demonstrated iron deficiency anemia. Which of the following statements regarding iron deficiency anemia is correct?
option_a: Endomysial antibody serology to investigate for coeliac disease should always be requested in addition to duodenal biopsies
option_b: Low serum iron with a low total iron-binding capacity confirms iron deficiency
option_c: Microcytosis may be absent where there is combined iron and folate deficiency
option_d: The presence of Howell-Jolly bodies on blood film would go against coeliac disease
explanation:
Distal duodenal (D2) biopsies should be taken in any patient with iron deficiency anemia undergoing a gastroscopy as 2-3% of patients will have celiac disease.

Endomysial antibody serology can be useful to confirm that subtotal villous atrophy found at histology is not due to another cause.Antibody titres help to determine whether or not the patient is adhering to a gluten free diet.

In the investigation of iron deficiency anemia serology for coeliac disease would be performed prior to an OGD. Low serum iron (< 10 pmol/L) with a high total iron-binding capacity (> 70 pmol/L) confirms iron deficiency.

Howell-Jolly bodies on blood film indicate hyposplenism and are consistent with a diagnosis of coeliac disease.

Thrombocytosis may occur in acute hemorrhage but is also found in a number of other situations such as inflammatory conditions.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 325, Pg: 2463

question_text: A 25-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism presents with chronic oral mucocutaneous candidiasis persisting for 5 years. She is diagnosed with Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy Syndrome (APS) Type 1. Which of the following statements about this condition is incorrect?

Explanation:

Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is strongly associated with APS Type 2 (Schmidt syndrome) but not typically seen in APS Type 1.

  • Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1) also known as APECED (Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy, Candidiasis, and Ectodermal Dystrophy) is a rare, monogenic autoimmune disorder that primarily affects children.
  • It results from a mutation in the AIRE gene (Autoimmune Regulator), leading to a breakdown of central immune tolerance and the formation of multiple autoantibodies against endocrine and non-endocrine tissues.

APS Type 1 is more associated with conditions like hypoparathyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.

Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy Syndrome (APS):

Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy Syndrome iis a group of autoimmune disorders characterized by the immune system mistakenly attacking multiple endocrine glands, leading to hormonal imbalances.

It is classified into two main types.

question_text:
A 33 year old lady presents with stiffness, pain and swelling of her hands and wrists.
Investigations reveal a normocytic, normochromic anemia, elevated ESR and CRP.
What antibody would you use if you wanted to do A test for detecting RA factor?
explanation:
IgM, IgG, and IgA isotypes of RF occur in sera from patients with RA, although the IgM isotype is the one most frequently measured by commercial laboratories.

The sensitivity of RA is only 75%, therefore a negative test does not exclude the presence of the disease.

False positive in other connective tissue diseases, such as primary Sjogren's syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, and type II mixed essential cryoglobulinemia, as well as chronic infections such as subacute bacterial endocarditis and hepatitis B and C.

Serum RF may also be detected in 1-5% of the healthy population.

Anti CCP has a role in predicting the outcomes too, as it is associated with worse outcomes.

question_text:
A 40-year-old woman presents with left flank pain. On examination she was febrile, had livedo reticularis and a blood pressure of 190/100 mmHg. She has also had a history of a butterfly rash in the past.
Investigations revealed:
Hb 13.9 g/dL
WBC 6.5 x 10^9/L
Platelet count 110 x 10^9/L
Serum Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL
Urine dipstick analysis: blood ++, protein -
Which one of the following tests is likely to be positive?
explanation:
The patient is an adult female with history of butterfly rash in the past, which points to the diagnosis of SLE.

Causes of flank pain includes Acute pyelonephritis or Renal vein thrombosis.

Urinalysis here is not favoring a pyelonephritis and hence can be ruled out. So the possibility here is renal vein thrombosis

How can renal vein thrombosis be linked to SLE?

  • Lupus Nephritis causing Nephrotic range proteinuria and renal vein thrombosis
  • A secondary APS causing renal vein thrombosis.

Hypertension can be seen in both lupus nephritis and APS with renal vein thrombosis.

Thrombocytopenia can occur in both SLE and APS, but the presence of a clinical evidence of thrombosis despite thrombocytopenia points towards an underlying APS.

So this patient is having a renal vein thrombosis due to Secondary APS with SLE.

So the antibodies that should be tested are the Antiphospholipid antibodies. Among the given options it is the anti Cardiolipin.

Anti Ro antibody is not a marker of thrombosis, but of cutaneous disease and neonatal lupus with CHB. Hence option A is ruled out

Anti GBM antibody is seen in Goodpasture's syndrome. The disease has got a very different clinical presentation and is included under the pulmonary renal syndromes. It presents with hemoptysis and hematuria.

ASOT is probably ASO titre which is seen in acute rheumatic fever and not APS

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:357 Pg:2749

question_text:
A 26 year old female who is planning to conceive has come to you for advice. She gives a history of stroke 6 years back and was diagnosed with Antiphospholipid Syndrome and is on Warfarin. Which among the following statements are incorrect.
1. Warfarin has to be stopped prior to a planned pregnancy as it is teratogenic.
2. The patient has to be started only on prophylactic dose of heparin as it is her first pregnancy.
3. The patient has to be started on therapeutic dose of heparin as she gives a history of thrombosis in the past.
4. Newer oral anticoagulants are approved for treatment of APS.
5. With anticoagulation, the risk of IUGR decreases substantially.
explanation:
This question deals with the recommendations for anticoagulation in APS.

Statement 1: it is a known fact that Warfarin is teratogenic, which makes statement 1 true.

Statement 2 and 3: These statements deal with recommendations for anticoagulation in pregnancy in patients with APS.

  • In patients who have had previous history of thrombosis due to APS, regardless of their previous pregnancy morbidity, should receive therapeutic dose (1mg/kg LMWH twice daily) of heparin and warfarin post partum that has to be continued life long.
  • In patients with APS and previous pregnancy morbidity( defined as ≥ 1 fetal loss or ≥ 3 embryonic loss), but no history of thrombosis prophylactic dose of heparin( 0.5mg/kg LMWH once daily) should be given with low dose aspirin, through out pregnancy and continued 4-6 weeks post partum.
  • In patients with diagnosed APS and first pregnancy: no treatment is required.

So statement 2 is incorrect and 3 is correct.

Statement 4: DOAC are not recommended in treatment of APS and hence it is incorrect.

Statement 5: Even with therapeutic anticoagulation IUGR can occur in APS, hence it is wrong

So statements 2, 4 and 5 are wrong

Treatment of APS in general


Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:357 Pg:2749

  • Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is a disorder characterized by recurrent venous or arterial thrombosis and/or fetal losses associated with typical laboratory abnormalities.   • Aspirin or warfarin is recommended for patients with thrombotic syndromes.

question_text: A 40-year-old female presents with pain and stiffness of the small joints of hand. She also has difficulty in getting up from the chair. She has no dermatologic symptoms. question_text: A 35-year-old woman experiences skin thickening, muscle weakness, and pale peripheries upon cold exposure. Her creatine kinase is increased with positive ANA, and biopsy revealed scl-70 positivity and perifascicular infiltration. What is the antibody linked to this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The simultaneous presentation of Raynaud's phenomenon and anti-Scl-70 positivity is indicative of systemic sclerosis, specifically the diffuse subtype. Peri-fascicular inflammation and elevated creatine kinase levels are characteristic of dermatomyositis or polymyositis. When these clinical and serological features coexist, an overlap syndrome most notably scleroderma-myositis overlap should be suspected. This particular overlap is strongly associated with the presence of anti-PM/Scl antibody.
  • Overlap syndromes are defined by the co-occurrence of dermatomyositis or polymyositis with one or more additional connective tissue diseases, such as systemic sclerosis, mixed connective tissue disease, Sjögren's syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, or rheumatoid arthritis.
  • The clinical presentation of systemic sclerosis can be broadly categorized into two main subtypes: diffuse and limited cutaneous disease.

Histopathology and Pathogenesis of polymyositis

Polymyositis exhibits diverse muscle changes, with inflammatory cell infiltration that is more prominent in the perimysium than in the endomysium.

The predominant inflammatory cells are CD8+ T lymphocytes and macrophages, which are mainly located in the endomysial, perimysial, and perivascular areas.


  • Autoantibodies in systemic sclerosis

Explanation of other options:

Anti-Jo-1 Antibody (Option B): This antibody is a marker for antisynthetase syndrome. The clinical presentation of this syndrome includes a combination of symptoms such as myositis, non-erosive arthritis, interstitial lung disease, Raynaud's phenomenon, mechanic's hands, and fever. Since these findings are not described in the provided scenario, this antibody is not the most specific answer.

Anticentromere Antibody (Option C): This antibody is highly associated with the limited cutaneous form of systemic sclerosis, also known as CREST syndrome. The acronym CREST represents its key features: Calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, and Telangiectasia.

Anti-Nuclear Antibody (Option D): This antibody is a general screening test for autoimmunity and is positive in a wide range of autoimmune disorders, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). However, since the scenario already states that the ANA is positive, the question is asking for a more specific antibody that would confirm the diagnosis, making this option insufficient on its own.

question_text:
A 57-year-old woman with longstanding well controlled seropositive Rheumatoid Arthritis, treated with methotrexate (20 mg/week) and folic acid 5 mg/day, presents with cough productive of green phlegm, fever (38.5°C), and severe sore throat. On examination, the BP is 110/70 mmHg, SaO2 is 98% on air. There is an occasional crackle at the right lung base. Chest x ray is normal. CBC, RFT, and LFTs are also normal. The CRP is 34 mg/L.
Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?
option_b: IV antibiotics, stop methotrexate, and give folinic acid rescue
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis in this scenario is a lower respiratory tract infection (because of the presence of productive cough).

In the setting of acute infection, most DMARDs (except hydroxychloroquine) should be discontinued until the infectious process has resolved.

Option 1 - Methotrexate should be stopped until the infection resolves.

Option 2 - Taken in overdose, methotrexate can cause multiple organ damage. Folinic acid is indicated and should be given intravenously as soon as it is suspected to limit toxicity. There is no suggestion of methotrexate overdose in this patient, and therefore folinic acid is not indicated.

Option 4 - Oral antibiotics can be used to control the infection but methotrexate should be stopped until the infection resolves.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition, Ch:358, Pg:2762

question_text:

Peri epithetlial involvement is characterized by accumulation of activated lymphocytes and hence is called autoimmune epithelitis.

Sjogren's Syndrome predisposes to the development of MALTOMA.

Explanation:

question_text: The image shown below depicts a specific physical finding (Palmar Erythema). Which of the following conditions is not associated with this finding?
explanation:
Explanation:

Palmar erythema is associated with states of increased estrogen or vasodilation. The condition listed that is not associated with this finding is Menopause, which is characterized by low estrogen levels.

Associations of Palmar Erythema

  • Pregnancy (Option B ruled out): A classic physiologic cause due to high estrogen levels and increased cardiac output.
  • Liver Cirrhosis (Option C ruled out): Impaired liver function leads to decreased metabolism of estrogen, causing relative hyperestrogenism.
  • Rheumatoid Arthritis (Option A ruled out): An autoimmune cause, likely related to increased vascularity and chronic inflammation.

Key Takeaways:

  • Palmar erythema is a sign of hyperestrogenic states (pregnancy, cirrhosis) or chronic inflammatory diseases (RA).
  • Menopause, with its low estrogen state, is not associated with this finding.

question_text: Felon most common complication

question_text: Cairo bishop criteria include all except
explanation:
Cairo Bishop criteria for the diagnosis of Tumor lysis Syndrome (TLS) includes -

  • High potassium ( ≥6 mmol/L or 25% increase from baseline)
  • High uric acid (≥ 476 μmol/l or 25% increase from baseline)
  • High phosphorous (≥ 2.1 mmol/l (children)/ ≥1.45 mmol/l (adults) or 25% increase from baseline)
  • Low calcium (≤ 1.75 mmol/l or 25% decrease from baseline)

Tumor lysis Syndrome (TLS) is caused by the destruction of a large number of rapidly proliferating neoplastic cells. It is an oncological emergency which can progress to acute kidney injury, cardiac arrhythmias and death if untreated.

TLS is most often associated with the treatment of Burkitt's lymphoma, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and other rapidly proliferating lymphomas, but it also may be seen with chronic leukemias and, rarely, with solid tumors.

Laboratory findings - high potassium, high uric acid, high phosphorous, low calcium, high LDH, acidosis

Treatment of TLS -

  • Rigorous hydration
  • Management of hyperuricemia
  • Allopurinol or febuxostat beginning 2-3 days prior to chemotherapy and continued for 10-14 days (OR)
  • Rasburicase single dose is indicated in patients with the following risk factors -
  • Urgent need to initiate therapy in a high bulk patient
  • Situations where adequate hydration may be difficult
  • Acute renal failure
  • Frequent monitoring of electrolytes and correction as needed.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 75, Pg: 573

question_text:
A 58-year-old female presented to her family doctor with pain in the left side of her neck radiating down the lateral aspect of her arm and forearm. She had also noticed some weakness of her left shoulder and struggled to elevate her arm. She had a longstanding history of rheumatoid arthritis, treated with steroids and penicillamine. She was a non-smoker and did not drink any alcohol. On examination there was some wasting over the left deltoid and evidence of fasciculations. Neck movements appeared full except that lateral movement exacerbated the left arm pain. On examination of the upper limb, tone appeared reduced at the elbow and wrist and the biceps jerk was only present on re-enforcement. The left supinator jerk was inverted and the triceps jerk appeared brisk. There was some weakness of left shoulder abduction, elbow flexion and supination, but finger movements and elbow extension were intact. There was a sensory deficit over the lateral aspect of the left upper arm and forearm. The right arm appeared normal. On examination of her lower limb, tone was increased, but power appeared normal. All reflexes were brisk and both plantar responses were extensor.
Investigations showed:
Haemoglobin 11.4 g/dl(13.0 18.0 g/dL)
White cell count 3.4 x 10^9/L (4 11 x 10^9/L)
Platelets 245 x 10^9/L (150 400 x 10^9/L)
ESR (Westergren) 45 mm/1st hour (0-15 mm/1st hour)
Serum Sodium 145 mmol/L(137-144 mmol/L)
Serum Potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-4.9)
Serum urea 66 mg/dl (high)
Serum Creatinine 1.6 g/dl (high)
Serum creatine kinase 178 U/L (2D-170 U/L)
Fasting blood glucose 136 (high)
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• This patient has a cervical myelopathy, most likely as a result of her rheumatoid arthritis.
  • The likely level is C5/C6 given that there is weakness of the deltoid, biceps and supinator and the supinator jerk is inverted. She also has long tract signs in her legs with hypertonia and hyperreflexia.
  • A circumflex neuropathy would account for the weakness and fasciculations of the deltoid, but would not explain the upper motor neuron signs in the legs, or weakness of the biceps and supinator.
  • Inclusion body myositis, an inflammatory myopathy, would present with bilateral often asymmetrical weakness, which has a tendency to affect distal musculature. The tendon reflexes would be normal and the creatine kinase would be normal or mildly elevated.
  • Motor neuron disease presents with upper and lower motor signs in absence of sensory disturbance .
  • A steroid induced myopathy would cause proximal weakness and wasting with normal reflexes and sensation.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 442, Pg: 3452

question_text:
A 51 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis was referred with iron deficiency anemia. She had been taking undisclosed medications for a long time. Endoscopy showed gastritis and antral erosions, small bowel biopsy showing mild villous blunting, and apoptotic bodies, Colonoscopy was normal.
What could lead to such a presentation for this woman?
explanation:
NSAIDs were formerly viewed as the core of RA therapy, but they are now considered to be adjunctive agents for management of symptoms uncontrolled by other measures. NSAIDs exhibit both analgesic and anti-inflammatory properties. Chronic use should be minimized due to the possibility of side effects, including gastritis and peptic ulcer disease as well as impairment of renal function.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition, Ch:358, Pg:2761

question_text: A 31 year old man has had a year's history of bilateral hip pains and back pains with early morning stiffness. There is no past medical history of trauma to the back. Non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs helped to relieve his symptoms. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pain and stiffness in the lower back or buttocks, especially in the morning is typical of sacroiliitis. It is typically helped by NSAIDS or steroids. X rays will help to confirm the diagnosis. It is associated with various inflammatory diseases e.g. ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, arthritis associated with IBD, Reactive arthritis etc

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 362, Pg: 2790

question_text:
A 58 year old lady has polyarthritis due to Rheumatoid Arthritis.
Which one of the following molecules plays a central role in its pathogenesis?
explanation:
RA is considered to be a macrophage driven disease.

The key inflammatory cytokines released by the macrophages include TNFα, Il-1,6,12,15,18 and 23. Of these TNF α is the pivotal cytokine in the pathogenesis of synovial inflammation.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:358 Pg:2758

question_text: A 54 year old man presents with a 6 week history of lethargy and diffuse purpuric rash. He is noted to have a right foot drop and a left ulnar nerve palsy. He complains of arthralgia but has no clinical evidence of inflammatory joint disease. Echocardiogram is unremarkable, blood cultures are negative, ESR 80 mm/hr, ANCA negative, ANA negative, rheumatoid factor strongly positive, C3 1.1 g/l (0.75 - 1.6), C4 0.03 g/l (0.14 - 0.5). Dipstick urinalysis shows blood ++. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A low C4 together with a strongly positive rheumatoid factor suggests cryoglobulinemia as a cause of mononeuritis multiplex and rash. Palpable purpura, arthralgia, hepatosplenomegaly, diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis, Raynaud's phenomenon and thrombosis may occur.

Type I cryoglobulinemia may be associated with lymphoproliferative disorders, multiple myeloma, and monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance, and macroglobulinemia. Plasmapheresis may reduce the levels of cryoglobulin.

Type II cryoglobulinemia (mixed monoclonal) is usually composed of a monoclonal component (usually IgG, IgM or IgA) and a polyclonal component (mainly IgG). Causes are connective tissue diseases, Hepatitis B and C infection, infectious mononucleosis and lymphoma.

Reference: Harrison's Principles Of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:363 Pg:2814

question_text:
A 48 year old woman has severe rheumatoid arthritis. She is currently on ibuprofen and methotrexate. There is no palpable lymphadenopathy and no abdominal masses.

platelets 55 x 10^9/l.

In this question, the affection of three cell lines with reticulocytopenia, in the absence of splenomegaly, is suggestive of pathology of the bone marrow.

The patient has an aplastic anaemia which can be caused by methotrexate or azathioprine,

In patients with cutaneous psoriasis, systemic corticosteroids predispose to pustular
