question_text: A 54-year-old homeless man presents with a six month history of periodic knee pains and aching legs. These have been occurring monthly and episodes last up to two weeks. He has noticed a 'bumpy' rash to his lower legs and complains of feeling more tired than usual. He has no significant past medical history. He is currently reporting to a pharmacy daily for methadone. Clinical examination demonstrated; pulse 88 (regular), normal heart sounds and chest sounds, painful but full active range of knee motion and palpable purpura to the lower extremities. Blood tests revealed; Hb 11.9 g/dL(1C-18)MCV 93fL(80 - 96)WCC 9.8 x 109/L (4 - 11)ALT 150 iu/L(5 - 35)AST 90 iu/L(1 - 31)Complement C4 64 mg/dL(75-135) Which test is most likely to assist you in the management of this man's illness?
explanation:
The background of a destitute male who is on methadone currently indicates possibility of an IV opioid abuser who is currently on deaddiction. IV drug abuse predisposes the patient to blood borne infections like chronic Hepatitis and HIV.

Apart from that, now the patient has arthralgia, rash and hypocomplementemia. He has transaminase elevation as well.

This points to the possibility of a Hepatitis C associated Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.

Learning points:

Presentation of mixed cryoglobulinemia (MCG), Risk factors for (MCG) and Haematological profile of MCG.

Mixed cryoglobulinemia manifests as

Purpura

Cutaneous ulcers

Polyneuropathy

Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and non-erosive polyarthralgia is associated with hepatitis C.

Laboratory investigations show positive rheumatoid factor, low C4, active urine sediments, and type II or III serum cryoglobulins. There may be axonal polyneuropathy.

Active urinary sediment suggests the presence of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.

Type II (mixed essential) cryoglobulinemia is closely associated with persistent hepatic infection (transaminitis, inferred IVDU) most commonly hepatitis C and to a lesser extent hepatitis B.

Management involves treating the underlying cause in the absence of any immediate life, organ or limb threatening complications. In this case with pegylated interferon alpha and ribavirin.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:363 Pg:2586

question_text:
A 54 year old female has been on long-term steroids for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She complains of pain in her right groin radiating down the anteromedial thigh. She has an antalgic gait. On examination of the hip, there is decreased range of movement especially flexion, abduction and internal rotation.
What is the likely diagnosis?
option_d: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
explanation:
In a patient on long term steroids presenting with groin pains radiating to the thigh associated with an antalgic gait and decreased range of movement of the hip, the most likely diagnosis is avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

In this condition, MRI is the most sensitive and specific technique and is useful for early diagnosis before collapse of bone occurs. CT scan and X-ray are useful to rule out advanced disease if duration is not clear. Bone scanning is more sensitive than X-ray but is non-specific.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 370, Pg: 2847

question_text:
A 21-year-old lady has a swinging fever, significant weight loss over 2 months, generalised myalgia, polyarthralgia affecting wrists, knees, ankles, elbows metacarpophalangeal joints and a sore throat. Investigations show : Hb 9.5g/l, MCV 85 fl, ESR 92 mm in first hour, CRP 45 g/l, serum ferritin 1600 mg/dl, RF negative, ANA negative, ENA negative, ASO titre <200iu.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The most appropriate answer from among the option is C.

Adult Onset Still's Disease (AOSD) is an acute febrile illness in young adults. It usually affects multiple organs, but is a diagnosis of exclusion. The presence of high ferritin and negative serological markers of other autoimmune diseases makes the possibility of Adult Onset Still's Disease.

Clinical features include a high fever, arthralgia and arthritis, phayngitis, typical rash (evanescent salmon-colored, macular or maculopapular eruption), lymphadenopathy, and serositis. Chronic arthritis and constitutional symptoms are common.

The triad of fever, rash, and arthralgia are often absent during the first month of the illness. The usual joints affected are wrists, knees, and ankles in descending order.

Two thirds of cases experience polyarticular arthritis and one third have monoarticular symptoms.

Approximately 1/3 of patients have chronic persistent disease with progressive joint damage.

Reference: Harrison's Principles Of Internal Medicine, 21st ed Ch: 19, Pg: 135

question_text:
A 68 year old woman with ischaemic heart disease and rheumatoid arthritis presents with worsening angina. Bloods show: hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL; MCV: 80 fl; MCH: 29 pg; WBC: 7000/μL; platelets 300000/μL;
S. Iron: 37 μg/dL (NR: 50-150 μg/dL)
Transferrin saturation 12% (NR: 15-50%)
Total iron-binding capacity 200μg/dL (NR: 240-450 μg/dL)
Vitamin B12 400 ng/L (NR: 160-950 ng/L)
folate 8 ng/mL (NR: 3-10 ng/mL)
What is the most likely cause of her anemia?
explanation:
She has a normochromic, normocytic anemia with low iron, iron-binding capacity and transferrin saturation in keeping with anemia of chronic disease. Anemia of chronic disease results from impaired iron handling. In iron deficiency anemia, the patient is iron depleted, leading to a raised iron-binding capacity in the context of low iron and transferrin saturation. Folate deficiency, myelodysplasia and autoimmune haemolysis are associated with an elevated MCV.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 97 pg. 752-753

question_text: A 68 year old woman has been found to have a low hemoglobin in the context of long-term rheumatoid arthritis and chronic kidney disease. What does the mechanism of the anemia of chronic disease include?
option_b: High hepcidin levels inhibiting iron export from macrophages
option_c: Iron toxicity to the bone marrow
option_d: Poor iron absorption because of achlorhydria
explanation:
The anemia of chronic disease largely results from induced hepcidin production from the liver. This occurs secondary),' to increased interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels in inflammation. Iron is trapped in iron-exporting cells, including duodenal enterocytes and macrophages. Iron does not cause direct marrow toxicity. Chronic Gl tract bleeding leads to iron deficiency anemia, as does achlorhydria, e.g. post-gastrectomy

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 97 pg. 752

question_text: A 73-year-old man has had increasingly severe, throbbing headaches for several weeks, centered on the right. There is a palpable tender cord-like area over his right temple. His heart rate is regular with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Pulses are equal and full in all extremities, BP is 110/85 mmHg. A biopsy of this lesion is obtained, and histologic examination reveals a muscular artery with luminal narrowing and medial inflammation with lymphocytes, macrophages, and occasional giant cells. He improves with a course of high-dose corticosteroid therapy. Which of the following laboratory test findings is most likely to be present with this disease?
explanation:
The features described here are classical for giant cell arteritis (GCA).

GCA affects large and medium sized arteries, with a predilection for the external carotid, ciliary and retinal arteries.

The typical presentation of GCA is a temporal headache, with myalgia, malaise and fever. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C reactive protein (CRP) are usually raised.

Anti-double stranded DNA antibodies are associated with systemic lupus erythematosus.

Reduced high-density lipoprotein (HDL) contributes to increased cardiovascular risk, and can be caused by a number of inherited metabolic conditions or may be secondary to other factors such as smoking. It is not commonly associated with rheumatological disease.

Perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (pANCA) is associated with microscopic polyangiitis and Churg-Strauss syndrome, neither of which present as described above.

Rheumatoid factor is non-specific, and may be seen in patients with GCA but this is less likely than a raised ESR.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:363 Pg:2811-2812

question_text:
A 74 year old woman with longstanding Rheumatoid arthritis has great difficulty walking and comments that both her legs are stiff and 'jumpy'.
What is the most likely cause of the presentation?
explanation:
Stiff and jumpy legs suggest-> spasticity-> suggestive of Upper motor neuron disorder.

The problem can be at the level of the brain or spinal cord. Now, we need to think about where RA affects the spinal cord.

RA affects the cervical spine. Unlike Spondyloarthropathy it does not affect the thoracic or lumbar spine.

Cervical cord compression due to atlanto-axial instability at C1/C2 is the most likely cause of UMN nerve weakness.

The laminations of the pyramidal tract in the spinal cord is in such a way that the sacral fibres are lateral and the cervical fibres are medial. Hence, in a long standing upper cervical cord compression, as in the case of an atlanto axial instability, the symptoms will first begin in the lower limbs and then involve the upper limbs and may be asymmetrical too.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:358 Pg:3752

question_text: A 47 year old man had suffered from classical seropositive rheumatoid arthritis for 10 years. He has never received treatment with phenylbutazone, gold, or antimalarials. He presents with intense pain in the right hand. Over a course of 3 weeks, he noticed pain, numbness, and tingling on the lateral aspect of the palm and in the fourth and fifth fingers of the right hand. On examination, he has weakness in the abductors and adductors of the fingers, and his hand is held in a clawed position. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
• The ulnar nerve supplies the lumbricals (claw hand) and also the Interossei- Dorsal:
  • Abductors (DAB) and Palmar: Adductors (PAD).
  • A lesion in the anterior interosseous nerve results in weakness of the terminal phalanges of the thumb and index fingers.
  • It can be a mononeuritis due to Rheumatoid Vadvulitis, a compication of long standing RA


Claw Hand

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

question_text: A 48 year old secretary noticed tingling and numbness over the palmar surface of her thumb, index and middle fingers after several hours at her computer. Pain in the same areas often occur at night.What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Pain and numbness in the distribution of the median nerve indicates Carpal Tunnel Syndrome.

CTS is a compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel at the wrist

The symptoms of CTS consist of numbness and paresthesias variably in the thumb, index, middle, and half of the ring finger.

The paresthesias can include the entire hand and extend into the forearm or upper arm or can be isolated to one or two fingers.

The signs of CTS are decreased sensation in the median nerve distribution

Reproduction of the sensation of tingling when a percussion hammer is tapped over the wrist (Tinel sign)

Parasthesia in the median nerve distribution evoked by a 30 minute compression of the Carpal Tunnel( Durkan’s Test)

The wrist is flexed for 30–60 s (Phalen sign)

Weakness of thumb opposition and abduction.

Edx is extremely sensitive and shows slowing of sensory and, to a lesser extent, motor median potentials across the wrist.

Ultrasound can show focal swelling of the median nerve at the wrist.

Treatment options consist of avoidance of precipitating activities; control of underlying systemic-associated conditions if present; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications; neutral (volar) position wrist splints, especially for night use

Glucocorticoid/anesthetic injection into the carpal tunnel

Surgical decompression by dividing the transverse carpal ligament, should be considered if there is a poor response to nonsurgical treatments; if there is thenar muscle atrophy and/or weakness; and if there are significant denervation potentials on EMG



Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 446 Pg: 3497

question_text: Patients well controlled on theophylline should not be given which antibiotic?
explanation:
Macrolides increase the level of theophylline by inhibiting Cyp450 and causes theophylline toxicity. Hence co administration should be avoided.

Agents which enhance theophylline metabolism primarily by inducing CYP1A2 lower its plasma level: dose has to be increased by the factor given in parenthesis.

Smoking, phenytoin, rifampicin, phenobarbitone, charcoal broiled meat meal.

Drugs which inhibit theophylline metabolism and increase its plasma level are-erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, oral contraceptives, allopurinol; dose should be reduced to 2/3.

question_text: A 56 year old woman presents with a 2 month history of pain affecting the cervical spine and both shoulders, this was preceded by pain in the lower back and both hips. Early morning stiffness lasts until lunchtime and she feels markedly tired and weak. Investigations demonstrate a normochromic normocytic anaemia of Hb 9.8 g/dl, ESR 72 mm in the first hour, CRP 12 g/l, serum immunoglobulins and protein electrophoresis show a polyclonal increase in gamma globulins and elevated alpha 1 and alpha 2 globulins but no paraprotein band. RA factor, anti CCP and ANA were negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pain and stiffness in an elderly woman with proximal joint pain and morning stiffness in the absence of RA factor points towards Polymyalgia Rheumatica.

ESR and CRP will be elevated. About 40-50% of patients with GCA will have PMR. 10-15% of patients with PMR will develop GCA in the course of time.

Proximal joint pain is against the diagnosis of RA.

It shows prompt response to low dose steroids.

Low back and hip pain with stiffness may be seen in Ankylosing Spondylitis. But there is no other history to suggest enthesitis or any other manifestations of AS.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch: 363 Pg: 2811-2812

question_text: In which of the following conditions is pneumomediastinum commonly found?
explanation:
Explanation:

Pneumomediastinum is one of the complication associated with Boerhaave syndrome.

Boerhaave syndrome

  • It is a spontaneous esophageal rupture caused by a sudden increase in intraesophageal pressure.
  • Results from forceful vomiting against a closed glottis, leading to a left-sided oesophageal perforation, which allows gastric contents to spill into the pleural cavity, leading to a left pleural effusion and subcutaneous emphysema.

Clinical features

  • Manifests as Mackler's triad
    • Vomiting
    • Chest pain
    • Subcutaneous emphysema
  • Other symptoms include fever, tachycardia, and tachypnea in the presence of sepsis.
  • Physical examination reveals Hamman's sign
    • Crunching sound on auscultation due to surgical emphysema.
  • Commonly affects the lower third of the oesophagus and results in a direct communication between the esophageal lumen and mediastinal space.
  • The rupture allows oesophagal contents to spill into the mediastinum, which can occasionally lead to complications such as:
    • Pneumomediastinum
    • Chemical mediastinitis.
    • Pneumothorax
    • Sepsis

Explanation of other options:

Pulsion diverticulum (Option A): Pulsion diverticulum occurs due to increased intraluminal pressure in the esophagus, forming an outpouching of the esophageal wall. While it can cause symptoms like dysphagia and regurgitation, it does not typically result in pneumomediastinum as the esophageal wall remains intact.

Mallory-Weiss syndrome (Option C): Mallory-Weiss syndrome involves longitudinal mucosal tears at the gastroesophageal junction, typically following forceful vomiting. While it can cause hematemesis, the tear is superficial and does not extend through the full thickness of the oesophageal wall, thus not causing pneumomediastinum. ;

Pericarditis (Option D): Pericarditis is the inflammation of the pericardium, the fibrous sac surrounding the heart, and causes chest pain and other symptoms related to inflammation.

question_text: Which of the following statements concerning industrial lung disorders is correct?
option_a: Pneumoconiosis can be diagnosed in the absence of chest X-ray abnormalities
option_b: Occupational asthma occurs more frequently in atopic persons
option_c: Silo fillers disease is caused by allergy to grain
option_d: Widespread crepitations are typically heard in extrinsic allergic alveolitis
explanation:
a-Pneumoconiosis is an X-Ray diagnosis. It is due to deposition of coal dust in parenchyma and reaction to its presence. The types - simple / complicated - are diagnosed on XRay appearance

b-It also occurs more frequently in smokers.

c-Silo fillers' disease is pulmonary oedema caused by inhalation of oxides of nitrogen generated by fresh silage.

d - examination in EAA usually reveals inspiratory crepitations which tend to be basal rather than widespread, sometimes squeaks, but wheeze is not typical.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: Ch: 288, Pg: 2160-2171

question_text:
A couple attend the GP with their 2 year old daughter. She has a history of repeated chest infections, failure to thrive, and steatorrhoea (fatty stools). They also have an 8 year old child who is fit and well.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• The gene defect in cystic fibrosis is in a mutation on chromosome 7. The inheritance is autosomal recessive so the other child without symptoms has not inherited two CF genes.
  • Pulmonary disease develops over a few months after birth. Common infective organisms are pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 291 Pg 2176

question_text: A 65 year old patient with COPD is on maximal treatment. Which one of the following is likely to prevent further disease progression?
explanation:
• In COPD, discontinuation of smoking is the only feature which has been shown to reduce disease progression.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:292 Pg: 2186

question_text: Omalizumab is used in treatment of:
explanation: Omalizumab is a blocking antibody that neutralizes circulating IgE without binding to cell- bound IgE; it thus inhibits IgE-mediated reactions. This treatment has been shown to reduce the number of exacerbations in patients with severe asthma and may improve asthma control. However, the treatment is very expensive and only suitable for highly selected patients who are not controlled on maximal doses of inhaler therapy and have a circulating IgE within a specified range. Ref: Harrison’s principle of internal medicine 17th edition, chapter 248.

question_text: A 45-year-old woman with obstructive lung disease is on salmeterol and tiotropium but still has persistent breathlessness and frequent exacerbations. Which treatment option would be most appropriate next?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The clinical manifestations indicate persistent symptoms of obstructive lung disease despite optimal bronchodilator therapy with salmeterol (LABA) and tiotropium (LAMA).
  • Long-Term Oxygen Therapy (LTOT) is the most appropriate next step in management as it addresses potential hypoxemia, which is often present in patients with chronic obstructive lung disease experiencing persistent symptoms.

Interventions for Improved Survival in COPD

  • Smoking Cessation:
    • Most crucial intervention for improving survival.
    • Slows decline in lung function (FEV1), altering disease progression.
  • Long-Term Oxygen Therapy (LTOT):
    • Improves survival in severe hypoxemia (PaO2 < 7.3 kPa).
    • Recommended use: at least 15 hours/day, with greater benefit at >20 hours/day.
  • Pulmonary Rehabilitation:
    • Improves symptoms, exercise tolerance, and health status.
    • May contribute to better survival, though direct link needs more research.
  • Management of Exacerbations:
    • Crucial for reducing mortality.
    • Key components:
      • Controlled oxygen therapy (24%-28%) to maintain PaO2 > 8 kPa.
      • Nebulized bronchodilators: salbutamol + ipratropium.
      • Oral glucocorticoids: prednisolone 30 mg for 10 days.
      • Antibiotics for increased sputum purulence/volume, breathlessness.
      • Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) for mild-moderate acidosis (pH < 7.35).
  • Vaccination:
    • Annual influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations to prevent infections and exacerbations.
    • Multidisciplinary Management:
    • Address comorbidities (e.g., obesity, malnutrition, depression, social isolation).
    • These factors impact overall health and survival.

question_text: A 63 year old man is on treatment for chronic heart failure with diuretics. He has previous history of asthma. He presents with sudden onset of pain and swelling of the metatarso-phalangeal joint of his right big toe. Aspiration of the joint demonstrates crystals of monosodium urate. What is the recommended treatment?
explanation:
In this particular patient, colchicine is the best option. In acute gout, either colchicine or NSAIDs can be used. However, asthma contraindicates NSAIDs.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 372, Pg: 2865

question_text: Which of the following is not a characteristic finding of Gaisbock syndrome?
explanation:
Explanation:

Hypotension is not a characteristic finding of Gaisbock syndrome.

  • Gaisbock syndrome, commonly linked with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), involves secondary polycythemia caused by long-standing hypoxemia.
  • In response to low oxygen levels, the body increases erythropoietin production, resulting in erythrocytosis.
  • Patients usually present with high blood pressure rather than low blood pressure, due to the underlying lung condition and greater blood viscosity.

question_text: A 60-year-old man presents with a small amount of haemoptysis and breathlessness. He does not have pleuritic chest pain and has normal oxygen saturation. In considering the potential diagnosis, haemoptysis can occur with which of the following diagnoses?
explanation:
• Haemoptysis can be caused by pulmonary embolism, tuberculous infection, aspergilloma, bronchial carcinoma, good pasture's syndrome and Wegener's granulomatosis.
  • Interstitial lung disease presents with dry cough along with progressive dyspnoea.
  • Asthma presents with episodic breathlessness and cough in exposure to cold or allergens.
  • Goitre presents as neck swelling; if large, it may compress the trachea causing stridor and breathlessness; retrosternal extension causes venous congestion due to compression of superior vena cava.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 39, Pg:270-272

question_text: A 26-year-old man presents to his GP with rapidly increasing shortness of breath and haemoptysis for the second time within 3 weeks. He is referred urgently to the medical on-call team. Apart from smoking 20 cigarettes per day and having mild asthma, he has no other significant past medical history. Urinalysis reveals microscopic haematuria and proteinuria. Chest X-ray reveals fluffy pulmonary infiltrates. Haemoglobin is 10.5 g/dl, serum creatinine is 345 m mol/l, serum-ANCA is negative and C3 is normal. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
This is a young male, who presents with pulmonary hemorrhage and acute glomerulonephritis. This fits into the category of pulmonary-renal syndromes.

The DDs of pulmonary renal syndromes include-Goodpasture's Syndrome, ANCA associated vasculitis, HSP, Cryoglobulinemia, SLE.

ANCA negativity makes Wegener's Granulomatosis less likely. SLE too is less likely given the history and normal C3 levels.

Goodpasture's syndrome is characterised by the triad of glomerulonephritis, pulmonary haemorrhage and anti-GBM antibody.

Goodpasture's syndrome occurs due to autoantibody against the α3 NC 1 domain of the Type IV collagen. Linear deposition of IgG antibodies are seen on electron microscopy.

Goodpasture's syndrome predominantly affects young male smokers.

Smoking, infection and oxidants or solvents can expose the collagen domain.

In elderly patients the incidence is equal in males and females and will have less incidence of pulmonary hemorrhage and have bad prognosis.

Goodpasture's syndrome accounts for 5% of all cases of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Some 80% of patients with Goodpasture's syndrome are HLA-BR2 positive.

Acute management may involve treatment with prednisolone and cyclophosphamide or plasma-exchange therapy. In patients with severe renal failure, haemodialysis may be required.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 314, Pg: 2338-2339.

question_text: Reslizumab is a monoclonal antibody approved for the management of bronchial asthma. What is the target molecule of this antibody?
explanation:
Monoclonal antibodies used in asthma


Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine, 21st Edition, Ch: 287, Pg: 2157

question_text: A 65-year-old male patient came to the emergency department with a complaint of severe dyspnea. He refuses to lie down. His SpO2 on air is 75%, respiration rate (RR) is 24/min, pulse rate is 124/min, and BP is 130/86 mm Hg. Oxygen therapy was started immediately. On examination, bilateral crepitus was heard over lung fields and the chest X ray showed emphysematous changes. On asking, relatives of the pt. gave a history of chronic smoking. He was diagnosed with COPD. Which beta agonist should be administered for management of acute attack of dyspnea?
explanation:
• In the management of COPD, short acting beta agonists are preferred for acute attacks of dyspnea.
  • Salmeterol and Indacaterol are long-acting beta agonist agents and are used mainly as prophylaxis.
  • For relief of acute symptoms, inhalation of a short-acting β agonist (e.g., albuterol), of an anticholinergic drug (e.g., ipratropium bromide), or of the two in combination is usually effective.
  • For patients with persistent symptoms of exertional dyspnea and limitation of activities, regular use of a long-acting bronchodilator, whether a long-acting β agonist (e.g., Salmeterol) or a long-acting anticholinergic (e.g., tiotropium) is indicated.
  • For patients with severe airflow obstruction or with a history of prior exacerbations, regular use of an inhaled corticosteroid reduces the frequency of future exacerbations.

Reference: LANG' Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor, 12th Edition, Page Number-353.

question_text: A 40 year man presents with shortness of breath. On admission he is unwell and has a respiratory rate of 32 breaths per minute. His chest is wheezy on auscultation. Arterial blood gases show :pO2 71.2 mmhg, pCO2 26.25 mmhg, pH 7.48, HCO3 25, BE +2.What is the likely clinical scenario?
explanation:
• The patient has a respiratory alkalosis (pH > 7.45) which is acute since the bicarbonate levels are normal (22-28). There is hypoxia and the patient is hyperventilating in response and blowing off CO2.
  • This would be consistent with an asthma attack.
  • In an anxiety attack, hypoxia would not be present.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 55, pg: 359

question_text:
A 63-year-old male is referred due to inadequate pain relief for his hip osteoarthritis.
His GP has prescribed paracetamol and codeine 30 mg four times daily but he has found little improvement in his pain relief.
He has a past history of asthma for which he occasionally takes an inhaler.
What is the most likely explanation for the lack of clinical efficacy associated with this medication?
option_a: Ipratropium accelerates the metabolism of codeine
explanation:
The most likely explanation is that the codeine dose is inadequate.

Studies have shown that paracetamol 1 g combined with codeine at dose of 60 mg have the best analgesic outcomes.

Ipratropium does not increase the metabolism of codeine.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 371 Pg: 2861

question_text: What is the minimum percentage rise in the FEV1/FVC ratio, after giving a bronchodilator, that confirms reversibility of airway obstruction in diagnosing bronchial asthma?
explanation:
Explanation:

According to clinical criteria, a notable bronchodilator response suggestive of bronchial asthma is defined as an improvement of more than 12% in the FEV1/FVC ratio from baseline following bronchodilator use.

  • This criterion is useful in distinguishing asthma from other chronic obstructive airway disorders, as asthma typically demonstrates marked reversibility with bronchodilator therapy.
  • In asthma, airflow obstruction often results in air trapping and lung hyperinflation, leading to an increase in total lung capacity.
  • The airways are overly sensitive to different triggers, causing contraction of the bronchial smooth muscles. Administration of bronchodilators relaxes these muscles, enhances airflow, and thereby improves the FEV1/FVC ratio.

question_text: Which of the following features of an asthma attack is classified as 'life-threatening' in asthma?
option_a: Inability to complete sentences in one breath
explanation: Reference: Harrison 20th 1968

question_text: A hypertensive patient who is non-compliant with his medications presents with sudden-onset severe breathlessness. Chest X-ray findings are consistent with pulmonary edema. What is the most appropriate immediate management for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation indicates acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema (ACPE), a medical emergency often precipitated by severe hypertension, myocardial infarction, or medication non-compliance.

  • Intravenous nitroglycerin is the drug of choice as it provides rapid relief by reducing preload and afterload via venodilation, thereby decreasing pulmonary venous pressure.

Clinical Features of ACPE:

  • Symptoms: Sudden dyspnea, pink frothy sputum, cyanosis, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.
  • Signs: Tachypnea, rales and rhonchi on auscultation, raised jugular venous pressure, gallop rhythm.
  • Chest X-ray findings: Interstitial edema, alveolar edema in "butterfly pattern," cardiomegaly.

Management of Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema:

  • IV Nitroglycerin: First-line agent; start sublingual, escalate to IV if required. Rapid symptom relief without hypotension.
  • Oxygen therapy: Maintain SpO2 >92%; non-invasive ventilation (NIPPV) or intubation if severe.
  • Diuretics (e.g., furosemide): Used after stabilization to remove excess fluid.
  • Morphine: Reduces anxiety and provides venodilation; use cautiously due to risk of respiratory depression.
  • Positioning: Upright posture with legs dependent reduces venous return.

Explanation of other options:

Intravenous salbutamol (Option A): Salbutamol is a β2-agonist used in asthma and hyperkalemia, not in pulmonary edema.

Nebulization with salbutamol (Option C): Similar to Option A; appropriate in obstructive airway disease, not ACPE.

Oxygen and antibiotics (Option D): Oxygen is beneficial, but antibiotics are unnecessary unless infection (e.g., pneumonia) coexists.

Key Takeaways:

  • Intravenous nitroglycerin is the first-line drug in ACPE.
  • Oxygen and diuretics are supportive measures after stabilization.
  • Antibiotics are not part of routine management unless secondary infection is present.

References:

  1. https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/JAHA.119.013441
  2. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31587602/

question_text: Antibody used in the treatment of Bronchial Asthma is:
explanation: Answer is A (Omalizumab): Omalizumab is a recombinant IgE Antibody approved for use in treatment of moderate and severe persistent asthma Omalizumab is a recombinant IgE blocking antibody that neutralizes circulating IgE. It prevents circulating IgE from binding to receptors on the surface of Basophils and Mast cells and thus inhibits IgE mediated reactions. Omalizumab is indicated for treatment of 'moderate to severe' persistent asthma in patients who react to perennial allergens (Allergic Asthma). Treatment with Omalizumab has shown to reduce the number of exacerbations in patients with severe asthma and may improve asthma control. However this treatment is very expensive and is only suitable for highly selected patients who are not controlled on maximal doses of inhaler therapy and have a high circulating IgE (within a specified range). Omalizumab is usually given as a subcutaneous injection for 2 to 4 weeks and may be used in adults and adolescents more than 12 years of age.

question_text: Which one of the following statements is true of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
option_a: Patients show at least a 15 %  improvement in the FEV1 after nebulised bronchodilator
option_b: Inhaled corticosteroid usage does not improve long-term prognosis
option_c: Breathlessness is uncommon until the FEV1 falls to approximately 50 % of predicted
option_d: Emphysema is associated with increased transfer factor
explanation:
1. 15% improvement in FEV1 level of improvement would mean the presence of asthma.
  2. High dose inhaled steroids have been shown (ISOLDE) to improve quality of life and reduce hospitalisation rates by reducing the number of exacerbations, but it does not slow the rate of decline of FEV1 (hence does not affect prognosis).
  3. Breathless is common but subjective. Mild COPD (60 - 79% predicted FEV1) are often unknown to their GP. Those with moderate COPD (40 - 59% predicted) are seen intermittently seen by GP, whilst those with severe disease (< 40% predicted) have frequent hospital and GP visits.
  4. It is asthma which is associated with normal or increased transfer factor. COPD is associated with decreased transfer factor.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: Ch:202, Pg: 2187

question_text: Pulsus paradoxus is seen in:
option_b: Severe Asthma or Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
explanation:
Explanation:

Pulsus paradoxus is defined as an abnormally large drop in systolic blood pressure (>10 mmHg) during inspiration. While classically associated with cardiac tamponade, it is also a critical sign in severe obstructive lung diseases like asthma and COPD.

Pathophysiology in Obstructive Lung Disease

During an acute exacerbation, severe airway obstruction leads to markedly negative intra-thoracic pressures during inspiration. This exaggerated pressure change has two main effects:

  1. It increases the gradient for venous return, enhancing right ventricular (RV) filling.
  2. The significantly negative pressure around the heart increases the afterload on the left ventricle (LV).

The combination of a volume-loaded RV (which causes the interventricular septum to bulge into the LV) and the increased LV afterload results in a dramatic reduction in LV stroke volume and systolic pressure during inspiration.

Key Associations


Explanation of other options:

Coronary artery disease (Option A): While CAD can cause various symptoms and signs, it does not typically produce the specific hemodynamic alterations necessary to cause pulsus paradoxus.

Atrial fibrillation (Option C): This arrhythmia causes an irregular pulse volume, but this variation is random and not synchronized with the respiratory cycle, which is a defining feature of pulsus paradoxus.

Right ventricular myocardial infarction (Option D): RV infarction primarily causes elevated jugular venous pressure and hypotension, but not the phasic, inspiration-related blood pressure drop characteristic of pulsus paradoxus.

Key Takeaways:

  • Pulsus paradoxus is an exaggeration of the normal slight drop in BP during inspiration.
  • Its key causes can be remembered as the "3 T's and Asthma/COPD": Tamponade, Tension pneumothorax, and massive pulmonary Thromboembolism, plus severe Obstructive Lung Disease.
  • It is a sign of severe physiological compromise in both cardiac and pulmonary conditions.

question_text: Creola bodies are seen in -

Found in a patient's sputum, they are ciliated columnar cells sloughed from the bronchial mucosa of a patient with asthma. question_text:
A 52-year-old man enquired about the advisability of vaccination prior to a holiday abroad. He had been treated for asthma with long-term steroids and regularly required doses of Prednisolone in excess of 30mg daily to control acute exacerbations.
Which one of the following vaccinations would be contra-indicated in this man?
explanation:
• Some individuals, particularly those that are immunosuppressed, are at risk if they are given live vaccines. Inactivated vaccines are generally not dangerous but may be ineffective. They are also at risk of severe manifestations to vaccines such as disseminated infection with BCG.
  • Those patients who receive prednisolone 40mg/day for more than a week or who are on lower doses for more prolonged periods should be considered to be immunosuppressed.
  • Asthma alone is not a contra-indication to vaccination even if patients are taking inhaled corticosteroids.

question_text: A 75 year old lady is admitted with an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). One hour after admission she remains distressed with a respiratory rate of 35 per minute and is peripherally cyanosed. Repeated arterial blood gases show a severe respiratory acidosis with a pH of <7.2. Which of the following treatments is recommended?
option_c: Repeat bronchodilator therapy and arrange repeat arterial gases
option_d: Arrange for non-invasive positive pressure ventilation
explanation:
• Non invasive positive pressure ventilation should be considered, especially in COPD patients when there is a need for ventilatory assistance as indicated by worsening dyspnoea, acute respiratory acidosis and worsening oxygenation. If this does not work then intubation and ventilation may be necessary.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:292 Pg 2189

question_text: In the diagnosis of asthma, reversibility is defined as increase in FEV1 by > __% after administration of  albuterol.
explanation:
• Reversibility is defined as a ≥12% increase in the FEV1and an absolute increase of ≥200 mL at least 15 min after administration of a β2 -agonist or after several weeks of corticosteroid therapy

question_text: Aspirin sensitive asthma is associated with:
explanation:
• A subset of patients (5–10%) present in adulthood with difficult-to control asthma and type 2 inflammation with eosinophilia, sinusitis, nasal polyposis, and severe asthma exacerbations that are precipitated by ingesting inhibitors of cyclooxygenase, with aspirin being the most prominent of such inhibitors.
  • Such patients, classified as having aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, overproduce leukotrienes in response to inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1, probably secondary to inhibition of PGE2 .
  • These patients should avoid inhibitors of cyclooxygenase-1, (aspirin and NSAIDs) but can generally tolerate inhibitors of cyclooxygenase-2 and acetaminophen.
  • They should be treated with leukotriene modifiers.


Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 21st Edition, Ch: 287, Pg: 2159

question_text: A 65 year old man has been diagnosed with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Spirometry confirms severe COPD with a FEV1 of less than 25% predicted. In the last year he has been admitted to hospital on 6 occasions with COPD exacerbation.Which one of the following can help to reduce hospital admissions?
explanation:
Severe COPD is diagnosed if the FEV1 is less or equal to 30% predicted. Studies have shown that patients treated with long acting anticholinergic (e.g. Tiotropium) have fewer exacerbations per year.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:292 Pg:2186

question_text: A 35 year old man has significant wheezing and breathlessness. Recordings of peak flows show diurnal variation. He was prescribed salbutamol but continues to have frequent wheezy episodes. What is the next step in management?
explanation:
• Diurnal PEFR variation points towards a diagnosis of asthma. GINA does not recommend SABA only treatment for asthma in adults and adolescents and does not recommend the scheduled day use of SABAs.
  • Although SABA is effective as a quick relief medication, patients who are treated with SABA are at increased risk for asthma-related death even if their symptoms are controlled. Increased use (more than one cannister a month) indicates diminished asthma control and the need for adding long term therapy.

  • Leukotriene antagonists are less effective than inhaled corticosteroids for exacerbation reduction but may be considered as alternatives in patients with asthma who are unable to take inhaled corticosteroids or who experience undesirable steroid side effects.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:287 Pg:2158

question_text: A lifelong non-smoker is diagnosed with emphysema. Which of the following would be the most likely aetiological agent ?
explanation:
• Coal inhalation is a recognised risk factor of emphysema. Other industrial associations with COPD include gold, cotton, grain and cement.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:292 Pg: 2184

question_text: A 50 year old female, diagnosed with  COPD 2 years ago has had 1 exacerbation in the past 1 year which did not require hospitalization. On assessing her symptoms, she reported to get breathless after walking a few minutes on a level ground. What is her category of severity as per current GOLD classification?
explanation:
• This patient has mMRC grade 3 breathlessness and only 1 exacerbation which did not require hospitalization, hence she is having category B (high symptoms, low risk) COPD.
  • COPD severity categories are based on respiratory symptoms (based on the Modified Medical Research Council Dyspnea Scale [mMRC] or COPD Assessment Test [CAT]) and annual frequency of COPD exacerbations.

mMRC grading

question_text:
A 17-year-old female presents after taking an overdose of her grandmother's medication.
Investigations revealed:
Serum potassium 6 mmol/L (3.5-4.9)
Which one of the following drugs is the most likely cause of this abnormality?
explanation:
Beta blockers, particularly propranolol, in overdose can cause hyperkalaemia by transmembrane shifts. It is useful to think of the opposite - beta-agonists such as salbutamol are far more widely known to cause hypokalaemia.

Overdose of digoxin therapy most commonly manifests as rhythm disturbance, and may be exacerbated by hyper- or hypokalaemia.

Salicylate overdose causes metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, pg:423

question_text: An asthmatic patient on salbutamol and ipratropium continues to have nocturnal exacerbations. Which of the following is the next best step?
option_b: Add long-acting beta agonist + inhaled corticosteroid
explanation:
Explanation:

For a patient with uncontrolled asthma despite use of a short-acting beta agonist (salbutamol) and an anticholinergic (ipratropium), the next recommended step is to add an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) and a long-acting beta agonist (LABA). This combination addresses airway inflammation (ICS) and provides prolonged bronchodilation (LABA), improving symptom control and reducing nocturnal exacerbations.

Bronchial asthma management depends on the severity and frequency of symptoms, as well as objective measures of lung function, such as forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1).

  • Patients with intermittent asthma, who experience symptoms less than twice a week and have normal FEV1 (>80%), usually require only as-needed inhaled β2-agonists (e.g., albuterol).
  • However, if:
    • Symptoms occur more than twice per week,
    • Nocturnal symptoms are present more than twice a month, or
    • FEV1 < 80% of predicted, Then, additional maintenance therapy is warranted.
  • The first-line controller medication is a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS). Alternatives include leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRAs) or mast cell stabilizers like cromolyn.
  • Theophylline is now rarely used due to its narrow therapeutic window and side effect profile and is typically reserved for cases unresponsive to standard therapies.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Add oral corticosteroids (Option A): Reserved for severe exacerbations and not for routine long-term control due to side effects.

Increase frequency of salbutamol (Option C): Can cause side effects and does not address the underlying inflammation.

Add montelukast (Option D): Used as an add-on in mild-to-moderate asthma, but evidence is stronger for ICS+LABA at this stage.

question_text:
A 26-year-old patient with a history of bronchial asthma experiences two daytime episodes and one night time episode per week. He uses albuterol as needed. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows an improvement in FEV1 from 76% to 83%.
What is the most appropriate next step in management?
option_d: Change to salbutamol MDI twice daily
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

The patient has mild persistent asthma and requires initiation of an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) like fluticasone for long-term control.

  • This patient's symptoms; daytime attacks more than once weekly and nighttime symptoms, fulfill the criteria for mild persistent asthma.
  • The partial reversibility of airway obstruction seen on spirometry (FEV1 improving from 76% to 83% after a bronchodilator) also supports this diagnosis.
  • In such cases, relying solely on short-acting β2-agonists like albuterol is not sufficient.
  • Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) such as fluticasone are the cornerstone of controller therapy, reducing airway inflammation and the frequency of exacerbations.
  • According to the stepwise approach to asthma management:
    • Step 1 (intermittent): PRN short-acting β2-agonists (SABAs) for symptoms less than once a week.
    • Step 2 (mild persistent): Regular low-dose ICS is introduced, typically when symptoms occur ≥3 times per week or nocturnal symptoms occur ≥1 per week.
    • Step 3-5: Progressive escalation depending on control, including higher ICS doses, LABAs, oral steroids, and biologics like omalizumab or mepolizumab.

Explanation of other options:

Add oral prednisolone 10 mg daily (Option A): Oral corticosteroids are reserved for severe cases or acute exacerbations; their chronic use is avoided due to systemic side effects.

Continue albuterol whenever required (Option B): While effective for symptom relief, albuterol alone does not address the underlying inflammation seen in persistent asthma.

Change to salbutamol MDI twice daily (Option D): Salbutamol is not intended for regular scheduled use. Maintenance therapy in persistent asthma requires an ICS, not increased use of a SABA.

question_text: A known case of COPD with acute exacerbation of COPD. On examination patient is conscious and alert, pulse 110/min on examination bilateral wheeze is noted. Which of the following is not true?
explanation:
The question deals with the management of acute exacerbation of COPD. It includes

  • Inhaled bronchodilators, beta agonist or anticholinergics, either separately or together.
  • Systemic methylxanthines can be given
  • Antibiotics
  • Systemic steroids reduces length of hospital stay and future exacerbations.
  • Oxygen: to maintain SpO2≥90%.
  • NIV is indicated in patients with PCO2> 45

Invasive ventilation is indicated in patients with severe respiratory distress or hypercapnia despite initial therapy, severe hypoxia, hemodynamic instability, altered mentation, acidosis or respiratory arrest.

Permissive hypercapnia is allowed in COPD management and should not deter physicians from giving O2 to correct hypoxia, as O2 can cause modest increase in CO2 levels.

question_text: In asthma diagnosis is by
explanation: Answer- A. FEVi Asthma is classified according to the frequency of symptoms, forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), and peak expiratory flow rate. Spirometry is recommended to aid in diagnosis and management. It is the single best test for asthma. If the FEV1 measured by this technique improves more than 12% and increases by at least 200 milliliters following administration of a bronchodilator such as salbutamol, this is supportive of the diagnosis.

question_text:
Child presented with a severe acute exacerbation of asthma with spO2-80%. In treatment of this patient in ER what will you do?
a. Order an urgent CXR
b. Nebulization with SABA for 60 min 3 times
c. Inhaled steroids
d. High flow O2
explanation: For severe acute asthma, an emergency Chest radiograph is not indicated. Treatment for severe persistent asthma consists of inhaled corticosteroids. Additional long-term controller medicines, such as long-acting beta 2 agonists (LABA), montelukast or theophylline, are added if asthma is still uncontrolled.

question_text: For which of the following groups is pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine not routinely recommended?
option_a: Otherwise healthy adults aged 50 to 65 years
option_b: Adults aged 19 to 65 years who have immunocompromising conditions
explanation:
• Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine is not recommended for otherwise healthy adults aged 50 to 65 years.
  • This vaccine is, however recommended for persons who have immunocompromising conditions or lung disease (such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or asthma) and for persons who are cigarette smokers and heavy consumers of alcohol. Post splenectomy or hyposplenism is another indication
  • There are 2 types of pneumococcal vaccine pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) and a protein conjugate pneumococcal vaccine (PCV13)
  • Routine use of PCV13 is recommended among adults aged 65 and older. Individuals 65 years of age or older who have never received a pneumococcal vaccine should first receive PCV13 followed by a dose of PPSV23 6-12 months later. Individuals who have received more than one dose of PPSV23 should receive a dose of PCV13 more than 1 year after the last dose of PPSV23 was administered.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 146, Pg: 1177

question_text: A 55 year old male who has a history of COPD since 15 years presents with complaints of fever, productive cough and breathlessness on exertion. Chest X ray reveals a non homogeneous air space opacity in the right mid lobe of the lung. Which of the following organisms may be responsible for causing this condition?
explanation:
COPD is a risk factor for pneumonia. Organisms implicated in COPD patients include:

  • H influenzae
  • P aeruginosa
  • Legionella
  • Pneumoniae
  • Moraxella catarrhalis
  • Chlamydia pneumoniae


Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal medicine 21st edition chapter.126 page number 1011

question_text: A 68-year-old male with a known history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is admitted with acute exacerbation. He is placed on mechanical ventilation due to respiratory distress. During ventilation, his oxygen saturation begins to fall consistently. On auscultation, vesicular breath sounds are heard on the right side, and chest X-ray was done and shown below. What is the most likely finding on auscultation of the left side of the chest?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Chest X-ray reveals a hyperlucent left hemithorax with absent vascular markings and mediastinal shift to the right.

In left-sided pneumothorax, air in the pleural space prevents transmission of breath sounds, resulting in absent breath sounds on auscultation.

  • In a patient with COPD on mechanical ventilation, the sudden drop in oxygen saturation, along with hyperlucency on chest X-ray and absent vascular markings, strongly suggests the development of a pneumothorax, specifically on the left side in this case.
  • Mechanical ventilation, especially with positive pressure, increases the risk of barotrauma, which may cause rupture of already fragile lung tissue (common in emphysematous lungs of COPD patients), leading to a secondary spontaneous or tension pneumothorax.

Classic signs of pneumothorax:

  • Inspection: Asymmetric chest movement, respiratory distress
  • Palpation: Reduced/absent tactile fremitus on affected side
  • Percussion: Hyperresonant note on the side of pneumothorax
  • Auscultation: Absent or markedly reduced breath sounds over the affected side
  • Other signs: Tracheal/mediastinal shift (if tension pneumothorax), hypoxemia, hypotension

Explanation of other options:

Bronchial breath sounds (Option B): Bronchial breath sounds are heard over areas of lung consolidation (e.g., pneumonia), not in pneumothorax, where the lung is collapsed and displaced by air in the pleural space.

Increased vesicular breath sounds (Option C): Vesicular breath sounds are normal and may be slightly increased over hyperinflated but aerated lungs; in pneumothorax, breath sounds are typically absent, not increased.

Increased vocal fremitus (Option D): Fremitus is increased in consolidated lung, but decreased or absent in pneumothorax due to the insulating effect of free air in the pleural cavity.

Reference:

https://pubs.rsna.org/doi/abs/10.1148/radiol.2282020524?journalCode=radiology

https://radiopaedia.org/articles/pneumothorax

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17419871/

question_text: A 13 year old male has recent onset breathlessness. He has a history of wheezing particularly during the summer when the pollen count is high.Which of these tests would help to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
• The history of wheezing during pollen exposure suggests asthma. The best diagnostic test for asthma would be demonstration of variable airways obstruction with Bronchodilator reversibility and serial peak flow measurements.
  • Reversibility is defined as a ≥12% increase in the FEV1 and an absolute increase of ≥200 mL at least 15 min after administration of a β2 -agonist or after several weeks of corticosteroid therapy.
  • Diurnal peak flow variability of >20% has also been proposed as an indicator of reversible airways disease, but it is less reliable due to difficulties with quality control and variability of home assessments

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:287 Pg:2154

question_text:
A 70 year old man with known chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is admitted with symptoms of worsening breathlessness and confusion. Following a dose of 200mg iv hydrocortisone and two doses of salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisers, arterial blood gases were taken.
His arterial blood gases are as follows: pH 7.18, pO2 49.5 mmhg, pCO2 90 mmhg. What should be done next?
explanation:
• This patient has type II respiratory failure with acidosis, and hence should be considered for ventilation, either straight away or with a trial of NIPPV beforehand.

Mechanical ventilation is indicated for:

  • patients with severe respiratory distress despite initial therapy
  • life-threatening hypoxemia
  • severe hypercarbia and/or acidosis
  • markedly impaired mental status
  • respiratory arrest
  • hemodynamic instability

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 292 Pg 2189

question_text: Which of the following goes against a diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
explanation:
• Clubbing is not a feature of COPD, its presence should raise the suspicion of an underlying lung malignancy.

Physical findings of COPD:

  • Nicotine staining of fingernails
  • Signs of respiratory distress: pursed lip breathing, accessory muscle use, tripod position, inspiratory in drawing of ribs (esp lower ribs, ka Hoover's sign)
  • Cachexia (poor prognostic finding)
  • Signs of hyper inflated lungs: barrel chest, hyper resonance on percussion
  • Auscultation: coarse crepitations (fibrosis), polyphonic rhonchi
  • Signs of right heart failure (cor pulmonale): Elevated JVP, Pedal edema, ascites.

Labs may show a 2° polycythaemia and chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic alkalosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st edition, chapter. 292 page number. 2185

question_text: A 24-year-old asthmatic female is admitted with acute severe asthma. Which of the following statements regarding the diagnosis is correct?
option_a: Agitation should be managed with a benzodiazepine
option_b: A high inspired Oxygen concentration should be used routinely
option_c: Inhaled salmeterol is indicated as first line therapy
explanation:
• A normal or raised arterial pCO2 is an indication of severe asthma. Pluses paradoxus is not reliable and is not part of the criteria in assessing severity of asthma attack. Salmeterol is used in management of chronic asthma (Step 3).
  • High dose oxygen (40-60% should be used in severe asthma attacks, together with steroids and nebulised bronchodilators. Sedation must be avoided as it can cause respiratory failure and arrest.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 287, Pg-2158

question_text: What should be the subsequent course of action in managing a 60 year old patient, who is known case of COPD patient, admitted to the ICU, and currently receiving 2 liters of oxygen therapy, but observed to be hypoventilating with an arterial blood gas analysis revealing a pH level of 7.33 and pCO2 levels of 64 mmHg?
explanation:
Explanation:
The patient is in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (pH < 7.35, pCO2 > 45 mmHg) due to a COPD exacerbation. The first-line treatment for this scenario is Non-Invasive Positive Pressure Ventilation (NIPPV or NIV). NIPPV improves gas exchange, reduces the work of breathing, and decreases the need for intubation and its associated complications.

Treatment of Acute Exacerbation of COPD:

Management begins with recognition of increased breathlessness, cough, sputum, often triggered by infection or air quality changes.

At home, patients may increase bronchodilators, use a short oral glucocorticoid course, and start antibiotics if needed. Hospital referral is warranted with cyanosis, oedema, or altered consciousness.

Investigations include ABG (to assess hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, acidaemia and guide oxygen/ventilation) and chest X-ray (to detect pneumonia, pneumothorax, effusion).

Management in hospital:

  • Oxygen:Controlled 24-28% to keep PaO2 > 8 kPa or SaO2 > 90%, with ABG monitoring.
  • Bronchodilators:Nebulised short-acting β -agonists (salbutamol, terbutaline) plus anticholinergics (ipratropium); compressed air if oxygen-sensitive.
  • Glucocorticoids:Prednisolone 30 mg orally for 10 days; consider osteoporosis prophylaxis with repeated courses.
  • Antibiotics:For increased sputum purulence, volume, or breathlessness (aminopenicillin, tetracycline, macrolide; co-amoxiclav if resistant organisms suspected).
  • NIV:For mild-moderate respiratory acidosis, reduces intubation need/mortality; avoid if airway protection is impaired.
  • Mechanical ventilation:Consider if reversible cause, no prior chronic failure, or failed/contraindicated NIV, with shared decision-making.

Explanation of other options:

Invasive PPV should be given and Intubate and start on ventilator (Option B and D): Invasive mechanical ventilation is reserved for patients with severe acidosis (pH <7.25), hemodynamic instability, impaired mental status, or those who have failed a trial of NIPPV.

Increase the oxygen flow rate (Option C): Increasing oxygen in a hypercapnic COPD patient can worsen hypoventilation by reducing the hypoxic respiratory drive, leading to further CO2 retention.

Key Takeaways:

  • NIPPV is the first-line intervention for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure in COPD exacerbations.
  • The goal is to correct acidosis and avoid intubation.

question_text: A patient has presented with features of cardiac tamponade. Which of the following is correct regarding this condition?
option_d: Jugular veins column is visibly distended without pulsations
explanation:
Explanation:

In cardiac tamponade, the pericardial effusion causes elevated and equalized pressures throughout the heart. This leads to elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP). A key finding is the loss of the y descent in the JVP waveform due to impaired early diastolic filling, making the veins appear distended but quiet, without the normal visible pulsations.

  • In cardiac tamponade the Compression of cardiac chambers by pericardial effusion, limiting cardiac inflow; can occur with 200 ml-2 L of fluid.
  • Beck's Triad:
    • Jugular venous distension (↑ CVP, prominent x, absent y descent)
    • Hypotension (↓ cardiac output)
    • Muffled heart sounds (fluid dampens sounds)
  • Other Feature:Pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg fall in systolic BP on inspiration).
  • Causes of Pulsus Paradoxus:
    • Lung:Acute asthma, COPD, tension pneumothorax, pleural effusion, PE
    • Heart:Cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis

JVP Waveform in Cardiac tamponade

Explanation of other options:

Pulsus Paradoxus is always present (Option A): While a highly specific sign, it may be absent in patients with pre-existing conditions like aortic regurgitation, atrial septal defect, or severe hypotension.

Kussmaul sign is always present (Option B): Kussmaul sign (a rise in JVP on inspiration) is characteristic of constrictive pericarditis, not cardiac tamponade.

Tall A wave is present (Option C): Tall A waves are seen in conditions causing reduced right ventricular compliance (e.g., pulmonary hypertension, pulmonic stenosis), not in tamponade where the waveform is dampened.

Key Takeaways:

  • Cardiac tamponade is a clinical diagnosis characterized by Beck's triad: hypotension, JVD, and muffled heart sounds.

The JVP is elevated with a prominent x descent and an absent y descent.

question_text: Which of the following is/are an indications for long term oxygen therapy to patients of COPD?
option_c: Resting O2 saturation ≤89% with signs of pulmonary arterial hypertension
explanation:
• For patients with resting hypoxemia (resting O2 saturation ≤88% in any patient or ≤89% with signs of pulmonary arterial hypertension, right heart failure or erythrocytosis), the use of O2 has been demonstrated to have a significant impact on mortality.

Therapies showing a mortality benefit in COPD patients:

  • Smoking cessation
  • Long term Oxygen therapy
  • Lung volume resection surgery

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st edition, chapter. 292 ,page number 2188

question_text:
A 25 year old male with a 5 year long history of bronchial asthma, presented with worsening of asthma and fever of 20 days duration. The patient was well controlled on budesonide metered dose inhalations (400µg/day) and rarely ever required to take salbutamol inhalations. For the past 20 days, the patient was experiencing increasing breathlessness, fever, cough and production of mucoid expectoration for the past 20 days. Examination had a BP of 130/80 mmHg, and temperature 38.2°C. Respiratory examination revealed bilateral widespread wheezes. Investigations revealed- Haemoglobin- 12.4 g/dl, total white count -13,000/µL Neutrophils 6 (2-7.5) x 109/L, Lymphocytes 3 (1.3-3.5) x 109/L, Eosinophils 4 (0.04-0.44) x109/L. Serum IgE was 800 (0-380) kIU/ml. The chest X-ray revealed pulmonary infiltrates in the right mid and lower zones.

What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• ABPA usually occurs in association with asthma, but can occur in cystic fibrosis.
  • Peripheral Eosinophilia and high IgE levels>1000
  • It is treated with either oral or inhaled steroids. There is some evidence supporting antifungal agents like itraconazole, but amphotericin is not used. IgG and IgE are raised. In addition, skin-testing or examination of sputum with fungal stains can be used.
  • Sputum culture is not often helpful. ABPA can lead to proximal bronchiectasis affecting the upper lobes if left untreated.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 288, Pg:2165

question_text: A patient who has undergone cardiac surgery suddenly develops low blood pressure, elevated central venous pressure, and pulsus paradoxus four hours after the operation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The symptoms observed in the postoperative cardiac surgery patient strongly suggest cardiac tamponade. This is a medical emergency caused by the buildup of fluid or blood within the pericardial sac, which compresses the heart and disrupts its normal function.

Cardiac Tamponade

Definition:

A condition in which the heart chambers are compressed by a tense pericardial effusion, restricting the heart’s ability to fill properly. Fluid accumulation ranging from as little as 200 ml to over 2 liters can cause cardiac tamponade.

Clinical Features:

  • Beck's Triad:
    • Jugular Venous Distension: Due to increased central venous pressure, with a prominent x descent and absent y descent.
    • Hypotension: Caused by reduced cardiac output.
    • Muffled Heart Sounds: Fluid in the pericardial space dampens the heart sounds.

Other Features:

  • Pulsus Paradoxus: A drop in systolic blood pressure of more than 10 mm Hg during inspiration.

Causes of Pulsus Paradoxus:

  • Lung-related: Acute asthma, COPD, tension pneumothorax, pleural effusion, pulmonary embolism.
  • Heart-related: Cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis.

Low-Pressure Cardiac Tamponade

Definition:

A form of tamponade occurring when pericardial pressure is relatively low, often seen in cases of intravascular volume depletion such as hypovolemia.

Features:

  • Jugular venous distension is often absent.
  • Pulsus paradoxus is rare.
  • Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion since classic signs like jugular venous distension and pulsus paradoxus may be missing.

Explanation for other options:

Ventricular dysfunction (Option A): can lead to hypotension and cardiac symptoms, but it usually does not cause raised central venous pressure or pulsus paradoxus. Moreover, the sudden onset of symptoms in this case indicates an acute condition like cardiac tamponade rather than a chronic ventricular dysfunction.

Congestive heart failure (CHF) (Option C): may result in fluid retention, causing increased venous pressure and symptoms such as shortness of breath and edema. However, it rarely presents with sudden hypotension, elevated central venous pressure, or pulsus paradoxus.

Excessive mediastinal effusion (Option D): can compress the heart and produce symptoms similar to cardiac tamponade. Still, the presence of raised central venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus more specifically suggests cardiac tamponade as the most probable diagnosis.

Reference:

  1. Low-Pressure Cardiac Tamponade | Circulation
  2. Fluid amount
  3. Pulsus paradoxus

question_text:
A 55-year-old female presents with tremor of the hands which has been present for approximately five years.
She has a past medical history which includes anxiety and she receives salbutamol for asthma.
Examination revealed titubation and an upper limb postural tremor.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Anxiety and drugs (for example, salbutamol, sodium valproate, theophylline, amiodarone) are commonly associated with tremor of the limbs.

However, head tremor (titubation) is unusual. Essential tremor is the commonest cause of head tremor.

Parkinson's disease is associated with rest tremor but not titubation.

Multiple sclerosis is associated with titubation and intention tremor.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 436, Pg: 3401

question_text: A 40-year-old man has a 3-month history of cough, dyspnoea and sputum production. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and has a history of asthma. There is no history of asbestos exposure. His WBC count is 24 x 10∧9/L with 70% neutrophils and 3.0 x 10∧9/L (5%) eosinophils. IgE level is elevated. He has decreased breath sounds corresponding to parenchymal infiltrates on the CXR. Which is the best test to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
• The condition described is Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis, commoner among asthmatics and cystic fibrosis patients. Wheeze, shortness of breath and productive Allergic Bronchopulmonary aspergillosis results from an allergic reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus which actually grows in the walls of the bronchi.
  • Eosinophilia and high IgE levels are suggestive of the condition. Aspergillus precipitins (lab test to detect antibodies) is diagnostic. The chest radiograph often shows evidence of proximal bronchiectasis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 288, Pg:2165

explanation:
Bacteria that frequently implicated in COPD exacerbations include:

question_text: A 40-year-old worker presents with wheezing and breathlessness which seem to improve over weekends and holiday periods when he is not working. What is he most likely to be exposed to at work?
explanation:
• Disinfectants and preservatives including glutaraldehyde, chlorhexidine and formaldehyde can cause occupational asthma.
  • Metals causing occupational asthma include isocyanates cobalt, aluminium, chrome, manganese, nickel, zinc, and platinum.
  • Exposure to Actinomyces (farmer's lung, mushroom workers' lung), avian bloom (bird fanciers' lung) and aspergillus clavatus (malt worker's lung) cause extrinsic allergic alveolitis.

question_text: A 65 year old man with emphysema presented with increasing dyspnoea and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. A chest radiograph reveals a left-sided pneumothorax with a lung edge measured 5 cm away from the chest wall. The most appropriate management of his condition is:
option_c: Refer to a respiratory outpatient clinic
explanation:
The lung edge measurement suggests a greater than 50% pneumothorax. A smaller pneumothorax may be amenable to aspiration. In the context of chronic underlying respiratory disease such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder and a large pneumothorax, patients are best managed by pleural drainage.


Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 294 Pg: 2200

question_text: Which of the following respiratory conditions may cause a non caseating granuloma in the lungs?
explanation:
• Farmer's lung is hypersensitivity pneumonitis is a TH1 mediated type 4 hypersensitivity which results in formation of non caseating granuloma.
  • It presents with a subacute onset progressive dry cough with exertional dyspnoea.
