question_text:
A 40 year old woman has been breathless and is undergoing investigations for the cause. She has a previous history of being a smoker and has a dry cough as well. Her ABGs show a pO2 of 67 mmHg and pCO2 of 37 mm Hg. Lung function tests show reduced vital capacity, reduced TLCO but increased KCO.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• In this scenario, the lung function indicates that the surface area for exchange are inadequate (low TLCO) hence suggesting that lung expansion is reduced. However, cardiac output is increased to compensate, and hence KCO is increased. Kyphoscoliosis would restrict lung expansion, or a neuromuscular disorder (e.g. spina bifida) could cause this.

KCO = Transfer coefficient = DLCO/volume of air in alveoli


Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 285Pg 2138

question_text: Identify the diagnosis based on the CT image provided.
explanation:
Explanation:

A CT scan demonstrating a signet ring sign is highly indicative of bronchiectasis. This sign occurs when a dilated bronchus is larger than its accompanying pulmonary artery, creating the appearance of a ring with a gemstone. It reflects permanent airway dilation, which is a defining feature of bronchiectasis.

Bronchiectasis is a disorder marked by irreversible dilatation of the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to impaired mucus clearance and recurrent infections. CT imaging is the diagnostic modality of choice for confirming the condition.

Chest CT findings in bronchiectasis include:

  • Airway dilation - visible as parallel "tram tracks" or on cross-section as the signet-ring sign.


  • Loss of bronchial tapering - bronchi fail to narrow normally toward the periphery.
  • Bronchial wall thickening - walls of dilated bronchi appear thickened.
  • Inspissated secretions - sometimes seen as a "tree-in-bud" pattern.
  • Signet-ring sign - particularly prominent in cystic bronchiectasis.

Imaging modalities:

  • X-ray - may show tram-track shadows.
  • High-resolution CT (HRCT) - gold standard for detecting airway changes.
    • Black arrows - indicate tram-track sign.
    • Red arrows - highlight signet-ring sign.

Explanation of other options:

Pulmonary TB (Option A): Cavitary lesions, upper-lobe fibrosis.

Bronchial Asthma (Option B): Reversible airway disease, no structural bronchial dilation.

COPD (Option C): Emphysema, bullae, hyperinflation; no bronchial dilation.

question_text:
A 30 year old man gives a six-month history of worsening breathlessness and coughs up half a cupful of sputum daily. He was occasionally wheezy with viral illnesses as a young child, works in a factory and has smoked 25 cigarettes per day for the last four years.
The most likely diagnosis is:
explanation:
• Bronchiectasis is most likely due to the extensive amounts of sputum production. In a young person, cystic fibrosis and hypogammaglobulinemia should be considered.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 290 Pg 2173

question_text: A 55 year old lady presents with worsening breathlessness. She has a history of Raynaud's phenomenon, heartburn and reflux. On examination, the skin over her fingers is tight and shiny. She has multiple telangiectasia over her face and nail fold capillary loops are seen. Her investigations show she has Anticentromere antibodies. What respiratory complication may occur?
explanation:
• The patient has the clinical features of limited cutaneous scleroderma ( formerly CREST syndrome). Anticentromere antibodies occur in 70-80% of these patients. A significant respiratory complication is pulmonary hypertension. Treatment is with prostaglandin analogues e.g. iloprost (intravenous infusions) or bosentan (oral).
  • Churg Strauss syndrome presents with asthma, haemoptysis and pulmonary infiltrates; it is associated with ANCA antibodies and does not allow mail fold changes
  • Pulmonary fibrosis is a complication of diffuse systems sclerosis; it is associated with anti Scl-70
  • ABPA affects patients of long standing asthma or cystic fibrosis., It presents as asthma refractory to treatment, haemoptysis and is characterized by elevated IgE levels

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 360 Pg 2780

question_text: A 34-year-old woman presented with a dry cough, thorax constriction, and generalised weakness. During the preceding 5 months, she had experienced these dry cough episodes twice a week. A lung function test showed a restriction of the vital capacity (71% of the adjusted reference value), and the diffusion capacity was also reduced (66 to 68%). Broncho alveolar lavage specimens were obtained, the lymphocytes were increased up to 41% (norm, <10%), and neutrophils were increased up to 6% (norm, <2%) with a normal total cell count. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis is type IV hypersensitivity.
  • There is no eosinophilia, IgG and lymphocytes are involved in immune response.
  • Antigens of micropolyspora faeni and thermoactinomyces are 0.5-5 microns.
  • Assaying for IgG antibodies against specific antigens, either through precipitin testing or direct serum measurement, can be a useful adjunct in the diagnosis of HP
  • High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) is a common component in the diagnostic workup; In subacute forms of the disease, ground-glass airspace opacities are characteristic, as is the presence of centrilobular nodules. Expiratory images may show areas of air trapping that are likely caused by involvement of the small airways
  • BAL shows a lymphocytic predominance with a greater proportion of CD8 positive T cells.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 288, Pg: 2161

question_text: A 60-year-old male patient comes to your clinic with an 8-month history of shortness of breath and non-productive cough. He has smoked half a pack of cigarettes for the past 30 years. On physical examination, clubbing is seen and fine crackles are heard on both sides during inspiration. You perform pulmonary function tests and it shows an FEV1/FVC ratio of 92%. The CT scan of the chest is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation is classic for a restrictive lung disease, specifically Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF). Key indicators include:

  • Symptoms:Progressive dyspnea, dry cough.
  • Examination:Clubbing, bilateral inspiratory crackles ("Velcro" crackles).
  • PFTs:Normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio (ruling out obstructive disease like COPD) indicating a restrictive pattern.
  • Imaging:The CT image shows the presence of honeycombing (black arrows), traction bronchiectasis (white arrow), and a reticular pattern (black dotted arrows). Bronchiectasis in a subpleural and basal distribution.

Explanation of other options:

Bronchial asthma and Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) (Option A and D): These are obstructive diseases, characterized by a low FEV1/FVC ratio on PFTs.
Pulmonary tuberculosis (Option C): Typically causes upper lobe infiltrates, cavitation, or lymphadenopathy on imaging, not the classic subpleural honeycombing of IPF.

Key Takeaways:

  • IPF is a restrictive lung disease with a characteristic HRCT pattern of usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP).

question_text: Patient presents with fever, nocturnal cough, breathlessness and wheezing for 4 weeks. Absolute eosinophil count >5000. X-ray shows a military pattern. Diagnosis?
explanation:
The given history and lab findings suggestive of tropical pulmonary Eosinophilia.

TROPICAL PULMONARY EOSINOPHILIA

Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE) is a distinct syndrome that develops in some individuals infected with the lymphatic- dwelling filarial species.

The majority of cases have been reported from India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Brazil, Guyana, and Southeast Asia; the decreasing incidence of TPE in last decade probably reflects global MDA efforts.

CLINICAL FEATURES

The main features include a history of residence in filaria-endemic regions, paroxysmal cough and wheezing (usually nocturnal probably related to the nocturnal periodicity of microfilariae), weight loss, low-grade fever, lymphadenopathy, and pronounced blood eosin- ophilia (>3000 eosinophils/µL).

Chest x-rays or CT scans may be normal, but generally show increased bronchovascular markings. Diffuse miliary lesions or mottled opacities may be present in the middle and lower lung fields.

Tests of pulmonary function show restrictive abnor- malities in most cases and obstructive defects in half.

Characteristically, total serum IgE levels (4-40 KIU/mL) and anti filarial antibody levels are markedly elevated.

question_text: After performing spirometry, the flow-volume curve of a patient is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis based on this curve?
explanation:
Explanation:

The case describes a typical flow-volume loop pattern observed in patients with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD).

Options A, C and D are incorrect.

question_text:
A 71-year-old man presents with difficulty speaking. He has a history of diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He is currently on aspirin, simvastatin, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. On examination the patient is awake, his blood pressure is 150/70 mmHg. His pulse is irregularly irregular. He has 4/5 strength in the right arm and leg and 5/5 strength on the left. When asked to point to the window he does this correctly. When told to raise his arms and place his hands out he is seen to have a pronator drift on the right. He is shown a pen and asked what it is. He responds fluently but makes some paraphasic errors. He is asked to use it appropriately and begins to write on a piece of paper. When asked to repeat 'Today is a sunny day', he is unable to do so.
Which of the following terms best describes these signs?
explanation:
• In Broca's or nonfluent or expressive aphasia the patient is unable to name objects with poor comprehension and repetition. It localises to the Broca's area in the left posterior inferior frontal gyrus.
  • In transcortical motor aphasia, which localises to the anterior superior frontal lobe, the patient is has good comprehension and repetition but has halting, effortful speech. Patients also have impaired writing skills.
  • Transcortical sensory aphasia is characterised by impaired auditory comprehension with intact repetition and fluent speech, and is caused by damage to the temporal lobes. It differs from Wernicke's aphasia in that patients still have intact repetition, and exhibit echolalia (the compulsive repetition of words). Improvement may be seen with speech therapy.



  • Anomic aphasia (also known as nominal aphasia) results in word finding difficulties. On closer examination there may also be repetition problems and comprehension problems but these are typically mild compared to other aphasia syndromes.
  • This scenario describes conduction aphasia. It is characterised by frequent speech errors, impaired repetition, reduced phonological short-term memory and naming difficulties.
  • In contrast to other forms of dysphasia, speech output is otherwise fluent and grammatically correct. Comprehension is intact. It is thought to be caused by left temporo-parietal region damage.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 30, Pg: 196

question_text: A 50 year old male chronic smoker was recently diagnosed to have chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He has a FEV1 of 40% predicted. What is his severity of the disease according to GOLD classification?
explanation:
This patient is in GOLD stage 3 (FEV1 30-49% predicted) which is considered severe COPD.


Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st edition chapter. 292, page number. 2182

question_text: A 65-year-old man presents with a five day history of lower abdominal pain and diarrhea.He has a history of chronic obstructive airways disease (COAD) and has had numerous acute infective exacerbations over the last three months.On examination he was dehydrated, with a temperature of 38.6°C, a blood pressure of 102/72 mmHg and has a distended, tender abdomen.Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation for this patient?
explanation:
This is pseudomembranous colitis due to Clostridium difficile secondary to antibiotic usage for his COPD.

Plain AXR is useful for diagnosing toxic dilatation and would be the investigation of choice here due to his abdominal distension, so toxic dilatation should be excluded prior to sigmoidoscopy. However it does not establish the diagnosis.Stool microscopy has no value but stool toxin assay is useful.

A patient with diarrhea normally has involvement of the distal colon and rectum, and sigmoidoscopy with biopsy is helpful for rapid diagnosis but should not be performed if toxic dilatation is suspected.Patients with involvement of right colon usually have little or no diarrhoea.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 138, Pg: 1069

question_text:
A 66-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and ischaemic heart disease is taken to the Emergency Department with dyspnoea. On examination his respiratory rate is 24/min, JVP is not elevated and crackles are heard in both lung bases.
Which other finding would most strongly indicate that his dyspnoea is secondary to isolated left Ventricular failure?
explanation:
Gallop rhythm (S3) is an early sign of LVF

The classic clinical examination triad in patients with left ventricular failure include

  • Pulsus alternans
  • Gallop rhythm (LV S3)
  • Bibasal crepitations

Pulsus bisferiens, where two peaks are present in systole, is observed in Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, combined AS and AR.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1937

question_text: A 74-year-old man presents with difficulty speaking. He has a history of diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He is currently on aspirin, simvastatin, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. On examination the patient is awake, his blood pressure is 150/70 mmHg. His pulse is irregularly irregular. He has 4/5 strength on the right arm and leg and 5/5 strength on the left.When asked to point to the window he appears unable to do so. When told to raise his arms and place his hands out he does not. When visually shown the same action he is able to perform it. When asked to repeat 'Today is a sunny day', he is able to do so.With what is this type of dysphasia consistent?
explanation:
• In Broca's or non-fluent or expressive aphasia the patient is unable to name objects with poor comprehension and repetition. It localises to the Broca's area in the left posterior inferior frontal gyrus.
  • In Wernicke's or fluent or receptive aphasia the patient is able to form correct grammatical sentences but language content is incorrect. It localises to the dominant superior temporal gyrus. There is poor comprehension and repetition but verbal output is fluent.
  • In transcortical motor aphasia, which localises to the anterior superior frontal lobe, the patient has good comprehension and repetition but has halting, effortful speech. Patients also have impaired writing skills.
  • Global aphasia results in an almost mute patient: there is poor verbal output, comprehension, repetition and understanding.
  • Transcortical sensory aphasia is what is described in this case. It is characterised by impaired auditory comprehension with intact repetition and fluent speech, and is caused by damage to the temporal lobes. It differs from Wernicke's aphasia in that patients still have intact repetition, and exhibit cholalia (the compulsive repetition of words). Improvement may be seen with speech therapy.



Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 30, Pg: 196

question_text: A 73-year-old man presents with difficulty speaking. He has a history of diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He is currently on aspirin, simvastatin, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. On examination the patient is awake; his blood pressure is 150/70 mmHg. His pulse is irregularly irregular. He has 4/5 strength on the right arm and leg and 5/5 strength on the left.When asked to point to the window he does this correctly. When told to raise his arms and place his hands out he is seen to have a pronator drift on the right. He is shown a pen and asked what it is. He is unable to identify it by name and appears frustrated, applying much effort to speak a sentence. He is asked to use it appropriately and begins to write on a piece of paper but no makes no legible words despite being a retired journalist. When asked to repeat 'Today is a sunny day', he is able to do so. With what type of dysphasia is this consistent?
explanation:
• In Broca's or nonfluent or expressive aphasia the patient is unable to name objects with poor comprehension and repetition. It localises to the Broca's area in the left posterior inferior frontal gyrus.
  • In Wernicke's or fluent or receptive aphasia the patient is able to form correct grammatical sentences but language content is incorrect. It localises to the dominant superior temporal gyrus. There is poor comprehension and repetition but verbal output is fluent.
  • Transcortical sensory aphasia is similar to transcortical motor aphasia in that there is good repetition but comprehension and fluency are poor.
  • Global aphasia results in an almost mute patient: there is poor verbal output, comprehension, repetition and understanding.


Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 30, Pg: 196

question_text: A 74-year-old man presents with difficulty speaking. He has a history of diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He is currently on aspirin, simvastatin, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. On examination the patient is awake, his blood pressure is 150/70 mmHg. His pulse is irregularly irregular.He has 4/5 strength in the right arm and leg and 5/5 strength on the left. When asked to point to the window he does this correctly. When told to raise his arms and place his hands out he is seen to have a pronator drift on the right. He is shown a pen and asked what it is. He is unable to identify it by name. He is asked to use it appropriately and begins to write on a piece of paper. When asked to repeat 'Today is a sunny day', he is able to do so.What type of dysphasia is this consistent with?
explanation:
• In Broca's or non-fluent or expressive aphasia the patient is unable to name objects with poor comprehension and repetition. It localises to the Broca's area in the left posterior inferior frontal gyrus.
  • An injury to the anterior superior frontal lobe results in transcortical motor aphasia with good comprehension but poor verbal output with the exception of echolalia or repetition. Writing is usually also impaired. Repetition is also spared as the arcuate fasciculus is not involved.
  • Conduction aphasia has poor repetition and naming but intact comprehension and fluent verbal output.
  • It is different to the transcortical sensory and motor aphasias in that there is intact comprehension and fluency which are not seen in each of the transcortical aphasias respectively.


Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 30, Pg: 196

question_text: A 65-year-old man comes to see you for chronic back pain, which worsened 1 week ago. He has been wheelchair bound for 6 months because of severe osteoporosis with multiple lumbosacral spine fractures. He has severe asthma, which has required large doses of glucocorticoids for many years. The patient reports progressive loss of height and kyphosis over the past year. Significant physical findings include bilateral cataracts, multiple ecchymoses and a prolonged expiratory phase with bilateral wheezes. Which of the following treatments is the first choice in this patient?
explanation:
• This patient has severe osteoporosis as evidenced by multiple fragility fractures, almost certainly related to chronic use of glucocorticoid therapy for his asthma.
  • First-line therapy in this case would be bisphosphonates, which improve bone mass in the lumbar spine and the hip. Older preparations are associated with significant gastrointestinal (GI) side-effects (predominantly oesophagitis and ulceration), so newer treatments that may be dosed weekly over significant advantages in terms of side-effect reduction.
  • Zoledronic acid is the most effective bisphosphonate for improving bone mass and is administered as IV infusion once yearly,
  • In patients with renal dysfunction or not tolerating bisphosphonates, denosumab injection given s/c every 6 months is also an option.
  • Calcium and vitamin D supplementation should be given for all patients with osteoporosis and are not a replacement for anti-osteoporotic medications
  • Testosterone supplementation is only of use in patients with low testosterone levels and osteoporosis, where it does improve bone mass.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 3202

question_text: A patient came with the complaints of fatigue and difficulty breathing. On examination, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds were found. X-ray is shown below. Identify the condition.
explanation:
Explanation:

The chest X-ray shows a normal-sized heart with a thickened, fibrosed/calcified pericardium, producing the classic 'egg-in-cup' appearance. Along with the clinical triad of dyspnea, distended neck veins (reflecting elevated JVP), and muffled heart sounds, these findings are characteristic of constrictive pericarditis.

Constrictive Pericarditis:

  • Constrictive pericarditis is characterised by the progressive thickening, fibrosis, and calcification of the pericardium, restricting heart filling.
  • Calcification can extend into the myocardium, impairing myocardial contraction.
  • Restricted ventricular filling leads to elevated atrial pressures, causing:
    • Atrial hypertrophy
    • Atrial dilation
    • Atrial fibrillation (common).
  • Primarily manifests as systemic venous congestion (lung congestion is rare).
  • Shows"Egg in cup appearance" on Xray

Examination Findings:

Explanation of other options:

Acute pericarditis (Option A): The most common symptom of acute pericarditis is pleuritic chest pain. It worsens on lying supine and improves on sitting up or leaning forward. While causes like TB, uremia, post-irradiation, and neoplasia may be painless, the CXR is usually normal in uncomplicated pericarditis, showing cardiomegaly only if effusion is present.

Bronchial asthma (Option B): Bronchial asthma in chest xray shows pulmonary hyperinflation with bronchial wall thickening.

Atrial myxoma (Option D): Typically presents with cardiomegaly, left atrial enlargement, and vascular redistribution.

question_text: While reviewing medications for an elderly male with COPD, hypertension, and diabetes, what key factors should the physician take into account?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The Beers criteria is a guideline developed to optimize medication use in older adults.
  • It provides detailed guidance for recognizing potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs) for older individuals, taking into account age-related physiological changes and possible drug-disease interactions. The framework includes:
  • Explicit Criteria: Specifies drugs that should generally be avoided in the elderly.
  • PIMs and Drug Classes:Highlights medications that carry greater risks in older populations.
  • Rationale: Outlines reasons why certain drugs are considered inappropriate.
  • Considerations: Reflects changes in how aging affects drug absorption, metabolism, and response.
  • Regular Revisions: Updates regularly based on new research and evolving clinical practices.

Explanations of other options:

Duke's criteria (Option A): The diagnostic framework for infective endocarditis consists of major criteria (such as positive blood cultures and echocardiographic findings) and minor criteria (including fever, vascular manifestations, and predisposing factors). A definite diagnosis of IE is established when a patient meets either two major criteria, one major plus three minor criteria, or five minor criteria.

Light criteria (Option B): These criteria are used to distinguish between transudative and exudative pleural effusions based on certain parameters: a protein ratio above 0.5, an LDH ratio over 0.6, and pleural fluid LDH greater than two-thirds of the upper normal serum LDH level. If any two of these are fulfilled, the effusion is classified as exudative. They are mainly applied in assessing respiratory and pleural disorders.

Jones criteria (Option D): For the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever, the criteria include major features (carditis, arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules) and minor features (fever, raised ESR/CRP, joint pain, and prolonged PR interval). A confirmed diagnosis requires either two major criteria or one major plus two minor criteria, along with evidence of a preceding streptococcal infection.

Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5325682/

question_text: A 40-year-old woman presents with chest pain and shortness of breath. She reported a viral illness one week prior. Her chest X-ray is given below. What is not true about this condition?
option_d: ECHO showing diastolic collapse of RA and RV walls during inspiration
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's presentation of chest pain, dyspnea, and a water-bottle configuration of the cardiac shadow on X-ray following a viral infection strongly suggests pericardial effusion, which may progress to cardiac tamponade.

In this setting, heart sounds are muffled, not loud, due to the insulating layer of fluid around the heart. Therefore, a loud S1 is not characteristic of pericardial effusion.

question_text: A 42-year-old woman presents with numbness and weakness of her upper and lower limbs. She developed asthma at the age of 30, which is poorly controlled with medications. On examination she looks unwell. She has palpable purpura over her face and over her elbows and knees. On neurological examination she has a right sided wrist drop and there is weakness of dorsiflexion of her right foot. Sensation is also impaired over the dorsum of her right foot. Investigations:CXR is normal. Hb 10.9 g/dLMCV 90 fl WBC 23 x 10^9 /l Eosinophils 12% ANCA negative. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The combination of mononeuritis multiplex, asthma, eosinophilia points to the diagnosis of Churg Strauss Vasculitis.

The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) has proposed 6 criteria for diagnosis of Churg Strauss syndrome. The presence of 4 or more criteria yields a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 99.7%.

These criteria are

  1. Asthma (wheezing, expiratory rhonchi)
  2. Eosinophilia of more than 10% in peripheral blood
  3. Paranasal sinusitis
  4. Pulmonary infiltrates (may be transient)
  5. Histological proof of vasculitis with extravascular eosinophils
  6. Mononeuritis multiplex or polyneuropathy

Vasculitic rash on the skin of a patient with Churg Strauss syndrome

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:363 Pg:2809

question_text:
A 50-year-old woman, is admitted with malaise and fever. Four weeks previously she had suffered a chest infection for which she was given a course of oral amoxycillin. She felt better initially, but is now getting worse, complaining of intermittent fevers. Her chest radiograph shows a left sided pleural effusion.

question_text: What is The Most common infectious complication of varicella?
option_a: Secondary bacterial superinfection of the skin
explanation:
The most common infectious complication of varicella is secondary bacterial superinfection of the skin, which is usually caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus, including strains that are methicillin-resistant

question_text: In Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL), What are the dominant cells?
explanation:
In Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL), Lymphocytes are the dominant cells; next most common are histiocytes and plasma cells. In about half of cases, epithelioid cells--scattered individually or forming compact granulomas are seen

question_text: Patient is scheduled for an elective splenectomy. At least how long before the operation should pneumovax be given?
explanation:
All patients undergoing an elective splenectomy should be immunised with polyvalent pneumococcal vaccine (Pneumovax), which currently gives variable protection against 23 strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae.

Where possible, it should be given at least 2 weeks and preferably at least 4 weeks prior to splenectomy to allow immunoglobulin G (gG) antibody production.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 146, Pg: 1177

question_text: A 76-year-old man with a long history of COPD was admitted with pneumonia. Prior to admission he had become increasingly confused. On examination he was drowsy, had a BP of 142/75 mmHg and was clinically euvolemic. Chest auscultation was consistent with pneumonia. Blood biochemistry investigations revealed Na 121 mmol/l, K 3.9 mmol/l, urea 14 mg/dl, creatinine 0.70 mg/dl and glucose 75 mg/dl. Plasma osmolarity was 261 mOsmol/kg, and thyroid function testing was normal. Urine testing revealed an osmolality of 560 mOsmol/kg and a sodium concentration of 55 mmol/l.What was the most likely cause of his hyponatremia?
explanation:
• SIADH is not an uncommon consequence of pneumonia, particularly in patients of this age group. Small-cell bronchial carcinoma is another cause of SIADH.
  • Diagnostic criteria for SIADH
    • Low serum Na
    • Low serum osmolality (<275 mOsm/kg)
    • urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg
    • High urine Na > 30 mEq/L
    • Euvolumia
    • Normal renal, adrenal and thyroid function

Hyponatremia with low urine osmolality (<100 mOsm/kg) is suggestive of primary polydipsia

  • The normal potassium level here makes Addison's disease unlikely. Additionally, these patients have hypotension and episodes of hypoglycemia.
  • A number of drugs can cause SIADH, including chlorpropamide, phenothiazines and carbamazepine.
  • Both fluid restriction and demeclocycline precipitate renal diabetes insipidus, which may be of assistance in the treatment of SIADH.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2924

question_text: What is the common cause of SIADH?
option_b: Small cell carcinoma of the lung
explanation:
Common causes of SIADH include pulmonary disease (e.g., pneumonia, tuberculosis, pleural effusion) and central nervous system (CNS) diseases (e.g., tumor, subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis). SIAD also occurs with malignancies, most commonly with small-cell lung carcinoma (75% of malignancy-associated SIAD); ~10% of patients with this tumor will have a plasma Na+ concentration of < 130 mM at presentation. SIAD is also a frequent complication of certain drugs, most commonly the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). Other drugs can potentiate the renal effect of AVP, without exerting direct effects on circulating AVP levels.

Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 343

question_text: Complications of Viral hepatitis does not include:
explanation:
Rare complications of viral hepatitis include pancreatitis,myocarditis, atypical pneumonia, aplastic anemia, transversemyelitis, and peripheral neuropathy. In children, hepatitis B may present rarely with anicteric hepatitis, a nonpruritic papular rash of the face, buttocks, and limbs, and lymphadenopathy (papular acrodermatitis of childhood or Gianotti-Crosti syndrome)

Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 339 pg. 2565

question_text: A 30 year old lady is referred for investigation of abnormal liver function tests. She has been taking several drugs to treat tuberculosis for a long period of time.Her albumin is 3.0 g/dl, bilirubin 5 mg/dl, ALP is 250 U/l and ALT is 300 U/l.She has a liver biopsy which shows histological evidence of liver necrosis eroding the portal zone and extending into the liver lobule. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Periportal necrosis, portal inflammation, bridging necrosis and interface hepatitis are features of active liver inflammation.

Inflammatory conditions (e.g Wilson's disease) and drugs such as methyldopa and isoniazid can precipitate chronic active hepatitis.

Autoimmune hepatitis is associated with antinuclear antibodies (70%), anti-smooth muscle (30%) and liver specific antibodies (ASGP-R asialoglycoprotein receptor; LKM liver kidney microsomal antibodies).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 341, Pg: 2592

question_text: A 36-year-old HIV-positive man, evaluated for weight loss and weakness has been found to have disseminated tuberculosis. On examination, he is hypotensive and has hyperpigmentation of the mucosa, elbows and skin creases. Further investigations confirm a diagnosis of Addison's disease. Which of the following is likely in this condition?
explanation:
• In adrenal destruction, serum Na, Cl and HCO3 levels are reduced, and serum potassium is elevated. The hyponatraemia is due to both loss of sodium in the urine (due to aldosterone and cortisol deficiency) and to movement into the intracellular compartment.
  • Hyperkalemia is due to a combination of aldosterone deficiency, impaired glomerular filtration (due to hypotension) and acidosis. Mild to moderate hypercalcemia occurs in 10-20% patients, the cause of which is uncertain.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2971

question_text: Which criterion helps differentiate exudative from transudative pleural effusion?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • High protein content in pleural fluid is a key criterion in Light's Criteriafor distinguishing exudative from transudative pleural effusions.
  • An exudative pleural effusion occurs due to inflammation or infections such as bacterial pneumonia, malignancy, or viral infection, while a transudative pleural effusion results from an imbalance between hydrostatic and osmotic pressures.

Lights Criteria

  • Helps to differentiate transudative from exudative pleural effusions based on LDH and protein levels in pleural fluid.
  • Exudative pleural effusions meet at least one of the following criteria, whereas transudative pleural effusions meet none:
    • Pleural fluid protein/serum protein > 0.5
    • Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH > 0.6
    • Pleural fluid LDH exceeds two-thirds of the normal upper limit for serum.
  • ~25% of transudates may be misidentified as exudates.
  • If exudative criteria are met but a transudative condition is suspected, measure protein difference; if >31 g/L (3.1 g/dL), likely transudative.
  • A transudative pleural effusion occurs when systemic factors that influence the formation and absorption of pleural fluid are altered.
  • The leading causes of transudative pleural effusions in the United States are left ventricular failure and cirrhosis.
  • An exudative pleural effusion occurs when local factors that influence the formation and absorption of pleural fluid are altered.
  • The leading causes of exudative pleural effusions are bacterial pneumonia, malignancy, viral infection, and pulmonary embolism.

question_text: A patient with Parkinson's disease had aspiration pneumonitis. How will you manage this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

PEG gastrostomy tube insertion is the best appropriate step for long-term prevention of recurrent aspiration pneumonia.

Chronic neurological illnesses such as Parkinson's disease or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis often cause oropharyngeal dysphagia, creating a high risk of recurrent aspiration.

  • Nasogastric feeding can provide temporary nutrition but does not prevent aspiration of saliva or refluxed gastric contents.
  • For long-term support, a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) is frequently chosen to deliver food directly into the stomach and reduce episodes of aspiration pneumonia.

A PEG tube offers several advantages: it avoids nasal irritation, is less prone to accidental displacement, and allows more reliable feeding.

  • After placement, a fibrous tract typically matures in about 10 days.
  • If the tube is removed or dislodged before this tract is established, gastric contents can leak into the peritoneal cavity, posing a significant risk of peritonitis.

Explanation for other Options:

High frequency chest oscillation (Option A): This airway-clearance technique is used in conditions with thick secretions (e.g., cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis).

It does not address the root cause of aspiration in Parkinson's disease and will not prevent further aspiration episodes.

Macrolides (Option B): Antibiotics such as azithromycin are indicated for bacterial pneumonia, not for chemical aspiration pneumonitis, which is an inflammatory injury from gastric/oral contents.They do not prevent future aspiration.

N-acetylcysteine (Option C): Functions as a mucolytic or an antidote for acetaminophen toxicity. It has no established role in treating or preventing aspiration pneumonitis.

question_text: A young man came to the medical OPD with complaints of early morning backache and stiffness, which improves on exercise, and persistent red eyes. On examination, lung expansion was less than 3 cm. X-ray is shown in the image given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The classic triad of inflammatory back pain, reduced chest expansion, and uveitis strongly suggests ankylosing spondylitis, supported by the “bamboo spine” seen on X-ray. 

  • Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory seronegative spondyloarthropathy that primarily affects the spine and sacroiliac joints.
  • The hallmark feature is inflammatory back pain, which is worse in the morning or after periods of inactivity, and improves with exercise.
  • Reduced lung expansion (<3 cm) is due to costovertebral joint involvement.
  • The patient also has persistent red eyes, suggesting anterior uveitis, the most common extra-articular manifestation of AS.
  • Characteristic radiological features of AS seen in this case:
    • Sacroiliitis: bilateral and symmetrical involvement with erosion, sclerosis, and eventual fusion.
    • Syndesmophyte formation leads to bamboo spine appearance on X-ray.
    • Dagger sign: a radiodense line due to ossification of interspinous and supraspinous ligaments.
  • Other clinical features include:
    • Enthesitis (especially at Achilles tendon, plantar fascia)
    • Peripheral large joint arthritis (hip, shoulder)
    • Postural changes: forward stooping due to thoracic kyphosis
    • Fatigue, anemia of chronic disease, and rarely cardiac/aortic involvement
  • Investigations:
    • HLA-B27 positive in >90% of patients
    • Elevated ESR, CRP
    • MRI is more sensitive than X-ray in early disease

Explanation of other options:

Paget's Disease (Option B): Characterized by abnormal bone remodeling with cortical thickening and lytic-sclerotic lesions, not vertebral fusion or syndesmophytes. Does not cause morning stiffness or uveitis.

Healed Tuberculosis (Option C): Pott's spine may cause vertebral collapse or gibbus deformity, but not the bamboo spine appearance. Uveitis and reduced lung expansion are uncommon.

Osteopetrosis (Option D): A genetic disorder with diffuse bone sclerosis due to defective osteoclast function. X-rays show dense bones, but there is no inflammatory back pain, uveitis, or vertebral fusion.

question_text: The following statement about keloid is true ?

Features- It continues to get worse even after 1 year and up to a few years. Severe itching is present Margin is tender Vascular, red, erythematous (immature blood vessels) Extends to normal tissues, has a claw-like process. Hence the name. question_text:
A 28-year-old woman is referred with intermittent diarrhoea present for a couple of years. She states that her weight has been steady but describes watery motions up to six stools per day and has also noted abdominal discomfort with bloating. She has not been aware of any blood in the motions or melaena. She describes no other medical history and denies taking any medication.
Investigations show:
Complete blood count : Normal
Urea and electrolytes : Normal
Albumin 3.9 g/dL(3.7-4.9)
Corrected Calcium 8.6 mg/dl
Alkaline phosphatase 94 U/L(45-105)
C-reactive protein 6 mg/L (<10)
Prothrombin time 12 s(11.5-15.5)
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The normal albumin and C-reactive protein levels count against a diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's or ulcerative colitis) or an infectious pathology such as intestinal tuberculosis.

Whilst small bowel bacterial overgrowth does not typically produce a raised C-reactive protein level it is very unusual in patients without risk factors for the condition (previous bowel surgery, Crohn's disease, motility disorders such as scleroderma).

This leaves laxative abuse as the most likely diagnosis. Laxative abuse, where not a function of chronic constipation, is usually closely linked to eating disorders (Bulimia and Anorexia) and as such is typically over-represented in young, female patients.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 46 Pg: 303

question_text: Correct about treatment of newly diagnosed tuberculosis and HIV patients when CD count is greater than 50 cells/μL?
option_b: ATT first then ART after 2 weeks
option_c: ART first then ATT after 2 weeks
explanation: Initiation of ART and/or anti-TB therapy may be associated with clinical deterioration due to immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) reactions. These are most common in patients initiating both treatments at the same time, may occur as early as 1 week after initiation of ART therapy, and are seen more frequently in patients with advanced HIV disease. For these reasons it is recommended that initiation of ART be delayed in antiretroviral-naive patients with CD4 counts >50 cells/μL until 2-4 weeks following the initiation of treatment for TB. For patients with lower CD4 counts the benefits of more immediate ART outweigh the risks of IRIS, and ART should be started as soon as possible in those patients.

question_text: A patient with AIDS has developed miliary tuberculosis with apical calcifications. What is the appropriate management?
option_a: Start antiretroviral therapy (ART) 2 weeks after initiating anti-tubercular therapy (ATT)
option_c: Start ART after completing the course of ATT
option_d: Start ART first, then initiate ATT
explanation:
Explanation:

In patients with HIV/AIDS and newly diagnosed tuberculosis, anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) should be started first. ART is then initiated 2 weeks later in those with low CD4 counts or severe disease (such as miliary tuberculosis). This delay helps reduce the risk of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), a potentially life-threatening complication, while ensuring both infections are appropriately managed.

  • If a person is positive for both HIV and TB, Treatment for TB should be started first.
  • In a person positive with both HIV and TB, signs and symptoms of TB are less prominent due to decreased cellular immunity (due to decreased CD4 count )
  • If ART is given 1st to this person, the cellular immunity will be increased, and there will be a flare-up of signs and symptoms of TB. This is known as Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome ( IRIS).
  • Hence, ATT is given first to prevent this.
  • ATT is given for a minimum of 2 weeks, followed by ART.
  • With rifampicin-containing regimen :
    • An additional dose of DTG 50mg should be taken after 12 hours on the same day, as rifampicin decreases the bioavailability of dolutegravir ( DTG)

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Start ATT and ART simultaneously (Option B): Starting both at once increases the risk of IRIS and can make management of drug interactions and side effects challenging.

Start ART after completing the course of ATT (Option C): Delaying ART until ATT is completed may result in immunological decline and increased mortality in people with low CD4 counts.

Start ART first, then initiate ATT (Option D): ATT should always be started first to control active tuberculosis and reduce the risk of worsening disease upon immune recovery.

question_text:
A 20 year old Armenian man presents with pain and swelling of the left knee. He also gives a history of recurrent episodes of fever, pleuritic pains in the chest,and generalised rash. These episodes typically last for 2-3 days. Examination reveals splenomegaly, swollen knees and ankles.Urine dipstick reveals 2+ proteinuria.
What is the likely diagnosis ?
explanation:
A young male presenting with history of recurrent fevers, arthritis and serositis especially in a person belonging to the Armenian descent points to the possibility of an autoinflammatory syndrome. Among the given options, Familial Mediterranean fever is the autoinflammatory syndrome seen in Armenians.

Autoinflammatory syndromes are characterized by recurrent fevers, serosal, synovial and cutaneous inflammation and the eventual development of AA amyloidosis. They are called so because of the relative infrequency of autoantibodies or antigen specific T cells.

The diseases included in this disease are:

  1. Familial Mediterranean Fever.
  2. TNF receptor associated periodic syndrome
  3. Hyperimmunoglobulinemia D with periodic fever syndrome
  4. NLRP 3 associated autoinflammatory disease.

FMF occurs predominantly in Armenians, Arabs and Non Ashkenazi Jews.

Hyperimmunoglobulin D with periodic fever is seen predominantly in Dutch and northern European.

The rest of the autoinflammatory syndromes don't show any ethnic propensity.

Familial Mediterranean fever:

AR mainly, can be AD too.

Fever lasting for 24-72 hours.

Associated with abdominal pain in 90% cases.

Unilateral pleurisy.

Monoarticular arthritis, non erosive, without warmth or erythema.

Skin rash resembling erysipelas.

Exercise induced myalgia.

Mutations in PYRIN gene, which is involved in host defense, where the threshold of activation of pyrin is reduced.

Treatment is Cochicine or anti IL1β( Canakinumab)

Rash seen in familial mediterranean fever

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21stedition Ch:369 Pg:2841-2842

question_text: Complication of joint TB
explanation: Answer- A. Fibrous ankylosis The outcome of tubercular arthritis is fibrous ankylosis, except in spine. Spine is the only site where tuberculosis heals with bony ankylosis.

question_text: A 30-year-old man with a history of tuberculosis now complains of abdominal distension and pedal edema. On examination, his neck veins are prominent. His chest x-ray is given below. Which of the following findings will be likely seen in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The chest X-ray shows an increased cardiothoracic ratio, and clinically the patient presents with distended neck veins (elevated JVP), abdominal distension, and pedal edema, consistent with cardiac tamponade.
  • Given the patient's history of tuberculosis, the most likely underlying cause is tuberculous pericarditis leading to tamponade.
  • In cardiac tamponade, there is typically a significant drop in systolic blood pressure during inspiration (pulsus paradoxus), which in this case is represented by the fall in SBP from 80mmHg to 60mmHg (>10mmHg drop).

Cardiac tamponade

  • A condition where the cardiac chambers are compressed by a tense pericardial effusion, limiting cardiac inflow.
  • Fluid accumulation of as little as 200 ml to upwards of 2L may lead to cardiac tamponade development.

Clinical features

  • Beck's triad
    • Jugular Venous Distension: Due to increased central venous pressure. Prominent x descent and an absent y descent.
    • Hypotension: Resulting from impaired cardiac output.
    • Muffled Heart Sounds: Caused by fluid accumulation in the pericardial space, dampening heart sounds.
  • Pulsus Paradoxus: A hallmark finding. A drop in systolic BP during inspiration, greater than 10 mm Hg. Causes of Pulsus paradoxus:
    • Lung Conditions: Acute asthma, COPD, tension pneumothorax, pleural effusion, pulmonary embolism.
    • Heart Conditions: Cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis.

Explanation of other options:

Pulsus bisferiens (Option A): Pulsus bisferiens is a double-peaked pulse typically seen in aortic regurgitation and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Kussmaul breathing (Option B): Kussmaul breathing refers to deep and laboured breathing seen in metabolic acidosis, particularly diabetic ketoacidosis; not a characteristic finding in cardiac tamponade.

Fine crepitations (Option D): Fine crepitations are typically heard in pulmonary edema or pneumonia.

question_text: A 42-year-old male presents with a six hour history of profuse vomiting and over the last two hours had developed left-sided chest pain and dyspnoea. On examination he had a pulse of 110 beats per minute regular and a blood pressure of 168/90 mmHg. On palpation, he had crepitus over the left supraclavicular region and neck, reduced heart sounds and left basal sided crackles, plus some dullness to percussion over the right base of the chest. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This man has a history of vomiting which then progressed to chest pain.

The most relevant finding on examination is the crepitus over the chest, indicating surgical emphysema. The most probable cause is therefore spontaneous rupture of the oesophagus, secondary to forceful vomiting, called the Boerhaave's Syndrome.

Mackler's triad (vomiting, chest pain and surgical emphysema) is classical but absent in almost half the cases. The chest x ray (CXR) may reveal the surgical emphysema and a gastrografin swallow is diagnostic.

A CT scan should be performed if a gastrografin swallow is not possible or negative.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2433

question_text: A 46-year-old male chronic alcoholic visits the outpatient department with a two-day history of fever, headache, shortness of breath, chest pain, and a productive cough producing red currant jelly sputum. Examination reveals bronchial breath sounds on the right side, increased vocal fremitus, heightened vocal resonance, and dullness on percussion. Given the plain chest radiograph shown below, what is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture of a chronic alcoholic with fever, productive cough producing red currant jelly sputum, and the described examination findings strongly suggest pneumonia caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae.

In patients with alcohol use disorder, the most common organisms linked to lung abscesses include Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Actinomyces.

Etiology of pneumonia based on specific contexts:

  • Alcoholic patient with pneumonia: commonly caused by Pneumococcus pneumoniae.
  • Alcoholic patient with red currant jelly sputum: typically Klebsiella pneumoniae (Friedlander pneumonia).
  • COPD patients and smokers: often infected with Haemophilus influenzae (Option D).
  • Structural lung diseases such as cystic fibrosis with thick mucus plugs: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Option C) or Burkholderia cepacia.
  • Exposure to birds: Chlamydia psittaci.
  • Exposure to bats: Histoplasmosis.
  • Exposure to rabbits: Francisella tularensis (Tularemia).
  • Exposure to goats or sheep: Coxiella burnetii, causing Q fever.
  • Exposure to hotels or cruises: Legionella pneumophila.

Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option A) is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia, typically presenting with a sudden onset and rust-colored sputum, but it is less likely in this case based on the symptoms and sputum description.

Reference:

  1. The Epidemiology of Alcohol Abuse and Pneumonia - PMC
  2. Klebsiella Pneumonia - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
  3. Haemophilus influenzae in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
  4. Microbial Epidemiology of the Cystic Fibrosis Airways: Past, Present, and Future
  5. Psittacosis Pneumonia - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf.
  6. Living With Bats
  7. Tularemia - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
  8. Q fever pneumonia - PubMed
  9. Legionnaire's Disease & Pontiac Fever | CDC Yellow Book 2024

question_text: Most common symptom of genitourinary TB
explanation: Answer- B. Increased frequency The clinical manifestations are variable. The onset of clinically evident genitourinary tuberculosis is usually insidious. The most common symptoms are :- Dysuria, increased frequency of urination and gross hematuria

question_text: Following type of pulmonary TB is most likely to be associated with AFB sputum positivity:
explanation:
Cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis is more likely to be associated with Acid-Fast Bacilli (AFB) sputum positivity. In cavitary TB, cavities or cavitations (hollow spaces or gaps) form within the lung tissue as a result of the disease process. These cavities often contain a high concentration of mycobacteria, making it more likely for AFB to be present in the sputum of affected individuals. Sputum from cavitary TB lesions is more infectious and has a higher likelihood of yielding positive AFB smear results compared to other forms of pulmonary TB.

  • Cavities represent necrosis of tissue resulting in communication of the infected material with the airways. The bacteria are thus discharged in the bronchial tree from where they can be coughed out with sputum.
  • The infected material can cause tubercular bronchopneumonia in the host by spreading to other parts of lungs or gastro-intestinal tuberculosis by means of swallowed secretions. The risk of spreading to other individuals is very high with cavitary tuberculosis.

Other options

  • Primary complex: This is usually associated with the initial infection and may not always yield AFB-positive sputum.
  • Fibro nodular: While fibro nodular lesions can be seen in tuberculosis, they are not typically associated with the highest likelihood of AFB sputum positivity.
  • Pleural effusion: Tuberculous pleural effusion can occur, but it involves fluid in the pleural space rather than cavities within lung tissue. The presence of AFB in pleural effusion is less common compared to cavitary TB.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch:178 Pg:1362-1364

question_text: Nucleic acid amplification (NAA) tests for the diagnosis of TB
option_a: Are not approved by the FDA.
option_b: Require more than one month for results.
option_c: May not be used with smear-positive specimens.
option_d: Are able to differentiate between different species of M. tuberculosis.
explanation:
• The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved three commercially available nucleic acid amplification (NAA) tests for use in confirming tuberculosisin procured specimens. The first is the Amplicor Test, which is based on the polymerase chain reaction. It amplifies a specific portion of the RNA from the TB organisms and measures the results with a photometer. The findings of this test are usually available within six to seven hours. The FDA has approved the Amplicor Test only for smear-positive specimens.
  • The second approved probe is the amplified tuberculosisdirect (Amplified MTD) test, which uses transcription-mediated amplification in order to identify and magnify the RNA target. Results are generally available within three to four hours. This test is approved for the detection of tuberculosis in both smear-positive and smear-negative cultures.
  • The third NAA test is the Xpert MTB/RIF Assay, which is able to detect the presence of tuberculosisorganisms as well as resistance to rifampicin. This automated, cartridge-based system requires a sputum sample and results are available within two hours. Non-FDA approved NAA tests (often called "in-house" tests) may be used to diagnose TB and to test for drug-resistant TB.
  • These tests are also able to differentiate the DNA of different species of tuberculosis, also called DNA fingerprinting or genotyping. Because most strains of bacteria share patterns, it has been difficult to follow the person-to-person transmission of certain strains. Using genotyping, researchers have shown that each strain has a distinct DNA fingerprint and that all samples sharing the same DNA fingerprint were isolated from people who live together. This will help track the path of transmission and aid public health researchers to pinpoint patterns of infection, which in turn helps to plan prevention programs that target the areas of heightened infection rates.
  • Truenat MTB and MTC Plus are two newly introduced rapid molecular tests with a sensitivity of 83% and 89%, respectively, if compared to bacteriological culture. They were developed in India.
  • Loop Mediated Isothermal Amplification, is another method using the DNA amplification and can be substituted for microscopy

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 178, Pg: 1369

question_text: Which of the following is not common in primary pulmonary tuberculosis?
explanation:
• Because most inspired air is distributed to the middle and lower lung zones, these areas are most commonly involved in primary TB.

  • Pleural reaction overlying a subpleural focus is also common.
  • The Ghon focus, with or without overlying pleural reaction, thickening, and regional lymphadenopathy, is referred to as the Ghon complex.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 172 Pg: 1362

question_text: A 70-year-old smoker presents with high fever, cough, confusion, and diarrhea. Chest X-ray demonstrates bilateral lower lung infiltrates. Sputum Gram stain shows no organisms. Lab findings include sodium 126 mEq/L, AST 62, ALT 56, random blood sugar 112 mg/dL, bilirubin 0.8 mg%, and a positive HIV test. Which organism is the likely cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture is consistent with Legionnaires' disease, a severe type of pneumonia, characterized by high fever, cough, confusion, hyponatremia, and raised liver enzyme levels.

  • Legionella is an obligate aerobe that does not stain well with Gram stain, which accounts for the negative result despite active infection.
  • The patient's advanced age and immunocompromised state (HIV positivity) further heighten the susceptibility to Legionella infection.

Explanations of other options:

Streptococcus (Option A): Streptococcus pneumoniae is a frequent cause of community-acquired pneumonia and usually presents with a productive cough producing rust-colored sputum. Here, the sputum Gram stain was negative, making pneumococcal infection less probable. Moreover, the presence of extrapulmonary features is not characteristic of pneumococcal pneumonia.

Pneumocystis jiroveci (Option C): Although the patient is HIV positive, the clinical features and chest X-ray showing bilateral infiltrates are not typical of Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia (PJP). PJP usually develops more slowly with dry cough and progressive shortness of breath, without the hyponatremia and elevated liver enzymes noted in this case. Radiologically, PJP often shows pneumatoceles, thin-walled cysts, or reticular opacities with septal thickening.

Klebsiella (Option D): Klebsiella pneumonia usually occurs in patients with alcoholism or COPD. Although this patient has a smoking history, the presence of confusion and diarrhea does not fit the typical presentation of Klebsiella infection. Furthermore, Klebsiella organisms are generally detectable on Gram stain, unlike in this case.

Key takeaway:

Pneumonia - Etiology and Major Pathogens

Common Causative Agents:

  • Bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa
    • Typical bacteria: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA).
    • Atypical bacteria: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Legionella species.
    • Viruses: Influenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and coronaviruses (e.g., SARS-CoV-2).

question_text: In the stage of Grey hepatization -
explanation: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Accumulation of fibrin Pathological changes of bacterial pneumonia A.Lobar pneumonia Large confluent area of the lung or entire lobes are consolidated. The lower lobes are affected most commonly. There are four stages of the inflammatory response (Laennec's stages) ? Stage of congestion (initial phase) The affected lobe is enlarged, heavy, dark red and congested. Cut surface exudes blood-stained frothy fluid. There is dilatation and congestion of alveolar capillaries. There are few neutrophils and numerous bacteria in the alveolar fluid. Stage of red hepatization (early consolidation) The term hepatization refers to liver-like consistency of the affected lobe on cut section. o The affected lobe is red and firm. The edema fluid of preceding stage is replaced by strands of fibrin. There is marked cellular exudate of neutrophils with extravasation of red cells. Stage of gray hepatization (late consolidation) The affected lobe is grayish brown, firm and dry. The fibrin strand are dense and more numerous. There is progressive disintigration of red cells and neutrophils. The macrophages begin to appear in the exudate. The organisms are less numerous and appear as degenerated forms. Resolution The previously solid and fibrinous constituent is liquefied by enzymatic action. Granular and fragmented strands of fibrin in the alveolar spaces are seen due to progressive enzymatic digestion. There is progressive removal of fluid content as well as cellular exudate from the air spaces, resulting in restoration of normal lung parenchyma with areation. B.Bronchopneumonia Patchy areas of red or grey consolidation, more often multilobar and frequently bilateral and basal (lower zones) because of tendency of secretions to gravitate into lower lobes. There is suppurative exudate, consisting chiefly neutrophils, filling bronchi, bronchioles and adjacent alveolar spaces. Alveolar septa thicken due to congested capillaries and leucocytic infiltration.

question_text: Most common complication of pneumococcal pneumonia?
explanation:
• Empyema is the most common focal complication of pneumococcal pneumonia, occurring in <5% of cases.
  • When fluid in the pleural space is accompanied by fever and leukocytosis (even low-grade) after 4-5 days of appropriate antibiotic treatment for pneumococcal pneumonia, empyema should be considered.
  • Parapneumonic effusions are more common than empyema, representing a self- limited inflammatory response to pneumonia.
  • Pleural fluid with frank pus, bacteria (detected by microscopic examination), or a pH of 7.1 indicates empyema and demands aggressive and complete drainage, usually through chest tube insertion

Complications of pneumonia:

  • Respiratory failure
  • Shock and multiorgan failure
  • Exacerbation of comorbid illnesses
  • Metastatic infection
  • Lung abscess
  • Complicated pleural effusion.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 146 Pg: 1175

question_text: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) tuberculosis is characterized by resistance to which of the following anti-tubercular drugs?
explanation:
Explanation:

MDR-TB is specifically defined as resistance to both isoniazid and rifampicin, the two most powerful first-line anti-tubercular medications. This form of TB poses major therapeutic challenges as these drugs form the backbone of standard treatment regimens.

  • Drug-Sensitive Tuberculosis (DSTB): Refers to tuberculosis that responds to the main first-line drugs such as isoniazid and rifampicin.
  • Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis (DR-TB): Defined as TB caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains resistant to at least one first-line anti-TB drug.
  • Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis (MDR-TB): TB caused by strains resistant to both isoniazid and rifampicin.
  • Extensively Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis (XDR-TB): A severe subset of MDR-TB where the bacilli are resistant to isoniazid, rifampicin, any fluoroquinolone, and at least one second-line injectable drug (such as amikacin, kanamycin, or capreomycin).

Explanation of Other Options:

Immediately (Option A): Incorrect, as MDR-TB does not require resistance to fluoroquinolones. This definition corresponds to XDR-TB.

Fluoroquinolones (Option B): Wrong, since resistance to only fluoroquinolones defines neither MDR-TB nor XDR-TB by itself.

Isoniazid, rifampicin, and kanamycin (Option D): Incorrect, as this again falls under the definition of XDR-TB rather than MDR-TB.

References:

  1. NCBI Bookshelf - Tuberculosis MDR Overview
  2. PMC - Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis Review

question_text: A 40-year-old man with pneumonia is being examined. Which one of the following positive auscultatory signs is diagnostic of bronchial breathing?
explanation:
• Whispering pectoriloquy is a diagnostic sign for bronchial breathing.
  • Refers to an increased loudness of whispering on auscultation. In areas of consolidation of the lungs, these whispered spoken sounds by the patient will be heard clearly through the stethoscope.
  • This increase in sound occurs because sound travels through solid or liquid medium versus gaseous (air in the lung) media. It is usually performed in cases of consolidation or mass.

Reference: “Bates Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking” 11th edition, 314-5

question_text: Hospital acquired pneumonia can be labelled if it develops after __ hours after hospital admission.
explanation:
• Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) occurs more than 48 hours after admission to the hospital or other health care facility and excludes any infection present at the time of admission.
  • If it develops within 48 hours it is considered as community acquired pneumonia (CAP)
  • Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) develops more than 48 hours following endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation.
  • It presents as At least two of the following: fever, leucocytosis, purulent sputum OR a new or progressive parenchymal opacities on chest radiograph.

Reference: CMDT 2020 page number 285

question_text: A 30-year-old man came with complaints of fever and cough for 3 days. On examination, creatinine is 1.5 and BUN is 45. Chest-x ray shows infiltrates in the right lung and patchy infiltrates in the left lung. A nasopharyngeal swab shows only  Rhinovirus. The patient is shifted to the ICU. Which antibiotics are suitable for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In this case, the patient presents with fever, cough, and chest X-ray findings of patchy infiltrates, which most likely indicate pneumonia. Since the condition qualifies as severe pneumonia requiring ICU admission, the preferred treatment is a combination of a beta-lactam and a macrolide, such as ceftriaxone with azithromycin.
  • The treatment protocol in an inpatient with pneumonia would be chosen based on the severity of the disease.
  • CURB-65 Score: Used to stratify patients with the following factors:
  • Hospitalisation Criteria:
    • CURB-65 score 0: Outpatient treatment
    • Score 1 or 2: Indicates hospitalization
    • Score ≥3: Indicates ICU admission and more intensive therapy.
  • In non-severe case a B-lactam with a macrolide or a respiratory fluoroquinolone is used and in a severe pneumonia case a B-lactam with a macrolide (ceftrioxone+azithromycin) or a B-lactam+ respiratory fluoroquinolone is used.

Explanation of other options:

  • Amoxicillin with clavulinic acid (Option A): Inadequate for this patient due to the severity of his illness and the risk of resistant organisms. Monotherapy with amoxicillin does not provide sufficient coverage for his condition, especially considering the possibility of Pseudomonas and MRSA.
  • Azithromycin (Option B): Not appropriate for this patient due to the severity of his condition, indicating he requires more intensive treatment. Azithromycin is preferred for outpatient therapy, suitable for lower-risk patients without significant comorbidities.
  • Piptaz + ciprofloxacin (Option D): Piptaz (piperacillin/tazobactam) is a beta-lactam antibiotic combination, while ciprofloxacin belongs to the fluoroquinolone class. However, in this patient's case, these options alone are not appropriate, as the management of severe pneumonia requires the addition of a macrolide along with either a fluoroquinolone or a beta-lactam.

question_text: Which of the following statements is NOT true of primary pulmonary tuberculosis:
option_b: Miliary spread is commoner in a younger age group
option_c: pleural effusion occurs before tuberculin skin testing is positive
option_d: A positive tuberculin skin test develops within two weeks of infection
explanation:
• Primary TB is usually asymptomatic, with miliary TB most likely to occur in young children.
  • The Ghon focus is the area of consolidation from cellular infiltration and response to uptake of organisms by macrophages, which transform into epithelioid cells and group into granulomata.
  • Bacilli are transported via lymphatics early in the disease process to regional lymph nodes to cause marked lymphadenopathy. Positive tuberculin test occurs between 3 weeks to 3 months after primary infection. Pleural and pericardial infections occur at or shortly after primary infection.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 178, Pg: 1362

question_text: Urinary antigen is a useful test to detect which of the following organisms causing pneumonia?
explanation:
• Two commercially available tests detect pneumococcal and Legionella antigen in urine. The test for Legionella pneumophila detects only serogroup 1, but this serogroup accounts for most community-acquired cases of Legionnaires’ disease in the United States.
  • The sensitivity and specificity of the Legionella urine antigen test are as high as 70% and 99%, respectively. The pneumococcal urine antigen test is also quite sensitive and specific (70% and >90%, respectively).
  • Although false-positive results can be obtained with samples from pneumococcus-colonized children, the test is generally reliable. Both tests can detect antigen even after the initiation of appropriate antibiotic therapy


C&S: Culture & Sensitivity

PCR: Polymerase Chain Reaction

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st ed, ch:126 Pg: 1012

question_text: Peribronchial pneumonia is typically seen in chest radiographs. It is caused by-
explanation:
On physical examination, wheezes or rales are detected in ~80% of patients with M. pneumoniae pneumonia. In many patients, however, pneumonia can be diagnosed only by chest radiography. The most common radiographic pattern is that of peribronchial pneumonia with thickened bronchial markings, streaks of interstitial infiltration, and areas of subsegmental atelectasis. Segmental or lobar consolidation is not uncommon. While clinically evident pleural effusions are infrequent, lateral decubitus views reveal that up to 20% of patients have pleural effusions

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page Number-1442.

question_text: A patient has been diagnosed with chlamydia pneumonia. What is the most appropriate antibiotic therapy?
explanation:
Macrolide antibiotics (erythromycin and clarithromycin) are the treatment of choice
for chlamydia and other atypical pneumonias. The diagnosis of chlamydia pneumonia is difficult.

The organism is cultivated like a virus using tissue cultures, but few laboratories offer this test.

Serology is difficult to interpret; the usual titres for IgM or serial changes with acute and convalescent sera are arbitrary.

Like mycoplasma, this is an organism that is often suspected, infrequently proven, but easily treated empirically

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 189 Pg: 1447

question_text: Most common organism causing overwhelming infection in post-splenectomy patients is:
explanation:
Splenic individuals are at increased risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infections (OPSI).

Patients without spleen are 58 times more likely to succumb to sepsis than the general population.

Most OPSIs occur within 2 years of splenectomy. Most OPSIs are caused by encapsulated organisms such as S. pneumonia, H. influenzae & N. meningitidis. Streptococcus pneumoniae accounts for up to 40-70% of cases of OPSI.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, ch:146 Ch: 1173

question_text: Which pathogen causes Pneumonia and signifies that the patient's immune system is so compromised that death is almost certain?
explanation:
Stenotrophomonas maltophilia causes Pneumonia which is a marker for a patient whose immune system is so compromised that death is almost certain.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 164Pg: 1291

question_text: Antibiotic of choice for Legionella pneumonia is
explanation:
• Because Legionella is an intracellular pathogen, antibiotics that reach high intracellular concentrations are more likely to be effective. The macrolides (especially azithromycin) and the quinolones (especially levofloxacin or ciprofloxacin) are the antibiotics of choice and are effective as monotherapy.
  • Compared With erythromycin, the newer macrolides have superior in vitro activity, display greater intracellular activity, reach higher concentrations in respiratory secretions and lung tissue, and have fewer adverse effects.
  • Quinolones are the preferred antibiotics for transplant recipients because both macrolides and rifampin interact pharmacologically with cyclosporine and tacrolimus.

Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:159 Pg: 1256
