question_text: A patient with lung cancer reports difficulty in breathing. On auscultation over the left infrascapular region, bronchial breath sounds are heard along with dullness on percussion. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

In patients with malignancy, pleural effusion is a frequent complication. The finding of dull percussion with bronchial breathing suggests underlying consolidation due to compression from effusion. In this context, malignant pleural effusion is the most probable cause.

  • Etiologies:
    • Transudates: CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome.
    • Exudates: TB, pneumonia, malignancy, connective tissue diseases, drugs.
  • Clinical features: Dyspnea, cough, pleuritic pain. Dullness, decreased breath sounds, reduced fremitus. Egophony at fluid upper level.
  • Radiology: X-ray shows blunting of costophrenic angle, homogeneous opacity, Ellis S-shaped curve. Ultrasound detects fluid more accurately.

  • Pleural fluid analysis: Light's criteria differentiates transudates from exudates. Exudative effusions → protein-rich, high LDH.
  • Management: Diagnostic/therapeutic thoracentesis, pleurodesis for recurrent malignant effusions.

Explanation of other options:

Cardiac tamponade (Option A): Causes Beck's triad (muffled sounds, hypotension, distended veins), not pleural effusion signs.

Constrictive pericarditis (Option B): Produces right heart failure findings (ascites, hepatomegaly), no dullness or bronchial breathing.

Pulmonary embolism (Option C): Presents with acute dyspnea and chest pain, not bronchial breathing with dullness.

Key Takeaways:

  • Malignant pleural effusion is a common cause of dyspnea in lung cancer.
  • Diagnostic confirmation is by thoracentesis and pleural fluid analysis.

question_text:
A 24-year-old man was found to have iron deficiency anemia when he went to donate blood. Generally, the patient was very well. He had a good appetite, his weight was steady and he ate a normal diet. He had a normal bowel habit and had never passed any blood, mucus or diarrhea in his stools. There is no history of any overt blood loss. His general practitioner got an open access endoscopy which was normal; duodenal biopsies were unremarkable. His father had died of what he thought was secondary liver and lung cancer but he was unsure. On general physical examination he was fit and athletic. The skin and mucosal membranes were unremarkable. Vitals were normal. Heart sounds were normal and the chest was clear. His abdomen was soft and nontender with no palpable masses or organs. Rectal examination was normal. On viewing the rectal mucosa through a rigid sigmoidoscope the colonic mucosa was covered in innumerable polyps.
What specific genetic abnormality is responsible for this appearance?
option_a: Germline mutation of the STK11 gene on chromosome 19
option_b: Heterozygous mutation of the MYH gene
option_c: Loss of the APC gene on chromosome 5
option_d: Mutations in mismatch repair genes (for example, MSH2)
explanation:
The patient will need a full colonoscopy and biopsy but the information presented is highly suggestive of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), caused by the loss of the APC gene on the short arm of chromosome 5.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is an autosomal dominant inherited disorder caused by a germline mutation of the STK11 (serine threonine kinase 11) gene, usually located on the long arm of chromosome 19. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is associated with intestinal hamartomatous polyps, but is usually (90%) associated with perioral pigmentation.

Hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer (HNPCC) and MYC polyposis do not cause multiple polyps as suggested in this case. InHNPCC, affected individuals inherit a mutation in one of several genes involved in DNA mismatch repair, including MSH2, MLH1, and PMS2.

Homozygous mutations in the MYH gene have been associated with a phenotype of multiple colorectal adenomas with or without cancer.

This accounts for a proportion of FAP patients without a pathogenic APC mutation. Mutations in the p53 tumor suppressor gene are found in many different cancers. While mutations in p53 are seen in cases of colon cancer, the question asks for the specific mutation associated with polyposis coli. The main differential in this question is between FAP and PJS but the lack of perioral pigmentation favors FAP as the diagnosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 81, Pg: 638

question_text: A lung cancer patient has hyperpigmentation of palmar and sole creases. Which of the following is responsible for this presentation?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The clinical features are suggestive of ectopic Cushing's syndrome, a paraneoplastic condition frequently linked to lung cancer.
  • In this setting, tumour-derived proopiomelanocortin is cleaved into ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH), resulting in hyperpigmentation.
  • This represents one of the most common hormone-mediated paraneoplastic syndromes in small cell lung cancer (SCLC).

Paraneoplastic Syndromes Caused by Ectopic Hormone Production

Explanation of other options:

C-peptide (Option B): C-peptide is a byproduct formed during the conversion of proinsulin to insulin. It has no role in the hyperpigmentation seen in paraneoplastic syndromes associated with lung cancer.

Neuropeptide Y (Option C): Neuropeptiode C is involved in appetite regulation through hypothalamic signaling. This peptide does not contribute to the hyperpigmentation observed in paraneoplastic syndromes.

Melanin (Option D) : Melanin is the end product of melanogenesis responsible for skin pigmentation. While it is the final pigment, the question asks about the hormone responsible for triggering the hyperpigmentation, which is MSH.

Key Takeaway:

Lung tumors and their associated paraneoplastic syndromes

question_text: Which lung cancer stains positive for CD56, NCAM, synaptophysin and chromogranin?
explanation:
CD 56, NCAM, synaptophysin and Chromogranin are neuroendocrine markers and will be positive in small cell carcinoma lung.

Nap-A and TTF 1 are other immunohistochemical markers that can be used in the diagnosis of lung cancer.

Primary lung adenocarcinoma (Nap-A positive, TTF-1 positive)

Primary lung squamous cell carcinoma (Nap-A negative, TTF-1 negative)

Primary SCLC (Nap-A negative, TTF-1 positive).

Cytokeratins 7 and 20 used in combination can help narrow the differential diagnosis; nonsquamous NSCLC, SCLC, and mesothelioma may stain positive for CK7 and negative for CK20, whereas squamous cell lung cancer often will be both CK7 and CK20 negative

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 78, Pg: 596

question_text: A 50-year-old man receiving therapy for lung cancer reports breathlessness and dizziness. On examination, reduced breath sounds are detected over the left lower scapular area. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The symptoms point toward pleural effusion, a frequent complication in lung cancer, with dyspnea, dizziness, and the notable finding of decreased breath sounds over the left lower scapular area being typical indicators.

  • Pleural effusion develops when cancer cells infiltrate the pleural cavity or trigger inflammation, leading to fluid accumulation.
  • The malignancies most often associated include lung cancer (mesothelioma more than adenocarcinoma), breast cancer, ovarian cancer, and gastrointestinal cancers.

Explanations of other options:

Constrictive pericarditis (Option A): This disorder is marked by pericardial thickening and scarring, which restricts cardiac filling. Although shortness of breath may occur, it more often manifests with features of right-sided heart failure, such as jugular venous distension and a pericardial knock. Focal reduction in breath sounds is not usually seen.

Cardiac tamponade (Option C): This condition is characterized by Beck's triad-low blood pressure, neck vein distension, and muffled heart sounds-along with pulsus paradoxus. Although breathlessness is common, it does not produce localized reduction in breath sounds, and the presentation is typically more sudden and severe than in this scenario.

Pneumothorax (Option D): It is marked by abrupt chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, and a hyperresonant percussion note on the affected side. The presentation is usually more acute, with breath sounds being absent rather than merely reduced.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448189/#

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559322/#

question_text: A 65 year old male presents with history of hemoptysis and is admitted in hospital. He has been a heavy smoker for 25 years. A chest  X-ray shows a mass in the right upper lobe. Which is the best test to investigate at present?
explanation:
The initial evaluation of a patient with hemoptysis is a plain radiograph of the chest.

In a low risk individual (age <40 years, non smoker), if the chest radiograph is normal, further investigations can wait if we can ensure a close follow up.

In individuals who are high risk for lung malignancy( age > 40 years or smokers), even if the initial chest xray is normal, they should undergo a contrast enhanced CT of the chest. If a lesion is visible on the CT it should be sampled for histopathology.

If a sampling is not possible or a lesion is not visible, a bronchoscopy should be done.

So our patient is at high risk for a bronchogenic carcinoma,and has a lesion visible on the chest xray. The next step will be a CT of the lung to characterize the lesion and to find the feasibility of a percutaneous biopsy.

Sputum cytology has a very low yield.

Pleural biopsy is indicated if there is evidence of pleural involvement.

A bronchoscopy should be done if the lesion is central or if no lesion is visible even on CT.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 78, Pg: 271

question_text: A chronic smoker presents with dysphagia. Which type of lung cancer is most likely?
explanation:
Explanation:

SCC is centrally located, strongly associated with smoking, and can compress the esophagus, causing dysphagia.

Types of Lung Cancer and Their Features

Adenocarcinoma:

  • Most common histologic subtype (~45% of lung cancers).
  • Early spread, often to the CNS.
  • Produces mucin; shows glandular differentiation.
  • Location: Peripheral.

Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC):

  • Strongly linked to smoking (~90% cases).
  • Histology: keratinization, intercellular bridges, central necrosis, cavitation.
  • Location: Central.

Large Cell Carcinoma:

  • Aggressive tumor, poorly differentiated.
  • Lacks defining histologic features.
  • Tends to grow slowly but has high vascularity.
  • Location: Peripheral.

Small Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma:

  • Very aggressive, with early nodal and distant metastasis.
  • Arises from neuroendocrine cells.
  • Location: Central.

Typical/Atypical Carcinoid Tumors:

  • Typical: Indolent course.
  • Atypical: More aggressive behavior.
  • Location: Variable.

Pancoast's Tumor (Apical):

  • Located at lung apex, invades brachial plexus.
  • Causes severe local pain.
  • Associated with Pancoast's syndrome.

Clinical Features of Lung Cancer

  • Cough: Common but non-specific.
  • Hemoptysis: Present in <50% of initial cases.
  • Chest pain: Severe pain indicates chest wall or intercostal nerve involvement.
  • Dyspnea: Due to reduced lung function, lymphatic spread, or pleural effusion.
  • Dysphagia: From mediastinal node enlargement or upper lung involvement compressing the esophagus.
  • Pleural fluid: Hemorrhagic fluid suggests pleural invasion.
  • Clubbing/Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy: Sometimes present, may regress after tumor removal.
  • Mediastinal invasion: May cause hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve), dysphagia, or SVC obstruction.
  • Pancoast's syndrome: Due to apical invasion with brachial plexus involvement.

Explanation of other options:

Adenocarcinoma (Option B): The most common lung cancer in non-smokers, usually arising in the lung periphery. It is less often associated with dysphagia compared to squamous cell carcinoma.

Large Cell Carcinoma (Option C): A relatively uncommon lung cancer that often presents with vague, non-specific symptoms. Dysphagia is not typically seen with this type.

Bronchogenic Carcinoma (Option D): A general term describing cancers originating from the bronchial epithelium, which includes subtypes such as squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma. However, it is not a precise diagnosis and therefore does not specifically address the question.

question_text: A 55 year old shipbuilding worker presents with dyspnea. He has been working in this industry for the past 25 years. Which is the most specific malignancy that we can expect in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

A long-term history of occupational asbestos exposure (common in shipbuilding) is the primary risk factor for malignant mesothelioma, a cancer arising from the mesothelial cells of the pleura. While asbestos also increases the risk for bronchogenic carcinoma, mesothelioma is the most specific malignancy linked to this exposure.

  • Pathology:Advanced pleural thickening/fibrosis makes the hemithorax rigid; mediastinal fixation may occur, but mediastinal shift is uncommon. Most common cytogenetic abnormality: 9p homozygous deletion (CDKN2A loss).
  • Clinical Features:Progressive dyspnea, chest pain, weight loss, chronic cough, hemoptysis; decreased breath sounds and dull percussion due to effusion or thickening.
  • Diagnosis:
  • CT scan:Pleural thickening, effusion, 'frozen hemithorax'(no mediastinal shift).
  • Biopsy:
    • Epithelioid: Tubules/nests/papillary structures, uniform nuclei, eosinophilic cytoplasm
    • Sarcomatoid: Spindle cells, fibrosarcoma-like
    • Biphasic: Mixed pattern
  • Markers:Calretinin, epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), cytokeratin, mesothelin.
  • Gross Findings:Lobulated pleural mass encasing lung, rib erosion, massive effusion, calcified pleural plaques (bilateral, prior asbestos exposure).

Explanation of other options:
Bronchogenic carcinoma ,Small cell carcinoma and Squamous cell carcinoma (Option A,C and D): These are types of lung cancer. Asbestos exposure is a risk factor, especially when combined with smoking, but they are not as specifically linked to asbestos as mesothelioma.

Key Takeaways:

  • Malignant mesothelioma is strongly and specifically associated with asbestos exposure.
  • Shipbuilding, construction, and insulation work are high-risk occupations.

question_text: A 45-year-old male complains of daytime sleepiness and nighttime insomnia. His wife reports that he snores loudly. Which of the following statements about his condition is incorrect?
option_a: Increased tone of the pharyngeal muscle worsens obstruction
option_b: Fall of oxygen saturation triggers waking up at night
option_c: Episode of apnea increases stress on heart
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient has Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA), a sleep disorder caused by repetitive upper airway collapse during sleep leading to intermittent hypoxia and sleep fragmentation.

Pathophysiology:

  • During sleep, pharyngeal muscle tone decreases, causing collapse of the upper airway.
  • This leads to airflow obstruction despite continued respiratory effort → apnea episodes.
  • The fall in oxygen saturation activates chemoreceptors, triggering brief arousals → fragmented sleep → daytime fatigue.
  • It is decreased, not increased, tone of the pharyngeal muscles that worsens obstruction.
  • Increased tone would actually help maintain airway patency.

Clinical Features:

  • Loud snoring
  • Witnessed apnea episodes
  • Excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS)
  • Morning headaches
  • Poor concentration, irritability

Complications:

  • Cardiovascular: Hypertension, arrhythmias, pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure
  • Metabolic: Insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome

Explanation of Other Options:

Fall of oxygen saturation triggers waking up at night (Option B):

  • True as hypoxia activates chemoreceptors → stimulates arousal reflex.
  • Restores muscle tone and breathing effort.
  • Leads to repeated micro-arousals → daytime sleepiness.
  • Oxygen desaturation is a key diagnostic feature on polysomnography.

Episode of apnea increases stress on heart (Option C):

  • True as repeated hypoxia increases sympathetic activation.
  • Raises heart rate and blood pressure transiently.
  • Leads to arrhythmias, hypertension, and cardiac failure in chronic cases.
  • Also increases risk of sudden cardiac death during sleep.

Low oxygen stimulates respiratory effort (Option D):

  • True as hypoxemia and hypercapnia stimulate medullary respiratory centers.
  • Increased respiratory effort against obstruction causes chest retractions.
  • Effort continues until arousal restores airflow.
  • Seen as thoraco-abdominal asynchrony on sleep studies.

question_text:
A 24-year-old man comes to the clinic complaining that he has begun waking from sleep in the early hours of the morning, unable to move. He is very distressed by this and is worried that he will become paralysed.
Additionally, he has begun to suffer from excessive sleepiness during the day and fell asleep once whilst out for dinner with a new girlfriend during the middle of the meal.
On examination his BP is 132/70 mmHg, pulse is 72 and regular. Neurological examination is entirely normal.
Investigations show
Haemoglobin 13.2 g/dl(13.5-18)

question_text: A 61-year-old, heavy smoker, with a BMI of 37 kg/m2, presents with impotence, nocturia and depression. He is hypoxic at rest on air and has ankle oedema. Which is the most appropriate investigation to determine the aetiology?

question_text: Which of the following is true regarding diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnoea?
option_a: Snoring along with 5 episodes of apnoea overnight fulfills the criteria
option_b: Lack of symptoms along with 15 episodes of apnea overnight fulfills the criteria
option_c: Each episode of apnoea or hypopnea lasts at least 10 seconds
explanation:
• options A and B are incorrect because the given number of episodes should occur per hour of night to satisfy the criteria

Diagnosis of OSA requires the patient to have:

(1) either symptoms of nocturnal breathing disturbances (snoring, snorting, gasping, or breathing pauses during sleep) or daytime sleepiness or fatigue that occurs despite sufficient opportunity to sleep and is unexplained by other medical problems; and

(2) five or more episodes of obstructive apnoea or hypopnea per hour of sleep (the apnoea-hypopnea index [AHI], calculated as the number of episodes divided by the number of hours of sleep) documented during a sleep study.

OSA also may be diagnosed in the absence of symptoms if the AHI is ≥15 episodes/h. Each episode of apnoea or hypopnea represents a reduction in breathing for at least 10 s and commonly results in a ≥3% drop in oxygen saturation or a brain cortical arousal

Polysomnography is used for the diagnosis of OSA.

Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 21st Edition, chapter 297, page number.2205

question_text: A 55 year old gentleman has pickwickian syndrome. He has poor exercise tolerance of 50 yards and often feels lethargic at work. Which of the following is the best investigation?
explanation:
• The classic features of Pickwickian syndrome or obesity hypoventilation syndrome are obesity and daytime hypercapnia.
  • The differences between Pickwickian syndrome and OSA are that former has longer and more continuous episodes of hypoventilation overnight( there may or may not be upper airway obstruction).
  • The diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnoea can be made with a sleep study (polysomnography). In sleep apnoea, there is gross obesity and airways obstruction, occasionally leading to type II respiratory failure. During the sleep study, > 10 episodes of apnoeic episodes (pauses in breathing) satisfies the criteria for obstructive sleep apnoea.
  • A sleep study is the gold standard test for diagnosing OSA. It involves monitoring the patient's breathing, heart rate, and oxygen levels during sleep. The sleep study will also show the number and duration of apneas and hypopneas (breathing pauses).
  • The other options are not as accurate for diagnosing Pickwickian syndrome.
  • Echocardiography can be used to assess cor pulmonale, which is a heart condition that can develop in people with Pickwickian syndrome. However, it is not the best test for diagnosing the condition.
  • CT scan of the chest can be used to visualize the lungs and airways, but it is not as sensitive as a sleep study for detecting OSA.
  • Blood gas can be used to measure the levels of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood, but it is not as specific as a sleep study for diagnosing Pickwickian syndrome.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 296, Pg:2203, 2204

question_text: A 33-year-old woman presents with a one-year history of daytime sleepiness and memory impairment. She has a BMI of 43 and blood pressure of 170/98 mmHg. Arterial blood gas analysis while awake shows pO<sub>2</sub> 70 mmHg, pCO<sub>2</sub> 53 mmHg, and HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> 33 mmol/L. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient shows typical signs of Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS), such as marked obesity (BMI 43), excessive daytime sleepiness, impaired memory, and high blood pressure.

  • The hallmark of OHS diagnosis is arterial blood gas findings that reveal hypoxemia (pO2 70 mmHg), hypercapnia (pCO2 53 mmHg), and increased bicarbonate (HCO3 33 mmol/L), consistent with chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation, considered pathognomonic for OHS.
  • It develops in individuals with severe obesity who demonstrate hypoventilation both while asleep and awake.

Explanations of other options:

Central Sleep Apnea (Option B): Although central sleep apnea may lead to daytime drowsiness, it stems from impaired central nervous system regulation of breathing during sleep. However, the ABG findings of chronic compensated respiratory acidosis align more with obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) than with a CNS-related disorder.

Narcolepsy (Option C): Narcolepsy typically presents with excessive daytime sleepiness along with cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations. Since these features are absent, and instead there is marked obesity with respiratory acidosis, this diagnosis is less probable.

Obstructive Sleep Apnea (Option D): While OSA often coexists with OHS, the presence of daytime hypercapnia is not typical for isolated OSA. The chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation is more characteristic of OHS.

question_text:
A 40-year-old man presents with daytime sleepiness and impaired concentration and memory. On examination his BMI is 41 kg/m2, BP is 160/100 mm Hg. His awake ABG analysis is given:
PaO₂= 66mm Hg
PaCO₂= 50 mm Hg
HCO₃= 28 mEq/L
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS) is a medical condition characterized by persistent daytime hypercapnia (elevated arterial carbon dioxide pressure) in individuals with obesity, after other potential causes of hypoventilation have been ruled out.

Pathophysiology

  • The syndrome arises primarily because severe obesity mechanically restricts lung expansion, leading to chronic hypoventilation. This is compounded by several factors:
    • The increased work of breathing due to excess chest and abdominal weight.
    • Respiratory muscle impairment from adipose tissue.
    • A blunted ventilatory response to hypercapnia and hypoxemia.
    • Frequently co-existing obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), which further disrupts normal gas exchange during sleep.
  • Notably, the impaired ventilatory drive appears to be a consequence of the condition rather than its initial cause

Diagnostic Criteria

  • A diagnosis of OHS is confirmed when the following three criteria are met:
  • Body Mass Index (BMI): A BMI ≥30 kg/m².
  • Daytime Alveolar Hypoventilation: An awake arterial PaCO2 ≥45 mmHg, without other explanations such as severe lung or neuromuscular disease.
  • Sleep-Disordered Breathing: The presence of a disorder like obstructive sleep apnea (OSA).

Risk Factors

  • The primary risk factors for developing OHS are:
  • Severe obesity (BMI >40 kg/m²)
  • Severe obstructive sleep apnea (Apnea-Hypopnea Index, AHI >30 events per hour)
  • Treatment :

Explanation of other options:

Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) (Option A) :is a disorder that is characterized by obstructive apneas and hypopneas due to repetitive collapse of the upper airway during sleep. The clinical features against OSA include hypercapnia and hypoxemia in an awake individual.

Narcolepsy (Option B): is characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness, sudden loss of muscle tone (cataplexy), and disrupted sleep patterns. While impaired concentration and memory can be seen in narcolepsy, the ABG is normal.


Central sleep apnea (Option D): is a condition in which there is a lack of respiratory effort during sleep, leading to pauses in breathing. Impaired concentration and memory can occur in central sleep apnea.

question_text: A 46 year old female with morbid obesity is brought to the physician by her husband for complaints of excessive snoring at night. On further questioning, she reports to have day time sleepiness occasionally. A polysomnography is done which shows 6 episodes of apnoea per hour of sleep. What is the best modality to treat this patient?
option_b: Continuous positive alveolar pressure (CPAP) machine overnight
explanation:
• This patient fits in the criteria for obstructive sleep apnoea (≥ 5 Apnoea hypopnea index)

Management of OSA:

  • Weight loss
  • CPAP: standard medical therapy with the highest level of evidence for efficacy. Delivered through a nasal or nasal-oral mask, CPAP works as a mechanical splint to hold the airway open, thus maintaining airway patency during sleep.
  • Mandibular advancement devices: used for treating patients with mild/moderate OSA or patients who do not tolerate CPAP
  • Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty: less successful than treatment with oral appliances; reserved for the treatment of patients who snore, have mild OSA, or cannot tolerate CPAP
  • Upper airway neurostimulation: Unilateral stimulation of the hypoglossal nerve through a surgically implanted device; reserved for patients who cannot tolerate or fail CPAP therapy. with moderate to severe OSA

Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 21st Edition, chapter 297, page number2208,2209

question_text:
A 17-year-old female student is admitted for confusion and acute kidney injury. She is able to give some history that she had a fight with her boy friend 2 days ago, and she drank some liquid that was in their garage. She has no any other significant medical or illicit drug history. In the Emergency Department, her vital signs are stable. Other than altered mental status and confusion, her physical examination is normal. She weighs 60 kg. Laboratory values:

Which one of the following toxic alcohol ingestions is the MOST likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
This patient has a high AG metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis. She has also an osmolal gap of 16, which is elevated. The presence of calcium oxalate crystals (envelope-like) in the urine sediment is the clue for her acid-base disturbance, which is ethylene glycol ingestion (B is correct). One of the final products of ethylene glycol is oxalic acid, which is excreted as oxalate. Antidote for ethylene glycol is fomepizole. The initial dose is 15 mg/kg followed by 10 mg/kg every 12 h for 4 doses. Continue fomepizole, if ethylene glycol levels are not below 20 mg/dL. At the same time, hydration with D5W and 3 ampules (150 mEq) of NaHCO3 to run at 120 mL/h to improve volume status should be started. Hemodialysis is indicated, if no improvement in renal function and metabolic acidosis following adequate hydration and NaHCO3 administration is observed.

Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:55 Pg: 361

question_text:
Which of the following is true regarding proteinuria?
1. 8-10mg/day of albuminuria may be seen in normal individuals.
2. Sustained proteinuria >1g/day is associated with glomerular diseases.
3. Proteinuria in adults is selective, whereas proteinuria in Minimal Change Disease is non selective.
4. Benign proteinuria is seen with CCF, fever, exercise, obesity, stress etc.
explanation:
Abumin has negative charge and so does the Glomerular basement membrane, the size of albumin is 3.6mm, whereas the size of the pores of the slit pore is 4 mm. so some amount of albumin will be filtered across the glomerulus. They are reclaimed at the PCT by the cubulin and the megalin receptors. Ultimately around 8-10mg/day of albumin is excreted and it forms 20-60% of the total excreted protein.

<30mg/day of albumin excretion is normal. Albumin in the range of 30-300mg/day is called microalbuminuria and it indicates renal disease.

Sustained proteinuria of >1-2g/day indicates glomerular disease. Benign proteinuria or non sustained proteinuria of <1g/day is associated with fever, exercise, obesity, sleep apnoea, cardiac failure etc.

The proteinuria seen in adults is non selective, whereas in Minimal Change Disease it is selective.

question_text: What is observed in the case of an abnormal accumulation of misfolded protein?
explanation:
Explanation:

The condition directly caused by the abnormal accumulation of misfolded proteins is Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD). This is a rare, fatal neurodegenerative disorder that rapidly impairs brain function.

CJD is classified as a prion disease. Prions are infectious, misfolded proteins that cause normally folded proteins in the brain to also misfold. This leads to the accumulation of abnormal protein aggregates, resulting in progressive and severe damage to nerve cells, giving the brain a sponge-like (spongiform) appearance.

Clinical Presentation

The disease progresses rapidly and is characterized by:

  • Severe mental deterioration (dementia)
  • Involuntary muscle jerks (myoclonus)
  • Lack of coordination and balance problems
  • Behavioral changes, anxiety, and confusion
  • Vision problems and unusual sensations
    As it advances, it leads to coma and ultimately death, often from secondary infections like pneumonia.

Types of CJD

  • Sporadic (sCJD): The most common form (85% of cases) with no known cause.
  • Genetic (gCJD): Inherited through a gene mutation (10-15% of cases).
  • Acquired (vCJD): The rare "variant" form, linked to consuming products from cattle with bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE or "mad cow disease").

Diagnosis and Management

  • Diagnosis is supported by clinical signs, characteristic EEG patterns, MRI brain imaging, and detecting the 14-3-3 protein in cerebrospinal fluid. Definitive diagnosis often requires brain biopsy or postmortem examination.
  • Treatment: There is no cure. Management focuses on palliative care to alleviate symptoms and provide comfort.

Explanation of other options:

Nephritic syndrome (Option B): It is primarily associated with immune-mediated damage and not the accumulation of misfolded proteins.

Sickle cell anaemia (Option C): This is a genetic hemoglobinopathy caused by a mutation in the beta-globin gene, leading to abnormally shaped red blood cells.

Megaloblastic anaemia (Option D): It is a type of anaemia characterized by the presence of large, immature red blood cells (megaloblasts) in the bone marrow. Megaloblastic anaemia does not involve the accumulation of misfolded proteins.

Reference:

https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/creutzfeldt-jakob-disease

question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents with high fever, purpura occurring on her arms and legs, haematuria and renal dysfunction. Investigation results were: sodium 135 mmol/l potassium 4.5 mmol/l urea 90 mg/dl creatinine 3 mg/dl. Urine showed 2+ protein and 3+ blood. A p-ANCA is positive. Serum C3 is normal. Renal biopsy before steroid therapy confirmed the diagnosis of pauci-immune-type crescentic glomerulonephritis. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
The patient in this question is suffering from Glomerulonephritis.

Temporal arteritis and Takayasu arteritis are large vessel vasculitis. Large and medium vessel vasculitis can affect the main renal vessel or its branches, which does not result in glomerulonephritis.

Glomerulonephritis can be of three types

  1. Systemic immune activation and complement consumption, resulting in immune complex deposition in vessels, which consists of immunoglobulins of varying classes and Complement, seum complement levels will be low. Eg: Lupus Nephritis, Cryoglobulinemia.
  2. Local activation of complement and/or immune system, resulting in local deposition of immunoglobulin and complement in the vessels. Normal serum complement. Eg: IgA Nephropathy, Glomerular Basement membrane dissease, HSP.
  3. No activation of complement or systemic antigen antibody response, hence no deposition of immunoglobulins or complements. There will be circulating ANCA but serum complement will be normal. Eg: Pauci immune small vessel vasculitis and renal limited vasculitis.

Post streptococcal glomerulonephritis results in low S C3 and biopsy also shows immunoglobulin and complement deposition.

Here the S C3 is normal and biopsy is also pauci immune. So the pauci immune glomerulonephritis among the following is Microscopic polyangiitis.

PANCA(perinuclear staining) is usually due to myeloperoxidase and is found in:

  • Microscopic polyarteritis(80%)
  • Idiopathic crescentic GN(65%)
  • Churg-Strauss Syndrome
  • Polyarteritis nodosa
  • Wegener's granulomatosis
  • SLE

Although pANCA can be positive in many conditions, cANCA is found more commonly in Wegener's Granulomatosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2340.

question_text: Which of the following diseases present mainly as Glomerulonephritis?
explanation:
Glomerular diseases can present in 2 ways- Nephritic Syndrome or Nephrotic Syndrome. Clinical distinction of both is required to identify the disease process and to plan investigations.

NEPHRITIC SYNDROME:

  1. Hematuria.
  2. RBC cast.
  3. Hypertension.
  4. Proteinuria of the range 1-2g/day.
  5. Varying degrees of decline in GFR.

Diseases that present predominantly as Nephritis are: Post streptococcal Glomerulonephritis, Sub acute bacterial endocarditis, Lupus Nephritis, IgA Nephropathy, Basement Membrane Disease, ANCA associated vasculitis, Membraneoproliferative glomerulonephritis.

NEPHROTIC SYNDROME:

  1. Heavy proteinuria, >3gm/day
  2. Edema/anasarca
  3. Hypertension
  4. Hypercholesterolemia
  5. Hypoalbuminemia
  6. Hematuria, variable.

Diseases that predominantly present as Nephrotic syndrome: Minimal change disease, Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, Membranous glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, Amyloidosis, Light chain deposition disease, Fabry’s Disease.

There can be overlap between these two, eg: heavy proteinuria in Glomerulonephritis, known as Nephritic-nephrotic Syndrome.

Reference: Harrison's principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2334.

question_text:
Which of the following features are characteristic of glomerular hematuria? Statements:
1. Brown-colored urine
2. Dysuria absent
3. Crystals present
4. Edema rare
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Glomerular hematuria occurs when damage to the glomerular filtration barrier allows red blood cells (RBCs) and plasma proteins to leak into the urinary space.
  • It typically presents with cola-colored (brown) urine, absence of dysuria, and may be associated with edema when part of a nephritic syndrome.
  • The presence of urinary crystals is not a feature of glomerular bleeding, it suggests a metabolic or post-renal causesuch as stones or hyperuricosuria.

Explanation of Other Statements:

Brown-colored urine (Statement 1) - True

  • The urine appears cola- or tea-colored due to oxidation of hemoglobin released from RBCs that have traversed damaged glomeruli.
  • Indicates bleeding originating above the renal pelvis.

Dysuria absent (Statement 2)- True

  • Dysuria (painful micturition) suggests inflammation or infection of the lower urinary tract (urethra, bladder).
  • Glomerular hematuria is non-irritative and painless.

Crystals present (Statement 3) - False

  • Crystalluria is associated with renal calculi or metabolic disorders (e.g., hyperuricemia, cystinuria), not glomerular diseases.

Edema rare (Statement 4) - True in isolated glomerular hematuria

  • Mild or no edema may be seen in isolated microscopic hematuria.
  • However, when hematuria occurs as part of nephritic syndrome, edema can be marked.

question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents with dipstick positive haematuria. Her blood tests reveal a urea of 150 mg/dl and creatinine of 2.9 mg/dl. Which of the following most strongly suggests post streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
explanation:
Post streptococcal glomerulonephritis is caused by Group A beta haemolytic streptococci.

A second episode is unusual in those who have previously had the disease because there is good immunity to the cell wall proteins of Group A strep.

Acute Rheumatic Fever, which is also a disease caused by β hemolytic Sterptococci, is known for recurrences without secondary prophylaxis.

Although features of hypertension with papilledema, complete anuria and nephrotic syndrome can occur, the strongest predictor is the clinical history of sore throat suggesting infection with streptococci leading to nephritic syndrome.

question_text: A 17-year-old male presents with proteinuria >4g/day, edema, and hypoalbuminemia, consistent with nephrotic syndrome. What is the recommended management for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Management of Nephrotic Syndrome in a 17-Year-Old Male

  • First-line Treatment: Steroids (Prednisone)
    • Based on high remission rates in minimal change disease (MCD), the most common cause in children and adolescents.
    • Leads to complete remission in 90-95% of children, 80-85% of adults.
    • Given daily or on alternate days.
    • Other immunosuppressants (cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, mycophenolate mofetil) are used for frequent relapsers, steroid-dependent, or steroid-resistant

Presentation & Epidemiology

  • Features:
    • Proteinuria >4 g/day, edema, hypoalbuminemia, hypercholesterolemia
    • Minimal hematuria, possible hypertension
  • Without treatment: Risk of progression to renal failure

Therapeutic Overview

  • Edema: Managed with diuretics
  • Hypercholesterolemia: Treated with lipid-lowering agents
  • Hypercoagulability: May need anticoagulants
  • Proteinuria: May use RAAS inhibitors

Minimal Change Disease (MCD)

  • Prevalence:
    • 70-90% of pediatric cases
    • 10-15% of adult cases
  • Histology:
    • Normal on light microscopy, foot process effacement on electron microscopy
  • Etiology:
    • Linked to T-cell dysfunction; triggered by infections, allergies, or medications

Clinical Features of MCD

  • Sudden onset of edema
  • Classic nephrotic syndrome signs
  • Hypertension and microscopic hematuria are uncommon
  • Renal function usually returns to normal after remission

Outcomes & Prognosis

  • Relapses common, especially in children
  • Long-term prognosis is poorer in cases of acute renal failure or steroid resistance
  • Children: Remission typically within 8 weeks
  • Adults: Remission may take 20-24 weeks

Explanation of other options:

Steroids and Cyclophosphamide (Option B): Cyclophosphamide is NOT first-line for nephrotic syndrome. It is reserved for steroid-resistant or frequently relapsing cases.

IV Albumin (Option C): Albumin infusion can be used temporarily for severe edema but does NOT treat the underlying disease. Main treatment is still steroids.

Cyclophosphamide (Option D): Cyclophosphamide is used for steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome or frequent relapses, NOT as initial therapy.

Key Takeaways:

Nephrotic syndrome in adolescents is most commonly due to Minimal Change Disease, which responds well to corticosteroids. First-line treatment is prednisone.

question_text: An 8-year-old girl presents with sudden onset of fever, decreased urine output (oliguria), nausea, dark-colored (smoky) urine, and swelling around the eyes (periorbital puffiness). Her parents mention that she had facial lesions similar to those shown in the image below about two weeks ago, which are now healing. Which of the following findings is likely to be present in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The skin lesions described by the parents, which appeared about two weeks ago and are now healing, suggest a recent streptococcal infection. This infection has likely progressed to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), leading to the presence of red blood cells in the urine (hematuria).

Explanation for other options:

Nephrotic range proteinuria (Option D): defined as heavy protein loss exceeding 3.5 grams per day, is not commonly seen in PSGN. Instead, PSGN typically presents with hematuria and mild to moderate proteinuria.

Abnormal liver enzyme levels (Option C): and neurological symptoms (Option D) are also not characteristic features of PSGN.

question_text: Aldosterone synthesis is stimulated by which of the following?
explanation:
• Mineralocorticoid secretion is stimulated by hypotension, hyperkalemia, angiotensin II, ACTH and hyponatremia, in reducing order of efficacy.
  1. Aldosterone secretion in response to hyperkalemia is the most important and forms the basis for renal regulation of body potassium balance.
  2. Stimulation of aldosterone by angiotensin II (through renin-angiotensin system) is important for the correction of hypovolemia and hypotension in conditions like salt depletion or renal ischemia.
  3. Stimulation of aldosterone secretion by ACTH results in diurnal variation of aldosterone secretion.
  4. However, ACTH is not an important physiological regulator for aldosterone secretion. Hyponatremia is a weak stimulator of aldosterone secretion.

Factors stimulating release of aldosterone release:

  • Hypotension
  • Hyperkalemia
  • Acidosis
  • Angiotensin 2

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2958

question_text: Which of the following is not a characteristic feature of Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)?
explanation:
Explanation of Correct Answer:

Renal Failure may occur in patients with Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) due to widespread microvascular injury, it is not a defining or predominant feature of the condition.

Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) is a rare hematological disorder characterized by:

  • Thrombocytopenia (Option A ruled out)
  • Thrombosis (Option B ruled out)
  • Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (Option C ruled out)

question_text: A 65-year-old man is brought in with a sudden inability to speak coherently, producing nonsensical grammar despite speaking fluently and rapidly. He had normal communication ability before this event. Which type of defect does this patient have?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario of quick speech, which does not make sense, is suggestive of fluent aphasia, also known as Wernicke's aphasia.

  • Fuent aphasia, or Wernicke's aphasia, arises from injury to Wernicke's area in the brain.
  • It is characterised by effortless and well-structured speech, but the content is nonsensical or filled with invented words.
  • Patients usually retain normal rhythm and fluency yet produce meaningless language, and they are generally unaware of their communication difficulties.

Explanation of other options:

Motor aphasia (Option A): Motor aphasia, or Broca's aphasia, is marked by impaired speech production, including reduced vocabulary, slow and effortful speech, and poor grammar. Affected individuals find it hard to construct complete sentences and often become frustrated with their inability to communicate. Since the patient can speak smoothly and rapidly, this condition is unlikely.

Anomic aphasia (Option B): Anomic aphasia involves difficulty retrieving words, causing pauses and the use of substitute terms, though grammar and speech fluency are usually preserved. Since the patient shows meaningless speech content rather than problems with word retrieval, this diagnosis is improbable.

Conduction aphasia (Option D): Conduction aphasia arises from injury to the arcuate fasciculus, which links Broca's and Wernicke's areas. It is marked by impaired ability to repeat words or phrases, despite having relatively preserved comprehension and spontaneous speech. Because this patient's main problem lies in the meaning of their speech rather than repetition, this diagnosis is less likely.

question_text: A 19-year-old woman complains of stiff joints and a facial rash. Her blood pressure is 146/96 mmHg, she has +1 oedema, slightly swollen metacarpophalangeal joints and some ulceration of her buccal mucosa. Plasma creatinine is 1.2 mg/dl, Hb is 8.9 g/dl and platelet count is 92,000/µl. Urinalysis shows +3 blood and +3 protein. High titres of double-stranded DNA antibodies are detectable in her serum. What would histological examination of renal tissue demonstrate?
option_a: Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis with deposits of IgG, IgM and C3
explanation:
The scenario describes a young female who has arthritis, oral ulceration, edema, bicytopenia, hematuria and proteinuria.

This woman clearly has lupus nephritis. The most common(and most severe) form, one which is entirely compatible with the clinical history, is type IV - proliferative GN affecting > 50% of glomeruli, often with crescents present. This form of lupus nephritis frequently progresses to cause renal failure when untreated and is associated with extensive immune deposits on immunofluorescence staining. Therefore, patients with type IV(and sometimes type III, where < 50% of glomeruli are involved) should be treated with a combination of cyclophosphamide and steroids, a treatment combination that is frequently extremely emotive in this population. Additional types of lupus nephritis are type I(abnormal urine sediment with normal light microscopy), type II(mesangioproliferative GN), type V(membranous nephropathy) and type VI(advanced scleroses).

Option C: FSGS will present as a nephrotic syndrome rather than a nephritic syndrome

Option D: Pauci-immune proliferative glomerular lesions, with and without crescents, tend to be associated with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody(ANCA)-associated small-vessel vasculitis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition, Ch:314, Pg:2337, 2338.

question_text: A 40-year old man presents with dyspnoea and massive haemoptysis for the last 1 week. On urinalysis, he has 2+ protein, RBCs, and RBC casts. Which disease is least likely to be present?
explanation:
The patient has massive pulmonary hemorrhage along with glomerulonephritis on urinalysis.

Glomerulonephritis with pulmonary hemorrhage (Pulmonary Renal Syndrome) occurs in ANCA associated small vessel vasculitis, Henoch Schoenlein purpura, Goodpasture's Syndrome, Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis and SLE. They often present as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page Number-2334.

question_text: A 70-year-old male with a 3-month history of constitutional symptoms including weight loss, night sweats, fatigue and malaise presents with rapidly progressive acute renal failure, haemoptysis and diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. Biopsy demonstrates a pauci-immune focal segmental proliferative, necrotizing and sclerosing glomerulonephritis with crescent formation and a superimposed necrotizing and granulomatous arteritis involving small intrarenal arteries. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient is an elderly male with pulmonary renal syndrome, as evidenced by the presence of pulmonary infiltrates, hemoptysis and renal failure. Among the given options Goodpasture's syndrome and Wegener's Granulomatosis cause pulmonary renal syndromes.

But the biopsy is showing granulomatous arteritis, which is seen in Wegerner's Granulomatosis(Granulomatosis with angiitis) and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

The presence of "crescents" is not specific for any particular type of glomerular disease, but is common for all diseases causing Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis.

NON CASEATING Granulomatous arteritis + necrotizing Glomerulonephritis= Wegener's Granulomatosis

Differential Diagnosis:

  • Microscopic Polyarteritis Nodosa(PAN) with Glomerular Involvement: This condition presents with crescentic glomerulonephritis and is characterized by immune complex deposition in the blood vessel walls. While it may involve the kidney, it typically and granulomatous vasculitis, which are more indicative of Wegener's granulomatosis.
  • Wegener's Granulomatosis(Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis - GPA): Wegener's granulomatosis is characterized by crescentic glomerulonephritis and often presents with both renal and extrarenal manifestations, such as destructive sinusitis and pulmonary involvement and granulomatous vasculitis. This combination of findings is more consistent with Wegener's granulomatosis.

Explanation for Ruling Out Other Options:

  • Polyarteritis Nodosa(PAN): While PAN can involve the kidney in the form of involvement of main renal artery or its branches and does not cause glomerulonephritis.
  • Goodpasture Syndrome: Goodpasture syndrome primarily involves the kidney and lung, but it is caused by autoantibodies against the basement membrane antigen, leading to pulmonary hemorrhage. It does not typically present with granulomatous vasculitis.
  • Post Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis: This condition is usually associated with a recent streptococcal infection and manifests with different histological findings('lumpy-bumpy' appearance). It does not typically cause granulomatous vasculitis or the systemic symptoms described.

In summary, the presence of extrarenal(pulmonary) involvement and granulomatous vasculitis, along with the crescentic glomerulonephritis, strongly favors the diagnosis of Wegener's granulomatosis(Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis - GPA). It's important to note that GPA is a severe condition that requires prompt immunosuppressive treatment.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 356 Pg: 2340.

question_text: A 40-year-old male with fleeting cough and uncontrolled asthma now presents with decreased urine output and minimal pedal edema of 1 week duration. His BP is 180/110mm Hg. The ESR is 110. His Urinalysis shows 2+ protein and dysmorphic RBC. His peripheral blood eosinophils count is 20000/µL. Which of the following statements is false?
option_a: His serum will contain P ANCA directed against Myeloperoxidase.
option_b: His renal biopsy will show necrotizing glomerulonephritis, with pauci immune vasculitis without granulomas or eosniophils.
option_c: ANCA may be used for monitoring response to treatment.
option_d: Relapses of glomerulonephritis is less common in these group.
explanation:
ANCA has limited role in assessing response to treatment in any pauci immune glomerulonephritis. But it has a definite role in detecting relapses.

Now, this question deals with a patient having uncontrolled asthma, peripheral eosinophilia, who now presents with acute glomerulonephritis. So it basically deals with Churg Strauss Syndrome(Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis).

It is a small vessel vasculitis with peripheral eosinophilia, allergic rhinitis, asthma, mononeuritis and can present with glomerulonephritis. The glomerulonephritis is pauci immune, as with other small vessel vasculitis. But unlike Wegener’s granulomatosis, there is no granuloma formation or eosinophilia in renal biopsy, but necrotizing glomerulonephritis with vasculitis.

The ANCA that is seen in Churg strauss and microscopic polyangiitis is P ANCA directed against myeloperoxidase, where as in Wegener it is C ANCA, directed against PR3.

Renal disease in Churg Strauss and Microscopic polyangiitis has got less chance of relapse than Wegeners Granulomatosis.

Though clinical features of these diseases are different, the management of renal disease is the same:

  • RPGN is managed by plasma exchange.
  • Otherwise glomerulonephritis is manged with induction with high dose steroids + Cyclophosphamide/Rituximab, followed by tapering dose of oral steroids with cyclophosphamide/methotrexate/azathioprine for an year.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch:314, Pg: 2340.

question_text: Two weeks after an episode of infective diarrhoea, a 15-year-old child presents with fever, hypertension and haematuria. A possible diagnosis could be:
explanation:
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura(TTP) and hemolytic-uremic syndrome(HUS) represent a spectrum of thrombotic microangiopathies. TTP and HUS share the general features of idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, hemolytic anemia, fever, renal failure and neurologic disturbances.

  • When patients, particularly children, have more evidence of renal injury, their condition tends to be called HUS.
  • In adults with neurologic disease, it is considered to be TTP.

Childhood HUS is caused by a toxin released by Escherichia coli 0157:H7 and occasionally by Shigella dysenteriae. This shiga toxin(verotoxin) directly injures endothelial, enterocytes and renal cells, causing apoptosis, platelet clumping and intravascular hemolysis by binding to the glycolipid receptors(Gb3). Investigations reveal anemia with schistocytes; a normal bleeding profile and impaired renal function.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2348.

question_text: A 40-year-old woman has a history of Raynaud's phenomenon, stiffness in the hands, butterfly rash on her face and arthralgia. She has a blood pressure of 175/90 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows protein ++ and blood +. Blood tests reveal a creatinine of 1.6 mg/dl, ESR 60 mm/hour and positive ANA 1/160 titres. Which of the following is most likely to be the result of the renal biopsy?
option_a: Mesangial IgA staining and proliferative glomerulonephritis
option_b: Subendothelial deposits seen as humps with focal glomerulonephritis
option_c: Deposition of IgA, IgG, IgM and complements with proliferative glomerulonephritis
option_d: Focal or diffuse glomerular necrosis with crescents and liner IgG deposits along the basement membrane in IF.
explanation:
So this question deals with a young woman with history suggestive of SLE. So we have to find out, from the options, the most likely finding in lupus nephritis. There are 6 classes of lupus nephritis.

  • The histological pattern is membranoproliferative or mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis, where you can see focal or diffuse, segmental or global endocapillary proliferation.

The immune deposits are seen sub endothelially along the basement membrane.

There will be variable degree of mesangial proliferation.

All classes of immunoglobulins and complement will be seen(Full house staining)

  • Sub endothelial deposits of immunoglobulins IgG, M and complements with endocapillary and mesangial proliferation and polymorphonuclear infiltration is seen in PSGN. There will be sub epithelial humps on electron microscopy.
  • Focal necrosis of the glomeruli with linear IgG deposits along the basement membrane is seen in Anti GBM disease. There will not be any proliferation seen.
  • Mesangial IgA staining with mesangial hypercellularity, known as mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis is seen in IgA nephropathy. Here the immunoglobulin deposits are IgA class and there will be no staining of sub epithelium or sub endothelium of the basement membrane.

Note: Sub endothelial deposits occur with pre formed immune complexes precipitating along the sub endothelial side. Immune complexes that are formed in situ will be seen along the sun epithelial side.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 21st edition, Ch: 314, Pg: 2332-2343.

question_text: A 45-year-old patient with chronic hepatitis C has a creatinine of 1.5 mg/dl. His BP is 150/90. He has a urine dipstick showing blood ++, protein +++. Which of the following might be demonstrated in histology?
explanation:
This question deals with another cause of glomerulonephritis. Our patient is a chronic Hepatitis C infected individual who presents with Glomerulonephritis.

The type of glomerulonephritis that we see in such a patient is Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.

Unlike the glomerulonephritis that we learned so far which is specific for a particular etiology, MPGN is a histology patten that is common for many diseases.

In a simplified form, the causes of MPGN can be broadly divided into three:

  1. Type I: Immune complex or monoclonal antibody mediated: Hep B or Hep C, Malaria, Schsitosomiasis, Infective endocarditis, SLE, Sjogren's syndrome, Cryoglobulinemia, MGUS or myeloma.
  2. Type II: Dense deposit disease
  3. Type III: Idiopathic

Hepatitis C infection as well as Cryuoglobulinemia associated with it can lead to glomerulonephritis and the MC histology will be MPGN

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 314, Pg: 2341.

question_text: A 20-year-old patient complains of ankle swelling and breathlessness. Her CXR shows pleural effusions. Blood tests show: urea 17 mg/dl creatinine 0.90 mg/dl sodium 138 mmol/l potassium 4.2 mmol/l alanine transferase 20 U/L bilirubin 0.9 mg/dl albumin 2 gm/dl total cholesterol 340 mg/dl. What is the next best investigation?
explanation:
The given patient has hypoalbuminemia, hyper cholesterolemia, edema and pleural effusion. So the edema is attribute to hypoalbuminemia. Hypoalbuminemia can be due to either decreased albumin production as in CLD or excessive albumin loss through urine or gut. However here the cholesterol levels are high which is an indirect indicator of nephrotic syndrome. So the next investigation will be to confirm the urinary loss, which is 24 hour urine estimation. Followed by a renal biopsy, once proteinuria is confirmed.

The classic features of nephrotic syndrome are:

  • Proteinuria >3g/24 hours
  • Hypoalbuminemia(<3.5 g/dl)
  • Generalized Oedema
  • Hypercholesterolemia
  • Lipiduria

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2341.

question_text: A 33-year-old man presents with rapid progressive glomerulonephritis and nephrotic syndrome. A renal biopsy shows Wegener's granulomatosis. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
The management of renal disease is the same for all pauci immune glomerulonephritis:

  • RPGN is managed by plasma exchange.
  • Otherwise glomerulonephritis is manged with induction with high dose steroids + Cyclophosphamide/Rituximab, followed by tapering dose of oral steroids with cyclophosphamide/methotrexate/azathioprine for an year.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2340.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, Ch:356, Pg:2581.

The primary pulmonary pathology in COVID 19 is excessive clotting, activation of inflammation and endothelial injury.

question_text: A hepatitis B-positive patient presented to your OPD with massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day). A renal biopsy was subsequently performed, as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

This renal biopsy shows the condition membranous glomerulonephritis

Investigations in Membranous Nephropathy/Glomerulonephritis:

  • Kidney function tests: Elevated creatinine levels.
  • Urine protein: Proteinuria exceeding 2 grams per gram of urinary creatinine.
  • Renal biopsy findings:
    • Light Microscopy: Shows uniform thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, especially along peripheral capillary loops.
    • Immunofluorescence: Displays diffuse granular deposits of IgG and C3.
    • Electron Microscopy: Reveals dense subepithelial deposits with a characteristic 'spike and dome' pattern.
  • Autoantibody testing:
    • Autoantibodies against M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) are found in about 70% of cases.
    • Thrombospondin type-1 domain containing 7A (THSD7A) autoantibodies are seen in 3-10% of cases.
    • Secondary membranous nephropathy usually lacks these autoantibodies.

Management:

  • Symptomatic treatment: Includes control of edema (using thiazide diuretics), dyslipidemia, and hypertension (using ACE inhibitors or ARBs).
  • Immunosuppressive therapy: Considered for primary membranous nephropathy patients with persistent proteinuria above 3 g/day. Options include corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine, and rituximab (an anti-CD20 antibody).
  • Prophylactic anticoagulation: May be advised in patients with hypoalbuminemia due to an increased risk of thrombotic events.

Complications:

  • High risk of renal vein thrombosis.
  • Other thrombotic complications such as deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism due to the hypercoagulable state associated with nephrotic syndrome.

Prognosis:

  • Approximately one-third of patients progress to advanced disease.
  • One-third achieve spontaneous remission.
  • One-third maintain stable disease without progression.
  • Poorer outcomes are linked to male sex, older age, hypertension, and ongoing nephrotic-range proteinuria.

Explanation of other options:

Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) (Option A): involves scarring and sclerosis that affects some glomeruli (focal) and only portions of each affected glomerulus (segmental).

Membranoproliferative Glomerulonephritis (MPGN) (Option C): is defined by a combination of basement membrane thickening and mesangial cell proliferation.

Minimal Change Disease (Option D): is the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, but it occurs less frequently in adults.

question_text: Renal vein thrombosis is associated with all of the following except: September 2011
explanation: Ans. B: Sickle cell anemia Conditions associated with RVT are: Trauma, extrinsic compression (lymoh nodes, aneurysm), invasion by renal cell carcinoma, dehydration (infants), nephritic syndrome and Pregnancy/ oral contraceptives RVT: Acute cases occurs in children and presents with sudden loss of renal function Gradual thrombosis occurs in elderly and only manifestation may be recurrent pulmonary emboli or development of hypertension Definitive diagnosis can be done through selective renal venography with visualization of the occluding thrombus Treatment options consists of anticoagulation and thrombectomy

question_text: A 30-year-old lady has haematuria on the dipstick and was referred by the GP for further investigation. She eventually has a renal biopsy which shows mesangial hypercellularity with IgA deposition. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
The diagnosis is IgA nephropathy.

Epidemiology:

IgA nephropathy is the commonest glomerulonephritis worldwide

Males are more commonly affected; peak incidence affecting individuals in 2nd & 3rd decades

Pathogenesis:

Deposition of immune complexes in the mesangium; antibodies are formed against galactose deficient polymeric IgA1.

Presentation:

Recurrent gross hematuria during or immediately following an upper respiratory tract infection(unlike PSGN, where there will be a period of 1-3 weeks)

Persistent microscopic hematuria ± proteinuria

Biopsy shows mesangial IgA deposits, which is composed of polymeric IgA joined by J chain.

Prognosis:

Renal failure develops in 30% patients over 20-25 years.

MEST C score is used for prognosis.

Treatment:

Conservative; ACE inhibitors in patients with proteinuria; steroids for patients with persistent proteinuria or presenting with Rapidly progressive Glomerulonephritis

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 314, Pg: 2339.

question_text: A 35-year-old man has been given some painkillers by his GP for pleuritic chest pains following a chest infection. 2 weeks later he presents again with ankle oedema. His blood pressure is 130/70 mmHg, and urine dipstick reveals protein +++ and no blood. Plasma creatinine is 1.4 mg/dl.What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Here the patient has mild renal impairment with urine dipstick showing 3+ proteinuria.

The very short history points against renal amyloidosis. Amyloidosis can cause heavy proteinuria with bland urinary sediments. But the patient lacks other features that may predispose to renal amyloidosis.

FSGS and Membraneous nephropathy causes variable degree of hematuria along with proteinuria.

So the most appropriate option is an acute interstitial nephritis. The point against an interstitial nephritis is the 3+ proteinuria. Tubulointerstitial diseases usually cause mild proteinuria<1g/day. Heavy proteinuria is seen in glomerular diseases. But here the semiquantitative method is used which may not reflect the actual amount. Also NSAIDs can cause heavy proteinuria by involving the glomerulus.

The most frequent causes of acute interstitial nephritis can be found in one of three general categories:

  • drug-induced (NSAID, anti TB drugs, sulphonamides)
  • infection-associated (legionella, HIV, Hep C)
  • immune or neoplastic disorders (SLE, Sjogrens, Wegeners).

The clinical presentation can range from asymptomatic elevation in creatinine or blood urea or abnormal urinary sediment, to generalized hypersensitivity syndrome with fever, rash, eosinophilia, and oliguric renal failure.Proteinuria is much more common in NSAID-induced nephritis than other causes. Resolution of proteinuria should occur with discontinuation of NSAID drugs, although steroids can be used in cases of heavy proteinuria.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 310, Pg: 2302

question_text: A 57-year-old man has presented with chest pain and pulmonary oedema. He has acute coronary syndrome. His blood pressure was 85/60 mm Hg. He is also suffering from pneumonia caused by streptococcus and was treated with augmentin (amoxicillin + clavulanic acid). His blood pressure improved on the second day of admission. His blood tests on admission show a creatinine of 1.45 mg/dl rising up to 1.90 mg/dl and then 2.50 mg/dl the day after. Urine dipstick showed 1+ proteinuria, with muddy brown hyaline casts. On the 5ᵗʰ day, the serum creatinine became 1.3 mg/dL. What is the likely cause of renal failure?
explanation:
We have a patient who suffered from hypotension due to an acute coronary syndrome, with a rapidly improving renal failure. Here the spontaneous improvement along with the presence of muddy hyaline casts points to the diagnosis of an Acute tubular necrosis.

In UTI, there pyuria on urinalysis, along with typical symptoms.

Post streptococcal glomerulonephritis will lead to presence of RBC or RBC casts and not hyaline cast. Interstitial nephritis due to Augmentin may also be considered, but the typical muddy casts rules it out. Urine in interstitial nephritis will also show hyaline casts, (but not muddy), WBC cast or WBCs.

URINALYSIS in AKI:


Acute tubular necrosis or (ATN) involves the death of tubular cells that form the tubule that transports urine to the ureters while reabsorbing 99% of the water. Tubular cells continually replace themselves and if the cause of ATN is removed then recovery is likely.

Causes of ATN

  • Sepsis
  • Ischemia
  • Toxins -
    1. Endogenous: Hemolysis, rhabdomyolysis, myeloma, intratubular crystals
    2. Exogenous: Iodinated contrast, aminoglycosides, cisplatin, amphotericin B, PPIs, NSAIDs

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:310 Pg: 2304

question_text: A 55-year-old man presents with chest pain and is thrombolysed for an acute myocardial infarction. His blood pressure was 85/40 for several hours on admission. Two days later his blood tests showed a urea of 140 mg/dl and creatinine of 3 mg/dl (Urea and Electrolytes were normal on admission). What would a renal biopsy show?
option_d: IgG deposition in the basement membrane
explanation:
So this question again deals with ischemic acute tubular necrosis.

The outer medulla, which contains the S3 segment of the proximal tubule is particularly vulnerable to hypoxia because of its high metabolic rate.

Contributing factors for ATN include: reduced renal reserve as in CKD, elderly, sepsis, nephrotoxins, rhabdomyolysis, co-existing SIRS.

Due to hypoperfusion, acute tubular necrosis may occur. This would show necrosis or loss of tubular cells.


The epithelium of the tubules seen here is ragged from undergoing necrosis with acute tubular necrosis (ATN) from ischemia.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:310 Pg: 2298,2299.

question_text: A 20-year-old registered drug addict is brought unconscious to the emergency department. It's not known how long he was on the floor of his apartment. Blood tests on admission revealed a bicarbonate of 19 mmol/l, creatinine of 2.80 mg/dl, urinary sodium of 60 mmol/l and a urine osmolality of 220 mOsmol/l. There is evidence of acute sepsis.(Ref values: s. creat: 0.6-1.4 mg/dl; S. urea:  17- 43 mg/dL; s. sodium: 135-145 meq/L; S. potassium: 3.5-5 meq/L; urinary sodium: 20 mmol/l; urine osmolality: 50 to 1200 mOsm/kg)What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
option_a: Pre-renal failure due to a prolonged period of unconsciousness
option_d: Renal artery embolus secondary to drug injecting
explanation:
So this question basically deals with utilizing the blood and urine parameters to differentiate pre renal from intrinsic renal failure.


So we can exclude option A.

Sepsis is initially leads to reduced GFR by vasodilation, mimicking pre renal AKI. Later in its course, sepsis leads to endothelial damage and will show features of intrinsic renal failure. so we don’t know the duration of disease and since sepsis can cause both the pictures, it is not the appropriate answer.

Acute tubular necrosis is possible here, as it causes a low urine osmolarity and loss of sodium in urine.

Renal artery embolism, as in infective endocarditis, produces glomerulonephritis like picture with hematuria and RBC cast, which is not mentioned.

Since we have the option of ATN, that should be chosen

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 310 Pg:2305

question_text: Fractional Excretion <1% occurs in which of the following?
explanation:
The FeNa is the fraction of the filtered sodium load that is not reabsorbed by the tubules, and is a measure of both the kidney’s ability to reabsorb sodium as well as endogenously and exogenously administered factors that affect tubular reabsorption.With prerenal azotemia, the FeNa may be <1%, suggesting avid tubular sodium reabsorption. In patients with CKD, a FeNa significantly >1% can be present despite a superimposed prerenal state.The most common clinical conditions associated with prerenal azotemia are hypovolemia, decreased cardiac output, and medications that interfere with renal autoregulatory vascular responses such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and inhibitors of angiotensin II.

Option A: In ATIN, since there is tubular inflammation sodium reabsorption is affected hence FeNa is >1%

Option B: In ischemic AKI, the FeNa is frequently >1% because of tubular injury and resultant impaired ability to reabsorb sodium

Reference: Harrison's principles of internal med 21st ed, chap 310 pg. 2296, 2305

question_text: Oliguria is defined as urine output <__/24hrs
explanation:
Oliguria defined as U.O. <400 mL/24 hrs

Anuria is defined as U.O <100 mL/24 hrs

Causes of Anuria: complete bilateral urinary tract obstruction, a vascular catastrophe (dissection or arterial occlusion) renal vein thrombosis, acute cast nephropathy in myeloma, renal cortical necrosis, severe ATN, combined therapy with NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and/ or ARBs, and hypovolemic, cardiogenic, or septic shock.

Reference: Harrison’s principles of internal med 21ˢᵗ ed, chap 52 pg. 336

question_text: Which of the following is/are novel biomarkers for acute kidney injury?
explanation:
Option A: Kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1) is a type 1 transmembrane protein that is abundantly expressed in proximal tubular cells injured by ischemia or multiple, distinct nephrotoxins, such as cisplatin. It can be detected after ischemic or nephrotoxic injury in the urine and plasma

Option B: Neutrophil gelatinase associated lipocalin (NGAL, also known as lipocalin-2 or siderocalin) is another biomarker of AKI. NGAL was first discovered as a protein in granules of human neutrophils. It is highly upregulated after inflammation and kidney injury and can be detected in the plasma and urine within 2 h of cardiopulmonary bypass–associated AKI.

Other biomarkers include:

  • Plasma levels of soluble urokinase Plasminogen Activator Receptor(suPAR)
  • Urinary concentration of two cell-cycle arrest biomarkers, insulin-like growth factor binding protein 7 (IGFBP7) and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-2 (TIMP-2) (option C) - predictive biomarkers for higher risk of the development of moderate to severe AKI.
  • Cystatin C
  • Osteopontin
  • β-D-glucosaminidase
  • Clusterin

Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 21st ed, Chap 310 Pg. 2305

question_text: Which of the following procedures is most likely to cause postoperative Acute Kidney Injury?
explanation:
The procedures most commonly associated with AKI are cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (particularly for combined valve and bypass procedures), vascular procedures with aortic cross clamping, and intraperitoneal procedures.Severe AKI requiring dialysis occurs in ~1% of cardiac and vascular surgery procedures.Longer duration of cardiopulmonary bypass is a risk factor for AKI.

Mechanisms of AKI in Cardiopulmonary bypass procedures:

  • Ischemic injury from sustained hypoperfusion
  • extracorporeal circuit activation of leukocytes and inflammatory processes 
  • hemolysis with resultant pigment nephropathy
  • aortic injury with resultant atheroemboli.

Reference: Harrison's principles of internal med 21st ed, chap 310, pg. 2299
