question_text: A 66-year-old lady, post-myocardial infarction, is suspected to have a left ventricular apical thrombus. What is the most suitable imaging technique for confirming this diagnosis?
explanation:
The most suitable imaging technique for confirming the presence of a left ventricular apical thrombus is Transthoracic Echocardiography (Option D).

  • Transthoracic Echocardiography (TTE) is the initial imaging modality of choice in evaluating cardiac structure and function. It is non-invasive and can provide real-time images of the heart. In the case of a suspected left ventricular apical thrombus, TTE can visualize the thrombus directly, allowing for a reliable diagnosis.

Now, let's consider the other options:

  • Cardiac MR (Option A): Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is a powerful tool for assessing cardiac structure and function. While it can detect thrombi, it is typically used for more detailed evaluation after an initial diagnosis has been made, often with TTE.
  • Left Ventricular Angiography (Option B): This involves injecting contrast dye into the coronary arteries to visualize the heart's chambers. While it can detect thrombi, it's an invasive procedure and this technique carries a risk of dislodging and embolisation of the intraventricular thrombus, So it's generally reserved for cases where other imaging methods like TTE have provided inconclusive results or when planning interventions.
  • Multiple Uptake Gated Acquisition Scanning (Option C): This is not a standard imaging technique for evaluating cardiac thrombi. It's more commonly used in nuclear medicine for assessing myocardial perfusion and function.

In summary, while multiple imaging modalities can contribute to the evaluation of cardiac thrombi, Transthoracic Echocardiography (TTE) is typically the initial and most suitable choice due to its non-invasive nature and direct visualization capabilities.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition

question_text:
A 12 year old patient has Down's syndrome. He has over the past year become progressively more breathless, is losing weight and feeling lethargic. He is also becoming blue when running with the dog during walks.
Which of the following cardiac lesions might be responsible?
option_d: Ventricular septal defect with Eisenmenger syndrome
explanation:
Down's syndrome leads to an endocardial cushion defect (between the atrial and ventricular septum). This can present as atrial septal defect (ASD), ventricular septal defect(VSD) or an Atrioventricular Septal Defect.

Given the clinical presentation including the development of severe fatigue and cyanosis, VSD with Eisenmenger syndrome (reversal of left to right shunt) is most likely.

VENTRICULAR SEPTAL DEFECTS -

  • Most common cause of congenital heart disease.
  • They close spontaneously in around 50% of cases.
  • The most common site for a VSD -Perimembranous.
  • Classically a pan-systolic murmur which is inversely proportional to the defect size is present in the left sternal border. Heard loudest in a small defect.

Fallot's tetralogy presents with VSD, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (pulmonary stenosis), right ventricular hypertrophy along with an over-riding aorta.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:264 pg:1833

question_text: Which of the following is correct about 1 degree AV block?
option_a: Normal PR and prolonged RR interval
option_c: Normal heart rate and short PR
explanation:
Explanation:

First-degree AV block is characterized by a prolonged PR interval on the electrocardiogram (ECG) but with a normal RR interval, indicating that all atrial impulses are still being conducted to the ventricles, albeit with a delay. This type of AV block typically involves a delay within the AV node, but other parts of the conduction system can also be involved. The prolongation of the PR interval (greater than 200 milliseconds) is the defining feature of first-degree AV block.

First-Degree AV Block:

  • Definition:First-degree AV block involves a fixed prolongation of the PR interval more than 200 milliseconds on an ECG.
  • Conduction Delay:The delay in conduction typically occurs within the AV node, although other parts of the conduction system like the atria, His bundle, and Purkinje system can be involved.
  • Conduction Characteristic:Despite the delay, electrical conduction is not interrupted; hence, all atrial impulses are conducted to the ventricles, which is why the term "block" is somewhat of a misnomer.
  • ECG Appearance:
    • The PR interval is consistently prolonged.
    • The RR interval remains normal as atrial impulses continue to be conducted regularly to the ventricles.

Comparison with Other AV Blocks:

  • Second-degree AV block (Type I and Type II) involves intermittent failures of conduction, with Type I showing progressive prolongation of the PR interval until a beat is dropped, and Type II showing a fixed PR interval with sudden loss of conduction without prior prolongation.
  • Third-degree (complete) AV block shows complete interruption of atrial to ventricular conduction, leading to complete AV dissociation.

Explanation of other options:

Normal PR and Prolonged RR Interval (Option A): First-degree AV block requires a prolonged PR interval, not a normal one. A prolonged RR interval suggests bradycardia, which is not a defining feature of first-degree AV block.

Prolonged PR and Prolonged RR (Option B): While PR is prolonged, the RR interval remains normal in first-degree AV block. Prolonged RR is more common in bradyarrhythmias like sinus bradycardia or second-degree AV block.

Normal Heart Rate and Short PR (Option C): First-degree AV block is defined by PR prolongation, so a short PR interval rules it out. Short PR intervals are seen in conditions like Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome due to an accessory pathway.

Key Takeaways:

First-degree AV block is characterized by a prolonged PR interval (>200 ms) with a normal RR interval, indicating delayed but consistent conduction of atrial impulses to the ventricles.

question_text: Which condition is characterized by absence of P waves?
explanation:
Explanation:

AF is an arrhythmia with irregularly irregular ventricular response and absent P waves due to chaotic atrial activity.

Explanation of other options:

Ventricular tachycardia (Option A): In VT, the heart rate is markedly increased. P waves are usually still present, but they may not correlate with the QRS complexes because of the abnormal ventricular rhythm.

Focal atrial tachycardia (Option B): This rhythm arises from a single ectopic atrial focus, producing rapid atrial activity. P waves remain visible and identifiable.

Ventricular fibrillation (Option C): A life-threatening arrhythmia marked by chaotic and disorganized ventricular electrical activity. Since atrial activity is absent, P waves are not seen. However, the key characteristic of VF is the irregular fibrillatory pattern, not simply the absence of P waves.

question_text: An intern observed that a patient in the ward was unresponsive. An urgent ECG showed a rhythm as depicted below. A DC shock was delivered, but the arrhythmia persisted, and the patient remains unresponsive. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The ECG depicts ventricular fibrillation (VF), a shockable rhythm. According to the Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) protocol, after a failed first defibrillation attempt, the immediate next step is to resume high-quality CPR for 2 minutes before delivering a second shock.

Rationale for Starting CPR

The initial defibrillation attempt may not successfully reorganize the heart's electrical activity. The period immediately following a shock is characterized by myocardial stunning and poor perfusion. CPR is critical during this interval to provide coronary and cerebral perfusion, making the heart more likely to respond to a subsequent defibrillation attempt. Delivering another shock immediately (Option C ruled out) or administering drugs (Option D ruled out) without CPR is less effective.

ACLS Algorithm for Persistent VF/VT

The correct sequence after the first unsuccessful shock is:

  1. Resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes.
  2. Establish IV/IO access and secure the airway.
  3. Then, administer Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO.
  4. After 2 minutes of CPR, check the rhythm and deliver a second shock if VF/VT persists.

Algorithm for Management of Cardiac arrest in adults by the American Heart Association


Explanation of other options:

Synchronized cardioversion (Option A): This is used for unstable tachyarrhythmias with a pulse (e.g., atrial fibrillation, VT with a pulse). It is contraindicated in pulseless rhythms like VF, as the shock must be delivered asynchronously (defibrillation).

Deliver another DC shock (Option C): ACLS protocol mandates 2 minutes of CPR between shock attempts to perfuse the heart. A second shock without intervening CPR has a very low success rate.

Administer 1 mg epinephrine (Option D): While epinephrine is a key drug in cardiac arrest, it is administered during CPR, not before initiating chest compressions. Starting CPR takes precedence over drug administration.

Key Takeaways:

  • For persistent VF after the first defibrillation, the next step is always to resume CPR for 2 minutes.
  • The sequence is Shock → CPR (2 min) → Rhythm Check → Shock.
  • Synchronized cardioversion is not used for pulseless arrest.

question_text: Which of the following is the most appropriate position for placement of a single-lead pacemaker?
explanation:
Explanation:

A single-lead pacemaker, also known as a VVI pacemaker, is designed to pace and sense only the ventricles. The standard and most appropriate position for its lead is the right ventricle, typically anchored in the right ventricular apex or the septum.

Rationale for Right Ventricular Placement

  • Primary Goal: The main purpose of a single-lead pacemaker is to prevent life-threatening bradycardia (e.g., complete heart block, symptomatic sinus node dysfunction). Pacing the right ventricle ensures ventricular contraction and maintains an adequate cardiac output.
  • Safety and Stability: The right ventricle provides a stable anatomical location for lead fixation. Placing a lead in the left side of the heart (Options B and C ruled out) would require crossing the interatrial or interventricular septum, which is not standard practice for a simple single-lead system and carries a risk of thromboembolism.
  • Functionality: The lead in the right ventricle effectively captures the ventricular myocardium, initiating a depolarization wave that leads to a QRS complex and ventricular systole.

Pacemaker Types

  • Single-Chamber (VVI): One lead in the Right Ventricle.
  • Dual-Chamber (DDD): Two leads in the Right Atrium and Right Ventricle.
  • Biventricular (CRT-P): Three leads in the Right Atrium, Right Ventricle, and Left Ventricle (via the coronary sinus).

Explanation of other options:

Left atrium (Option B): This is not a standard site for any permanent pacemaker lead. Atrial pacing, when needed, is performed from the right atrium.

Left ventricle (Option C): The left ventricle is paced only in biventricular pacemakers (CRT) for cardiac resynchronization therapy in heart failure. This requires a specialized lead placed via the coronary sinus, not as a single-lead system.

Superior vena cava (Option D): The pacemaker lead must pass through the superior vena cava to reach the heart, but it is never the final placement site. The lead must contact the endocardium to deliver the electrical impulse.

Key Takeaways:

  • The standard placement for a single-lead (VVI) pacemaker is the right ventricle.
  • Leads are never placed in the systemic circulation (left atrium/ventricle) for standard pacing due to thromboembolic risk.
  • The superior vena cava is a transit route, not a placement site.

question_text: The HV interval shown in the His bundle electrogram below represents conduction time from:
option_b: From AV node to bundle of His
option_d: From a bundle of His and bundle branches to ventricles
explanation:
Explanation:

The HV interval measures the time taken for electrical conduction to travel from the His bundle through the bundle branches to the ventricles.

A typical His bundle electrogram consists of:

  • A: Atrial deflection
  • H: His bundle deflection
  • QRS: Ventricular depolarization

The measured intervals are:

  • P-H: Time from the start of the P wave (on standard ECG or high atrial lead) to the initial rapid deflection of the His bundle spike (Option B ruled out).
  • A-H: Time from the onset of the atrial deflection on the His bundle electrogram (low right atrium) to the His bundle deflection (Option A ruled out)..
  • H-V: Time from the first rapid deflection of the His bundle to the start of ventricular depolarization, measured on either the His bundle electrogram or standard ECG leads.

Option C is incorrect.

Reference:

https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/pdf/10.1161/01.cir.47.4.897

question_text: Which of the following drugs will cause Torsades de Pointes if given with erythromycin?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Astemizole significantly prolongs the QT interval, and when co-administered with erythromycin (a CYP3A4 inhibitor), it increases the risk of life-threatening Torsades de Pointes.

  • Torsades de Pointes (TdP) is a distinctive form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that occurs in the setting of prolonged QT interval, often drug-induced.
  • It can deteriorate into ventricular fibrillation and cause sudden cardiac death.
  • Risk factors include electrolyte imbalance (especially hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia), bradycardia, congenital long QT syndromes, and most importantly drugs that prolong the QT interval.

Astemizole

  • Astemizole is a non-sedating H1 antihistamine, previously used for allergic rhinitis and urticaria.
  • It has now been withdrawn in many countries due to its high risk of cardiac arrhythmias.
  • Mechanism:
    • Astemizole and its active metabolite desmethylastemizole inhibit the (Ikr/hERG) potassium channel, which is critical for ventricular repolarization.
    • This blockade prolongs the QT interval on ECG, predisposing to early after depolarizations (EADs) and triggering Torsades de Pointes.
    • When combined with erythromycin, a known CYP3A4 inhibitor, metabolism of astemizole is inhibited, leading to elevated plasma levels and exacerbated QT prolongation.
    • This interaction is synergistically proarrhythmic and potentially fatal.

Explanation of other options:

Levofloxacin (Option B): A fluoroquinolone that can prolong the QT interval on its own. However, it is less likely to interact significantly with erythromycin as it is not extensively metabolized by CYP3A4, and the risk of Torsades is lower than with astemizole.

Amoxicillin (Option C): A beta-lactam antibiotic with no known effect on cardiac repolarization or QT interval. It does not interact with erythromycin in a way that would cause QT prolongation or TdP.

Ceftriaxone (Option D): A third-generation cephalosporin that is cardiac-neutral. It neither affects QT interval nor interacts with CYP enzymes in a way that predisposes to TdP.

Reference:

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9165570/#

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8023479/#

https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/astemizole

question_text: What is the next best step in management of a pulseless patient with the following rhythm?
option_c: Check pulse and give synchronized DCP
option_d: Give synchronized DC and continue chest compression
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

In a pulseless patient with suspected ventricular tachycardia (VT), the immediate step is unsynchronized defibrillation with continued chest compressions.

  • The clinical situation describes a pulseless patient with a wide complex regular rhythm, strongly suggesting pulseless monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT).
  • In this scenario, defibrillation is the cornerstone of management.

Understanding Ventricular Tachycardia (VT):

  • VT is a potentially life-threatening arrhythmia that arises from the ventricles.
  • Defined as ≥3 consecutive wide QRS complexes at a rate >100 bpm.
  • Monomorphic VT: All QRS complexes appear similar; usually due to a reentrant circuit in scarred myocardium.
  • Polymorphic VT: Varying QRS morphology; often associated with prolonged QT or electrolyte abnormalities.
  • ECG Findings in Monomorphic VT:
    • Wide QRS complexes (>120 ms)
    • Regular rhythm
    • Absence of clear P waves
    • May mimic bundle branch block patterns
  • Management Approach Based on Hemodynamic Status:
    • Stable VT (with pulse):
      • Antiarrhythmic drugs like amiodarone, procainamide, or lidocaine
    • Unstable VT (with pulse):
      • Synchronized cardioversion
    • Pulseless VT or VF (ventricular fibrillation):
      • Immediate unsynchronized defibrillation (not synchronized cardioversion)
      • High-quality CPR must be continued without delay
    • Why Defibrillation + CPR is Critical:
      • Defibrillation delivers a shock at a random phase of the cardiac cycle (unsynchronized), aiming to stop the chaotic electrical activity and allow the heart to reestablish a perfusing rhythm.
      • CPR maintains circulation until return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) is achieved.

Explanation of other options:

Defibrillate and check pulse (Option B): Pulse check should be done after delivering the shock and resuming CPR for 2 minutes, not before.

Check pulse and give synchronized DC (Option C): Synchronized DC cardioversion is indicated for hemodynamically unstable VT with pulse-not in a pulseless patient.

Give synchronized DC and continue chest compression (Option D): Synchronized shocks are not appropriate for pulseless rhythms; defibrillation (unsynchronized) is required.

question_text: What does the ECG in the following image depict?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The ECG demonstrates a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a characteristic spindle-like pattern of the QRS complexes twisting around the baseline, along with a prolonged QT interval, confirming the diagnosis of Torsades de Pointes.

ECG features:

  • Polymorphic VT: Characterized by variation in QRS direction and amplitude.
  • Spindle-shaped pattern: The QRS complexes form a twisting or spindle-shaped "envelope".
  • Prolonged QT interval
  • PVC initiation: Often triggered by a premature ventricular contraction (PVC) on a prolonged T-U wave, creating an "R on T" phenomenon.
  • Postectopic pause: A pause following the PVC, further prolonging repolarization.
  • Causes of QT Prolongation (A TIGERS BITE Mnemonic)

Treatment:

  • Administer IV magnesium sulfate (even with normal magnesium levels).
  • Discontinue all QT-prolonging drugs.
  • Correct electrolyte imbalances, focusing on hypokalemia.
  • Increase heart rate with temporary pacing or isoproterenol to shorten the QT interval.

Explanation of other options:

Acute pericarditis (Option A) : It shows T-wave inversion following ST-segment elevation in the ECG.
Viral myocarditis (Option B) : It shows prolonged QRS, QT prolongation, diffuse T wave inversion, ventricular arrhythmias, and AV conduction defects in the ECG.
Cardiac tamponade (Option D) : It shows consecutive normally-conducted QRS complexes that alternate in height (electrical alternans) and low QRS voltage with tachycardia in the ECG.

question_text:
Sequence after p wave?
A. A wave
B. 1st heart sound
C. Rapid filling of ventricles
D. T wave
explanation: P wave corresponds to the electrocardiographic atrial systole, which corresponds to the a wave of JVP. Atrial systole(reduced filling phase) is followed by ventricular systole, marked by the closure of the AV valves or the first heart sound. This is followed by the ventricular ejection(QRS) into the aorta and pulmonary artery. This is followed by the ventricular diastole(T wave), which is marked by the closure of the semilunar valves 2nd heart sound, the AV valves are already closed. During this phase the atria gets filled. When the ventricular pressure falls below the atrial, the AV valves open and the passive filling or the rapid filling phase occurs. Followed by atrial systole.

question_text: Patient is on metoprolol and if he is given Verapamil, what is the effect that occurs ?
explanation:
Metoprolol is a beta blocker. It causes bradycardia by acting on the β 1 receptor in the heart.

Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker and is an AV nodal blocking agent. It causes bradycardia by blocking the AV node.

In the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, where depolarization is due primarily to a Ca2+-dependent slow inward current, the Verapamil slow the sinus pacemaker and inhibit atrioventricular conduction.

So the combined effect will be bradycardia with AV blocks.

question_text: Athletic syndrome is characterized by:
explanation: The answer is A (Increased amplitude of QRS complex): Athletic Heart Syndrome Athletic Heart Syndrome is a benign condition consisting of physiologic adaptations to the increased cardiac workload of exercise in trained athletes. It represents a constellation of clinical findings that are the result of normal physiologic adaptation to strenuous physical activity. In response to the increased physical demand, the left ventricles dilate and wall thickness increases. The mass to volume ratio, however, does not change. Physical examination Decreased body fat and increased muscle mass (generally very physically fit) Pulse slow and often irregular (sinus bradycardia or bradycardia with first-and second-degree blocks) Grade I or II mid-systolic murmurs (benign functional ejection murmur resolves with Valsalva maneuver) Third and fourth heart sounds very common (benign filling sounds) Blood pressure typically remains normal Electrocardiogram rhythm Rhythm - Sinus bradycardia of 40 to 55 beats /min while at rest - Sinus pauses of more than 2.0 seconds due to increased vagal tone - Wandering atrial pacemaker found only in dynamic athletes - First degree atrioventricular block present only at rest; P-R interval normalizes with exercise - Second degree atrioventricular block present only at rest: Mobitz I (wenckebach block) common in marathon runners; Mobitz II rare in athlete's heart. Voltage: TORS voltage (Amplitude) - Left ventricular hypertrophy found in 85% of Olympic marathon runners - Right ventricular hypertrophy common in dynamic athletes but rarely seen in sedentary controls and static athletes sedentary control and static athletes Repolarization - S-T segment elevation with peaked T waves normalizes with exertion - S-T segment depression may be rarely found in athletes T-wave inversion in lateral leads associated with interventricular septal hypertrophy in static athletes (can be a normal finding in dynamic athletes) Chest radiography - The heart is globular in appearance, particularly in endurance athletes. - Cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio >0.50)

question_text: Paradoxical splitting of second heart sound is seen in?
explanation: Answer is C (LBBB) Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB) is typically associated with Reversed or Paradoxical Splitting of S2 Paradoxical splitting of second heart sound is caused by delayed A2 or early P2. Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB) is associated with delayed Aortic closure (delayed A2) due to delayed electrical activation of the left ventricle. ASD and RBBB are associated with a wide physiological (non- paradoxical) split of second heart sound due to delayed pulmonic closure (Delayed P2) while VSD is associated with a wide physiological (non-paradoxical) split second heart sound from early aortic closure (Early A2).

question_text: A 65 year old woman who is on digoxin has symptoms of nausea and dizziness. On examination, her heart rate is 35 bpm and an ECG shows prolonged PR interval with first degree heart block.Digoxin toxicity is more likely with which of the following conditions?
explanation:

question_text: Tall and tented T waves, wide QRS, and absent P wave are features of:
explanation:
Explanation:

The triad of peaked (tented) T waves, QRS complex widening, and loss of P waves is the classic and progressive ECG presentation of hyperkalemia. This occurs due to impaired cardiac conduction and depolarization from elevated serum potassium levels.

Explanation of other options:

Bundle branch block (Option A): Causes QRS widening and secondary T-wave changes (discordance) but does not characteristically cause peaked T waves or absent P waves

Acute MI (Option B): Can cause hyperacute T waves (broad and asymmetric), but these are transient and are not associated with QRS widening or absent P waves in isolation.

Ventricular ectopic (Option D): Produces a wide QRS complex but is a single beat, not a sustained rhythm with the described triad.

Key Takeaways:

  • Hyperkalemia causes a sequence of ECG changes: Peaked T waves → QRS widening → Loss of P waves → Sine wave pattern → Asystole.
  • Recognizing this pattern is critical for emergent management

question_text: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The ECG demonstrates ventricular tachycardia (VT), characterized by wide, regular QRS complexes and a heart rate typically exceeding 100 beats per minute.

Ventricular Tachycardia (VT):

Definition:

VT is defined as three or more consecutive premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) with a ventricular rate greater than 100 bpm. It can be classified into:

  • Monomorphic VT: All QRS complexes have a similar shape.
  • Polymorphic VT: QRS complexes vary in shape and amplitude.

Causes:

  • Monomorphic VT is commonly due to a re-entry circuit around a scarred area of the myocardium, often following a myocardial infarction.
  • Polymorphic VT, including Torsades de Pointes, is often linked to prolonged QT interval, ischemia, or electrolyte disturbances (like low magnesium or potassium).

ECG Characteristics:

  • Monomorphic VT:
    • Wide QRS complexes (>120 ms)
    • Regular rhythm
    • QRS complexes maintain a uniform morphology
    • QRS axis and morphology depend on the site of origin (e.g., resembles LBBB or RBBB)

Certainly! Here's the rephrased explanation of Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia in bullet points:

  • Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia (VT)
  • Involves QRS complexes that vary in shape and amplitude throughout the rhythm.
  • Displays an irregular or varying ventricular rate.
  • Commonly associated with a prolonged QT interval.
  • A classic form is Torsades de Pointes, which shows a twisting of the QRS complexes around the isoelectric line.
  • Often triggered by:
  • Electrolyte imbalances (e.g., low potassium or magnesium)
  • Medications that prolong the QT interval

Treatment:

  • Stable Monomorphic Ventricular Tachycardia (VT):
    • Administer IV procainamide or amiodarone.
  • Unstable Monomorphic VT:
    • Requires immediate synchronized cardioversion.
  • Polymorphic VT (e.g., Torsades de Pointes):
    • Give IV magnesium sulfate.
    • Correct electrolyte imbalances (e.g., hypokalemia).
    • Stop any QT-prolonging medications.

Explanation for other options:

Normal ECG (Option A): Incorrect, as the ECG shows tachycardia, absent P waves, and broad QRS complexes - features not seen in a normal ECG.

Ventricular Fibrillation (Option B): Unlikely, because ventricular fibrillation lacks identifiable QRS complexes, unlike the ECG shown.

Misplaced Leads (Option D): Misplacement of ECG leads does not cause this pattern, making this option incorrect.

question_text: The use of prostaglandin to keep the ductus arteriosus open is necessary in which of the following?
explanation:
Ductus dependent congenital heart disease (require a patent ductus for maintaining pulmonary / systemic circulation)

- Transposition of Great arteries

- Tetralogy of Fallot

- Tricuspid atresia (Ebstein anomaly)

- Coarctation of aorta

- Hypoplastic left heart syndrome

- Pulmonary stenosis

PGE1 is used to maintain an open ductus arteriosus in neonates with heart lesions that depend on it for survival.

In Gerbode defect, there is a direct communication between right atrium and left ventricle.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2011-12

question_text:
A 39 year old lady has a pulmonary systolic murmur which is louder on inspiration. The second heart sound is wide and fixed with splitting.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The second heart sound typically has A2 (aortic) and P2 (pulmonary) components.

Wide fixed splitting of second heart sound is heard in Atrial Septal Defect (ASD).

  • In ASD, there is a left to right shunt which leads to prolonged right ventricular ejection and increased pulmonary artery capacitance, which, in turn, delays pulmonary valve closure.

A systolic murmur is heard inthe pulmonary area because of increasedpulmonary valve flow due to pulmonaryhypertension.


ASD is the most common symptomatic congenital heart disease diagnosed in adults. Bicuspid aortic valve may be more common in adults, but is often an incidental finding.

In RBBB there is wide splitting of S2 but it is not fixed.

Aortic stenosis leads to reversed splitting (also seen with LBBB and ventricular pacemaker).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:234,264 pg:1671, 1832

question_text: A patient with a history of coronary artery disease presents with chest pain and palpitations. The ECG provided below is suggestive of a specific arrhythmia. Which of the following is the preferred drug for management?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given case and ECG features are consistent with ventricular tachycardia (VT) in the setting of ischemic heart disease.

  • ECG Findings:
    • Wide QRS complexes (>120 ms)
    • Absence of P waves or evidence of atrioventricular dissociation
    • Ventricular rate exceeding 100 bpm
  • Symptoms of VT: Palpitations, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, and syncope
  • Management:
    • Hemodynamically stable VT: The drug of choice is intravenous amiodarone.
      • Mechanism: Class III antiarrhythmic, prolongs repolarization and increases refractory period.
    • Hemodynamically unstable VT: Requires immediate synchronized electrical cardioversion.
    • Torsades de Pointes (Polymorphic VT): Managed with intravenous magnesium sulfate.

Resuscitation Algorithms: Shockable vs Non-Shockable Rhythms

Shockable Rhythms:

  • Ventricular fibrillation (VF)
  • Pulseless VT

Non-shockable Rhythms:

  • Asystole
  • Pulseless electrical activity (PEA)

Shockable Rhythm Algorithm (VF/Pulseless VT):

  1. Recognition: Identify rhythm as VF or pulseless VT.
  2. Activate Emergency Response: Call for advanced life support.
  3. Initiate CPR: Perform high-quality compressions at a rate of 100-120/min, depth of 5-6 cm, with minimal interruptions. Continue for 2 minutes.
  4. Defibrillation: Deliver a non-synchronized DC shock.
    1. If no return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), deliver a second shock immediately.
  5. Resume CPR: Continue for 2 minutes post-shock.
  6. IV/IO Access: Establish intravenous or intraosseous line.
  7. Administer Epinephrine: 1 mg IV/IO (1:10,000) after 2 minutes of CPR; repeat every 3-5 minutes.
  8. Airway Management:
    1. Secure airway with endotracheal intubation if indicated.
    2. Monitor with capnography (end-tidal CO2).
    3. Provide ventilation at 1 breath every 6 seconds once intubated.
  9. Further Defibrillation:
    1. Deliver third non-synchronized shock if VF/pulseless VT persists.
    2. Continue CPR for another 2 minutes.
  10. Antiarrhythmic Therapy: Administer amiodarone 300 mg IV for shock-refractory VT/VF.
  11. Identify and Treat Reversible Causes: Focus on 5 H's (hypoxia, hypovolemia, hydrogen ion [acidosis], hyper-/hypokalemia, hypothermia) and 5 T's (tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis coronary, thrombosis pulmonary).

Non-Shockable Rhythm Algorithm (Asystole/PEA):

  1. Recognition: Confirm rhythm as asystole or PEA.
  2. Activate Emergency Response: Call for advanced life support.
  3. Initiate CPR: Perform high-quality compressions (100-120/min, 5-6 cm depth) for 2 minutes.
  4. IV/IO Access: Establish intravenous or intraosseous line.
  5. Administer Epinephrine: 1 mg IV/IO (1:10,000) every 3-5 minutes, beginning after first CPR cycle.
  6. Rhythm Check:
    1. If rhythm remains non-shockable, continue CPR and epinephrine.
    2. If rhythm converts to shockable (VF/pulseless VT), deliver a DC shock.
  7. Airway and Ventilation:
    1. Secure airway with endotracheal intubation if required.
    2. Monitor ventilation with capnography.
    3. Provide 1 breath every 6 seconds with advanced airway.
  8. Reversible Causes: Identify and correct underlying causes (5 H's & 5 T's).
  9. Repeat Cycles: Continue CPR and epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, reassess rhythm after each cycle.

Explanation of Other Options:

Oral Metoprolol (Option A): A selective β1-blocker used in angina, hypertension, and chronic heart failure. Not appropriate in acute VT where immediate control is necessary.

Oral Amiodarone (Option B): Utilized in long-term suppression of VT, AF, and VF. Due to delayed onset, it is not effective in acute management.

Intravenous Metoprolol (Option D): Sometimes used in acute MI to reduce myocardial oxygen demand but is not first-line for VT.

question_text: Patient comes with palpitations to ER. His pulse-180 bpm and BP -70/50 mm of hg. ECG shows narrow qrs complex tachycardia with regular heart rate. What is the next step in management?
explanation: The patient in the given question is having a regular narrow complex tachycardia with a blood pressure of <90mmHg systolic, which is considered as unstable hemodynamics, which should be managed by cardioversion.

question_text: A 28-year-old asymptomatic male undergoes routine medical evaluation for job recruitment. His ECG reveals a PR interval of 0.21 seconds, but no dropped beats or irregular rhythms are noted. He has no history of cardiovascular disease and no symptoms like palpitations or syncope. What is the most appropriate diagnosis based on the ECG findings?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

A PR interval >0.20 seconds with no dropped beats is diagnostic of first-degree AV block.

  • First-degree AV block is defined by a prolonged PR interval (>0.20 seconds) on ECG, representing delayed conduction through the AV node or proximal conduction system.
  • Importantly, every P wave is followed by a QRS complex, indicating that conduction is delayed but not blocked.
  • Etiologies include:
    • Increased vagal tone (in athletes or young individuals)
    • Fibrosis of the conduction system in the elderly
    • Myocardial ischemia, MI
    • Drugs (e.g., beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin)
    • Infectious/inflammatory diseases (e.g., Lyme disease, rheumatic fever, myocarditis)
    • Infiltrative diseases (sarcoidosis, amyloidosis)
  • Clinical features:
    • Usually asymptomatic
    • Rarely, patients with very prolonged PR intervals may experience symptoms due to atrial contraction occurring too early before ventricular filling ("pseudo-pacemaker syndrome")
  • ECG Features:
    • PR interval >0.20 seconds
    • Regular rhythm
    • No dropped QRS complexes
  • Management:
    • Typically no treatment is needed
    • Periodic follow-up with ECG
    • Consider pacing only if associated with symptoms or other conduction disease

ECG's of Heart Blocks

Explanation of other options:

Normal ECG (Option B): The upper limit of a normal PR interval is 0.20 seconds; a PR of 0.21 seconds is prolonged, thus not a normal finding.

2nd-degree block (Option C): Characterized by intermittent dropped QRS complexes:

  • Mobitz I (Wenckebach): Progressive PR lengthening followed by a dropped beat.
  • Mobitz II: Sudden dropped beats without PR prolongation. Neither are seen in this case.

Complete heart block (Option D): There is no AV conduction; the atria and ventricles beat independently, and PR intervals are variable or unrelated. This is not consistent with a constant prolonged PR interval and 1:1 conduction.

Reference:

First-Degree Heart Block - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

1st degree heart block: Causes, symptoms, and treatment

question_text: Whilst attending the clinic, the staff nurse measures the blood pressure of a 61-year-old man, and finds that it is 183/100 mmHg sitting and 190/105 mmHg standing. He has a heart rate of 81/minute, with an irregularly irregular rhythm. On auscultation of the heart, there are no murmurs, but he has bibasilar crackles on chest examination. Which of the following pathological findings is most likely to be present?
explanation:
This patient is likely to have a hypertensive cardiomyopathy with a left ventricle hypertrophy.

The LVH is secondary to increased afterload, as a result of chronic hypertension. The atrial fibrillation suggested by an irregularly irregular pulse, is an indicator of diastolic dysfunction and poor ventricular filling.

This in turn indicates pulmonary congestion, as evidenced by the bibasal crackles.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1932-33

question_text: A 66-year-old man who is known to have ischaemic heart disease is due to start a chemotherapy regime which includes doxorubicin. You want to accurately assess his left ventricular function as you are concerned the doxorubicin may damage his myocardium.Which one of the following is the most accurate method to determine his left ventricular function?
explanation:
Cardiac imaging: non-invasive techniques excluding echocardiography

The ability to image the heart using non-invasive techniques such as MRI, CT and radionuclides has evolved rapidly over recent years.

Nuclear imaging

These techniques use radiotracers which are extracted by normal myocardium. Examples include:

  • Thallium
  • Technetium (99mTc) sestamibi: a coordination complex of the radioisotope technetium-99m with the ligand methoxyisobutyl isonitrile (MIBI), used in 'MIBI' or cardiac Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) scans.
  • Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG): used in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scans
  • The primary role of these scans are- to assess myocardial perfusion and myocardial viability.

MUGA (radionuclide angiography)

Multi Gated Acquisition Scan, also known as radionuclide angiography

  • Radionuclide (technetium-99m) is injected intravenously
  • The patient is placed under a gamma camera
  • Can accurately measure left ventricular ejection fraction. Typically used before and after cardiotoxic drugs are used.

Cardiac Computed Tomography (CT)

  • Cardiac CT is useful for assessing suspected ischaemic heart disease, using two main methods:
  • Calcium score: there is known to be a correlation between the amount of atherosclerotic plaque calcium and the risk of future ischaemic events. Cardiac CT can quantify the amount of calcium producing a 'calcium score'

Cardiac MRI

  • Cardiac MRI (commonly termed CMR) has become the gold standard for providing structural images of the heart. Useful in assessing LV mass and differentiating forms of cardiomyopathy

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2037

question_text: A 70-year-old male presents with recurrent fainting episodes. His ECG shows P waves at a rate of 75 bpm and QRS complexes at a rate of 35 bpm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The clinical manifestations indicate Stokes Adams syndrome - sudden, transient episodes of syncope resulting from intermittent complete heart block or severe bradyarrhythmia.
  • The ECG findings show P waves at 75 bpm with QRS complexes at 35 bpm, demonstrating AV dissociation typical of complete heart block or IIIrd degree heart block.
  • This indicates a complete interruption of electrical conduction between the atria and ventricles, leading to independent atrial and ventricular rhythms.

Third-degree atrioventricular block

  • Refers to the complete failure of conduction between atria and ventricles, resulting in independent beating (AV dissociation).
  • Ventricular Activity is maintained by an escape rhythm from:
    • The AV node or bundle of His (narrow QRS complexes).
    • Distal Purkinje tissues (broad QRS complexes).

Clinical features

  • Recurrent syncope or 'Stokes-Adams' attacks- sudden loss of consciousness and collapse.
  • Brief anoxic seizure.
  • Pallor and a death-like appearance during the attack; characteristic flush upon recovery.
  • Rapid recovery distinguishes it from epilepsy.

ECG Findings

  • Prolonged PR interval
  • Broad QRS complex
  • Number of P waves will not be equal to the number of R waves
  • P-R interval (atrial rate) will not match the R-R interval (ventricular rate)

Fig: ECG showing complete heart block - AV dissociation, with the atrial rate (~100 bpm) independent of the ventricular rate (~40 bpm).

Management

  • Transient AV block in acute inferior myocardial infarction, requires no treatment if the patient remains stable.
  • Symptomatic third-degree AV block are managed with intravenous atropine or intravenous isoprenaline to maintain circulation until temporary pacing is inserted.
  • Permanent pacemaker.

Explanation of other options:

Mobitz type II heart block (Option A): A form of 2nd degree AV block in which there is intermittent non-conducted P waves without progressive prolongation of the PR interval. Thus, in Mobitz type II heart block there is normal PR intervals of 200ms.

First degree heart block (Option C): A first degree heart block will show prolonged PR interval >200ms with 1:1 AV conduction. This is typically asymptomatic and would not cause the presenting symptoms of recurrent syncope.

Wolf-Parkinson white syndrome (Option D): WPW Syndrome refers to the presence of a congenital accessory pathway (AP) and episodes of tachyarrhythmias. It presents with a short PR interval <120ms and delta waves. This represents pre-excitation through an accessory pathway and does not cause the AV dissociation seen in this case.

question_text: A 65-year-old man with no significant past medical history is admitted to the Emergency Department. His ECG is consistent with an anterior myocardial infarction. Unfortunately, he develops cardiac arrest shortly after arriving in the department. What is the most common cause of death in patients following a myocardial infarction?
explanation:
Myocardial infarction: Complications

Patients are at risk of a number of immediate, early and late complications following a myocardial infarction (MI).

Cardiac arrest

This most commonly occurs due to patients developing ventricular fibrillation and is the most common cause of death following a MI. Patients are managed as per the ALS protocol with defibrillation.

Cardiogenic shock

If a large part of the ventricular myocardium is damaged in the infarction the ejection fraction of the heart may decrease to the point that the patient develops cardiogenic shock. Other causes of cardiogenic shock include the 'mechanical' complications such as left ventricular free wall rupture. Patients may require inotropic support and/or an intra-aortic balloon pump.

Chronic heart failure

As described above, if the patient survives the acute phase their ventricular myocardium may be dysfunctional resulting in chronic heart failure.

Tachyarrhythmias

Ventricular fibrillation is the most common cause of death following a MI. Other common arrhythmias including ventricular tachycardia.

Bradyarrhythmias

Atrioventricular block is more common following inferior myocardial infarctions.

Pericarditis

Pericarditis in the first 48 hours following a transmural MI is common (c. 10% of patients). The pain is typical for pericarditis (worse on lying flat etc), a pericardial rub may be heard and a pericardial effusion may be demonstrated with an echocardiogram.

Dressler's syndrome tends to occur around 2-6 weeks following a MI. The underlying pathophysiology is thought to be an autoimmune reaction against antigenic proteins formed as the myocardium recovers. It is characterized by a combination of fever, pleuritic pain, pericardial effusion and a raised ESR. It is treated with NSAIDs.

Left ventricular aneurysm

The ischaemic damage sustained may weaken the myocardium resulting in aneurysm formation. This is typically associated with persistent ST elevation and left ventricular failure. Thrombus may form within the aneurysm increases the risk of stroke. Patients are therefore anticoagulated.

Left ventricular free wall rupture

This is seen in around 3% of MIs and occurs around 1-2 weeks afterwards. Patients present with acute heart failure secondary to cardiac tamponade (raised JVP, pulsus paradoxus, diminished heart sounds. Urgent pericardiocentesis and thoracotomy are required.

Ventricular septal defect

Rupture of the interventricular septum usually occurs in the first week and is seen in around 1-2% of patients. Features: acute heart failure associated with a pansystolic murmur. An echocardiogram is diagnostic and will exclude acute mitral regurgitation which presents in a similar fashion. Urgent surgical correction is needed.

Acute mitral regurgitation

More common with infero-posterior infarction and may be due to ischaemia or rupture of the papillary muscle. A pansystolic murmur is typically heard. Patients are treated with vasodilator therapy but often require emergency surgical repair.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page no: 2063

question_text:
A 27 year old patient with systemic lupus erythematosus attends the obstetric clinic at 25 weeks into her pregnancy. The fetal heart rate is 45 beats per minute. Foetal echocardiography shows complete heart block.
Which one of the following is false?
option_a: Anti Ro (SSA) antibody will be seen in maternal serum
option_b: Complete heart block of the fetus can be reversed with Dexamethasone
option_c: HCQ should be given to mothers with previous history of CHB in fetus
option_d: Structural heart disease can also be associated with anti Ro antibodies
explanation:
Complete heart block, once developed always require pacing. Dexamethasone is given to mother for first and second degree heart block in fetus, so that progression to CHB is prevented.

NEONATAL LUPUS:

  • Congenital heart block with or without cardiomyopathy- life-threatening
  • Vigilant monitoring of heart rate in Ro antibody positive mothers.
  • HCQ treatment of an anti-Ro-positive mother - reduces the chance that subsequent fetuses will develop heart block.
  • No treatment for heart block. -Dexamethasone(and not prednisolone, since fluorinated steroids cross the placenta) treatment of a mother in whom fetal first- or second-degree heart block is detected only prevents progression to complete heart block.
  • Structural heart diseases like ASD, VSD, PDA, PFO can be seen with neonatal lupus.
  • Rash is similar to Sub acute cutaneous lupus.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:356 Pg:2747

question_text:
A 74-year-old man who has a history of ischaemic heart disease and left Ventricular dysfunction is admitted with dyspnoea. He has not taken his diuretics for three days as he ran out. On examination you note bilateral crackles to the midzones and a respiratory rate of 30/min.
Which other clinical finding is specific with this presentation?
explanation:
Pulsus alternans is the presence of alternating strong and weak pulse- seen in left ventricular failure

Pulsus paradoxus

  • Greater than the normal (10 mmHg) fall in systolic blood pressure during inspiration → faint or absent pulse during inspiration; seen in severe asthma, cardiac tamponade

Slow-rising/plateau

  • Aortic stenosis

Collapsing pulse

  • Aortic regurgitation

  • Hyperkinetic (anaemia, thyrotoxic, fever, exercise/pregnancy)

Bisferiens pulse

  • 'Double pulse' - two systolic peaks
  • seen in mixed aortic valve disease and Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

'Jerky' pulse

  • Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1937

question_text:
An elderly man develops syncope. He is known to have ischaemic heart disease. Peripheral pulses are absent, and ECG reveals wide-complex tachycardia.
Immediate management consists of which of the following?
option_c: A bolus dose of intravenous lidocaine
explanation:
• The patient has ventricular tachycardia and is hemodynamically unstable indicated by loss of consciousness.
  • Immediate treatment consists of cardioversion followed by a suitable anti-arrhythmic such as lidocaine IV or amiodarone and correction of any electrolyte imbalance.
  • Myocardial infarction (MI) is the likely cause of ventricular tachycardia, hence treatment for MI would be indicated if required. Programmed stimulation may only be carried out when the patient is stable.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page no: 2252

question_text: What is the most likely diagnosis in the patient with the ECG shown in the image?

question_text: A 19-year-old woman presents with numbness and paraesthesia of fingers, triggered by cold or stress. The image shows characteristic findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Primary Raynaud's phenomenon is characterized by excessive constriction of blood vessels in the fingers or toes in response to cold or emotional stress. This leads to episodic numbness, tingling, and sequential color changes (white → blue → red). It occurs without any associated systemic disease and is most commonly seen in young women.

In this patient, the absence of comorbid conditions supports Primary Raynaud's phenomenon as the most likely diagnosis.

Raynaud's Phenomenon:

Primary Raynaud's:

  • No underlying systemic disease
  • Normal nail fold capillaries
  • Accounts for over 50% of cases
  • Generally has a favorable prognosis
  • Spontaneous improvement occurs in ~15%, while progression is seen in ~30%

Explanation of other options:

Secondary Raynaud's (Option B): Associated with connective tissue disorders, vascular disease, drugs, or occupational exposure.

Cold sores (Option C): Herpes simplex virus; affects lips, not fingers.

Scleredema (Option D): Thickening and hardening of skin, unrelated to episodic digital color changes.

question_text: Which of the following is not a feature associated with acute aortic regurgitation?
explanation:
Acute Aortic regurgitation

- occurs due to infective endocarditis, aortic dissection or trauma

- Unlike chronic AR, LV cannot adapt to the large regurgitant volume resulting in backflow to LA and pulmonary edema

- Reduction is stroke volume in acute severe AR can result in profound hypotension and cardiogenic shock

- Peripheral vasodilation leading to waterhammer pulse observed with chronic AR is absent in acute AR

- Surgical correction is mandatory after initial stabilisation with inotropic and peripheral vasodilatory agents.

explanation:
The different mechanisms for occurrence of mitral regurgitation in acute MI include:

  1. Papillary muscle dysfunction due to ischemia
  2. Partial or complete rupture of chordae tendinae

question_text: A 40 year old patient presents with vomiting episodes followed by severe abdominal pain, blood in stool and prostration. His bp IS 90/50 mm hg and pulse is 180 bpm with irregularly irregular rhythm. Per abdomen finding is unremarkable except for absent bowel sounds. Past medical history of CAD. Which is the most probable cause?
explanation:
A severe abdominal pain with hypotension and AF, with minimal abdominal findings is the most common presentation in acute mesenteric ischemia(95%).

Acute mesenteric ischemia can be embolic or thrombotic.

Embolic mesenteric ischemia is suspected in elderly patients with risk factors for embolism like AF, infective endocarditis, previous embolic events.

Thrombotic acute mesenteric ischemia is suspected in a patient with underlying thrombotic atherosclerotic disease.

AMI is a surgical emergency. In a suspected patient the gold standard investigation is CT angiography with 1mm cuts. If an acute embolic occlusion is detected, surgical exploration with resection of the ischemic bowel. A transverse arteriotomy is made and the thrombus should be removed. The return of blood flow is assessed clinically by noting the return of hyperemia to the bowel or by applying duplex at the antimesentric border. Second look surgery should be done in case of questionable bowel viability.

The gut is supplied by the Coeliac trunk, SMA and IMA.

There is extensive collateral formation along the gut wall. These collaterals meet at the splenic flexure and the sigmoid colon, where they are prone fro ischemia, known as the Griffiths and the Sudecks point respectively. These are the commonest sites of colonic ischemia.

Acute mesenteric ischemia may be, arterio occlusive, non occlusive or venous thrombosis. 50% of AMI is due to occlusion of mid to distal SMA. Embolic etiology includes AF, valvular heart disease, IE, recent cardiac catheterization, recent MI, soft atherosclerotic plaque. In >75% cases the source of emboli comes from the heart and lodges in the SMA

Non occlusive ischemia is seen in acute hemodynamic instability as seen in hypovolemic shock or drugs causing vasoconstriction. It is the most important and prevalent GI complications following a cardiovascular surgery.

Venous thrombosis is seen in hypercoagulable states either congenital or acquired.

question_text: A 30-year-old man is brought to ER with severe acute chest pain radiating to the back. He is pale and anxious.On examination the blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg and he was noted to have blue sclerae. Which of the following conditions has predisposed to this complication?
explanation:
Marfan's syndrome is one of the causes of blue sclerae. The clinical diagnosis is aortic dissection.

Disorders predisposing to aortic dissection are: essential hypertension, atherosclerosis, bicuspid aortic valve, connective tissue disorders, Marfan's syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, adult polycystic kidney disease.

Marfan's syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by a defect in the fibrillin-1 gene on chromosome 15.

Clinical features:

  • Tall stature with arm span to height ratio > 1.05
  • Upper to lower body ratio is decreased (head to symphysis pubis: symphysis pubis to toes).
  • High-arched palate
  • Arachnodactyly
  • Pectus excavatum
  • Pes planus
  • Scoliosis of > 20 degrees à Low back pain
  • Dural ectasia (ballooning of the dural sac at the lumbosacral level) – seen in 60% of patients. It may cause lower back pain associated with neurological problems such as bladder and bowel dysfunction like incontinence.
  • Heart - Dilatation of the aortic sinuses (seen in 90%) which may lead to aortic regurgitation, aortic aneurysm, aortic dissection, and mitral valve prolapse (75%) which causes systolic murmur at mitral area.
  • Lungs: repeated pneumothoraxes
  • Eyes: Upwards lens dislocation (supertemporal ectopia lentis), blue sclera, retinal detachment and myopia.

The life expectancy of patients used to be around 40-50 years. With the advent of regular echocardiography monitoring and beta-blocker/ACE inhibitor therapy this has improved significantly over recent years. 

Aortic dissection and other cardiovascular problems remain the leading cause of death however.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:274 pg:1917

question_text: A 44 year old man visit his family doctor with symptoms of flushing and dizziness. He also has watery diarrhoea several times a month. On examination he has a systolic murmur in the tricuspid area and a parasternal heave over the left sternal edge. A 24 hour urine shows raised 5HT levels. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a case of carcinoid syndrome.

  • Occurs due to increased metabolism of tryptophan into serotonin (5 HT).
  • Presents with episodic flushing, diarrhea, wheezing.
  • Right-sided valvular heart disease (eg, tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonic stenosis) can be seen.
  • Niacin deficiency (pellagra) Niacin is derived from tryptophan. In carcinoid syndrome, all the tryptophan is converted to serotonin. This causes a deficiency of niacin.
  • Diagnosed by raised urinary 5-HT levels.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 333, Pg: 2527

question_text: A 45-year-old patient has been commenced on nifedipine for hypertension.Which of the following effect describes the action of nifedipine?

explanation:
Nifedipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker.

The mechanism of action is smooth muscle relaxation and reduction in peripheral vascular resistance.

However, peripheral capillary pressure is increased (this causes oedema in the ankles), there is increased sympathetic activity and increased activation of the renin angiotensin aldosterone axis. There is also increased vascular release of nitric oxide.

question_text: A 5-year-old child has hyperflexible fingers and can touch the back of his hand with his wrist extended. The child also demonstrates the sign shown in the image below (Gorlin's sign: touching the nose with the tongue). On auscultation, a click is heard after S1, followed by a late systolic murmur. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The constellation of findings is classic for Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS), specifically the hypermobile type. The diagnosis is supported by the following key features:

  1. Generalized Joint Hypermobility: Demonstrated by the ability to touch the back of the hand with the wrist extended.
  2. Gorlin's Sign: The ability to touch the nose with the tongue is a classic, though not pathognomonic, sign of generalized connective tissue laxity seen in EDS.
  3. Cardiac Findings: The auscultatory finding of a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur is diagnostic of Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP), a common cardiovascular manifestation of EDS.

Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome

EDS comprises a group of heritable disorders characterized by defects in collagen synthesis and processing. The hypermobile type is the most common and is defined by:

  • Primary Features: Joint hypermobility, soft/smooth skin, and tissue fragility.
  • Systemic Involvement: Chronic musculoskeletal pain, autonomic dysfunction (e.g., POTS), and MVP are frequent associations.

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is classified into 13 clinical types associated with 20 genes, with common mutations involving COL1A1, COL1A2, COL3A1, COL5A1, and COL5A2.

Explanation of other options:

Marfan's syndrome (Option B): While Marfan's can cause MVP and some joint hypermobility, it is characterized by dolichostenomelia (long limbs), arachnodactyly, and ectopia lentis (lens dislocation), not the extreme skin and joint laxity seen here. Gorlin's sign is not typical.

Loeys-Dietz syndrome (Option C): This syndrome features arterial tortuosity and aggressive aortic aneurysms, hypertelorism, and bifid uvula. Joint hypermobility may be present, but the severe vascular phenotype dominates the clinical picture.

Osteogenesis imperfecta (Option D): This disorder is characterized by bone fragility leading to frequent fractures, blue sclerae, and hearing loss. Joint hypermobility and MVP are not hallmarks.

Key Takeaways:

  • The triad of joint hypermobility, Gorlin's sign, and mitral valve prolapse strongly points to Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
  • MVP presents auscultatorily as a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur.
  • EDS is a disorder of collagen, leading to systemic connective tissue laxity.

question_text: Female patients present with progressive worsening of dyspnea. On examination there is left parasternal heave, palpable liver, on auscultation a systolic murmur is heard. Investigation reveals right axis deviation of heart, what is the most probable cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most probable cause of the symptoms described - progressive worsening of dyspnea, left parasternal heave, palpable liver, and a systolic murmur heard on auscultation, combined with right axis deviation on the ECG - is Pulmonary stenosis (PS).

In pulmonary stenosis (PS), there is an obstruction at the level of the pulmonary valve or right ventricular outflow tract that impedes blood flow from the right ventricle to the pulmonary artery. Severe PS can lead to right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH) as the right ventricle works harder to overcome the obstruction. This condition presents clinically with features such as:

  • Dyspnea and fatiguedue to reduced cardiac output and right heart strain.
  • Physical signsincluding a left parasternal heave due to right ventricular hypertrophy.
  • Palpable liverwhich may indicate right heart failure.
  • Systolic murmurcaused by the turbulent flow across the stenotic pulmonary valve.

The right axis deviation seen on ECG is indicative of right ventricular hypertrophy, common in severe PS. This is a classic finding associated with conditions that put a strain or increase the workload on the right heart.

Explanation of other options:

Mitral Regurgitation (MR) (Option A): MR leads to left-sided heart failure → pulmonary congestion and pulmonary edema, not systemic venous congestion. Left parasternal heave and right axis deviation are not typical of isolated MR.

Pulmonary Edema (Option B): Pulmonary edema occurs in left-sided heart failure, not right-sided. No left parasternal heave or palpable liver, which are indicative of right heart strain. Pulmonary edema presents with bilateral crackles rather than a systolic murmur.

Pulmonary Hypertension (PH) (Option D): PH can cause right heart strain, but it typically presents with a loud P2 (accentuated pulmonary component of S2) rather than a systolic murmur. Right ventricular heave and palpable liver can be present, but PH is usually secondary to other conditions rather than a primary valvular issue.

Key Takeaways:

Pulmonary stenosis presents with a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur, left parasternal heave, right axis deviation, and signs of right heart failure (hepatomegaly, systemic congestion).

question_text: A 40-year-old female presents with complaints of chest pain, palpitations, and shortness of breath. On examination, a mid-diastolic murmur is heard, and a prominent 'a'wave is noted in the jugular venous pulse (JVP). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

A mid-diastolic murmur with a prominent 'a' wave in JVP points towards tricuspid stenosis, due to impaired right atrial emptying and elevated right atrial pressure.

  • Tricuspid stenosis (TS) is characterized by narrowing of the tricuspid valve, leading to obstruction of blood flow from the right atrium to the right ventricle during diastole.
  • This results in elevated right atrial pressure, producing a prominent 'a' wave in JVP, due to forceful atrial contraction against a stenotic valve.
  • The mid-diastolic murmur is typically heard best at the lower left sternal border or over the xiphoid and is accentuated during inspiration (Carvallo's sign), due to increased venous return to the right heart.
  • Other features include right atrial enlargement, evident as tall, peaked P waves in inferior leads (II, III, aVF) on ECG.
  • Hepatomegaly, ascites, and peripheral edema may also be present in advanced cases.

Types of Murmurs:

question_text: What is the clinical diagnosis for a young male who has no symptoms but is found to have a wide fixed split S2 during auscultation?
explanation:
Explanation:

A wide and fixed split of the second heart sound (S2) is the auscultatory hallmark of an Atrial Septal Defect (ASD). The shunt from the left to the right atrium causes increased blood flow through the pulmonic valve, delaying its closure (P2). This split does not vary with respiration because the shunt volume compensates for the normal respiratory variation in venous return.

Explanation of other options:
VSD (Ventricular Septal Defect) (Option B): Typically causes a harsh holosystolic murmur, not a

haracteristic S2 finding.

TOF (Tetralogy of Fallot) (Option C): It is characterized by a single S2 due to severe pulmonic stenosis.

BAV (Bicuspid Aortic Valve) (Option D): May cause an ejection click or a murmur of aortic stenosis/regurgitation, but not a fixed split S2.

Key Takeaways:

  • A wide, fixed split S2 is pathognomonic for an ASD.
  • Patients with ASDs are often asymptomatic until adulthood.

Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK535440/

question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic finding of Tricuspid regurgitation?

explanation:
Tricsupid regurgitation

- Around 90% is secondary to left sided valvular heart disease and pulmonary hypertension

- Syndromes associated with primary TR include Marfan syndrome, Carcinoid syndrome and with Ebstein anomaly

- Clinical examination shows elevated JVP with prominent c-v waves (Lancisi sign) and pulsatile hepatomegaly

- Pansystolic murmur is typically heard in the left lower sternal border that increases during inspiration (Carvallo sign)

Pansystolic murmur at apex is typically caused by mitral regurgitation. PSM at left lower sternal border can be caused by TR and VSD.

question_text: Identify the condition associated with the murmur depicted in the image below.
explanation:
Explanation:

A pansystolic murmur best heard at the apex and radiating to the axilla is characteristic of mitral regurgitation.

  • The image provided shows a pansystolic murmur, also known as a holosystolic murmur, which is a hallmark of mitral regurgitation (MR).
  • MR occurs when the mitral valve fails to close properly during systole, leading to retrograde flow of blood from the left ventricle (LV) to the left atrium (LA).
  • This murmur:
    • Begins with S1 and continues through to S2, hence the term pansystolic.
    • Is best heard at the apex of the heart.
    • Characteristically radiates to the axilla.
    • May be associated with a soft or absent S1, especially in chronic MR where the mitral valve leaflets are already poorly mobile.
    • Clinical signs of MR include:
      • Dyspnea (due to pulmonary congestion)
      • Fatigue (from reduced cardiac output)
      • Orthopnea, and
      • Atrial fibrillation (due to left atrial dilation)

The Janeway lesions of endocarditis are nontender, slightly raised hemorrhages on the palms and soles.

question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, palpitations, and breathlessness. On examination, blood pressure and oxygen saturation are normal, jugular venous pressure is elevated, the pulse is irregular, and tender hepatomegaly is present. Cardiac examination reveals a heaving apex and a mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. She has a past history of acute rheumatic fever. Which of the following statements regarding this patient is false?
option_a: This patient has an increased risk of stroke
option_c: This patient has features of right heart failure
option_d: Pre-systolic accentuation of the mid-diastolic murmur is a hallmark feature
explanation:
Explanation:

This patient likely has rheumatic mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation (AF)-suggested by paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, irregularly irregular pulse, elevated JVP with absent "a" wave, and a mid-diastolic murmur. Pre-systolic accentuation of the mid-diastolic murmur is typically heard only when sinus rhythm is present, due to atrial contraction. In atrial fibrillation, the "pre-systolic accentuation" is absent because there is no organized atrial kick.

  • Mitral stenosis (MS), most commonly caused by rheumatic fever, is characterized by obstruction to left ventricular inflow, leading to elevated left atrial pressure, pulmonary congestion, and eventually pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure.
  • A key auscultatory feature of MS is the opening snap, a high-frequency sound occurring shortly after the second heart sound (S2), due to the sudden tensing of the stenotic but still mobile mitral valve leaflets. However, when the valve becomes heavily calcified and immobile, the opening snap disappears.
  • AF leads to irregular rhythm and variable S1 intensity, making the auscultatory findings less consistent. A classic loud S1 and opening snap are typically not heard in persistent AF.
  • AF abolishes presystolic accentuation of the diastolic murmur, but the opening snap remains as long as the valve is still mobile.

Clinical Signs of Mitral Stenosis:

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

This patient has an increased risk of stroke (Option A): True-mitral stenosis with AF significantly increases embolic (stroke) risk.

"a" wave is absent on JVP (Option B): True-in AF, there is loss of coordinated atrial contraction, so no "a" wave.

This patient has features of right heart failure (Option C): True-elevated JVP and tender hepatomegaly suggest right-sided congestion.

question_text: Which of the following describes an aortic regurgitation murmur?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Aortic regurgitation (also known as aortic insufficiency) is a valvular heart disease where the aortic valve fails to close properly during diastole. This allows blood to flow backward from the aorta into the left ventricle.
  • The murmur associated with this backward flow occurs during ventricular relaxation (diastole), as the aortic valve should be closed but is incompetent.
  • It is typically described as a high-pitched, decrescendo diastolic murmur, best heard at the left sternal border with the patient leaning forward and holding expiration.
  • Clinical Features of Aortic Regurgitation
  • Blood Pressure Changes
    • Widened pulse pressure: Characterized by an elevated systolic pressure and a decreased diastolic pressure.
    • Low diastolic BP may also occur in conditions like atrioventricular malformation or fistula, due to continuous Korotkoff sounds.
    • Hill's sign: A positive sign refers to an abnormally higher systolic blood pressure in the lower limbs compared to the upper limbs (typically >20 mmHg difference).
  • Palpation Findings
    • Apical impulse: A heaving left ventricular impulse, displaced laterally and inferiorly due to left ventricular volume overload and dilation.
    • Thrills:
      • Diastolic thrill: May be felt at the left lower sternal border.
      • Systolic thrill: Sometimes detected in the suprasternal notch.
  • Auscultation - Heart Sounds
    • A₂ (aortic component of S₂): Often soft or absent.
    • Ejection sound: May be heard in cases with a bicuspid aortic valve.
    • S4 (atrial sound): Occasionally audible due to increased atrial contraction into a noncompliant, volume-loaded left ventricle.
  • Auscultation - Murmurs
    • Early diastolic murmur: A high-pitched, decrescendo blowing murmur, best heard at the left sternal border with the patient sitting up and leaning forward. Becomes holodiastolic as severity increases.
    • Musical diastolic murmur (cooing dove murmur): Results from flutter or eversion of an aortic cusp in the regurgitant stream.
    • Austin Flint murmur: A low-pitched mid- to end-diastolic rumble heard at the apex, caused by the regurgitant jet impinging on the anterior mitral valve leaflet, leading to functional mitral stenosis.
    • Ejection systolic murmur: Often present due to increased stroke volume across the aortic valve; may be mistaken for concomitant aortic stenosis

Classification of Murmurs
