question_text: Mitral stenosis is characterized by ?
explanation:
Explanation:

The opening snap is associated with mitral stenosis, and occurs after S2 due to the rapid opening of the stenotic mitral valve. The opening snap (OS) of the mitral valve is an important auscultatory finding in mitral stenosis (MS). It occurs as the stenotic mitral valve opens abruptly at the beginning of diastole when the left atrial pressure exceeds the left ventricular pressure. This sharp sound is:

  • Best heard at the apex of the heart, slightly medial to the apex.
  • Follows the aortic component of the second heart sound (A2) shortly after S2.
  • The time interval between A2 and OS is inversely related to the severity of mitral stenosis; a shorter interval indicates more severe stenosis.

Explanation of other options:

Midsystolic murmur (Option B): Midsystolic murmurs are typically associated with conditions like mitral valve prolapse or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, not mitral stenosis, which produces a diastolic murmur.

Mid diastolic murmur (Option C): Mitral stenosis is characterized by a mid-diastolic murmur. But the typical characteristic of this mid-systolic murmur is presystolic accentuation. As mid diastolic murmur can be seen in other conditions. This low-pitched, rumbling diastolic murmur is best heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral recumbent position and is accentuated by mild exercise.

Ejection click (Option D): Ejection clicks are typically associated with valvular stenosis but more commonly refer to aortic or pulmonary valve stenosis, not mitral stenosis.

Mitral Stenosis:

Inspection and Palpation:

  • Facial Features:Malar flush with pinched, blue facies may be noted.
  • Jugular Venous Pulse:Prominent a waves reflecting vigorous right atrial contraction, especially in patients with severe pulmonary hypertension or tricuspid stenosis (TS).
  • Arterial Pressure:Usually normal or slightly low.
  • Right Ventricle:Parasternal lift indicating RV enlargement.
  • Apex:Diastolic thrill may be rarely palpable with the patient in the left lateral recumbent position.

Auscultation:

  • First Heart Sound (S1):Usually accentuated and slightly delayed in the early stages.
  • Second Heart Sound (S2):Pulmonic component often accentuated with elevated pulmonary artery pressures (PAPs); S2 closely split.
  • Opening Snap (OS):Audible in expiration, just medial to the cardiac apex, follows A2 by 0.05-12 seconds.
  • Diastolic Murmur:Low-pitched, rumbling, heard best at the apex; duration correlates with the severity of stenosis.
  • Presystolic Accentuation:Murmur often reappears or becomes louder during atrial systole in patients with sinus rhythm.

Associated Findings:

  • Systemic Signs:Hepatomegaly, ankle edema, ascites, and pleural effusion, especially in the right pleural cavity, in cases of MS with RV failure.
  • Pulmonary Hypertension:Pansystolic murmur of functional tricuspid regurgitation (TR) along the left sternal border, louder during inspiration (Carvallo's sign).
  • Silent MS:Auscultatory findings may disappear when CO is severely reduced but may reappear as cardiac function improves.

Key Takeaways:

Mitral stenosis is best characterized by an "opening snap," which occurs due to the sudden tensing of thickened mitral valve leaflets. The disease also presents with a low-pitched, rumbling mid-diastolic murmur and a loud first heart sound (S₁).

question_text: Which is the preferred drug for managing acute rheumatic fever presenting with migratory joint pain and polyarthritis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Aspirin is the first-line anti-inflammatory therapy for symptomatic relief in a patient with acute rheumatic fever presenting with joint pain and polyarthritis.

Acute rheumatic fever: Management

  • Acute rheumatic fever (ARF) is a multisystem autoimmune disease that occurs as a post-infectious complication of group A Streptococcus infection.
  • Management of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) aims to relieve symptoms and prevent cardiac damage.
  • Bed rest is important as it reduces joint pain and cardiac workload.
  • Cardiac failure should be treated as needed, and severe cases with fulminant mitral or aortic regurgitation may require valve replacement; AV block usually resolves spontaneously, with pacemaker rarely required.
  • Antibiotics:
    • A single dose of benzathine penicillin or a 10-day course of oral phenoxymethylpenicillin are given to eradicate residual streptococcal infection.
    • Long-term penicillin prophylaxis is recommended to prevent recurrence, especially in high-risk individuals or those with residual heart disease.
  • Aspirin
    • Aspirin rapidly relieves arthritis, with doses of 60 mg/kg/day in children and up to 100 mg/kg/day in adults, continued until ESR normalizes.
  • Glucocorticoids
    • Indicated in severe arthritis or carditis, given as prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day and tapered once ESR normalises.

Explanation of other options:

Furosemide (Option A): Furosemide is a loop diuretic, used in management of congestive heart failure and as an antihypertensive.

Digoxin (Option B): Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside used in the treatment of heart failure, where it helps improve symptoms and significantly reduce mortality. It has also been used for rate control, particularly in patients prone to congestive heart failure.

Amiodarone (Option D): Amiodarone is a Class III antiarrhythmic used to treat atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. It prolongs the cardiac action potential and has multi-class antiarrhythmic effects.

question_text: A 50-year-old woman presents with exertional dyspnea and chest pain on exertion. Physical examination reveals a harsh systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. Echocardiography confirms the presence of aortic stenosis. Which of the following findings best distinguishes aortic stenosis from aortic regurgitation in terms of myocardial oxygen consumption?
option_a: Increase in preload causes more reduction in myocardial oxygen demand than increase in afterload
option_b: Workload is independent of myocardial oxygen consumption
option_c: Aortic stenosis results in lower pressure compared to aortic valve
option_d: Increase in myocardial oxygen consumption is more significant with pressure overload than volume overload
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Myocardial oxygen consumption increases more significantly in pressure overload (as in aortic stenosis) than in volume overload (as in aortic regurgitation).

  • Aortic stenosis (AS) leads to pressure overload on the left ventricle due to obstruction of blood flow across a narrowed aortic valve.
  • This pressure overload results in concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, which increases myocardial wall tension and oxygen demand.
  • The myocardium has to work harder to overcome the elevated pressure gradient across the valve, leading to a significant increase in myocardial oxygen consumption.
  • In contrast, aortic regurgitation (AR) primarily causes volume overload, resulting in eccentric hypertrophy.
  • Although this also increases myocardial workload, the oxygen demand rises more steeply in pressure overload than in volume overload, making this distinction important in clinical practice.
  • This explains why patients with aortic stenosis can develop angina even in the absence of coronary artery disease-due to a mismatch between the high oxygen demand of the hypertrophied myocardium and the compromised coronary blood flow.

Explanation of other options:

Increase in preload causes more reduction in myocardial oxygen demand than increase in afterload (Option A): Incorrect. Preload increases tend to augment stroke volume, but do not reduce myocardial oxygen demand. In fact, increased afterload (as in AS) raises oxygen demand more significantly.

Workload is independent of myocardial oxygen consumption (Option B): Incorrect. Myocardial oxygen consumption is directly proportional to the workload of the heart, especially in terms of pressure or volume stress.

Aortic stenosis results in lower pressure compared to aortic valve (Option C): Incorrect. Aortic stenosis causes increased intraventricular pressure due to obstruction at the aortic valve, not reduced pressure.

question_text: Mitral stenosis murmur coincides with:
explanation:
Explanation:

The murmur of mitral stenosis corresponds to the P wave of the ECG.

Mitral stenosis raises left-atrial pressure, which produces characteristic electrocardiographic and auscultatory changes.

Electrocardiographic features

  • Left atrial enlargement results in a broad, notched P wave in the limb leads and a biphasic P wave in lead V1, with a prominent terminal negative component reflecting delayed left-atrial depolarization.
  • When pulmonary hypertension is marked or when tricuspid stenosis is also present, right atrial enlargement may occur, giving a tall, peaked P wave in lead II and an upright P wave in V1.
  • The QRS complex generally remains normal, but significant pulmonary hypertension can lead to right-axis deviation and signs of right-ventricular hypertrophy.

Auscultation

  • An accentuated first heart sound (S1) is typical.
  • Following the aortic component of the second heart sound (A2), an opening snap (OS) is heard-best appreciated at the cardiac apex during expiration.
  • A low-pitched, rumbling, mid-diastolic murmur then follows the OS, most audible at the apex with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position. The intensity of this murmur correlates with the degree of mitral narrowing.

Explanation for other Options:

ST segment (Option A): Represents the period when the ventricles are fully depolarized and in the plateau phase of the action potential. This corresponds to the early part of ventricular systole, not the time of atrial contraction or diastolic filling.

QRS (Option B): Marks ventricular depolarization and the onset of ventricular systole. The mitral valve is closed during systole, so the mid-diastolic murmur of mitral stenosis does not coincide with this phase.

T wave (Option D): Reflects ventricular repolarization (end of systole and start of early diastole). While diastole begins here, the specific accentuation of the murmur occurs during atrial contraction, which happens later in diastole and aligns with the P wave, not the T wave.

question_text: A 25-year-old woman who is known to have a cardiac murmur becomes pregnant. It is noted that the intensity of her murmur diminishes during her pregnancy.Which cardiac abnormality is she likely to have?
explanation:
During pregnancy, cardiac output and blood volume increase from the second month up to the thirtieth week to 30-50% above the normal levels.

The decrease in peripheral vascular resistance during pregnancy cause a reduction in the regurgitant volumes in AR and MR. The MVP murmur remains same or reduced in intensity during pregnancy.

Murmurs of stenotic valve and coarctation increases during pregnancy due to increased force of contraction of heart and stroke volume.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1987

question_text: A 42-year-old woman is admitted with a stroke after a prolonged pyrexial illness. On examination she is in sinus rhythm, has splenomegaly and a pansystolic murmur at the apex. Blood cultures confirm an infective endocarditis.Which of the following is the most common causative organism?
explanation:
Most common cause for native valve endocarditis :

Streptococcus viridans > Staph aureus > Enterococcus

Most common cause for prosthetic valve endocarditis :

Coagulase negative Staph aureus > Staph aureus (Early, < 1 year)

Streptococcus viridans (Late, > 1 year)

Infective endocarditis in IV drug abusers : Staph aureus (right sided endocarditis)

Members of the viridans group of streptococci are the commonest cause of subacute endocarditis on native valves.These commensals of the upper respiratory tract may enter the bloodstream on chewing,tooth brushing or at the time of dental treatment. Staphylococcus aureus is a common cause of acute endocarditis originating from skin infections, abscesses,vascular access sites or intravenous drug misuse. Staphylococcus epidermidis is the most common organism causing postoperative endocarditis following cardiac surgery.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1023

question_text: Which of the following cardiac lesion confers the lowest risk for developing infective endocarditis?
explanation:

  2. Moderate risk: MVP with MR, MS, TS, TR
  3. High risk: AR, AS, MR, VSD, Coarctation of aorta, Prosthetic valves

question_text: A 42-year-old woman presents with a 1-month history of fatigue, weight loss, night sweats and a degree of exertional dyspnea. Her past history includes a prosthetic mitral valve replacement 2.5 years ago. Examination showed petechial hemorrhages in nails.ECHO confirms moderate paravalvular mitral regurgitation. Diagnosis of infective endocarditis was suspected and blood cultures are taken and a diagnosis of infective endocarditis made. What is the most likely culprit organism?
explanation:
• The commonest infective cause is Streptococcus viridans, accounting for around 40% of all cases.
  • Enterococcus species account for approximately 10% of cases, and they are more prevalent in the elderly.
  • Staphylococcus species account for around 25% of cases of endocarditis.

Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis (First Year After Replacement):

  • In the first year following prosthetic valve replacement, the spectrum of infecting organisms is somewhat different.
  • Coagulase-negative staphylococci, primarily Staphylococcus epidermidis, are the most common, accounting for around 50% of cases.

Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis (After the First Year Following Surgery):

  • After the first year following valvular surgery, the spectrum of infecting organisms is very similar to that for native valve endocarditis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1023

question_text: Which of the following give a clue regarding the severity of mitral stenosis in clinical examination?
explanation:
The clinical examination findings suggestive of severity of mitral stenosis include:

- duration of MDM (more duration suggests severity)

- gap between S2 and opening snap (shorter gap indicate more severe disease)

Mitral valve area less than 1 cm2 is indicative of severe MS (normal mitral valve area is 4 to 6 cm2)

The loudness of S1, presence of opening snap and intensity of murmur are not indicative of severity of mitral stenosis.

question_text: A 15 year old female developed rheumatic fever with carditis. There was no significant residual cardiac lesions. This patient need to take prophylaxis for rheumatic fever until the age of ____.
explanation:
For patients with RF without carditis, prophylaxis to be given for 5 years after last attack or till 18 years, whichever is longer

For patients with carditis and no severe involvement and significant residual disease, prophylaxis for 10 years or till the age of 21, whichever is longer

For patients with severe valvular involvement / post-surgery, prophylaxis need to be instituted lifelong.

Our patient had carditis with no significant cardiac involvement, hence she need prophylaxis for 10 more years (till 25 years)

question_text: A 23-year-old woman is seen in outpatients and is found to have loud first heart sound, an early diastole sound followed by a mid-diastolic murmur.What is the likely diagnosis?
option_a: Mitral stenosis with a calcified valve
explanation:
A loud first heart sound and when an opening snap is heard this indicates that the mitral valve is mobile. The snap occurs when the superior systolic bowing of the anterior mitral valve leaflet is rapidly reversed towards the left ventricle in early diastole, due to the high left atrial pressure.

When the valve leaflets are calcified, S1 is typically soft. (If the S1 is loud,  patient may be a likely candidate for balloon mitral valvuloplasty)

In patients with atrial fibrillation, S1 intensity varies depending on RR interval

Pulmonary hypertension would be associated with loud pulmonary component (P2) of 2nd heart sound

Atrial myxoma can produce an early diastolic sound(tumour plop), which is due to the abrupt diastolic seating of the tumour within the right or left atrioventricular orifice.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1992

question_text: A 24-year-old man's blood pressure is consistently 30 mmHg higher when measured in his right arm compared with his left arm.What is the most likely diagnosis?
option_b: Artifact due to lack of simultaneous recording
explanation:
In supravalvular aortic stenosis, the jet is preferentially directed up the innominate artery. Other findings might include a difference in carotid pulsation, as well as the murmur of aortic stenosis. In coarctation of the aorta, the narrowing is usually found just beyond the origin of the left subclavian artery. Hypertension in the arms and weak femoral pulses are the classic features of coarctation. The other choices are possibilities, but not the most likely diagnosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1980-81

question_text: Which if the following is not a documented cause of Mitral stenosis?
explanation:
Rheumatic fever contributes to >90% of all mitral valve stenosis. Other less common causes include:

  • Radiation therapy
  • Calcium deposition (age related)

Marfan syndrome is associated with aortic root dilatation, aortic regurgitation and mitral valve prolapse.

question_text: A 24-year-old student with a murmur which on assessment was found to have a harsh systolic murmur over his precordium, which did not change with inspiration. ECG showed features of biventricular hypertrophy.What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Right-sided murmurs increase with inspiration (eg: tricuspid regurgitation, TR), whereas left-sided murmurs show no change. The clue to diagnosis is in the ECG finding. Aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation produce left ventricular hypertrophy, TR produces right ventricular hypertrophy and a ventricular septal defect produces biventricular hypertrophy.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2011

question_text: A 52-year-old obese woman was noticed to have a systolic murmur over her precordium. Isometric exercise by handgrip intensified the murmur. What is the most likely cause of her murmur?

Decreased murmur intensity with handgrip

Sudden standing also decreases the MR murmur.

question_text: A 42-year-old healthy man attends a health check-up. He is found to have a faint systolic murmur. An echocardiogram reveals a bicuspid aortic valve.What should he be told?
option_a: His family members should be checked for a similar condition
option_b: He should start treatment with a cholesterol-lowering drug
option_c: He should undergo further tests to check for any autoimmune disorder
option_d: He may require heart surgery at a later date
explanation:
Bicuspid aortic valve occurs in 1-2% of adults and is one of the commonest forms of congenital heart disease in adults.

There is a familial incidence of around 9% but the occurrence tends to be sporadic. Around 1-2% of affected individuals require surgery in their fifth or sixth decade for worn out or calcified valves.

Long standing complications which may be associated with bicuspid aortic valve include aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation and aortic aneurysm

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1979

question_text: Which of the following is not true regarding the Modified Duke Criteria for diagnosis of infective endocarditis?

explanation:
Diagnosis of Infective endocarditis by Duke's criteria requires either clinical or pathological criteria to be met.

If clinical criteria are used, definitive IE is denoted by presence of 2 major / 1 major + 3 minor or 5 minor criteria

Presence of single pathological criteria is definitive of infective endocarditis

Clinical criteria

Pathological criteria

  1. Microorganisms demonstrated by culture or histologic examination, in vegetation, embolus from vegetation or intracardiac abscess

OR

  1. Histologic confirmation of active endocarditis in vegetation or intracardiac abscess

question_text: Which one of the following is the strongest risk factor for developing infective endocarditis?
explanation:
Infective endocarditis - strongest risk factor is previous episode of infective endocarditis

Infective endocarditis

  • The strongest risk factor for developing infective endocarditis is a previous episode of endocarditis. The following types of patients are affected:
  • Previously normal valves (50%, typically acute presentation)
  • Rheumatic valve disease (30%)
  • Prosthetic valves
  • Congenital heart defects
  • Intravenous drug users (IVDUs, e.g. Typically causing tricuspid lesion)

Causes

  • Streptococcus viridans (most common cause - 40-50%)
  • Staphylococcus epidermidis (especially prosthetic valves)
  • Staphylococcus aureus (especially acute presentation, IVDUs)
  • Streptococcus bovis is associated with colorectal cancer
  • Non-infective: systemic lupus erythematosus (Libman-Sacks)

Malignancy: marantic endocarditis

Culture negative causes

  • Prior antibiotic therapy
  • Coxiella burnetii
  • Bartonella
  • Brucella
  • HACEK: Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella)

Following prosthetic valve surgery Staphylococcus epidermidis is the most common organism in the first 2 months and is usually the result of perioperative contamination. After 2 months the spectrum of organisms which cause endocarditis return to normal, except with a slight increase in Staph. aureus infections.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1024

question_text: Which of the following is true regarding mitral stenosis?

explanation:
Mitral stenosis is typically a consequence of childhood rheumatic fever but congenital disease is well recognised.

It is associated with a tapping apex beat, a loud S1, Opening snap and Mid diastolic rumble with presystolic accentuation in those in sinus rhythm.

The opening snap is characteristically lost with heavy valvular calcification.

In particular Mitral stenosis is poorly tolerated in pregnancy due to volume overload. It is well characterized by doppler echocardiography.

Acute pulmonary edema occurs relatively early in the course of disease compared to other vavular lesions.

question_text: A 25-year-old patient is scheduled for a tooth extraction due to dental caries. In which of the following conditions is prophylaxis against infective endocarditis not required?
explanation:
Explanation:

Patients with atrial septal defect (ASD) generally do not require prophylaxis for infective endocarditis (IE) unless associated with additional complications such as large shunts or right-sided failure. Hence, ASD alone is not considered a high-risk condition.

Infective Endocarditis (IE):

  • Infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, most often involving valves.
  • Prophylaxis is recommended only for high-risk groups undergoing invasive procedures such as dental extraction.

High-Risk Conditions Requiring Prophylaxis:

  • Prosthetic heart valves (Option D) - both mechanical and bioprosthetic.
  • History of infective endocarditis (Option A) - prior infection increases recurrence risk.
  • Congenital heart disease (CHD):
    • Unrepaired cyanotic CHD (Option C)
    • Repaired CHD with prosthetic material (first 6 months)
    • Repaired CHD with residual defects
  • Cardiac transplant patients with valvulopathy.

Procedures where prophylaxis is indicated:

  • Dental: Extractions, periodontal procedures, root canal, implants.
  • Respiratory: Tonsillectomy, adenoidectomy, bronchoscopy with biopsy.
  • GI/GU: Endoscopy with biopsy, colonoscopy, cystoscopy (in high-risk patients).

Prophylaxis Regimen:

  • Amoxicillin: 2 g orally, 30-60 min before procedure.
  • Penicillin allergy alternatives: Clindamycin 600 mg or Azithromycin 500 mg orally.

Causative Organisms in Infective Endocarditis:

Explanation of other options:

Prior history of infective endocarditis (Option A): Requires prophylaxis since recurrence risk is high.

Unrepaired cyanotic CHD (Option C): Considered high-risk, prophylaxis mandatory.

Prosthetic heart valves (Option D): Strongest indication for prophylaxis due to high risk of infection.

Key Takeaways:

  • IE prophylaxis is restricted to a select group of high-risk patients.
  • Atrial septal defect alone does not warrant prophylaxis.
  • Amoxicillin is the standard prophylactic drug; alternatives available for penicillin allergy.

question_text: Large, Irregular, Friable deposits on the heart valves are seen in?

question_text: Which of the following statements is true regarding blood sample collection for infective endocarditis?

Explanation:

For infective endocarditis, the ideal practice is to collect 3 blood culture sets:

  • Each set contains 2 bottles: one aerobic and one anaerobic.
  • Samples are taken from 3 different sites over 24 hours, with a minimum gap of 2 hours between sets.
  • This maximizes the detection of causative organisms, as bacteremia may be intermittent.

question_text: A 55-year-old man presents to the hospital with complaints of palpitations. On physical examination, a diastolic murmur is heard at the left third intercostal space, and a pistol-shot sound is noted over the femoral arteries. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of a diastolic murmur along with a pistol-shot sound over the femoral arteries, combined with symptoms such as palpitations, is indicative of aortic regurgitation.

Aortic Regurgitation - Clinical Features

Blood Pressure Findings

  • Wide pulse pressure: Elevated systolic and decreased diastolic pressure.
  • Continuous Korotkoff sounds may be heard in cases with arteriovenous malformations or fistulas due to low diastolic pressure.
  • Positive Hill's sign: A notable difference in blood pressure between the upper and lower limbs (higher in the legs).

On Palpation

  • Heaving left ventricular impulse, often displaced laterally and downward due to left ventricular hypertrophy.
  • Thrills:
    • Diastolic thrill felt at the left lower sternal border.
    • Systolic thrill may be palpable at the suprasternal notch.

On Auscultation

Heart Sounds:

  • A2 (aortic component of second heart sound) may be diminished or absent.
  • Systolic ejection click may be heard if a bicuspid aortic valve is present.
  • Fourth heart sound (S4) may occasionally be heard.

Murmurs:

  • Early diastolic murmur: High-pitched, decrescendo type, best heard at the left third intercostal space, especially when the patient is sitting up and leaning forward.
  • In severe cases, this murmur may become holo-diastolic.
  • Musical diastolic murmur: Caused by fluttering of the aortic cusp in the regurgitant stream.
  • Mid-diastolic murmur (Austin Flint murmur): Low-pitched and rumbling, results from functional mitral stenosis due to the regurgitant jet hitting the anterior mitral leaflet.
  • Ejection systolic murmur may coexist, especially if aortic stenosis is also present.

Explanation for other options:

Aortic stenosis (Option B): typically presents with a midsystolic ejection murmur heard best at the upper left sternal border.

Tricuspid regurgitation (Option C): is characterized by a holosystolic murmur heard along the lower left sternal border.

Mitral regurgitation (Option D): presents with a systolic murmur best heard at the cardiac apex, often radiating to the left axilla.

Marfan syndrome commonly causes mitral valve prolapse and mitral regurgitation due to connective tissue abnormalities.

  • The image and clinical features suggest Marfan Syndrome, a connective tissue disorder inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern due to FBN1 gene mutation on chromosome 15, leading to abnormal fibrillin-1 protein.
  • This weakens connective tissue, particularly affecting the cardiovascular, ocular, and musculoskeletal systems.
  • Cardiac manifestations include aortic root dilation, aortic dissection, mitral valve prolapse, and mitral regurgitation-the latter being the most common cardiac complication.
  • Mitral regurgitation occurs due to valve floppiness and improper closure, causing backflow of blood into the left atrium during systole.
  • Key features of Marfan Syndrome:
    • Facial/Ocular: Long face, high-arched palate, ectopia lentis (superotemporal), myopia.
    • Musculoskeletal: Tall stature, arachnodactyly, pectus excavatum/carinatum, scoliosis, positive thumb (Steinberg) and wrist (Walker-Murdoch) signs.
    • Cardiovascular: Aortic root dilation, dissection (most common cause of death), mitral regurgitation.
    • Diagnosis: Based on Ghent criteria, supported by genetic testing and echocardiography.
      • Major criteria:
        • Aortic root dilation.
        • Ectopia lentis.
        • Skeletal features (e.g., arachnodactyly, scoliosis).
        • Family history of Marfan syndrome.
      • Minor criteria:
        • Joint hypermobility, myopia, high palate.
        • Genetic testing for FBN1 mutation confirms diagnosis
    • Management: Beta-blockers/ARBs, regular imaging, surgical repair of aortic root or mitral valve if needed.

Explanation of other options:

Aortic Stenosis (Option B): Typically due to calcific degeneration or congenital bicuspid valve; not a classic feature of Marfan syndrome.

Aortic Regurgitation (Option C): Can occur in Marfan's due to aortic dilation, but mitral regurgitation is more common and primary in early stages.

Mitral Stenosis (Option D): Usually post-rheumatic in origin and unrelated to connective tissue disorders like Marfan's.

question_text: Which part of the jugular venous waveform may be exaggerated in tricuspid regurgitation?
explanation:
JVP: giant v waves in tricuspid regurgitation

Jugular venous pulse

JVP refers to the pulsatile movement of blood within the internal jugular vein as it reflects the dynamic changes in right atrial pressure throughout the cardiac cycle

A non-pulsatile JVP is seen in superior vena cava obstruction.

Kussmaul's the sign describes a paradoxical rise in JVP during inspiration seen in constrictive pericarditis and restrictive cardiomyopathy.

'a' wave

  • Due to atrial contraction
  • Large a waves in high pressure e.g. tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary stenosis, pulmonary hypertension
  • Absent in atrial fibrillation
  • Cannon 'a' waves when atria contracts against a closed tricuspid valve – complete heart block, ventricular ectopics

'c' wave

Due to closure of tricuspid valve; not normally visible

'v' wave

  • Due to passive filling of blood into the atrium against a closed tricuspid valve
  • 'giant v waves' in tricuspid regurgitation

'x' descent

  • due to fall in atrial pressure during ventricular systole
  • Increased x descent in constrictive pericarditis and restrictive pericarditis

'y' descent = opening of tricuspid valve

  • Sharp and deep y descent in constrictive pericarditis (Friedreich's sign)

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page

question_text: A patient presents with progressive exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and hemoptysis. On examination, he has an irregularly irregular pulse, tapping apex beat, loud S1, and a low-pitched rumbling murmur. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation

  • The patient has classical features of mitral stenosis (MS):
    • Progressive exertional dyspnea and orthopnea due to pulmonary venous congestion.
    • Hemoptysis from rupture of bronchial veins secondary to elevated left atrial pressure.
    • Irregularly irregular pulse suggests atrial fibrillation, a common complication of MS.
    • Tapping apex beat and loud S1 are hallmark signs of MS.
    • The murmur of MS is a low-pitched, rumbling, mid-diastolic murmur best heard at the apex in left lateral position, often preceded by an opening snap.

Mitral Stenosis (MS):

  • Aetiology:
    • Primary Cause: Rheumatic fever is the leading cause of mitral stenosis, accounting for about 40% of cases in patients with a history of rheumatic heart disease.
    • Congenital abnormalities (e.g., parachute valve, cor triatriatum)
    • Mitral annular calcification with involvement of leaflets
    • Autoimmune diseases (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis)
    • Left atrial myxoma
    • Infective endocarditis with large vegetation
  • Pathology: Chronic inflammation leads to thickening of the valve leaflets, fibrous tissue formation, calcific deposits, and fusion of the mitral commissures and chordae tendinae. This process results in a narrowed, funnel-shaped valve. (Fish-mouth Appearance)
    • Normal mitral valve area: 4-6 cm²; significant obstruction of <2 cm².
    • Hemodynamics: In severe MS (<1.5 cm²), a left atrial (LA) pressure of ~25 mmHg is needed to maintain normal cardiac output (CO).
    • Effects of Heart Rate: Increased heart rate diminishes diastolic filling time, raising the LA pressure and transvalvular gradient
  • Symptoms:
    • Exertional dyspnea, cough, and progressive limitation of daily activities.
    • Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea can develop as MS worsens.
    • Atrial fibrillation (AF) often accelerates symptom progression.
  • Findings:
    • Inspection: Malar flush, jugular venous distension, and right ventricular (RV) enlargement.
    • Auscultation: A loud S1, an opening snap (OS) after S2, and a low-pitched, rumbling mid-diastolic murmur with presystolic accentuation- heard best at the apex.
      • Characteristics of a murmur in severe MS:
        • Decreased interval between A2 & OS.
        • Wide splitting of S2.
        • Palpable systolic thrill.
        • The duration of the murmur increases.
  • Investigations:
    • ECG: Often shows LA enlargement, right axis deviation, and RV hypertrophy.
    • Echocardiogram: Measures mitral inflow velocity and transvalvular gradients and evaluates for associated mitral regurgitation (MR) or other valvular lesions.
    • Chest X-ray: Shows LA enlargement, pulmonary vein dilation, and Kerley B lines indicating pulmonary congestion.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Mitral Stenosis - End diastolic murmur (Option A):

  • MS produces a mid-diastolic murmur, not a true end-diastolic one.
  • End-diastolic murmurs are more typical of aortic regurgitation (diastolic decrescendo murmur), not MS.

Tricuspid Stenosis - Pan systolic murmur (Option C):

  • Tricuspid stenosis produces a diastolic rumble, not a pan-systolic murmur.
  • A pan-systolic murmur is typical of tricuspid regurgitation, mitral regurgitation, or VSD, not TS.

Tricuspid Stenosis - Mid diastolic murmur (Option D):

  • While TS does cause a diastolic murmur, it is heard best at the left lower sternal border, increases with inspiration (Carvallo's sign), and is associated with systemic venous congestion (edema, hepatomegaly, ascites).
  • The patient's features (AF, tapping apex, hemoptysis, loud S1) are typical of mitral, not tricuspid, stenosis.

question_text: A 65-year-old man presents with chest pain, shortness of breath on exertion, and episodes of syncope. He is diagnosed with aortic stenosis, and a chest X-ray is performed (as shown below). What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Given the patient's symptoms - chest pain, exertional dyspnea, and syncope along with the confirmed diagnosis of aortic stenosis and supporting chest X-ray findings, the most likely diagnosis is post-stenotic dilatation of the aorta.

Aortic Stenosis (AS)

  • AS becomes hemodynamically significant when the aortic valve area narrows to around 1 cm².
  • Despite this severity, patients can remain asymptomatic for years due to left ventricular (LV) compensation.
  • Symptoms commonly emerge between the 6th and 8th decades, though patients with bicuspid aortic valves (BAV) may present 10-20 years earlier.

Classic Symptom Triad:

  • Exertional dyspnea
  • Angina pectoris
  • Syncope with exertion

Other clinical features:

  • Early signs: Fatigue, decreased exercise tolerance
  • Later stages: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, pulmonary edema
  • Advanced/late findings: Right heart failure, systemic venous congestion, hepatomegaly, atrial fibrillation, tricuspid regurgitation

Post-Stenotic Aortic Dilatation (PSAD)

Definition: PSAD refers to the enlargement of the ascending aorta just beyond a narrowed or abnormal aortic valve. It is typically diagnosed when the aortic diameter exceeds 4.0 cm and shows progressive enlargement of more than 0.3 cm/year.

PSAD can predispose patients to life-threatening complications such as:

  • Aortic dissection
  • Aortic rupture

Causes and Associations:

  • Seen in aortic stenosis (AS), aortic regurgitation (AR), and bicuspid aortic valve (BAV)-even when the valve is functioning normally
  • Can also develop after aortic valve replacement (AVR)
  • It's not always related to AS severity; genetic factors and hemodynamic stress also play a role
  • Bicuspid aortic valve is a major risk factor for both AS and progressive aortic dilatation

Imaging Features (e.g., on X-ray or echocardiogram):

  • Enlargement of the aorta just beyond the stenotic valve
  • Normal or narrowed aortic root proximal to the stenosis
  • Additional findings depend on the underlying cause

Explanation for other options:

Aortic root dilatation (Option A): is usually asymptomatic and often detected incidentally. However, in rare cases, it can lead to serious complications such as aortic dissection, rupture, or heart failure due to aortic regurgitation. This does not match the current clinical scenario.

Widening of the aortic knob (Option B): may be seen in conditions like congenital heart disease, aortic dissection, systemic hypertension, or post-stenotic dilatation. However, in this case, the lesion's location does not correspond to the aortic knob.

Widening of the vascular pedicle (Option C): refers to the horizontal distance between specific anatomical landmarks (from the superior vena cava crossing the right main bronchus to the origin of the left subclavian artery). This finding is not consistent with the current chest X-ray.

Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1464384/

question_text: 60 year old male, known case of Rheumatic Heart Disease presents with shortness of breath, on examination hyperdynamic precordium is noted with water hammer pulse and pistol shot gun sound over femoral arteries is heard. What is the predominant valvular lesion associated?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation described in the scenario is characteristic of aortic regurgitation (AR), particularly in a patient with a history of rheumatic heart disease. The hyperdynamic precordium, water hammer pulse, and pistol shot sound over the femoral arteries are classic signs of severe AR. These symptoms and signs indicate a significant backflow of blood from the aorta into the left ventricle during diastole, leading to increased stroke volume and characteristic pulses.

  • General Impact:In chronic severe AR, the abrupt distention and collapse of the larger arteries can be visibly noted. The whole body may show a jarring motion with each systole.
  • Arterial Pulse:
    • Water-Hammer Pulse (Corrigan's pulse): A rapidly rising and collapsing pulse due to the high stroke volume entering the arteries and then rapidly ebbing during diastole.
    • Capillary Pulsations (Quincke's pulse): Visible at the root of the nail when pressure is applied to the nail tip, showing alternate flushing and paling.
    • Pistol-Shot Sound (Traube's sign): A booming sound heard over the femoral arteries.
    • Duroziez's Sign: A to-and-fro murmur heard over the compressed femoral artery.
  • Blood Pressure:Widened pulse pressure due to high systolic and low diastolic pressures. Measurement may reveal persistent systolic sounds even with a fully deflated cuff.
  • Palpation:
    • Left Ventricle (LV) Impulse:Heaving and displaced laterally and inferiorly.
    • Apex:Systolic expansion and diastolic retraction are pronounced.
    • Thrills:Diastolic thrill along the left sternal border and systolic thrill in the suprasternal notch.
  • Auscultation:
    • Aortic Valve Closure Sound (A2):Usually absent in severe AR.
    • Murmur:High-pitched, blowing, decrescendo diastolic murmur best heard along the left sternal border. It extends throughout diastole as AR severity increases.
    • Austin Flint Murmur:Soft, rumbling mid-to-late diastolic murmur due to diastolic displacement of the mitral valve by the AR stream.
  • Other Features:Increased afterload and systemic vascular resistance can intensify AR's auscultatory features, and acute AR can result in a soft S1 and a narrow pulse pressure due to rapid equalization of aortic and LV diastolic pressures.

Explanation of other options:

Hyperthyroidism (Option A): Hyperthyroidism can cause a hyperdynamic circulation with bounding pulses, but it does not produce aortic regurgitation murmurs or characteristic signs like the water hammer pulse or pistol shot femoral sounds.

Mitral Stenosis (MS) (Option C): MS causes a low-pitched diastolic murmur with an opening snap, typically heard best at the apex. Unlike AR, MS leads to pulmonary congestion and right heart failure rather than hyperdynamic circulation and bounding pulses.

Aortic Stenosis (AS) (Option D): AS produces a harsh, systolic ejection murmur best heard at the right upper sternal border with radiation to the carotids. Patients with AS often have pulsus parvus et tardus (weak and delayed carotid upstroke), not the bounding pulse seen in AR.

Key Takeaways:

Aortic regurgitation (AR) is characterized by a hyperdynamic precordium, water hammer pulse, and pistol shot sounds over the femoral arteries due to widened pulse pressure from diastolic backflow into the left ventricle. The hallmark murmur is a high-pitched, early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border.

question_text: An 11-year-old child with a history of streptococcal pharyngitis presents with fever and joint pain. There is no prior history of rheumatic heart disease or carditis. How frequently should 600,000 IU of benzathine penicillin be administered for the prophylaxis of rheumatic heart disease?
option_c: Once in three weeks for 5 years or till the age of 18, whichever is longer
option_d: Once in three weeks for 10 years or till the age of 25, whichever is longer
explanation:
Explanation:

The given case represents acute rheumatic fever (ARF) in a child following group A streptococcal pharyngitis. Secondary prophylaxis is crucial to prevent recurrent ARF episodes and to lower the risk of progression to rheumatic heart disease (RHD).

  • Secondary prophylaxis regimen:
    • < 27 kg: 600,000 IU benzathine penicillin intramuscularly every 3 weeks
    • ≥ 27 kg:1.2 million IU benzathine penicillin intramuscularly every 3 weeks

Duration of Secondary Prophylaxis

Revised Jones Criteria for Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF)

Major Criteria

Minor Criteria

Diagnostic Requirements

  • Initial ARF: 2 Major, or 1 Major + 2 Minor
  • Recurrent ARF: 2 Major, or 1 Major + 2 Minor, or 3 Minor

Evidence of preceding Group A Streptococcal infection:

  • Elevated ASLO/anti-DNase B titers
  • Positive throat culture
  • Rapid antigen detection test

Explanation of other options:

Immediately (Option A): Starting prophylaxis should indeed be immediate, but this option does not specify the required interval regimen. The correct schedule is every 3 weeks, not a one-time dose.

Thrice weekly lifelong (Option B): This is incorrect because benzathine penicillin is a long-acting preparation given every 3-4 weeks, not multiple times per week. Lifelong prophylaxis may be required only in patients with persistent valvular disease, but the schedule remains once every 3 weeks.

Once in three weeks for 10 years or till the age of 25, whichever is longer (Option D): This regimen is indicated for patients with a history of carditis but without residual valvular damage. Since this child has no carditis, the shorter 5-year/age 18 regimen (Option C) applies.

Key Takeaways:

  • Secondary prophylaxis is vital to prevent recurrence of ARF and progression to RHD.
  • Duration of prophylaxis depends on the presence and persistence of carditis/valvular disease.
  • Jones criteria remain the cornerstone for ARF diagnosis, with adjustments based on population risk.

question_text:
A 74-year-old man is referred to with a 6-month history of progressive exertional dyspnea and pedal edema. There is no associated chest discomfort. He is a reformed smoker and non-alcoholic. His father died of a myocardial infarct at the age of 55 years. The patient's blood pressure is 150/86 mmHg. Results of investigations are as follows: HbA1C of 6.1%; LDL-cholesterol 160 mg/dl; ECG shows sinus rhythm; Echocardiogram showed dilated and impaired left ventricular function with ejection fraction of 30%, mild to moderate mitral regurgitation and no LVH.
What is the most likely underlying etiology?
explanation:
• Chronic heart failure is not an absolute diagnosis and an etiological evaluation is mandatory. The commonest etiology is underlying ischaemic heart disease (50-65% cases). This patient has several risk factors for ischaemic heart disease including smoking, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and family h/o CAD.
  • It is important to exclude other potentially reversible causes such as thyroid disease, ethanol, nutritional deficiencies, primary valvular pathology, and uncontrolled prolonged tachycardia.
  • The mitral regurgitation in this patient is most likely to be secondary to left ventricular dilatation and subsequent annular dilatation of the mitral valve ring. This will contribute to the development of pulmonary hypertension.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page Number-2034.

question_text: A patient has been diagnosed with enterococcal infective endocarditis and has a documented penicillin allergy. Which of the following antibiotics should be used for empiric therapy?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In a patient with enterococcal infective endocarditis (IE) who is allergic to penicillin, vancomycin is the antibiotic of choice for empiric treatment.
  • Vancomycin is effective against Enterococcus faecalis and Enterococcus faecium, the most common causative species in enterococcal IE.
  • It is particularly valuable in patients who cannot tolerate β-lactams due to allergy or resistance.

Mechanism of Action

  • Glycopeptide antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to D-alanyl-D-alanine termini of peptidoglycan precursors.
  • Bactericidal for most Gram-positive organisms, including enterococci, staphylococci, and streptococci.
  • Administered intravenously for systemic infections; oral form is used only for C. difficile colitis.

Explanation of Other Options:

Piperacillin (Option A):

  • Class: Extended-spectrum ureidopenicillin (β-lactam antibiotic).
  • Spectrum of Activity: Broad-spectrum, active against many Gram-negative organisms, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and some Enterococcus species (especially E. faecalis).
  • Mechanism: Inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs).
  • Clinical Use:
    • Often combined with tazobactam (β-lactamase inhibitor) for hospital-acquired infections, sepsis, and intra-abdominal infections.
  • Limitation in this Case:
    • Contraindicated in penicillin allergy due to cross-reactivity with other β-lactams.
    • Risk of anaphylaxis or angioedema in penicillin-hypersensitive patients.

Aztreonam (Option C):

  • Class: Monobactam antibiotic (β-lactam group, structurally distinct).
  • Mechanism: Inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to PBP-3, leading to cell lysis.
  • Spectrum:
    • Narrow spectrum - exclusively aerobic Gram-negative bacilli, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
    • No activity against Gram-positive organisms (including Enterococcus and Staphylococcus).
  • No anaerobic coverage.
  • Use:
    • Effective for Gram-negative infections in penicillin-allergic patients (as it has no cross-reactivity with penicillin).
    • Often used in sepsis, UTI, or pneumonia caused by Gram-negative rods.
  • Limitation:
    • Ineffective in enterococcal infective endocarditis due to lack of Gram-positive activity.

Ceftriaxone (Option D):

  • Class: Third-generation cephalosporin.
  • Mechanism: Inhibits cell wall synthesis by binding to PBPs, preventing peptidoglycan cross-linking.
  • Spectrum:
    • Broad coverage against Gram-negative bacteria and some Gram-positive organisms (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria).
    • Poor activity against Enterococcus species due to intrinsic resistance.
  • Pharmacokinetics:
    • Long half-life (once-daily dosing).
    • High protein binding.
    • Biliary excretion (contraindicated in neonates with hyperbilirubinemia).
  • Clinical Use:
    • Bacterial meningitis, pneumonia, gonorrhea, and typhoid fever.
    • Sometimes used in combination (e.g., Ampicillin + Ceftriaxone for enterococcal IE with aminoglycoside resistance).
  • Limitation:
    • Enterococci are inherently resistant to all cephalosporins.
    • Therefore, ineffective as monotherapy in this case.

question_text: What is a macrovascular complication commonly seen in the later stages of diabetes?
explanation:
Explanation:

In the advanced stages of diabetes, coronary artery disease is a common macrovascular complication.

Macrovascular Complications of Diabetes Mellitus

These complications are major contributors to illness and death in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. They involve damage to large blood vessels and typically present as:

  • Coronary artery disease - causing myocardial ischemia or infarction
  • Cerebrovascular disease - resulting in transient ischemic attacks or strokes
  • Peripheral arterial disease - leading to limb ischemia and claudication

Important Considerations:

  • Myocardial infarction and stroke are leading causes of death in people with diabetes.
  • Atherosclerosis develops earlier and is more severe in diabetic patients.
  • Risk factors such as smoking, high blood pressure, and abnormal lipid profiles amplify cardiovascular risk.
  • Metabolic syndrome, often seen in type 2 diabetes, includes:
    • Hypertension
    • Elevated fasting glucose
    • High triglycerides
    • Low HDL cholesterol
    • Central obesity

Pathophysiological Links Between Hyperglycemia and Vascular Disease:

  • Vascular permeability increases in response to chronic high blood glucose.
  • Atherogenic lipoprotein deposition is promoted by hyperinsulinemia and hypertension.

Prevention & Risk Reduction:

  • Tight glycemic control helps reduce both macrovascular and microvascular complications.
  • Blood pressure management, especially with ACE inhibitors or ARBs, provides cardiovascular protection.
  • Lipid control with statins is strongly recommended.
  • Lifestyle interventions-including smoking cessation, physical activity, and healthy weight maintenance-are essential.

Explanation for other options:

Foot ulcers (Option B): often linked to microvascular damage and neuropathy

Diabetic nephropathy (Option C): affects kidney microvasculature

Diabetic retinopathy (Option D): damages retinal blood vessels

These are all microvascular, not macrovascular, in origin.

question_text: Which of the following is not true regarding management of vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina?
option_b: Classically cause transmural ischemia compared to subendocardial ischemia in angina pectoris.
option_c: Associated with rest pain and ST segment elevation on ECG
option_d: Beta blockers and nitrates are the preferred treatment
explanation:
• Transient coronary artery spasm is the basis for Prinzmetal (vasospastic) angina which can result in transient ST elevation and spasm which is evident on coronary angiography.
  • Nitrates and calcium channel blockers are the preferred treatment options for vasospastic angina. Beta blockers are not used as unopposed alpha receptor action of catecholamines would worsen coronary vasoconstriction.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page no: 2052

question_text: Female patient presents to AIIMS ER. She is a known case of chronic stable angina that comes with severe fatigue and prostration. During the blood sample you notice that blood has a brown hue. Diagnosis is?
explanation:
Nitrates used for the treatment of angina can convert hemoglobin to methemoglobin in the absence of CYB5R3 which is needed to reduce methemoglobin back to hb. Other drugs include dapsone and benzocaine.

O2 transport is reduced and reflected by the left-shift in the hemoglobin-O2 binding curve. CYB5R3 deficiency usually affects only erythrocytes (type I), causing a mild disorder; when all cells are affected (type II), a severe disease results. Intravenous methylene blue is the preferred treatment in symptomatic patients with acquired methemoglobinemia and 40-60% methemoglobin. The usual dose is 1-2 mg/kg. Alternative treatment with ascorbic acid is preferable in people who are glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficient. Methylene blue interferes with co-oximetry, reducing the value of co-oximetry for monitoring treatment.

question_text: A 50-year-old man had a history of myocardial infarction 6 months ago. He had two episodes of syncope and the ECG tracing during one such episode is given below. Coronary angiography showed a 99% LAD artery stenosis and angioplasty was unsuccessful due to the tortuosity of the vessel. Echocardiography shows a dilated LV at 5.9 cm with an ejection fraction of 28%. Which is the most appropriate therapy?
explanation:
The indications for Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator (ICD) include:

  • Patients with a history of sustained VT/VF not due to acute MI or any reversible cause.
  • History of previous MI and EF < 35% for NYHA Class II or III, EF < 30% for Class 1.
  • Familial or inherited condition with predisposition for VT/VF.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page Number-1873.

question_text: A 20 year old male patient presented to OPD with the given presentation, he reports fluctuation in size of the swelling, mild numbness in hand and occasional pain. Identify the swelling on the dorsal aspect of the wrist?
explanation:
Explanation:

Location: Ganglion cysts commonly occur on the dorsal aspect of the wrist.

Symptoms: They are known to fluctuate in size and can cause mild numbness or pain, particularly if they impinge on nerves. Consistency: They typically feel firm and are filled with a jelly-like fluid.

Explanation of other options:

Sebaceous Cyst (Option B): Originates from blocked sebaceous glands (not synovial tissue). Filled with keratinous material, not fluid, and does not transilluminate. More common on scalp, back, or face, not typically on the wrist.

Lipoma (Option C): Soft, mobile, and painless, unlike the firm consistency of a ganglion cyst. Does not fluctuate in size or cause numbness. Composed of fat tissue, not fluid-filled.

Hematoma (Option D): Typically follows trauma with a history of recent injury. More likely to be tender and ecchymotic (bruised appearance). Does not fluctuate in size over time.

Key Takeaways:

Ganglion cysts are fluid-filled swellings commonly found on the dorsal wrist, known to fluctuate in size and occasionally cause numbness or pain. Aspiration or surgical excision may be considered if symptomatic.

question_text: The 'snowman' appearance of heart on chest xray is seen in which congenital heart disease:
explanation:
Eponymous chest X ray appearances in congenital heart disease

  • Snowman sign : Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection
  • Egg on side appearance: Transposition of great arteries
  • Boot shaped heart : Fallot's tetralogy
  • Scimitar sign : Partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection
  • Figure of 3 sign : Coarctation of aorta

question_text: A 50-year-old man reports recurrent chest pain episodes occurring only during physical exertion, each lasting 2 to 5 minutes. He has been diagnosed with stable angina, but his blood pressure remains consistently high. What is the most suitable antihypertensive medication for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The best antihypertensive choice for a patient with stable angina and persistently high blood pressure is amlodipine.

Amlodipine is especially effective in stable angina because it improves coronary blood flow by reducing vasospasm and lowering myocardial oxygen demand. It also effectively controls blood pressure, making it an ideal option for patients managing both stable angina and hypertension.

Explanation for other options:

Thiazide diuretics (Option B): are commonly used to treat hypertension by promoting diuresis and reducing fluid volume. However, they are not the ideal choice here because they do not specifically address stable angina, which is the patient's primary condition.

Enalapril (Option C): an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, is effective for managing hypertension, but it may not be the first choice in this scenario given the patient's main symptom of stable angina.

question_text: In a patient with NSTEMI, which of the following would not be given?
explanation:
The drugs that are used in the treatment of NSTEMI are anti ischemic therapy, oral or parenteral antiplatelets and anticoagulants.

Streptokinase is a thrombolytic agent used for STEMI.

question_text: A 48-year-old man presented with chest pain, facial flushing and elevated jugularvenous pressure but no leg oedema. He had been exposed to tuberculosis in childhood,had a strongly positive tuberculin test and had been followed up in the tuberculosissurveillance program with regular chest x-rays, but had never been diagnosed withtuberculosis. Chest x-ray on presentation showed calcified plaques and masses in thepericardium and mediastinum.Coronary angiography showed 70% stenosis in the left anterior descending artery. Cardiaccatheterization showed equalisation of diastolic pressures in all four chambers, with apositive square root sign.What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Equalisation of diastolic pressures in all four chambers of heart, with a positive square root sign is seen in constrictive pericarditis.

Tuberculous pericarditis is seen in 1%-2% of all cases of pulmonary tuberculosis and can lead to constriction. Treatment is with corticosteroids and anti TB therapy.

The atrial waveform manifests as:

  • Augmented "a" wave, reflecting enhanced atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle
  • A rapid "x" descent attributable to subsequent accelerated atrial relaxation
  • A steep "y" descent reflecting rapid, resistance-free early diastolic filling.

Right and left heart chamber filling pressures are typically increased and equalized (LVEDP = RVEDP), reflecting the common constraining effects of the pericardium.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:265 pg:1845

question_text: Based on the provided ECG findings, which wall of the myocardium is affected in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The ECG shows ST elevation in leads V2, V3, and V4, indicating an anterior wall myocardial infarction (MI).
  • The convex upward ST segment elevation (Pardee sign) in the precordial leads is characteristic of an acute anterior wall MI, typically supplied by the left anterior descending artery.

ECG in MI

  • In the initial stage of an acute myocardial infarction, total occlusion of an epicardial coronary artery produces ST-segment elevation.
  • Most patients presenting with ST elevation eventually develop Q waves on the ECG, although their magnitude and duration can vary depending on reperfusion and restoration of transmembrane potentials.
  • Some patients may not develop Q waves if the occlusion is partial, transient, or if a rich collateral circulation exists.
  • In patients with ischemic symptoms but without ST-segment elevation, the detection of a serum cardiac biomarker of necrosis confirms a diagnosis of NSTEMI.
  • Cardiac biomarkers include cardiac-specific troponin T and cardiac-specific troponin

question_text: You review an 84-year-old lady in the gastroenterology clinic. She has been referred by her family doctor with a three month history of change in bowel habit and weight loss. Recently she has noticed PR bleeding with blood in the stool. There is a history of ischaemic heart disease with a previous myocardial infarction three years ago. She suffers from stable angina and congestive cardiac failure. Which of the following investigations would be most appropriate to make the diagnosis?
explanation:
Colorectal carcinoma needs to be excluded in this case.

Three quarters of cases occur in people aged over 65y. Around 50% survive for over 5 years following diagnosis.

With regard to the investigation of colorectal carcinoma, colonoscopy should be offered to patients without major comorbidity. If a lesion suspicious of cancer is detected, a biopsy should be performed to obtain a histological diagnosis.

If the colonoscopy is incomplete, it should be repeated or CT colonography or barium enema should be performed.

Flexible sigmoidoscopy then barium enema should be offered for patients with major comorbidity. CT colonography is an alternative if the local radiology service is competent in this technique. A small dose of oral contrast is administered 24 hours prior to the procedure and then the colon is imaged using helical CT scanning. Most CT colonography protocols require the use of bowel cleansing agents. The advantages over colonoscopy include no requirement for sedation, smaller risk of perforation, and extra-colonic pathology can also be demonstrated.

If a lesion suspicious of cancer is detected on CT colonography, a colonoscopy and biopsy should be offered (unless there are absolute contraindications).

CT chest, abdomen, pelvis should be offered after the diagnosis is made to estimate the stage of the disease. Patients with a rectal tumour should also undergo MRI to assess local disease. Endorectal ultrasound can then be offered if MRI shows disease amenable to local excision (or if MRI is contraindicated).

Digital rectal examination is not part of the staging investigations.

In this case, the presence of congestive cardiac failure is a major comorbidity. A flexible sigmoidoscopy should therefore be first line (especially as she complains of fresh red bleeding, increasing the chance that this is a left-sided lesion). This would allow biopsy if a lesion is seen. If the flexible sigmoidoscopy is normal, a barium enema or CT colonography would be done.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:322 Pg:2390

question_text: A 50-year-old patient has tearing interscapular chest pain. His ECG shows no ST changes, but a CT scan with contrast showed aortic dissection. His blood pressure is 190/106 mmHg. Which is the most important management?
explanation:
Immediate management of aortic dissection is aggressive blood pressure control. Intravenous labetalol or sodium nitroprusside can be used.

Once this is done, the patient can be further assessed with coronary angiography or be referred for urgent surgery.

There are two main types of Aortic Dissection:

Stanford Type A Aortic Dissection:

  • Occurs in the first part of the aorta, closer to the heart, and can be immediately life-threatening.
  • It usually requires emergency open chest surgery to repair or replace the first segment of the aorta where the tear started (ascending aorta +/- the arch and/or aortic valve).
  • This is a more common type of dissection than Type B, and the dissection of the aorta usually extends through the entire length of the aorta.

Stanford Type B Aortic Dissection:

  • This type of tear begins farther down the aorta (descending aorta beyond the arch), and farther from the heart. It usually extends into the abdominal segment (abdominal aorta), but doesn't involve the first part of the aorta in the front of the chest.
  • Surgery may or may not be needed immediately, depending on exactly where the dissection is located and if it is or isn't cutting off blood flow to your organs. These operations usually can be performed with a stent-graft device inserted into the aorta.

Another classification system (DeBakey Classification) defines dissection by three types.

  • Type 1 originates in the ascending aorta and extends through the downstream aorta.
  • Type 2 originates and is limited to the ascending aorta (both would be considered Stanford Type A).
  • Type 3 originates in the descending aorta and extends downward (similar to Type B).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:274 pg:1921

question_text: Identify the false statement regarding the management of NSTEMI.
option_a: Aspirin loading dose should be initiated immediately
option_b: ACC/AHA guidelines recommend a P2Y12 inhibitor (clopidogrel, prasugrel, or ticagrelor) as Class I therapy
option_c: Glycoprotein IIB/IIIA inhibitors are useful adjuncts
option_d: Fibrinolytic therapy is useful in acute coronary syndrome without ST-segment elevation
explanation:
Explanation:

Fibrinolytic therapy is not indicated in NSTEMI as it does not improve outcomes and may increase bleeding risk. Preferred strategies include antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulation, and early invasive interventions.

Management of NSTEMI-ACS

The management of Non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) involves initial assessment in the emergency setting for patients with low probability of ischemia, which includes continuous ECG monitoring, stress testing, and serial serum troponin measurements. Patients meeting the criteria for non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS) should be admitted for further observation and medical therapy aimed at stabilizing the condition and preventing subsequent cardiac events.

Medical Management

  • Anti-ischemic Therapy:
  • Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate (GTN)/nitroglycerin:

First-line therapy for unstable angina; used to relieve ischemic chest discomfort.

  • Intravenous beta-blockers (Atenolol, Metoprolol):

Reduce myocardial oxygen demand, relieve chest pain, decrease the incidence of arrhythmias, and lower short-term mortality.

  • Calcium channel blockers (Verapamil, Diltiazem):

Considered when symptoms persist despite optimal beta-blocker and nitrate therapy; reduce heart rate and myocardial oxygen consumption.

  • Intravenous morphine sulfate or diamorphine:

For analgesic relief in severe chest pain.

  • Antiemetics (e.g., Metoclopramide):

For symptomatic relief of nausea.

  • Nifedipine or Amlodipine:

Used if ischemic chest discomfort continues despite other therapy.

  • Lipid-lowering therapy:
    • Statins (Atorvastatin and other HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors): Reduce the risk of myocardial infarction and recurrence of acute coronary syndrome.
    • Additional agents (Ezetimibe, Alirocumab, Evolocumab): Administered if full-dose statins are insufficient; effectively lower LDL cholesterol and further prevent cardiovascular events.
  • Antithrombotic Therapy:
  • Antiplatelet agents:
    • Cyclooxygenase inhibitor: Aspirin
    • P2Y12 receptor inhibitors: Clopidogrel, Prasugrel, or Ticagrelor
  • Anticoagulants:
    • Unfractionated heparin
    • Low-molecular-weight heparin: Enoxaparin
    • Direct thrombin inhibitor: Bivalirudin
    • Synthetic factor Xa inhibitor: Fondaparinux

Invasive Management:

Invasive strategies are indicated if medical management fails or if symptoms persist. Coronary arteriography should be performed within 48 hours of presentation. Coronary revascularization options include:

  • Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI): Often performed with Glycoprotein IIB/IIIA inhibitors as adjunct therapy.
  • Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG): Considered for patients with extensive coronary artery disease or unsuitable anatomy for PCI.

Explanation of other options:

Aspirin loading dose should be initiated immediately (Option A):

A loading dose of 162-325 mg is crucial in acute coronary syndrome (ACS) as it irreversibly inhibits thromboxane A2, preventing platelet aggregation and limiting clot propagation. Early administration is associated with improved outcomes.

ACC/AHA guidelines call for either a P2Y12 inhibitor (Option B):

P2Y12 receptor inhibitors-such as clopidogrel, prasugrel, or ticagrelor-are class I recommended in ACS. They are used in combination with aspirin as dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) to further reduce platelet aggregation and prevent thrombotic events.

Glycoprotein IIB/IIIA inhibitors are useful adjuncts (Option C):

Drugs like abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban block platelet aggregation by inhibiting the GPIIb/IIIa receptor. They are typically used in high-risk PCI patients to reduce the risk of periprocedural thrombotic complications.

question_text: A patient presents with acute-onset chest pain for one hour, accompanied by profuse sweating and restlessness. The ECG demonstrates ST-segment depressions in leads V<sub>2</sub> and V<sub>3</sub>. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient's presentation, along with ECG findings of ST depressions in leads V2 and V3, suggests posterior wall myocardial infarction (MI).
  • Clinical Presentation: Chest pain, sweating, and anxiety are classic symptoms of acute myocardial infarction.

Infarct Localization based on ECG

Explanation of Other Options:

NSTEMI (Option A):

  • ECG may show ST depression or T wave inversion, but not confined to reciprocal anterior leads.
  • No specific localization like posterior MI.
  • Cardiac biomarkers (troponin I/T) are elevated, confirming infarction.
  • Lacks the tall R wave and reciprocal ST depression pattern seen in posterior infarction.

Unstable Angina (Option B):

  • Presents with anginal pain at rest or minimal exertion.
  • ECG may show transient ST depression or T wave inversion, but biomarkers are normal (no myocyte necrosis).
  • Represents pre-infarction ischemia.
  • Pain relief after nitrates is typical.

Acute Myocarditis (Option D):

  • Presents with anginal pain at rest or minimal exertion.
  • ECG may show transient ST depression or T wave inversion, but biomarkers are normal (no myocyte necrosis).
  • Represents pre-infarction ischemia.
  • Pain relief after nitrates is typical.

Reference:

https://www.cardiologymedjournal.com/articles/jccm-aid1082.php

question_text: Which of the following statements is true of raised cardiac troponin levels in the blood?
option_b: Remain elevated for up to two days after myocardial damage
option_c: Are seen in patients with NSTEMI
option_d: Can be used to distinguish Non-Q from Q MI
explanation:
• The most sensitive markers of myocardial cell damage are the cardiac troponins T and I. Troponins are regulatory elements of the contractile apparatus in muscle. They are released within 4-6 hours and remain elevated for up to two weeks.
  • Troponin levels are elevated in patients with NSTEMI and STEMI while it is normal in subjects with stable and unstable angina.
  • Cardioversion can give rise to raised creatine kinase (CK) levels due to skeletal muscle damage and mildly raised troponins in a small share of patients.
  • Non-Q and Q MI are electrocardiographic diagnoses. Raised troponin levels indicate heart muscle damage: the commonest cause being ischaemic damage. Myocarditis or myocardial contusion can also cause raised troponin levels.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page no: 2055

question_text:
A 69-year-old male presents with cognitive impairment and a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease is suspected.
What is the most appropriate test of short term memory?
option_c: Knowledge of the capital of the India
option_d: Recall of the doctor's name at the end of the consultation
explanation:
Short term memory impairment is the commonest clinical presentation of Alzheimer's disease.

Usually patients are fully orientated in time, person and place. Long term memory is usually intact.

The best way to test short term memory is to ask the patient to recall new information in the next few minutes.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 29, Pg: 192

question_text:
A 74-year-old diabetic man is admitted to ER with a 40 minute history of central, crushing chest pain. The pain eases after an hour with bedrest, oxygen and morphine. ECG shows mild anterior ST flattening. The troponin T level is slightly raised.
What would be the optimal management of the underlying cause of his chest pain be besides usual medical measures?
option_a: Discharge home with referral to the outpatients department
explanation:
This patient falls into the high-risk category of acute coronary syndrome.

Acute coronary syndrome is a medical emergency, which, if untreated, will progress to myocardial infarction in over 10% of cases.

High-risk patients may have one or more of the following features:

  • Prolonged, ongoing (> 20 min) rest pain
  • Pulmonary oedema or angina with hypotension
  • Rest angina with dynamic ST changes > 1 mm
  • Raised troponin (I and T)
  • Age > 70 years
  • Diabetes mellitus

Those at high-risk should proceed promptly to angiography with a view to proceeding to revascularisation, where appropriate, during that admission.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page no: 2059
