question_text: In which clinical scenarios is rescue percutaneous coronary intervention indicated?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Rescue PCI is indicated when thrombolytic therapy fails to restore coronary blood flow in acute myocardial infarction.
  • It is performed if symptoms persist, ST-segment elevation continues > 90 min, or the patient remains hemodynamically unstable despite thrombolysis, serving as a secondary intervention to mechanically reestablish coronary perfusion.

Fig: Reperfusion therapy for patients with STEMI (CABG, coronary artery bypass graft; DIDO, door-in-door-out; FMC, first medical contact; LOE, level of evidence. While the infarct-related coronary artery is typically occluded in Type I MI's, subtotal occlusion may be present in Type II MI's.

Explanation of other options:

Chronic stable angina (Option B): Chronic stable angina is characterized by predictable chest pain triggered by exertion or stress. While PCI can be performed for symptom relief when medical therapy fails, this is elective or planned intervention, not rescue PCI, which is reserved for urgent cases where thrombolysis has failed.

Prinzmetal angina (Option C): Prinzmetal (variant) angina is caused by coronary artery spasm and usually responds to medical therapy with calcium channel blockers and nitrates. PCI is generally not indicated unless a significant fixed obstruction coexists, as the main treatment targets relieving vasospasm rather than performing mechanical intervention.

NSTEMI (Option D): In NSTEMI, management primarily begins with medical therapy, and PCI is performed based on risk stratification and treatment response. Although PCI may be indicated, it is planned or early invasive management, not rescue PCI, which is specifically reserved for cases where initial thrombolytic therapy has failed.

question_text: Which of the following is not true regarding Dressler syndrome?
option_a: Pericarditis occurring in the setting of MI
option_c: Occurs in the first week post MI
option_d: NSAIDS and steroids are used to reduce inflammation
explanation:
• Dressler syndrome is characterised by immune complex deposition in pericardium approximately around 2-4 weeks following an episode of MI as part of autoimmune phenomenon.
  • ECG findings include PR segment depression and ST segment elevation.
  • Aspirin is the preferred treatment while NSAIDs and steroids are not given as they can interfere with healing of infarct area in the post-infarction period.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 21st edition 2064

question_text: A patient with acute inferior wall myocardial infarction develops hypotension and shock. Which of the following complications of his MI is most likely to be the cause?
explanation:
• Right ventricular infarction occurs in one-third of cases of inferior wall myocardial infarction, which leads to pooling of blood in the right ventricle and a consequent decreased preload in the left ventricle and consequent hypotension.
  • Papillary muscle rupture and atrial fibrillation are other complications which are also more common in inferior myocardial infarction.
  • Interventricular septal rupture is commoner in anterior myocardial infarction. Atrial fibrillation occurs as a complication in 10% of patients with myocardial infarction.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page no: 2035

question_text: Patient came to the hospital within 3 hrs of onset of chest pain. ECG revealed ST depression in Anterior chest leads and t wave inversion. She is best managed by?
explanation:
The initial treatment of these consist of providing pain relief. The main anti ischemic treatments given are nitrates, Beta blockers and bed rest.

Anti thrombotic treatment remains the corner stone of treatment. This

includes antiplatelets and anticoagulants.

Antiplatelets: in patients with NSTEMI or UA two antiplatelets should be used. Cyclooxygenase inhibitor aspirin should be given in a dose of at least 162 mg followed by 75-100mg/day. A P2Y12 inhibitor should be added, if there is no high risk for bleeding. Clopdogrel 600mg loading followed by 75mg/day. Other P2Y12 inhibitors are Prasugrel, 60mg loading followed by 10 mg per day. It is preferred for those in whom an invasive strategy is planned. It is contra indicated in the previous stroke, TIA. It is associated with a high bleeding risk. Ticagrelor is reversible. 180mg loading dose followed by 90mg twice daily is used. Beneficial for both invasive as well as conservative management. Cangrelor is an IV P2Y12 inhibitor which is rapid and IV. It is recommended as an adjunct in patients undergoing PCI to reduce post-procedure MI, recurrent revascularization and stent thrombosis.

Anti coagulants: unfractionated heparin, LMWH, fondaparinux and Bivaluridin are the anticoagulants used.

After giving the initial treatment, the patient has to be risk stratified to determine if the patient has to be taken up for an early PCI VS conservative management. In high risk patients, those with multiple risk factors, ECG changes and positive troponin, an early invasive strategy should be followed which is definitely beneficial than a conservative strategy. In low risk patients, early invasive or conservative approach has similar outcomes. In a low risk patient, a PCI is carried out if the CT Coronoary angio shows occlusion, positive stress test or raising biomarkers.

In the question, the patient's pain is subsiding with sublingual nitrates, but has recurrent angina and multiple risk factors, the ideal treatment would be an early invasive treatment. But since that is not there LMWH or heparin is the next best.

So the best treatment would be PCI.

question_text: A 52-year-old man with angina has a percutaneous coronary intervention with insertion of a drug-eluting stent. What is the single most important risk factor for stent thrombosis?
option_c: Failing to adhere to cardiac rehabilitation program
explanation:
PCI: Stent thrombosis - withdrawal of antiplatelets biggest risk factor

Diabetes mellitus is a risk factor for restenosis rather than stent thrombosis

Percutaneous coronary intervention

Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is a technique used to restore myocardial perfusion in patients with ischaemic heart disease, both in patients with stable angina and acute coronary syndromes. Stents are implanted in around 95% of patients undergoing PCI.

Complications following stent placement

  1. Stent thrombosis: due to platelet aggregation as above. Occurs in 1-2% of patients, most commonly in the first month. Usually presents with acute myocardial infarction
  2. Restenosis: due to excessive tissue proliferation around the stent. Occurs in around 5-20% of patients, most commonly in the first 3-6 months. Usually presents with the recurrence of angina symptoms. Risk factors include diabetes, renal impairment and stents in venous bypass grafts

Types of stent

  • Bare-metal stent (BMS)
  • Drug-eluting stents (DES): Stent coated with paclitaxel or rapamycin which inhibit local tissue growth. Whilst this reduces restenosis rates the stent thrombosis rates are increased as the process of stent endothelialization is slowed

Aspirin should be continued indefinitely. The length of clopidogrel treatment depends on the type of stent, reason for insertion and consultant preference.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page no: 2067

question_text:
For which type(s) of cancer is prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) typically given?
1. Lung cancer
2. Liver cancer
3. Prostate cancer
4. Breast cancer
explanation:
Explanation:

Prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) is primarily used to reduce the risk of brain metastases in cancers that have a high likelihood of spreading to the central nervous system.

Lung Cancer:

  • PCI is most commonly administered in small cell lung cancer (SCLC) due to its aggressive nature and high tendency to metastasize to the brain.
  • It has been shown to improve overall survival and decrease the incidence of brain metastases in patients who respond to initial treatment.

Breast Cancer:

  • PCI may be considered in select cases of breast cancer, particularly in patients at high risk for brain metastases.
  • This includes aggressive subtypes such as HER2-positive and triple-negative breast cancer. 

Options A, B, and D are incorrect.

question_text: Which of the following explains type 5 MI according to the Third Universal Myocardial Infarction Classification?
option_a: Myocardial Infarction Related to Stent Thrombosis
option_b: Myocardial Infarction Related to Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting
option_c: Myocardial Infarction Resulting in Death When Biomarker Values Are Unavailable
option_d: Myocardial Infarction Related to Percutaneous Coronary Intervention
explanation:
Third Universal Myocardial Infarction (MI) Classification of Type

Type 1: Spontaneous Myocardial Infarction

Spontaneous MI related to atherosclerotic plaque rupture, ulceration, fissuring, erosion, or dissection with resulting intraluminal thrombus in one or more of the coronary arteries.

Type 2: Myocardial Infarction Secondary to Ischemic Imbalance

In cases of myocardial injury with necrosis in which a condition other than CAD contributes to an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and/or demand (e.g., coronary endothelial dysfunction, coronary artery spasm, coronary embolism, tachy/bradyarrhythmias, anemia, respiratory failure, hypotension, hypertension ± left ventricular hypertrophy).

Type 3: Myocardial Infarction Resulting in Death When Biomarker Values Are Unavailable

Cardiac death with symptoms suggestive of myocardial ischemia and presumed new ischemic changes on the ECG or new LBBB, but death occurring before blood samples could be obtained.

Type 4a: Myocardial Infarction Related to Percutaneous Coronary Intervention

Type 4b: Myocardial Infarction Related to Stent Thrombosis

Type 5: Myocardial Infarction Related to Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting

Reference: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine 11th Ed Page 1096

question_text: A 60-year-old male patient presented with myocardial infarction and planned for urgent percutaneous coronary intervention. Bivalirudin was used as an anticoagulant in this patient. Which of the following statement is true about the drug used?
option_a: It is a parenteral direct thrombin inhibitor.
option_b: Antidote of bivalirudin toxicity is protamine.
option_c: No dose adjustments required in renal failure patients.
option_d: It is contraindicated in heparin induced thrombocytopenia.
explanation:
• Bivalirudin is a synthetic polypeptide that can be used in patients undergoing PCI or coronary bypass surgery for STEMI and NSTEMI as an anticoagulant along with antiplatelet drugs like aspirin.
  • Bivalirudin is a parenteral direct thrombin inhibitor
  • Lepirudinand argatroban are licensed for the treatment of HIT, whereas bivalirudin is approved as an alternative to heparin in patients undergoing PCI, including those with HIT
  • Protamine is the antidote for heparin, not bivalirudin.
  • Bivalirudin is eliminated by the kidneys, so dose adjustments may be needed in patients with severe renal impairment.

Reference: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine 11th Ed, chap 93 Pg: 1839

question_text:
A 62-year-old male is admitted with an inferior myocardial infarction and receives thrombolysis with streptokinase, aspirin, atenolol, simvastatin and ramipril. His ECG shows good ST segment resolution. The following day he develops some pain in the legs and a dusky discolouration of the lower limbs. On closer examination there is a diffuse petechial rash over the lower legs particularly the feet but all peripheral pulses are palpable. Investigations reveal:
Hemoglobin 13.3 g/dl (12-16)
Platelets 145 x 10^9/L (140-450)
White cell count 12.1 x 10^9/L (4-10)
Neutrophils 6.5 x 10^9/L (2-7)
Lymphocytes 3.5 x 10^9/L (1-3.5)
Eosinophils 1.2 x 10^9/L (0.3-06)
Which of the following is the most likely cause for his current problems?
explanation:
• This patient has acute MI and one day after thrombolysis develops this petechial rash in the lower limbs with raised white cell count - marked eosinophilia. This is the classical picture of cholesterol embolism syndrome where cholesterol crystal breaks off from an atherosclerotic plaque in an artery and lodges in smaller arteries elsewhere.
  • The most commonly involved organs include kidneys, skin, GI tract and brain.
  • Renal involvement would lead to eosinophiluria and AKI while embolism to the legs can cause a mottled appearance and purple discoloration of the toes, small infarcts, areas of gangrene, and a marbled pattern on the skin known as livedo reticularis.
  • Biopsy of the affected organ would confirm the diagnosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page no: 2090

question_text: A 30-year-old woman visits the outpatient department complaining of palpitations and weight loss. On examining her legs, a lesion is observed that, when pressed, does not leave a lasting indentation after the pressure is released. Her ECG reveals a sinus rhythm. What is the most likely cause of her edema?
explanation:
Explanation:

Given the clinical presentation and examination findings, the most likely cause of the edema in this case is nephrotic syndrome.

Explanation for other options:

Myxedema (Option A): is associated with severe hypothyroidism and does not match the symptoms of palpitation and weight loss in this case.

Chronic lymphangitis (Option C): involves inflammation of lymphatic vessels and typically causes lymphedema affecting the entire limb. However, this case involves pedal edema linked to nephrotic syndrome.

Dilated cardiomyopathy (Option D): usually causes pitting edema, but here the edema is described as non-pitting, which does not fit with this condition.

question_text: Which of the following is not seen in a patient with Pheochromocytoma ?
explanation:
• The classical triad of Pheochromocytoma include headache, palpitations and diaphoresis.
  • The most common sign is hypertension
  • Pheochromocytoma can also have a set of less common manifestations including:
  • Takotsubo cardiomyopathy / arrhythmias
  • Weight loss
  • Constipation or diarrhea
  • Hyperglycemia
  • Hypercalcemia
  • Raynaud phenomenon
  • Increased haematocrit
  • Orthostatic hypotension
  • The gold standard for diagnosis is measurement of plasma or urine free metanephrine and normetanephrine
  • Pre-operative preparation of pheochromocytoma is done using alpha blockers initially, later followed by beta blockers. (Beta blockers, if started upfront can paradoxically worsen the hypertensive crisis)

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2979

question_text: A 5 year old boy presents with history of fever of 1 week duration, along with bilateral cervical adenopathy, bilateral conjunctival congestion, erythema of the oral cavity and desquamation, especially of the finger tips. He has evidence of myocarditis too. He has an ESR of 100mm/1st hour, elevated CRP, and elevated liver enzymes. Which infection will you suspect?
explanation:
This patient presents with a multi system involvement. The salient features are involvement of mucosa and desquamation of the skin especially the finger tips. He also has myocarditis. This fits into the picture of Kawazaki Disease.

An infection which presents with clinical features resembling Kawazaki Disease is MIS-C, caused by COVID 19.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:363 Pg:2816

question_text: A middle aged man presents with features of polyneuropathy and ataxia. Which of the following disease is least likely?
explanation:
Diseases that present with features of polyneuropathy and ataxia are:

Friedreich's Ataxia

Abetalipoproteinemia

Spinocerebellar ataxia

Vitamin E deficiency

Refsum's Disease

All these may be characterized by the absence of ankle jerk but with an extensor plantar response.

Friedreich's ataxia is associated with cardiomyopathy and musculoskeletal abnormalities like pes cavus.

Abetalipoproteinemia is associated with steatorrhoea, acanthocytosis and retinitis pigmentosa.

Vitamin E deficiency is associated with night blindness, pigmentary retinopathy, ophthalmoplegia.

Refsum's disease is characterized by the tetrad of neuropathy, retinitis pigmentosa, cerebellar ataxia and high CSF protein concentration

Tangier's disease is an AR disease due to mutations in the ATP binding cassette protein 1 gene, that leads to very low levels of HDL and high TG. It is characterized by asymmetric multiple mononeuropathies or symmetric polyneuropathy or a pseudosyringomyelia pattern. It is characterized by enlarged yellowish orange tonsils, splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy.

Peripheral neuropathy with retinitis pigmentosa is seen in: Vitamin E deficiency, abetalipoproteinemia, Refsum's disease

Peripheral neuropathy with abnormal lipid levels are seen in Tangiers disease and abetalipoproteinemia. Tangier's disease causes very low HDL and high TG. Abetalipoproteinemia leads to absent LDL and very low TG and HDL.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3487

question_text: A 65-year-old male attends a clinic complaining of breathlessness and persistent fatigue. He has end stage cardiac failure due to dilated cardiomyopathy. Currently he takes Furosemide, Lisinopril, Spironolactone and Carvedilol. Which one of the following drugs should be added to his current therapy?
explanation:
Digoxin has a positive inotropic effect; it can be used in patients with heart failure who are in sinus rhythm but presenting with severe symptoms with no response to guideline mediated medical therapy including an ACE inhibitor, diuretic and beta blocker.

Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic window, hence should be used cautiously to avoid the risk of serious adverse effects including arrhythmias.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1946

question_text: Arrange in sequence for manifestations of iron toxicity
explanation:
The clinical course of iron toxicity is divided into five stages. The progression from stage to stage may be very rapid, and not every patient goes through every stage.

  1. During the first stage (0.5 to 6 hours), the patient mainly exhibits gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms including abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hematemesis, and hematochezia.
  2. The second stage (6 to 24 hours) represents an apparent recovery phase, as the patient's GI symptoms may resolve despite toxic amounts of iron absorption.
  3. The third stage (6 to 72 hours) is characterized by the recurrence of GI symptoms, shock, and metabolic acidosis. Iron-induced coagulopathy, hepatic dysfunction, cardiomyopathy, and renal failure are also observed in this stage.
  4. The fourth stage (12 to 96 hours) is characterized by an elevation of aminotransferase levels and possible progression to hepatic failure.
  5. The fifth stage (2 to 8 weeks) represents the consequences of the healing of the injured GI mucosa including pyloric or proximal bowel scarring and obstruction.

A patient may present in or skip any of the five stages. Determination of the iron toxicity stage should be based on symptoms and clinical manifestations and not on time of ingestion.

question_text: A 22-year-old student presents with a history of breathlessness on exertion and orthopnoea, fatigue and anorexia. On examination he has peripheral oedema, ascites, hepatomegaly, a low volume pulse, elevated JVP with a rapid y descent, no inspiratory increase in JVP, and S4 was heard on auscultation. ECG shows a low voltage QRS complex with diffuse nonspecific repolarization changes. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The patient has features suggestive of predominant right sided (edema, hepatomegaly, ascites, raised JVP) as well as left sided heart failure (breathlessness, orthopnea, low volume pulse)..

Predominant right sided heart failure is seen in both constrictive pericarditis and restrictive cardiomyopathy. Elevated JVP with rapid y descent is seen in both conditions while an inspiratory increase in JVP (Kussmaul sign), is more common in constrictive pericarditis however may also be seen in the latter. The fourth heart sound (S4) reflecting increased atrial contraction in an effort to overcome the reduced compliance of the ventricle is classically seen in restrictive cardiomyopathy and almost never occurs in constrictive pericarditis.Low voltage QRS with non-specific repolarisation changes are also commonly seen.

Classical features of constrictive pericarditis include elevated JVP with prominent x descent, rapid y descent and positive Kussmaul sign, presence of pericardial knock on auscultation and pericardial calcification on imaging.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1967

question_text: A 65-year-old female presents to the OPD with complaints of shortness of breath and tiredness. On examination, there were engorged neck veins, and the JVP showed rapid X and Y descents. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation of right heart failure symptoms (shortness of breath, tiredness) with engorged neck veins and a characteristic JVP showing rapid X and Y descents is highly specific for constrictive pericarditis.

Pathophysiology of the JVP Waveform

The fibrotic and non-compliant pericardium in constrictive pericarditis encases the heart, limiting its total filling volume. However, early diastolic filling is rapid and unimpeded until the heart abruptly reaches the limit set by the constrictive pericardium. This creates a steep pressure gradient early in diastole, resulting in the rapid Y descent, which signifies a precipitous drop in right atrial pressure as blood rushes into the right ventricle. The rapid X descent is also prominent due to preserved systolic atrial relaxation.


The "square root sign" on ventricular pressure tracings (rapid early filling followed by a plateau) corresponds to this physical finding. This pattern is a key differentiator from other causes of elevated JVP.

Explanation of other options:

Cardiac tamponade (Option B): In tamponade, the pericardial fluid compresses the heart throughout the cardiac cycle, impairing diastolic filling. This results in a prominent X descent but a markedly diminished or absent Y descent.

Dilated cardiomyopathy (Option C): The JVP is usually elevated but does not show the classic rapid descents. The primary issue is impaired systolic contraction (pump failure), not restricted filling.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy (Option D): While clinically very similar to constrictive pericarditis (both cause restrictive physiology), the JVP typically shows a rapid X descent but a slow Y descent due to impaired ventricular relaxation and compliance from myocardial infiltration or fibrosis.

Key Takeaways:

  • The combination of elevated JVP with rapid X and Y descents is the hallmark of constrictive pericarditis.
  • This contrasts with cardiac tamponade (absent Y descent) and restrictive cardiomyopathy (slow Y descent).
  • Kussmaul's sign (a rise in JVP on inspiration) is also commonly associated with constriction.

question_text: Which of the following best describes 'Holiday heart syndrome'?
option_b: Dilated cardiomyopathy following long standing alcohol intake
option_c: Atrial fibrillation after binge alcohol consumption
explanation:
Holiday heart syndrome is defined as 'an acute cardiac rhythm and/or conduction disturbance associated with heavy ethanol consumption in a person without other clinical evidence of heart disease'. The most common arrhythmia in this condition is atrial fibrillation.

Alcohol cardiomyopathy is a type of dilated cardiomyopathy. Atrial fibrillation followed by ventricular tachycardia is the most commonly reported arrhythmias in this condition.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1964

question_text: A young female presents to the emergency department with palpitations and syncopal episodes following physical exertion. She reports having had similar episodes previously. An ECG performed during this episode shows characteristic findings. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's symptoms of palpitations, syncope following exercise, and a suggestive ECG pattern are characteristic of Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Dysplasia (ARVD), a condition that often leads to arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death, particularly in young, athletic individuals.

question_text: An athlete fell while running and died suddenly. The cut-section of a heart is shown. What of the following is correct about the condition?
option_a: Structural heart disease and check family members for atherosclerosis
option_b: Screening in close relatives for risk of arrhythmias
explanation:
The patient in the given question has HCM. They are at high risk of developing ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. 80% have mutations in the MYH7 or MYBPC3 gene.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is characterized by age-dependent and incomplete penetrance. Ventricular hypertrophy is rarely present at birth and usually develops later in life. Women appear to have lower penetrance of sarcomere mutations and an older age at hypertrophic cardiomyopathy diagnosis but increased rates of heart failure and mortality.

Screening of family members should begin in adolescence and extend through adulthood.

In MYBPC3 mutation carriers, the average age of disease development is ~40 years, while 30% remain free from hypertrophy after 70 years.

Related individuals who carry the same mutation may have a different extent and pattern of hypertrophy (e.g., asymmetric vs concentric), occurrence of outflow tract obstruction, and associated clinical outcomes, although sudden death and progression to heart failure occur more commonly in families with that history.

question_text: A 28 year old man presents with a history of syncope related to exercise. There is a family history of sudden cardiac death. On examination, the carotid pulse is jerky, there is a double apical pulsation. On auscultation there is a fourth heart sound, an ejection systolic murmur heard at the base of the heart.The inheritance of this condition is most likely:
explanation:
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is most commonly of Autosomal dominant inheritance. It occurs in at least one in 1,000 to one in 500 of the general population.

Inherited forms of dilated cardiomyopathy also have predominant autosomal dominant inheritance.

Some important Inherited syndromes with cardiac disease

  1. Duchenne muscular dystrophy: Dilated cardiomyopathy, X linked recessive inheritance (Dystrophin gene)
  2. Friedreich ataxia: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, autosomal recessive inheritance (Frataxin gene)
  3. Fabry disease: Restrictive cardiomyopathy, X linked recessive inheritance (Alpha galactosidase A)
  4. Kearns Sayre syndrome: Conduction defects, mitochondrial (maternal) inheritance
  5. Noonan syndrome: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, pulmonary stenosis, Autosomal dominant inheritance (PTPN11 gene)

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1966

question_text: Most common CVS finding in AIDS is:
explanation:
In patients with long-standing but treated HIV infections, accelerated atherosclerosis with myocardial infarction is increasingly common Coronary artery disease is the most common form of cardiovascular manifestation of HIV.

Others include:

  • HIV associated cardiomyopathy (leading to CHF)
  • Pericarditis
  • Non bacterial thrombotic endocarditis

Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 21st Ed Ch: 202 pg. 1568

question_text: Which of the following is not a cause for elevated Troponin T?
explanation:
Troponins are not elevated in a patient with stable or unstable angina. Raised troponins are markers of myocardial injury and is present in patients with myocardial infarction.

Other causes for raised cardiac troponins include:

  • Myocarditis
  • Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
  • Post cardioversion
  • Sepsis
  • Pulmonary embolism (causing RV strain)

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page no: 2055

question_text: A 25-year-old previously healthy woman has worsening fatigue with dyspnoea, palpitations, and fever over the past one week. Her clinical examination showed temperature 38.9C, respiratory rate 30/min, pulse rate of 105 bpm and BP of 95/65 mmHg. An ECG showed diffuse ST-T segment changes.Echocardiogram showed slight mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, global left ventricular hypokinesia, but no valvular vegetations. Her troponin I was 12 ng/mL (NR<0.04). She recovers over the next two weeks with no apparent sequelae. Which of the following laboratory test findings best explains the underlying etiology for these events?
option_c: Blood culture positive for Streptococcus, viridans group
explanation:
She was suffering from myocarditis, which is supported by the fever, tachycardia, echo finding of global LV hypokinesia and markedly raised troponin. Myocarditis can have features similar to cardiomyopathy and the mild valvular disease is quite compatible.

Most common infectious cause of myocarditis is viruses – commonly Coxsackie virus and parvo virus B19.

The important bacterial infections causing myocarditis include Staphylococcus, streptococcus, Lyme disease, Diphtheria.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1961

question_text: Which of the following is seen in subclinical acute myocarditis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Subclinical acute myocarditis is myocardial inflammation without symptoms such as chest pain, palpitations, or dyspnea. (Option A ruled out)
  • It is usually detected incidentally during evaluation for abnormal biomarkers ( Elevated pro-BNP, Trop T) or imaging and is diagnosed when there is evidence of myocardial injury without cardiovascular symptoms, but with at least one abnormal finding raised cardiac biomarkers, ECG changes, or impaired function on echocardiography or MRI.(Option C ruled out)
  • Probable acute myocarditis is considered when cardiac symptoms are present with at least one supportive finding (elevated biomarkers, ECG abnormalities, or abnormal imaging).
  • Definite myocarditis requires histological or immunohistological confirmation for inflammation , irrespective of symptoms.
  • Elevated creatinine Indicates renal dysfunction, unrelated to myocarditis.(Option D ruled out).

Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5814111/

question_text: Which of the following is not true regarding dilated cardiomyopathy?
option_a: Functional mitral regurgitation may be seen
option_c: Ejection fraction is usually preserved till later stages
option_d: Left sided failure occurs earlier than right sided heart failure
explanation:
Dilated cardiomyopathy

  • Ejection fraction is usually significantly reduced (<30%) when the patient develops significant symptoms
  • Left ventricular wall thickness is reduced with increase in LV diastolic dimension
  • Mitral regurgitation is commonly seen due to annular and atrial dilatation
  • Left sided symptoms are predominantly present unlike restrictive cardiomyopathy which presents with right predominant disease
  • Most common cause is ischemic followed by infectious, toxin related, inflammatory and endocrine diseases related.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 21st edition, pg:1955

question_text:
A 27-year-old man who is known to have Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy has an out of hospital cardiac arrest and is successfully resuscitated.
What is the most appropriate mode of treatment?
explanation:
Patients with HCM are at increased risk of sudden cardiac death (SCD) due to VF/VT. Patients at high risk of SCD like those with sustained ventricular tachycardia, syncope, LV septal thickness more than 3 cm, family history of sudden cardiac death, abnormal BP response to exercise should be treated with Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator (ICD) implantation.
Implantable Cardiac Defibrillators (ICD) are superior to Amiodarone or Beta Blockers for preventing this. Reducing outflow tract obstruction with myomectomy or Alcohol Septal Ablation does not reduce the risk of SCD.

Other indications for ICD implantation include

  1. Cardiac arrest due to VF/VT
  2. Sustained VT causing haemodynamic compromise
  3. Chronic Heart Failure, LVEF<40% and associated syncopal episodes due to Non Sustained VT
  4. Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy causing cardiac arrest
  5. Congenital Long QT with family history of sudden cardiac death at young age

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1972

question_text: The cardiomyopathy characterised by fibrofatty replacement of the myocardium is:
explanation:
Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC)

  • Genetically determined cardiomyopathy characterised by fibrofatty replacement of myocardium
  • Defective cell signalling leading to transformation of myocytes to adipocytes
  • Syndromes associated with ARVC: Naxos disease, Carvajal syndrome
  • Patient may present with ventricular arrhythmias or heart failure

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1966

question_text: A 21-year-old man presents with recurrent chest pain, and on examination has a bisferiens pulse and a heaving apex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of a bisferiens (double-peaked) pulse and a heaving apex are characteristic physical findings of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM).

Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM)

  • A condition characterised by asymmetric hypertrophy of the ventricular septum, which can cause dynamic obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract.
  • HCM is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder, resulting from mutations in beta-myosin heavy-chain, troponin, and myosin-binding protein C, leading to inappropriate left ventricular hypertrophy
  • Patients may present with angina, dyspnea and syncope
  • It is the most common cause of sudden death
  • Pathologically, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is characterized by
    • Misaligned myocardial fibers
    • Myocardial fibrosis
    • Rigid left ventricle
    • Impaired diastolic filling.

Explanation of other options:

Dilated Cardiomyopathy (Option A): Dilated cardiomyopathy is characterized by left ventricular dilation and impaired systolic function. Physical exam findings typically include signs of heart failure, such as elevated jugular venous pressure and displaced apex beat.

Mitral Stenosis (Option C): In mitral stenosis, obstruction of blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle, leads to findings like diastolic murmur best heard at the apex and possible signs of left atrial enlargement.

Aortic Stenosis (Option D): Aortic stenosis causes obstruction of blood flow from the left ventricle into the aorta. While it can present with chest pain, the classic physical findings include a systolic ejection murmur and a reduced or delayed carotid pulse, not a bisferiens pulse.

Reference:

Dynamic Auscultation in HOCM

Auscultatory Findings in HOCM

Reverse splitting

question_text: All of the following conditions are associated with elevated JVP ~12 cm H<sub>2</sub>O that increases on deep inspiration except:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The elevation of JVP on deep inspiration refers to the Kussmaul sign, which is not seen in Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM).
  • HOCM is typically characterized by a bisferiens (double-peaked) arterial pulse and a heaving, displaced apex beat on physical examination.

Kussmaul's sign

Kussmaul's sign is defined as a rise or a lack of fall of the JVP during inspiration. It is classically associated with conditions like:

  • Constrictive pericarditis (Option B ruled out)
  • Restrictive cardiomyopathy (Option D ruled out)
  • Massive pulmonary embolism
  • Right ventricular failure
  • Advanced left ventricular systolic heart failure.
  • Cor Pulmonale (Option C ruled out)

question_text: A young athlete presented with chest pain and dyspnea. His brother passed away due to sudden cardiac death. He is diagnosed with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). A harsh systolic murmur is heard along the left sternal border. Which of the following maneuvers will increase the intensity of this murmur?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

The Valsalva maneuver reduces preload, exacerbating left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO) in HCM and thereby increasing the murmur.

  • This is a classic case of Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM), an autosomal dominant genetic disorder characterized by asymmetric septal hypertrophy, dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO), and increased risk of sudden cardiac death, especially in young athletes.
  • Genetic mutations:
    • β-myosin heavy chain: Associated with significant hypertrophy and earlier presentation.
    • Troponin T: May cause minimal hypertrophy but high risk of sudden cardiac death due to myocardial disarray.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • The thickened septum narrows the LVOT.
    • Systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve further blocks the outflow.
    • LV becomes non-compliant, impairing diastolic filling.
    • Myocyte disarray increases risk of arrhythmias, especially ventricular fibrillation.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Exertional angina, dyspnea, and syncope due to dynamic obstruction and poor diastolic filling.
    • Sudden cardiac death often during exertion, especially in genetically predisposed athletes.
    • Jerky or bifid pulse due to dynamic changes in LV ejection.
    • Harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur, best heard at the left sternal border, which mimics aortic stenosis but lacks radiation to the neck.
  • Why murmur increases with Valsalva:
    • The Valsalva maneuver reduces venous return and preload, leading to a smaller LV cavity. This enhances septal-mitral valve contact, worsening the dynamic LVOT obstruction and increasing the intensity of the murmur in HOCM.

Auscultatory changes with maneuvers:

Explanation of other options:

Squatting (Option A): Increases both venous return and afterload, which distends the LV cavity and relieves the obstruction, thereby reducing murmur intensity.

Leaning forward with head down/up (Option B): This maneuver accentuates diastolic murmurs, particularly of aortic regurgitation, but has no significant impact on HOCM murmur.

Hand grip (Option C): Increases afterload, which reduces the gradient across the obstructed LVOT and diminishes murmur intensity in HCM.

Reference:

https://litfl.com/hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy-hcm-ecg-library/

https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article-abstract/37/5/498/2466086?redirectedFrom=fulltext

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1168371/

https://www.healio.com/cardiology/learn-the-heart/cardiology-review/topic-reviews/s2-heart-sound#

question_text: Which of the following is the most common infective cause of cardiomyopathy?
explanation:
Chagas disease, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi and transmitted by reduviid bug is the most common infectious cause of cardiomyopathy. Typical features include conduction system abnormalities commonly AV blocks

Parvovirus B19, Coxsackie and Echoviruses are the most common infectious causes of myocarditis

Bacterial causes of myocarditis include legionella, salmonella, Corynebacterium diphtheria etc

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1972

question_text: A 55-year-old man with a longstanding history of alcohol excess has had a progressive abdominal distension for several months.On physical examination he has a non-tender abdomen with no masses palpable, but there is a fluid thrill. An abdominal ultrasound scan shows a large abdominal fluid collection with a small cirrhotic liver. A chest x ray shows increased cardiothoracic ratio with bilateral pleural effusion. Which of the following conditions is most likely to be present?
explanation:
Alcohol when consumed in significant amounts for 5-10 years is a risk factor for development of alcohol induced cardiomyopathy which presents with features of dilated cardiomyopathy.

Toxicity is attributable to acetaldehyde, the primary metabolite of ethanol.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 259, Pg: 1959

question_text: A 25-year-old man whose brother had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) was referred for a cardiological assessment. His echocardiogram confirmed the condition. Which one of the following echocardiographic features is the most important risk factor for sudden cardiac death in a patient with HCM?
option_b: Systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve
option_d: Gradient across left ventricular outflow tract
explanation:
The most important echocardiographic risk factor of sudden cardiac death in HCM is increased LV wall thickness > 3 cm (major) followed by resting LV outflow gradient > 30 mmHg (minor).

Other risk factors for sudden cardiac death in HCM:

  • History of cardiac arrest or sustained VT
  • Family history of HCM and sudden cardiac death
  • Unexplained syncope
  • Lack of increase in BP or reduction in BP on exercise.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1972

question_text: Which of the following is not true regarding hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)?
option_a: Hand grip accentuates the murmur in HCM
option_b: Dynamic LVOT obstruction is a typical feature
option_c: Beta blockers are the preferred agents in medical management
option_d: ECG shows LVH with prominent Q waves
explanation:
Hand grip (increased afterload) cause a reduction in intensity of murmurs in HCM and aortic stenosis and a delayed onset of click / murmur in Mitral valve prolapse. Valsalva manoeuvre cause an increase in intensity of murmur in HCM and earlier onset of murmur in MVP. Standing also increases the murmur intensity in HCM.

Systolic anterior motion of mitral leaflet and Asymmetric septal hypertrophy are the major contributors of dynamic LVOT obstruction in HCM

Beta blockers and non-dihydropyridine CCBs (verapamil) are the preferred agents of medical management in HCM ECG findings of HCM include LVH changes with strain pattern and prominent q waves.

LVH in Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy LVH in Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1970

question_text: A 40-year-old man presented to your clinic because he is concerned about his family history of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy. His brother has recently deceased  due to the condition.  Which is the preferred investigation for screening for HCM in the patient ?
explanation:
Relatives of patients with HOCM should be offered screening especially in the context of a fatality. Transthoracic echocardiogram is the preferred screening modality in patients with suspected diagnosis.

Cardiac MRI may also be performed as a second line investigation in patients with HOCM especially during followup after surgical myomectomy or septal ablation therapy.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1969

question_text:
A 21-year-old man with Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy presents in a clinic with dizzy spells but has not had any syncopal episodes.
Which of the following, if present, would indicate an increased risk of sudden cardiac death?
option_a: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with maximum wall thickness of 2.1 cm
option_b: Blood Pressure drop of 20mmHg during peak exercise tolerance testing
option_c: Presence of ejection systolic murmur of Grade 6/6
option_d: Systolic Anterior Movement of the mitral valve on echocardiography
explanation:
Patients with Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) are at increased risk of sudden cardiac death due to VF/VT. The five poor prognostic markers which are predictive of sudden cardiac death are:

  1. Syncope
  2. Family History of HCM and sudden cardiac death
  3. Maximum Left Ventricular Wall Thickness >3cm
  4. BP drop during peak exercise on stress testing
  5. History of cardiac arrest / sustained VT

LVOT obstruction causes symptoms and can lead to deterioration of LV function but does not predict sudden cardiac death. Asymmetric Septal Hypertrophy is a feature of HCM, in order to assess the risk for sudden cardiac death a detailed echocardiogram with measurements of the maximum left ventricular wall thickness is required.

Systolic anterior movement of the mitral valve is often seen on echocardiogram and is thought to be the mechanism behind the left ventricular outflow tract obstruction.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1972

question_text: Which of the following nutrient deficiencies is not associated with dilated cardiomyopathy?
explanation:
The nutrient deficiencies associated with dilated cardiomyopathy include:

  • Thiamine (Wet beriberi)
  • Selenium (Keshan cardiomyopathy)
  • Carnitine
  • Taurine
  • Niacin

The electrolyte abnormalities like hypocalcemia and hypophosphatemia have also been linked with causation of dilated cardiomyopathy.

Pyridoxine deficiency can lead to peripheral neuropathy, sideroblastic anemia, skin lesions.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1965

question_text: A 65 year old female presented to the emergency department with chest discomfort and breathlessness after she heard the news about the demise of her husband. She had no fever, hypotension or syncope. ECG was suggestive of anterolateral wall ischemia. ECHO showed global ventricular dilation with ballooning of apex and basal contraction. What is the likely diagnosis ?
option_d: MI due to left anterior descending coronary artery occlusion
explanation:
The condition described in question is Takotsubo cardiomyopathy a.k.a apical ballooning syndrome or acute stress induced cardiomyopathy. The ventricle shows global ventricular dilation with apical ballooning and hypercontractility of segments at the base.

Clinical presentation may mimic acute MI with features of angina, hypotension or pulmonary edema. Coronary angiogram is required to rule out coronary artery occlusion

Treatment include beta blockers and Angiotension receptor blockers.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1966

question_text: The 9 month old child of a diabetic mother presents with tachypnea and hepatomegaly. Echocardiography of the heart showed normal cardiac morphology with asymmetric septal hypertrophy. Which of the following you will give to treat this child :
explanation: Answer is C (Propranolol) The symptoms of the patient and echocardiographic finding of asymmetrical septal hypertrophy almost confirms the diagnosis of Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Beta Blockers should be the initial drug Q in symptomatic individuals Management of HOCM Avoidance of strenuous physical activity Beta Blockers should be the initial drug Q in symptomatic individuals. They reduce: - Heart rate - Blood pressure - Stiffness of left ventricle - Fatal arrythmias Calcium channel BlockersQ (verapamil and diltiazem) are alternative drugs. - They reduce-stiffness of ventricle - Elevated diastolic pressures Amiadarone may be used to reduce arrythmias. Surgical myomectomy

question_text: Which is the Gold Standard Investigation for confirming the diagnosis of myocarditis?
explanation:
Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing myocarditis.

Patients with recent or ongoing viral syndromes have been classified into three levels of myocarditis diagnosis.

  1. Possible subclinical acute myocarditis is diagnosed when a typical viral syndrome occurs without cardiac symptoms, but with elevated biomarkers of cardiac injury, ECG suggestive of acute injury, and/or reduced left ventricular ejection fraction or regional wall motion abnormality.
  2. Probable acute myocarditis is diagnosed when the above criteria are met and accompanied by cardiac symptoms, such as shortness of breath or chest pain, which can result from pericarditis or myocarditis. When clinical findings of pericarditis are accompanied by elevated troponin or CK-MB or abnormal cardiac wall motion, the terms perimyocarditis or myopericarditis are sometimes used.
  3. Definite myocarditis is diagnosed when there is histologic or immunohistologic evidence of inflammation on endomyocardial biopsy and does not require any other laboratory or clinical criteria

When biopsy is performed, the key Dallas criteria for myocarditis include lymphocytic infiltrate with evidence of myocyte necrosis and are negative in 80-90% of patients with clinical myocarditis. Negative Dallas criteria can reflect sampling error or early resolution of lymphocytic infiltrates, but may also be influenced by the insensitivity of the test when inflammation results from cytokines and antibody-mediated injury.

question_text: A 55 year old patient presented with breathlessness, abdominal distension and ankle oedema. The blood pressure is 135/80 mmHg. On examination, her JVP rises with inspiration. She has a soft systolic murmur and a third heart sound. ECG shows poor R wave progression. An echocardiogram shows no pericardial effusion, the ventricles are stiff and systolic function is mildly impaired. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The predominant right sided heart failure point towards either constrictive pericarditis or restrictive cardiomyopathy. The rise in JVP with inspiration is also seen in both conditions.

Echocardiography showing no pericardial effusion / calcification and presence of stiff ventricles suggest restrictive cardiomyopathy rather than constrictive pericarditis. The transmitral dopplers on the echo may show E/A wave reversal and high velocities which may suggest a restrictive picture.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy is usually caused by inflitrative diseases like haemochromatosis, endomyocardial fibrosis, sarcoidosis, myeloma, lymphoma or connective tissue disease.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1967

question_text: A 65 year old lady, diagnosed with ischaemic cardiomyopathy has breathlessness walking up one flight of stairs. Her lung fields are clear. Chest X ray shows cardiomegaly and clear lung fields. She is currently on frusemide 40mg bd, ramipril 5 mg and Metoprolol 100 mg per day. Which of the following medication would be the most appropriate addition?
explanation:
The agents proven to have mortality benefit in subjects with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction include ACE inhibitors / ARBs, beta blockers, ARNI, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors. Hence the best answer would be spironolactone which is an MRA.

Diuretics are used for symptomatic relief in fluid overload patients with chronic heart failure but does not confer any mortality benefit. In patients with HFrEF and heart rate > 70 bpm, ivabradine can be used to control the rate. .

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1947

question_text: A 75-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy has fatigue and exertional dyspnea NYHA class 3. On examination his BP was 150/95. He is currently taking Ramipril 10 mg od and Furosemide 80 mg OD. Which of the following drugs would be the best addition to his current regimen ?
explanation:
The five pillars of treatment in patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) are:

  • ACE inhibitors / ARBs
  • Angiotensin receptor / neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI)
  • Beta blockers
  • Mineralocorticoid receptor blockers
  • SGLT2 inhibitors (with or without Diabetes mellitus)

The beta blockers approved for this condition include Carvedilol, Metoprolol, Bisoprolol(COPERNICUS, MERITHF, CIBIS trials). They should be initiated once patients are stable (rather than in the acute setting) and can be used in all classes of heart failure.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1947

question_text: Which of the following about Dapagliflozin in heart failure is true?
option_a: Associated with a reduction in CV deaths and heart failure events
option_b: Useful only in patients with Type 2 DM and HF
option_c: Useful only in patients with Type1 DM and HF
option_d: Only benefit in HF events but no role in reduction of CV deaths.
explanation:
Dapagliflozin is an SGLT2 inhibitor that reduces the renal reabsorption of glucose and induces glycosuria.

Apart from reduction of blood glucose, it also improves cardiac function and reduce mortality rates in patients with heart failure with both preserved and reduced ejection fraction. SGLT2 inhibitors also reduce the progression of Diabetic nephropathy by reducing albuminuria and GFR fall.

SGLT2 inhibitors are advocated in patients with heart failure irrespective of the presence of Diabetes mellitus.

The use of SGLT2 inhibitors is discouraged in Type 1 Diabetes patients due to risk of DKA.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1948

question_text: 25 year old village man presented to OPD with complaints of RUQ pain and fever since 2 week and started developing productive cough since last 2 days. On investigations Chest X-Ray shows normal lung fields and there is altered echogenicity in liver in right lobe in USG confirming the diagnosis of Amebiasis. What can be the possible case of cough in this patient?
explanation:
Amebiasis is common in rural areas and it matches with presenting complaints of the patient except cough. Hepatobronchial fistula is the known complication of amebiasis which causes productive cough but has a excellent prognosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 223Pg 1717

question_text:
A 79 year-old-man known to have chronic congestive heart failure is readmitted with worsening heart failure. His furosemide (frusemide) dosage is increased to 200 mg/day to aid the relief of his symptoms. His other medications are bendrofluazide, ramipril and bisoprolol.
Which of the following effects can be encountered up on dose modification?
explanation:
Adverse effects of Frusemide therapy

  1. Electrolyte disturbances: hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia
  2. Acid-base disturbance: metabolic alkalosis
  3. Dehydration and hypotension
  4. Hyperuricemia and gout
  5. Hyperglycemia
  6. Ototoxicity (when IV doses exceed 80 mg/hour)

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1946, 1949

question_text: An elderly woman is taking furosemide and ramipril for heart failure. She visited her family doctor complaining of pain in her left knee and was prescribed rofecoxib. Two weeks later she is admitted in emergency room with breathlessness and pedal oedema.What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
Rofecoxib does not interact with or affect the actions of furosemide. It may act in conjunction with ramipril to cause deterioration of renal function. Rofecoxib is a cyclo-oxygenase-2 (Cox-2) specific inhibitor and has a reduced adverse effect on the gastrointestinal tract. However, rofecoxib can cause fluid retention and worsen a pre-existing heart failure. It is therefore contraindicated in patients with severe congestive heart failure.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1936

question_text: Which of the following is not a component assessed in NYHA functional classification in heart failure
explanation:
The NYHA Functional Classification categorizes heart failure patients based on their limitations during physical activity.

The clinical parameters assessed include undue fatigue, palpitation, dyspnea and angina. 

Class I: Ordinary physical activity does not cause undue fatigue, palpitation, dyspnea, or anginal pain.

Class II: They are comfortable at rest, but ordinary physical activity results in fatigue, palpitation, and dyspnea.

Class III: Marked limitation of physical activity. Patients are comfortable at rest, but less than ordinary activity causes symptoms

Class IV: Symptoms of heart failure occur even at rest, and any physical activity exacerbates discomfort

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1798

question_text:
A 77-year-old male with type 2 diabetes requires improved glycaemic control. He also suffers from heart failure which is controlled with diuretic and ACEis.
Which of the following hypoglycaemic agents is contraindicated in this patient?
explanation:
Rosiglitazone can result in fluid retention of unknown etiology which may cause a mild dilutional anaemia (haemoglobin typically falls by 1 to 2 g/dl) and ankle oedema. It is contraindicated in hepatic dysfunction and congestive heart failure

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1936

question_text: A patient presented with features of severe heart failure and was diagnosed with Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF). What is the treatment of ARF-induced carditis in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation

  • In Acute Rheumatic Fever, the most serious manifestation is carditis, which can lead to severe heart failure.
  • In such cases, glucocorticoids (e.g., Prednisone, Prednisolone) are the treatment of choice because they suppress the autoimmune inflammatory response and help control myocardial inflammation.
  • Supportive therapy for heart failure (diuretics, ACE inhibitors, oxygen) is also given, but the specific therapy for ARF-induced carditis is glucocorticoids.
  • Long-term secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin is also indicated but not as the acute treatment for severe carditis.

Glucocorticoids in ARF

  • Indication:
    • Reserved for moderate to severe carditis, especially if accompanied by heart failure.
  • Preferred agent:
    • Oral prednisone or prednisolone is the typical choice.
  • Dosage:
  • Children: ~1-2 mg/kg/day, up to 60-80 mg/day
  • Duration & tapering:
    • Continue for approximately 2-3 weeks, then taper gradually-reducing dose

Secondary prophylaxis for Rheumatic Fever:

Dose and Frequency:

Patients weighing <27 kg: 600,000 IU benzathine penicillin every 3 weeks.

Patients ≥27 kg: 1.2 million IU benzathine penicillin every 3 weeks.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Aspirin (Option A):

  • Aspirin (or other NSAIDs) is used for migratory polyarthritis in ARF, where it provides symptomatic relief.
  • However, it is not effective in treating severe carditis with heart failure.

Benzathine penicillin (Option B):

  • Essential for eradication of group A streptococcus and secondary prophylaxis.
  • While mandatory for preventing recurrence, it does not reverse or treat acute carditis with heart failure.

Surgical valve replacement (Option C):

  • Considered in cases of chronic rheumatic heart disease with severe valvular damage or failure of medical therapy.
  • In the acute phase, especially with active ARF carditis, glucocorticoids are first line. Surgery is not the immediate treatment.

Key Takeaway:

Revised Jones Criteria for the diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF)

question_text: A 35-year-old female with a history of hypertension presents to the emergency department with complaints of palpitations and shortness of breath. On examination, she has bilateral basal crackles and an irregularly irregular pulse. ECG done is shown below. Which of the following management methods is least useful in this patient?
option_a: Cardioversion in a hemodynamically unstable patient
option_c: Beta blockers are to be given for rate control if the patient is intolerant to calcium channel blockers
option_d: IV digoxin for ventricular rate control
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

ECG shows absent P waves with an irregularly irregular ventricular rate, suspecting atrial fibrillation with acute decompensated heart failure. Beta-blockers are not preferred in acute decompensated heart failure due to their negative inotropic effect, which may worsen cardiac output.

  • This patient presents with acute atrial fibrillation (AF) and signs of acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF)-dyspnea, basal crackles, and irregularly irregular pulse.
  • Management in this setting prioritizes rate control, rhythm control, and stroke prevention through anticoagulation.
  • In acute settings with hemodynamic instability, synchronized cardioversion is the treatment of choice to rapidly restore sinus rhythm.
  • In stable patients with ADHF, rate control is preferred initially.
  • However, beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers (like diltiazem/verapamil) should be avoided in the acute decompensated phase due to their negative inotropic effect, which can reduce myocardial contractility and worsen heart failure.
  • Therefore, giving beta blockers when calcium channel blockers are not tolerated is not appropriate in this setting.
  • In contrast, IV digoxin can be used for rate control in AF with heart failure, especially when systolic function is compromised, as it has minimal impact on contractility acutely.
  • Additionally, Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs) are essential in AF to reduce the risk of thromboembolic complications, such as stroke.

Explanation of other options:

Cardioversion in a hemodynamically unstable patient (Option A): Appropriate and often life-saving in AF with hemodynamic instability. This is the treatment of choice in acute decompensated heart failure with AF when the patient is unstable.

Direct oral anticoagulants (Option B): Crucial to prevent thromboembolic complications like stroke in patients with AF. DOACs are preferred over warfarin unless contraindicated.

IV digoxin for ventricular rate control (Option D): Useful in controlling ventricular rate in AF when beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers are contraindicated, particularly in patients with heart failure.

question_text: A patient presents with frothy sputum, hemoptysis, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and dyspnea on exertion. Lung biopsy reveals hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Which of the following conditions is least likely to be associated with this finding?
explanation:
Explanation:

Hemosiderin-laden macrophages ("heart failure cells") in the lungs result from chronic pulmonary congestion, most often due to increased pressure on the pulmonary venous side-commonly seen with left-sided heart failure, pulmonary vein obstruction, or volume overload. Right ventricular failure generally causes systemic venous congestion (e.g., peripheral edema, ascites) and is not a typical cause of pulmonary congestion or hemosiderin-laden macrophages in the lungs.

Hemosiderin-laden macrophages, known as heart failure cells, are characteristic of long-standing pulmonary venous congestion.

  • In chronic pulmonary congestion, persistent high pressure in the pulmonary veins causes red cell extravasation into the alveoli.
  • Alveolar macrophages phagocytose RBCs, break down haemoglobin, and store iron as hemosiderin, leading to the formation of heart failure cells.
  • These cells are typically found in lung biopsy specimens from patients with left-sided heart failure.
  • The interalveolar septa also become thickened and fibrotic over time.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Volume overload (Option A): Can increase pulmonary capillary pressure, resulting in pulmonary congestion and hemosiderin-laden macrophages.

Pulmonary vein obstruction (Option C): Causes increased back pressure in the pulmonary circulation, leading to this finding.

Protein-losing enteropathy (Option D): Primarily affects protein absorption but may result from chronic right heart failure; however, it is less directly related than RV failure.

question_text: Which of the following classifications is used for etiology of chronic pancreatitis?
explanation:
Option A: The Killip Classification for Heart Failure quantifies severity of heart failure in NSTEMI and predicts 30-day mortality.

Option B: Atlanta classification is used to diagnose, assess severity and classify radiological findings in acute pancreatitis

Option D: hinchey classification is used for perforated diverticular disease Alcoholism is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis in adults.

Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 21st Ed chap 348, pg. 2665,2661

question_text: Which of the following anti-diabetic drug is recently approved to be used in patients with heart failure with low ejection fraction and reduced urine output?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Empagliflozin is an SGLT2 inhibitor that blocks glucose and sodium reabsorption in the renal proximal tubule, promoting urinary excretion.
  • This mechanism provides cardiorenal benefits, reducing cardiovascular mortality and heart failure hospitalizations even in non-diabetic patients and slows chronic kidney disease progression. It also induces mild diuresis, weight loss, and reduces systolic blood pressure. However, it may cause genital infections, UTIs, dehydration, or hypotension.
  • It is not recommended when eGFR is below 45 mL/min due to reduced efficacy. Along with other SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists, it is among the few anti-diabetic agents proven to lower cardiovascular mortality.

Explanation of other options:

Linagliptin (Option A): It is a DPP-4 inhibitor, works by preventing the breakdown of incretin hormones. While it is generally cardiovascularly safe, it provides no specific benefit for heart failure, and some drugs in its class are associated with an increased risk of heart failure hospitalization.

Pioglitazone (Option C): a thiazolidinedione (TZD), is contraindicated in this clinical scenario. It causes significant, dose-dependent fluid retention and edema, which can dangerously exacerbate heart failure and is particularly unsafe for a patient with already impaired cardiac function and low urine output.

Insulin degludec (Option D): It is a long-acting basal insulin analogue used for glycemic control. Although it is cardiovascularly neutral, it offers no specific cardiorenal advantages and does not improve outcomes in heart failure or renal function.

question_text:
A 70-year-old male is referred by his family doctor for management of recently diagnosed congestive heart failure.
The patient has a history of poorly controlled hypertension. Over the last three months he has been aware of deteriorating shortness of breath, fatigue, and orthopnea. Over the last month he had been commenced on digoxin (62.5 μg daily), furosemide (80 mg daily), and amiloride 10 mg.
On examination he has a pulse of 96 bpm regularly, a blood pressure of 132/88 mmHg. His JVP was not raised, he had some scattered bibasal crackles on auscultation with a displaced apex beat in the anterior axillary line, sixth intercostal space. Auscultation of the heart revealed no murmurs and he had peripheral oedema to the mid tibia. An ECG reveals left ventricular hypertrophy and chest x ray shows cardiomegaly and calcified aorta.
Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
option_a: Add an ACE inhibitor to the current regimen
option_b: Add atenolol at a dose of 25 mg daily
option_d: Increase furosemide to 80 mg twice daily
explanation:
This patient would be classified as probably NYHA grade III - IV heart failure (dyspnea on minimal exertion - rest). With the persisting symptoms despite 80 mg of furosemide, guidelines would initially suggest the addition of an ACE inhibitor. There is no evidence that increasing a dose of digoxin above 62.5 µg in a patient in sinus rhythm would have any added benefit. Although beta blockers would be of further benefit in this patient, it is important first to establish him on ACEi and then introduce beta blockers such as carvedilol, metoprolol, or bisoprolol in a small dose and gradually increase.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1947

question_text: Which of the following medications are known to lower mortality in patients with heart failure?
explanation:
Explanation:

Clinical studies show that beta-blockers, such as metoprolol, play a key role in lowering mortality among patients with heart failure.

  • Beta-blockers counteract the harmful effects of prolonged sympathetic stimulation seen in heart failure.
  • Metoprolol in particular has been shown to improve left ventricular performance, lower mortality, reduce hospital admissions, and mitigate the adverse impact of sustained sympathetic activity.
  • When combined with ACE inhibitors, it provides clear survival benefits in heart failure patients.

Explanations of other options:

Furosemide (Option B): Although furosemide is frequently prescribed in heart failure to control symptoms and fluid overload, it has not demonstrated a mortality benefit. Its main role is to relieve congestion and improve comfort, without altering disease progression or long-term survival.

Prazosin (Option C): While prazosin, an alpha-blocker, can lower afterload, studies have not shown it to improve survival in heart failure patients. In fact, its vasodilatory action and reflex sympathetic stimulation may actually worsen heart failure.

Torsemide (Option D): Like furosemide, torsemide is a loop diuretic used to control fluid retention and relieve symptoms in heart failure, but it has not been shown to lower mortality. Although torsemide offers better bioavailability than furosemide, neither drug has demonstrated a survival advantage in clinical studies.

question_text: Which of the following conditions is most likely to produce a wide, relatively fixed split of S2?
option_d: Right bundle-branch block and heart failure
explanation:
Fixed splitting refers to a constant and unchanged splitting of S2 throughout the cardiac cycle. Atrial Septal Defect is the classical cause for the same. In a patient with RBBB and heart failure, the former makes the split wide and heart failure fixes the split. (Heart failure does not permit much of a change in ventricular volume with respiration, because breathing with congested lungs is shallow.)

In cases of moderate ventral septal defects, the widening is due to delayed P2, but it is not fixed. In WPW and other causes of electrical delay of LV conduction, including LBBB, there is a narrowly split S2.

Causes of paradoxical splitting of S2 (P2 before A2)

  • Severe aortic stenosis
  • Left bundle branch block (may also cause narrowly split S2)

Reference: Bilton Samuel J, Carande Elliott J (2018) The Mechanism of S2 (Second Heart Sound) Splitting in Normal Physiology and Congenital Heart Defects. J Pediatr Care Vol.4 No.2:3

question_text:
A 52-year-old woman who is already on ramipril, furosemide and bisoprolol for heart failure, decompensates and presents to ER with pulmonary oedema. Her heart rate is 120 bpm and her blood pressure is 100/65 mmHg. She is given oxygen and diamorphine.
Which of the following actions is indicated in her further management?
option_a: Increase diuretics and maintain the current dose of β-blocker
option_d: Increase diuretics, stop β-blockers and later increase the β-blocker dose when her lungs are dry
explanation:
Although β-Blockers are not started for the first time in a patient with pulmonary oedema, in a case like this, when the patient is already on β-Blockers, it is wise to carry on with the same dose. Beta blockers may be beneficial in acutely decompensated heart failure because they help break the neurohormonal vicious circle associated with worsening HF.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1945-47

question_text: A 68-year-old man is admitted with chronic congestive heart failure. Which of the following is true regarding the management principles in this patient ?
option_a: Loop diuretic administration would result in a decrease in mortality
option_b: Digoxin is more effective than ACE inhibitors in providing symptomatic relief
option_c: Administration of a β-blocker improve symptoms and exercise tolerance
option_d: Administration of spironolactone has no effect on the incidence of sudden cardiac death
explanation:
Beta-adrenoceptor blocking agents (metoprolol, bisoprolol and carvedilol) have been found to be useful in patients with chronic stable heart failure. The studies MERIT and CIBIS 2, using the β-blockers metoprolol and bisoprolol, respectively, have shown improved symptomatic class, exercise tolerance, left ventricular function and reduced mortality in heart failure of any cause.

Diuretic administration is associated with a rapid decrease in symptoms, but mortality rates are unchanged. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and ARBs have been found to be equally effective in chronic heart failure. Spironolactone reduces the mortality and sudden cardiac death rates, hence should be added to the treatment.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1948

question_text: A person experiencing shortness of breath with slight limitation during physical activity, where ordinary activities trigger symptoms but they remain symptom-free at rest, falls under which class according to the New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classification?
explanation:
Explanation:

This scenario corresponds to Class II in the New York Heart Association (NYHA) classification of heart failure.
