option_a: At high risk of heart failure without structural heart disease
option_b: Structural heart disease with prior symptoms of HF
option_c: Structural heart disease with current symptoms of HF
option_d: Structural heart disease without signs or symptoms of HF
explanation:
ACC/AHA has divided heart failure evolution into 4 stages.


Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page

question_text: Which is increased in plasma of chronic heart disease pts
explanation: Answer- A. BNP The plasma concentrations of both hormones are increased in patients with asymptomatic and symptomatic left ventricular dysfunction, permitting their use in diagnosis. BNP levels are simple and objective measures of cardiac function. These measures can be used to diagnoose heart failure including diastolic function.

question_text: A patient with stable angina develops symptoms of heart failure. Which of the following medications reduces mortality in this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitor) that lowers mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) by preventing vasoconstriction and fluid retention, thereby decreasing both preload and afterload.

It enhances survival, reduces hospital admissions, and relieves symptoms such as fatigue and dyspnea.

Mechanism: Inhibits the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, resulting in vasodilation, lower blood pressure, and improved cardiac output.

First-line agents for chronic CHF (mortality benefit):

  • ACE inhibitors: Captopril, Enalapril, Lisinopril
  • ARBs: Telmisartan, Olmesartan
  • ARNI (preferred): Sacubitril-Valsartan (ARB + Neprilysin inhibitor) → Any of these can be started initially.

Adverse effects:

  • ACE inhibitors: Cough, angioedema

Beta-blockers:

  • Cardioselective
    • 2nd generation: Metoprolol, Bisoprolol
    • 3rd generation: Carvedilol (α- and β-blocker; most effective in HF)
  • ADR: Bradycardia, hypotension

SGLT-2 inhibitors: Dapagliflozin, Empagliflozin

  • ADR: UTI, Fournier's gangrene, Euglycemic DKA

Aldosterone antagonists: Spironolactone

  • ADR: Gynecomastia

Management of CHF with cardiogenic shock:

  • Vasopressors: Norepinephrine, Dobutamine, Dopamine
  • Inodilators: Milrinone, Amrinone
  • Ca2+ sensitizer: Levosimendan
  • Direct myosin activator: Omecamtiv mecarbil

Management of refractory CHF:

  • LVAD (HeartMate)
  • Cardiac resynchronization therapy
  • Heart transplant

Explanation of Other Options:

Nifedipine (Option A): A calcium channel blocker mainly prescribed for hypertension and angina. It has no mortality benefit in heart failure and may even worsen the condition, particularly with short-acting forms due to reflex tachycardia.

Digoxin (Option B): Provides symptomatic improvement in heart failure, useful for rate control in atrial fibrillation and relief of HFrEF symptoms, but does not decrease mortality.

Torsemide (Option D): A loop diuretic that helps relieve fluid overload in heart failure, reducing edema and congestion, but offers no survival advantage.

question_text: A 63-year-old man with known chronic heart failure is admitted with dyspnea at rest. Examination reveals pitting oedema to his knees, elevated jugular venous pressure and basal crepitations. He is in sinus rhythm at a rate of 80 bpm and his blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg. Current medication includes bisoprolol 10 mg once daily, frusemide 80 mg once daily and ramipril 2.5 mg twice daily. The doctor commences him on iv frusemide 80 mg twice daily and increases his ramipril to 5 mg twice daily. When you review him the following day what other drug would be most appropriate to add in?
explanation:
This man has decompensated heart failure with symptoms at rest (New York Heart Association class IV). Examination has revealed significant fluid retention. The initial management plan of changing to iv furosemide is sensible since coexistent gut wall oedema is likely to impinge on oral absorption.

Spironolactone, mineralocorticoid receptor blocker, has been shown to improve the mortality rate and symptoms and reduce hospitalization in patients with severe CHF already on conventional treatment. In addition to diuretic effect, it will also improve the myocardial function by modifying the cardiac remodelling. Notable adverse effects include hyperkalemia, gynecomastia and worsening of renal function.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 21st edition, Page 1947

question_text: A patient presents with congestive heart failure. Which drug may be effective in reducing mortality?
explanation:
Standard drugs like digitalis and diuretics have not been shown to improve survival rates. Lidocaine and other antiarrhythmic agents are useful only when There is arrhythmia associated with heart failure. Aspirin is indicated only in cases of coronary occlusion or myocardial infarction.

The agents hown to have mortality benefit in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) are:

  • ACE inhibitors / ARBs
  • Angiotensin receptor / neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI)
  • Beta blockers
  • Mineralocorticoid receptor blockers
  • SGLT2 inhibitors (with or without Diabetes mellitus)

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1947

question_text: A 52 year old male with NYHA 3 chronic heart failure has a normal ejection fraction (54%) on echocardiography. Which of the following has been found to be useful in the management?
explanation:
The conventional drug therapy to reduce mortality in patients with HFrEF are less effective in those with HFpEF. Only two groups of drugs approved by FDA in HFpEF are ARNI (Sacubitril-Valsartan) and SGLT2 inhibitors. Diuretics are used only if there is fluid overload. Though not proven to have mortality benefit, ACEI/ARBs and beta-blockers are also given in HFpEF.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1948-49

question_text:
A 72-year-old woman is admitted with acute dyspnoea to the Emergency Department. Oxygen saturations are 94% on 30% supplementary oxygen and her respiratory rate is 30/min. A rapid B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) assay is reported as follows:BNP 62 pg/ml
What is the best interpretation of this result?
option_a: No conclusion can be drawn from this result
option_b: Pulmonary embolism is the most likely cause of her symptoms
option_c: If a further BNP level is above 50 pg/ml after one hour then this is diagnostic of heart failure
option_d: Heart failure is unlikely to be the cause of her dyspnoea
explanation:
B-type natriuretic peptide

B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is a hormone produced mainly by the left ventricular myocardium in response to strain. BNP Whilst heart failure is the most obvious cause of raised BNP levels any cause of left ventricular dysfunction such as myocardial ischaemia or valvular disease may raise levels. Raised levels may also be seen in patients with chronic kidney disease. Factors which reduce BNP levels include treatment with ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-2 receptor blockers and diuretics.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1939

question_text: Which of the following can result in a pseudo low BNP / NT proBNP?
explanation:
False increase in BNP levels

  • Advanced age
  • Renal impairment
  • Anemia
  • Stroke
  • Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension
  • Sepsis

Falsely low BNP levels

  • Flash pulmonary edema
  • Heart failure due to causes upstream from left ventricle (constrictive pericarditis, mitral stenosis, restrictive cardiomyopathy)
  • Obesity

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1939

question_text:
A 55 years old man presented with shortness of breath of acute onset. He was having a similar episode a month ago, for which he had taken some injections on an outpatient basis. On examination, his BP was 140/88 mmhg, PR of 108/min, oxygen saturation of 97% on room air and bilateral basal crepitations on auscultation. His 2-D echo revealed an ejection fraction of 20%. A diagnosis of HF with reduced EF was made.
NT pro BNP - > 2000 pg/ml
Based on above findings, what would be the ideal role of Sacubitril-Valsartan combination?
option_a: Improve clinical symptoms and reduce hospitalization.
option_c: No role as it is useful only in HF with preserved EF
option_d: Diuretics, ACE inhibitors are better options.
explanation:
Sacubitril/valsartan is a combination of 2 different drugs. Sacubitril is a pro-drug that, upon activation, acts as a neprilysin inhibitor. It inhibits neprilysin, thus preventing the breakdown of natriuretic peptides. This leads to a prolonged duration of the favourable effects of these peptides.

Valsartan is an angiotensin receptor blocker, Because neprilysin breaks down angiotensin II, inhibiting neprilysin will result in an accumulation of angiotensin II. Hence neprilysin inhibitor should always be combined with an ARB.

Neprilysin inhibition will also cause a build-up of bradykinin. Therefore, sacubitril cannot be used with an ACEI due to an increased risk of angioedema if ACEI and ARNI are used together or dosed in a short timeframe.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1948

question_text: In a patient with heart failure who is intolerant of ACE inhibitor / ARB, which of the following is best suited to provide survival benefit?
explanation:
In patients with HFrEF having intolerance to RAAS blockers, hydralazine with nitrates have been shown to improve mortality outcomes.

Ivabradine is an inhibitor of funny current (If) in SA node and is indicated if the patient remain symptomatic despite optimal therapy, cannot use beta-blockers or if HR > 70 bpm after therapy.

Digoxin and frusemide, though may offer symptomatic benefit to the patients, won't improve the survival in heart failure.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1947

question_text: Which of the following best describes the mechanism with which beta blockers improve outcomes in HFrEF?
option_c: Reduce heart rate by inhibiting funny currents in SA node
explanation:
Beta blockers improve mortality and quality of life in chronic heart failure (COPERNICUS, MERIT, CIBIS trials). They reduce heart rate and myocardial contractility thereby reducing the myocardial oxygen consumption

Ivabradine reduce the heart rate by inhibiting the funny current (If) in SA node.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1948

question_text: Which of the following is not true regarding NT-proBNP ?
option_a: It is released in response to ventricular volume and pressure overload
option_b: Level of NT-proBNP correlate with severity of heart failure
option_c: Levels fall after initiation of definitive therapy for heart failure
option_d: Levels fall in old age and renal dysfunction
explanation:
NT-proBNP

  • Marker of cardiac stress used in the diagnosis and prognostication of heart failure
  • BNP and its N-terminal fragment is produced from the ventricular myocytes
  • Levels are < 125 pg/ml in normal individuals and values > 300 - 400 pg/ml is highly suggestive of heart failure
  • Wide variety of conditions can result in elevated levels apart from heart failure including renal failure, old age, stroke, critical illnesses, anemia, hyperthyroidism etc.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1939

question_text:
Sign(s) of heart failure?
a. Non pulsatile elevated JVP
b. Orthopnea
c. Dyspnea occurring after 2 hours of getting bed rest
d. Right upper quadrant pain
explanation:
The JVP in cardiac failure is pulsatile. Option c is suggestive of PND(Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea). Right Upper quadrant pain is suggestive of hepatic congestion. Shortness of breath with activity or when lying down.

Fatigue and weakness, Swelling in the legs, ankles and feet, Rapid or irregular heartbeat, Reduced ability to exercise, Wheezing are some of the signs of Cardiac failure.

question_text: Anti androgen used in heart failure ?
explanation: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Spironolactone o Spironolactone and eplerenone are the aldosterone antagonists. They are used as potassium sparing diuretics. Their diurectic effect is quite feeble, but in CHF these drugs reduce the mortality (at doses lower than diuretic doses) by antagonizing the effect of aldosterone (reversal of remodelling). Spironolactone also possesses anti- androgenic effects.

question_text: A 64-year-old male with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus has fatigue and exertional dyspnea. He is compliant with his medications. Echo reveals normal systolic function and grade 2 diastolic dysfunction, left ventricular hypertrophy, left atrial enlargement, and EF 60%. His BNP is elevated at 980 pg/mL. He has had two hospital admissions for heart failure in the past year. He is currently euvolemic and is on optimal doses of beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
option_b: lvabradine - to decrease heart rate and improve ventricular filling
option_c: Loop diuretic + SGLT2 inhibitor - to improve long term outcome
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's clinical presentation, with an ejection fraction of 60%, is indicative of Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF). Long-term management primarily focuses on symptom control, decongestion, and addressing comorbidities. Currently, initiating SGLT2 inhibitors along with loop diuretics is considered beneficial in managing HFpEF.

In patients with diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitors have demonstrated a reduction in the risk of developing heart failure, suggesting their potential effectiveness in HFpEF as well. Additionally, angiotensin receptors-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs) are being investigated as part of emerging therapies. Overall, management of HFpEF emphasizes controlling fluid overload, optimizing treatment of comorbid conditions, and minimizing factors that can worsen symptoms.

Explanation for other Options:

Digoxin - to increase myocardial contractility (Option A): Digoxin primarily increases systolic function. HFpEF patients have preserved EF, so increasing contractility is not beneficial and does not improve mortality or hospitalizations.

lvabradine - to decrease heart rate and improve ventricular filling (Option B): Ivabradine selectively lowers heart rate and can improve filling in HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) with sinus rhythm. In HFpEF, evidence for ivabradine improving outcomes is limited and not guideline-recommended.

Ranolazine - to reduce angina (Option D): Ranolazine is an antianginal agent. It does not improve heart failure symptoms, hospitalizations, or long-term outcomes in HFpEF.

question_text: Which is not associated with congestive cardiac failure?
explanation:
Explanation:

Non-pulsatile elevated JVP is not seen in cardiac failure.

In congestive cardiac failure (especially right-sided or biventricular failure) systemic venous pressure is raised because the right atrium and venous system are volume/pressure-overloaded. The raised jugular venous pressure (JVP) in CCF retains the normal venous waveform (visible a- and v-waves), so the elevation is pulsatile. Loss of the normal pulsations (a non-pulsatile venous distension) is therefore not typical of heart failure.

A non-pulsatile raised neck venous pressure suggests an extrinsic or intraluminal obstruction of the superior vena cava (e.g., mediastinal mass, thrombosis) or other causes that blunt transmission of right-atrial waves to the neck veins. In SVC obstruction the veins are distended but the normal cardiac pulsations are lost or very faint.

Explanation for other Options:

Orthopnea (Option A): Difficulty breathing when lying flat occurs in left-sided heart failure due to redistribution of fluid from the lower limbs to the lungs, worsening pulmonary congestion. This is a classic feature of CCF.

PND (Option B): Sudden breathlessness that awakens the patient from sleep is another hallmark of left-sided heart failure, caused by pulmonary venous hypertension and interstitial edema.

Right hypochondrium pain (Option D): Seen in right-sided heart failure due to hepatic congestion and stretching of the liver capsule. Patients may also show hepatomegaly and tenderness in the right upper quadrant.

Key takeaway:

explanation: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Spironolactone o Among potassium sparing diuretics, aldosterone antagonists (Spironolactone, eplerenone) reduce mortality in CHF.

question_text:
A 56-year-old woman with a history of myocardial infarction two years ago is now presenting with a cough and shortness of breath during minimal exertion. On physical examination, there was dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds on the right side. A chest X-ray revealed a moderate right-sided pleural effusion. Ultrasound-guided thoracocentesis was performed, and the laboratory findings are as follows:
Pleural fluid findings: :
1. Appearance: turbid:
2. pH: 7.1:
3. Protein: 3.2 g/dL:
4. Lactate dehydrogenase: 80 U/L (normal serum LDH- 50-150 U/L) :
5. Pleural fluid protein/serum protein ratio: 0.34:
6. Pleural fluid LDH /serum LDH: 0.3:
7. Glucose: 54 mg/dL:
8. WBC count: 4000 cells/µL with >50% lymphocytes:
9. Adenosine deaminase: 30 U/L:
10. AFB smear microscopy: Negative:
11. Gram staining and microscopy: No organisms, no pus cells
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical scenario described is consistent with a diagnosis of congestive heart failure (CHF). According to Light's criteria, the pleural effusion is classified as transudative.

Congestive Heart Failure - Clinical features:

  • Reduced cardiac output
  • Decreased stroke volume
  • Increased heart rate
  • Enhanced sympathetic activity, leading to palpitations and diaphoresis
  • Orthopnea
  • Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea

Explanation for other options:

Parapneumonic pleural effusion (Option A): typically shows an increased white blood cell count, particularly neutrophils, and the fluid often appears cloudy.

Both malignant pleural effusion (Option B) and tuberculous pleural effusion (Option D) are characterized as exudative.

Reference:

://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4753987/#sec4

question_text: Which of the following anticoagulants has a mechanism of action involving antithrombin-dependent inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa?
explanation:
Dalteparin is a low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), the effect of which is mediated by enhanced avidity of antithrombin for its natural substrates, thrombin and factor Xa. Apixaban and edoxaban are direct-acting inhibitors of factor Xa, while dabigatran and bivalirudin are direct thrombin inhibitors

PCC: Prothrombin Complex Concentrates

FFP: Fresh Frozen Plasma

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 118 Pg: 929-936.

question_text:
A 26 year old woman has symptoms of lethargy, bloody diarrhoea and a previous history of DVT in the leg. On examination, the left eye was inflamed and multiple mouth ulcers were noted. Colonoscopy was organized and this confirmed colitis. She also has vulval ulcers.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Recurrent oral ulceration is the commonest manifestation and the presenting feature in Behcet's disease.

Diagnosis of Behcet’s disease requires - Recurrent oral ulcers plus two of the following four clinical manifestations:

  • Recurrent genital ulcers – cause scarring
  • Skin lesions - Erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis, papulopastular or acneiform nodules
  • Eye lesions - Anterior or posterior uveitis, corneal ulceration, conjunctivitis, papillitis,
  • Positive pathergy test

Vasculitis, pustules and subcutaneous nodules can also occur. Vascular thrombosis occurs in about 10% of patients.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 364, Pg: 2818

question_text: A 44-year-old man presents with a week history of a painful right leg. He has had previous episodes of erythema nodosum, recurrent oral and scrotal ulceration. Examination reveals a diffusely swollen left leg.What is the likely cause of his swollen leg?
explanation:
The overall diagnosis is Behcet's syndrome. There is a thrombotic tendency (venous>>arterial), hence the likely cause of a DVT.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:364 Pg:2817

question_text: A 25-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Room (ER) after a car accident. He has multiple injuries, including a fractured tibia. He was treated and stabilized, but 48 hours later, he suddenly developed difficulty in breathing, tachypnoea, tachycardia, and visible cyanosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Occurs 24-72 hours after long bone fractures (e.g., tibia, femur).
  • Classic triad:
    • Respiratory distress (hypoxemia, tachypnea, cyanosis)
    • Neurologic symptoms (confusion, agitation, altered mental status)
    • Petechial rash (often on upper body, conjunctiva)
  • Pathophysiology: Fat globules from bone marrow enter circulation, lodge in the pulmonary microvasculature, and cause inflammation and microvascular obstruction.
  • Diagnosis: Clinical; MRI brain may show "starfield" pattern (microemboli).

Explanation of other options:

Pulmonary embolism (Option B):

  • Less likely in this setting, as PE is typically associated with prolonged immobility, hypercoagulability, or recent surgery.
  • PE usually presents with pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, and sudden cardiovascular collapse, which are not mentioned

Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) (Option C):

  • Occurs later (4-7 days post-injury) and involves progressive hypoxia, not sudden respiratory distress.
  • Would be expected in severe systemic inflammation (sepsis, aspiration, or massive trauma).

Pulmonary edema (Option D):

  • This is fluid accumulation in the lungs, usually due to heart failure or volume overload, not trauma.
  • Would present with bilateral crackles, pink frothy sputum, and cardiogenic findings.

Key Takeaways:

Fat embolism syndrome (FES) is the most likely diagnosis in a trauma patient with respiratory distress 48 hours after a tibia fracture, especially if associated with neurological symptoms and petechiae.

question_text: Which of the following is not an aetiology for exudative pleural effusion?
explanation:
• Myxoedema causes a transudative pleural effusion
  • Pulmonary embolism may cause both exudative or transudative effusion.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 294 Pg 2199

question_text: Which of the following  associations is matched correctly?
option_c: Pulmonary embolism and left bundle branch block
explanation:
Pneumoconiosis is not associated with clubbing. Pulmonary embolism causes right heart strain and may present with RBBB Rv strain and Ischemia in ECG. Lung Carcinoids are rarely associated with pleural effusion. Bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is associated with wheezing.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: Ch: 288, Pg: 2165

question_text: An older man confined to bed for several months develops shortness of breath and chest pain. What should be the next appropriate step in his management?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In an elderly patient with prolonged immobility, breathlessness, and chest pain, pulmonary embolism secondary to DVT is strongly suspected, and CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) serves as the gold standard for confirmation.
  • CTPA offers high-resolution imaging of the pulmonary vessels, allowing for a definitive diagnosis or exclusion of pulmonary embolism.

Explanations of other options:

ECG (Option B): Although ECG may reveal findings like the S1Q3T3 pattern or signs of right ventricular strain in pulmonary embolism, these changes lack both sensitivity and specificity and cannot be relied upon as a substitute for pulmonary angiography.

CT thorax (Option C): A routine non-contrast CT scan of the chest is insufficient for detecting pulmonary embolism because it does not clearly show the pulmonary arteries; contrast in CTPA is crucial to reveal filling defects within the pulmonary circulation.

Echocardiography (Option D): Although echocardiography may reveal right heart strain and McConnell's sign (RV free wall hypokinesis as an indirect marker of PE) in severe cases, it is not the primary diagnostic tool. It serves more in post-diagnosis risk assessment rather than providing a definitive confirmation or exclusion of pulmonary embolism.

question_text: A 60-year-old bedridden patient suddenly develops breathlessness and chest pain, and a CTPA is performed. Which non-invasive test would help confirm the underlying cause of this presentation?
explanation:
Explanation:

The CT showing filling defects in both pulmonary arteries, along with the patient's bedridden state, suggests PE secondary to DVT, for which Doppler ultrasound is the preferred non-invasive test to confirm the embolic source.


Explanations of other options:

D-dimer (Option A): D-dimer reflects fibrin breakdown and rises in conditions involving clot formation and lysis, such as DVT and PE. In this case, since CTPA has already demonstrated PE, a D-dimer test would add no further diagnostic value. It is a non-specific marker and is primarily useful as a screening test before imaging rather than after PE has been confirmed.

MRI (Option B): MRI can be a useful imaging modality, but it is not the investigation of choice for determining the cause of PE. Since CTPA has already been done and serves as the gold standard for diagnosing PE, MRI is not preferred in this context.

Coagulogram (Option C): A coagulogram assesses multiple components of the clotting process and is useful for identifying bleeding disorders or coagulopathies. Although it can give information about the patient's coagulation profile, it is not the most specific test to establish the underlying cause of PE.

question_text: A 60 year old asthmatic lady is admitted with sudden onset left sided pleuritic chest pain accompanied by shortness of breath. Arterial blood gases are as follows: pH of 7.30, pO2 of 56.2 mmhg, and pCO2 of 28.5 mmhg. Chest XR is normal. She is commenced on oxygen. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
option_a: Request a chest XRay in expiration
option_c: Start low molecular weight heparin and request CT pulmonary angiography
option_d: Start low molecular weight heparin and request a V/Q scan
explanation:
• The symptoms and findings clearly point out towards pulmonary embolism (PE). As the clinical probability of PE is high, measurement of D-dimer should not be performed, since the result would not alter the need for definitive investigation.
  • Measurement of D-dimer should only be performed when the probability of PE is low, when a normal value would be taken as reassuring and further investigation would not be pursued.
  • V/Q scan less likely to be unhelpful in view of her asthma; hence a CT pulmonary angiogram would be the imaging procedure of choice.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:279 Pg 2097

question_text: Which one of the following is true regarding acute pulmonary embolism?
option_a: A normal ECG excludes the diagnosis
option_b: Embolectomy is more effective than thrombolysis in improving survival
option_c: Heparin is as effective as thrombolytic therapy
option_d: Thrombolysis administered through a peripheral vein is as effective as through a pulmonary artery catheter
explanation:
Embolectomies are rarely done nowadays due to the excellent results with thrombolysis.

Thrombolytic therapy is reserved for those with severely compromised circulation (equally effective through peripheral vein or via catheter in pulmonary artery).

Heparin reduces risk of further embolism (anticoagulant) and reduces pulmonary vasoconstriction.

Results of a trial of submassive PE, using the thrombolytic agent tenecteplase versus heparin alone, showed that death or hemodynamic collapse within 7 days of therapy was reduced by 56% in the tenecteplase group.

ECG is not a reliable diagnostic imaging tool for acute pulmonary embolism (PE) because most patients with PE have normal ECGs.

However, echocardiography is a very useful diagnostic tool for detecting conditions that may mimic PE, such as acute myocardial infarction, pericardial tamponade, and aortic dissection.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:273 pg:1915,1916

question_text: A 50-year-old woman with diabetes and recurrent DVT presents with a progressive skin rash spreading to her limb and abdomen despite anticoagulation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's presentation of a progressive skin lesion, long-standing diabetes, and recurrent deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is highly indicative of glucagonoma, a rare pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor characterized by excess glucagon secretion.

Glucagonoma

Glucagonomas are neuroendocrine tumors originating from multipotent stem cells of endodermal origin.

Clinical Features:

Characteristic dermatitis:

  • Presents as necrolytic migratory erythema (NME), predominantly affecting intertriginous areas such as the groin and buttocks.
  • The rash often fluctuates in severity (waxing and waning).

Other Common Symptoms:

  • Glucose intolerance
  • Significant weight loss

Tumor Characteristics:

  • Most glucagonomas are large at diagnosis and are usually located in the tail of the pancreas.

Diagnosis:

  • Confirmed by elevated plasma glucagon levels, typically >1000 pg/mL.

Initial Treatment:

  • Somatostatin analogues (octreotide, lanreotide) reduce symptoms and control rash by inhibiting glucagon secretion.
  • Nutritional support with total parenteral nutrition, amino acids, and zinc supplementation to counteract weight loss and malnutrition.
  • Adjunctive therapies such as antibiotics, zinc replacement, and steroids may improve recovery from NME.

Surgical Recommendations:

  • Distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy is recommended for localized disease and is the only curative option for the minority of patients with localized tumors.

Complications:

  • Up to 33% of patients may develop a hypercoagulable state; perioperative anticoagulation is typically advised.

Explanation of Other Options:

Insulinoma (Option A): Results in excessive insulin secretion, causing hypoglycemia with symptoms like sweating, confusion, and palpitations. This patient, however, has hyperglycemia, which rules out insulinoma.

Gastrinoma (Option B): Leads to recurrent peptic ulcers, abdominal pain, and diarrhea due to high gastrin and acid levels, but it does not typically cause skin lesions or DVT.

VIPoma (Option D): Causes WDHA syndrome (Watery Diarrhea, Hypokalemia, Achlorhydria) and dehydration, but is not strongly associated with DVT or diabetes.

Key Takeaways:

  • Necrolytic migratory erythema + diabetes + DVT = glucagonoma.
  • Somatostatin analogues are first-line for symptom control.

question_text: A 60-year-old patient develops respiratory distress on the third postoperative day following major surgery. What is the most likely initial differential diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely differential in a postoperative patient on day 3 who develops sudden respiratory distress is pulmonary embolism.

  • Most pulmonary emboli originate from thrombi in the deep veins of the lower limbs or pelvis.
  • Other possible sources include the vena cava or the right atrium (especially in atrial fibrillation).
  • When a deep vein thrombus detaches, it travels through the vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary arteries, where it becomes lodged, causing acute pulmonary embolism.
  • Clinical presentation depends on the size and extent of obstruction, ranging from mild dyspnoea, cough, and pleuritic chest pain to sudden cardiovascular collapse in massive embolism.

Common postoperative complications

Explanation of other options:

Air embolism (Option B): Usually occurs intraoperatively or immediately post-op, often due to central venous catheter manipulation or neurosurgery in the sitting position.

Atelectasis (Option C): Common in the first 24-48 hours post-op, presents with gradual hypoxia and low-grade fever.

Pneumothorax (Option D): Can cause sudden breathlessness and chest pain, but usually occurs after thoracic or central line procedures, not spontaneously on day 3 after general surgery.

question_text: Which of the following imaging tests should be performed to confirm a diagnosis of pulmonary embolism in a patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is the first-line and gold standard imaging test for diagnosing acute pulmonary embolism (PE). It directly visualizes thrombi in the pulmonary arteries and has high sensitivity and specificity.

Clinical Evaluation of Pulmonary Embolism (PE):
PE symptoms are often nonspecific, making CT pulmonary angiography the primary diagnostic tool.

  • D-dimer:Highly sensitive but nonspecific; normal levels help rule out PE. Age-adjusted cutoff is recommended in patients >50 with low-to-moderate probability.
  • ECG:Most common finding is sinus tachycardia; most specific is S1Q3T3. T-wave inversions in V1-V4 suggest RV strain.
  • Venous ultrasonography:Demonstrates DVT via loss of vein compressibility; Doppler assesses blood flow.
  • Chest X-ray:Usually normal but may show Westermark's sign (oligemia), Hampton's hump (wedge-shaped opacity), or Palla's sign (enlarged pulmonary artery).
  • CT with contrast (CTPA):Gold standard; shows intraluminal filling defects or abrupt cut-off. RV enlargement suggests higher mortality risk.
  • Lung scan:Second-line for patients intolerant to contrast; high-probability perfusion scans strongly suggest PE.
  • MR imaging:MR venography with gadolinium detects DVT when USG is inconclusive; MR pulmonary angiography is less reliable for small PEs.
  • Echocardiography:Not diagnostic but helps identify alternate causes; McConnell's sign indicates RV dysfunction.

Explanation of other options:

Doppler echocardiography (option A): Useful for assessing right ventricular strain in massive PE but cannot directly visualize pulmonary artery clots.

Ventilation perfusion (V/Q) scan (Option C): A second-line test used when CTPA is contraindicated (e.g., contrast allergy, renal failure). It shows mismatched perfusion defects.

MR pulmonary angiography (Option D): An alternative for patients who cannot undergo CTPA or V/Q scanning, but it is less readily available and has lower sensitivity for subsegmental PEs.

Key Takeaways:

  • CTPA is the preferred initial imaging modality for confirming a diagnosis of PE.
  • It provides fast, accurate results and can identify alternative diagnoses.

question_text: An otherwise healthy 32-year-old man was the driver of a car involved in a high speed RTA 3 days ago. He has sustained a closed fracture of his femur which has been treated surgically with an intramedullary nail, as well as fractures of his right clavicle and left radius. He was managed according to ATLS protocol when he attended the emergency department. On examination, he is acutely short of breath and has a temperature of 37.5 C. The patient seems confused when you speak to him, and as you examine him, you note petechial haemorrhages.What do you think is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• The two diagnoses which should be considered first in this scenario are pulmonary embolism and fat embolism. Although the patient is at high risk of pulmonary embolism, and appropriate measures should be undertaken to reduce this, the clinical scenario is more suggestive of fat embolism.
  • Fat embolism is thought to occur as a result of release of lipid globules from damaged bone marrow fat cells. Another mechanism that has been suggested is the increased mobilisation of fatty acids peripherally.
  • The effects that are seen clinically depend on what part of the microvasculature is affected by the lipid globules. Pulmonary symptoms are caused by ventilation - perfusion mismatch.
  • Confusion (cerebral effects) may be seen, as well as a petechial rash caused by capillary damage in the skin.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 279, Pg-2095

question_text: A 55-year-old female presents with respiratory distress and hemoptysis on day 7 after knee replacement surgery. Her respiratory rate is 28/min, and pulse is 120/min. What is the most appropriate investigation?
explanation:
Explanation:

In a post-operative patient with acute onset of respiratory distress, tachycardia, and hemoptysis, pulmonary embolism is highly suspected. CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is the gold standard for the diagnosis of pulmonary embolism in hemodynamically stable patients.

Pulmonary Embolism (PE)

  • Pulmonary embolism occurs when a thrombus (most often from the deep veins of the legs or pelvis) travels to the pulmonary arteries, causing obstruction of pulmonary blood flow, ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch, and impaired gas exchange.
  • It is a life-threatening emergency

Causes & Risk Factors (Virchow's Triad)

  • Stasis of blood flow: Prolonged immobilization, post-surgery, long travel, heart failure
  • Endothelial injury: Trauma, surgery, indwelling catheters
  • Hypercoagulability: Malignancy, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, inherited thrombophilia

Clinical Features

Classic Triad (though not always present):

  1. Dyspnea (sudden-onset shortness of breath)
  2. Chest pain (pleuritic, worse on inspiration)
  3. Hemoptysis

Other features include:

  • Tachypnea (most common sign)
  • Tachycardia
  • Hypoxemia (↓ SpO2)
  • Cough, syncope, anxiety, diaphoresis
  • Signs of DVT (swollen, tender calf)

Severe/massive PE: Hypotension, shock, right heart failure, sudden death

Pathognomonic Sign

  • Hampton's Hump: Wedge-shaped pleural-based opacity on CXR
  • Westermark's Sign: Regional oligemia (focal decrease in vascular markings)

Investigations

  • ABG: Hypoxemia, respiratory alkalosis (low PaCO2)
  • D-dimer: Elevated (sensitive, not specific) (Option D ruled out)
  • Chest X-ray: Often normal; may show Hampton’s hump / Westermark's sign (Option B ruled out)
  • CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA): Gold standard imaging test
  • V/Q Scan: Used when CTPA contraindicated (Option A ruled out)
  • Doppler Ultrasound leg veins: To detect the source of DVT
  • ECG: Sinus tachycardia is the most common; may show S1Q3T3 pattern (acute cor pulmonale)

question_text: A 28-year-old lady presented to the Emergency department with a diagnosis of DVT. She is in the third trimester of her first pregnancy and she has been 'taking it easy' by resting a lot at home. In the department she develops a right hemiparesis. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cardiac abnormality?
explanation:
• This is a 'paradoxical embolus' where a right sided thrombus has crossed into the arterial circulation.
  • The commonest cause is a patent foramen ovale. Although atrial septal defects are also a cause, they are more rare.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 427, Pg: 3340

question_text:
A 55 year old woman is admitted with a history of syncopal episodes and breathlessness. There is no prior history of recent travel. 
On examination she looks distressed. Her pulse rate is 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 85/60, JVP is elevated by 5 cm. Respiratory rate 26 per minute, there is a soft systolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Breath sounds are clear. 
Investigations show : HB 12.4 g/dL, Blood gases pH 7.42, PaCO2 24.7 mmhg, PaO2 63.75 mmhg. 
She was put on high flow oxygen and given low molecular weight heparin. 
The next step in management of this patient should be:
explanation:
• The diagnosis massive central pulmonary embolus as the patient is hypoxic and hypotensive.
  • The best management is to obtain an urgent CTPA and then thrombolysis if there are no contraindications (e.g. high risk of bleeding).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:279Pg 2097

question_text: A female with a history of mitral stenosis presents with sudden-onset dyspnea, limb swelling, and calf pain. What is the most likely clinical diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In mitral stenosis, narrowing of the mitral valve impedes blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle, causing elevated left atrial pressure.
  • This pressure backs up into the pulmonary veins and capillaries, leading to pulmonary congestion and acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
  • Increase in pulmonary vascular resistance will lead to pulmonary hypertension.
  • Severe pulmonary hypertension due to mitral stenosis can lead to right ventricular enlargement, secondary tricuspid and pulmonic regurgitation, and ultimately right-sided heart failure.
  • Patients will present with symptoms like
    • Dyspnoea associated with cough
    • Orthopnoea
    • Exercise intolerance
    • Symptoms due to RV dysfunction include ema, hepatomegaly and ascites.

Explanation of other options:

Pulmonary embolism (Option A): Pulmonary embolism typically causes sudden respiratory difficulty due to reduced blood flow to the lungs, but it does not cause sudden limb oedema or cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.

Cerebral embolism (Option C): Cerebral embolism will present with neurological deficits like weakness or aphasia.

Paradoxical embolism (Option D): Paradoxical embolism occurs when a venous thrombus enters the arterial circulation via a PFO or ASD. This will also result in a stroke, which will present as neurological deficits.

question_text:
A 30 year old woman has a deep vein thrombosis. Her previous history included investigations for miscarriages.Investigations revealed: Haemoglobin 11.9 g/dl, White cell count 4 x 10^9/L, Platelet count 30 x 10^9/L.
Which of these are likely to be abnormal?
explanation:
• Antiphospholipid syndrome leads to venous and arterial thrombosis, livedo reticularis, splinter haemorrhages, leg ulcer, multi-infarct dementia, chorea, Thrombocytopenia (40% of patients), hemolytic anaemia and late term miscarriages.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Chapter:351, page number 2749

question_text: Which of the following is not used in the management of COVID 19?
explanation: The agents that are approved for the treatment of COVID 19 are Dexamethasone, Remdesivir with or without the JAK 1 and 2 inhibitor Baricitinib, Tocilizumab (IL6 monoclonal antibody) and SARS CoV 2 specific monoclonal antibody.

question_text:
A 62 year old man presents with lethargy. He has frequent diarrhoea.
On examination, he has an erythematous rash across his face and chest. He is confused and disorientated. On examination, he has an MMSE score of 21 /30. Tone and reflexes are normal but he is weak throughout the body.
Which vitamin is his diet likely to be deficient?
explanation:
The diagnosis is pellagra. There is a triad of dementia, diarrhoea and dermatitis. Niacin (nicotinamide or nicotinic acid) deficiency causes pellagra only if tryptophan, an amino acid, is also deficient. People who live in areas where maize (Indian corn) is the main food source are at risk of developing pellagra because maize is low in niacin and tryptophan.

Pellagra affects the skin, digestive tract, and brain. A photosensitive rash may occur. Skin abnormalities are persistent, and the affected areas may become brown and scaly.

The whole digestive tract is affected. Other symptoms include nausea, vomiting, constipation, and diarrhea. Later, fatigue, insomnia, and apathy develop.

Encephalopathy usually follows. It is characterized by confusion, disorientation, hallucinations, and memory loss.



Photosensitive rash seen in Pellagra

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, CH: 29, Pg: 190

question_text: Loss of pain/temperature sensation on ipsilateral face & c/l body due to thrombosis in?
explanation:
This sensory pattern is seen in Lateral medullary syndrome.

The arteries responsible may be vertebral> PICA>Superior, middle or inferior lateral medullary arteries.

So if vertebral artery is there in the option that should be the answer. Here it is given as anterior vertebral artery. So the most appropriate would be PICA.

The lateral medullary arteries are penetrating branches and lead to partial syndromes.

question_text: Imaging changes in frontotemporal dementia (FTD) start initially in which parts of the brain?
explanation:
Damage to the hippocampus and parahippocampus results in memory problems and has early involvement in Alzheimer's disease. Entorhinal cortex is also involved

The corpus callosum can be involved in multiple sclerosis where so-called Dawson's fingers can be seen.

Posterior parietal lobe is involved in DLB

Cortical ribboning and basal ganglia and thalamus hyperintensity is seen in CJD

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 29, Pg: 192

question_text: Left atrial myxoma may be associated with all except-
explanation:
• Atrial myxoma in the heart make up 50% of primary cardiac tumours.
  • They are most common in the left atrium arising from a pedicle on the fossa ovalis.
  • One third present with emboli, a third with systemic inflammation (ESR elevated in 1/3) and a third are asymptomatic when detected.
  • The mass can intermittently flop through the mitral valve, and cause a mid-diastolic click (tumour plop) when they stop moving.
  • Elevated left atrial pressures cause dilatation.
  • Syncope can occur due to obstruction.
  • They are more common in women.

Carney complex is a familial multiple neoplasia and lentiginosis syndrome associated with -

  • Primary adrenal hypercortisolism
  • Lentigenes and naevi of the skin

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:266 pg:1847,1848

question_text: What is the most common site of dissemination in hematogenously disseminated mucormycosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Hematogenously disseminated mucormycosis can originate from any primary site of infection (often pulmonary).The most common site of dissemination is the brain, but metastatic lesions may also be found in the spleen, heart, skin, and other organs.

Cerebral infection following dissemination is distinct from the more common rhinocerebral mucormycosis (which spreads by direct extension); disseminated cerebral infection typically results in abscess formation and infarction due to the angioinvasive nature of the fungus.

Explanation of other options:

  • Bone (Option B): Osteomyelitis is a rare manifestation of disseminated mucormycosis, though direct extension to bone (e.g., palate/orbit) occurs in rhinocerebral forms.
  • Liver (Option C) & Spleen (Option D): The spleen, liver, and heart are known sites of metastatic spread, but they are less frequently the primary target of dissemination compared to the brain.

Key Takeaways:

  • Most common form of Mucormycosis: Rhino-orbital-cerebral (Direct extension).
  • Most common site of spread in Disseminated (Hematogenous) Mucormycosis: Brain.
  • Hallmark pathology: Angioinvasion causing vessel thrombosis and tissue necrosis (black eschar).
  • Risk Factors: DKA (Rhinocerebral), Neutropenia (Pulmonary), Iron overload/Deferoxamine use (Disseminated).

question_text: A 68-year-old man has been very ill for months following the onset of chronic liver disease with hepatitis C infection and suspected transformation to hepatocellular transformation. He experiences a sudden loss of consciousness and then exhibits hemiplegia on the right. A cerebral angiogram reveals lack of perfusion in the left middle cerebral artery distribution. The most likely cardiac lesion to be associated with this finding is?
explanation:
Marantic endocarditis / non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis has sterile, platelet-fibrin thrombi that are prone to embolize. This form of non-infective endocarditis can be seen in persons who are very debilitated or who have a hypercoagulable state.

The order of preference in involvement of valves in marantic endaocarditis is mitral > aortic > tricuspid > pulmonary.

Libman-Sacks endocarditis is characterized by sterile, verrucous valvular lesions with a predisposition for the mitral and aortic valves. Classically associated with SLE and less commonly Anti phospholipid antibody syndrome.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1024

question_text:
A 64 year old man has had a 6 month history of progressive worsening of confusion. He had left the cooker on several times and accused the neighbours of spying on him.
On examination, his face is expressionless and he has a monotonous speech. Cranial nerve are normal.
Increased tone is present in all 4 limbs. Reflexes, power and sensation are all normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient has parkinsonism, with bradykinesia and rigidity. In view of the deterioration in mental function and delusion, Lewy body dementia is more likely than Parkinson's disease.

In Parkinson's disease dementia occurs in long standing disease.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 434 Pg: 3385

question_text: A 60-year-old woman experiences a gradual loss of language abilities. She struggles to find the right words, has difficulty understanding spoken language, and exhibits reduced vocabulary. The relatives also  notice changes in personality, socially inappropriate behavior. She also exhibits changes in personality, loss of empathy, and increased preference for sweet foods. Neurological examination shows no significant motor deficits. What is she most likely suffering from?
explanation:
This patient is definitely suffering from a dementing disease. The chief domains affected are language, social skills and hyperorality. These are the characteristic features of Frontotemporal dementia. Other features that may be seen include, symptoms of MND and dystonia.

PD presents with memory loss only later after the progression of motor symptoms.

In DLB, the chief domain affected are visuospatial skills and psychiatric manifestations like visual hallucination.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 432, Pg: 3378

question_text: A 52 year old patient is assessed for gradually progressive dementia over several months. Whilst he was on the ward he was noticed to have myoclonic jerks of his hands. What is the likely cause?
explanation:
• Creutzfeldt Jakob disease (CJD) usually occurs in the 45-75 year age group and most commonly presents as a rapidly evolving multifocal dementia with myoclonic jerks in the latter stages.
  • New variant CJD, which has been strongly linked to infection from meat products of cows with BSE, tends to present with behavioural and psychiatric disturbances progressing to incoordination and dementia with myoclonic jerks.
  • Epidemiology – Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is the most frequent of the human prion diseases, although it is still rare. The mean age of onset is approximately 62 years.
  • Pathogenesis – sCJD is the most common prion disease; the prion protein in sCJD is thought to be generated endogenously rather than acquired. Iatrogenic CJD (iCJD) has followed administration of cadaveric human pituitary hormones, dural graft transplants, and other procedures and is rare now that these vectors have been removed from the health care system.
  • Clinical features – Rapidly progressive mental deterioration, often with behavioural abnormalities, and myoclonus are cardinal clinical manifestations of sCJD. Extrapyramidal signs such as hypokinesia and cerebellar manifestations are also common

Evaluation and diagnosis

  • MRI shows an abnormal hyper intense signal in the putamen and head of the caudate and in a cortical ribboning pattern of the cortex.
  • EEG reveals periodic sharp wave complexes
  • CSF has elevated levels of 14-3-3 protein (non specific)

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 438, Pg: 3420

question_text: Decorticate child - Flase statement is ?
option_d: Flexion of arm & extension of lower limb
explanation: Ans. is 'c' i.e., More dangerous than decerebrate lesion Decortical Posture o Also known as flexor posturing or Mummy baby o Arms flexed/bent over chest, hand fisted, leg extended & rotated inward o Damage to area in cerebral hemisphere, internal capsule, thalamus & upper part of brain. o Decorticate posture is ominous sign of severe brain damage. Decerebrate posture o Also known as extensor posturing o Extension of upper limb & lower limb (ELBOW EXTENDED) o Indicates brain stem damage (Below level of red nucleus) o Decerebrate posture is more ominous than decortical posture

question_text: Which of the following is not a scoring system used to assess severity of illness in ICU?
explanation:
MoCA – Montreal cognitive Assessment tool is used to assess cognitive function in patients with dementia. Others are scoring systems used in ICU.

In the ICU, illnesses are frequently categorized by degree of severity. Numerous severity-of-illness (SOI) scoring systems have been developed for this.The most commonly utilized scoring systems are:

  • SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment)
  • APACHE (Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation)
  • SAPS (Simplified Acute Physiology Score) systems.

Reference- Harrison 20th edition chap 293, pg. 2023

question_text: All of the following are subcortical dementia except?
explanation: Wilsons disease, Parkinsons disease and Huntingtons disease affect the subcortical structures like basal ganglia and have dementia as an associated feature. Picks disease is a cause for cortical dementia.

question_text:
A 65-year-old obese man presents with night time sweats, nocturia, poor concentration and day time somnolence.
To which of the following conditions does this diagnosis predispose?
explanation:
This history is typical of sleep apnoea. Sleep apnoea is an independent risk factor:

  • hypertension

  • stroke
  • motor vehicle collisions
  • polycythaemia
  • pulmonary hypertension

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 297, Pg-2208

question_text: Which of the following features are not compatible with the diagnosis of motor neurone disease (MND)?
explanation:
• Optic atrophy is not a feature of MND.
  • Other features not compatible with the diagnosis are sensory impairment and bladder and bowel dysfunction.
  • Muscle cramps occurring with volitional activities especially in early morning hours can be seen in very early disease.
  • Even though there is severe brain stem dysfunction, Ocular motility will also be spared in MND till late stages
  • ALS especially familial ALS is associated with behavioural dysfunction suggesting a frontal lobe dysfunction.
  • Cognitive changes don't occur in MND.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 437, Pg: 3411-3412

question_text: A 55-year-old man who has been on haemodialysis for 20 years has progressive dementia. Which one of the following is most likely to have caused this?
explanation:
Aluminium was used in dialysis and also for the treatment of hyperphosphatemia. It causes acute dementia, osteomalacia, proximal myopathy, bone pain and non iron deficient microcytic hypochromic anemia. Use of Aluminium free dialysate and avoidance of aluminum containing antacids for the treatment of hyperphosphatemia has reduced the incidence. Deferoxamine is an Aluminium chelator is the mainstay of treatment of aluminium toxicity.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition, Ch:410, Pg:3182

question_text:
A 68 year old man has early signs of cognitive impairment. His wife describes urinary incontinence and unsteadiness on walking in the past six months. Examination reveals ataxia and he has an MTS score of 7/10.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) is a clinical symptom complex characterized by abnormal gait, urinary incontinence, and dementia. Ventricular enlargement occurs out of proportion on the CT scan. Surgical CSF shunting remains the main treatment modality.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 29 Pg: 194

question_text:
A 67-year-old man has a monotonous, slurred speech. He has an expressionless face and a festinant gait.
There is also impairment of vertical gaze.
What is the most likely underlying aetiology?
explanation:
Parkinson's disease is a triad of

Bradykinesia

Tremor and

Rigidity.

Speech may be slurred and without accents or emphasis. Impairment of vertical gaze suggests the diagnosis of Steele-Richardson-Olszewski syndrome or supranuclear gaze palsy, which also cause pyramidal signs, dementia or frontal lobe syndrome.

Response to L-dopa is poor and median survival is about seven years.

Shy-Drager syndrome is associated with autonomic dysfunction and postural hypotension.

Wilson's disease presents in children and young adults with cirrhosis and parkinsonism, which later leads to dementia, dysphagia and immobility.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed Ch: 435, Pg: 3388

question_text:
A 54 year old man has been progressively getting more confused. His symptoms begin about three years ago when he noticed leg stiffness. At present his entire body feels stiff and he has a resting tremor in the limbs. His writing has become small. Over the last six months, he has developed hallucinations and reports seeing ghost figures, and is also becoming forgetful, on one occasion leaving the gas cooker fire on.
On examination, his mini-mental score was 10/30. He has increased tone throughout which is spastic and cogwheeling. There is a tremor in all limbs. Cranial nerve examination reveals mild restriction of conjugate upgaze eye movement. His gait was shuffling with a tendency to fall backwards.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Whenever we come across a question on dementia, we have to see what are the cognitive domains that are affected, that will help us reach a diagnosis. Dementia is the term used to denote loss of cognitive functions like memory, language, execution, visuospatial skills, attention, learning and social skills. In addition to the cognitive decline, they may have additional neurological findings according to the disease.

Here , the patient has forgetfulness, along with extrapyramidal symptoms, visual hallucinations. This is basically a dementia syndrome. The various diseases causing dementia can be identified by the symptoms that accompany them.

The given combination of parkinsonian features and memory loss is characteristic of Lewy Body Dementia.

DLB is characterized by :

  • A relative sparing of episodic memory compared to other dementias
  • With sever executive dysfunction, in attention and visuospatial problems.
  • Fluctuations in the symptoms.
  • There will be REM sleep disorder characterized by enacting during dreams and injuring others.
  • Early visual hallucinations is prominent.
  • Capgras syndrome is seen, where care taker is mistaken for an imposter.

Parkinsons disease can also present with dementia symptoms, but there will be history of long standing motor symptoms. If Parkinsonian Features occur along with or after the development of neuropsychiatric symptoms, DLB should be suspected.

Pick's Disease is the other name for Frontotemporal dementia. It is characterized by executive dysfunction, social disinhibition and language dysfunction. The neurological findings that may be seen include dystonia, vertical gaze palsy.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 434, Pg: 3385

question_text: Pulmonary infarction occurs with all except -
option_b: Blockage of 2nd and 3rd gen end arteries
explanation: Ans. is 'd' i.e., None The morphologic consequences of embolic occlusion of the pulmonary arteries depend on the size of the embolic mass and the general state of the circulation. Large emboli may impact in the main pulmonary artery or its major branches or lodge at the bifurcation as a saddle embolus. Sudden death often ensues, owing largely to the blockage of blood flow through the lungs. Death may also be caused by acute failure of the right side of the heart (acute cor pulmonale). Smaller emboli can travel out into the more peripheral vessels, where they may cause infarction. In patients with adequate cardiovascular function, the bronchial arterial supply can often sustain the lung parenchyma despite obstruction to the pulmonary arterial system. Under these circumstances, hemorrhages may occur, but there is no infarction of the underlying lung parenchyma. Only about 10% of emboli actually cause infarction. Although the underlying pulmonary architecture may be obscured by the suffusion of blood, hemorrhages are distinguished by the preservation of the pulmonary alveolar architecture; in such cases, resorption of the blood permits reconstitution of the preexisting architecture.

question_text: A 60-year-old individual presents with psychiatric symptoms, including personality changes, depression, and anxiety. He has insomnia and visual hallucinations. The patient also reports visual disturbances especially decreased visual acuity.  Following this, there was a rapidly progressive decline in all the cognitive function and the patient became bed bound, is akinetic mute accompanied by repeated episodes of startle like muscle movements occurring during sleep also. EEG reveals characteristic periodic sharp wave complexes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a dementing disease which begins with psychiatric symptoms, including visual hallucinations, and a rapid decline in cognitive function leading to akinetic mutism, and myoclonus(startle like movements) and periodic sharp waves in EEG. This is the characteristic presentation of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD).

Visual symptoms are common in CJD, especially reduced visual acuity.

Myoclonus is not specific of CJD, but is also seen in Alzheimer's Disease, Corticobasal degeneration, and DLB.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 438, Pg: 3420

question_text: A 72-year-old retired pilot, accompanied by his wife, presents to a neurologist with rapidly progressing dementia, myoclonus, ataxia, and visual disturbances. The FLAIR MRI images provided may help confirm the diagnosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation, along with the FLAIR MRI showing the characteristic "hockey stick" sign, is indicative of variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD).

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a rare, rapidly progressive neurodegenerative disorder that impairs coordination, memory, and cognitive function.

Explanation for other options:

In the early stages of Alzheimer's disease (Option A):the MRI appears normal, with temporal and parietal lobe atrophy becoming evident in later stages.

Since there is no history of stroke, vascular dementia (Option B): is an unlikely diagnosis.

The hockey stick sign is not characteristic of sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (Option C).

Reference:

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16442343/

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507860/

question_text: Length time bias in cancer screening is defined as
option_a: Detecting the cancer earlier without an effect on survival
option_b: Indolent cancers are detected on screening and may not affect survival, whereas aggressive cancers are likely to cause symptoms earlier in patients and are less likely to be detected
option_c: Diagnosing cancers so slow growing that they are unlikely to cause the death of the patient
explanation:
With any screening procedure, it is important to consider the possible influence of Lead-time bias (detecting the cancer earlier without an effect on survival), length-time bias (indolent cancers are detected on screening and may not affect survival, whereas aggressive cancers are likely to cause symptoms earlier in patients and are less likely to be detected), and over diagnosis (diagnosing cancers so slow growing that they are unlikely to cause the death of the patient)

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 78, Pg: 597

question_text: What is the second most common cause of death among the parasites?
explanation:
Entamoeba histolytica is the second most common cause of death related to parasitic infection (after malaria).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 223Pg 1715

question_text: Visual field assessment in this patient shows a specific pattern of vision loss. Based on this pattern, the most probable location of the lesion within the visual (optic) pathway can be identified accordingly.
explanation:
Explanation:

A lesion involving the occipital lobe-particularly within the territory supplied by the Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA)—often results in a congruous homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

This pattern of visual field loss occurs because the primary visual cortex is mainly supplied by the PCA. However, the macular region of the visual field is often preserved due to dual blood supply, including collateral flow from the middle cerebral artery (MCA).

Lesions in the Visual Cortex:

  • Commonly lead to congruous homonymous hemianopia, meaning the visual field defect is identical in both eyes.
  • Macular sparing is a distinguishing feature when the lesion is limited to the occipital cortex.

Explanation of other options: 

Frontal visual field (option A): is incorrect, as lesions in the frontal lobe primarily impact functions such as attention, visual scanning, and executive decision-making. The visual field defect shown in the image does not correspond to a lesion in this region.

question_text: An elderly patient was brought to the OPD with complaints of tremors, stoop posture and slow movements. His son also gives a history of the patient forgetting day to day activities. What is the possible cause of this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation combining parkinsonian motor symptoms (tremors, stooped posture, bradykinesia) with progressive cognitive decline is highly characteristic of Lewy Body Dementia (LBD).
  • LBD is a neurodegenerative disorder and xrepresents the second most common form of neurodegenerative dementia after Alzheimer's disease. It encompasses two related diagnoses:
    • Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB): Cognitive deficits appear concurrently with or before motor symptoms.
    • Parkinson's Disease Dementia (PDD): Dementia emerges in the context of well-established Parkinson's disease.

Clinical Features

  • Motor Symptoms: The presence of parkinsonism (tremor, rigidity, slow movement, postural instability) is a core feature.
  • Cognitive Symptoms: Patients exhibit significant deficits in attention, executive function, and visuospatial ability, while episodic memory may be relatively spared in early stages. A hallmark is fluctuating cognition, with pronounced variations in alertness and performance throughout the day.
  • Neuropsychiatric Features: Recurrent visual hallucinations are another core diagnostic feature. REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD), where patients act out their dreams, is a very common and often early sign.
  • Other Symptoms: Autonomic dysfunction (e.g., constipation), loss of smell (anosmia), depression, and anxiety are frequently present.

Explanation of other options:

Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) (Option A): It can cause a triad of symptoms known as Hakim's triad, which includes gait disturbances, urinary incontinence, and cognitive impairment. The triad is not present in the given scenario.

Hypothyroidism (Option B): It can lead to various symptoms, including cognitive impairment, depression, and memory problems. But the given scenario does not provide any relation to it.

Vitamin B12 deficiency (Option D): It can lead to neurological symptoms, including cognitive impairment and dementia-like symptoms. However, the given scenario is not associated with this.

question_text: In a patient with Dialysis Dementia, which substance is deposited in the cerebral cortex?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Dialysis dementia, or dialysis-related amyloidosis, occurs when amyloid beta-2 microglobulin, which is normally cleared by healthy kidneys, builds up in the blood due to impaired renal function in end-stage kidney disease.
  • Long-term dialysis causes elevated beta-2 microglobulin levels, which deposit as amyloid in different tissues, including the cerebral cortex, leading to cognitive decline and neurological features typical of dialysis dementia.

Explanations of other options:

Amyloid beta microglobulin (Option B): This term is not valid or recognised as a deposit-forming substance in relation to dialysis dementia or amyloid buildup.

Amyloid transthyretin (Option C): Transthyretin amyloidosis is a distinct disorder in which the transthyretin protein accumulates as amyloid in multiple organs, leading to systemic dysfunction. Although it may involve the nervous system, it is not directly linked to dialysis dementia or kidney failure.

Amyloid Beta (Option D): This protein contributes to Alzheimer's disease by forming plaques in the brain, but in dialysis dementia, the implicated protein is beta-2 microglobulin rather than amyloid beta.

question_text: A patient with an aortic valve replacement develops right hemiparesis. CT scan shows cerebral infarction. There is no evidence of cerebral haemorrhage. The INR is 2.0.How would you manage this case?
option_a: Reverse the anticoagulation with vitamin K
option_b: Stop warfarin and start intravenous heparin
option_d: Continue warfarin and add intravenous heparin
explanation:
Use of oral anticoagulation may result in haemorrhage in the infarcted area. As the patient has a mechanical valve, anticoagulation must be continued. The best the option therefore would be to stop the warfarin and start intravenous heparin. The reason for this is that heparin can be more easily controlled than oral anticoagulation during the acute period of stroke recovery.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1991

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding CADASIL (cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy) is correct?
option_a: Computerised tomography (CT) of the brain is diagnostic
option_c: It is associated with an abnormality of the X chromosome
explanation:
• CADASIL is a diffuse disease of small arteries, predominantly in the brain.
  • It starts during mid adulthood and is characterised by:
  • Recurrent ischaemic events (transient or permanent)
  • Attacks of migraine with aura
  • Severe mood disorders
  • Sub-cortical dementia and
  • A wide spread leukoencephalopathy on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
  • CT brain is not diagnostic. Characteristic MRI changes include T2 weighted hyperintensity of the periventricular white matter.
  • A family history is almost always present, as it is an autosomal dominant condition, located to chromosome 19.
  • Infarcts are subcortical, and the thalami and basal ganglia are usually involved.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 427, Pg: 3343

question_text: In a patient on maize diet with diarrhea, dermatitis and dementia which vitamin is deficient?

• Pellagra is caused due to deficiency of vitamin B3 i.e niacin.

question_text: A 30-year-old boy present with fever for the last 5 days. Then he developed drowsiness and a coma. What will be used in treatment based on peripheral smear of the patient?
