question_text:
A 74-year-old man is diagnosed with a Lewy body dementia.
Which one of the following drugs would be contraindicated for this patient?
explanation:
Patients with DLB are sensitive to Dopeminergic agonists and anticholinergics that worsen their symptoms. Hence Dopeminergic agonists should be used with careful titration of the dose and addition of cholinesterase Inhibitors.

They are also sensitive to typical antipsychotics that causes Neurolept Malignant Syndrome.

The drug absolutely contra indicated is Haloperidol, among the options.

Management of DLB includes:

Cholinestrase inhibitors like Rivastigmine.

Pimavanserin is an atypical antipsychotic approved for treatment of Psychosis.

Low dose clozapine can also be used.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 434, Pg: 3386

question_text: Which is the most common variant of Frontotemporal dementia?
explanation:
The types of FTD are:

  • The behavioral variant is the most common type of FTD. It manifests mainly as dysfunction of social abilities and emotional control, with hyperorality.
  • Semantic Primary progressive aphasia: Inability to understand language
  • Agrammatic Primary Progressive Aphasia: inability to produce words.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 432, Pg: 3378

question_text: A 76 year old male with hypertension and history of recurrent minor strokes comes to you with complaints of cognitive impairment. His affect is labile with the patient becoming tearful on trivial things. On examination, he has mild deviation of angle of mouth to left, exaggerated gag reflex, release reflexes and bilateral extensor plantar. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Memory impairment occurring in the context of recurrent strokes is the clue to multi infarct or vascular dementia. Here the pseudobulbar affect is due to the recurrent strokes involving the corticobulbar tracts on both the sides.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch:433, Pg:3382

question_text: A 61 year old man presents with drowsiness and confusion. A friend says he has been confabulating about having his wallet stolen. On examination, he is unkempt, his pupil reflexes are normal and eye movements are normal. There were otherwise no focal neurological deficits. A CT scan of the brain showed mild cerebral atrophy. He has a MCV of 105 fl. Which diagnosis is most likely?
explanation:
• The high MCV suggests heavy alcohol drinking. He is delusional (having his wallet stolen) and also there are no signs of nystagmus or cerebellar signs to support Wernicke's encephalopathy.
  • Short term memory loss, amnesia and personality changes are also seen in Korsakoff's psychosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch:333, Pg: 2526

20th edition Chapter:445 Page number:3279

question_text:
A 72-year-old man attends the memory clinic with his wife. She has noticed that he has become progressively more forgetful over the past few years and has begun to wander at night. Most recently he became lost whilst shopping in the local village and had to be brought home by the police. This caused his wife significant distress.
On examination in the clinic he has easily demonstrable short-term memory loss, with relative preservation of memory for events from his 40s. He also has visuospatial dysfunction.
His BP is 142/72 mmHg, his pulse is 78 and regular. There are no murmurs or bruits on auscultation.
Investigations showed
Haemoglobin 12.9 g/dl(13.5-17.7)
White cells 7.4 x 10^9/L (4-11)
Platelets 193 x 10^9/L (150-400)
Sodium 141 mmol/l (135-146)
Potassium 4.6 mmol/l (3.5-5)
CT head Mild cortical atrophy
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a dementing disease characterised chiefly by episodic memory loss and visuospatial dysfunction, characterised by way finding difficulty. This is characteristic of Alzheimer's Disease.

This is the most common cause of dementia in elderly.

The characteristic clinical features are:

Episodic memory loss, for recent memory, followed by

Executive dysfunction

Language dysfunction

Visuospatial disorientation

As the disease progresses, there will be difficulty in day to day activities.

Patient will eventually develop rigidity and become mute and incontinent and bed ridden. Hyperactive tendon reflexes or myoclonus occur at late stages.

Cause of death is malnutrition, secondary infections or pulmonary embolism

The neurological examination will be normal.

Patients may have depression or social withdrawal.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 431, Pg: 3370

question_text:
A 77-year-old lady has four months of memory loss, urinary incontinence and falls.
On examination she has mild memory loss and a broad-based, slow gait. Muscle tone is normal and both plantar reflexes are downgoing.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus is characterised by abnormal gait, urinary incontinence, and dementia.

It is an important clinical diagnosis, because it is a potentially reversible cause of dementia.

Frontal lobe dementia is characterised by loss of 'executive' functions and multi-infarct state usually has a step-wise history.

TO SUMMARIZE, THE VARIOUS DEMENTIAS



Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 431, Pg: 3375

question_text:
A 70 year old patient has progressive dementia. His wife mentions that he has urinary incontinence and an ataxic gait.
What is his CT scan likely to show ?
explanation:
The diagnosis is normal pressure hydrocephalus. Dementia, urinary incontinence and unsteady gait are seen.

Typically there is no papilloedema. There are large ventricles caused by communicating hydrocephalus. Ventricular shunting may help improve the symptoms.



Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 29 Pg: 194

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding CADASIL (cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy) is correct?
option_a: Computerised tomography (CT) of the brain is diagnostic
option_c: It is associated with an abnormality of the X chromosome
explanation:
• CADASIL is a diffuse disease of small arteries, predominantly in the brain. It starts during mid adulthood and is characterised by:
    • Recurrent ischaemic events (transient or permanent)
    • Attacks of migraine with aura
    • Severe mood disorders
    • Sub-cortical dementia and
    • A wide spread leukoencephalopathy on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
    • CT brain is not diagnostic. Characteristic MRI changes include T2 weighted hyperintensity of the periventricular white matter.
    • A family history is almost always present, as it is an autosomal dominant condition, located to chromosome 19.
    • Infarcts are subcortical, and the thalami and basal ganglia are usually involved.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, Ch:427, Pg: 3343-3344

question_text: An 82 year-old male presented with acute right-sided weakness. Examination revealed minimal right facial weakness, impaired elevation of the right shoulder, with relatively preserved right hand strength. There was global weakness in the right leg which appeared to be maximal in the foot. Which of the following arteries is most likely to have been affected?
explanation:
• The confusion could be due to middle or anterior artery circulation stroke but the aim is to choose which is the more likely.
  • Unilateral occlusion (distal to ant. comm. origin) of anterior cerebral artery produces contralateral sensorimotor deficits mainly involving the lower extremity with relative sparing of face and hands (think of the homunculus).
  • The lateral lenticulostriate artery is a branch of the middle cerebral artery. Occlusion causes damage to the internal capsule resulting in contralateral hemiparesis and sensory deficit. Speech may be affected (medial temporal lobe) as well as visual function (Meyer's loop: optic radiations affected).
  • Middle cerebral artery:
  • Occlusion at the stem (proximal segment) results in: Contralateral hemiplegia affecting face, arm, and leg (lesser) Homonymous hemianopia - ipsilateral head/eye deviation
  • If on the left: global aphasia.
  • Posterior cerebral artery: A variety of neurological syndromes including:
  • Pure hemisensory loss
  • Visual field loss- a variety
  • Visual agnosia
  • Disorders of reading (alexia, dyslexia).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3327

question_text: Cannabinoid oil not indicated in which of the following conditions?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Cannabidiol (CBD) oil, a non-psychoactive compound derived from the cannabis plant, has been FDA-approved for use in specific epilepsy syndromes that are refractory to standard therapy.
  • It is not approved for Rett syndrome, which is a neurodevelopmental genetic disorder associated with MECP2 mutations and not primarily a seizure syndrome responsive to cannabinoids.

question_text: A 72-year-old man is admitted to hospital in a comatose condition. His wife gives a history of past episodes of sweating and palpitations, confusion, fits and occasional abnormal behaviour. On examination his pulse is 92 bpm and his blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg. His plasma catecholamine level is normal and blood glucose is 66 mg/dl. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• This patient most probably has an insulinoma.
  • Phaeochromocytoma either isolated or as part of the MEN-II syndrome, is unlikely as his blood pressure and catecholamine levels are normal.
  • Hypoglycaemia is not associated with this disorder.
  • The history and tests are not suggestive of epilepsy.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page:3133

question_text:
A 64-year-old man is brought to the Emergency department with a grand-mal seizure. You are aware from his notes that he has undergone chemotherapy for small cell carcinoma of the bronchus a few months earlier. His wife tells you that he was drowsy and not himself for a day or two before the seizure. On examination he is very drowsy but you can wake him up with stimulation. He is very thin with evidence of muscle and fat loss consistent with his carcinoma. Neurological examination reveals no focal signs. Labs:
Na+ 123 mmol/l
K+ 4.0 mmol/l
Creatinine 0.8 mg/dl
Urea 10 mg/dl
Hb 11.1 g/dl
WCC 4500/mm3
PLT 230000/mm3
You suspect SIADH and fluid restrict him. Despite no evidence of him having taken in more fluids than documented his sodium deteriorates to 119 mmol/l the following day. His drowsiness has increased. Which of the following represents the most appropriate management for him?
explanation:
• This man remains drowsy and has suffered a further dangerous fall in his serum sodium despite fluid restriction. It seems unlikely on a closely monitored ward that he would have access to fluids beyond his restriction, therefore another intervention is required.
  • Treatment of acute symptomatic hyponatremia should include hypertonic 3% saline (513 mM) to acutely increase plasma Na+ concentration by 1-2 mM/h to a total of 4-6 mM; this modest increase is typically sufficient to alleviate severe acute symptoms
  • Demeclocycline is an efficient oral treatment for SIADH which fails to respond to intake restriction but is not the first line treatment in symptomatic acute hyponatremia.
  • Dexamethasone may exacerbate salt and water retention further.
  • Tolvaptan (V2 receptor blocker) may also be useful in SIADH but not in an acute situation.
  • IV normal saline can also cause deterioration of Na levels in a patient with SIADH.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2925

question_text: A 63 year woman with a long history of alcohol abuse has been on Phenytoin for epilepsy. On examination, she has a palpable a liver edge. Her full blood count reveals: Hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL MCV 116 fL white blood count 2.3 x 10^9/L platelet count 95 x 10^9/L What is the likely explanation for these results?
explanation:
This patient presents with a clinical picture consistent with megaloblastic anemia.

Megaloblastic anemia is either due to Folic acid or Vitamin B12 deficiency.

Given her history of heavy alcohol intake and phenytoin usage, folate deficiency is the most likely cause.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, ch: 99, Pg: 773

question_text: What is the Most common complication of meningococcal disease ?
option_a: Scarring after necrosis of purpuric skin lesions
explanation:
The most common complication of meningococcal disease (10% of cases) is scarring after necrosis of purpuric skin lesions, for which skin grafting may be necessary

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 155 Pg: 1231

question_text: Inhaled Nitric oxide is used in treatment of ?
explanation: Nitric oxide is a gaseous agent that produces pulmonary vasodilation by cGMP.

question_text:
A 60 year old man presents with breathlessness, visual blurring and headaches to ER. During examination, he has a generalized tonic clonic seizure. He has a blood pressure of 240/120. Fundoscopy reveals retinal hemorrhages and exudates. The optic disc margin is not visualized.
Which of the following medications is the first line?
explanation:
Malignant hypertension is defined as severely elevated blood pressure (BP > 180/120 mmHg) with evidence of new / progressive target organ damage.

Target organ damage may involve cardiovascular (MI, pulmonary edema). Renal (hematuria, worsening GFR), CNS (encephalopathy) or ophthalmic (hard exudates, papilledema).

The intravenous drugs used for urgent BP reduction in malignant hypertension include:

  • Sodium nitroprusside
  • Labetolol
  • Nitroglycerin
  • Nicardipine
  • Esmolol
  • Hydralazine
  • Fenoldopam

Sodium Nitroprusside has an immediate onset of action and short half-life. It acts by causing relaxation of vascular smooth muscle, resulting in vasodilation and inotropy. The dose is 0.25-10 mcg/kg/min IV.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2086

question_text: A 60 year old man is brought to hospital having collapsed to the ground suddenly and was unable to move his left leg and arm. There was no loss of consciousness. He has a past medical history of hypertension only. The episode lasted a few seconds and he has been relatively well. Examination reveals a mild hemiparesis of the left arm and leg. Which is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pontine bleed would have caused alteration in consciousness with pupillary abnormalities and quadriparesis.

Epilepsy may cause transient paralysis, but there would be history of convulsions.

Medullary haemorrhage will be associated with cranial nerve paralysis.

  • This patient is likely to have a lacunar infarct involving the internal capsule, causing transient contralateral hemiparesis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3328-3333

question_text: Patient presented with seizure, urine osmolality 1000 mosm/kg ,serum osmolality 270 mosm/kg. On further evaluation what electrolyte abnormality is expected?
explanation: The scenario described here suggests SIADH.

question_text: A 34-year-old woman presents to the Emergency department following a witnessed first ever seizure. She is drowsy and confused postictally.A CT brain shows petechial haemorrhages in the right hemisphere. An MRI shows cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.Which of the following would be the best initial treatment?
explanation:
• Venous sinus thrombosis is more common in young women.
  • It may present with headaches or symptoms of raised intracranial pressure.

It can cause seizures.

  • The underlying problem is a thrombosis and the petechial haemorrhages are caused by venous outflow blockage. It is therefore important that anticoagulation is started immediately to relieve the cause.
  • Heparin is the most appropriate anticoagulant to use in this circumstance.
  1. Antibiotics are not the best answer. The underlying cause may be infection and it would be important to look for this and treat it. However, there is no sign of this in this case. It would be most important here to get on and treat the thrombosis.
  2. Aspirin is not the best answer. The clot is venous therefore heparin is more appropriate.
  3. Heparin is the correct answer.
  4. Supportive management is not the best answer. The underlying thrombosis should be treated to relieve symptoms. The petechial haemorrhages should not put you off anticoagulating the patient.

The haemorrhages are secondary to the venous outflow blockage.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 427, Pg: 3342

question_text: A 30-year-old woman with epilepsy has been diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and is about to be started on quadruple therapy. Which drug may cause urine discolouration?
explanation:
Discoloration of urine is due to rifampicin. Rifampicin is a liver enzyme inducer but isoniazid is an enzyme inhibitor.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page Number 1372-1373.

question_text: A young lady visits her neurologist complaining of episodes of generalised weakness after arguments with her partner. She also complains of seeing goblins upon waking up. At work as a secretary, she has difficulty staying awake and may have sleep attacks. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• The condition described is narcolepsy. The episodes described are likely to be cataplexy.
  • The HLA association is DQB1, Clomipramine is a tricyclic antidepressant which may help, there is early REM sleep and hypnagogic hallucinations occur.
  • Narcolepsy typically begins in the teens and early twenties, but may occur as early as five years of age or after 40 years of age. Cardinal symptoms of narcolepsy include:
  • Moderate to severe daytime sleepiness
  • Transient facial weakness or falls caused by episodes of cataplexy (ie, emotionally triggered muscle weakness)
  • Hallucinations when falling asleep or awakening (Hypnagogic hallucinations)
  • Inability to move for one or two minutes immediately after awakening

Generalized seizure would have an episode of unconsciousness along with tonic or tonic clonic or myoclonic movements

Petit mal epilepsy (absence seizures) would present with abrupt episodes of impaired consciousness with staring, eye movements or automatisms.

OSA may present with excess snoring, daytime sleepiness, irritability and sleep attacks but hallucinations are not a feature

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 31, Pg: 209

question_text: A 26-year-old woman with epilepsy and a low IQ presents with flank pain, hypotension and anaemia. A CT scan of her abdomen shows a large haemorrhage into a mass in her right kidney, which is composed primarily of fat. There are two similar lesions(without haemorrhage) in her left kidney. Renal function is normal. What is the underlying condition?
explanation:
The CT scan appearance is typical of angiomyolipoma, which when bilateral and associated with epilepsy, is highly suggestive of a diagnosis of tuberous sclerosis.

Inheritance: Autosomal-dominant trait with incomplete penetrance.

Genetics: Two genetic defects have been identified, one on chromosome 9(TSC1) and one on chromosome 16(TSC2). Interestingly, the latter is adjacent to the PKD1 gene, which is deficient in adult polycystic kidney disease.

Presentation:

The renal lesions are hamartomas, which tend to grow slowly over time and occasionally undergo malignant transformation. Bleeding into the angiomyolipoma is the most common presentation.

The principal differential diagnosis is von Hippel-Lindau disease, which is manifested by retinal and cerebellar hemangioblastomas, pancreatic cysts, pheochromocytoma and renal cysts. The latter frequently undergo malignant transformation such that these patients often end up on dialysis because of bilateral nephrectomy. ADPKD usually presents with loin pain, recurrent UTIs with an ultrasound suggestive of bilaterally enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Ch:315, Pg:2354.

question_text: Which is the most likely presentation of leptospirosis?
explanation:
High fever, myalgia, and headache are common clinical manifestations of leptospirosis. Leptospirosis can be associated with acute abdominal pain, sometimes mimicking acute cholecystitis; however, diarrhea rarely occurs. Localized seizure would be an atypical presentation of leptospirosis, which is generally not considered to be associated with focal neurologic findings.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 184 Pg: 1419

Goldman Cecil's Medicine 26th Ed. Chap 307 pg. 1999

question_text: A patient is evaluated for recurrent seizures. EEG shows hypsarrhythmia. What is the preferred drug?
explanation:
Explanation

  • Hypsarrhythmia on EEG is the classical finding in Infantile Spasms (West Syndrome).
  • ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone) is considered the first-line therapy for infantile spasms.
  • It improves seizure control and may also help in neurodevelopmental outcomes.
  • Alternative treatments include oral corticosteroids and vigabatrin (especially when spasms are due to tuberous sclerosis).

Antiepileptic drug choice according to seizure type:

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Carbamazepine (Option A): Used for focal seizures and trigeminal neuralgia. Not effective for infantile spasms and may actually worsen generalized seizures.

Lamotrigine (Option B): Effective in generalized tonic-clonic and absence seizures.Not preferred for hypsarrhythmia/infantile spasms.

Vigabatrin (Option D): Can be used in infantile spasms due to tuberous sclerosis, but ACTH remains the preferred first-line drug in general cases.

question_text: A patient stopped alcohol for 3 days and presented with irritability disorientation, paranoid delusion, visual hallucinations and altered sensorium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Delirium tremens:-

  • Severe alcohol withdrawal symptoms such as shaking, confusion and hallucinations.
  • Delirium tremens usually start two to five days after the last drink and it can be fatal.
  • Some symptoms are shaking, confusion, high blood pressure, fever, seizures (worst at night), and hallucinations.

Wernicke's encephalopathy:

  • Global confusion
  • Ophthalmoplegia
  • Ataxia

Korsakoff psychosis:

The triad of symptoms for Korsakoff psychosis is memory loss, learning deficits, and confabulation.

question_text:
Which of the following combinations of seizure and its corresponding medication is not accurate?

1. Generalized onset tonic-clonic seizures: Lamotrigine
2. Focal seizures: Levetiracetam
3. Typical absence seizures: Topiramate
4. Myoclonic seizures: Valproic acid
explanation:
Explanation:

The incorrect pairing is Typical absence seizures: Topiramate. The first-line medications for typical absence seizures are Ethosuximide and Valproate. While topiramate has broad-spectrum activity, it is not a primary or preferred agent for absence seizures.

Ethosuximide is used in children <2 years as valproate has higher chances of fulminant hepatic failure as the age lowers.

Explanation of other options:

  • Generalized tonic-clonic seizures: Lamotrigine (Option A): Lamotrigine is a broad-spectrum antiepileptic effective for generalized seizures.
  • Focal seizures: Levetiracetam (Option B): Levetiracetam is a first-line treatment for focal seizures.
  • Myoclonic seizures: Valproic acid (Option D): Valproate is a first-line broad-spectrum drug, highly effective for myoclonic seizures (e.g., in Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy).

Key Takeaways:

  • Typical Absence Seizures: First-line = Ethosuximide or Valproate.
  • Topiramate is a broad-spectrum drug used for various seizure types but is not a first-line choice for absence seizures.

question_text: All of the following are correct statements except?
option_a: EEG is required for diagnosis of Epilepsy
option_b: Scalp eeg is used for diagnosis of frontal lobe seizures
option_c: In progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy the EEG shows rhythmic spikes and diffuse slow wave pattern
option_d: 10% of normal people show epileptic activity
explanation:
• The EEG is always abnormal during generalized tonic-clonic
  • The absence of electrographic seizure activity does not exclude a seizure disorder, however, because focal seizures may originate from regions of the cortex that cannot be detected by standard scalp electrodes.
  • EEG may also be helpful in the interictal period by showing certain abnormalities that are highly supportive of the diagnosis of epilepsy. Such epileptiform activity consists of bursts of abnormal discharges containing spikes or sharp waves. The presence of epileptiform activity is not entirely specific for epilepsy, but it has a much greater prevalence in patients with epilepsy than in other individuals. However, even in an individual who is known to have epilepsy, the initial routine interictal EEG may be normal 50-80% of the time. Thus, the EEG has limited sensitivity and cannot establish the diagnosis of epilepsy in many cases.
  • Focal interictal epileptiform discharges would support the diagnosis of a focal seizure disorder such as temporal lobe epilepsy or frontal lobe seizures, depending on the location of the discharges
  • The routine scalp-recorded EEG may also be used to assess the prognosis of seizure disorders; in general, a normal EEG implies a better prognosis, whereas an abnormal background or frequent epileptiform activity suggests a worse outcome. Unfortunately, the EEG has not proved to be useful in predicting which patients with predisposing conditions such as head injury or brain tumor will go on to develop epilepsy, because in such circumstances epileptiform activity is commonly encountered regardless of whether seizures occur.
  • Magnetoencephalography (MEG) provides another way of looking noninvasively at cortical activity. Instead of measuring electrical activity of the brain, it measures the small magnetic fields that are generated by this activity. The epileptiform activity seen on MEG can be analyzed, and its source in the brain can be estimated using a variety of mathematical techniques. These source estimates can then be plotted on an anatomic image of the brain such as an MRI (discussed below) to generate a magnetic source image (MSI). MSI can be useful to localize potential seizure foci.

question_text: An 18-year-old woman presents to the clinic having had five blackouts over the last year, all while she is standing up. She gets warnings of blurred vision, nausea, and feeling hot. She has been witnessed twice to have jerking of all limbs while she is unconscious. The attacks last 30 to 60 seconds. She recovers quickly after the attacks. She has never bitten her tongue or sustained any injuries. Physical examination and an ECG are normal. Her grandmother and sister suffer from epilepsy. Which of the following investigations is the most appropriate?
explanation:
• The most likely diagnosis is vasovagal syncope.
  • The gradual onset of the attack is typical. It is common for patients with syncope to have jerking of their limbs while they are unconscious.
  • Warning symptoms of darkening/blurring of vision, dizziness and feeling hot are characteristic in syncope. Patients usually recover very quickly after the event.
  • Tilt table test is a useful test to support the diagnosis of vasovagal syncope.


Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 440, Pg: 3432

question_text: A 19-year-old woman presents to the clinic having had 5 blackouts over the last year, all while she is standing up. She gets warnings of blurred vision, nausea, feeling hot. She had been witnessed twice to have jerking of all limbs while she is unconscious. The attacks last 30-60 seconds. She recovers quickly after the attacks. She has never bitten her tongue or sustained any injuries. Physical examination and an ECG are normal. Her grandmother and sister suffer from epilepsy. Which of the following investigations is the most appropriate?
explanation:
• The most likely diagnosis is vasovagal syncope.
  • The gradual onset of the attack is typical. It is common for patients with syncope to have jerking of their limbs while they are unconscious (due to brain hypoxia).
  • Warning symptoms of darkening/blurring of vision, dizziness, feeling hot, is characteristic in syncope.
  • Patients usually recover very quickly after the event.
  • Tilt table test is a useful test to support the diagnosis of vasovagal syncope.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:265 pg: 122,128-129

question_text: An 8-year-old child with a history of generalised tonic-clonic seizures presents with continuous convulsions lasting more than 45 minutes without regaining consciousness. What is the most appropriate stepwise pharmacological management?
explanation:
Explanation:

An 8-year-old child seizing for >45 minutes is in status epilepticus, which is treated first with IV lorazepam, the first-line benzodiazepine to abort the seizure, followed by IV levetiracetam as a second-line antiepileptic.

Status epilepticus

  • Refers to continuous convulsive activity lasting 5 min or longer (or)
  • Multiple generalised convulsions without gain of consciousness, lasting 5 min or longer
  • If activity > 30 min, serious neuro sequelae may develop.
  • Status epilepticus (SE) is a medical emergency that should be anticipated in any patient who presents with an acute seizure.
  • The most common cause of status epilepticus is a febrile seizure (febrile status epilepticus ~ 40% cases of status epilepticus).
  • In the case of impending and early SE, the standard protocol involves administering IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg followed by levetiracetam 20-30 mg/kg.
  • For established and early refractory SE, the treatment progresses to Propofol 2 mg/kg IV followed by 2-10 mg/kg/hr with the addition of anticonvulsants like levetiracetam.

Management of Status Epilepticus

Explanation of other options:

Valproate followed by gabapentin (Option B): Valproate is indeed effective in generalized tonic-clonic seizures and can be used intravenously in status epilepticus, but it is not the first-line drug (benzodiazepines are always first). Gabapentin, on the other hand, is not used in acute seizure control; it is an oral drug reserved for chronic seizure management and neuropathic pain.

Carbamazepine followed by lorazepam (Option C): Carbamazepine is mainly used for partial/focal seizures and is given orally, making it unsuitable for acute management of status epilepticus. Moreover, the correct sequence in status epilepticus is to give a benzodiazepine first (lorazepam), not after another anticonvulsant.

Levetiracetam followed by valproate (Option D): This sequence is incorrect as benzodiazepines should be the first-line treatment in early status epilepticus.

Key Takeaway:

Antiepileptic drugs: Indications

question_text: What is correct about febrile seizures
explanation: Answer- A. Normal EEG Spontaneous remmission occurs with no postictal neurological deficit and EEG changes few days after the seizure is normal. Recurrent febrile seizures occur in 30-50% of cases. More than 90% of febrile seizures are generalized. Acute respiratory illness are most commonly associated with febrile seizures.

question_text:
A 18-year-old girl presents with recurrent episodes of loss of consciousness.
 Over the last two years she has had blackouts which last approximately 2 minutes. They typically occur when she is standing. These have occurred more frequently over the last week. The last episode was witnessed by her friend who noted that she collapsed without any abnormal movements. On coming round she was rather drowsy initially but generally fine and recovered relatively quickly.
 What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This young girl has features suggestive of vasovagal syncope.

The story suggests that the episodes always occur when she is standing (whereas cardiac syncope could occur at any time but may be precipitated by exercise), that there are no abnormal movements (making epilepsy less likely) and that there is an almost full recovery (again making epilepsy less likely).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:253 pg:122,127-129

question_text: Which of the following drugs are used for absence seizures?
explanation: Valproate, ethosuximide and Lamotrigine are the drugs used in typical absence seizures.

question_text:
A 28-year-old previously healthy woman has a sudden onset of mental confusion.
She has a seizure and is brought to the hospital.
Her vital signs show blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, temperature 37°C, pulse 89, and respirations 22. A lumbar puncture reveals a normal opening pressure, and clear, colourless cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is obtained with 1 RBC and 20 WBCs (all lymphocytes), with normal glucose and protein.
An MRI scan reveals swelling of the right temporal lobe with haemorrhagic areas.
Which of the following infectious agents is the most likely cause for these findings?
explanation:
• Haemorrhagic lesions of the temporal lobe are typical for Herpes simplex virus infection.
  • Haemophilus influenzae is the organism most associated with meningitis in children.
  • Neisseria meningitidis would cause meningitis - however, in this case there are lymphocytes not neutrophils in the CSF and a normal, not low, glucose.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:137 Pg: 1095-1097

question_text:
A 68 year old man presents with a history of falls. He has difficulty reading and walking down stairs. He has dysarthria, akinesia and rigidity. Power of the muscles is normal, reflexes are brisk.
What physical sign will help to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
The patient has progressive supranuclear palsy - parkinsonian features and gaze palsy.

Demonstration of impairment of voluntary gaze will help confirm the diagnosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed Ch: 435, Pg: 3388

question_text: Which of the following syndromes is not associated with patent ductus arteriousus (PDA) ?
explanation:
Syndromes associated with PDA:

  • Edward syndrome (Trisomy 18- ASD, VSD)
  • Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13 - ASD, VSD)
  • Cri du chat syndrome (deletion of 5p)
  • Noonan syndrome (Pulmonary stenosis, HCM, ASD)
  • Congenital rubella syndrome
  • Cardiac manifestations of Marfan syndrome include Mitral valve prolapse, Aortic root dilatation, Aortic regurgitation, Aortic dissection (rarely)

Reference: Harrison,s Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:264 pg:1833

question_text: A 40-year female has several episodes of vomiting and loose stool. She was managed at the periphery by IV fluids and hyponatremia was corrected. She presented to ER with paralysis, dysarthria, dysphagia, loss of consciousness. What might be the cause?
option_d: Excessive infusion fluids leading to fluid overload
explanation:
Overly rapid correction of hyponatremia (>8-10 mM in 24 h or 18 mM in 48 h) causes Osmotic demyelination syndrome. Hypertonic stress in astrocytes within brain regions prone to ODS, leading to generalized protein ubiquitination and endoplasmic reticulum stress due to activation of the unfolded protein response; this is accompanied by apoptotic and autophagic cell death. Rapid correction of hyponatremia also causes a disruption in integrity of the blood-brain barrier, allowing the entry of immune mediators that may contribute to demyelination.

The lesions of ODS classically affect the pons, a neuroanatomic structure wherein the delay in the reaccumulation of osmotic osmolytes is particularly pronounced; clinically, patients with central pontine myelinolysis can present 1 or more days after overcorrection of hyponatremia with paraparesis or quadriparesis, dysphagia, dysarthria, diplopia, a "locked-in syndrome", and/or loss of consciousness.

Other regions of the brain can also be involved in ODS, most commonly in association with lesions of the pons but occasionally in isolation; in order of frequency, the lesions of extrapontine myelinolysis can occur in the cerebellum, lateral geniculate body, thalamus, putamen, and cerebral cortex or subcortex. Clinical presentation of ODS can, therefore, vary as a function of the extent and localization of extrapontine myelinolysis, with the reported development of ataxia, mutism, parkinsonism, dystonia, and catatonia.

However, even appropriately slow correction can be associated with ODS, particularly in patients with additional risk factors; these include alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia, and liver transplantation.

question_text:
A 34 year old man has bradykinesia and rigidity of his limb movements. He was also noticed to have choreiform movements when observed. He has a history of poor development during the latter part of school education.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
In Huntington's disease, as the disease progresses, chorea coexists with and gradually is replaced by dystonia and parkinsonian features, such as bradykinesia, rigidity, and postural instability. It is also associated with cognitive impairment as well as psychiatric manifestations.

In CJD, there will be dementia and myoclonus.

Alzhiemer's Disease presents in later age group mainly as memory impairement.

Parkinsonisn is not associated with Chorea

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 436, Pg: 3405

question_text:
A 65 years old man has had longstanding tremors in both his hands and forearms. Examination reveals normal tone, power and reflexes in his arms. The tremors improve when he drinks alcohol.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
The Following features support a diagnosis of Essential Tremor:

  1. bilateral action tremor of the hands and forearms
  2. absence of other neurological signs, except the cogwheel phenomenon
  3. may have isolated head tremor with no signs of dystonia

Secondary criteria include a long disease duration (more than three years), a positive family history and beneficial response to alcohol (not anticholinergics).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 436, Pg: 3401

question_text:

question_text: A patient presents with spastic quadriplegia. What is the most likely site of lesion?
explanation:
Explanation:

Periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) refers to ischemic necrosis of the white matter adjacent to the lateral ventricles, typically seen in preterm infants due to hypoxic-ischemic injury.

  • It affects the descending corticospinal tracts → spasticity and motor deficits.
  • If extensive, both upper and lower limbs are affected → spastic quadriplegia.

Pathogenesis:

  • Hypoxia → ischemia of watershed zones near ventricles → demyelination and necrosis → cystic cavitations in periventricular white matter.

Explanation of Other Options:

Basal ganglia calcification (Option B):

  • Seen in hypoparathyroidism or Fahr's disease.
  • Produces extrapyramidal symptoms (rigidity, tremor, dystonia).
  • Does not cause spasticity or pyramidal signs.
  • Usually bilateral and symmetric on CT scan.

Cerebellar degeneration (Option C):

  • Causes ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor, and hypotonia.
  • Gait becomes wide-based and unsteady.
  • No hyperreflexia or spastic quadriplegia.
  • Seen in chronic alcoholism, paraneoplastic syndromes, or vitamin E deficiency.

Cystic encephalomalacia (Option D):

  • Post-hypoxic destruction of brain parenchyma forming cystic cavities.
  • Causes focal neurological deficits depending on area affected.
  • Usually results in seizures or cognitive delay, not pure spasticity.
  • Common sequel of severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.

question_text: A 78-year-old woman presents with a progressive decline in daily activity. She gives a history of convulsions and visual hallucinations. She does not talk to anyone and keeps looking at the sky. Pathological examination shows the presence of Lewy bodies within the neurons. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Lewy bodies in neurons along with progressive motor and cognitive decline are hallmark features of Parkinson's disease.

  • Parkinson's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder marked by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra.
  • A key pathological feature is the presence of Lewy bodies-eosinophilic, intracytoplasmic inclusions primarily composed of alpha-synuclein.
  • Patients typically present with motor symptoms like bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and postural instability.
  • In later stages, non-motor symptoms such as cognitive decline, visual hallucinations, sleep disturbances, and behavioral changes can occur-consistent with this patient's clinical presentation.
  • Convulsions are rare but can be seen in late-stage disease or in Parkinson's disease dementia.
  • Management involves dopaminergic therapies like levodopa/carbidopa, dopamine agonists, and MAO-B inhibitors.

question_text: Which part of the brain is most commonly involved due to rapid correction of sodium in extrapontine myelinolysis?
explanation:
Overly rapid correction of hyponatremia (>8-10 mM in 24 h or 18 mM in 48 h) is also associated with a disruption in integrity of the blood brain barrier, allowing the entry of immune mediators that may contribute to demyelination. The lesions of ODS classically affect the pons, a neuroanatomic structure wherein the delay in the re accumulation of osmotic osmolytes is particularly pronounced; clinically, patients with central pontine myelinolysis can present 1 or more days after overcorrection of hyponatremia with paraparesis or quadriparesis, dysphagia, dysarthria, diplopia, a 'locked-in syndrome,' and/or loss 301 of consciousness. Other regions of the brain can also be involved in ODS, most commonly in association with lesions of the pons but occasionally in isolation; in order of frequency, the lesions of extrapontine myelinolysis can occur in the cerebellum, lateral geniculate body, thalamus, putamen, and cerebral cortex or subcortex. Clinical presentation of ODS can, therefore, vary as a function of the extent and localization of extrapontine myelinolysis, with the reported development of ataxia, mutism, parkinsonism, dystonia, and catatonia. Relowering of plasma Na+ concentration after overly rapid correction can prevent or attenuate ODS.

Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 344

question_text: A patient is unable to perform the heel-to-shin test properly and repeatedly misses during the finger-to-nose test. What is the most likely site of the lesion?
explanation:
Explanation:

Inability to perform the heel-to-shin and finger-to-nose tests is indicative of a cerebellar lesion, reflecting impaired coordination and dysmetria.

Cerebellar Lesion: Key Clinical Signs

  • Cerebellar ataxia: Uncoordinated voluntary movements, producing a drunken gait.
  • Dysmetria: Inability to accurately reach a target; finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin tests are impaired.
  • Dysdiadochokinesia: Difficulty performing rapid alternating movements.
  • Nystagmus: Involuntary oscillation of the eyes.
  • Intention tremor: Tremor during voluntary movement, worsening near the target (different from Parkinson's resting tremor).
  • Pendular knee jerk: Leg swings like a pendulum due to hypotonia.
  • Rebound phenomenon: Inability to stop a movement suddenly, causing exaggerated response.

Explanation of other options:

Caudate (Option B): The caudate nucleus, a component of the corpus striatum, when affected, can cause chorea, which consists of involuntary, purposeless, jerky, dancing movements.

Globus pallidus (Option C): Lesions of globus pallidus can cause athetosis, characterized by slow, writhing, purposeless, involuntary movements that are often described as snake-like.

Subthalamic nucleus (Option D): A lesion of the subthalamic nucleus causes hemiballismus, characterised by involuntary, purposeless, flailing movements of the extremities.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562317/

explanation:
Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) is a clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder characterized by disordered cell proliferation, impaired differentiation, and aberrant hematopoiesis, resulting in cytopenias and risk of progression to leukemia.

Both chromosomal and genetic instability have been implicated; both are aging-related.

Cytogenetic abnormalities are found in approximately one-half of patients. Aneuploidy (chromosome loss or gain) is more frequent than translocations.

Loss of all or part of chromosomes 5, 7, and 20, and trisomy of 8 may be related to etiology (11q23 following topoisomerase II inhibitors).

The type and number of cytogenetic abnormalities strongly correlate with the probability of leukemic transformation and survival.

question_text:
Which of the following findings are typical of an upper motor neuron lesion (UMNL)?
1. Rigidity
2. Exaggerated reflexes
3. Fasciculations
4. Severe muscular atrophy
5. Spasticity
explanation:
Explanation:

Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesions result from damage to the descending corticospinal or corticobulbar tracts, which normally exert inhibitory control over lower motor neurons. When this control is lost, characteristic motor signs emerge due to unopposed reflex activity and altered muscle tone regulation.

Key clinical features of UMNL:

  • Spasticity: A velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone, classically described as "clasp-knife rigidity", where resistance to passive movement is initially high but then suddenly gives way.
  • Hyperreflexia: Deep tendon reflexes become exaggerated as inhibitory supraspinal modulation is lost.
  • Positive Babinski sign: Upgoing plantar response due to corticospinal tract involvement.
  • Minimal muscle atrophy: Only from disuse, not denervation.
  • Absence of fasciculations: Because the lower motor neuron remains intact.

question_text: What is segawa syndrome?
explanation:
Dopa-responsive dystonia (DRD; also known as Segawa syndrome) is caused by mutations in the GCH1 gene (GTP cyclohydrolase-1) that encodes for the rate-limiting enzyme in the biosynthesis of dopamine via the biopterin pathway. It manifests as a childhood-onset form of dystonia with diurnal fluctuations and is important to recognize as the condition dramatically responds to low doses of levodopa. Parkinsonism can be a major, or even the only finding, and there may be a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit as evidenced by SPECT. To date, more than 100 different mutations have been reported with a penetrance of around 50% which is considerably higher in women compared to men. Recessively inherited (biallelic) mutations in GCH1 result in a much more severe clinical phenotype with developmental delay and infantile onset. Due to the enzymatic defect in the levodopa biosynthesis, there is a lifelong and dramatic response to levodopa therapy. Indeed, all young onset forms of dystonia should be tested with levodopa to exclude the possibility of DRD.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 436, Pg: 3402

question_text: Which of the following conditions leads to the development of a wing-beating tremor?
explanation:
Explanation:

A wing-beating tremor is a highly characteristic, low-frequency, high-amplitude tremor that is provoked when the patient's arms are extended and is a classic neurologic manifestation of Wilson's disease.

Pathophysiology

Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism, leading to copper accumulation in the liver, cornea, and brain-particularly the basal ganglia. This toxic accumulation disrupts neural circuits controlling movement, producing tremors, dystonia, and parkinsonism. The "wing-beating" quality is distinctive.

Wilson's disease presents with hepatic involvement such as chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis with portal hypertension, or acute liver failure.

Neurological features include tremors, dystonia, ataxia, dysarthria, and parkinsonism-like symptoms, along with psychiatric changes like depression and cognitive decline.

Ocular signs include Kayser-Fleischer rings and, rarely, sunflower cataracts. Renal manifestations include Fanconi syndrome, hematologic involvement is hemolytic anemia, and skeletal features include osteopenia, osteoporosis, and arthropathy.

Differentiation from Other Movement Disorders

  • Huntington's chorea and Sydenham's chorea (Option B and D ruled out): These conditions present with chorea (brief, irregular, dancelike movements), not a rhythmic, postural tremor.
  • Parkinsonism (Option D ruled out) : The classic tremor is a pill-rolling tremor at rest, which is finer and disappears with voluntary movement, unlike the large, flapping tremor of Wilson's.

Key Takeaways:

  • The wing-beating tremor is a pathognomonic sign of Wilson's disease.
  • Other key features include Kayser-Fleischer rings, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and liver disease.
  • It is a treatable condition, making early recognition critical.

question_text: Patient presents to the neurology clinic with complaints of difficulty switching from one movement to another. He also reports having uncontrolled hand movements when trying to perform rapid alternating movements, particularly when asked to tap his fingers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Dysdiadochokinesia is a medical term used to describe a difficulty in performing rapid, alternating movements. It is often considered a sign of cerebellar dysfunction.
  • The cerebellum is a part of the brain that plays a crucial role in motor control and coordination. When there is damage or dysfunction in the cerebellum, it can lead to impaired ability to coordinate these movements, manifesting as dysdiadochokinesis.
  • Patients with dysdiadochokinesis will have trouble performing tasks that require quick and alternating movements, such as tapping their foot quickly or rapidly alternating hand movements, like the finger-tapping task described. The symptoms are typically due to the inability of the cerebellum to correctly time muscle contractions needed for smooth execution of these movements.

Clinical Presentation:

  • Difficulty with rapid alternating movements: This includes tasks like quickly switching the position of the hands or feet.
  • Uncoordinated movement: Movements may appear clumsy or jerky.
  • Other associated cerebellar signs: These might include ataxia, nystagmus, or a wide-based gait.

Explanation of other options:

Ataxia (Option B): Ataxia refers to a broad lack of coordination in voluntary movements, including gait instability, limb incoordination, and speech issues. While dysdiadochokinesia is a specific sign of cerebellar dysfunction, ataxia is a more general term encompassing various coordination deficits.

Tremors (Option C): Tremors are involuntary rhythmic movements, often seen at rest (e.g., Parkinson's disease) or during movement (e.g., essential tremor). The patient's main issue is difficulty switching movements, not rhythmic oscillations.

Bradykinesia (Option D): Bradykinesia (seen in Parkinson's disease) is slowness of movement with difficulty initiating motion. Unlike dysdiadochokinesis, it is not primarily a coordination problem but rather a movement initiation and execution issue due to basal ganglia dysfunction.

Key Takeaways:

Dysdiadochokinesia is a hallmark of cerebellar dysfunction, characterized by difficulty performing rapid alternating movements, as seen in this patient's inability to switch movements smoothly.

question_text: A patient is brought to the OPD by his wife complaining about difficulty in expressing emotions and not taking part in daily activities. On examination, resting tremors and rigidity are noted. Given the possible diagnosis, which part of the brain is affected in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Basal ganglia degeneration, particularly in the substantia nigra, leads to the classic motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease including resting tremors and rigidity.

  • The patient's symptoms-difficulty expressing emotions, reduced participation in daily activities, along with resting tremors and rigidity-are classic features of Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder primarily involving the basal ganglia.
  • More specifically, the substantia nigra pars compacta, a component of the basal ganglia, undergoes dopaminergic neuron degeneration, leading to dopamine deficiency in the striatal pathways.
  • This disrupts the balance of the direct and indirect motor pathways, resulting in motor symptoms like bradykinesia, resting tremors, rigidity, and later, postural instability.
  • Additionally, non-motor features such as emotional blunting and apathy are linked to dysfunction in the limbic circuits of the basal ganglia.
  • Key features of Parkinson's disease:
    • Rigidity: Resistance to passive limb movement ("lead-pipe" or "cogwheel").
    • Resting tremor: Classically described as "pill-rolling" tremor.
    • Bradykinesia: General slowness of voluntary movement.
    • Postural instability: Late features causing impaired balance and frequent falls.

Explanation of other options:

Hippocampus (Option B): Involved mainly in memory consolidation and spatial learning; not associated with motor features like tremor or rigidity.

Cerebellum (Option C): Lesions cause intention tremor, ataxia, and dysmetria-;not the resting tremor or rigidity seen in Parkinson's disease.

Premotor cortex (Option D): Responsible for motor planning and initiation. Lesions here may cause apraxia but are not the primary site of pathology in Parkinson's disease.

The Parkinson's symptoms associated with multi-system atrophy usually respond poorly to dopamine agonists or L-dopa, in contrast to idiopathic Parkinson's.

Urinary retention can be managed with an indwelling catheter if required, and postural hypotension managed with support stockings plus mineralocorticoids if required.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed Ch: 435, Pg: 3388

question_text: A patient presented with hyponatremic encephalopathy with Na 126 meq/L. She was administered 3% NS over the next 24 hours. Following this, the patient deteriorated and developed quadriparesis. What is the next best step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

Overly rapid correction of hyponatremia, particularly with hypertonic (3%) saline, can result in central pontine myelinolysis (osmotic demyelination syndrome), presenting with new neurological deficits including quadriparesis. The next best diagnostic step is MRI brain, which can detect characteristic demyelinating lesions (especially in the pons) and confirm the diagnosis.

  • Overly rapid correction of hyponatremia (>8-10 mM in 24 h or 18 mM in 48 h) is also associated with a disruption in the integrity of the blood-brain barrier, allowing the entry of immune mediators that may contribute to demyelination.

Extrapontine Myelinosis:

  • Extrapontine myelinolysis (EPM) is a form of osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS) that occurs outside the pons. It is often associated with the rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia.
  • Other regions of the brain can also be involved in ODS, most commonly in association with lesions of the pons but occasionally in isolation.
  • In order of frequency, the lesions of extrapontine myelinolysis can occur in the cerebellum, lateral geniculate body, thalamus, putamen, and cerebral cortex or subcortex. (Other options ruled out)
  • Clinical presentation of ODS can, therefore, vary as a function of the extent and localisation of extrapontine myelinolysis, with the reported development of ataxia, mutism, Parkinsonism, dystonia, and catatonia.
  • Relowering of plasma Na+ concentration after overly rapid correction can prevent or attenuate ODS.

Central Pontine Myelinolysis


Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Brainstem evoked potential (Option A): Not used for diagnosis of osmotic demyelination, but may be used for brainstem function in other contexts.

Electroencephalogram (EEG) (Option B): Detects electrical activity, useful for seizures or encephalopathy but not for demyelinating lesions.

Nerve conduction study (Option D): Evaluates peripheral nerves, not central demyelination.

question_text:
A 33 year old woman presents with double vision that is worst when trying to read a book or walk down stairs. The most likely diagnosis is:
A Progressive supranuclear palsy
explanation:
• The superior oblique muscle is innervated by the fourth nerve. The action is to depress the eye and is maximally effective when the eye is looking medially, hence diplopia on reading or going downstairs is typical of fourth nerve paralysis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 441, Pg: 3441

question_text: A 50-year-old man presents with hand tremors and movement abnormalities, along with emerging cognitive and emotional disturbances. Which of the following conditions is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of choreiform movements, progressive cognitive impairment, and psychiatric symptoms is characteristic of Huntington's disease, an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative condition resulting from a mutation in the HTT gene.

  • Huntington's disease typically presents in middle adulthood between ages 30-50 and involves a trinucleotide repeat expansion (CAG repeats) in the HTT gene, leading to the accumulation of abnormal protein in the brain.

Explanations of other options:

Parkinson's disease (Option A): Parkinson's disease usually affects people over the age of 60 and is marked by movement issues, most notably a resting tremor, which differs from the involuntary choreiform movements of Huntington's disease. Although cognitive and emotional symptoms may arise, they tend to appear later in the illness or alongside related conditions such as Lewy body dementia.

Friedreich's ataxia (Option B): Friedreich's ataxia is an inherited condition that mainly impacts the nervous system, leading to progressive damage of the spinal cord and peripheral nerves. It usually begins in childhood or adolescence and presents with ataxia rather than chorea, while cognitive and emotional disturbances are not key features of the disease.

Alzheimer's disease (Option C): Alzheimer's disease mainly impairs memory, cognition, and behaviour, with its defining feature being gradual memory decline. Although psychiatric symptoms can occur, movement abnormalities such as tremors or chorea are not typical, and the condition usually presents at an older age.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559166/

question_text: A 41 year old man complains of pain in the right eye, which has worsened over the last few days. On examination, he had a ptosis of the right eye. He also had a weakness of superior upgaze of the right eye and loss of accommodation reflex, with a dilated pupil. Which of the following is likely?
explanation:
Complete Ptosis of the right eye with loss of accommodation reflex indicates a 3rd nerve palsy.

  • Patients with painful, isolated third nerve palsy with pupillary involvement is most likely due to a posterior communicating artery aneurysm. Other causes of mononeuritis multiplex (diabetes, vasculitis, syphilis), can also cause a third nerve palsy, but seldom are painful.


Arteriogram - Lateral view showing a posterior

communicating artery aneurysm.

Option A: Myasthenia gravis would cause diurnal symptoms of ptosis and diplopia which would occur a few hours after waking up.

Option B: Neurosyphilis would cause an Argyll Robertson Pupil which is characterized by absent pupillary reflex with a preserved accommodation reflex. It occurs due to lesion in the pretectal region

Option C: Multiple sclerosis would cause an internuclear ophthalmoplegia which causes a loss of adduction of ipsilateral eye on abduction of contralateral eye. It occurs due to lesion in medial longitudinal fasciculus

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 429, Pg: 3355

question_text: A 33-year-old banker presents for to the clinic. Apart from a past history of reflux symptoms, her previous medical history is unremarkable. She gives a history of increasing fatigue, being sometimes unable to leave her bedroom;  She feels unable to concentrate, has headaches, intermittent sore throats and feels that when she is able to sleep, she awakes unrefreshed. Full blood count, viscosity, urea and electrolytes, liver function testing, thyroid function testing and a Synacthen test have all been normal. On examination in the clinic there are no abnormal physical findings in this normal weight, normal height young woman. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
• The prevalence of chronic fatigue syndrome is estimated at 1-3 per 1000 individuals. The predominant age at presentation is young adulthood to middle age, and there is a slight female preponderance. Sufferers often report a short flu-like illness at the point of onset and some scientists believe that an initial viral trigger may be responsible.
  • Conventional investigation and physical examination prove normal.
  • EBV infection was thought to be a trigger but there’s no definitive evidence
  • Education, counselling and goal setting have proved useful in stimulating recovery, and trials have demonstrated improvements with amitriptyline use, but many patients take years to return to normal life.
  • Physical exam is normal.
  • Myasthenia Gravis is an autoimmune disorder of NMJ causing skeletal muscle weakness commonly those of eyes, face and swallowing. It can cause diplopia, ptosis, difficult in talking and walking. Often associated with thymoma.
  • Hypothyroidism is excluded as thyroid function tests are normal.
  • Addison's is less likely as Synecthen test (ACTH stimulation test) is normal.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20th edition Chapter:442 Page number:3254-56

question_text: A 20-year-old student is brought to emergency after he had been playing that afternoon, and while resting (after having had a pasta meal), complained of generalized weakness. He was unable to stand and had to be carried in by his friends. His potassium level was noted to be 2.1 mmol/l. Urine screen for diabetic and laxative abuse was normal. Apparently, he has had similar attacks since his early teenage years. Symptoms were aborted by potassium chloride. What type of mutation best fits the underlying pathology of this autosomal-dominant condition involving intermittent paralysis?
option_a: Mutation of a muscle voltage-gated sodium channel
option_b: Mutation in a muscle voltage-gated potassium channel
option_c: Mutation in a renal potassium channel
option_d: Mutation in a muscle voltage-gated calcium channel
explanation:
• Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis is related to a muscle calcium-channel mutation (CAClN1A3).
  • It is an autosomal-dominant condition; attacks usually begin in the teenage years and may remit after around 35 years of age. Potassium is normally below 3 mmol/l during an attack and symptoms resolve with the administration of potassium chloride. Attacks appear to be precipitated either by a high carbohydrate meal or by a period of rest after extreme exercise. Loss of function of muscles concerning speech, bulbar or generalized weakness may occur and attacks can last for several hours.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20th edition Page number:304, 305, 3251

question_text:
A 42-year-old man has weakness in the extensors of the upper limb and flexors of the lower limb muscles. His speech has a nasal quality. There is tongue fasciculation.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The patient has only motor symptoms like weakness of muscles of the upper and lower limbs and possibly of the palate, causing the nasal twang. There is fasciculation too. So among the given options the diseases that presents with pure motor weakness are MND and Myasthenia gravis. But fasciculation is seen in diseases of the neurons and not the neuromuscular junction. So the best possible answer is Motor Neuron Disease.

Motor neuron disease presents with muscle weakness with either UMN features, or LMN features or both.

  • In motor neuron disease, UMN signs include muscle spasticity, slowed recruitment of voluntary muscle strength, weakness especially in the extensors of the upper limb and flexors of the lower limb muscles and hyperreflexia with extensor plantar.
  • LMN features include muscle wasting and fasciculation, depressed reflexes and bulbar palsy.
  • Onset of the disease is usually in mid to late adult life with the incidence increasing with advancing age.

Wilson's Disease presents with extrapyramidal features and neuropsychiatric manifestations.

Creutzfeldt Jacob disease presents with rapidly progressive dementia and death.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 437, Pg: 3410-3415

question_text: A case of progressive weakness of right left leg for 1 year and weakness of upper limb for the last 6 months. On examination spasticity and brisk reflexes are noted in the left leg and wasting and weakness in muscles of the upper limb. Bladder and bowel control is maintained. What is the Diagnosis?
explanation: Here the patient is having features of both UMN and LMN weakness with sparing of bowel and bladder and without sensory symptoms. Cervical myelopathy causes sensory symptoms. Tropical spastic paraparesis causes UMN type weakness and motor neuropathy with conduction block causes LMN weakness.

question_text: A 52 year old man presents with a history of slowly progressive, abnormal movements of his body. On examination there are jerky, semi-purposive movements involving the entire body and abnormal tongue movements. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Huntington's disease is a genetic disorder characterized by abnormal, involuntary movements known as chorea. These movements can involve the entire body and often affect the face, resulting in abnormal tongue movements. The condition typically progresses slowly and is associated with neurological and cognitive symptoms. It is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the HTT gene.
  • There are many causes of chorea.
    • Inherited- Ataxia-telangiectasia, Huntington disease, Wilson disease.
    • Drugs - Anticonvulsants (eg, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital), Antidopaminergic agents (eg, phenothiazines, haloperidol, metoclopramide)
    • Behcet disease, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, Bacterial endocarditis, Herpes simplex encephalitis, Lyme disease.

The other options can be ruled out as follows:

  • A) Parkinson's disease: Parkinson's disease primarily presents with symptoms such as resting tremors, bradykinesia (slowness of movement), rigidity, and postural instability, which are different from the choreiform (chorea-like) movements seen in Huntington's disease.
  • B) Motor neuron disease: Motor neuron disease, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), typically presents with muscle weakness, muscle atrophy, and spasticity rather than the choreiform movements seen in this case.
  • C) Frontal lobe tumor: Frontal lobe tumors may present with various neurological symptoms, but the combination of jerky, semi-purposive movements affecting the entire body and abnormal tongue movements is not characteristic of frontal lobe tumors.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 436, Pg: 3405

question_text:
A 32-year-old woman has an 18 month history of unsteady gait, difficulty to speak and to perform fine movements with the fingers. She has a history of moderate alcohol intake. Neurological examination showed scanning dysarthria, horizontal nystagmus in the lateral gaze, severe bilateral dysmetria in the upper and lower limbs, bilateral dysdiadochokinesis, severe gait ataxia and inability to maintain the sitting.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Cerebellar signs include - Vertigo, Ataxia, Nystagmus, Intention tremor, Scanning speech, Hypotonia and Dysdiadochokinesis.

Cerebellar syndromes are commonly due to alcohol, cerebellar space occupying lesions, multiple sclerosis, and rarely, inherited sydromes such as Friedrich's Ataxia or Spinocerebellar ataxia.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 439, Pg: 3423

question_text: What is the most probable diagnosis for a 30-year-old man who experiences increased tiredness at the end of the day that gets better with rest, along with symptoms of drooping eyelids, difficulty in speaking, and swallowing?
explanation:
Explanation:
The presentation is classic for myasthenia gravis (MG), an autoimmune disorder affecting the neuromuscular junction. Key features include:

  • Fatigable muscle weaknessthat worsens with activity and improves with rest.
  • Ptosis(drooping eyelids).
  • Bulbar symptomslike dysarthria (difficulty speaking) and dysphagia (difficulty swallowing).

Explanation of other options:

Lambert-Eaton syndrome (Option B): Also causes weakness, but it typically improves with brief exercise and is associated with reduced reflexes and autonomic dysfunction, often linked to small cell lung cancer.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy (Option C): An X-linked recessive disorder presenting in early childhood with progressive, non-fatigable proximal muscle weakness and pseudohypertrophy of calves.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (Option D): A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause various symptoms, including rash, arthritis, and serositis, but not typically isolated, fatigable bulbar and ocular weakness.

Key Takeaways:

  • Myasthenia gravis is characterized by fatigable weakness of ocular, bulbar, and limb muscles.
  • Symptoms fluctuate and are typically worse later in the day.

question_text: In thymoma, all are seen except -
explanation: Ans is (b) i.e. hyperalbuminemia Thymoma is the most common Anterior mediastinal mass. Thymomas are seen to be associated with Myasthenia gravis Acquired hypogammaglobulinemia Pure red cell aplasia Grave's ds - Pernicious anemia - Dermatomyositis-polymyositis - Cushing syndrome

question_text: In a patient with Addison's disease, which of the following also occur with increased frequency?
explanation:
• The most common cause for Addison disease overall is autoimmune adrenalitis which has multiple autoimmune associations.
  • Antibodies are most commonly directed against 21 hydroxylase enzyme.
  • There is an increased incidence of chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, premature ovarian failure, type 1 diabetes mellitus, hypo- or hyperthyroidism, pernicious anemia, vitiligo, alopecia, non-tropical sprue & myasthenia gravis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2970

question_text: Gas gangrene is caused by which organism?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) is most commonly caused by Clostridium perfringens, an anaerobic, spore-forming, gram-positive bacillus.
  • The organism produces the potent alpha-toxin (lecithinase), which destroys muscle tissue, causes hemolysis, and produces gas within tissues.
  • It is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection requiring urgent surgical debridement with high-dose penicillin and clindamycin, and sometimes hyperbaric oxygen therapy.

Explanation of other options:

Clostridium difficile (Option A): Causes pseudomembranous colitis due to toxins A and B after broad-spectrum antibiotic use, not gas gangrene.

Clostridium tetani (Option C): Produces tetanospasmin, leading to spastic paralysis, risus sardonicus, and opisthotonus, but not muscle necrosis with gas.

Clostridium botulinum (Option D): Produces botulinum toxin, causing flaccid paralysis and foodborne botulism, not gas gangrene.

question_text:
A 64-year-old male is accompanied to the office by his wife who has noticed that his memory is deteriorating. She also reports that at dinner parties he is inappropriate in his behaviour and she thinks that his personality has changed. On examination the patient has frontal lobe release signs. He is hypotonic in the arms but his reflexes are brisk. He has fasciculations in the tongue and in all four limbs. You suspect frontotemporal dementia (FTD) with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
On which chromosome is the responsible gene located?
explanation:
• Although frontotemporal dementia is associated with chromosome 17, when there is motor neuron disease (MND) associated the chromosome linked to the disorder is 9.
  • It is linked to a hexa nucleotide (GGGGCC) expansion at the non coding region of C9orf72 gene on Chr 9
  • The disorders that are associated with Frontotemporal lobar involvement are: Frontotemporal dementia, Corticobasal degeneration and Progressive Supranuclear palsy .
  • The entities categorized under the umbrella of FTD are - Behavioral variant FTD, the semantic Primary progressive aphasia and the agrammatic Primary Progressive aphasia.
  • The behavioural variant FTD is usually associated with ALS.
  • ALS can also be heritable as AD pattern. The majority(45-50%) of cases of AD ALS is caused by mutation in the C9orf7 gene. The rest of it are caused by mutation of Superoxide dismutase gene(20%) and TDP43 and FUS/TLS gene in 5%.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 437, Pg: 3412

question_text: With regard to a patient with a neuromuscular disorder on the critical care unit which is true:
option_a: Potassium-sparing diuretics should be avoided in patients with hypokalemic periodic paralysis.
option_b: Rocuronium use should be avoided in patients with myasthenia gravis
option_c: Patients with motor neurone disease typically require double the standard dose of suxamethonium to provide optimum intubating conditions.
option_d: Local anesthesia can exacerbate symptoms of multiple sclerosis
explanation:
The use of suxamethonium is challenging in patients with neuromuscular disorders. Key points to remember include relative resistance to depolarisation in myasthenia gravis, often requiring an increased dosage, and the development of extrajunctional receptors in many of the myotonias, leading to extensive depolarisation and potentially fatal hyperkalemia with the use of depolarising neuromuscular blockade. In addition, there are disease-specific aspects of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade that should be noted,including the relative sensitivity in conditions such as Guillain-Barré syndrome. Hence dose reduction to 10-20% should be considered in addition to ongoing monitoring of blockade.

Reference: Harrison 20th 3188-3200

question_text: A 67-year-old male has a diagnosis of myasthenia gravis (MG). All of the following medications should be avoided to reduce the risk of exacerbation except?
explanation:
Some of the medications reported to cause exacerbations of myasthenia gravis (MG) include the following:

  • Antibiotics: macrolides, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides,tetracycline, and chloroquine.
  • Antiarrhythmic agents beta -blockers, calcium channel blockers, quinidine, lignocaine, procainamide, and trimethaphan.
  • Miscellaneous - diphenylhydantoin, lithium, chlorpromazine, musclerelaxants, levothyroxine, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), and, paradoxically, corticosteroids.

Reference: Harrison 20th pg. 3239

question_text: In Myasthenia gravis, antibodies are targeted at the NMJ on receptor:
explanation:
Explanation

  • Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction.
  • Autoantibodies are directed against the postsynaptic acetylcholine (ACh) receptors.
  • This prevents normal neuromuscular transmission, leading to fluctuating muscle weakness that worsens with activity (fatigability).
  • Common symptoms: ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, proximal limb weakness.
  • Associated with thymic hyperplasia or thymoma.

Myasthenia Gravis

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Presynaptic Ach receptors (Option A): The presynaptic terminal releases acetylcholine; however, MG antibodies do not target presynaptic receptors.Presynaptic pathology is instead seen in botulism and Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS) (where calcium channels are affected).

Voltage gated calcium channels (Option C): These are the antibody targets in Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS), not MG.In LEMS, impaired calcium influx leads to reduced ACh release.

Motor end plate (Option D): The motor end plate is the anatomical site where the NMJ exists, but MG specifically targets the postsynaptic ACh receptors, not the entire motor end plate structure.

question_text: A 30-year-old woman presents with unilateral ptosis that worsens by evening and is diagnosed with myasthenia gravis. What is the drug of choice for her management?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The goals of treatment in myasthenia gravis are to maximize acetylcholine activity at remaining neuromuscular junction receptors and limit or abolish the immune attack on motor end plates.
  • The duration of acetylcholine action is prolonged by acetylcholinesterase inhibition, with pyridostigmine being the most commonly used drug.

Myasthenia gravis: Management

Anticholinesterase medication

  • Anticholinesterase medications produce at least partial improvement in most myasthenic patients, although complete recovery is uncommon.
  • Patients with anti-MuSK myasthenia generally benefit less from these agents and may even worsen.
  • Pyridostigmine, the most widely used anticholinesterase, is started at 30-60 mg three to four times daily.

Immunological treatment includes:

Acute treatments

  • Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG): Rapidly reduces antibody levels and weakness.
  • Plasmapheresis: Produces a short-term reduction in anti-AChR antibodies, leading to temporary improvement in myasthenic symptoms.
  • IVIG and plasmapheresis are reserved for myasthenic crisis or preoperative preparation. (Option D ruled out)

Long-term treatments

  • Glucocorticoids:
    • Glucocorticoids effectively improve myasthenic weakness in most patients.
    • To minimise adverse effects, prednisone should be given as a single daily dose rather than in divided doses. (Option B ruled out)
    • In patients with more severe weakness or those already hospitalized, starting at a high dose is reasonable to achieve a faster therapeutic effect.
  • Pharmacological immunosuppression:
    • Azathioprine5 mg/kg daily reduces steroid requirements and may allow withdrawal, though effects are delayed for months.
    • Mycophenolate mofetil is widely used in myasthenia gravis due to its presumed effectiveness and relatively favourable side-effect profile.
    • Calcineurin inhibitors such as cyclosporine and tacrolimus and monoclonal antibodies like Rituximab and Eculizumab are also currently used. (Option C ruled out)
  • Thymectomy: Indicated in antibody-positive patients under 45 years with generalized symptoms, or in patients with thymoma; less effective if disease duration exceeds 7 years or symptoms are confined to extraocular muscles.

question_text: A young man presents with drooping eyelids and muscle weakness that becomes worse by evening and improves after rest in the morning, with symptoms alleviated by neostigmine. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:
