  • The diagnosis of myasthenia gravis is indicated by the typical features of fatigable muscle weakness that progresses over the day (diurnal variation), drooping eyelids (ptosis), and improvement with neostigmine.
  • Symptom relief with neostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that boosts acetylcholine levels at the neuromuscular junction, is a key diagnostic feature of myasthenia gravis.

Explanations of other options:

Huntington chorea (Option B): Huntington's chorea is an inherited disorder marked by involuntary movements, cognitive impairment, and psychiatric disturbances. It is not associated with ptosis, does not exhibit diurnal variation, and does not improve with neostigmine.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Option C): ALS causes gradually worsening muscle weakness but does not display the diurnal fluctuation typical of myasthenia gravis. It rarely starts with ptosis and does not respond to neostigmine.

External ophthalmoplegia (Option D): External ophthalmoplegia may lead to ptosis, but it does not show the typical fatigue pattern or recovery with rest. It also does not respond to neostigmine and lacks the diurnal variation that is characteristic of myasthenia gravis.

question_text: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is seen in myasthenia gravis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune condition caused by IgG autoantibodies against acetylcholine receptors (AChR) at the neuromuscular junction. This leads to complement-mediated cytotoxicity and receptor destruction, producing fatigable muscle weakness.

Since the disease mechanism involves antibody-mediated cellular damage, it is classified under Type II hypersensitivity reaction.

Explanation of Other Options:

Type 1 hypersensitivity reaction (Option A): IgE-mediated immediate reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis, asthma). Not applicable in MG.

Type 3 hypersensitivity reaction (Option C): Immune complex-mediated (e.g., SLE, RA). Different from antibody cytotoxicity.

Type 4 hypersensitivity reaction (Option D): T-cell mediated delayed hypersensitivity (e.g., contact dermatitis, Mantoux). Not relevant here.

question_text: A patient with excessive tiredness towards the end of the day which improves with rest. He also has ptosis, speech difficulty. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
In the given question, a fatigable weakness which improves with rest is classical Myasthenia gravis.

Lambert Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome is similar to myasthenia Gravis but is differentiated by

  • Absence of reflexes
  • Autonomic dysfunction
  • Antibodies are directed against the pre synaptic P/Q type Ca channels.
  • Proximal muscles of the lower limb are more commonly affected.
  • It occurs as a paraneoplastic syndrome in association with Small Cell Carcinoma Lung in elderly patients. In young females it is usually not associated with malignancy.

Duchenne and Becker are inherited and progressive muscle dystrophies and do not show fatigability.

question_text: Which of the following exacerbates myasthenia?
explanation:
This table shows the drugs that interact in M gravis. Among the antibiotics, quinolones and macrolides exacerbate myasthenia. Among the local anesthetics, procaine and lignocaine in large quantities also worsen myasthenia. Magnesium is an ion that worsens myasthenia.

Among the given options Digene is an antacid that contains MgOH and Mg aluminum silicate. So the most appropriate answer is Digene.

question_text: Myasthenia gravis is associated with
explanation: Answer- A. Antibodies against Ach receptors The characteristic pathological feature of myasthenia gravis is presence of antibodies against acetyl choline receptors. These autoantibodies against the acetylcholine receptors lead to loss of functional acetylcholine receptors at the neuro muscular junction.

question_text: A 16-year-old girl presents with generalized muscle weakness and ptosis that worsens as the day progresses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical manifestations of muscle weakness and fatigability, especially worsening as the day progresses, are highly suggestive of myasthenia gravis.

Myasthenia Gravis

  • Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is a neuromuscular junction disorder characterized by skeletal muscle weakness and fatigability.
  • The underlying mechanism is a reduction in available acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the neuromuscular junction due to antibody-mediated autoimmune destruction.

Clinical Features of Myasthenia Gravis:

  • Fatigable muscle weakness: Muscle strength decreases with continued use, especially:
    • Later in the day as day progresses
    • After exercise
  • No sensory or CNS involvement, distinguishing it from other neurological disorders.
  • Common initial symptoms
    • Ptosis (drooping eyelid)
    • Diplopia (double vision)
  • Weakness can spread to:
    • Chewing, swallowing, and speaking muscles
    • Limb muscles

Muscle Weakness Patterns:

Diagnosis

  • Anti-AChR Ab: + in 85% generalized, 50% ocular; confirms diagnosis if positive; AChR-negative: 40% MuSK+, 2% LRP-4+.
  • Repetitive Nerve Stimulation: >10% decrement → probable MG.
  • SFEMG: Jitter/blocking; confirmatory, not specific.
  • Edrophonium Test: Positive → probable MG.
  • Ice-Pack Test: Improves ptosis; highly sensitive.
  • CT/MRI: Exclude intracranial lesions in ocular/cranial MG.

Explanation of other options:

Fibromyalgia (Option B): This chronic condition is characterized by widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, and tender points rather than true muscle weakness. It does not present with ptosis or demonstrate diurnal variation in symptoms.

Myotonic Dystrophy (Option C): A genetic disorder causes progressive muscle weakness with myotonia (delayed muscle relaxation) and primarily affects distal muscles. The absence of myotonia and the presence of generalized muscular weakness points away from this diagnosis.

Guillain-Barré Syndrome (Option D): Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy. GBS typically presents with acute-onset symmetric flaccid limb weakness that begins in the lower extremities and progresses upward.

question_text: A young male presents with eyelid drooping that worsens by evening, fatigue improving with rest, and relief of ptosis with an ice pack. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Myasthenia gravis (MG) is suspected due to ptosis worsening with activity, fatigue improving with rest, and a positive ice pack test (cooling decreases acetylcholinesterase activity, increasing ACh availability).

Definition & Pathophysiology:

  • Autoimmune antibodies (Anti-AChR, Anti-MuSK, Anti-LRP4) damage postsynaptic NMJ.
  • Complement-mediated injury reduces receptor density, impairing transmission.

Etiology:

  • Autoimmune most common.
  • Thymic abnormalities (thymoma, thymic hyperplasia).
  • Drug-induced (penicillamine, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, beta-blockers, MgSO4).

Clinical Features:

  • Ocular (50-60%): Ptosis, diplopia.
  • Bulbar: Dysarthria, dysphagia, chewing fatigue.
  • Limb: Proximal > distal weakness.
  • Respiratory: Dyspnea, risk of myasthenic crisis.

Diagnostic Tests:

  • Bedside: Edrophonium test, Ice pack test.
  • Antibodies: Anti-AChR (85%), Anti-MuSK (10%), Anti-LRP4 (rare).
  • Electrophysiology: Repetitive nerve stimulation (decremental response), SFEMG (↑ jitter).
  • Imaging: Chest CT/MRI for thymoma.

Management:

  • Symptomatic: Pyridostigmine (DOC).
  • Immunosuppression: Steroids, azathioprine, mycophenolate.
  • Severe/Refractory: IVIG, plasmapheresis, eculizumab.
  • Surgical: Thymectomy if thymoma.

Explanation of Other Options:

Huntington chorea (Option B): Movement disorder with dementia, psychiatric features, not fatigable weakness.

ALS (Option C): Progressive upper + lower motor neuron disease; no ocular weakness or rest improvement.

External ophthalmoplegia (Option D): Eye muscle paralysis, not fatigable and no ice pack response.

Key Takeaways:

  • Fatigable weakness improving with rest = MG hallmark.
  • Ice pack test is simple bedside confirmatory tool.
  • Always evaluate for thymic pathology.

question_text: A 30-year-old woman presents with ptosis, diplopia, and generalised fatigable muscle weakness, along with difficulty chewing and swallowing, which worsens later in the day. A Tensilon test is positive. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient's symptoms of ptosis, diplopia, fatigable muscle weakness, and diurnal variation strongly suggest Myasthenia Gravis (MG).
  • A positive Tensilon test supports this clinical suspicion.
  • The most sensitive confirmatory investigation is Single Fiber Electromyography (SFEMG), with sensitivity up to 99%.
  • While SFEMG is the most sensitive, Repetitive Nerve Stimulation (RNS) is more commonly performed as a confirmatory test in clinical practice.

Myasthenia Gravis

  • Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction characterized by skeletal muscle weakness and fatigability.
  • The underlying mechanism involves antibody-mediated destruction of acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the neuromuscular junction.

Clinical Features:

  • Fatigable muscle weakness: Strength worsens with continued use, especially later in the day or after exercise.
  • No sensory or central nervous system involvement, distinguishing MG from other neurological disorders.
  • Common initial symptoms include ptosis and diplopia.

Evaluation and Diagnosis

Diagnosis involves a comprehensive approach integrating clinical evaluation and specific diagnostic tests.

Explanation of other options:

MRI of the brain (Option D): MRI may be useful in ruling out other neurological conditions that can present with similar symptoms, such as multiple sclerosis or brainstem lesions. However, it does not provide specific diagnostic information for MG and is primarily used to exclude other conditions.

question_text: Botulism is most commonly due to -
explanation: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Meat Following new types of botulism have been added in 18th/e of Harrison . Adult intestinal toxemia botulism :- results from absorption of toxin produced in situ after rarely occuring intestinal colonization with toxigenic clostridia. . Iatrogenic botulism :- results from injection of botulism toxin.

question_text: A 64-year-old man develops swallowing difficulties and complains of difficulty walking up stairs. On examination, there is weakness and wasting of the distal muscles of the arms. There are visible fasciculations. Reflexes are brisk and the plantars are up going. There are no sensory abnormalities. Speech and language assessment suggests the presence of pharyngeal muscle weakness.What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient presents with pure motor weakness, with UMN features like hyper-reflexia and extensor plantar and LMN features like fasciculations.

  • This is a classical presentation of motor neuron disease.
  • There is a pseudobulbar palsy in association with fasciculations of the muscles and a mixture of upper and lower motor neuron signs.
  • GBS is less likely as it is not acute onset, no preceding infection.
  • Moreover,fasciculation and muscle wasting are the classic features found in MND and not in GBS. This features also differentiates it from Myasthenia gravis.
  • As sensory is normal, CIDP is less likely.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 437, Pg: 3410

question_text: A middle aged man comes to the ER with altered sensorium of insidious onset. Upon detailed history his wife said that he had difficulty in extending the wrist over the past 3 weeks without any sensory symptoms. You are suspecting a heavy metal poisoning. What additional findings will you see?
option_c: Microcytic hypochromic anemia with Basophilic stippling of RBC on peripheral smear
explanation:
A pure motor neuropathy with encephalopathy points to toxicity with lead. Lead poisoning causes microcytic hypochromic anemia with basophilic stippling of RBC, due to the abnormal porphyrin metabolism. There will be increased serum coproporphyrin levels. Bluish black discolouration of gums may also be seen.

Mee's lines are transverse lines seen in the finger and toe nails. It is classically described in Arsenic poisoning but may be seen in Thallium as well. Arsenic leads to sensorimotor neuropathy with abdominal symptoms. Patchy areas of skin pigmentation may be seen. The diagnosis is made by excessive levels of arsenic in the urine, nail and hair and not in blood. Encephalopathy is not seen.

Acneform lesion is seen in chronic poisoning with Thallium. Thallium toxicity causes sensorimotor neuropathy, encephalopathy and abdominal symptoms.

Another heavy metal that causes encephalopathy is mercury

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3495-3496

question_text: The basic abnormality in increased fasting blood glucose is:
explanation:
• The basic abnormality in increased fasting glucose is high hepatic glucose output mainly due to reduced basal secretion of insulin or hepatic insulin resistance
  • Raised post-prandial glucose values is due to decreased peripheral utilization (muscle and adipose tissue)
  • First and second phase insulin secretion occurs in response to meals

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 3096-3099

question_text: A 75-year-old patient with long-standing diabetes presents with loss of ankle reflex. Which of the following patterns describes neuropathy most commonly seen in diabetes?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most common type of diabetic neuropathy is distal symmetric polyneuropathy. It primarily affects the sensory and motor nerves in a “stocking and glove” distribution, starting distally in the feet and progressing proximally.

  • Diabetic distal Sensory and Sensorimotor Polyneuropathy (DSPN) is the most common form of diabetic neuropathy and manifests as sensory loss beginning in the toes that gradually progresses over time up the legs and into the fingers and arms.
  • Loss of ankle reflex is a hallmark sign.
  • Symptoms may include numbness, tingling, burning pain, and sometimes weakness.
  • This neuropathy develops gradually and is the typical neuropathic pattern seen in long-standing diabetes.
  • The most common cranial nerve involvement in Diabetes mellitus is the Oculomotor nerve, followed by the abducens and facial nerves.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Mononeuritis multiplex (Option B): Involves asymmetric involvement of individual nerves, often in an acute or subacute fashion, not the typical pattern in diabetes.

Proximal neuropathy (Option C): Also called diabetic amyotrophy; less common and usually involves the thigh and hip muscles with pain and weakness.

Amyotrophy (Option D): Refers to muscle wasting and weakness, often associated with proximal neuropathy, not the classic diabetic sensory polyneuropathy.

question_text: A 21-year-old female, who was 32 weeks pregnant is brought to the ER, with 1 week history of fever. She had been complaining of sever fatigue, decreased urine output and high coloured urine. This morning she developed two episodes of seizures and is unconscious. There were no focal deficits and both the plantar were extensor. Her investigations showed Hb: 6g/dL, Total Count of 20,000 cells/μL, Platelet of 10,000/μL, S. Cr was 4.5mg/dL. Her peripheral smear showed shistocytes. Her Prothrombin time and activated thromboplastin time were normal. Which of the following statements is false?
option_a: HELLP Syndrome can be a possible differential diagnosis.
option_b: TTP can be triggered by pregnancy
option_c: Renal impairment is life threatening in HELLP
option_d: ADAMTS 13 activity can be decreased in HELLP syndrome also.
explanation:
Renal failure is a common manifestation of HELLP but is not life threatening. Life threatening complications are neurological complications and hepatic hematoma.

HELLP syndrome is a Thrombotic Microangiopathy that occurs in pregnancy. It is usually associated with pre-ecclampsia. It is different from other TMAs by the presence of liver injury that defines its severity. Liver sub capsular hematoma can be life threatening as it can cause rupture of liver. Neurological complications include cerebral infarction, hemorthage in brainstem and cerebral edema.

aHUS and TTP can also be triggered by pregnancy and hence be a differential diagnosis of HELLP syndrome. In HELLP syndrome anti thrombin III will be decreased and D Dimer will be elevated. ADAMTS 13 activity may be reduced to 30-60%.

DIC can be considered as a DD, but it causes prolongation of PT and aPTT.

In TTP, there will be a classical pentad of fever, neurological symptoms, renal failure, thrombocytopenia and MAHA. It is due to decreased activity of ADAMTS 13 to < 10%, which results in accumulation of ultra large multimers of vWF, that clogs the microcirculation and causes MAHA. The low level of ADAMTS13 activity alone is not enough but TTP is usually triggered by pregnancy, pancreatitis or infection in such individuals.

Acquired TTP can occur due to antibodies to ADAMTS13 which inhibits its activity. It is common in females. It is very severe with mortality of >90% if untreated.

TRERATMENT OF TMAs:

Plasma infusion or plasma exchange is enough to treat congenital TTP.

Acquired TTP and DEAP HUS requires immunosuppression in addition to plasma exchange.

Caplacizumab is the monoclonal antibody approved for the treatment of acquired TTP.

Atypical HUS is treated with Eculizumab

Neuraminidase associated HUS is treated with antibiotics and plasma exchange. Blood should not be given as it has IgM.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:317, Pg: 2365-2367.

question_text: A 34-year-old woman has been admitted to hospital for investigation of progressive weakness in her legs. For the past 5 years. The patient's mother has similar difficulties with weakness and sensory problems. Examination revealed power of 3/5 distally in the upper and lower limbs with a glove and stocking pattern sensory loss to pain and touch. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
In view of the family history, this patient is most likely to have hereditary sensory motor neuropathy type I (Charcot Marie Tooth disease).

  • CMT 1 is the most common form of hereditary neuropathy.
  • Hallmarks of the disease include -
  • Severely and uniformly slowed nerve conduction velocities (NCVs)
  • Primary hypertrophic myelin pathology with prominent onion bulbs
  • Secondary axonal changes
  • Motor symptoms predominate over sensory symptoms.
  • Often, patients report loss of balance, muscle weakness, and foot deformities.
  • Onset in the first decade of life is typical, but disease develops in some patients in young or mid adulthood.

Friedreich's ataxia is an autosomal-recessive genetic disease that causes difficulty walking, a loss of sensation in the arms and legs, and impaired speech that worsens over time. Complications of the disease include hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, scoliosis and diabetes mellitus.

Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) is an acquired autoimmune disease of the peripheral nervous system characterized by progressive weakness and impaired sensory function in the legs and arms. CIDP is closely related to Guillain-Barre syndrome and it is considered the chronic counterpart of that acute disease. Its symptoms are also similar to progressive inflammatory neuropathy.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch: 446, PG: 3483-3485

question_text: GBS in a child treatment -
explanation: Answer- D. All of above Treatment of Guillain-barre syndrome - Self limited in majority of cases. Intravenous immunoglobin shows good response. Plasma pharesis - Removal of autoantibodies. Assisted ventilation - If patient had respiratory muscle paralysis. Physiotherapy.

question_text: A 22-year-old man presents with tremor, sweating, flushing and weight loss. On examination his pulse is 135 bpm and his blood pressure is 160/110 mmHg. Which of the following is the least likely diagnostic possibility?
explanation:
• Pheochromocytomas are catecholamine secreting tumours arising from the adrenal gland.
  • Pheochromocytoma may occur in patients with von Recklinghausen's disease (NF-1) and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Skin neurofibromas and multiple cafe au-lait spots occur in peripheral (NF1) neurofibromatosis, while haemangioblastomas are commonly seen in those with the von Hippel-Lindau syndrome.
  • Carney's triad includes Pheochromocytoma /paraganglioma, pulmonary chondroma and Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST)
  • Ataxia telangiectasia is not associated with pheochromocytomas.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 2976

question_text:
A 54-year-old man presents with a two-month history of progressive painless weakness affecting the proximal arms and legs. He has noticed difficulty getting out of a low chair and some difficulty swallowing but denies any rashes or visual symptoms. Investigations shows a CK of 5000 IU/l.
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Proximal muscle weakness with high CPK suggests an inflammatory myopathy. Among the options Polymyositis is an Inflammatory myopathy. GBS does not cause elevated CPK. Hypothyroidism may cause weakness but here there are no clues to suggest a hypothyroidism. PMR causes girdle pain. Weakness is rare.

  • Polymyositis classically presents with relatively painless progressive proximal muscle weakness. Dysphagia is common but the ocular muscles are very rarely involved unlike myasthenia gravis where this is a predominant feature.
  • Diagnosis of polymyositis confirmed by elevated muscle enzymes (creatine kinase) and typical EMG and muscle biopsy findings.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:365 Pg:2819

question_text: Patient with End stage renal disease and peripheral edema. Is antihypertensive safe?
explanation: Safest drug in end stage, renal disease, and peripheral edema is thiazides

question_text: A 55-year-old man presents with weakness, general malaise and ankle swelling. He has been unwell for 4 months, the ankle swelling having developed quite rapidly over the previous 3 weeks. On examination he has marked peripheral oedema and 3+ proteinuria without haematuria on dipstick urinalysis. His daily urine albumin excretion rate is measured at 6.9 g/24 hours, creatinine is 1.30 mg/dl, serum albumin is 1.2 g/dl and Hb is 8.9 g/dl. Further investigation reveals a paraprotein band in his serum with kappa light chains demonstrated on immunofixation. What is the probable cause of the proteinuria?
explanation:
Multiple myeloma causes tubular dysfunction due to

  • Complete occlusion of the renal tubules by the light chains-Cast Nephropathy
  • Tubulointerstitial disesase due to immunoglobulin and hypercalcemia
  • Proximal tubular dysfunction

Tubular dysfunction causes mild proteinuria without hypertension and hematuria.

Glomerular involvement includes

  • Light chain deposition disease
  • Amyloidosis

Both cause massive proteinuria with variable hypertension and hematuria.

So our patient is having either Amyloidosis or Light Chain Deposition Disease or Amyloidosis, since there is massive proteinuria. So what is the difference?

Since the patient has circulating Kappa light chains, the biopsy is most likely to show LCDD.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Ch:314, Pg:2345.

question_text: A 16-year-old male presents with cardiac tamponade. On examination his peripheral pulse volume fell during inspiration. Which one of the following is the most likely explanation for this clinical sign?
option_a: The cardiac effect of high dose beta agonist bronchodilator drugs
option_b: A falling heart rate on inspiration
option_d: Reduced left atrial filling pressure on inspiration
explanation:
• This patient is demonstrating pulsus paradoxus.
  • The right heart responds directly to changes in intrathoracic pressure, while the filling of the left heart depends on the pulmonary vascular volume.
  • At high respiratory rates, with severe air flow limitation (eg cardiac tamponade, acute asthma) there is an increased and sudden negative intrathoracic pressure on inspiration and this will enhance the normal fall in blood pressure.

Reference: Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:265 pg:1843

question_text: Peripheral blood smear of a patient is given below. This is seen in which of the following conditions?
explanation:
The peripheral blood smear shows bite cells.

This is classically seen in glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page Number-784.

question_text: Which of the following investigations should be conducted in a 7-month-old child who has a hemoglobin level of 6.3, a history of recurrent blood transfusions, an MCV of 70 fl, normal MCH, normal MCHC, and a peripheral smear indicating a hypochromic microcytic image?
explanation:
Explanation:

In an infant with severe microcytic hypochromic anemia requiring transfusions, the most likely diagnosis is beta-thalassemia major. Hemoglobin electrophoresis is the definitive test, which would show a significant increase in Hemoglobin F (HbF) and possibly Hemoglobin A2 (HbA2), with absent or reduced Hemoglobin A (HbA).

Explanation of other options:

Serum iron (Option A): Would be normal or elevated in thalassemia (due to transfusions), but low in iron deficiency. It is not the definitive test.

Direct coomb's test (Option B): Used to diagnose autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

Osmotic fragility test (Option C): Used to diagnose hereditary spherocytosis, which causes a normocytic or macrocytic anemia, not microcytic.

Key Takeaways:

  • Thalassemia major presents in infancy with severe transfusion-dependent microcytic anemia.
  • Hemoglobin electrophoresis is the key diagnostic test.

question_text: A 20 year old boy presented with fever for 1 month, gum bleeding and easy bruisability. Examination showed petechial rashes. On evaluation Hb-3g%, total count 1500, platelet count 15,000/mm3 and peripheral smear showed macrocrocytes. Bone marrow examination showed fatty streaks, absent megakaryocytes and no immature cells. What is your diagnosis?
explanation:
Idiopathic aplastic anemia is the most appropriate answer.

  • The peripheral smear may show macrocytes in AA.
  • Also the marrow will be readily aspirated and pale on gross examination.
  • Hematopoietic stem cells occupy <25% of marrow space.
  • Marrow will be mostly replaced by fat.
  • The cells will be normal in morphology, except being mildly megaloblastic.

The patient is having bleeding manifestations, without any other remarkable physical examination and with pancytopenia in peripheral blood. So ITP can be ruled out since other cell lines will be normal in ITP.

Myelodysplasia occurs in middle aged to elderly and the marrow will be cellular.

So we are left with PNH or idiopathic aplastic anemia.

The history given to us does not have anything in common to suspect PNH. The rule is that PNH occurs in a patient with already established aplastic anemia.

question_text: Which of the following is not an FDA approved drug for Diabetic peripheral neuropathy?
explanation:
• Though tricyclic antidepressants like amitriptyline are commonly employed for managing positive symptoms of diabetic neuropathy, they are not FDA approved
  • Tapentadol is a central acting opioid analog with lesser evidence which is FDA approved
  • Capsaicin patch has also been approved by FDA which works by interfering with the function of TRPV1
  • Venlafaxine, Oxcarbexapine, tricyclic antidepressants, gabapentin etc are others useful in the symptomatic treatment of neuropathy

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 3124

question_text: A 37-year-old lady has developed progressive weakness in the hands and feet over a week. There is some associated numbness and tingling in the hands and feet. She complains of breathing difficulty. She had several episodes of diarrhea two weeks ago. On examination, there is slurring of speech. Her reflexes are all absent and there is sensory loss in a glove and stocking pattern. Which is the next appropriate step?
explanation:
This patient is having an LMN quadriparesis that is antedated by a history of diarrhoeal diasease. Guillain Barre syndrome is the likely diagnosis.

As she is complaining of breathlessness, vital capacity measurement would be essential to access respiratory function and determine the need for ventilation.

ICU admission is recommended when FVC is less than 20 mL/kg and intubation is recommended in most cases when FVC is less than 15 mL/kg.

Diaphragmatic weakness occurs in 30% of patients with patients with GBS and involvement of the neck muscles, tongue and palate leads to further respiratory compromise.

Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS): (Post-infectious polyradiculoneuropathy) -

  • Immune-mediated demyelination of the peripheral nervous system often triggered by an infection such as viral (CMV), viral pneumonia or bacterial (classically Campylobacter jejuni).
  • CSF findings - Elevated protein with no pleocytosis - (albuminocytologic dissociation). Glucose is normal.

Pathogenesis - Cross reaction of antibodies with gangliosides in the peripheral nervous system. Anti GM1 antibodies positive in 25% of cases.

Clinical features -

  • The characteristic features of GBS is progressive symmetric ascending weakness. It begins in the legs and progressively ascends to involve the trunk, upper limbs and finally the bulbar muscles.
  • However it tends to affect proximal muscles earlier than the distal ones.
  • Sensory symptoms tend to be mild (e.g., distal paraesthesia, peripheral sensory neuropathy) with very few sensory signs (NO sensory loss).
  • Usually there is painless progression over days or weeks.
  • Areflexia - All tendon reflexes are absent and the plantar responses were flexor.
  • Cranial nerve involvement e.g., bilateral facial palsy
  • Autonomic dysfunction: e.g., urinary retention and postural hypotension & tachycardia.

 Management -

  • IVIG (IV immunoglobulins) or plasmapheresis.
  • Regular monitoring of FVC (Forced vital capacity) to access respiratory function.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 447, Pg: 3501-3504

question_text: A 45-year-old man has developed weakness over the past 3 weeks which has affected his walking. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, he had decreased sensation peripherally in the legs and also flaccid reflexes in the ankles. A CT of the head was normal and lumbar puncture was done.Results were:Protein 0.75(<0.43 g/l)Glucose 4 (3.3 to 4.4 mmol/l)Lymphocytes 7 (< 5/mm3) What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The dissociation between a high CSF protein, normal glucose and a lack of CSF cellular response in a person with an acute or subacute polyneuropathy is diagnostic of Guillain-Barre syndrome.In GBS, CSF protein is elevated in most patients after the second or third week of illness. The gamma globulin fraction is usually raised. Cells, usually monocytes, are found in 20% of cases.

Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS): (Post-infectious polyradiculoneuropathy) -

  • Immune-mediated demyelination of the peripheral nervous system often triggered by an infection such as viral (CMV), viral pneumonia or bacterial (classically Campylobacter jejuni).

Pathogenesis - Anti GM1 antibodies positive in 25% of cases.

Clinical features -

  • The characteristic features of GBS is progressive symmetric ascending weakness.
  • No sensory loss
  • Areflexia - All tendon reflexes are absent and the plantar responses were flexor.
  • Cranial nerve involvement e.g., diplopia
  • Autonomic dysfunction: e.g., urinary retention and postural hypotension & tachycardia.
  • Diaphragmatic weakness occurs in 30% of patients.

Management -

  • IVIG (IV immunoglobulins) or plasmapheresis.
  • Regular monitoring of FVC (Forced vital capacity) to access respiratory function.

Poliomyelitis is a disease that occurs during childhood and has some disability. History of vaccine not taken may be there.

Tuberculous meningitis presents with acute history of fever, headache, altered sensorium, convulsions etc. History of TB foci may be there elsewhere in the body.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch:447, Pg: 3501-3504

question_text: A 32-year-old man presents with a 5-day history of weakness in the arms and legs, accompanied by tingling. He had several episodes of bloody diarrheal illness two weeks ago. On examination there was leg and arm weakness and flaccid deep tendon reflexes. Which test would best help confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
The diagnosis is likely to be Guillain Barre syndrome. The two best tests are -

  • NCS: Shows prolonged distal latencies and reduced CMAP in AIDP. In AMAN or AMSAN, there will be reduced CMAP without prolonged distal latencies.
  • CSF analysis - Shows raised protein.

Campylobacter serology should also be sent for this patient as he has history of bloody diarrhoea. GBS is often seen following Campylobacter infection.

Previous history of a diarrhoeal illness (specifically Campylobacter jejuni) is a poor prognostic feature.

Other poor prognostic features include

  • Age > 40 years
  • High anti-GM1 antibody titre
  • Poor upper extremity muscle strength
  • Need for ventilatory support

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21ST Ed, Ch: 447, Pg: 3503

question_text: Which of the following clinical manifestations suggests Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS)?
option_c: Bulbar involvement in about 50% of cases
explanation:
GBS is associated with bulbar involvement occurs in 50%, with a risk of aspiration and respiratory insufficiency.

In GBS,

  • Symmetric involvement is typical. Asymmetrical involvement is present in only 9% of patients.
  • CSF protein is elevated to more than twice the upper limit of normal, with normal glucose and no pleocytosis.
  • Areflexia is commonly present.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 447, Pg: 3501

question_text: A 57-year-old female is admitted with progressive weakness following a trivial flu-like illness. Which of the following would exclude Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) as the diagnosis?
explanation:
A sensory level is not a feature of GBS and would suggest cervical myelopathy.

Guillian Barre Syndrome (GBS) is a post-infectious acute polyneuritis typified by elevated CSF protein with few cells and often normal glucose.

  • There is a profound weakness associated with areflexia and peripheral sensory neuropathy.
  • Ophthalmoplegia is associated in particular with the Miller-Fisher variant.
  • Muscle wasting is typical with prolonged illness.
  • Autonomic dysfunction can also occur.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 447, Pg: 3501

question_text: The antibodies detected in Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy are of which immunoglobulin class?
explanation:
Explanation:

The antibody seen in Guillain-Barre Syndrome (GBS), also known as Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (AIDP), is predominantly IgG.

  • Guillain-Barre Syndrome (GBS) is an autoimmune condition in which the body's immune system mistakenly attacks the peripheral nervous system, leading to acute paralysis.
  • The main antibodies involved are of the IgG class, which target myelin in the peripheral nerves.
  • This immune response causes inflammation and demyelination, producing typical features such as muscle weakness, sensory disturbances, and progressive ascending paralysis.

Explanations of other options:

IgM (Option B): Although IgM antibodies may play a role in some autoimmune disorders, they are not commonly linked to Guillain-Barre Syndrome (GBS). IgM is generally involved in the initial stages of the immune response and is not the characteristic antibody type seen in GBS.

IgE (Option C): IgE antibodies are mainly linked to allergic responses and defence against parasitic infections. They are not typically involved in Guillain-Barre Syndrome (GBS), as their role is centred on hypersensitivity reactions rather than autoimmune activity.

IgA (Option D): IgA antibodies are predominantly present in mucosal surfaces and are crucial for protecting mucous membranes. They are not commonly linked to the immune mechanisms of GBS, since their main role is mucosal defence rather than systemic autoimmune activity.

question_text: A 26-year-old man, who had a respiratory infection 4 weeks earlier, has been unable to stand or walk for the past 2 weeks due to progressive, symmetrical, ascending weakness. The weakness started in the lower limbs and later involved the upper limbs. On examination, reflexes are absent, while pain and position sense remain intact. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient shows hallmark signs of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS), namely a preceding respiratory infection, gradually worsening ascending symmetrical weakness, and loss of reflexes.

Guillain-Barre syndrome is an autoimmune polyradiculopathy that leads to patchy, segmental demyelination of the spinal roots and peripheral nerves. Its link with recent infection, the pattern of ascending weakness, and the preservation of sensory function are typical features of the condition.


Explanation of other options:

Myasthenia gravis (Option B): In myasthenia gravis, muscle weakness usually becomes more pronounced with repeated activity and improves after rest. The condition often begins by involving the eye and facial muscles before progressing to the limbs. An ascending pattern of weakness with absent reflexes is not characteristic of this disorder.

Polymyositis (Option C): Polymyositis is characterized by symmetric weakness of proximal muscles, mainly involving the shoulders and hips, leading to difficulty in tasks such as climbing stairs or lifting the arms overhead. Reflexes remain intact, and sensation is preserved. Since this case lacks proximal muscle involvement, shows absent reflexes, and does not follow the typical ascending pattern, polymyositis is unlikely.

Multiple sclerosis (Option D): Multiple sclerosis usually progresses in a relapsing-remitting pattern with varied neurological signs. Typical features include visual disturbances such as optic neuritis and sensory issues like numbness and tingling. Affected individuals more often show increased reflexes rather than absent ones.

question_text: Guillain Barre Syndrome treatment consists of all except?
explanation:
Steroids have no role in the treatment of GBS.

Plasma exchange and I.V immunoglobulins are the mainstay treatment whereas ventilatory support may be needed during the course of GBS.

question_text: Predominantly sensory neuropathy is/are caused by:
explanation: Answer is A and B (Cisplatin and Pyridoxine excess): Cisplatin and Pyridoxine are associated with predominantly sensory neuropathies.

question_text: In a child diagnosed with Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS), which of the following statements is incorrect?
option_a: Areflexia of the affected limb is a mandatory diagnostic criteria
option_b: Plasmapheresis is not preferred in refractory cases
option_c: Intravenous immunoglobulin is the first line of management
option_d: Albuminocytological dissociation in CSF is characteristic
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Plasmapheresis is actually preferred in refractory cases of Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS), especially when the condition does not improve after initial treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG).
  • The standard treatment for GBS involves the use of either IVIG or plasmapheresis, depending on the patient's condition and response to initial therapy.

Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)

Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute autoimmune disorder that affects the peripheral nervous system. It often leads to ascending paralysis, starting from the lower limbs and spreading upwards.

GBS is considered a neurological emergency due to its potential to cause respiratory failure, autonomic dysfunction, and death without timely treatment.

Epidemiology and Triggers

  • Incidence: 1-2 cases per 100,000 persons per year.
  • Often follows an infection or vaccination (molecular mimicry).
  • Common triggers:
    • Campylobacter jejuni (most common)
    • Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
    • Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)
    • Mycoplasma pneumoniae
    • Zika virus, Influenza virus

These infections lead to molecular mimicry, where the immune system attacks nerve structures, particularly the myelin sheath, causing demyelination.

Variants of Guillain-Barré Syndrome:

Autoantibodies in Guillain-Barré Syndrome:

  • Diversity: GBS patients exhibit a range of autoantibodies targeting nerve cells and structures.
  • Common Antibodies: The most common are anti-ganglioside antibodies, which appear in up to 50% of GBS cases.
  • Prognostic Implications: The presence of anti-GM1 antibodies correlates with poorer clinical outcomes, especially in pure motor variants and Miller Fisher Syndrome.

Clinical Features:

Motor Symptoms

  • Symmetrical, ascending paralysis (starts in lower limbs → progresses proximally).
  • Hypotonia or flaccid paralysis.
  • Areflexia or hyporeflexia (deep tendon reflexes lost early).
  • In severe cases:
    • Facial nerve weakness.
    • Bulbar or respiratory muscle involvement (respiratory failure in 25-30%).

Sensory Symptoms

  • Paresthesias and numbness in distal limbs ("glove and stocking" pattern).
  • Loss of proprioception and vibration sense.
  • Pain in shoulders, neck, or back.

Autonomic Dysfunction

  • Orthostatic hypotension.
  • Cardiac arrhythmias (sinus tachycardia/bradycardia).
  • Blood pressure fluctuations.
  • Bowel and bladder dysfunction.

Diagnostic Findings:

Brighton Criteria for Diagnosis of GBS:

Treatment:

  1. Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG)
  • First-line therapy for both adults and children.
  • Dose: 2 g/kg total, administered over 2-5 days.
  • Mechanism: Neutralizes autoantibodies, blocks Fc receptors, and modulates immune response.
  1. Plasmapheresis (Plasma Exchange)
  • Equally effective as IVIG, especially useful in refractory cases or rapidly progressive weakness.
  • Removes circulating pathogenic antibodies and immune complexes.
  • Typically performed as 4-6 exchanges over 10-14 days.
  • Not recommended immediately after IVIG (should be spaced by ≥48 hours).
  1. Supportive Care
  • Respiratory monitoring (FVC < 15 mL/kg indicates need for ventilation).
  • Autonomic monitoring (for arrhythmias and BP fluctuations).
  • DVT prophylaxis and physiotherapy.
  1. Corticosteroids:
  • Ineffective in GBS and not recommended.

question_text: A patient presents with a history of viral infection 2 weeks back, the patient later develops acute ascending bilaterally symmetrical lower limb flaccidity over a week followed by upper limb weakness. On examination, there is loss of spinal reflexes. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP), also known as Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), is characterized by:

  • Rapidly evolving areflexic motor paralysis which may occur with or without sensory disturbances.
  • Commonly follows a preceding viral or bacterial infection, which often appears 1-3 weeks prior to the onset of neurological symptoms.
  • The progression of weakness generally starts in the lower limbs and ascends to the upper limbs and may include the cranial nerves.
  • Spinal reflexes are lost or significantly diminished early in the disease process.
  • Patients may experience autonomic dysfunction and severe cases might require respiratory support due to muscle weakness.

AIDP:

  • Clinical Manifestations:
    • Begins with weakness in the lower extremities progressing to the upper body.
    • Facial diparesis occurs in about 50% of patients.
    • Some patients may experience bulbar weakness leading to difficulty in managing secretions.
    • Pain is common and can be acute or a deep aching in weakened muscles.
  • Disease Course:
    • Symptoms typically peak within four weeks.
    • Hospitalization is required for most patients.
    • Up to 30% may require mechanical ventilation due to severe weakness.
  • Autonomic Involvement:
    • Includes fluctuations in blood pressure, postural hypotension, and cardiac dysrhythmias, necessitating close monitoring.
  • Subtypes and Variants:
    • The most common subtype is AIDP.
    • Other variants include acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN) and Miller Fisher syndrome (MFS), among others.
  • Antecedent Events:
    • About 70% of GBS cases follow a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection.
    • Common pathogens include Campylobacter jejuni and viruses such as CMV and Epstein-Barr virus.
  • Diagnosis and Treatment:
    • Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation and may be supported by electrodiagnostic studies and CSF analysis.
    • Immediate treatment with immunotherapies such as IVIG or plasmapheresis is recommended upon strong suspicion of GBS, even before all diagnostic criteria are met.

Explanation of other options:

Multiple Sclerosis (MS) (Option B): MS is a CNS demyelinating disease, not peripheral. Presentation is asymmetric, with relapsing-remitting episodes (not a rapidly ascending weakness). Reflexes are usually increased (UMN involvement), unlike the areflexia in GBS.

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) (OptionC): ALS causes both upper and lower motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia with spasticity and muscle atrophy). No sensory involvement in ALS (GBS has sensory symptoms). ALS progresses over months to years, while GBS is acute and rapidly progressing.

Transverse Myelitis (TM) (Option D): TM causes sudden, asymmetric weakness below the spinal lesion with bowel/bladder dysfunction. Reflexes are initially low but become hyperreflexic (UMN signs), unlike the areflexia in GBS. Not an ascending paralysis like in GBS.

Key Takeaways:

An acute ascending, bilaterally symmetrical, flaccid paralysis with areflexia following a viral infection strongly suggests Guillain-Barré Syndrome (AIDP subtype).

question_text: All are criteria for accelerated blast phase except
explanation:
Criteria of accelerated-phase CML (Chronic Myeloid Leukemia) includes the presence of -

  • 15% or more peripheral blasts
  • 30% or more peripheral blasts plus promyelocytes
  • 20% or more peripheral basophils
  • Cytogenetic clonal evolution (presence of chromosomal abnormalities inaddition to Ph)
  • Thrombocytopenia <100 × 109/L (unrelated to therapy)

Accelerated phase of CML is historically associated with median survival of <1.5 years.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 105, Pg: 821

question_text: A 74 year old patient with osteoarthritis of the right knee with joint pain. What should be tried for the patient first?
explanation:
NSAIDS tend to be better for pain control in osteoarthritis, but have significant side effects. Local NSAID application should be considered as well as intraarticular steroid injections. If multiple joints are involved-> we can start with paracetamol first.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 371 Pg: 2861

question_text: A 20 year old male has taken a drug overdose of multiple drugs. Which one of the following can be effectively removed by haemodialysis?
explanation:
Drugs with a large volume of distribution are poorly dialysed. Haemodialysis is effective in lithium poisoning.

LIST OF DIALYZABLE TOXINS

Dialysis should be considered in cases of severe poisoning due to:

  • Carbamazepine
  • Ethylene glycol
  • Isopropyl alcohol
  • Lithium
  • Methanol
  • Theophylline
  • Salicylates
  • Valproate.

Hemodialysis corrects the acid base balance as well as removal of toxins compared to hemoperfusion.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 459, Pg: 3589.

question_text: Water hammer pulse seen in which of the following?
explanation:
Water hammer pulse is seen in AR.

Corrigan pulse describes the excessive visible pulsations of arteries in patients with aortic valve insufficiency, most obvious in the head and superior extremity arteries when the patient is upright; in particular, the subclavian, carotid, temporal, brachial, and palmar arteries.

In MS the pulse will be low volume.

In AS the pulse will be slow rising low volume pulse(Parvus et tardus)

question_text: A patient presents with pigmented spots around the mouth and lips, along with abdominal pain and vomiting. History reveals that pigmentation has been present since childhood. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterised by mucocutaneous pigmented macules (especially on lips, mouth, fingers) and hamartomatous polyps in the GI tract.
  • Patients often present with abdominal pain, vomiting, or intussusception due to polyps. Pigmentation starting in childhood and gastrointestinal symptoms strongly support PJS.

Explanation of other options:

Familial adenomatous polyposis (Option A): Caused by APC gene mutation with hundreds of adenomatous polyps in the colon, but no mucocutaneous pigmentation.

Juvenile polyposis syndrome (Option C): Presents with multiple hamartomatous polyps and rectal bleeding, but pigmentation is absent.

Cronkhite-Canada syndrome (Option D): A rare non-hereditary disorder with GI polyps, alopecia, and nail atrophy, not pigmented spots around the lips.

question_text:
Comment on core criteria seen in case of Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Syndrome?
A) Focal Seizures
B) Bilateral Optic Neuritis
C) Area Postrema syndrome
D) Diencephalic Syndrome
Which of the above are correct?

A 20 year old man attends ER because of palpitations. Before they could do an ECG his palpitations self terminated. The ECG which was done showed sinus rhythm with a PR interval of 70 ms. What is the mechanism of the patient's tachycardia?
explanation:
The PR interval is short (<3 small squares or <120 ms) suggesting wolff parkinson white syndrome. There may be an accessory pathway which predisposes to AVRT rather than AVNRT.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, chapter:244 page number:1740

question_text: A 39-year-old lady has difficulty walking. On examination, she has an ataxic gait, increased tone in the legs with hyperreflexia and motor weakness. What diagnostic investigation should be arranged?
option_a: CT scan of the brain and spine
explanation:
The patient in this question has involvement of the pyramidal tract as evidenced by the hyperreflexia, hypertonia and the weakness. She also has ataxia, which could be either due to the involvement of the posterior column or the cerebellum. For imaging of the spinal cord and the structures in the posterior fossa MRI is the best investigation compared to CT. The diseases that can present like this are Multiple sclerosis, Vitamin B12 deficiency etc.

Lumbar spine X ray will help to reveal only the bony abnormalities and hence is not useful here. EMG is used if a muscle disease is suspected, which is unlikely in this case.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 423,Pg: 3284

question_text: A 74 year old has had increasing back and leg pains several years. X rays reveal bony sclerosis of sacroiliac, lower vertebral and upper tibial regions. He mentions greater difficulty hearing over the recent years. Blood tests reveal an elevated serum alkaline phosphatase. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The presence of bone pains, hearing impairement and isolated elevation of ALP points to the diagnosis of Pagets disease. Osteomalcia also causes high ALP, but there will be abnormalities of calcium and phosphorous. Osteoarthritis can cause one pains, but the ALP will be normal.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 412 Pg: 3211

question_text: Which disease is associated with the SOD1 mutation?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder involving both upper and lower motor neurons.
  • Mutations in the SOD1 (superoxide dismutase 1) gene are linked to familial ALS, leading to abnormal protein aggregation and neuronal injury.
  • Patients present with progressive weakness, fasciculations, spasticity, and eventual respiratory muscle involvement.

Explanation of other options:

Multiple sclerosis (Option B): An autoimmune demyelinating disorder of the CNS associated with HLA-DR2, not SOD1 mutation.

Alzheimer's disease (Option C): Linked to APP, presenilin-1, and presenilin-2 mutations, not SOD1.

Parkinson's disease (Option D): Associated with α-synuclein, PARKIN, and LRRK2 mutations, not SOD1.

question_text: A patient is diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. The disease mainly affects?

A 45-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of dysuria and suprapubic discomfort over the past 3 months. He has been treated multiple times with antibiotics for suspected urinary tract infections. He denies fever or hematuria. On examination, his prostate is non-tender and normal in size. Lab reports show leukocyte count (>50/UI) in Urine analysis  with no growth in urine culture. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

In this case, the patient presents with persistent urinary symptoms over the past 3 months, including increased frequency and suprapubic discomfort, along with a normal prostate examination. Urine analysis reveals a high leukocyte count (>50/μL), yet urine cultures remain negative for bacterial growth. These findings are most consistent with a diagnosis of sterile pyuria.

Explanations for other Options:

Chronic Bacterial Prostatitis (Option A): Chronic bacterial prostatitis usually presents with recurrent UTIs, perineal or low back pain, and sometimes a boggy or tender prostate on digital rectal exam.

Granulomatous prostatitis (Option B): This is a rare form of prostatitis usually due to tuberculosis, fungal infections, or after intravesical BCG therapy.

It often presents with prostate enlargement, nodularity, or tenderness, which are absent here. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy

Acute UTI (Option C): Acute UTIs generally present with dysuria, frequency, urgency, often accompanied by fever, chills, or flank pain, and show positive urine cultures.

This patient lacks systemic symptoms and has repeatedly negative cultures, which rules out a typical UTI.

question_text: A 66 year old man is admitted as an emergency with severe epigastric pain. He smokes 30 cigarettes a day and takes approximately 30 units of alcohol per week but admits to exceeding this amount occasionally. He also complains of sudden onset poor vision. Ophthalmoscopy shows multiple microinfarcts (cotton wool spots). What investigation should be considered next?
explanation:
This patient probably has acute pancreatitis precipitated by alcohol consumption. Ischaemic retinopathy, which causes retinal oedema and micro infarcts, is a complication of acute pancreatitis.

CT scan of the abdomen will be useful in confirming diagnosis and assessing for the presence of a pancreatic abscess/pseudocyst.

Causes of acute pancreatitis:

  • Gallstones (Most important risk factor) or other biliary diseases
  • heavy alcohol consumption
  • hypertriglyceridemia
  • hypercalcemia
  • Blunt Abdominal trauma
  • ERCP
  • Drugs: azathioprine, mercaptopurine, asparaginase, pentamidine, didanosine, valproic acid, tetracyclines, dapsone, isoniazid, metronidazole
  • Infections: hepatitis viruses, mumps, cytomegalovirus, M avium intracellulare complex, SARS CoV-2
  • Cardiopulmonary bypass

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 348, Pg: 2658

question_text: A 28 year old female comes with sensory symptoms in the form of hypoesthesia beginning from the nipple downwards of subacute onset. She was evaluated suspecting a demyelination and the diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis was made with MRI and positive oligoclonal bands. She has no visual symptoms, and her VEP is normal. She does not have any bladder symptoms or motor symptoms. Which of the following is a highly efficacious disease modifying therapy for her treatment?
explanation:
This patient has a first episode of demyelination consistent with MS. Treatment should be started in all patients with an isolated demyelinating event which has high risk of MS

The long term treatment of MS mostly relies on the use of highly efficacious disease modifying treatments, which includes:

  1. Anti CD 20 agents: Rituximab, Ofatuzumab and Ocrelizumab
  2. Anti CD 52 agents: Alemtuzumab
  3. Natalizumab : Antibody against α4β1 integrin
  4. Mitoxantrone

Moderately efficacious agents include:

  1. S1P receptor modulators: Fingolimod
  2. Dimethyl Fumarate
  3. Cladrabine

Modestly effective:

  1. Teriflunamide
  2. Interferons
  3. Glatiramir acetate

For all patients highly efficacious agents are preferred

For those with normal physical examination or those with minimal MRI findings or those who want oral treatment Fingolimod or Dimethyl fumarate is preferred.

Siponimod is the agent preferred for Secondary Progressive MS

Ocrelizumab is the agent showing benefit in Primary Progressive MS

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine 21st edition, page no.3496

question_text: Which of the following drugs are approved for the treatment of NMO, to prevent relapse ?
explanation:
The drugs that are approved for preventing relapses in NMO are

Eculizumab Monoclonal antibody against C5 complement

Inebilizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to the B-cell-specific surface antigen CD19

Satralizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to the interleukin-6 receptor, blocking engagement of IL-6.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 445, Pg: 3477-3479

question_text: Which of the following is the preferred drug treatment in the treatment of primary progressive multiple sclerosis?
Which of the following is true regarding Behcet disease?
option_a: The most common and the earliest lesion of Behcet disease is genital ulcers
option_b: The most specific lesion is oral ulcer
option_c: While oral ulcers do scar, genital ulcers usually do not
option_d: Pathergy test is a non-specific hyperreactivity test to trauma
explanation:
• The most common symptoms are associated with mucocutaneous tissues. Oral ulcers are seen in virtually all patients and are commonly the first manifestation. Commonly, like ordinary cancer sores, they are usually multiple. They scar only uncommonly.
  • Genital ulcers are the most specific lesions, most commonly occurring on the scrotum or labia. They are larger and deeper and take longer to heal than oral ulcers and tend to form scars.
  • Pathergy reaction is a nonspecific hyperreactivity of the skin to trauma. Typically, a papule or pustule forms in 24–48 h after a needle prick. It is rather unique for Behçet syndrome and is part of the ISG diagnostic criteria.
  • Eye involvement is seen in half of all patients and in ~70% of males. It is most commonly a bilateral panuveitis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:364 Pg:2817

question_text: A diabetic patient came to you and wished you namaste. While doing namaste you as a doctor observe his hand has this deformity?
explanation:
The patient in the given question is unable to oppose the palmar surfaces of the hands and fingers(prayer sign). This is due to limited joint mobility syndrome or diabetic cheiroarthropathy or stiff hand syndrome.

It is not an arthropathy, but a process that involves the periarticular structures. It is a fibrosing syndrome resulting in thick waxy and tight skin on the dorsal aspect of MCP, PIP and DIP of fingers. Larger joints can also be involved.

It is seen in both type i and type ii diabetes and increases in frequency with age, disease duration and poor glycemic control.

NSAIDs and steroids are ineffective in management. Physical therapy and glycemic control are the treatment.

question_text: A 66 year old man has been admitted Following an episode of confusion. He was on two different diuretic drugs on admission which were discontinued due to hyponatremia. On day 1, he had a sodium of 112 mmol/l and on day 3 he had a sodium of 145 mmol/. He had developed by day 3, spastic quadriparesis and pseudobulbar palsy. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• The upper motor neuron features and rapid correction of hyponatremia suggests central pontine myelinolysis. The neurological features may improve gradually but certain patients have permanent neurological deficits from rapid changes in serum sodium.

Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome:

  • The neurologic manifestations associated with overly rapid correction have been called the osmotic demyelination syndrome.
  • The clinical manifestations of ODS are typically delayed for two to six days after overly rapid elevation of the serum sodium concentration has occurred. The symptoms, which are often irreversible or only partially reversible, include dysarthria, dysphagia, paraparesis or quadriparesis, behavioural disturbances, movement disorders, seizures, lethargy, confusion, disorientation, obtundation, and coma. Severely affected patients may become "locked in"; they are awake but are unable to move or verbally communicate.

Risk factors for ODS:

  • Serum sodium at presentation ≤105 mEq/L.
  • chronic Hyponatremia (>48 hours)
  • Rapid correction of serum sodium (plasma Na+ concentration is corrected by >8–10 mm within the first 24 h and/or by >18 mm within the first 48 h)

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 53, Pg: 344-346

question_text: A 60-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department with hypertension and abdominal pain. Physical examination and initial laboratory work-up were unremarkable; except for severe abdominal tenderness and elevated lactate dehydrogenase. A CT scan showed a hypodense, triangle-shaped area in the right kidney suggestive of renal infarction. Renal duplex scanning revealed a focal increase of flow velocities followed by turbulence in multiple segments of the right renal artery. Arteriography showed multiple lesions in a "string of beads" pattern and a parenchymal filling defect. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
The presence of hypertension and "string of beads" appearance is characteristic of Fibromuscular Dysplasia.

Fibromuscular Dysplasia is an uncommon vascular disease, which results in arterial dilation and narrowing of vessel segments.

It causes stenosis, dissection, aneurysm and thrombosis.

Mainly involves renal and carotid/vertebral vessels. Can involve coronary, mesenteric, iliac and extremity vessels.

Non inflammatory obstruction, unlike vasculitis.

Definitive diagnosis can be made by selective renal arteriography and bilateral renal vein and systemic venous renin measurements.

Fibromuscular dysplasia(FMD), is a developmental lesion of unknown etiology which can affect multiple vessels. It consists of areas of heaped up intima, media and adventitia alternating with areas of medial destruction, the latter resulting in small focal aneurysms. The disorder can be progressive and affects females greater than males in a ratio of 3:1. It more commonly affects middle aged patients.

Image shows a diffusely beaded appearance of the right main renal artery to the level of the branch vessels.

Polyarteritis nodosa is a medium vessel vasculitis that can involve the renal vessels and cause hypertension, it does not cause the characteristic angiographic appearance.

Wegener's Granulomatosis is a small vessel vasculitis and does not involve the main renal vessels.

Polycystic kidney disease presents with large sized kidneys replaced by cysts of multiple sizes.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Ch:281, Pg:2110.

question_text:
A 75-year-old woman comes to the clinic for advice. Over the course of the past year or two she has had increasing problems with regurgitation of rotten food, has lost weight and acquired a chronic cough. According to her partner she has problems with halitosis which have not improved on multiple visits to the dentist. On examination her BP is 145/82 mmHg, pulse is 70 and regular and her BMI is 27. She has a neck mass which appears to gurgle when she swallows.
Investigations show:
Haemoglobin 13.2 g/dl (11.5-16.0)
White cell count 7.3 x 10^9/L (4-11)
Platelets 161 x 10^9/L (150-400)
Sodium 141 mmol/l (135-146)
Potassium 4.0 mmol/l (3.5-5)
Creatinine 0.7 mg/dl
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The history of regurgitation of rotten food, coupled with chronic cough and a gurgling mass on examination fits best with a pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's diverticulum). Aspiration of food from the pouch may lead to pneumonia in some cases.

Zenker's diverticulum is a pulsion diverticulum where pharyngeal mucosa herniates through the weak area between two parts of the inferior constrictor.

Management involves either diverticulectomy for larger lesions, or Dohlman's procedure for smaller pouches.

Whilst GERD is a possible alternative diagnosis, a pouch would not be found on examination.

Achalasia is usually associated with progressive dysphagia to both liquids and solids, oesophageal carcinoma with progressive dysphagia first to solids then liquids.

Plummer-Vinson's disease is associated with progressive dysphagia due to oesophageal webs.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2426

question_text: Chronic subdural haematoma in a 77-year-old man is not associated with the presence of which of the following?
explanation:
• Chronic subdural haematoma is classically associated with fluctuating conscious level and cognitive function.
  • Bilateral papilloedema may occur with raised intracranial pressure.
  • Bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia is associated with multiple sclerosis and unilateral lesions of medial longitudinal fasciculus may occur with small brain stem infarcts.
  • Unequal pupils are associated with rapid transtentorial coning in extradural haemorrhage leading to ipsilateral dilated pupil followed by bilateral fixed dilated pupils.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 443, Pg: 3457

question_text: In mitral stenosis loud S1 becomes soft in all of the following except?
explanation: Marked calcification, associated MR and bradycardia are causes of soft S1 in MS

question_text: A 40-year-old man has had decreased mentation with confusion as well as increasing incoordination and loss of movement in his right arm over the past six weeks. An MRI scan shows 0.5 to 1.5 cm lesions in cerebral hemispheres in white matter and at the grey-white junction that suggest demyelination. A stereotactic biopsy is performed, and immunohistochemical staining of the tissue reveals JC papova virus in oligodendrocytes. Which of the following laboratory test findings is most likely to be associated with these findings?
explanation:
• The findings are those of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), which is a condition that can develop in immunocompromised patients, such as those with AIDS.
  • PML is associated with papova (JC) virus infection.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:202 Pg: 1579

question_text: A homeless male presents with multiple lustreless nails. There is no other skin lesion. What is the most appropriate investigation?
explanation:
The diagnosis of fungal nail infection is usually based on clinical grounds. Nevertheless a useful, rapid and easy way to confirm the diagnosis is by using a Wood's lamp. Yellow to yellow-green fluorescence is characteristic of fine scales taken from active fungal lesions. However, the sensitivity of this procedure is reduced when patients have taken a recent shower. In this patient, waiting for mycology results is inappropriate as he may well not attend again

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 219 Pg 1690,1691

question_text: Where is the defect in multiple sclerosis?
explanation:
Multiple sclerosis is a disorder of the CNS characterized by chronic inflammation, demyelination and scarring.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease of the central nervous system (CNS) characterized by chronic inflammation, demyelination, gliosis (plaques or scarring), and neuronal loss; the course can be relapsing or progressive.

MS plaques typically develop at different times and in different CNS locations (i.e., MS is said to be disseminated in time and space).

Demyelination New MS lesions begin with perivenular cuffing by inflammatory mononuclear cells, predominantly T cells and macrophages, which also infiltrate the surrounding white matter.

At sites of inflammation, the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is disrupted, but unlike in vasculitis, the vessel wall is preserved.

At the leading edge of lesions, large numbers of cytotoxic CD8 cells are found. Involvement of the humoral immune system is also evident; small numbers of B lymphocytes infiltrate the nervous system, myelin-specific autoantibodies are present on degenerating myelin sheaths, and complement is activated.

question_text:
A 47 year old man was referred for assessment of unsteady gait, which has been present for 6 months. He has lost a stone in weight over the several months. An MRI of the brain shows multiple high signal areas. A biopsy was taken of one of the lesions. The report shows perivascular infiltrates of lymphocytes affecting white and gray matter. There was minimal myelin loss. CSF examination shows raised white cell count, and oligoclonal bands were not raised.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The white matter lesions suggest either multiple sclerosis or lymphoma. Infiltration with lymphocytes can be seen in Multiple Sclerosis too. In around 10% of patients with MS, OCB can be absent.

However, the presence of constitutional symptoms makes the possibility of CNS lymphoma more likely.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine. 21st Ed, Ch:90 Pg: 705

question_text:
A 32-year-old man has a painful right eye. On examination, there is decreased visual acuity and a relative afferent pupillary defect of the right eye.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
A painful eye with loss of vision, and also RAPD suggests optic neuritis.

Optic neuritis describes any condition that causes inflammation of the optic nerve; it may be associated with demyelinating diseases, or infectious or inflammatory processes.

It is also known as

  • Optic papillitis(when the head of the optic nerve is involved),
  • Neuro-retinitis(when there is a combined involvement of optic disc and surrounding retina in the macular area) and
  • Retro bulbar neuritis (when the posterior part of the nerve is involved).

Cause

TREATMENT : Steroids are the mainstay of treatment of Optic neuritis. There is no difference between oral and Iv steroids in the outcome of optic neuritis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 223

question_text:
A 38 year old teacher has a right sided headache and blurring of her vision in the right eye. She has previously had an episode of optic neuritis 3 years beforehand, in the right eye. On examination, there was a right afferent pupillary defect and pale optic disc. There was weakness of the facial muscles on the right. Tone and reflexes were brisk on the right with power of 3/5 in the arm and the leg. She was apyrexial. MRI of the brain reveals a 4 cm left temporo-parietal mass, which was incompletely ring enhancing. There were also two small white matter lesions also visible in the frontal area.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The patient gives a history of optic neuritis in the past, now with a second episode of ON as evidenced by the RAPD. She now presents with weakness of the right side of the body and face. The presence of optic neuritis with pyramidal type weakness should prompt us to think about demyelinating diseases like MS, NMO spectral disorders, and MOG antibody associated demyelinating disease. ADEM is also a demyelinating disease but is monophasic and does not present with recurrence.

So in the MRI we are expecting findings of demyelination. The two small white matter lesions in MRI may be demyelinating patches, but how to explain the 4 cm temperoparietal mass ?

 So, there are variants of MS that can present as space occupying lesions with incomplete or concentric ring enhancement, as shown below. It is called the Balo's Concentric sclerosis.

So the presence of mass lesions with incomplete contrast enhancement is also possible in MS.

CNS lymphoma presents with complete ring enhancement and is seen in the context of HIV.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine , 21st ed, Ch:444, Pg: 3474

question_text:
A 35 year old man has difficulty with his vision. On examination he has impaired adduction of the right eye looking left. The left eye has jerky nystagmus.
Which investigation is most likely to yield a diagnosis?
option_c: Paired CSF and serum for oligoclonal bands
explanation:
• The clinical scenario is internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
  • This is most commonly seen in multiple sclerosis. MRI of the brain and CSF are the best diagnostic tests. In this scenario the lesion is in the right medial longitudinal fasciculus.

Internuclear ophthalmoplegia - patient looking to the left

MR imaging of the brain showed multiple abnormal high signals on T2WI involving bilateral deep white matter, corpus callosum, occipital periventricular regions, and periaqueductal regions of the pons and medulla

Diagnostic tools in MS:

MRI

  • Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and spine may show areas of demyelination (lesions or plaques).
  • Gadolinium can be administered intravenously as a contrast agent to highlight active plaques and, by elimination, demonstrate the existence of historical lesions not associated with symptoms at the moment of the evaluation.
  • Central vein signs (CVS) have been proposed as a good indicator of MS in comparison with other conditions causing white lesions.
  • Brain atrophy is seen as an indicator of MS.

Cerebrospinal fluid

  • Testing of cerebrospinal fluid obtained from a lumbar puncture can provide evidence of chronic inflammation in the central nervous system.
  • The cerebrospinal fluid is tested for oligoclonal bands of IgG on electrophoresis, which are inflammation markers found in 75-85% of people with MS.

Evoked potential

Visual- and sensory-evoked potential tests measure brain responses; the nervous system in MS may respond less actively to stimulation of the optic nerve and sensory nerves due to demyelination of such pathways

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch:444, Pg: 3466

question_text: A 33 year old female comes with a 3 month history of multiple neurological symptoms. It started with a blurring of vision on the right eye. She has noted that the visual blurring increases when she takes a hot shower. She also has multiple episodes of electric shock like sensation radiating from her spine down to both lower limbs. On examination, she has afferent pupillary defect in the right eye, with a pale disc. She also has bilateral lower limb spasticity and hyperreflexia, with extensor plantar response. What will be the likely findings in the MRI of the brain and spinal cord in this patient?
option_a: Chronic infarct in the occipital lobe on the left side
option_b: Demyelination of the optic nerve of the right eye with multiple demyelinating patches in the brain and the spinal cord
option_d: Space occupying lesion in the occipital lobe
explanation:
Lets analyze the symptoms of this young female. She has a blurred vision in the right eye with Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect, which is suggestive of optic neuritis. A pale disc suggests optic atrophy secondary to a long standing optic neuritis. Her visual symptoms increase on taking hot shower. This is known as Uhthoff's Symptoms. Also she has electric shock like sensation that radiates down her spine to both lower limbs. This is known as Lhermitte's symptoms. She has UMN signs in the form of spasticity, hyperreflexia and extensor plantar. All these point to the diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis. The likely MRI finding that we will see will be demyelination of the optic nerve and other demyelinating patches, which may or may not be symptomatic, scattered in the brain and the spinal cord.

SYMPTOMS OF MS:

  • Sensory symptoms, girdle like sensation, pain.
  • Cranial nerve symptoms: Optic neuritis, Facial palsy with sparing of taste sensation in anterior 2/3rd of tongue, gaze disturbances like INO, one and a half syndrome, 6th nerve palsy, pendular nystagmus.
  • Motor symptoms: Weakness and spasticity
  • Ancilliary symptoms: which include Paroxysmal symptoms( brief and self limited neurological symptoms caused by hyperventilation or movement, without any loss of sensorium), Lhermitte's symptoms, Uhthoff's Symptoms, Bilateral trigeminal neuralgia, hemifacial spasm, glossopharyngeal neuralgia, facial myokimia, bladder dysfunction, constipation, fatigue, sexual dysfunction.

IMAGING IN MS:

MRI typically shows areas of hyperintensity in T2 and FLAIR images perpendicular to the ventricles, called Dawson's Fingers. There will be transient enhancement of these lesions on contrast appearance, but the enhancement disappears in one month. The lesion persists life long in MS. >90% of the lesions visualized in the MRI are asymptomatic.

Evoked potentials of the visual, auditory, somatosensory or motor pathways may be abnormal in 80-90% of patients.

CSF oligoclonal bands may be seen in> 90% of cases of MS

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 444, Pg: 3462-3467

question_text: A 24 year old man came from South America 5 years ago. Since a year ago, he has had two tonic clonic seizures a week. On examination, he appears well, with no focal neurological deficit. A CT scan shows multiple calcified cystic lesions in the brain. Which diagnosis is likely?
explanation:
• Neurocysticercosis is caused by Taenia solium (pork tape worm).
  • This disease is found in South America and Asia
  • It is typically benign, and most lesions resolve spontaneously within 2-3 months.
  • There may be seizures due to localised inflammation that accompanies their degeneration in the cerebral cortex when calcified cysts occur..
  • An enzyme linked immuno transfer blot (EITB) assay of a patient's serum may confirm the diagnosis.
  • Albendazole is the recommended treatment.


Neurocysticercosis

Here's why the other options are less likely:

A) Neurosarcoid (Neurosarcoidosis):

  • Neurosarcoidosis is a condition where sarcoidosis, an inflammatory disease, affects the nervous system. It can cause various neurological symptoms.
  • However, the presence of multiple calcified cystic lesions in the brain, as described in the case, is not typical of neurosarcoidosis.

C) Multiple sclerosis (MS):

  • Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system.
