explanation:
• The history is consistent with a subarachnoid haemorrhage, caused by rupture of a berry (saccular) aneurysm.
  • Migraine will not cause blood in the Sylvian fissure.
  • Carotid dissection will result in ischemia in the brain rather than bleed.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 429, Pg: 3355

question_text: A 42 year old obese woman presents with gradual onset severe headache and visual blurring. On examination, she has bilateral papilloedema, without any focal deficits or seizures. Which of the Following may help improve the condition?
explanation:
A chronic head ache with papilledema can occur with ICSOL or IIH. Given the presence of obesity and the absence of focal deficits or seizure, the possibility of IIH should be considered.

  • Vitamin A, prednisolone, minocycline and cyclosporin make idiopathic intracranial hypertension (used to be known as benign intracranial hypertension worse.
  • Acetazolamide is used to treat IIH. IIH is likely to be due to high pressure caused by the buildup or poor absorption of cerebrospinal fluid in the subarachnoid space surrounding the brain. The disorder is most common in women between the ages of 20 and 50. Symptoms include headache, nausea, vomiting, and pulsating intracranial noises, closely mimicking symptoms of brain tumors.
  • Acetazolamide may be used in vasogenic edema due to tumors also

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, ch: 307, Pg: 2270

question_text: A 26 year old lady presents with a severe headache, which woke her up from sleep. She is not pregnant and was on no drugs. On examination she was afebrile and alert. On examination of the optic fundus the cup of the optic disc was filled and the medial margins of the disc were blurred. There was no other CNS abnormality, in particular no neck stiffness. A CT scan was as normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• This is the most likely cause, despite not being pregnant or on the OCP. In only 10% of cases is cerebral venous thrombosis due to damage to the vessel wall by infection, tumour or trauma.
  • Commonest causes are inherited disorders of coagulation of which factor V Leiden mutation is found in around 20% of cases. Often there is a combination of causative factors: e.g. protein S deficiency and childbirth, pregnancy and Behcet's disease, OCP and factor V Leiden mutation.
  • A CT is often normal in VST, diagnosis requires MR with Venography
  • A meningioma presents often insidiously with symptoms depending on the location involved; CT may reveal a calcified extradural mass.
  • Benign intracranial hypertension: A typical presentation of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) is that of a female of childbearing age who presents with headaches and is found to have papilledema on fundoscopic examination.
  • MRI findings that suggest, but are not diagnostic for, IIH include empty sella, flattening of the posterior aspect of the globe, distension of the perioptic subarachnoid space (with or without a tortuous optic nerve), and transverse venous sinus stenosis.
  • Migraine presents with a unilateral throbbing headache with photophobia/phonophobia which may be preceded by a visual aura; there are no features of raised intracranial tension.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 427, Pg: 3342

question_text: A 33 year old lady presents with bilateral swelling and discomfort around her face. This caused her pain when she is chewing. It started 2 days ago and she also has mild fever and headache. She mentioned she had been in contact with someone with a similar illness 2 weeks ago. On examination, she has bilateral parotid enlargement which are tender.Which of the following is a likely cause?
explanation:
Fever, parotid swelling and pain during chewing indicates parotitis. Bilateral parotitis is usually due to viral infection by Mumps virus.

There are many causes of parotid swellings. Viruses include mumps, coxsackie A virus, parainfluenzae virus, CMV and varicella zoster virus.

Hypothyroidism can do so, but not hypoparathyroidism.

The incubation period for mumps is usually 18 to 21 days. Mumps is caused by a paramyxovirus, and are spread from person to person by saliva droplets or direct contact with articles that have been contaminated with infected saliva. The parotid glands (the salivary glands between the ear and the jaw) are usually involved.

Unvaccinated children between the ages of 2 and 12 are most commonly infected, but the infection can occur in other age groups. Orchitis (swelling of the testes) occurs in 10-20% of infected males, but sterility only rarely ensues; a viral meningitis occurs in about 5% of those infected.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 207, Pg: 1615-1618

question_text: A patient developed a severe headache after a lumbar puncture performed in the sitting position. Which of the following is not an appropriate management strategy for a post-lumbar puncture headache?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient's symptoms are consistent with a post-dural puncture headache (PDPH).
  • Restricting fluid intake is not recommended for managing PDPH.
  • Post-dural puncture headache results from intracranial hypotension due to cerebrospinal fluid leakage at the puncture site, causing traction on pain-sensitive structures.
  • PDPH is more likely with traumatic needles such as Quincke or Babcock and with lower-gauge needles.

Management of PDPH:

Conservative Measures:

  • Bed rest 8-12 hours
    • Lying in supine position reduces cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage and allows the dural puncture to seal. (Option A ruled out)
  • Analgesics
    • Pain relief with acetaminophen or NSAIDs.
  • Intravenous caffeine
    • Acts as a cerebral vasoconstrictor, reducing headache severity and increasing CSF production. (Option B ruled out)

Definitive Treatment for Persistent Headache: Epidural Blood Patch

  • For headaches unresponsive to conservative therapy, 10-30 mL of the patient's autologous venous blood is injected into the epidural space at the puncture site.
  • This forms a patch over the dural tear, reducing CSF leak or increasing intracranial pressure. (Option D ruled out)

Reference:

Postdural puncture headache

question_text: A 44 year old bank clerk presents with a headache, nausea and ptosis of the left eye with blurred vision. She does not have fatiguability of her eye movements. Examination revealed swelling on the left side of face, proptosis and chemosis of the left eye, left mastoid swelling and left ophthalmoplegia involving cranial nerves. The pupil sizes were equal. A CT of her head is normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• A history of headache and no other obvious cause of ptosis is suggestive of cavernous sinus thrombosis. Third nerve palsy is associated with dilated pupil and Horner's syndrome is associated with miosis. A CT can be normal, and diagnosis is confirmed with MRI.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 441, Pg: 3444

question_text:
A 47-year-old woman presented with a severe sudden onset headache, describing it as the worst headache she could imagine, but denying any head trauma.
On examination of her cranial nervous system she had a partial ptosis of her right eye, which was unable to look up or medially, and her right pupil was dilated. Her only past medical history is polycystic kidney disease.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
option_a: Subarachnoid haemorrhage caused by a ruptured right sided posterior communicating artery aneurysm
option_b: Subarachnoid haemorrhage caused by a ruptured left sided posterior communicating artery aneurysm
option_c: Subarachnoid haemorrhage caused by a ruptured right sided anterior communicating artery aneurysm
option_d: Subarachnoid haemorrhage caused by a ruptured left sided anterior communicating artery aneurysm
explanation:
• Posterior communicating artery aneurysms can compress the third cranial nerve. If the aneurysm ruptures it can cause the classic picture of an ipsilateral painful third nerve palsy, with the eye down and out, ptosis, and pupil dilation.
  • Cerebral aneurysms may be associated with polycystic kidney disease.

Regarding the options:

A is correct. It is the ipsilateral posterior communicating artery aneurysm that is compressing the third nerve.

B is incorrect as posterior communicating artery aneurysms do not cause contralateral compressive symptoms.

C and D are incorrect as anterior communicating artery aneurysms do not compress the third nerve.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 429, Pg: 3354

question_text: A man presents with his father, who collapsed while working outdoors in the hot sun at 42°C in May. On arrival, the patient was unconscious. There were no signs of dehydration, and serum electrolytes were normal. His body temperature measured 106°F. Which of the following findings is least likely in this scenario?
explanation:
Explanation:

This presentation is consistent with heat stroke, defined as a failure of thermoregulation with a core body temperature exceeding 40.5°C (104°F). In severe heat stroke, sweating ceases due to impaired thermoregulation and depleted sweat function. The absence of sweating and the presence of dry, hot skin are hallmark features, unlike other hyperthermic disorders where sweating is usually present.

Explanation of other options:

Nausea (Option A): Commonly occurs in heat exhaustion and heat stroke due to systemic stress.

Hypotension (Option B): Results from vasodilation and dehydration, frequently observed.

Headache (Option D): Prominent neurological symptom in heat stroke.

Key Takeaways:

  • Sweating is absent in classical heat stroke.
  • Heat stroke is a medical emergency with multi-organ dysfunction risk.

question_text:
A 65 year old woman has several episodes of dizziness particularly when she turns her head. 2 months ago, she had an attack of vertigo, without deafness or tinnitus, lasting for a few minutes. Over the last month, she had five further attacks of vertigo, accompanied by moderate headache and a left homonymous hemianopia, lasting for about a quarter of an hour. After the last episode she developed persistent unsteadiness of gait, and was admitted to hospital.
On examination there was normal visual fields. were full. There was rhythmic horizontal nystagmus, slight weakness of the right external rectus muscle without diplopia, and ataxia of gait, provoked by turning. The blood pressure was 160/80 mmHg. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
• Vertebrobasilar (posterior) circulation constitutes the arterial supply to the brain stem, cerebellum, and occipital cortex. Bilateral visual loss, dizziness, speech disturbances, drop attacks and transient global amnesia are features of vertebrobasilar insufficiency. MRI / MRA are good investigations to investigate for vertebral or basilar arterial disease.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3328

question_text: A 60 year old man recently diagnosed with Small cell carcinoma presented to the Emergency department with a history of headache and confusion for one day. On examination he was well; his BP 140/70 other was unremarkable. Laboratory examination showed Serum Urea 8 mmoL/L, Serum creatinine 1 mg/dL, Serum Na 105 mmoL/L, Serum K 4.3 mmol/L. Due to his neurological finding he was started on 3% normal saline, 2nd day his serum Na was 124 mmol/L and he improved. Next day he started to have slurred speech and exaggerated tendon reflexes while his serum Na was 130 mmol/L. T2 weighted MRI of brain was done showed hyperintense shadows in brainstem area, What is most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Patient developed central pontine myelinolysis secondary to rapid correction of serum Na. It was corrected 19 mmol over 24 hours.

Acute hyponatremia presenting with severe neurologic symptoms is life-threatening and should be treated promptly with hypertonic solutions, typically 3% NaCl ([Na+] = 513 mmol/L), because this represents the most reliable method to raise the serum [Na+ ] quickly. A continuous infusion of hypertonic NaCl is generally used in inpatient settings. One of the simplest methods to estimate an initial 3% NaCl infusion rate uses the following relationship:

Patient's weight in kg desired correction rate in mEq L h in ( ) ( ) × = fusion rate of 3% NaCl ( ) in mL h

This may not achieve the desired correction rate, but frequent monitoring of the serum [Na+] will inform the clinician about whether the rate should be increased or decreased, similar to using the measurement of the serum glucose level to guide the infusion rate of insulin drips.

If the correction exceeds 10 to 12 mmol/L in the first 24 hours, the infusion should be stopped and the patient monitored closely. Consideration should be given to administering sufficient water, orally or as intravenous 5% dextrose in water, to avoid a correction of more than 12 mmol/L/day. The maximum correction limit should be reduced to 8 mmol/L over the first 24 hours in patients with risk factors for ODS.

Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 344

question_text: A 20 year old male presents with fever, severe headache, vomiting and photophobia. On examination, neck rigidity and Brudzinski's sign is positive. Brain CT shows hydrocephalus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

In a patient presenting with sudden onset of severe headache, accompanied by vomiting, neck rigidity, photophobia, and a positive Brudzinski's sign, the most likely diagnosis-especially in the presence of hydrocephalus on CT without visible hemorrhage-is subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

About Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH):

Subarachnoid hemorrhage refers to bleeding into the subarachnoid space, the area between the pia mater and arachnoid membrane surrounding the brain.

This condition most commonly results from the rupture of a cerebral aneurysm or, less frequently, an arteriovenous malformation (AVM). The majority of ruptured aneurysms are found at the circle of Willis.

Clinical Features:

  • The hallmark symptom is a sudden, severe headache, often described as a "thunderclap headache" - the worst headache the patient has ever experienced.
  • Other symptoms may include:
    • Vomiting
    • Loss of consciousness
    • Seizures
    • Neck stiffness and photophobia, which may appear a few hours after the initial bleed due to meningeal irritation.

Diagnostic Approach:

  • The initial investigation of choice is a non-contrast CT scan of the head, especially if performed within 12 hours of symptom onset. This can detect hyperdense (bright) areas in the CSF spaces, indicating the presence of blood.
  • If the CT scan is inconclusive but clinical suspicion remains high, a lumbar puncture is indicated - ideally performed after 12 hours. This allows enough time for red blood cells in the CSF to break down, enabling the detection of xanthochromia (bilirubin), which confirms SAH.

Explanations for other Options:

Normal pressure hydrocephalus (Option A): Motor weakness is a common feature in MS, especially as the disease progresses. However, it is less likely to be the initial symptom compared to sensory disturbances. When present, motor symptoms often involve spasticity, stiffness, or weakness in the legs or arms.

Bacterial meningitis (Option B): Ataxia, or lack of coordination, may occur in MS due to cerebellar involvement. While it is a recognized manifestation, it is not typically the first symptom. It usually appears later in the disease course or during relapses affecting the cerebellum or its connections

Viral encephalitis (Option C): Seizures are relatively rare in MS, occurring in only a small percentage of patients. Although cortical lesions in MS can potentially lead to seizures, they are not a common presenting symptom and are far less frequent than sensory or motor signs.

question_text: A male patient presented to the emergency room with seizures. He has a history of fever, headache, and confusion. An MRI brain was done, and it showed inflammation involving the bitemporal lobes. What is the most likely aetiology for this presentation?
explanation:
Explanation:

HSV encephalitis classically involves the bitemporal lobes and presents with fever, seizures, confusion, and behavioural changes.

Explanation of other options:

Cytomegalovirus (Option A): Typically seen in immunocompromised individuals; MRI shows periventricular calcifications and ventricular enlargement, not bitemporal lobe involvement.

Toxoplasma gondii (Option B): Common in immunocompromised hosts; presents with multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia or corticomedullary junction, not the temporal lobes.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Option D): TB meningitis or encephalitis presents with diffuse cortical involvement and basal exudates; bitemporal localisation is not characteristic.

Reference:

Radiopaedia: Tuberculous Encephalopathy

question_text: What is the preferred medication for the presented case? A male patient, 54 years old, was brought to the emergency room with symptoms of fever, headache, and a focal seizure. The EEG results indicate the presence of spikes in the temporal lobe. Analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample reveals the presence of 50 cells, with 90% lymphocytes and 10% neutrophils.
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation of fever, headache, focal seizures, temporal lobe spikes on EEG, and a lymphocytic-predominant CSF pleocytosis is highly suggestive of Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) encephalitis. Intravenous Acyclovir is the empiric and first-line treatment of choice and must be initiated immediately to reduce mortality and morbidity.

Diagnosis of HSV encephalitis involves CSF analysis showing lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, and mildly elevated protein. CSF PCR for HSV is the gold standard, with 96% sensitivity and 99% specificity. MRI is the preferred imaging modality, detecting early T2 and diffusion-weighted lesions in the orbitofrontal and temporal lobes. EEG may demonstrate periodic slow-wave activity in the temporal regions.

Explanation of other options:
Valacyclovir (Option A): An oral prodrug of acyclovir, used for outpatient management of herpes zoster and genital herpes, but not for the initial, critical treatment of HSV encephalitis.

Ganciclovir (Option C): First-line treatment for Cytomegalovirus (CMV) CNS infections, not HSV.

Foscarnet (Option D): It is used for CMV infections resistant to ganciclovir or for acyclovir-resistant HSV strains, which are rare.

Key Takeaways:

  • HSV encephalitis is a neurologic emergency characterized by temporal lobe involvement.
  • Empirical intravenous acyclovir should be started immediately upon suspicion, before confirmatory PCR results.

question_text:
A 25 year old man has recently complains of fever, rigors and headache. On examination he had a temperature of 38°C, a blood pressure of 120/70 mmHg, a pulse of 110 bpm. His abdomen was tender in the right upper quadrant.Investigations showed:
Hb 10.5 g/dL
WBC 13500/μL
Neutrophils 11200/μl
Platelets 360000/μLBlood film No malaria parasites seen
Alk Phos 420 U/L
AST 60 U/L
CRP 110 mg/L
Stool culture Negative
Chest x-ray: Small right pleural effusion
Which of the following investigations would be of diagnostic value?
explanation:
The ultrasound would determine if there is a pyogenic liver abscess or amoebic liver abscess. The clinical history with associated pleural effusion suggests that an abscess needs to be excluded (and drained if necessary).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 132, Pg: 1059

question_text:
A 42 year old man presents to the emergency department complaining of severe lower back pain following carpentry work. The pain radiates to his left buttock and thigh. On examination, he was able to straight leg raise to 45 degrees only on the left side. The sciatic stretch test is positive. He has difficulty plantar flexing his left ankle and has abnormal sensation on the plantar aspect of the foot.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
• Ankle dorsiflexion is generally supplied by L4/L5 and plantar flexion supplied by S1/S2.this case is likely to be due to sciatic nerve palsy.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

question_text: A 50 year old male presents with unsteadiness of gait of one year duration. On examination, he has sensory loss in the stocking and glove pattern, with absent ankle jerk and pyramidal signs and sensory ataxia. Which of the following statements is false?
option_a: Cobalamine deficiency may be a cause of the above findings.
option_b: Dietary deficiency of copper may also lead to similar clinical features.
option_c: Haematological abnormalities if present points to the diagnosis of Vitamin B12 deficiency.
option_d: Excess Zinc is an known factor that reduced copper absorption.
explanation:
Symmetric sensory loss with distal areflexia and UMN signs is seen in Vitamin B12 deficiency, Copper deficiency and Vitamin E deficiency. It is also seen in adrenomyelkoneuronopathy. So all these can cause symptoms similar to subacute combined degeneration.

Haematological abnormalities are known to occur not only  in B12 deficiency, but also Copper deficiency and Vitamin E deficiency.

In Vitamin B12 deficiency, there will be macrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils and pancytopenia.

In copper deficiency, there will be microcytic anemia, neutropenia and occasionally pancytopenia.

In Vitamin E deficiency, there will be acanthocytosis.

Excess zinc upregulates intestinal metalothionine and decreases copper absorption.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Intrenal medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3496, 3497

question_text: A 40-year-old male presents with chronic back pain that has progressively worsened over the past few months. He also reports fever, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss. On examination, there is localized tenderness over the lower thoracic and lumbar spine. MRI spine is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Characterized by chronic back pain, fever, night sweats, and weight loss. MRI often shows involvement of two or more adjacent vertebral bodies, typically affecting the lower thoracic and upper lumbar spine in adults.
  • A hallmark feature is the destruction of the intervertebral disc space and adjacent vertebrae with potential abscess formation.
  • The patient's symptoms of systemic infection (fever, night sweats, weight loss) combined with localized spinal tenderness and the typical MRI findings strongly suggest Pott's spine.

Explanation of other options:

Osteoporotic Vertebral Fracture (Option B): Common in older adults or those with osteoporosis, presenting typically as a sudden onset of back pain after minimal trauma or even no apparent cause.

The patient's systemic symptoms like fever and weight loss are not typical of osteoporotic fractures.

Metastatic Spinal Tumor (Option C): Can cause back pain and may involve vertebral bodies, but is more likely to cause widespread or multifocal pain and neurological deficits. Lacks specific systemic symptoms such as fever and night sweats that are associated with an infection like tuberculosis.

Ankylosing Spondylitis (Option D): A chronic inflammatory disease primarily affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints, leading to pain and progressive spinal stiffness. Typically lacks systemic symptoms like fever and weight loss unless there is a concurrent secondary inflammation or infection.

Key Takeaways:

Pott's disease (spinal TB) should be suspected in patients with chronic back pain, systemic symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), and MRI findings of vertebral destruction with possible abscess formation. Early diagnosis and anti-tubercular treatment are essential to prevent complications such as neurological deficits and spinal deformity.

question_text: Sympathetic segments? supply to the heart arises from which of the following spinal
explanation: Sympathetic nerve cells supplying the heart are located in the intermediolateral horn of spinal segments T1 to T5. Sympathetic supply is cardio-acceleratory, and on stimulation, they increase the heart rate, and also dilate coronary arteries. Both parasympathetic and sympathetic nerves form the superficial and deep cardiac plexuses, the branches of which run along the coronary arteries to reach the myocardium.

question_text:
A 74-year-old man presented with intermittent chest pain at rest.
 Which one of the following would most strongly suggest that the pain was due to myocardial ischaemia?
option_c: Radiation of pain to the jaw
option_d: Relief of pain by sublingual nitrate
explanation:
The most specific feature of the given options which suggests that the pain is myocardial ischaemia, is the radiation to the jaw, which is relatively specific for pain of myocardial ischaemia.

Nerve convergence:

  • The nerves from the heart and the jaw converge at a similar point in the spinal cord, allowing pain signals from the heart to be perceived as jaw pain.
  • Nitrates may relieve the pain of oesophageal spasm, as well as that of myocardial ischaemia. Associated dyspnoea may be due to anxiety.
  • Coexistent claudication suggests the presence of peripheral vascular disease.
  • A past history of cigarette smoking is a risk factor for the development of cardiovascular disease.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:267 pg:1853

question_text: What is the Most common site of spinal TB in adults?
explanation:
• Weight-bearing joints (the spine in 40% of cases, the hips in 13%, and the knees in 10%) are most commonly affected in skeletal TB
  • The upper thoracic spine is the most common site of spinal TB in children
  • The lower thoracic and upper lumbar vertebrae are usually affected in adults

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 178, Pg: 1365

question_text: What is the Most common site of spinal TB in children?
explanation:
While the upper thoracic spine is the most common site of spinal TB in children, the lower thoracic and upper lumbar vertebrae are usually affected in adults

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 178, Pg: 1365

question_text: A 23-year-old male patient came with complaints of back stiffness, early morning stiffness for 30 min for 2 years. He now complains of bilateral heel pain. His eyes were always red looking. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
We have a young male with inflammatory back ache, enthesitis(bilateral heel pain) and ocular manifestation suggesting anterior uveitis, which points to ankylosing spondylitis.

Mechanical low back ache does not cause morning stiffness.

Disc prolapse presents with neurological symptoms. So these are ruled out.

Spinal TB is unlikely as the duration is prolonged and there are no constitutional symptoms mentioned.

question_text: A person experiences slight imbalance while trying to stand after getting off a roller coaster. Which neural tract is primarily responsible for maintaining balance in this situation?
explanation:
Explanation:

The vestibulospinal tract plays a crucial role in maintaining balance and posture. This neural pathway originates in the vestibular nuclei, which are located in the brainstem and are part of the vestibular system, crucial for processing sensory information related to motion, equilibrium, and spatial orientation. The vestibulospinal tract influences motor neurons that control the muscles of the limbs and trunk, enabling quick and reflexive adjustments to maintain balance and posture, particularly during unexpected movements.

When a person experiences an imbalance, especially after an activity like riding a roller coaster that significantly stimulates the vestibular system, the vestibulospinal tract is vital in helping to stabilize and orient the body correctly.

Vestibulospinal tract:

  • Receives inputs from the vestibular apparatus which detects changes in the position of the head relative to gravity and acceleration.
  • Sends outputs to spinal motor neurons that innervate muscles, particularly extensor muscles, which are activated to maintain posture and balance.

This neural pathway's activation is crucial when sudden adjustments are needed, such as after dismounting from a roller coaster, making option C the correct and relevant choice.

Explanation of other options:

Corticospinal tract (Option A): Primarily involved in voluntary motor control.

Rubrospinal tract (Option B): Helps with motor input, largely redundant in humans, and plays a role in the control of hand movements.

Vestibulocochlear tract (Option D): Incorrect terminology but closely related to the vestibulocochlear nerve, which is involved in hearing and balance; does not directly influence motor control for balance maintenance.

Key Takeaways:

The vestibulospinal tract is responsible for maintaining posture and balance by transmitting signals from the vestibular system to spinal motor neurons, ensuring quick adjustments to unexpected movements, such as after riding a roller coaster.

question_text: A 59-year-old man was previously diagnosed with pernicious anemia. He was non-compliant with medication for several years. He now has unsteadiness and difficulty walking. Lesion in which of the following is likely to be present?
explanation:
This patient has a long history of pernicious anemia and now presents with neurological symptoms. In pernicious anemia, antibodies against intrinsic factor are produced that lead to impaired absorption of vitamin B12. The diagnosis is Subacute Combined Degeneration (SACD) of the spinal cord due to vitamin B12 deficiency.

Signs and symptoms of SACD -

  • The onset is gradual and uniform.
  • The posterior columns and corticospinal tracts are specifically damaged.
  • Patient presents with subacute paresthesias in the hands and feet, loss of vibration and position sensation, and a progressive spastic and ataxic weakness.
  • A positive Babinski sign may be seen.
  • Loss of reflexes due to an associated peripheral neuropathy.

Treatment - Replacement therapy, beginning with 1000 μg of intramuscular vitamin B12 daily for 5 days and then continued as a once monthly maintenance dose; oral maintenance is also reasonable, except in cases of pernicious anemia.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page Number-3496.

question_text: The image was given of a clinician performing an ankle jerk. It is exaggerated in which type of lesion?
explanation:
Lower motor neurons are those whose axons terminate on skeletal muscles. Damage to these neurons is associated with flaccid paralysis, muscular atrophy, fasciculations (visible muscle twitches that appear as flickers under the skin), hypotonia (decreased muscle tone), and hyporeflexia or areflexia.

The development of cerebellar ataxia. Upper motor neurons typically refer to corticospinal tract neurons that innervate spinal motor neurons, but they can also include brainstem neurons that control spinal motor neurons. Damage to these neurons initially causes muscles to become weak and flaccid but eventually leads to spasticity, hypertonia (increased resistance to passive movement), hyperactive stretch reflexes, and abnormal plantar extensor reflex (positive Babinski sign).

question_text: A patient presents with tingling sensations in the hands and feet, generalized weakness, easy fatigability, pallor, and ataxia. Deficiency of which vitamin is responsible for these findings?
explanation:
Explanation:

The constellation of symptoms described - paresthesias in the extremities, generalized weakness, fatigue, pallor, and ataxia - are classical for Vitamin B12 deficiency. Cobalamin plays a critical role in neurological health and red blood cell production. Its deficiency results in megaloblastic (pernicious) anemia and neurological complications like subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, producing ataxia and peripheral neuropathy. These features highlight its essential role in maintaining the myelin sheath.

Explanation of other options:

Vitamin B1 (Option A): Deficiency leads to beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, but does not present with combined anemia and neuropathy as in this case.

Vitamin B2 (Option C): Deficiency manifests as ariboflavinosis, causing glossitis and cheilitis, without significant neurological deficits.

Vitamin B3 (Option D): Deficiency causes pellagra with the 3D's (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia), unrelated to the neurological and hematological findings here.

Key Takeaways:

Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia with neurological manifestations.

Neuropathy and ataxia point strongly toward subacute combined degeneration due to B12 deficiency.

References: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9710417/

question_text:
A 38 year old alcoholic presents with unsteadiness whilst walking. On examination he has increased tone and brisk reflexes in the right leg. Proprioception is abnormal in the right leg. There is loss of vibration sense in the right leg. There is decrease in pain and temperature sensation in the left leg.
Which one of the following conditions is most likely to be responsible for his weakness?
explanation:
• Brown Sequard syndrome which describes hemisection of the spinal cord, causes ipsilateral UMN signs and proprioception loss (corticospinal tract and dorsal column decussate at the medulla), and contralateral sensory loss in pain and temprature (the spinothalamic tracts decussate at the same level). The rest of the conditions (syringomyelia, subacute degeneration of cord, Friedrich's ataxia) can cause cerebellar signs or patchy sensory loss but should be bilateral.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 442, Pg: 3446

question_text:
A 44 year old woman has sensory loss and wasting of the small hand muscles.One examination, she also has a right sided Horner's syndrome. Her arms demonstrate thickening of the subcutaneous tissues. There is also evidence of Charcot's joints on the wrists.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
• Syringomyelia is chronic disorder characterised by the presence of glial-lined cavities situated in the central part of the spinal cord.
  • Recognised causes include Chiari type I malformation, central cord tumours, basal arachnoiditis and trauma.
  • There may be sensory loss, wasting of the small hand muscles, uni- or bilateral Horner's syndrome, abnormalities of sweating, thickening of subcutaneous tissues, atrophy and decalcification of bones, development of Charcot's joints and Chiari I malformation (due to arachnoiditis).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 442, Pg: 3453

question_text:
A 71 year old man has a 2 month history of progressive weakness in his legs. He has weakness in the hip and knee distribution. Knee and ankle reflexes are brisk. Plantars are upgoing bilaterally. He has sensory loss from legs upwards towards the T5 level.
Which one of the Following is a likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• A meningioma involving high in the spinal cord (thoracic region) can cause a T5 level. The rest are all causes of spastic paraparesis but are unlikely to cause a sensory level on clinical examination.
  • Friedrichs ataxia presents with prominent cerebellar signs along with upper motor neuron features due to degeneration of cerebellum, spinocerebellar and corticospinal tracts
  • Subacute combined degeneration is a neurological complication of B12 deficiency which has an absent ankle reflex due to a concomitant neuropathy
  • Hereditary (familial) spastic paraparesis is a group of rare hereditary disorders that cause gradual weakness with muscle spasms (spastic weakness) in the legs. It occurs due to motor neuron dysfunction and will not cause a sensory level as seen in this case.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 442, Pg: 3447

question_text: A 48-year-old man has drunk six units of alcohol a day for most of his adult life. He has worsening symptoms of difficulty walking, headaches and urinary incontinence for the past ten months.Of the following which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• There is no suggestion of memory loss so normal pressure hydrocephalus and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome are less likely.
  • Encephalopathy is more likely to be associated with symptoms of drowsiness.
  • Although meningovascular syphilis can present in many different forms it is rather rare.
  • Syringomyelia is associated with headaches, motor and bladder symptoms and is the likely diagnosis. There is syrinx (fluid-filled cavitation) in the central spinal cord, usually cervical. This can elongate and enlarge, causing compression of the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts and anterior horn cells. Syringobulbia describes the situation when the syrinx extends into the brainstem. The commonest cause is impaired cerebrospinal fluid circulation, usually due to a Chiari malformation (also associated with arachnoiditis, meningeal carcinomatosis, space-occupying lesions or idiopathic). It is more common in men than women, and usually presents in the 20s and 30s although it can present later in life.
  • Sensory features are pain and temperature loss, classically in a shawl-like distribution and dysaesthesia. Light touch, vibration and position sense are affected later. Motor signs start as muscle wasting and weakness that begins in the hands, and progresses to affect the forearms and shoulders. Tendon reflexes are lost and there may be respiratory muscle involvement. Bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction can develop, as can Horner's syndrome. Extension of the syrinx into the lumbar region can involve the legs.
  • Lumbar puncture should be avoided due to the risk of herniation. CT and MRI can be used to delineate the extent. Management involves physiotherapy, and neurosurgery to halt progression. Prognosis is variable, but early surgical involvement is beneficial.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 442, Pg: 3453

question_text: A 67-year-old woman presents with severe back pain and urinary retention with overflow. She says that her lower back has been aching for the past six weeks, but the pain has become significantly worse over the past 48 hours. There is a medical history of hypertension, but nothing else of note. Her BP is 142/82 mmHg, pulse is 73/min, regular. She is unable to get off the couch due to distal lower limb weakness. Tone is increased bilaterally and her reflexes are increased. As you chat to her you notice fasciculation. There is perianal loss of sensation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Conus medullaris syndrome presents with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs. These include bilateral distal weakness with increased tone and hyper-reflexia, fasciculation. Sensory loss is most marked in the perianal region. It is much rarer than cauda equina syndrome.
  • Spinal cord infarction related to anterior spinal artery disease presents most frequently with sudden onset pain and loss of power and sensation beginning in the thoracic region. The symptoms seen here have slowly built up over a few weeks and affect a more distal spinal cord distribution.
  • Sacroiliitis would not be associated with neurological deficit.
  • Cauda equina syndrome is associated with flaccid
  • Conus Medullaris Syndrome Cauda Equina Syndrome

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3500

question_text: At which level the lesion is located if all Extraocular muscles are paralyzed?
explanation:
Explanation:

A lesion affecting both the midbrain and pons would damage the nuclei of cranial nerves III (oculomotor), IV (trochlear), and VI (abducens), which collectively innervate all the extraocular muscles. This would result in complete paralysis of eye movement. Such an extensive lesion is typically seen in severe brainstem pathology.

Explanation of other options:

Frontal eye field (Option A): A lesion here would impair voluntary conjugate eye movements (saccades) but would not paralyze individual extraocular muscles.

Cerebral surface (Option B): A diffuse cortical lesion would not cause isolated, complete ophthalmoplegia.

Spinal cord (Option D): The spinal cord does not contain the cranial nerve nuclei responsible for eye movement.

Key Takeaways:

  • The brainstem (midbrain and pons) houses the nuclei for CN III, IV, and VI.
  • Complete external ophthalmoplegia localizes to the brainstem.

question_text:
LMN (Lower Motor Neuron) lesions are associated with:
1. Decrease in muscle tone
2. Spastic paralysis
3. Babinski positive
4. Fasciculations
explanation:
Explanation:

Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) lesions result from damage to the motor neurons in the anterior horn of the spinal cord or cranial nerve nuclei, leading to the following hallmark features.

  • Decreased muscle tone (hypotonia) (Statement 1)
  • Fasciculations (Statement 4)
  • Muscle atrophy
  • Absent Babinski reflex
  • Absent or reduced reflexes (hyporeflexia)
  • Flaccid paralysis

UMN vs LMN lesion


Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537305/

https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/lower-motor-neuron-lesion

question_text: Which sign is being elicited?
explanation:
The plantar reflex is elicited by stroking, with a noxious stimulus such as a tongue blade, the lateral surface of the sole of the foot beginning near the heel and moving across the ball of the foot to the great toe.

The normal reflex consists of plantar flexion of the toes. With upper motor neuron lesions above the S1 level of the spinal cord, a paradoxical extension of the toe is observed, associated with fanning and extension of the other toes (termed an extensor plantar response, or Babinski sign).

However, despite its popularity, the reliability and validity of the Babinski sign for identifying upper motor neuron weakness is limited, it is far more useful to rely on tests of tone, strength, stretch reflexes, and coordination.

question_text:
A 54-year-old man presents with a six day history of sharp shooting pain radiating from his back to the lateral aspect of his leg. The pain is associated with pins and needles.
On examination, he has sensory loss on the lateral aspect of leg, dorsum of foot, and there is a partial foot drop.
Which lumbar spine nerve root is affected?
explanation:
The L5 nerve root supplies sensation to the lateral aspect of leg and dorsum of foot (except for the lateral border which is supplied by S1). In addition, it supplies hip extensors, knee flexors (with S1), ankle dorsiflexors (with L4), and toe dorsiflexors.

Root-Dermatome distribution-Myotome distribution-Tendon reflex

L1Skin above, and below the inguinal ligament

L2Upper anterior, and medial thigh Psoas hip abductors

L3Mid anterior, and medial thigh Psoas quadriceps Patella (L3-4)

L4Medial aspect of leg, front of knee, and lower lateral thigh Tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis Patella (L3 - 4)

L5Lateral aspect of leg and dorsum of foot (except for the lateral border which is supplied by S1)Extensor halluces, peroneal, gluteus medius, dorsiflexors, hamstrings Plantar (L5, S1-2)

S1Posterior lateral thigh and calf Peroneal, plantar flexors Ankle (S1-2)

S3 - 5Medial buttock and perianal skin in a concentric manner with S3 most lateral, and s5 closest to the anus Bladder, rectum Ankle (S1-2)



Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

question_text: Most specific test of carpal tunnel syndrome?
explanation:
The tests mentioned here are used at the bedside for diagnosing median nerve compression at the carpal tunnel.

Phalen's test is prolonged full flexion of digits reproducing the symptom of carpal tunnel.

Tinel's test is percussion over the carpal tunnel.

Durkan's test is otherwise called the carpal compression test, where direct compression over the carpal tunnel reproduces the symptoms.It is the most specific and sensitive test.

question_text: All are true about Weber syndrome except?
explanation:
Weber syndrome is characterized by damage to the cerebral peduncle. This leads to damage to corticospinal pathway and oculomotor nerve. Hence the patient will develop ipsilateral third nerve palsy and contralateral hemiplegia.

The blood vessels compromised are paramedian branches of upper basilar and proximal posterior cerebral arteries

Dorsal midbrain syndrome is Parinaud syndrome/ Supranuclear vertical gaze disorder caused by damage to posterior commissure. It is characterized by:

  • Loss of up-gaze
  • Sun setting sign
  • Convergence retraction nystagmus
  • Lid retraction
  • Skew deviation
  • Pseudo-abducens palsy
  • Light near dissociation of pupils


Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition, chapter 426 page number. 3333

question_text: A patient presents with weakness of the right upper and lower limbs, along with left-sided facial nerve palsy and horizontal gaze palsy to the left side. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Foville syndrome results from a pontine lesion affecting the abducens nucleus, facial nerve, and corticospinal tract, producing ipsilateral facial and gaze palsy with contralateral hemiparesis.

  • The clinical presentation of right-sided hemiparesis (upper and lower limbs), along with left-sided cranial nerve VII palsy and horizontal gaze palsy to the left, is characteristic of Foville syndrome.
  • This syndrome arises from a lesion in the dorsal pons, typically involving the abducens nucleus (CN VI), facial nerve fascicles (CN VII), paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF), and corticospinal tract.
  • Key findings in Foville syndrome include:
    • Ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy (due to abducens nucleus or PPRF involvement)
    • Ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial palsy
    • Contralateral hemiparesis from corticospinal tract involvement
  • These findings distinguish Foville from other pontine syndromes that may share overlapping features but lack conjugate gaze deficits.

Brainstem stroke syndromes

  • Foville Syndrome: Ipsilateral CN VI palsy + VII palsy + contralateral hemiparesis + Conjugate gaze paralysis towards the side of brainstem lesion
  • Weber Syndrome: Ipsilateral CN III palsy (ptosis, pupillary dilation) + contralateral hemiparesis (corticospinal tract).
  • Millard-Gubler Syndrome: Ipsilateral CN VI and VII palsy + contralateral hemiparesis (No gaze paralysis - differentiates it from Foville syndrome) (Option A ruled out)
  • Benedikt Syndrome: Ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral ataxia and tremor (red nucleus involvement). (Option B ruled out)
  • Wallenberg Syndrome: Ipsilateral Horner syndrome, ataxia, dysphagia, and hoarseness + contralateral loss of pain/temperature.
  • Locked-In Syndrome: Quadriplegia and anarthria with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements. (Option D ruled out)
  • Raymond Syndrome: Ipsilateral CN VI palsy + contralateral hemiparesis.
  • Dejerine Syndrome: Ipsilateral CN XII palsy + contralateral hemiparesis and impaired proprioception/vibration.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560896/

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK544268/#

question_text: A 44 year old man has severe episodes of dizziness with associated vomiting and pain in the right ear. This occurs once or twice a week. During these attacks he feels the surrounding environment spinning around. He also mentions a high pitched sound frequently being present. On examination, during an attack, he has right horizontal nystagmus. Audiological testing reveals right-sided sensorineural deafness. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
• Meniere's disease is caused by distension of the endolymphatic compartment of the inner ear. The symptoms of Meniere's disease include vertigo, hearing loss and tinnitus. The dizziness is described as a spinning or whirling feeling and may cause problems with balance. Some people feel nauseated and vomit during an attack. Tinnitus refers to a ringing or roaring sound in the ear. Others may notice some hearing loss, especially with sounds that have a low frequency.
  • Horizontal nystagmus is more commonly seen on examination, but vertical nystagmus may also occur.
  • Option A: Vestibular neuritis presents with acute onset of vertigo with nausea, vomiting, and gait impairment.
  • Option C: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) presents with recurrent episodes of vertigo lasting one minute or less that are provoked by specific types of head movements. BPPV does not cause prolonged or sustained vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus, or neurologic deficits; these suggest an alternative diagnosis
  • Option D: The most common clinical manifestations of vestibular schwannomas are unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, often in association with tinnitus

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 22, Pg: 160

question_text:
A 64 year old man has symptoms of lethargy and vomiting. He drinks 10 pints of  beer a day. He was started on an intravenous glucose infusion and chlordiazepoxide. For a  day, he symptomatically improved. However, the next day, he became confused and started vomiting several times. He also had diplopia and was unable to stand.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a case of Wernicke's encephalopathy. It is a neurological disorder of acute onset caused by a thiamine (B1) deficiency.

People who are at risk for acute thiamine deficiency are:

Alcoholism, chronic diuretic use, bariatric surgery, hyperemesis, thiaminases in food

Symptoms include:

  • Ocular abnormalities (horizontal nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia)
  • Ataxia
  • Confusion.

The episode may be precipitated by intravenous dextrose administration which exhausts vitamin B reserves, especially in alcoholics and malnourished.Supplementation with vitamin B should be done in all alcoholic patients before dextrose administration.

Treatment is 200mg thiamine 3 times daily until there is no further improvement, followed by oral thiamine till complete recovery.

Cardiovascular and ophthalmoplegia recovers in 24 hours. Psychosis may be permanent or persist for months.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch:333, Pg: 2526

question_text:
An 80 year old lady is admitted complaining of acute onset weakness in both legs and low back pain for the previous 4 weeks. She has lost 5 kg of weight recently, and has a Hb of 8.5 g/dl. Her cranial nerves and upper limbs were normal but she has reduced power in both lower limbs of 3/5. She has a sensory level at T12 and plantar reflexes are upgoing. Rectal tone was normal.
Which is the best next investigation?
explanation:
• This patient is likely to have cord compression from a metastases to the spine.
  • Urgent MRI scan is required to confirm the diagnosis and a referral for either surgery or radiotherapy can then be made.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 442, Pg: 3447

question_text:
A 27-year-old female presents with drooping of the left side of her face and an inability to close her left eye. She had a viral illness in the preceding week. There is no past medical history.On examination, there is a left VIIth nerve palsy. The remaining cranial nerves are normal. Power, tone and reflexes are normal in the limbs.
What is the best course of treatment?
explanation:
• This is the classical history of a post-viral Bell's palsy.
  • There is some evidence to support a short course of steroids in the acute stages of the illness (NEJM 2007;357:1598-1607). This study suggests improved recovery of facial function with early treatment. No benefit was seen in acyclovir added to prednisolone in this study.
  • Oral valaciclovir has been evaluated with an RCT but consensus supports steroids (with some clinicians continuing to support the concomitant use of acyclovir).
  • You need to be confident that there are no features of Guillain-Barré (test reflexes), or brain stem vascular disease or space occupying lesion. The neurological examination of the cranial nerves thus needs to be completed with care.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 441, Pg: 3441

question_text: A patient with loss of the right half of the visual field loss on both sides. What would the probable diagnosis be?
explanation:
Lesion of the optic tract and beyond will lead to contralateral homonymous hemianopia Damage to the optic radiations in the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) produces a superior quadrantic homonymous hemianopia (lesion marked as J).

  • Lesions of the optic nerve will result in total blindness in the ipsilateral eye.
  • Lesion of the optic chiasm will lead to bitemporal hemianopia.
  • Injury to the optic radiations in the parietal lobe results in an inferior quadrantic homonymous hemianopia (K).
  • Lesions of the primary visual cortex give rise to dense, congruous hemianopic field defects. Occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery supplying the occipital lobe is a common cause of total homonymous hemianopia. Some patients have macular sparing, because the central field representation at the tip of the occipital lobe is supplied by collaterals from the middle cerebral artery (L).
  • Destruction of both occipital lobes produces cortical blindness. This condition can be distinguished from bilateral prechiasmal visual loss by noting that the pupil responses and optic fundi remain normal.

question_text:
A 24-year-old anorexic is admitted for parenteral nutrition and has a tunneled line inserted. A few days after parenteral feeding has begun you are asked to see her as she has begun complaining of diplopia, lethargy and muscle weakness. She also has paraesthesia affecting her hands and feet. Examination confirms global muscle weakness and peripheral sensory loss.
Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities is the most likely to have occurred?
explanation:
This patient is suffering from refeeding syndrome, where patients complain of a range of symptoms which can include

  • Muscle weakness
  • Peripheral neuropathy
  • Neurological impairment
  • Myocardial depression.

It is characterized by a fall in phosphate, magnesium, potassium and fluid accumulation, which in combination can lead to cardiac failure.

Patients at risk from re-feeding include those who are fed after a prolonged period of starvation, such as those with anorexia, and those with chronic alcoholism.

Reference: Harrison;s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 335, Pg: 2546

question_text: The correct description of Bruns garland syndrome is:
explanation:
• Bruns garland syndrome is also known as diabetic amyotrophy/lumbosacral radiculoplexopathy
  • Asymmetrical, painful weakness involving quadriceps, iliopsoas and adductors of thigh; spares the hamstring muscles
  • Most common form of Diabetic neuropathy is the distal symmetric sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy
  • Most common cranial nerve involvement in Diabetes mellitus is Oculomotor nerve followed by abducens and facial nerves.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 3124

question_text: A 44 year old lady has numbness in the right little finger and aspect of the palm shown in the picture. The small muscles of the hand are weak. Which nerve is affected?
explanation:
• The ulnar nerve innervates the third and fourth lumbricals, the interossei and adductor pollicis. Sensation is supplied to the fifth finger and the ulnar part of the fourth finger.


Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

question_text: A 47 year old woman complains of diplopia. On examination, she has double vision on looking to the left only. There is failure of adduction in the right eye, and nystagmus in the left eye whilst looking to the left. Which one of the following is likely?
explanation:
Diplopia on eye abduction is likely to be due to either a lateral rectus palsy or medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) defect. This scenario fits one of internuclear ophthalmoplegia (which is due to an MLF defect). In this scenario it is a right sided INO same side as the eye which fails to adduct.



Internuclear ophthalmoplegia

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 321

question_text: A 58 year old man has a right wrist drop. On examination he has an absent triceps jerk on the right as well as an area of sensory loss over the dorsum of the middle finger on the right hand. Where is the lesion?
explanation:
• Radial nerve dysfunction involves impaired movement or sensation of the back of the arm (triceps), the forearm, or the hand caused by damage to the radial nerve. There is weakness of wrist and elbow extension, and absent triceps jerk.

Wrist Drop


Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

question_text: A 24 year old tennis player finds that he is unable to extend his right wrist. On examination, there is weakness of the extensors of the wrist and digits. Which of the following structures are damaged?
option_d: Medial cord of the brachial plexus
explanation:
• The radial nerve may be damaged anywhere in its course. It is most commonly affected in the upper arm where it winds round the humerus and in the extensor muscle compartment of the forearm affecting the posterior interosseous branch.
  • Radial nerve palsy causes weakness of the wrist and elbow extension, and weakness of forearm supination. Sensory loss on the dorsum of hand and forearm may also be present.


Radial Nerve Palsy

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

20th edition Chapter:438 Page number:3222

question_text: What is The Most commonly affected nerve trunk in leprosy?
explanation:
The most commonly affected nerve trunk in leprosy is the ulnar nerve at the elbow, whose involvement results in clawing of the fourth and fifth fingers, loss of dorsal interosseous musculature in the affected hand, and loss of sensation in these distributions

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 179, Pg: 1387

question_text: A 48-year-old man presents with headaches and low libido. He is found to have hypopituitarism. The CT scan shows a pituitary tumour with suprasellar extension. Which of the following structures is likely to be compressed?
explanation:
In this case, with a pituitary tumor and suprasellar extension, the structure most likely to be compressed is the Optic chiasma. The optic chiasma is located near the pituitary gland and is particularly vulnerable to compression by pituitary tumors expanding upward. Compression of the optic chiasma can lead to visual disturbances, including bitemporal hemianopia, due to the partial crossing of optic nerve fibers at this location.

  • The optic chiasm lies 5-10 mm above the diaphragm sellar and anterior to the stalk.
  • Adenomas larger than 1.5 cm frequently have suprasellar extension, and a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan will show compression and upward displacement of the optic chiasm.

Other options:

  • Abducens nerve (Option A): The abducens nerve controls the movement of the lateral rectus muscle of the eye. Compression of this nerve can result in lateral rectus muscle weakness and difficulty moving the eye outward.
  • Hypothalamus (Option B): While the hypothalamus is located near the pituitary gland and is important for regulating many endocrine functions, it is less likely to be directly compressed by a pituitary tumor with suprasellar extension.
    • Superior extension of the tumour can lead to compression of firstly the optic apparatus and later the hypothalamus.
  • Oculomotor nerve (Option C): Lateral extension of the tumour with compression or invasion of the cavernous sinus can compromise third, fourth, or sixth cranial nerve functions, manifest as diplopia in 5 to 15% of pituitary tumour patients.
    • The oculomotor nerve controls several eye muscles and plays a role in eye movement. Compression of this nerve can lead to eye movement abnormalities, including ptosis (drooping of the eyelid) and diplopia (double vision).

In this case, the most likely structure to be affected based on the tumor's location is the optic chiasma, causing visual disturbances.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 380 Pg: 2901

question_text: A 16-year-old girl presented with a three week history of headache and horizontal diplopia on far right lateral gaze. On two separate occasions she noted dimmed vision whilst bending forwards. Over the last year she had gained 12 kilograms in weight. On examination, her weight was 95 kg, and height was 162 cm. Neurological examination revealed bilateral papilloedema and a partial right sixth cranial nerve palsy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• This patient is markedly obese with a BMI of 36 and the history suggestive of BIH.
  • Vision may be affected with enlargement of the blind spot and the visual obscuration with movements that provoke a rise in intracranial pressure (ICP) (for example, bending) is typical of BIH.
  • Dysthyroid eye disease would not present like this and is more commonly associated with hyperthyroidism.
  • The papilloedema would argue against multiple sclerosis (MS).
  • A Bitemporal hemianopia or a visual field defect would be expected with a pituitary tumour.
  • Venous sinus thrombosis is a possibility but would be expected to produce deteriorating symptoms.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 16Pg: 116

question_text: Which of the following cranial structures is not pain producing?
explanation:
The pain producing structures in brain includes: scalp, meningeal arteries, dural sinuses, falx cerebri and proximal portion of large pial vessels.

The ventricular ependyma, choroid plexus, pial veins, and much of the brain parenchyma are not pain producing

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 16 Pg:112

question_text: A 22  year old man injured himself whilst snowboarding. On examination, he has weakness of elbow flexion and loss of sensation over the radial aspect of her forearm. Which of the Following nerves is damaged?
explanation:
The fibers of the musculocutaneous nerve originate in the lower cervical spinal cord (usually C5 to C7) and travel via the lateral cord of the brachial plexus.

Innervation -

  • Sensory supply - Lateral forearm via the lateral cutaneous nerve.
  • Motor supply - To biceps brachi which helps in elbow flexion.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3499

question_text: A 59 year old lady presents with back pain that radiates to the knee and down the medial side of the calf towards the medial malleolus. Which nerve root is affected?
explanation:
• In contrast, L5 lesion can cause pain radiating through the buttock, down the postero lateral aspect of the thigh, lateral aspect of calf and across the dorsum of the foot.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

question_text: A 61 year old woman presents with diplopia. On examination, she has a fixed dilated pupil on the right side. Direct light reflex and accommodation reflex are totally absent. Which one of the Following is most likely?
explanation:
• Pilocarpine is a miotic, and all the rest are causes of small pupils as well. Although there is no mention of ptosis or oculomotor nerve palsy, this is the only answer which fits with a fixed dilated pupil.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 441, Pg: 3444

question_text:
A 41 year old man was injured in a road traffic accident. On examination, he is unable to extend his right hand at the wrist. The triceps jerk is diminished, and there is weakness of wrist flexion. A small area of over the right middle finger has sensory loss to pain and touch.
Where is the lesion?
explanation:
• A C5 root lesion causes weakness in abduction of the shoulder and biceps, as well as sensory loss in the upper arm.
  • A C7 root lesion causes weak wrist extensors and flexors, weak finger extensors and sensory loss to middle finger.
  • A radial nerve lesion would not involve finger flexors.
  • A ulnar nerve lesion would cause weak intrinsic hand muscles weakness of wrist flexion

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

question_text:
A 41 year old man presents with finger weakness which was diagnosed as an ulnar nerve lesion.
Which of the Following muscles is supplied by the ulnar nerve?
explanation:
• The interossei muscles and medial two lumbricals are supplied by the ulnar nerve. The lateral two lumbricals (anatomical position), opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis and flexor pollicis brevis are supplied by the median nerve.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

question_text: A 32 year old lady is found to have a left sided posterior communicating artery aneurysm on cerebral angiography. Which of the Following would you expect to find?
explanation:
• A posterior communicating artery aneurysm will cause compression of the third nerve, and therefore pupillary involvement from compression of the parasympathetic fibres that run on the outside of the third nerve. This leads to a dilated pupil. Other features of a third nerve palsy include ptosis, and a 'down and out' eye. Upgaze and adduction is affected.
  • On the contrary, ischemia of the 3rd nerve due to long standing diabetes and atherosclerosis would lead to a palsy which spares the pupillary reflex.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 441, Pg: 3441

question_text: A patient is undergoing examination of the eye. The patient has a direct response to light shone in the right eye, but no consensual response. Light shone in the left eye elicits a consensual response, but not a direct response. During pursuit eye movements, the left eye is fixed in an inferior and lateral position. Where is the lesion?
explanation:
• A left third nerve palsy will cause a dilated left pupil, with the eye in a 'down and out' position. The afferent pathway is controlled by the optic nerve and the efferent pathway by the oculomotor nerve - hence a dilated poorly reacting pupil.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 216

question_text:
A 47 year old teacher develops a sided facial weakness in association with hearing loss and pain in the right ear. On examination, there is a vesicular rash over the right ear, and right lower motor neuron 7th nerve palsy.
What is the likely cause?
explanation:
• This is Ramsay-Hunt syndrome. The primary pathophysiology of Ramsay Hunt syndrome is located in the geniculate ganglion of the seventh cranial nerve (CN VII).
  • Classically, Ramsay Hunt syndrome has been associated with VZV. It is associated with 7th nerve palsy, vertigo, ipsilateral hearing loss and tinnitus.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed,Ch: 35, Pg: 249

question_text:
A 61 year old patient has diplopia looking to the left. When the left eye is covered, the outer image disappears.
Which nerve is involved?
explanation:
• Covering the affected eye causes the false image (outer image) to disappear. In this case, the left eye is involved hence left lateral rectus (abducens nerve).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 441, Pg: 3441

question_text: Which of the following will not be affected by a lesion of the facial nerve in the internal auditory meatus?
explanation:
• The extent of dysfunction depends on the level of injury.
  • If it is proximal to geniculate ganglion, for example, internal auditory meatus, taste is lost in the anterior 2/3 of tongue. Also secretion from submandibular, sublingual and lacrimal glands is impaired.
  • Hyperacusis is due to paralysis of stapedius. Orbicularis oculi is affected causing inability to blink/close eyelids.
  • Sensation over the face is supplied by the trigeminal nerve, and sweat glands are controlled by the sympathetic nervous system, for example, anhidrosis in Horner's syndrome.

tests used to assess the lesion of the facial nerve clinically are as follows:

  • Blink test (corneal reflex)- when tapping on the patient's glabella, a suspension in blinking will occur on the affected side (the ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve controls afferent limb, the efferent limb is the temporal and zygomatic branch of the facial nerve)
  • Schirmer test (assessing lacrimation of the lacrimal gland) - lacrimation will be decreased by 75% compared to the normal side using a folded strip of blotting paper in the lower conjunctival fornix. It is important to note that a unilateral lesion within the geniculate ganglion can produce bilateral lacrimal deficiencies.
  • Stapedial test- This involuntary reaction in response to high-intensity sound stimuli causes contraction of the stapedius muscle and gets mediated by the facial nerve. Testing of the stapedius reflex can be performed using tympanometry.
  • Salivary Test- Salivation rate is assessed from a submandibular duct following stimulation with a 6% citric acid solution. If positive, there will be a reduction in salivation by 25% at the affected side and indicate a lesion at or proximal to the root of the chorda tympani.
  • Taste test- though using salt sweet, sour, and bitter tastes along the lateral aspects of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. A positive result will indicate a lesion at or proximal to the root of the chorda tympani.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed,Ch: 441, Pg: 3439

question_text: A 47-year-old man presents with an insidious onset of binocular horizontal diplopia and left sided facial pain. On examination he has a left abducens nerve palsy and numbness over the maxillary division of the left trigeminal nerve. Of the following which is the most likely anatomical site of his neurological lesion?
explanation:
• In the pre-antibiotic era, an abducens nerve palsy with ipsilateral pain and numbness was due to petrous osteitis (Gradenigo syndrome) but is now more likely the result of a meningioma or nasopharyngeal carcinoma of the petrous apex.

The cavernous sinus syndrome consists of variable involvement of

  • Oculomotor (III)
  • Trochlear (IV)
  • Abducens (VI)
  • Trigeminal (ophthalmic and maxillary division) (V) and
  • Oculo-sympathetic nerves.
  • The superior orbital fissure syndrome is similar to the cavernous sinus syndrome except for the presence of proptosis.
  • Lesions of the cerebellopontine angle causes compression of cranial nerves V (trigeminal), VII (facial) and VIII (vestibulocochlear).
  • Lesions of the midbrain cause a variety of symptoms, depending on the exact area affected.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 441 Pg: 3444

question_text: A 41 year-old male presents to his family doctor with a two week history of numbness and a burning sensation on the lateral aspect of the left upper thigh. Examination reveals sensory loss over the anterolateral thigh. Which one of the following nerves is most likely to be involved in this patient?
option_d: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
explanation:
• The pure sensory loss makes the diagnosis of meralgia paraesthetica and is a consequence of damage to the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh.
  • It is usually a consequence of entrapment at the lateral inguinal ligament or less likely, trauma, ischaemia or a retroperitoneal lesion.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

question_text:
A 27-year-old male is admitted following an altercation in which he is stabbed in the thigh by a bottle.
Which of the following features suggests injury to the femoral nerve?
option_b: Loss of sensation over lateral aspect of thigh
option_c: Weakness of abduction of the hip
option_d: Weakness of adduction at the hip
explanation:
• A lesion of the femoral nerve (L2,L3,L4) is characterised by weakness of the quadriceps femoris muscle and hence weakness of extension of the knee, loss of sensation over the front of the thigh and loss of the knee jerk.
  • The obturator nerve (LB-4) supplies adductors of hip and lateral cutaneous nerve to thigh supplies sensation to the outer part of the thigh.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

question_text:
A 27-year-old woman presents with new double vision. On examination she experiences horizontal diplopia on looking to her far right. Covering her left eye only obscures the innermost image. Covering her right eye only obscures the outermost image. In the neutral position her right eye is deviated medially. She has no problem on looking to the far left.Her neurological examination is otherwise normal.
What is the most likely problem?
explanation:
• The VIth nerve is motor to the lateral rectus muscle.
  • It is responsible for abduction of the ipsilateral eye.
  • In the neutral position the affected eye is deviated medially due to unopposed action of the medial rectus.
  • In patients with diplopia the 'cover test' can be used to determine the eye that has the problem. On covering the affected eye the outermost image disappears.
  • After finding a VIth nerve palsy the cause should always be looked for, it is not a diagnosis in itself.
  • Due to the long course and anatomy of the VIth nerve it can be damaged in any condition causing raised intracranial pressure. It can therefore be a 'false localising sign'.

Regarding the options:

  • Concomitant right esotropia is not the answer. An esotropia is a squint where one or both eyes turn inwards. This may alternate between the eyes or may be a problem in just one eye. A concomitant esotropia is a squint where the degree by which the eye turns inwards does not vary in any direction of gaze (as opposed to an incomitant esotropia where the direction of gaze does affect the size or presence of deviation). Concomitant esotropias usually begin early in childhood. The patient has diplopia in all directions of gaze if vision is normal in both eyes.
  • Left sided IVth nerve palsy is not the answer. The IVth nerve controls the superior oblique muscle. Lesions of it typically cause a vertical diplopia, usually noticed on going downstairs or reading.
  • Left sided VIth nerve palsy is not the answer. This would cause a horizontal diplopia but it would be on far left gaze. The outermost image would disappear with the cover test over the left eye if it was affected.
  • A medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion is not the answer. This connects the IIIrd and VIth cranial nerve nuclei in the pons and co-ordinates conjugate horizontal eye movements. Its lesions typically cause internuclear ophthalmoplegia. There will be impaired adduction on the side of the lesion with nystagmus of the contralateral eye. In the neutral position the eyes appear normal.
  • Right VIth nerve palsy is the correct answer (see above).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 441 Pg: 3444

question_text:
A 2B-year-old man presents to the Emergency department after punching a window. He has lacerated the medial aspect of his wrist, damaging the ulnar nerve.
What is he at risk of developing?
option_b: Inability to pinch paper between his thumb and index finger
option_c: Loss of sensation over the lateral three and a half fingers
option_d: Wasting of the second lumbrical muscle
explanation:
• Ulnar nerve damage at the wrist results in wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles (other than the lateral two lumbricals) and the hypothenar eminence. This produces the classic claw hand. It supplies sensation to the medial one and a half fingers.
  • The median nerve innervates the lateral two lumbricals and the thenar eminence (opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis and flexor pollicis brevis). It supplies sensation to the lateral one and a half fingers.
  • Damage to the motor branch, the anterior interosseous nerve results in inability to form and pinch grip, tip to tip, instead holding the paper between the pulp of the thumb and index finger.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

question_text: A 19-year-old male presents with blurring of vision in his right eye. Examination reveals visual acuity in the right eye of 6/18 and in the left eye 6/6. Visual fields to confrontation reveal a right temporal visual field defect and partial loss of the superior part of the temporal field of the left eye. Where is the most likely position of the lesion responsible for this defect?
explanation:
• The most likely localisation of the lesion is around the optic chiasma spreading up the right optic nerve. The signs indicate a bitemporal visual field defect with involvement of the right optic nerve (decreased visual acuity).
  • Occipital lobe lesion causes a congruous homonymous hemianopia whereas an optic tract lesion causes an incongruous homonymous hemianopia. Temporal lobe lesion causes an upper homonymous quadrantanopia. Optic nerve lesions in isolation lead to unilateral visual signs.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 219

question_text:
A 4B-year-old civil servant attends the clinic stating that she has difficulty swallowing. She gives a two months history of difficulty with solids which has progressed to difficulty tolerating liquids in the previous two weeks. She has noticed some weakness in her right arm which has affected her ability to lift certain objects like the kettle. Previously, she has enjoyed good health with no hearing loss or facial weakness. She describes no visual symptoms.On examination, she has an absent gag reflex on the right, with reduced palatal movements. There is weakness on rotating the head to the left with flattening and weakness of elevation of the right shoulder. Eye movements, visual acuity, hearing and tongue movements are all normal.
Where is the likely site of the lesion?
explanation:
• The clinical scenario is that of a right sided pathology affecting the IX, X and XI cranial nerves.
  • This produces the palatal weakness and the swallowing difficulties (IX/X), while the shoulder and sternocleidomastoid weakness are due to accessory nerve (XI) involvement.
  • The absence of hearing loss or facial weakness makes a cerebello-pontine angle lesion unlikely.
  • A lesion outside the skull may also involve the XII nerve (tongue).
  • The most likely site, therefore is the jugular foramen.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 441 Pg: 3444

question_text: A 2D-year-old man suffers a deep laceration to the forearm resulting in transection of the median nerve. Following this injury, the nerve will undergo which of the following pathological processes?
explanation:
• Wallerian degeneration is degeneration of the portion of the nerve distal to the injury. It occurs following axonal injury in both the peripheral and central nervous systems and usually begins within 2D24-36 hours of injury.
  • Coagulative necrosis is cell death following ischaemia or infarction. It is characterised by a 'ghostly' appearance of affected cells unders light microscopy.
