  • Fibrinoid necrosis is a form of necrosis in which there is an accumulation of material in the affected tissue with a staining pattern reminiscent of fibrin. It is associated with Henoch-Schönlein purpura, malignant hypertension and hyperacute transplant rejection.
  • Segmental demyelination is a feature seen in axons in the central nervous system with multiple sclerosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 437, Pg: 3411

question_text: A 42 year old man has a 4 week history of dizziness, and vomiting. The onset was acute. He feels that the world is spinning and his balance is poor. His hearing is normal. There is no family history. On examination, he has no cerebellar signs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Vestibular neuronitis often presents with acute vestibular disturbance that gradually resolves over a few weeks. It is associated with viral infections. Treatment is conservative and supportive.
  • Option A: BPPV is characterized by episodic vertigo and vomiting precipitated on head movement
  • Option B: Friedreich's ataxia is an autosomal recessive condition characterized by cerebellar and upper motor neuron manifestations
  • Option C acoustic neuroma is a tumour of the 8th cranial nerve which would cause progressive hearing loss along with tinnitus p

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 22, Pg: 160

question_text: Which of the following is true of tetanus?
option_a: Failure to culture Clostridium tetani from the wound would make the diagnosis doubtful
explanation:
A. Absence of a culture positivity from wound does not exclude tetanus.

B. Patients need to be actively immunised after recovery.

C. The toxin tetanospasmin does not cross the blood brain barrier, it diffuses through the blood to bind to receptors containing gangliosides on the neuronal membranes of presynaptic nerve terminals in muscles. The toxin does reach the brain by axonal transport.

D. Cephalic means involving the cranial nerves usually from a wound on the head and neck. It may be confused with rabies but hydrophobia never occurs.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 152 Pg: 1211-1214

question_text: A 66 year old lady presents to the hospital with an ataxic gait. On examination, the patient had difficulty standing without assistance and minor movements of her head and body caused vertigo. There was mild postural tremor and marked hypotonia of the right limbs, mostly the arm. Finger to nose testing elicited marked intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia in the right arm. Speech was dysarthric but comprehension was good.Where is the lesion likely to be?
explanation:
• Lesions of the cerebellum (intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia) lead to motor signs ipsilateral to the lesion.
  • Right pons or left medulla can also cause ipsilateral cerebellar sign, but there will be associated cranial nerve involvement.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3332-3333

question_text: A 45-year-old male presents with right-sided facial weakness. On examination, the patient is able to wrinkle his forehead on the right side but is unable to close his right eye completely, and his mouth droops to the left side when smiling. Based on these findings, which of the following statements best describes the type and location of the lesion?
option_a: Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion on the right side
option_b: Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion on the left side
option_c: Lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion on the right side
option_d: Lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion on the left side
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation described in the question indicates a pattern of facial weakness that involves an inability to fully close the right eye and a mouth droop to the left side when smiling, while still being able to wrinkle the forehead on the right side. This pattern suggests involvement of the facial nerve on the right side of the face.

  • Forehead Movement Preservation:In cases of lower motor neuron lesions affecting the facial nerve, the entire side of the face will show weakness, including the forehead. However, in upper motor neuron lesions, typically seen in strokes, the forehead receiving bilateral upper motor neuron inputs remains spared (patients can still wrinkle their forehead).
  • Facial Nerve (Cranial Nerve VII) Involvement:The facial nerve controls the muscles of facial expression. A lower motor neuron lesion affecting this nerve will impair its function on the affected side, leading to inability to close the eye and drooping of the mouth.
  • Side of Lesion:Since the patient cannot fully close the right eye and the mouth droops to the left (indicating weakness on the right), the lesion is on the same side as the deficits observed (right side).

The symptoms described are consistent with a classic presentation of Bell's Palsy or another form of peripheral facial nerve palsy, which are types of lower motor neuron lesions.

Explanation of other options:

Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion on the right side (Option A): A right UMN lesion would affect the contralateral (left) lower face, not the right side. Forehead sparing would be seen, but in this case, the right forehead is affected.

Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion on the left side (Option B): A left UMN lesion would cause lower facial weakness on the right, but the forehead would be spared. Since the patient has complete right-sided facial weakness (including the forehead), this is not a UMN lesion.

Lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion on the left side (Option D): The patient has right-sided facial weakness, indicating a right-sided lesion, not a left-sided one.

Key Takeaways:

A lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion of the right facial nerve (e.g., Bell's Palsy) causes complete right-sided facial weakness, including the forehead, and inability to close the eye.

question_text: Identify the defect in the given image:
option_c: Infranuclear facial palsy on the left side
option_d: Supranuclear facial palsy on the left side
explanation:
Explanation:

Infranuclear facial palsy on the left side, is the most likely diagnosis. This condition, also known as Bell's palsy or lower motor neuron facial palsy, affects the facial muscles on one side, leading to the kind of asymmetry seen in the image. The involvement of the facial nerve after it branches from the brain (infranuclear) leads to a lack of movement in all muscles on the affected side of the face.

Explanation of other options:

Erb's palsy (Option A): This typically affects the arm due to an injury to the upper brachial plexus, not facial muscles.

Congenital hypoplasia of orbicularis oculi (Option B): This would primarily affect the eyelid muscles and would not typically cause the asymmetry observed around the mouth.

Supranuclear facial palsy on the left side (Option D): This typically results in weakness predominantly in the lower half of the face on the opposite side due to the upper motor neuron lesion, which is not consistent with the full-face asymmetry observed here.

Bell's Palsy:

  • Overview and Incidence:
    • Bell's palsy is the most common form of facial paralysis.
    • The annual incidence is approximately 25 per 100,000 people, with a lifetime risk of about 1 in 60 individuals.
    • Common risk factors include pregnancy and diabetes mellitus.
  • Clinical Manifestations:
    • The onset of Bell's palsy is abrupt, usually reaching maximal weakness within 48 hours.
    • Early symptoms can include pain behind the ear and unilateral loss of taste sensation.
    • Hyperacusis (heightened sensitivity to sound) may be present.
    • In some cases, MRI findings include swelling and enhancement of the geniculate ganglion and facial nerve, sometimes with nerve entrapment in the temporal bone.
  • Prognosis and Recovery:
    • Approximately 80% of patients experience recovery within a few weeks to months.
    • Electromyography (EMG) can provide prognostic information; denervation observed after 10 days suggests axonal degeneration, predicting a longer recovery time, often around three months, and possibly incomplete recovery.
    • The presence of incomplete paralysis in the first week post-onset is a Favorable prognostic sign.
    • Recurrences occur in about 7% of cases.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Acute Bell's palsy involves inflammation of the facial nerve with mononuclear cells, indicative of an infectious or immune-mediated cause.
    • Herpes simplex virus (HSV) type 1 DNA is often found in the endoneurial fluid and posterior auricular muscle, implicating HSV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion as a common cause.
    • Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus accounts for up to one-third of cases, making it the second most frequent cause.
    • Other viruses and conditions, including HIV seroconversion, have also been linked to Bell's palsy less frequently.

Key Takeaway:

Lower motor neuron (infranuclear) facial palsy affects the entire ipsilateral half of the face, including the forehead, eye closure, and mouth movement. The most common cause is Bell's palsy, typically caused by HSV-1 reactivation.

question_text: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden-onset right-sided weakness lasting 3 hours. His blood pressure is 200/100 mmHg, and NCCT of the head reveals intracerebral haemorrhage with right-sided hemiparesis. Which of the following should not be included in his management?

question_text: A 60-year-old patient weighing 80 kg is diagnosed with acute ischemic stroke and is planned for thrombolysis using alteplase. What is the appropriate initial bolus dose (in mg) that should be administered?
explanation:
Explanation:

Among the given options, the appropriate initial dose of atleplase for a man of 80 kilograms is 8 mg.

  • In this case, the alteplase bolus dose for acute ischemic stroke needs to be determined.
  • The recommended regimen is 9 mg/kg body weight, with a ceiling of 90 mg.
  • For a patient weighing 80 kg, the total dose is 72 mg (80 × 0.9).
  • Of this, 10% (7.2 mg) is given as the initial bolus, which rounds up to 8 mg as the correct choice. (Options B, C, and D ruled out)
  • The remaining 90% (64.8 mg) should then be delivered via intravenous infusion over one hour.
  • Alteplase is a fibrinolytic drug belonging to the tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) class.
  • It works by converting plasminogen into plasmin, an enzyme that breaks down both fibrin and fibrinogen.
  • Produced using recombinant DNA technology, alteplase is FDA-approved for treating acute ischemic stroke, pulmonary embolism, acute myocardial infarction, and blocked catheters.

Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499977/

question_text:
A 75-year-old female is noted to have sustained hypertension with a blood pressure of 196/80 mmHg.
 Which of the following is the most appropriate strategy for this patient?
option_a: ACE inhibitors would be contraindicated in association with a creatinine above 1.5 mg/dl
option_b: Antihypertensive therapy would be associated with only a minor reduction in risk of stroke in this age group
option_c: Beta blockers are less effective in this age group than in younger patients
option_d: Doxazosin would be the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient
explanation:
This patient has isolated systolic hypertension with a persistent systolic BP over 140mmHg and diastolic BP below 90.

  • This is associated with increased risk of stroke and coronary events in those over 60 years.
  • This systolic hypertension should be lowered if persistent and is not responding to non-pharmacological measures, with calcium-channel blockers and thiazides as drugs of first choice.
  • Elderly patients have a higher absolute cardiovascular risk than younger individuals and therefore benefit more from control of blood pressure.

ACE inhibitors are not contraindicated when the serum creatinine is greater than 150umol/L but should be commenced under specialist supervision.

There is evidence that beta blockers maybe less effective in elderly patients.

question_text: A 45-year-old male has a history of 6 months of cutaneous symptoms in the form of Raynaud's Phenomenon and livido reticularis. He recently has history of numbness of the hands and feet. He presents to the emergency department with testicular pain. Which of the following complications is he least likely to develop?
explanation:
The patient in this question has a vasculitis as evidenced by the presence of involvement of multiple symptoms. The catch in the question is the presence of testicular pain, which is seen in Polyarteritis Nodosa.

Polyarteritis nodosa is a medium vessel vasculitis which is characterized by the absence of pulmonary involvement and glomerulonephritis. Microscopy shows transmural fibrinoid necrosis without granulomas.

Renal impairment can occur due to involvement of branches of renal artery.

Mesenteric ischemia and bowel infarction can also occur. Hepatic infarction can also occur. Dermatological manifestations are Raynaud’s Phenomenon, livido reticularis, nodules, rash, purpura etc.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 363, Pg 2811

question_text: J-wave is typically seen in which condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The J-wave or Osborn wave is a notching at the QRS junction on ECG, most strongly linked with hypothermia(<28°C). Cold alters cardiac conduction, producing this wave.

ECG Findings in Hypothermia:

  • Bradycardia
  • PR prolongation
  • QRS widening
  • J-waves in leads V3-V6 (camel hump appearance)

Explanation of Other Options:

Heat stroke (Option B): Hyperthermia-related (>40°C), no J-waves.

High-altitude pulmonary edema (Option C): Causes right heart strain, no J-wave.

Drowning (Option D): Hypoxia and acidosis, not J-waves.

Key Takeaways:

  • J-wave = Osborn wave = Hypothermia hallmark.
  • Prominent in precordial leads.

question_text: A 48-year-old man with chest pain of 1-hour duration is diagnosed as having acute myocardial infarction. Which of the following features, if present, would most contraindicate thrombolytic therapy?

Absolute contraindications for thrombolytic therapy

question_text: A 52-year-old woman develops sudden-onset facial droop, slurred speech, and inability to raise her right arm. The symptoms gradually improve and completely resolve within 24 hours. On examination, she has a mid-diastolic murmur over the left side of the heart and an irregular heart rhythm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient developed sudden-onset focal neurological symptoms that completely resolved within 48 hours, indicating transient cerebral ischemia without infarction, which defines a Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA).
  • The presence of irregular rhythm and mid-diastolic murmur is suggestive of atrial fibrillation with mitral stenosis pointing to a cardioembolic source, but since the symptoms resolved completely, the episode is classified as a TIA (Option C ruled out)

Transient ischemic attacks

  • Transient Ischemic Attacks (TIAs) are brief episodes of stroke-like symptoms that resolve completely, typically lasting less than 24 hours, without evidence of brain infarction on imaging.
  • Transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) represent brief vascular insults that can affect:
    • Brain → focal neurological deficits
    • Retina → amaurosis fugax (transient vision loss)
    • Cochlea → transient hearing loss or vertigo
    • Spinal cord → rare transient myelopathy
  • TIAs share the same etiologies as ischemic stroke, including:
    • Embolic events (from the heart or large arteries)
    • In situ thrombosis of intracranial vessels
  • In TIA, the occluded vessel reopens spontaneously, restoring neurological function.

Imaging and diagnosis

  • If brain imaging shows an infarction, the event is classified as a stroke, regardless of symptom duration.
  • A normal imaging study does not rule out TIA, as the diagnosis is primarily clinical.

Clinical significance

  • TIAs are important warning events, signaling high risk for subsequent stroke.
  • Risk of stroke after TIA: ~10-15% within the first 3 months, with most events occurring in the first 48 hours.

Treatment

  • For TIA, start dual antiplatelet therapy (Aspirin + Clopidogrel) for 21 days, followed by single antiplatelet therapy long-term for secondary prevention.

Explanation of other options

Thromboembolic stroke (Option B): A thromboembolic stroke results in persistent neurological deficits due to brain infarction and is diagnosed when symptoms last more than 24 hours or when brain imaging confirms infarction.

Paradoxical embolism (Option D): Paradoxical embolism occurs when a venous thrombus enters the arterial circulation via a PFO or ASD. The mid-diastolic murmur in this patient is instead associated with mitral stenosis, not the shunt.

question_text: A 60-year-old woman presents with weakness in her right arm lasting for 6 hours. The weakness gradually improved and eventually resolved. She has a history of diabetes, hypertension, and obesity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Based on the clinical presentation, the most likely diagnosis is Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA).

Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)

  • Defined as a brief episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal ischemia in the brain, spinal cord, or retina, without resulting in permanent tissue damage or infarction.
  • Symptoms usually last less than an hour, often just minutes, and resolve completely within 24 hours.
  • The risk of stroke is highest within the first 48 hours after a TIA.

Etiology:

  • Common risk factors include diabetes, hypertension, advanced age, smoking, obesity, alcohol use, poor diet, psychosocial stress, and lack of physical activity.
  • A history of prior stroke or TIA significantly increases the risk of recurrence.

Pathophysiology and Subtypes:

  • Large artery atherothrombosis (most common): Involves narrowing or blockage of large intracranial or extracranial arteries due to atherosclerosis, leading to reduced blood flow or artery-to-artery embolism.
  • Small vessel ischemic disease: Caused by lipohyalinosis or arteriolosclerosis of small vessels, commonly linked to hypertension, diabetes, and aging.
  • Cardiac embolism: Usually from clots forming in the heart chambers, often related to atrial fibrillation.
  • Cryptogenic: Ischemic events with no clear source, sometimes termed Embolic Stroke of Unknown Source (ESUS).
  • Other causes: Less common reasons include arterial dissection and vasculitis.

Explanation for other options:

Compressive neuropathy (Option A): usually causes persistent symptoms, unlike the transient symptoms described in this case.

Ischemic stroke (Option C): leads to longer-lasting neurological deficits due to sustained disruption of blood flow, and symptoms typically do not resolve within 24 hours.

Diabetic neuropathy (Option D): is unlikely to present with sudden, transient weakness affecting only one side of the body, as observed in this patient.

 

Reference:

  1. TIA

question_text: A stroke patient presents with an inability to identify objects but can determine the colour, texture, and shape of objects. Which of the following lobes is involved?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Visual agnosia is the inability to recognize objects despite intact vision, while preserving the ability to perceive their color, shape, and texture, typically resulting from lesions in the temporal lobe.
  • Temporal lobe stroke can cause memory impairment, difficulty recognizing faces or objects (prosopagnosia), fluent aphasia in left-sided lesions, visual agnosia, problems with visual perception and sound processing, and emotional or behavioral changes such as aggression, passivity, or trouble interpreting facial cues.

Explanantion of other options:

  • Frontal lobe (Option A) : It may result in difficulties with learning, visual-motor coordination, executive functions, and attention, including challenges in planning, focusing, and self-control.
  • Parietal lobe (Option B):
    • Right - Damage to this area can cause visuospatial deficits (e.g., the patient may have difficulty finding their way around new, or even familiar, places). Parietal Lobe,
    • Left: Damage to this area may disrupt a person's ability to understand spoken and/or written language.
  • Unilateral occipital lobe (Option D): Lesions of the occipital lobe, often from a posterior cerebral artery infarct, result in contralateral homonymous hemianopia a visual field loss on the same side in both eyes opposite to the lesion typically sparing the central (macular) vision.

question_text: A 35 year old male is evaluated for young stroke. He gives history of burning pains in both his feet since his late teenage. What can be seen on examining this patient?

question_text: A 60-year-old male presents to the emergency department with altered consciousness, vomiting, and left-sided weakness. His blood pressure on arrival is 220/120 mmHg. Which of the following statements regarding the management of hypertension in this clinical setting is incorrect?
option_a: In hemorrhagic stroke, reduce the BP to less than 160/100 mmHg with antihypertensives to prevent rebleed
option_b: In hemorrhagic stroke, aggressive use of IV antihypertensive if SBP > 220
option_c: In the ER, multiple blood pressure readings should be taken before starting antihypertensive therapy
option_d: In ischemic stroke, BP should be reduced to <140/90 mmHg immediately
explanation:
Explanation:

In acute ischemic stroke, cerebral autoregulation is impaired, and regional perfusion to the ischemic penumbra depends heavily on systemic blood pressure. A rapid or excessive drop in BP can reduce cerebral blood flow, thereby exacerbating ischemia and increasing infarct size.

Therefore, in ischemic stroke:

  • Blood pressure should not be reduced below 140/90 mmHg immediately.
  • If the patient is a candidate for thrombolysis, BP should first be lowered to <185/110 mmHg before administering tPA (alteplase).
  • If thrombolytic therapy is not planned, antihypertensive therapy is indicated only if BP exceeds 220/120 mmHg, or if there are other comorbid hypertensive emergencies (e.g., aortic dissection, acute MI, pulmonary edema).

Therefore, Option D is incorrect because immediate and excessive BP reduction can worsen cerebral ischemia.

Hemorrhagic Stroke:

  • BP should be lowered to <160/100 mmHg with antihypertensives to reduce the risk of rebleeding (Option A ruled out).
  • If SBP > 220 mmHg, aggressive use of IV antihypertensives is recommended (Option B ruled out).

Ischemic Stroke:

  • BP should only be reduced to <185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis.
  • If the BP is above this threshold and thrombolysis is considered, lowering it is necessary, but a reduction to <140/90 mmHg can worsen cerebral perfusion.
  • The ischemic penumbra depends on collateral flow maintained by systemic BP.
  • Aggressive BP reduction can cause secondary hypoperfusion, worsening infarct size, and poor neurologic outcomes.
  • Gradual control post-reperfusion or after the first 24-48 hours is safer.

Explanation of Other Options:

In the emergency room, blood pressure must be measured multiple times before initiating antihypertensive treatment(Option C): In a hypertensive emergency, multiple BP readings should be taken to ensure accurate assessment before starting antihypertensive therapy. This is important to avoid over- or under-treatment.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text:
A 65-year-old is investigated for dyspnoea and is shown to have an ejection fraction of 45% on echocardiography.
How is the left ventricular ejection fraction calculated?
explanation:
The left ventricle pumps only a fraction of the blood it contains. The ejection fraction is the amount of blood pumped (stroke volume=end diastolic volume - end systolic volume) divided by the amount of blood the ventricle contains (end diastolic volume). A normal ejection fraction (EF) is more than 55% of the blood volume.

Based on ejection fraction, heart failure is divided into:

  1. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) : EF > 40%
  2. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF) : EF > 50%
  3. HF with mid-range EF (HFmrEF) : EF 40-50%

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page

question_text:
A 7D-year-old woman presents with a two month history of episodic loss of vision in her right eye. Her electrocardiogram was normal and carotid ultrasound reveal a 49% stenosis of the right internal carotid artery, as assessed by the NASCAT criteria.
What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
explanation:
• The combination of aspirin and clopidogrel was found to prevent stroke following TIA better than aspirin alone in a large study(POINT STUDY).
  • Current NICE guidelines recommend that patients who have had a suspected TIA who are at high risk of a stroke (ABCD score of 4 or above) should have aspirin (300mg OD) started immediately. They also need specialist assessment and investigation within 24 hours of onset of symptoms. Secondary prevention measures should be introduced as soon as the diagnosis is confirmed, with consideration of individual risk factors.

The ABCD scoring system uses:

Age > or equal to 60 (1)

BP > or equal to 140/90mmHg at initial evaluation (1)

Clinical features (unilateral weakness 2, isolated speech disturbance 1, other 0)

Duration of symptoms (> or equal to 60 minutes, 10-59 minutes, <10 minutes)

Diabetes mellitus (1)

Although you cannot calculate the ABCD score with the information given in this question, aspirin remains the most appropriate answer.

  • Carotid endarterectomy has been established as an effective treatment for both symptomatic patients and asymptomatic patients who are shown to have carotid artery stenosis. It reduces the risk of disabling stroke or death by 48% in a person with severe symptomatic carotid stenosis (>70%) who has had a TIA. The peri-operative risk of disabling stroke or death is approximately 3%. Current guidelines recommend endarterectomy for symptomatic patients with greater than 70% stenosis, based on the North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial which showed clear benefit. The endarterectomy should be performed as soon as the patient is fit for surgery, preferably within two weeks of a TIA.
  • The benefit is marginal for symptomatic patients with 50-69% stenosis, but may be greater in male patients. NICE recommends these patients are also considered for endarterectomy. There is significantly less benefit for asymptomatic patients, even those with greater than 60% stenosis. Patients with less than 50% stenosis should not be considered for carotid surgery .
  • Recurrent stenosis can occur in 1-20% of patients following endarterectomy, and re-operation is needed in 1-3% of cases. Ipsilateral strokes occur in 9% of patients following endarterectomy, and 26% of those treated with medical management alone (within 2 years).
  • All patients with suspected non-disabling stroke or TIA who are considered as candidates for carotid endarterectomy should have carotid imaging within 1 week. If the patient has had a disabling stroke there is no real benefit in them undergoing the procedure.
  • Modified-release dipyridamole is indicated in combination with aspirin only once a TIA has been confirmed by a specialist. Alone, it is recommended only if aspirin is contraindicated or not tolerated.
  • Clopidogrel is recommended in patients who have had an ischaemic stroke, rather than a TIA.
  • Warfarin is only indicated with cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, or if the patient has atrial fibrillation.

Please note for this explanation, North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterecomy Trial (NASCET) criteria have been used. Carotid imaging reports will state which criteria are being used.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 427, Pg: 3345

question_text: Which of the following is a contraindication to treatment with intravenous tPA (tissue plasminogen activator) in a patient with an acute ischemic stroke?
option_d: Prior treatment with intravenous tPA for acute stroke 1 year ago
explanation:
A prior ischemic stroke within 3 months is a contraindication to tPA, but not a stroke a year ago. Patients cannot be treated with a systolic blood pressure above 185 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure above 110 mm Hg that does not respond to antihypertensive treatment. Patients who received intravenous tPA for a prior stroke can be treated, as long as they are beyond the 3-month period. Patients with ischemic stroke in any vascular distribution can be treated. However, intravenous tPA is contraindicated in patients with a prior history of intracerebral hemorrhage.

Contraindications for thrombolysis:

  • Significant head trauma or prior stroke in previous 3 months
  • Symptoms suggest subarachnoid hemorrhage
  • Arterial puncture at noncompressible site in previous 7 days
  • History of previous intracranial hemorrhage Intracranial neoplasm, arteriovenous malformation, or aneurysm
  • Recent intracranial or intraspinal surgery
  • Elevated blood pressure (systolic >185 mm Hg or diastolic >110 mm Hg)
  • Active internal bleeding
  • Acute bleeding diathesis, including but not limited to Platelet count <100,000/μL Heparin received within 48 hours, resulting in aPTT greater than the upper limit of normal Current use of anticoagulant with INR >1.7 or PT >15 seconds Current use of direct thrombin inhibitors or direct factor Xa inhibitors with elevated sensitive laboratory tests (such as aPTT, INR, platelet count, and ECT; TT; or appropriate factor Xa activity assays)
  • Blood glucose concentration <50 mg/dL (2.7 mmol/L)
  • CT demonstrates multilobar infarction (hypodensity > 1 3 cerebral hemisphere)

Inclusion Criteria for thrombolysis in stroke:

  • Diagnosis of ischemic stroke causing measurable neurological deficit
  • Onset of symptoms <3 hours before beginning treatment
  • Aged ≥18 years

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 427, Pg: 3338

question_text: A 67-year-old male with a history of diabetes, hypertension and hypercholesterolemia presents with dizziness. He reports that he woke up this morning and attempted to get out of bed but felt dizzy. He vomited and was unable to get out of bed to go to the bathroom. His wife was concerned as this had never happened before and called for the ambulance. On arrival at the emergency room his blood pressure was 180/70 mmHg, pulse was regular at 60 beats per minute and he was apyrexial. Blood sugar was within normal limits.On neurological examination his visual fields were full, and fundoscopy was notable for grade 2 hypertensive retinopathy. He had left jerk nystagmus on looking to the left and left jerk nystagmus on looking to the right. He was able to perform finger to nose and heel to shin in the bed. On standing the patient felt dizzy. His blood pressure was 170/80 mmHg after three minutes standing. He refused to walk for fear of falling. The rest of his examination was unremarkable.What is the leading diagnosis at this time?
explanation:
• Although there is no dysmetria a patient can have vertigo in isolation from a stroke.
  • Typically however the patient has direction changing nystagmus. You would be more reassured if the patient were able to walk. A trial of meclizine prior to walking may help.
  • A cerebrovascular accident should be considered and an MRI obtained of the brain.

question_text: During a scorching summer afternoon, a man, who had been toiling in a field, unexpectedly collapsed. Upon examination, there were no apparent physical indications of dehydration, although his radial pulse was detectable. The doctor determined that the man's serum electrolyte levels were within the normal range. Shockingly, the man's body temperature measured 106 degrees Fahrenheit. Considering these circumstances, which of the following should be administered as an initial form of immediate assistance?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient has heat stroke, defined by a core body temperature >40°C (104°F) with central nervous system dysfunction (collapse). The presence of a radial pulse indicates a perfusing rhythm, so CPR is not needed. The immediate life-threatening priority is rapid cooling. Covering the patient with cool, damp sheets (often combined with fanning) is an effective initial cooling method

Explanation of other options:

Inject epinephrine immediately (Option A): Epinephrine is used in cardiac arrest (ACLS); it is not indicated for heat stroke and could be harmful.

Cover with hot damp sheets (Option B): This would worsen hyperthermia.

Start CPR: Indicated only if the patient is pulseless and apneic, which is not the case here.

Key Takeaways:

  • Heat stroke is a medical emergency characterized by hyperthermia and CNS dysfunction.
  • The cornerstone of initial management is rapid cooling to prevent irreversible organ damage.

question_text: A 70-year-old patient with hypertension and atrial fibrillation presents with an acute episode of sensory and motor deficits. What is the next best step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

In a patient presenting with acute stroke symptoms and risk factors such as atrial fibrillation, the immediate priority is to restore cerebral blood flow if within the therapeutic window (usually within 4.5 hours of symptom onset). Intravenous recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rTPA) is the standard thrombolytic agent used for ischemic stroke management to dissolve the clot and reduce neurological damage.

  • Ischemic stroke is one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality. It is considered a clinical emergency, and timely diagnosis and treatment can improve the patient's outcome.
  • When a stroke is suspected, emergent brain imaging is essential to confirm the diagnosis of ischemic stroke before thrombolytics can be administered.
  • Noncontrast computed tomography (CT) scanning is the most commonly used form of neuroimaging to evaluate a patient suspected of having an acute stroke.
  • This patient presents with acute ischemic stroke (right MCA territory) within 2 hours, confirmed by CT (no haemorrhage) and MRI (ischemic injury).
  • Alteplase, a tissue plasminogen activator, is indicated within 3-4.5 hours of symptom onset in eligible patients to lyse clots and restore cerebral blood flow. It binds fibrin in thrombi, converting plasminogen to plasmin for fibrinolysis.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Defibrillation (Option B): Used to treat life-threatening arrhythmias, not indicated here.

Transesophageal echo (Option C): May identify cardiac sources of emboli, but is not part of acute management.

IV low molecular weight heparin (Option D): Anticoagulation is important for stroke prevention but not the first step in the acute management of ischemic stroke in the thrombolysis window.

question_text: Which of the following is not an absolute contraindication for fibrinolytic therapy in a patient with acute MI?

Absolute contraindications for use of fibrinolytic therapy in MI

  • Cerebrovascular events in the preceding year
  • Systolic blood pressure > 180 mmHg or diastolic BP > 110 mmHg at any time during presentation
  • Suspicion of aortic dissection
  • Active internal bleeding excluding menstrual bleed.

Relative contraindications

  • Current use of anti-coagulants
  • Pregnancy
  • Recent (< 2 weeks) invasive surgical procedure
  • Prolonged (> 10 min) CPR
  • Active peptic ulcer disease
  • History of severe hypertension that is controlled at present

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page no: 2059

question_text: An adult hypertensive male presented with sudden onset severe headache and vomiting. On examination, there is marked neck rigidity and no focal neurological deficit was found. The symptoms are most likely due to:
explanation: Ans. d. Subarachnoid hemorrhage The most likely diagnosis here is a subarachnoid bleed (SAH). The most common cause is trauma and is managed conservatively. The second most common cause is a rupture of a berry aneurysm. The typical presentation of a subarachnoid hemorrhage includes a ‘thunderclap’ headache. Meningitic features of neck stiffness and photophobia often develop over hours. Computed tomography (CT) is the investigation of choice. Lumbar puncture should be performed if the CT scan fails to establish the diagnosis of SAH; it shows a xanthochromic blood picture. Delayed ischemic neurological deficit (DIND) is attributed to vasospasm of the cerebral vasculature typically developing 3–10 days following ictus. It is the main cause of a poor outcome. Endovascular treatment ("coiling") is generally preferred over craniotomy and clipping for aneurysms amenable to this approach.

question_text:
In a case of meningitis, CSF sugar is 40 mg%, how will you proceed?
A. CSF sample must be taken before Antibiotics
B. Blood culture before start of Antibiotics
C. ATT initiated before CSF PCR for TB
D. 1 mL CSF centrifuged will have microbiological yield of > 95%CI
explanation:
CSF sugar < 40 indicates bacterial meningitis or chronic meningitis due to TB or fungus.

If LP is delayed in pyogenic, empirical antibiotic therapy should be initiated after blood cultures are obtained. Antibiotic therapy initiated a few hours prior to LP will not significantly alter the CSF WBC count or glucose concentration, nor is it likely to prevent visualization of organisms by Gram's stain or detection of bacterial nucleic acid by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay. CSF sterilization may occur more rapidly after initiation of parenteral antimicrobial therapy than previously suggested, with complete sterilization of CSF containing meningococci within 2 hours, and the beginning of sterilization of pneumococci by 4 hours into therapy.

Delay in treatment of tuberculous meningitis is associated with permanent neurological damage and death, hence treatment should be started without waiting for results, if clinically indicated. Centrifuged sample has more yield.

question_text: False about Pneumococcal Meningitis.

option_b: Drug of choice in the Penicillin resistant case is Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone.
option_c: Duration of therapy should be 2 weeks.
option_d: CSF sterilization occurs after completion of appropriate antibiotic therapy.
explanation:
A 2-week course of intravenous antimicrobial therapy is recommended for pneumococcal meningitis.

Patients with S. pneumoniae meningitis should have a repeat LP performed 24-36 h after the initiation of antimicrobial therapy to document sterilization of the CSF. Failure to sterilize the CSF after 24-36 h of antibiotic therapy should be considered presumptive evidence of antibiotic resistance.

Hyponatremia

So, among the given options, hydrocephalus is the most likely answer, as it has occurred after one week.

question_text: A patient presents with a 2-week history of fever, headache, and vomiting, along with nuchal rigidity. Lumbar puncture reveals elevated opening pressure, predominantly polymorphonuclear leukocytes, CSF glucose 35 mg/dL, protein 200 mg/dL and slightly cloudy CSF. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

CSF Findings in various types of meningitis:

Explanation of other options:

Meningoencephalitis (Option A): Meningoencephalitis involves inflammation of both meninges and brain parenchyma. While symptoms may overlap, the CSF profile with PMN predominance is more characteristic of bacterial meningitis. Meningoencephalitis typically shows mixed cellular response.

question_text:
A 24-year-old female presents with 3 days of fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, and ataxia. On exam, neck stiffness and positive Kernig's sign (hip and knee flexion on neck flexion) are present. CSF findings:

Opening pressure: Increased
Color: Cloudy white
WBC: 7000/μL (neutrophilic predominance)
Glucose: 15 mg/dL
CSF/serum glucose ratio: 0.2
Protein: 70 mg/dL
Latex agglutination: Positive
Limulus lysate test: Negative

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, and neck rigidity indicate meningitis. CSF shows high opening pressure, cloudy appearance, neutrophilic pleocytosis, very low glucose (15 mg/dl, ratio <0.4), and high protein, which are diagnostic of bacterial meningitis.

A positive latex agglutination test supports bacterial etiology, while a negative Limulus lysate test excludes Gram-negative endotoxin-associated causes.

Explanation of Other Options:

Tubercular meningitis (Option B): Cobweb CSF, lymphocytosis, very high protein.

Viral meningitis (Option C): Lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose.

Fungal meningitis (Option D): Lymphocytes, low glucose, often subacute onset.

Key Takeaways:

  • Bacterial meningitis = cloudy CSF, neutrophils, low glucose, high protein.
  • Latex agglutination test helps detect bacterial antigens.
  • Limulus lysate test rules out Gram-negative endotoxin.

question_text: A patient presented with fever, headache, mental confusion, nausea and neck stiffness. Lumbar puncture was performed and CSF analysis reveals proteins 45 mg/dl, glucose 7 mg/dl and increased neutrophils >80%. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's presentation and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings are indicative of bacterial meningitis. The most appropriate treatment for bacterial meningitis, given the clinical and CSF findings, would beCeftriaxone + Vancomycin. This combination is recommended to cover a broad spectrum of potential bacterial pathogens, including resistant strains such as penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis, until the specific organism can be identified and sensitivities are determined.

Based on the provided text and the diagnosis of bacterial meningitis is supported by:

  • Symptoms: Fever, headache, mental confusion, nausea, and neck stiffness.
  • CSF Findings:
    • Increased neutrophils: Predominance of polymorphonuclear cells (neutrophils) in the CSF is typical in bacterial infections.
    • Low glucose levels (7 mg/dL): Significantly reduced CSF glucose, compared to normal (40-70 mg/dL), which is common in bacterial meningitis due to glucose consumption by bacteria.
    • Elevated protein levels (45 mg/dL): Protein levels are elevated due to increased permeability of the blood-brain barrier.

These findings align with the classic signs of bacterial meningitis, which include low CSF glucose, high protein concentration, and a high percentage of neutrophils.

  • Immediate Actions: Obtain blood cultures and start empirical antimicrobial therapy along with adjunctive dexamethasone to reduce complications.
  • CSF Diagnosis: The diagnosis is confirmed by CSF analysis showing high protein, low glucose, high white blood cell count with a predominance of neutrophils, and positive results on Gram stain or culture.

Bacterial Meningitis Diagnosis:

  • Empirical Therapy Initiation: Start treatment immediately after obtaining blood cultures, before lumbar puncture if necessary, especially if neuroimaging is required.
  • Classic CSF Abnormalities in Bacterial Meningitis:
    • High white blood cell count: Mainly neutrophils.
    • Low glucose: Less than 40 mg/dL and a CSF/serum glucose ratio of less than 0.4.
    • High protein: Greater than 45 mg/dL.
    • Increased intracranial pressure: Opening pressure often above 180 mmH2O.
  • Gram Stain and Culture: More than 60% positivity in Gram stain and over 80% in culture, reinforcing the presence of bacterial pathogens.
  • PCR Testing: Useful for detecting bacterial DNA, which can help identify the specific causative organism.
  • Differential Diagnosis: Includes other conditions that can present with similar CSF findings but may require different management, such as viral, fungal, tuberculous, and carcinomatous meningitis.
  • Treatment Considerations: The administration of high-glucose solutions prior to lumbar puncture is unlikely to affect CSF glucose levels significantly unless there is a considerable delay.

Explanation of other options:

Ampicillin + Acyclovir (Option B): Ampicillin is used for Listeria monocytogenes, which is a concern in neonates, elderly, or immunocompromised-not the most common pathogen in this case. Acyclovir is used for herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE), which presents with temporal lobe involvement, seizures, and lymphocytic (not neutrophilic) CSF.

Cefotaxime + Ampicillin(Option C): Cefotaxime is an alternative to ceftriaxone but does not cover penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae unless combined with vancomycin. Ampicillin is used for Listeria, which is less likely in this patient.

Penicillin + Azithromycin (Option D): Penicillin alone is ineffective against penicillin-resistant pneumococci. Azithromycin is a macrolide used for atypical pneumonia and has no role in bacterial meningitis.

Key Takeaways:

For bacterial meningitis, the best empirical treatment is Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin to cover common pathogens, including resistant pneumococci.

question_text: A patient presented with an 11-day history of fever and neck stiffness. Lumbar puncture revealed lymphocyte predominance, glucose of 50 mg/dL, and protein of 3000 mg/dL, along with the presence of a cobweb-like coagulum. Gram stain was negative. Chest X-ray demonstrated upper lobe disease with hilar lymphadenopathy.
explanation:
The combination of subacute fever with neck stiffness, typical CSF profile (lymphocyte predominance, reduced glucose, markedly elevated protein), cobweb-like clot formation, and chest X-ray revealing upper lobe disease with hilar lymph node enlargement are hallmark findings of tuberculous meningitis.

A negative Gram stain favors a mycobacterial infection over common bacterial causes.


Explanations of other options:

Bacterial meningitis (Option B): Bacterial meningitis usually has a rapid onset (within 24-48 hours), shows neutrophil predominance in the CSF, and often yields a positive Gram stain. The slower progression and lymphocyte-rich CSF in this case argue against bacterial meningitis.

Fungal meningitis (Option C): Although fungal meningitis may show comparable CSF findings such as reduced glucose and elevated protein, it is more commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals and usually lacks the classic upper lobe changes on chest X-ray. Pulmonary involvement in this context strongly favors tuberculosis.

Viral meningitis (Option D): Viral meningitis is generally characterized by normal or only slightly raised protein, normal glucose, and no cobweb coagulum. The very high protein level (3000 mg/dL) together with low glucose makes a viral cause unlikely.

question_text: A 19-year-old boy was diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. What is the drug of choice (DOC) for prophylaxis to be given to his contacts?
explanation:
Explanation:

Rifampicin is the drug of choice for chemoprophylaxis of close contacts of a patient with meningococcal meningitis.

  • Meningococcal meningitis caused by Neisseria meningitidis is highly contagious and spreads through respiratory droplets.
  • Close contacts-such as roommates, family members, or anyone with prolonged exposure-are at high risk of acquiring the infection.
  • Chemoprophylaxis is essential to prevent secondary cases.
  • It is the drug of choice for adults unless contraindicated (e.g., pregnancy, resistance concerns). It effectively eliminates Neisseria meningitidis from the nasopharynx, thereby reducing secondary cases.
  • Alternatives (such as ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone) can be used in special situations, but rifampicin remains the standard recommendation in most guidelines.
  • Rifampicin 600 mg twice daily for 2 days in adults is the standard regimen

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Ethambutol (Option B): Used for tuberculosis, not effective against Neisseria meningitidis.

Doxycycline (Option C): Used for a variety of infections, but not recommended for meningococcal prophylaxis.

Amoxicillin (Option D): Not suitable for meningococcal chemoprophylaxis.

question_text: For MDR-RR TB, what is the indication of short course bedaquiline?
option_a: Resistance to rifampicin and sensitive to fluoroquinolones
option_b: Mutation only to INH A and kat G gene
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Short-course bedaquiline-containing regimens are indicated for MDR/RR-TB patients who are rifampicin-resistant but fluoroquinolone-sensitive.

  • Multidrug-resistant / Rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) is defined by resistance to rifampicin, with or without resistance to other first-line drugs.
  • The short-course bedaquiline-containing regimen (typically the 6-month BPaLM regimen) is indicated when the strain is resistant to rifampicin but remains sensitive to fluoroquinolones.
  • BPaLM Regimen Components:
    • Bedaquiline
    • Pretomanid
    • Linezolid (600 mg)
    • Moxifloxacin
  • WHO Endorsed Regimen Use:
    • Indicated when:
      • Confirmed Rifampicin resistance (MDR/RR-TB)
      • Confirmed Fluoroquinolone susceptibility
      • Age ≥14 years
      • Non-CNS involvement
      • No prior exposure to any BPaLM drugs >1 month unless drug resistance to them is ruled out
    • Not recommended in:
      • TB meningitis or CNS TB
      • Pregnancy and lactation
      • Age <14 years
      • Known exposure to BPaLM drugs for over 30 days without confirmed susceptibility

Explanation of other options:

Mutation only to INH A and katG gene (Option B): Indicates isoniazid resistance, but rifampicin resistance is required to define MDR/RR-TB. Without rifampicin resistance, the patient does not qualify for bedaquiline-based MDR therapy.

Rifampicin sensitive (Option C): First-line anti-TB drugs are used for rifampicin-sensitive TB. Short-course bedaquiline regimens are specifically for rifampicin-resistant cases.

Extrapulmonary TB like tubercular meningitis (Option D): Bedaquiline has poor CNS penetration, and tubercular meningitis is a contraindication for short-course regimens due to limited efficacy.

Reference:

https://pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2070942#

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11257606/

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4561400/

https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/365333/9789240065116-eng.pdf?sequence=1

question_text: True about cryptococcal meningitis is
explanation:
• The clinical manifestations of cryptococcosis reflect the site of fungal infection.
  • The spectrum of disease caused by Cryptococcus species consists predominantly of meningoencephalitis and pneumonia, but skin and soft tissue infections also occur; in fact, cryptococcosis can affect any tissue or organ.
  • CNS involvement usually presents as signs and symptoms of chronic meningitis, such as headache, fever, lethargy, sensory deficits, memory deficits, cranial nerve paresis, vision deficits, and meningismus.
  • Cryptococcal meningitis differs from bacterial meningitis in that many patients present with symptoms of several weeks In addition, classic characteristics of meningeal irritation, such as meningismus, may be absent in cryptococcal meningitis. Indolent cases can present as subacute dementia. Meningeal cryptococcosis can lead to sudden catastrophic vision loss

question_text: The commonest cause of acute bacterial meningitis in adults?
explanation:
pneumoniae is the most common cause of meningitis in adults >20 years of age, accounting for nearly half the reported cases(1.1 per 100,000 persons per year). There are a number of predisposing conditions that increase the risk of pneumococcal meningitis, the most important of which is pneumococcal pneumonia. Additional risk factors include coexisting acute or chronic pneumococcal sinusitis or otitis media, alcoholism, diabetes, splenectomy, hypogammaglobulinemia, complement deficiency, and head trauma with basilar skull fracture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea. The mortality rate remains ~20% despite antibiotic therapy.

The incidence of meningitis due to N. meningitides


GBS: Group B Streptococci Most common route of spread of bacteria causing meningitis: hematogenous

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 138, Pg: 1101

question_text: A patient presents with signs of meningeal irritation. CSF examination reveals lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, and elevated protein. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The CSF findings of lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, and mildly elevated protein along with signs of meningeal iritation are suggetsive of viral meningitis.

Viral meningitis

  • The most common causative agent is the enteroviruses, accounting for > 85% cases.
  • In adults, HSV is the major cause of viral meningitis.
  • Clinical manifestation
    • Headache: Present invariably; often retroorbital or frontal; associated with photophobia and pain on eye movements.
    • In viral meningitis, nuchal rigidity is usually present but often mild, appearing only near the limit of neck flexion.
    • Patients may show mild lethargy or drowsiness, but profound changes in consciousness, seizures, or focal neurological deficits are not typical and suggest encephalitis or another CNS pathology.

Diagnosis

  • CSF findings include:
    • Pleocytosis (generally <500 but occasionally as high as 1,000-­ 8,000 WBCs/μL; often predominantly polymorphonuclear cells in the first 48 hours before becoming mostly mononuclear)
    • Normal or slightly low glucose content (10% <40 mg/dL)
    • Normal or mildly increased protein content (generally <100 mg/dL).
  • PCR amplification of viral DNA/RNA from CSF is the most important diagnostic test for CNS viral infections.

CSF findings in meningitis

question_text: A child presents with two weeks of poor feeding and marked irritability. The sibling has confirmed tuberculosis and is receiving antitubercular therapy. As part of the evaluation, a lumbar puncture is done. Which of the following findings is most likely in the CSF?
option_a: Lymphocytosis with low sugar and high protein
option_b: Lymphocytosis with high sugar and high protein
option_c: Neutrophils with low sugar and low protein
option_d: Neutrophils with low sugar and high protein
explanation:
Explanation:

The history of two weeks of poor feeding and irritability, along with close contact with a tuberculosis case, points toward a diagnosis of tuberculous meningitis.

In tuberculous meningitis, cerebrospinal fluid usually demonstrates lymphocytic pleocytosis (up to 1000/μL), increased protein levels (100-800 mg/dL), and reduced glucose. This classic combination of findings represents the chronic inflammatory reaction seen in CNS tuberculosis.

Explanations of other options:

Lymphocytosis with high sugar and high protein (Option B): Although lymphocytosis and elevated protein are consistent with CNS infections, increased glucose (hyperglycorrhachia) is not characteristic of tuberculous meningitis. In TB meningitis, *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* typically lowers CSF glucose through heightened utilization. Therefore, elevated glucose would argue against this diagnosis.

Neutrophils with low sugar and low protein (Option C): A pattern of low glucose together with low protein is unusual in CNS infections, since infections generally cause protein to rise as part of the inflammatory process. In addition, neutrophilic predominance is more indicative of acute bacterial meningitis.

Neutrophils with low sugar and high protein (Option D): Although neutrophils may appear in the CSF during acute bacterial meningitis, their predominance is not typical of tuberculous meningitis, which is usually characterized by a lymphocytic response.

question_text: A young individual presents with an unusually severe headache, unlike any previous episodes. Examination reveals high blood pressure and neck stiffness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The sudden onset of an intense headache described as the 'worst ever,' together with hypertension, neck stiffness, and a CT scan demonstrating the classic 'Star of Death' pattern from blood in the basal cisterns, is indicative of a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

  • A subarachnoid hemorrhage happens when blood collects in the subarachnoid space, the area between the brain and its delicate coverings, most often caused by a ruptured aneurysm, and has a mortality rate of about 35% if left untreated.

Explanations of other options:

Cluster headache (Option A): Cluster headaches present as intense, one-sided pain usually located behind the eye, accompanied by autonomic symptoms. They appear in cyclical patterns or clusters, but unlike subarachnoid hemorrhage, they are not associated with neck stiffness or the 'Star sign' on CT scans.

Encephalitis (Option C): Encephalitis usually manifests with fever, confusion, seizures, and localized neurological signs. Since fever is absent and CT shows typical SAH features, encephalitis is an unlikely diagnosis.

Meningitis (Option D): Although meningitis may cause headache and neck stiffness, it usually also presents with fever and light sensitivity. The CT scan findings do not match meningitis, and the classic 'Star of Death' pattern on CT is specific for SAH.

question_text: What is the confirmatory test for the given condition?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

The given condition is Tuberculoma. NMR spectroscopy detects specific lipid peaks and metabolic profiles that help confirm tuberculoma and differentiate it from neurocysticercosis.

  • NMR spectroscopy (Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy) is a non-invasive biochemical imaging technique that analyzes the chemical composition of brain lesions.
  • It is especially helpful when CT or MRI shows ring-enhancing lesions, where the differential diagnosis includes tuberculoma vs. neurocysticercosis.
  • Key Spectroscopic Finding in Tuberculoma:
    • Prominent lipid peak at 1.3 ppm. This is the hallmark finding of caseating tuberculoma.
    • Helps differentiate from neurocysticercosis, which lacks a strong lipid peak and may show other metabolites like lactate.
  • Intracranial Tuberculoma - Diagnostic Imaging:

Explanation of other options:

CBNAAT of CSF (Option A): Useful in diagnosing tuberculous meningitis by detecting MTB DNA, but not confirmatory for parenchymal tuberculoma and does not distinguish it from other ring-enhancing lesions.

PET scan (Option B): Shows increased metabolic activity, but is non-specific and cannot biochemically differentiate tuberculoma vs. neurocysticercosis.

MRI aerial scan (Option D): Not a recognized term in clinical radiology. Standard MRI provides anatomical detail, but lacks metabolic resolution offered by spectroscopy.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4845155/

question_text: The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) specimen of a patient is shown below, along with microscopy. The report reveals mononuclear cytosis, raised protein levels, and reduced glucose. What is the most probable etiology?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of clinical details with CSF findings - lymphocytic predominance, elevated proteins, hypoglycorrhachia (low sugar), and the presence of a characteristic cobweb-like clot - points towards tuberculous meningitis (TBM).

Features of Tuberculous Meningitis (TBM):

  • Etiology: Caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis via hematogenous spread or rupture of subependymal tubercles into the subarachnoid space.
  • Presentation: Subacute onset with fever, headache, meningismus, and cranial nerve palsies (especially ocular nerves from basal meningeal involvement).
  • Complications: Hydrocephalus, elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), and ischemic infarcts.
  • CSF Findings:
    • Lymphocytic predominance
    • Elevated protein (100-500 mg/dL)
    • Decreased glucose (<40 mg/dL or <50% serum glucose)
    • Cobweb-like pellicle formation

Diagnosis:

  • Gold Standard: CSF culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
  • Supportive Tests: AFB staining, CSF ADA levels, or PCR for TB DNA.

Management:

  • Early initiation of antitubercular therapy (ATT).
  • Corticosteroids to minimize inflammation and reduce complications.

CSF Findings in Different Types of Meningitis:

Explanation of Other Options:

Aseptic meningitis (Option B): Typically viral, presents with lymphocytic predominance but normal glucose and near-normal protein levels.

Bacterial meningitis (Option C): Usually shows neutrophilic pleocytosis, very high protein, and markedly reduced glucose, with turbid CSF.

Chemical meningitis (Option D): Results from rupture of intracranial tumor contents (e.g., dermoid, glioma) into CSF. Shows variable inflammatory response, elevated protein, but absence of microbial organisms.

Reference:

  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8425579/
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8425579/

question_text: A 44 year old patient has been having fevers, neck stiffness and confusion. There was a past medical history of HIV infection and diabetes. A CT scan was normal and lumbar puncture was performed. The opening pressure during LP was normal, and there were elevated CSF lymphocytes (88), and elevated CSF protein (5.5 g/l), and a low glucose. Gram staining and India ink preparation revealed 4-7 micron, round budding yeasts with capsule and 8-10 lymphocytes per high power field. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
• Cryptococcal meningitis is often seen in immunosuppressed patients. The organism is Cryptococcus Neoformans. Meningitis manifests with diffuse, nonfocal findings (eg, altered mental status, vomiting).
  • A CT scan or MRI in patients with cryptococcal infection may reveal diffuse atrophy or cerebral edema with focal, homogenous, or contrast-enhanced areas.
  • An India ink preparation is commonly used with CSF to identify the organism and to support a presumptive diagnosis. If performed correctly, 25-50% of patients with cryptococcal meningitis show Cryptococci.
  • In patients with AIDS, amphotericin B is given for 2 weeks, with or without 2 weeks of flucytosine, followed by fluconazole at 400 mg/d for a minimum of 10 weeks.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 202, Pg: 1576

question_text:
A 16-year-old girl presented with a 12 hour history of fever and diffuse headache. On examination she was febrile (37.5°C). She was fully conscious. Mild neck stiffness was noted but there were no other neurological signs. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed:
Cell count 200/mL(60% lymphocytes)
Protein 0.8 g/L(0.15-0.45)
Glucose within normal range
Gram stain No organisms seen
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Enteroviruses and mumps are the commonest causes of viral meningitis.

Cerebrospinal fluid changes with bacterial meningitis typically include:

  • High protein
  • Low glucose and
  • Neutrophilic pleocytosis.

Cryptococcal meningitis is an infection of severely immunocompromised individuals, especially advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection.

Tuberculous meningitis is an insidious illness, presenting over weeks and months.



Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 138 Pg: 1106

question_text:
A 25-year-old primary school teacher presents to a local central hospital reported to be well at 8 a.m., confused by 10 a.m, and drowsy at 11 a.m.on examination she was restless and agitated; Glasgow Coma Scale 10/15, Pupil size were normal and reactive to light, the neck was stiff and there was no rash, Planter responses were down-going, Kernig's sign was positive, Chest and abdominal examinations were unremarkable,vitals were temperature 40°C, pulse 125 bpm, blood pressure 125/68 oxygen saturation 93% on room air.On CSF analysis :
Appearance : Turbid
Cells : 5000 cells/mm3 (60% Neutrophils)
Proteins : 320 mg/dL
Sugar : 18 mg/dlWhat will be the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
CSF findings in Acute Bacterial Meningitis:

  • Opening pressure >180 mmH2O
  • White blood cells 10/μL to 10,000/μL; (neutrophils predominant)
  • Red blood cells Absent in nontraumatic tap
  • Glucose <2.2 mmol/L (<40 mg/dL)
  • CSF/serum glucose <0.4
  • Protein >0.45 g/L (>45 mg/dL)
  • Gram's stain Positive in >60%
  • Culture Positive in >80%
  • PCR Detects bacterial DNA

Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 138, Pg: 1103

question_text: A 61 year old man is on high dose prednisolone for a diagnosis of giant cell arteritis 4 months ago. He complains of a headache, which had worsened for the past week and double vision. On examination, there is neck stiffness, and right sided 7th nerve palsy. His temperature is 38 degrees. A lumbar puncture reveals a protein of 0.8 g/l, glucose of 63 mg/dl, WCC of 30 (predominant neutrophils). What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
In this case, the patient presents with a headache, double vision, neck stiffness, and right-sided 7th nerve palsy, along with an elevated temperature. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis shows an elevated white cell count (WCC) with predominantly neutrophils, an elevated protein level, and a normal glucose level. These findings are indicative of acute bacterial meningitis.

The most likely causative organism in this scenario is Listeria monocytogenes (Option A). Listeria monocytogenes is a bacterium that can cause acute bacterial meningitis, particularly in older adults and immunocompromised individuals. It is known to present with a subacute or chronic course and can involve cranial nerve palsies, as seen in this patient.

  • The lumbar puncture findings are consistent with a bacterial meningitis but the glucose is not low enough to suggest TB. Listeria monocytogenes is an aerobic and facultatively anaerobic gram-positive bacillus.
  • The risk of listeriosis is markedly increased in immuno-compromised patients, particularly among those undergoing renal transplantation, receiving high doses of corticosteroids, or suffering with AIDS or cancer.
  • Ampicillin or penicillin has generally been recommended as the treatment of choice.
  • Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Option B): can cause tuberculosis meningitis, but it typically presents differently with a chronic course, a lymphocytic pleocytosis in the CSF, and elevated protein levels. It would be less likely to cause acute symptoms like those described here.
  • Option C: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a bacterium that causes atypical pneumonia, commonly known as "walking pneumonia." While it can cause respiratory symptoms, it is not a typical causative agent of acute bacterial meningitis.
    • Meningitis caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae is extremely rare. When it does occur, it often presents with milder symptoms and a more gradual onset compared to the acute bacterial meningitis seen in this patient.
  • Option D: Borrelia burgdorferi is the bacterium responsible for Lyme disease, which primarily affects joints, the skin, and the nervous system in some cases.
    • Lyme disease can lead to neurological complications, but it typically presents with symptoms such as Bell's palsy (facial nerve palsy), peripheral neuropathy, and rarely, meningitis.
    • It is less likely than listeria monocytogenes in this case because the patient does not have any of the typical symptoms of Lyme disease, such as a rash.
    • Meningitis due to Borrelia burgdorferi would usually have a different clinical course and CSF profile compared to the acute, suppurative (pus-containing) meningitis that this patient is experiencing.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 151, Pg: 1208-1211

question_text: An HIV-positive male presents with high fever and is found to have a positive Kernig's sign. CSF analysis reveals low glucose, elevated protein, and raised leukocyte count. He is diagnosed with cryptococcal meningitis. What is the correct treatment approach for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:  

  • In an HIV-positive patient with cryptococcal meningitis, liposomal amphotericin B is the first-choice initial treatment because of its superior effectiveness and CNS penetration.
  • The standard regimen includes liposomal amphotericin B (L-AMB) with 5-flucytosine for a 2-week induction phase, followed by fluconazole for 6 weeks as consolidation therapy.

Cryptococcal meningitis

Common Cause

  • The most frequent fungal cause of meningitis in AIDS patients is Cryptococcus neoformans.
  • Cryptococcus gattii accounts for up to 12% of cases.

Clinical Features

  • Symptoms include fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, and meningeal signs.
  • Seizures and focal neurological deficits are less common.
  • Kernig's sign: pain on passive extension of the knee, suggestive of meningeal irritation.

CSF Findings

  • May appear normal or show mild increases in white cells and protein.
  • Glucose is often reduced.
  • CSF opening pressure is typically elevated.

Diagnosis

  • India ink test on CSF reveals the organism.
  • Cryptococcal antigen detection in CSF or blood.
  • Blood fungal cultures are often positive.
  • Biopsy may be required for CNS cryptococcoma or to rule out immune reconstitution syndrome.

Induction Therapy

  • IV amphotericin B (0.7 mg/kg/day) or liposomal amphotericin (4-6 mg/kg/day) plus flucytosine (25 mg/kg every 6 hours) for at least 2 weeks.
  • Monitor kidney function to prevent flucytosine toxicity.

Maintenance therapy

  • Continue amphotericin until CSF culture is sterile, then switch to fluconazole:
  • 400 mg/day orally for 8 weeks
  • Then 200 mg/day until CD4+ T-cell count is >200 cells/µL for 6 months.

Explanation of other options:

Vancomycin (Option A): Vancomycin is mainly indicated for bacterial infections, especially those due to methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). It does not act against Cryptococcus neoformans and therefore is not effective in managing cryptococcal meningitis.

High dose fluconazole with flucytosine (Option B): Although these antifungal agents are part of cryptococcal meningitis management, they are not the preferred first-line therapy in severe cases. A combination of high-dose fluconazole with flucytosine does not provide the same rapid fungicidal effect as liposomal amphotericin B and is mainly used for maintenance treatment or when amphotericin B cannot be given.

Voriconazole (Option C): VVoriconazole is mainly indicated for invasive aspergillosis and other mold infections. It is not the preferred therapy for cryptococcal meningitis, as its effectiveness against Cryptococcus neoformans is limited compared to the standard treatment regimen.

question_text: Whole blood is stored at which temperature for maintaining erythrocyte viability?
explanation:
Whole blood provides both oxygen-carrying capacity and volume expansion. It is the ideal component for patients who have sustained acute hemorrhage of ≥25% total blood volume loss.

Whole blood is stored at 4°C to maintain erythrocyte viability, but platelet dysfunction and degradation of some coagulation factors occurs.

In addition, 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate levels fall over time, leading to an increase in the oxygen affinity of the hemoglobin and a decreased capacity to deliver oxygen to the tissues, a problem with all red cell storage.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 113, Pg: 885

question_text: A 22 year old man is admitted following a severe road traffic accident. He suffered significant blood loss at the scene. He is resuscitated with IV crystalloid and group O negative packed red cells. Intra-operatively the anesthetist phones you for advice. Bloods show: Hb: 6.6 g/dL; WBC: 11200/μL; platelet count 83000/μL; PT 28 seconds; APTT: 72 seconds; fibrinogen: 1.9 g/L. What is most appropriate to use to reduce his bleeding risk?
explanation:
The likely diagnosis is a disseminated intravascular coagulation following a road traffic accident.

His PT and APTT are significantly prolonged; therefore, FFP is indicated at a dose of 15 mU/ kg. He will likely require platelets; however, at present, they are greater than the recommended threshold of 20000/μL. Cryoprecipitate is primarily used to replace fibrinogen when below 1.5 g/L. Prothrombin complex concentrate is used to reverse warfarin.

For these situations, fibrinogen level should be maintained at >1.50 g/L and PT prolonged no more than 3 s above the upper limit of normal. Vitamin K should be given.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 116 pg. 917

question_text: Factor VII deficiency should be considered with which of the following coagulation abnormalities?
option_c: Prolongation of both PT and aPTT
explanation:
Commonly used tests of hemostasis provide the initial screening for clotting factor activity, and disease phenotype often correlates with the level of clotting activity.

An isolated abnormal prothrombin time (PT)suggests factor VII deficiency, whereas a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) indicates most commonly hemophilia or factor XI deficiency.

The prolongation of both PT and aPTT suggests deficiency of factors V, X, and II, or fibrinogen abnormalities.

The addition of the missing factor at a range of doses to the subject's plasma will correct the abnormal clotting times; the result is expressed as a percentage of the activity observed in normal subjects.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 116 pg. 911

question_text: Antiparasitic action of Metronidazole on E. histolytica is via :
explanation:
E histolytica lacks glutathione and glutathione reductase, it relies on its thioredoxin reductase system to prevent, regulate, and repair the damage caused by oxidative stress.

Metronidazole inhibits this antioxidant system.

Metronidazole is the drug of choice for the following parasitic infections:

  • Amoebiasis
  • Giardiasis
  • Trichomoniasis

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 223Pg 1718

explanation:

Islet D cells produce somatostatin

question_text: A 21-year old woman living in rural Indonesia is in her third trimester of pregnancy and is found to have severe microcytic anemia with a hematocrit of only 19%. She denies vaginal bleeding but consistently has darkened stools, which are positive when tested for occult blood. Blood laboratory testing is also remarkable for eosinophilia and low serum albumin concentration. Which of the following parasitic infections is the most likely to result in this syndrome?
explanation:
Intestinal blood loss is the principal clinical manifestation of hookworm infection, which can lead to iron deficiency and microcytic anemia. Pregnant women and children are at greater risk because of their higher iron needs.

Diphyllobothrium latum infection is associated with development of megaloblastic anemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency and is thus associated with an elevated,rather than low, red blood cell mean corpuscular volume.

Infection with Enterobius vermicularis and Entamoeba histolytica, is not usually associated with intestinal blood loss or iron deficiency.

Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 21st Ed , Ch: 232, pg.1775

question_text: A 12 year old male was admitted to the emergency department with significant lethargy which had worsened over the past year. On examination he was conscious and oriented. His heart rate was 70 beats per minute, blood pressure was 120/70mmHg and he was afebrile. Clinical examination of the abdomen revealed no organomegaly. His haemoglobin is 11.2 g/dL, white cell count of 8200/mm3 and a platelet count of 365000/mm3. The plasma urea was 30 mg/dL, creatinine 1.3 mg/dl, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 2.3 mmol/L, bicarbonate 38 mmol/L. The plasma liver function tests were within normal limits. His electrocardiogram demonstrated U waves. Which one of the following is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
So the given patient has hypokalemia with metabolic alkalosis as evidenced by a high bicarbonate. But his blood pressure is high. So barter and Gitleman are ruled out. ACE inhibitor causes hyperkalemia.

Hypokalemia with hypertension and alkalosis is caused by Liddle syndrome in the given options. Others include: Conns syndrome(primary hyperaldosteronism), renal artery stenosis(secondary hyperaldosteronism), Apparent mineralocorticoid excess, Cushing's syndrome.

Lets see how:

So in all these there will be excess sodium reabsorption mediated by the ENaC. In Liddle syndrome it is due to activating mutation of the channel, while in others, it is due to aldosterone excess. To maintain electrical neutrality of the interstitium, potassium and H+ ions are secreated. So the result is hypertension, hypokalemia and alkalosis.

In Liddle syndrome, the Renin and Aldosterone levels will be low, since the receptor is activated by a mutation, the sodium reabsorption will inhibit RAAS. There are two other conditions that will behave like Liddle syndrome. The first one is Cushing Syndrome, where the ENaC is activated by endogenous steroid, remember that glucocorticoids have mineralocorticoid action too. So that Renin and aldosterone will be suppressed.

The second one is Apparent mineralocorticoid excess, due to 11β hydroxy steroid dehydrogenase which converts Cortisol to Cortisone, so that there will be excess cortisol that acts on the ENaC.

So in all these conditions, the renin and aldosterone levels will be low.

Liddle's Syndrome and Apparent Mineralocorticoid excess are single gene mutations causing hypertension. Hypertension and hypokalemia in these can be treated with potassium sparing diuretics.

In Conns syndrome, there will be high aldosterone due to aldosterone secreting adenoma, which will inhibit Renin.

In Renal Artery stenosis and renin secreting tumors, there will be the same finding of hypokalemia, alkalosis and hypertension. But the Renin and aldosterone levels will be high.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 53, Pg:353.

A 72 year old woman with a history of multiple myeloma has a serum calcium of 11.6 mg/dl. She is prescribed pamidronate infusion over 4 days.

question_text: Glucose enters the pancreatic beta cell via:
explanation:
• GLUT increases glucose transport by facilitated diffusion
  • GLUT2 mediates glucose entry into pancreatic beta cells
  • Other locations for GLUT2 are liver, hypothalamus and renal tubular cells
  • GLUT4 mediates glucose entry to insulin dependent tissues muscle, adipose tissue and heart
  • Insulin increases glucose uptake in the liver by increasing glucokinase activity and inhibiting glycogen phosphorylase
  • SGLT1 is present in intestinal epithelial cells and transports glucose and galactose
  • Fructose is transporter by GLUT5
