question_text:
A 34-year-old woman has presented to the emergency department for the third time with abdominal pain which typically lasts several days. The previous two occasions she has been discharged home without a firm diagnosis. Between episodes the patient is symptom free. She complains of feeling anxious.
She has recently re-started the combined oral contraceptive pill after completing her family. On examination she is anxious and hypertensive at 155/98 mmHg with a pulse of 102. She has no rashes. Her abdomen is diffusely tender.
Investigations show
Haemoglobin 12.8 g/dl(13.5-18)
White cell count 8.1 x 10^9/L (4-10)
Platelets 220 x 10^9/L (150-400)
Sodium 135 mmol/l (134-143)
Potassium 3.9 mmol/l (3.5-5)
Creatinine 0.6 mg/dl
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is a rare disorder characterised by abdominal pain and neuropsychiatric symptoms which usually presents in the 20-40 age group. Rash is not a feature of AIP like other porphyrias. Hypertension and tachycardia are common examination findings.
  • The progesterone component of the combined oral contraceptive pill is known to precipitate porphyria attacks. Many other drugs have been described in association with an attack.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 416 Pg: 3237-3248

question_text: A man is admitted with acute abdominal pain and vomiting. He is diagnosed and treated for acute pancreatitis. Which of the following features is associated with a worse prognosis in acute pancreatitis?
explanation:
The Bedside Index of Severity in Acute Pancreatitis (BISAP)incorporates 5 clinical and laboratory parameters obtained within the first 24 hours of hospitalization.

They are BUN >25 mg/dl, Impaired mental status, SIRS, age >60 and pleural effusion on radiography.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 348, Pg: 2661

question_text:
A 16 year old boy with known sickle-cell disease is brought to the emergency department profoundly unwell. He has a reduced conscious level, temperature 39°C, pulse rate 160 beats/min and blood pressure 70/40 mmHg. Investigations:
Hb: 7.8 g/dL; MCV:68 fl; WBC: 17000/7mu;L; platelet count 480000/μL ,
Reticulocyte count: 10 X 109/L(NR:50-100 X 109/L )
Blood film: neutrophilia with toxic granulation; RBC consistent with sickle cell disease and hyposplenism. What is the most likely clinical diagnosis?
explanation:
Patients with sickle-cell disease have compromised splenic function resulting from microvascular occlusion. This puts them at risk of life-threatening infections from capsulated organisms.hyposplenism (through reduction in phagocytic capacity) increases the risk of meningococcal disease. Aplastic crises produce a very low hemoglobin with a reticulocytopenia.

There is no history of joint pain or shortness of breath to suggest a vaso-occlusive painful crisis or sickle chest syndrome.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 155 pg. 1227, 1229

question_text: Which of the following vasculitis is characterized by the presence of anti endothelial cell antibodies?
explanation:
Antibodies to Endothelial cells and smooth muscles are thought to be the pathogenetic mechanism in Kawazaki Disease.

question_text: Which one of the following proteins defect is most likely to be associated with very high levels of plasma chylomicrons?
explanation:
• Dietary triglycerides in cholesterol are packaged by gastrointestinal epithelial cells into large lipoprotein particles called chylomicrons. After secretion into the intestinal lymph and passage into the general circulation, chylomicrons bind to the enzyme lipoprotein lipase, which is located on endothelial surfaces.
  • This enzyme is activated by a protein contained in the chylomicron, apoprotein CII, liberating free fatty acids and monoglycerides, which then pass through the endothelial cells and enter adipocyte or muscle cells.
  • Patients with familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency usually presents in infancy with recurrent attacks of abdominal pain caused by pancreatitis. They also have eruptive xanthomas resulting from triglyceride deposition.
  • Treatment should consist of a low fat diet that may be supplemented by medium-chain triglycerides, which are not incorporated into chylomicrons. The absence of functional apoprotein CII, with consequent failure to activate lipoprotein lipase, presents with a similar phenotype, although the affected patients are typically detected at a somewhat later age than are patients with familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20th edition Chapter: 400 Page number:2889-90

question_text: A 55-year-old man with a history of multiple myeloma for 8 years presents with a 10-day history of loin pain and pink coloured urine. His BP is 126/78 mm Hg; Labs show a creatinine of 3.9 mg/dl and a urine examination reveals proteinuria and blood in urine. An ultrasound of the kidney suggests renal vein thrombosis. Which of the following is the next investigation to be done in this patient?
explanation:
The cause of loin pain could be either Pyelonephritis or Renal Vein thrombosis. Pyelonephritis is possible in a patient with myeloma, as myeloma predisposes to infection. But since there is no history of fever and the urine is showing proteinuria and blood, pyelonephritis is ruled out.

Next possibility is Renal Vein Thrombosis, which can definitely cause proteinuria and hematuria with loin pain.

How can we correlate myeloma with renal vein thrombosis.?

  1. Light chain can get deposited in the glomerulus and can cause heavy proteinuria and nephrotic range proteinuria can predispose to renal vein thrombosis.
  2. Nephrotic range proteinuria can develop in AL Amyloidosis, and around 10% of patients with Al amyloidosis have overt myeloma.

Because heat precipitation test does not give accurate measure of protein, the first step will be to confirm proteinuria with a 24 hour protein measurement.

After quantifying proteinuria, the next step would be a renal biopsy.

Diagnosis:

  • Screening: Doppler ultrasonography
  • Confirmatory: Computed tomography angiography (100% sensitive). Magnetic resonance angiography is another option but is more expensive

Angio should not be done in this patient as there is high risk of contrast induced nephropathy. Moreover, to establish the diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome it is essential to perform a 24-hr urinary protein which should be followed by a renal biopsy to establish the type of glomerulopathy.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 314, page: 2345

question_text: A 70-year-old woman is referred for investigation of a creatinine of 2.5 mg/dl. She mentioned several episodes of haematuria with symptoms of ureteric colic. explanation:
Our patient is an elderly female with renal impairment, with a background history of use of combination analgesics for low back ache. She also reports ureteric colic with hematuria episodes. There is bilateral scarred kidneys with papillary calcification.

This constellation of symptoms is known as analgesic nephropathy.

NSAID induced tubulointerstitial disease will not present with colic and hematuria.

There is no other information given in the question which suggests a myeloma other than low back ache. Myeloma does not produce colic and hematuria. It will not cause shrunken kidneys. Myeloma causes CKD with normal sized kidneys.

Chronic obstructive uropathy due to calculi is possible, but the history of analgesic intake is specified in the history which cant be ignored.

Analgesic nephropathy is usually a result of prolonged or chronic ingestion of combination analgesics, that contain phenacetin or acetaminophen and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs(NSAIDs) including aspirin or ibuprofen and caffeine.

There will be papillary necrosis and shedding of the necrosed papillae causing colic and hematuria. There will be normal anion gap metabolic acidosis due to loss of tubular function. The patients are at increased risk of urothelial malignancy. Ct scan will show garland calcification.

Usual NSAIDS does not cause Analgesic nephropathy

question_text: A 51-year-old male laborer presents with a haematemesis. Which of the following features confers the greatest risk of a poor outcome?
option_b: A history of ischaemic heart disease (IHD)
option_d: A pulse of 90 beats per minute
explanation:
Among the options given, history of ischemic heart disease confers the greatest risk of a poorer outcome.

There are a number of available scoring systems which stratify subjects with GI bleed into high and low risk groups.

The Rockall scoring system is based on:

  • Age (the higher the age the worse the prognosis)
  • Comorbidities (like IHD)
  • Presence of shock
  • Endoscopic abnormalities.

The Canadian Consensus Conference Statement utilizes a similar system, incorporating endoscopic factors including:

  • Active bleeding
  • Major stigmata of recent haemorrhage
  • Ulcers greater than 2 cm in diameter
  • The location of ulcers in proximity to large arteries.

The Blatchford score is based on clinical parameters alone:

  • Elevated blood urea nitrogen
  • Reduced haemoglobin
  • A drop in systolic blood pressure
  • Raised pulse rate
  • The presence of melaena or syncope
  • Evidence of hepatic or cardiac disease.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 48, Pg: 313

question_text: Which ratio is the quick indicator of water deprivation as a treatment in Hyponatremia?
explanation:
The urine-to plasma electrolyte ratio (urinary [Na+] + [K+]/plasma [Na+]) can be exploited as a quick indicator of electrolyte-free water excretion; patients with a ratio of >1 should be more aggressively restricted (<500 mL/d), those with a ratio of ~1 should be restricted to 500-700 mL/d, and those with a ratio < 1 should be restricted to < 1 L/d. In hypokalemic patients, potassium replacement will serve to increase plasma Na+ concentration, given that the plasma Na+ concentration is a functional of both exchangeable Na+ and exchangeable K+ divided by total-body water; a corollary is that aggressive repletion of K+ has the potential to overcorrect the plasma Na+ concentration even in the absence of hypertonic saline. Plasma Na+ concentration will also tend to respond to an increase in dietary solute intake, which increases the ability to excrete free water; this can be accomplished with oral salt tablets and with newly available, palatable preparations of oral urea.

Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 345

question_text: A 70-year-old man presents with lower back pain and increasing pallor. Investigations show abnormal renal function, normal liver function with preserved albumin, but markedly elevated gamma globulins. Spine X-ray reveals multiple lytic lesions. Which cell type is most likely responsible for this presentation?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of low back pain, pallor, impaired renal function, elevated gamma globulins, and lytic bone lesions is characteristic of multiple myeloma, which arises due to the accumulation of plasma cells.

  • Multiple myeloma develops when malignant plasma cells build up in the bone marrow and secrete large quantities of a monoclonal protein, resulting in widespread systemic effects.

Explanation of other options:

Lymphocyte (Option A): Although lymphocytes can lead to lymphomas, these usually present with lymph node enlargement and may affect organs such as the spleen and liver. The lack of lymphadenopathy, along with lytic bone lesions and elevated gamma globulins, makes a lymphocytic origin unlikely.

Histiocytes (Option C): Histiocyte-related disorders, such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, usually present with distinct clinical findings like skin rashes, enlarged liver and spleen, and blood cell deficiencies.

Monocytes (Option D): Monocytes, a type of white blood cell, can mature into macrophages and dendritic cells as part of the immune system. Disorders of monocytes usually show features such as skin involvement, gum enlargement, and blood abnormalities. However, the rise in gamma globulins is more indicative of a plasma cell disorder.

Capillary (Option C): Capillary blood can be used for bedside glucometers but is less accurate for laboratory diagnosis.

question_text: All of the statements regarding 'beer potomania' are true, except?
option_a: It occurs in alcoholics whose sole nutrient is beer
option_b: Typically urine Na+ concentration is > 20 mM
option_c: AVP levels are expected to be suppressed in this condition
option_d: Resumption of a normal diet and/or saline hydration will correct the causative deficit
explanation:
Hyponatremia can occasionally occur in patients with a very low intake of dietary solutes. Classically, this occurs in alcoholics whose sole nutrient is beer, hence the diagnostic label of beer potomania; beer is very low in protein and salt content, containing only 1-2 mM of Na+. The syndrome has also been described in nonalcoholic patients with highly restricted solute intake due to nutrient-restricted diets, e.g., extreme vegetarian diets. Patients with hyponatremia due to low solute intake typically present with a very low urine osmolality (< 100-200 mOsm/kg) with a urine Na+ concentration that is< 10-20 mM. The fundamental abnormality is the inadequate dietary intake of solutes; the reduced urinary solute excretion limits water excretion such that hyponatremia ensues after relatively modest polydipsia. AVP levels have not been reported in patients with beer potomania but are expected to be suppressed or rapidly suppressible with saline hydration; this fits with the overly rapid correction in plasma Na+ concentration that can be seen with saline hydration. Resumption of a normal diet and/or saline hydration will also correct the causative deficit in urinary solute excretion, such that patients with beer potomania typically correct their plasma Na+ concentration promptly after admission to the hospital.

Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 343

question_text: Elective splenectomy is preferred in which of the given conditions?
explanation:
Explanation:

Hereditary spherocytosis is a genetic condition where red blood cells are sphere-shaped rather than biconcave, and the main treatment is elective splenectomy.

  • In hereditary spherocytosis, splenectomy is highly beneficial since the spleen is chiefly responsible for destroying spherocytes.
  • The timing depends on disease severity: In severe cases it is done electively at 4-6 years, in moderate cases, it may be postponed until adolescence, while mild cases are usually managed with folic acid supplementation alone.

Explanations of other options:

G6PD deficiency (Option A): In G6PD deficiency, splenectomy can aggravate anaemia since the spleen plays a key role in clearing damaged red blood cells. Management mainly focuses on preventing exposure to oxidative triggers and treating acute hemolytic crises.

Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (Option B): In paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), hemolysis results from a complement system defect, making stem cell transplantation the only curative option. Splenectomy is not useful since the red cell destruction is complement-driven and occurs in the entire circulation.

Hairy cell leukaemia (Option D): In hairy cell leukaemia, the primary treatment is chemotherapy, while splenectomy is reserved for patients with significant splenomegaly or those who do not respond to standard therapy, rather than being the first-line approach.

question_text:
A 56-year-old man presents to his physician complaining of severe fatigue. He began to feel increasingly tired about 6 months ago, but believes that his fatigue has been worsening over the past 3 weeks. He also notes that he has had a nonproductive cough for about 2 weeks, and has experienced several episodes of drenching night sweats. On examination, he has several large bruises on his extremities but recalls no injuries. Abdominal examination reveals massive enlargement of both the liver and the spleen, without any lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests show:
WBC: 12,000/mm3 (Neutrophils 58% Eosinophils 7% Lymphocytes 30% Monocytes 0% Basophils 5%)
Hemoglobin 7.5 mg/dL
Platelet count 18,000/mm3
Peripheral blood smear reveals irregular nuclei and cell membranes, as well as cytoplasmic projections.
What is the patient's most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hairy cell leukemia is a rare malignancy of B lymphocytes. It is most common between the ages of 50 and 60 years, and shows a 5:1 male predominance. Patients generally present with the symptoms of pancytopenia, namely fatigue, easy bruising, and recurrent infection, as well as splenomegaly (and hepatomegaly in 50% of patients). Mycobacterial infections are common due to a striking monocytopenia that is nearly universal in these patients. Lymphadenopathy is rare. Examination of the spleen shows infiltration of the red pulp by these cells, which demonstrate the characteristic 'hairy cell' cytoplasmic projections and are typically tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase positive. Although patients may demonstrate markedly abnormal blood counts at presentation, > 90% of patients will live longer than 10 years with treatment.

Option A: Acute lymphoid leukemia (ALL) affects children much more often than adults. It may result in pancytopenia, as is seen in this patient, but would not cause such a striking monocytopenia. Immature blasts are evident on the peripheral smear of ALL patients.

Option B: Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura is an antibody-mediated thrombocytopenia caused by antibody response to platelets. It does not affect other cell lines, so is an unlikely cause of this patient's illness.

Option D: Infectious mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus) may affect patients of any age, although it is most common in adolescents. It may cause splenomegaly and a peripheral smear not unlike that shown. It does not, however, cause pancytopenia, a hallmark of hairy cell leukemia.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 110 pg. 856

question_text: A 71-year-old man is admitted to hospital in a comatose condition. His wife gives a history of past episodes of sweating and palpitations, confusion, and occasional abnormal behavior that improves with intake of glucose.. On examination his pulse is 92 bpm and his blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg. His plasma catecholamine level is normal and blood glucose is 65 mg/dl. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• This patient is suffering from hypoglycemic episodes as evidenced by the classical autonomic and neuroglycopenic symptoms which gets relieved with intake of glucose. (Whipple’s triad).
  • Insulinomas may be sporadic or associated with MEN1 syndrome.
  • Pheochromocytoma, either isolated or as part of the MEN-II syndrome, is unlikely as his blood pressure and catecholamine levels are normal.
  • Pseudodementia is associated with severe depressive illness. Memory impairment, slowed thinking and lack of spontaneity are characteristic features. Hypoglycemia is not associated with this disorder.

Hypoglycemia may be documented by Whipple's triad:

  1. symptoms consistent with hypoglycemia
  2. a low plasma glucose concentration measured with a precise method
  3. relief of symptoms after the plasma glucose level is raised. The lower limit of the fasting plasma glucose concentration is normally ~70 mg/dL (~3.9 mmol/L), but lower venous glucose levels occur normally, late after a meal, during pregnancy, and during prolonged fasting (>24 h).

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20th edition Page number:608, 2748, 2887

question_text: Which cell is primarily involved in causing structural damage to joints in RA?
explanation:
Osteoclasts are the cells that are ultimately responsible for the structural damage in RA.

The chief pathology of RA is bone not only bone destruction, but also decreased bone formation.

The first cells that are activated are CD4 + T cells. Macrophages are the chief inflammatory cells involved. But the bone damage is mediated by activated osteoclasts.

Bone erosions: The damage is typically located at the regions where the synovium is inserted to the periosteal surface at the edge of bone, at the rim of the articular cartilage. This also explains the development of bone erosions at the radial aspect of the MCP.

Juxtra-articular osteopenia is another pathology that is seen in the adjacent bone due to inflammation of marrow. It results in substantial thinning of bone trabeculae.

TNFα inhibits bone formation by inhibiting osteoblasts.

question_text: A 68-year-old man presents with chronic back pain, persistent fatigue, and a recent history of multiple urinary tract infections over the past three months. Laboratory tests reveal an elevated ESR, and his skull X-ray shows characteristic findings. Which of the following diagnostic tests would be most appropriate to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of chronic back pain, fatigue, and characteristic skull X-ray findings suggests multiple myeloma.

Investigations for Multiple Myeloma:

Hematological Analysis:

  • Anemia is common, and ESR is usually elevated.
  • In rare cases, plasma cell leukemia may occur with plasma cell counts exceeding 2000 cells/μL.
  • Serum calcium and blood urea nitrogen levels may be elevated.
  • Serum alkaline phosphatase is typically normal.
  • Peripheral blood smear may show rouleaux formation.
  • Albumin/globulin ratio is decreased.
  • β2 microglobulin levels are increased.
  • Renal function tests may reveal elevated creatinine and uric acid levels.

Imaging:

  • Chest and bone X-rays often show lytic lesions or diffuse osteopenia.
  • MRI (option A) is used to assess the extent of bone marrow infiltration and detect spinal cord or nerve root compression in patients with pain.
  • PET/CT (option B&C) scans help evaluate bone damage and identify extramedullary disease sites.

Serum or Urine Protein Electrophoresis:

  • The presence of an M spike (monoclonal immunoglobulin) is a hallmark of monoclonal gammopathies.
  • Serum Protein Electrophoresis (SPEP) is a preliminary and key test for diagnosing multiple myeloma. It separates serum proteins into albumin, α1, α2, β, and γ globulins. A sharp peak in the gamma region indicates monoclonal gammopathy.

Other Important Tests:

  • Anion gap calculation: Often decreased.
  • Serum free light chain assay: Increased in multiple myeloma.
  • Immunofixation: Identifies specific light chain subtypes.
  • 24-hour urine collection: Detects Bence Jones proteins (free light chains).
  • Fat pad biopsy: Used to detect amyloid deposits if suspected.
  • Flow cytometry: Identifies CD138+ plasma cells in bone marrow.
  • Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH): Detects chromosomal abnormalities such as chromosome 17 deletions and translocations associated with poor prognosis.
  • Bone marrow biopsy: Shows plasmacytosis greater than 10%.

Diagnostic Criteria:

Multiple myeloma diagnosis is based on the presence of clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow along with CRAB criteria -hypercalcemia, renal dysfunction, anemia, and bone lesions.

question_text: A patient underwent a cholecystectomy, during which black pigmented gallstones were identified. The patient's past medical history includes multiple episodes of shortness of breath and chest pain requiring hospitalization. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

Clinical Association: Black Pigmented Gallstones and Sickle Cell Anemia

  • Black pigmented gallstones are commonly associated with conditions involving increased red blood cell (RBC) turnover.
  • Sickle cell anemia is a genetic disorder characterized by the production of abnormal hemoglobin (hemoglobin S).
  • Hemoglobin S causes sickle-shaped red blood cells, which are:
    • Prone to destruction
    • Lead to chronic hemolytic anemia

Pathophysiology and Clinical Features of Sickle Cell Anemia

  • Hemolysis and Gallstone Formation:
    • Repeated hemolysis results in high levels of bilirubin.
    • Excess bilirubin leads to the formation of black pigmented gallstones.
  • Clinical History:
    • Patients often present with:
      • Recurrent shortness of breath
      • Chest pain
    • These symptoms are likely due to:
      • Vaso-occlusive crises
      • Acute chest syndrome
        → Both are hallmark complications of sickle cell disease.
  • Vaso-occlusion and Systemic Effects:
    • Sickled cells obstruct blood flow, causing vaso-occlusion.
    • Vaso-occlusive crises lead to acute painful episodes that:
      • Can affect any organ system
      • Result in complications such as:
        • Acute chest syndrome
        • Stroke
        • Chronic organ damage

Summary:

  • The combination of:
    • Chronic hemolytic anemia
    • Elevated bilirubin
    • Black pigmented gallstones
    • Recurrent vaso-occlusive symptoms
  • Strongly suggests a diagnosis of sickle cell anemia.

Explanation of other options:

Beta Thalassemia (Option B): Beta thalassemia is another hemoglobinopathy characterized by reduced or absent synthesis of the beta chains of hemoglobin. It can also lead to chronic hemolysis but is less likely to cause the same type of gallstones as seen in sickle cell anemia.

Hb Punjab (Option C): Hb Punjab is a variant of hemoglobin resulting from a mutation. It is generally benign but can be part of compound heterozygous states with other hemoglobinopathies. It is less likely to be associated with the clinical scenario described.

Sideroblastic Anemia (Option D): Sideroblastic anemia involves the presence of ringed sideroblasts in the bone marrow and is primarily a disorder of ineffective iron incorporation into hemoglobin. It does not typically present with the hemolytic features or complications like those seen in sickle cell anemia.

Key Takeaways:

Black pigmented gallstones in a patient with recurrent episodes of shortness of breath and chest pain strongly suggest sickle cell anemia, which is associated with chronic hemolysis and bilirubin stone formation.

question_text: A 56-year-old patient presents with fatigue, tingling sensation in the arms, weight loss, and a history of polyuria. A bone marrow biopsy was performed, and the findings are shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
option_a: Subacute combined degeneration due to cobalamin deficiency
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

The presence of plasmacytosis in the bone marrow, along with symptoms like polyuria (from hypercalcemia), neuropathy, fatigue, and weight loss, strongly indicates multiple myeloma.

Bone marrow biopsy findings: Numerous plasma cells with eccentric nuclei, perinuclear clearing (hof), and basophilic cytoplasm consistent with plasmacytosis.

  • Multiple myeloma (MM) is a plasma cell malignancy characterized by monoclonal proliferation of abnormal plasma cells in the bone marrow, leading to overproduction of abnormal immunoglobulin or light chains (M protein).
  • Key Clinical Clues in This Case:
    • Fatigue and weight loss → Constitutional symptoms
    • Tingling in arms → Neuropathy (common due to paraproteinemia or amyloidosis)
    • Polyuria → Due to hypercalcemia (part of CRAB criteria)
    • Bone marrow biopsy → Shows >10% abnormal plasma cells (as seen in the image)
  • Diagnostic Features of MM:
    • Bone marrow plasmacytosis >10% (as seen on histology)
    • CRAB Criteria:
      • C: Hypercalcemia
      • R: Renal dysfunction
      • A: Anemia
      • B: Bone lesions (lytic lesions on imaging)
    • Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP): M-spike
    • Urine: Bence Jones protein
    • Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation
    • Flow cytometry: CD138+ plasma cells
    • FISH: High-risk cytogenetics (e.g., 17p deletion)
    • Imaging:
      • Chest and bone radiographs: Lytic lesions/diffuse osteopenia
      • MRI: Extent of bone marrow infiltration and cord or root compression in patients with pain syndrome
      • PET/CT: Assess bone damage, extramedullary sites of the disease

Explanation of other options:

Subacute combined degeneration due to cobalamin deficiency (Option A): Presents with neurological symptoms like paresthesia and loss of proprioception but does not cause hypercalcemia or plasma cell proliferation in bone marrow.

Subacute degeneration due to diabetes (Option C): Refers to diabetic neuropathy, which causes tingling and numbness but no marrow abnormalities or CRAB features.

Megaloblastic anemia (Option D): Results from B12 or folate deficiency, causes macrocytic anemia and neurological symptoms, but not hypercalcemia or increased plasma cells on biopsy.

question_text: Which of the following situations would be in keeping with a diagnosis of monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance (MGUS)?
option_a: A light chain only paraprotein with immunoparesis for immunoglobulin G (lgG) and immunoglobulin A (lgA)
option_b: A low-level lgG paraprotein associated with a single lytic lesion in the femur
option_c: A low-level lgG paraprotein with normal serum free light chain ratio
option_d: An lgA paraprotein in someone presenting with acute renal failure
explanation:
In MGUS, the paraprotein is at a low level and with no evidence of end-organ damage, i.e. no evidence of anemia, bone disease or renal disease. lgM paraproteins are associated with low-grade lymphomas, most notably lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, but can present as MGUS if there is no clinical evidence of lymphoma. A normal serum free light chain ratio in MGUS carries a very good prognosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 111 pg. 871

question_text: A 46-year-old male presents with lower back pain and dysuria. Investigations reveal normocytic normochromic anaemia and hypercalcemia. Serum protein electrophoresis shows an M-spike in the gamma region. Which of the following tests is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Clinical features of hypercalcemia, renal dysfunction, anaemia, and bone lesions, along with the presence of a Gamma region M spike in serum electrophoresis, point towards the diagnosis of Multiple myeloma.

Multiple myeloma

A malignant proliferation of plasma cells producing a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M protein) with characteristic CRAB features.

  • C: Hypercalcemia
  • R: Renal dysfunction
  • A: Anemia
  • B: Bone lesions

Standard investigation workup in multiple Myeloma

Explanation of other options:

Liver function test (Option A): Liver function tests may sometimes be abnormal in multiple myeloma but are neither specific nor diagnostic and are mainly used to assess hepatic involvement or complications.

Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (Option C): The urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio helps evaluate kidney function and proteinuria but does not detect the characteristic Bence Jones proteins of myeloma.

Heat and acetic acid test (Option D): The heat and acetic acid test was historically used to detect Bence Jones proteins in urine, which precipitate on heating and redissolve at higher temperatures. It is now largely obsolete, replaced by more sensitive and specific methods like electrophoresis and immunofixation.

question_text: A 68-year-old male came to the physician with complaints of chronic back pain, easy fatigability, and a past history of multiple urinary tract infections in the last 3 months. His ESR is elevated, x-ray of his skull is shown below. Which of the following investigations is useful for diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture (bone pain, fatigue, recurrent infections) with lytic bone lesions is highly suggestive of multiple myeloma. The most useful initial diagnostic test is serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP), which detects the presence of a monoclonal (M) protein or "M-spike" produced by the malignant plasma cells.

Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell disorder characterized by uncontrolled proliferation of plasma cells in the bone marrow, often presenting with anemia, bone pain, recurrent infections, and renal impairment. Skull X-ray classically shows 'raindrop' lytic lesions.

Screening and Diagnostic Tests:

  • Serum and urine protein electrophoresis:Detect monoclonal M-protein spike; urine may show Bence Jones proteins.
  • Hematology:Anemia is common; ESR elevated, rare plasma cell leukemia (>2000 plasma cells/μL).
  • Biochemistry:Hypercalcemia, increased creatinine and urea, decreased albumin, decreased A/G ratio, elevated β2-microglobulin. Serum alkaline phosphatase usually normal.
  • Peripheral smear:Rouleaux formation.

Imaging:

  • X-ray:Lytic lesions, osteopenia.
  • MRI:Assesses marrow infiltration, cord or nerve compression.
  • PET/CT:Detects bone damage and extramedullary involvement.

Additional Tests:

  • Serum free light chain assay:Elevated kappa or lambda chains.
  • Immunofixation:Determines light chain subtype.
  • 24-hour urine:Bence Jones protein excretion.
  • Fat pad biopsy:Detects amyloid deposits.
  • Flow cytometry:CD138+ plasma cells.
  • FISH:Detects chromosomal abnormalities; del(17p) and translocations indicate poor prognosis.
  • Bone marrow biopsy:Plasmacytosis >10% (often >30%), presence of flame cells, Mott cells, Russell bodies, Dutcher bodies.

Explanation of other options:

MRI brain and Head CT scan with contrast (Option A and C) : It is not first-line for myeloma diagnosis. MRI spine is useful for evaluating cord compression from vertebral lesions.

PET scan (Option B): Used for staging and assessing metabolic activity of lesions, but not the primary test for establishing the diagnosis.
All options A, B, and C are imaging studies. While important for staging, the diagnosis is confirmed by laboratory tests demonstrating a clonal plasma cell disorder.

Key Takeaways:

  • Serum protein electrophoresis is a key screening test for multiple myeloma to identify a monoclonal paraprotein.
  • Lytic bone lesions on X-ray are a classic feature.

question_text: A patient presents with fatigue, pallor, and weakness. Laboratory tests show low hemoglobin with a normal reticulocyte count. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

A low hemoglobin level with a normal reticulocyte count indicates an inadequate bone marrow response specifically in the erythroid lineage, suggesting a diagnosis of pure red cell aplasia.

Pure Red Cell Aplasia

A condition characterized by anemia, reticulocytopenia, and absent or rare erythroid precursor cells in bone marrow with normal white cell and platelet production

  • In adults, PRCA is usually acquired.
  • A congenital form, Diamond-Blackfan anemia, presents at birth or early childhood, often responds to glucocorticoids, and is caused by mutations in ribosomal protein genes.
  • Temporary red cell failure can occur in transient aplastic crisis (e.g., acute parvovirus infection in hemolytic anemias) or transient erythroblastopenia of childhood in otherwise healthy children.

Clinical associations:

  • A minority of cases are associated with thymoma.
  • More commonly, PRCA can manifest in large granular lymphocytosis or complicate chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).
  • Deletion of a ribosomal protein gene in 5q- syndrome may cause MDS with acquired PRCA.
  • PRCA can rarely result from idiosyncratic drug reactions, subcutaneous EPO therapy (via neutralizing antibodies), or isoagglutinin antibodies after allogeneic stem cell transplant.
  • Most cases are thought to involve T-cell-mediated inhibition of erythropoiesis.

Persistent Parvovirus B19 Infection:

  • Parvovirus B19 can cause transient aplastic crises in patients with high RBC demand or persistent infection in immunodeficient individuals.
  • Bone marrow shows red cell aplasia with giant pronormoblasts, the cytopathic hallmark of infection.
  • The virus targets erythroid progenitor cells via the P antigen, causing direct cytotoxicity and anemia when RBC demand is high.
  • In immunocompetent individuals, infection is usually self-limited; skin and joint symptoms are immune-mediated, and temporary red cell suppression is often clinically silent.

Management:

  • Identify and treat underlying cause
  • Supportive Care: Long-term survival is possible with erythrocyte transfusions and iron chelation.
  • Persistent B19 Infection: Typically responds to intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy.
  • Acquired PRCA: Most patients respond well to immunosuppressive therapy, including glucocorticoids, cyclosporine, antithymocyte globulin (ATG), azathioprine, and cyclophosphamide.

Explanation of other options:

Aplastic Anemia (Option A): Aplastic anemia presents with pancytopenia, affecting all blood cell lines due to bone marrow failure.

Iron Deficiency Anemia (Option C): Typically shows microcytic, hypochromic red blood cells with an elevated reticulocyte count as the bone marrow attempts to compensate for the iron deficiency. The normal reticulocyte count in this scenario makes iron deficiency less likely.

Hemolytic Anemia (Option D): Hemolytic anemia is characterized by increased destruction of red blood cells, leading to an elevated reticulocyte count as the bone marrow responds to the increased demand.

question_text:
A 30-year-old woman with a history of recurrent headaches presents for evaluation. Laboratory investigations reveal normal hemoglobin and total white blood cell count, but a significantly elevated platelet count. Bone marrow aspiration demonstrates increased numbers of megakaryocytes, and genetic testing identifies the presence of a JAK2 mutation.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of a significantly elevated platelet count, JAK2 mutation, and increased megakaryocytes on bone marrow examination strongly suggests a diagnosis of Essential Thrombocytosis (ET).

Essential Thrombocythemia (ET)

ET is a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm primarily characterized by excessive platelet production.

Etiology:

  • Most cases are driven by mutations in one of three genes:
    • JAK2,
    • CALR, or
    • MPL (thrombopoietin receptor).
  • Additional less common mutations: SH2B3, TP53, IDH2, 20q deletion, etc.

Pathophysiology:

  • The JAK2 V617F mutation (valine replaced by phenylalanine) leads to continuous activation of cytokine signaling pathways, promoting abnormal blood cell proliferation.
  • CALR mutations alter protein function, affecting cell growth regulation.
  • MPL mutations disrupt thrombopoietin receptor signaling, promoting excessive platelet production.
  • Extreme thrombocytosis (>1 million/μL) may paradoxically cause bleeding due to acquired von Willebrand disease.

Clinical Features & Risks:

  • Persistent thrombocytosis.
  • Megakaryocytic proliferation in the bone marrow.
  • Increased risk of:
    • Thrombosis (arterial or venous),
    • Hemorrhagic events, and
    • Progression to myelofibrosis or acute leukemia in some cases.

Diagnosis:

  • Platelet count >450,000/μL
  • Presence of a driver mutation (JAK2, CALR, or MPL).
  • Bone marrow biopsy typically shows megakaryocyte hyperplasia with large, mature forms.

Management:

  • Cytoreductive therapy (e.g., hydroxyurea) may be used in high-risk patients to lower platelet counts.
  • Aspirin is often prescribed to reduce thrombotic risk unless contraindicated.
  • Regular monitoring of blood counts and molecular markers is essential for ongoing care.

Explanation for other options:

Polycythemia Vera (Option A): This myeloproliferative neoplasm is marked by excessive red blood cell production. Although white blood cells and platelets may also be elevated due to stimulation of the myeloid and megakaryocyte lineages, the hallmark feature is an increased red cell mass.

Primary Myelofibrosis (Option C): A chronic myeloproliferative disorder that leads to progressive fibrosis of the bone marrow. This fibrotic transformation disrupts normal hematopoiesis, ultimately causing bone marrow failure.

Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia (Option D): A myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by marked overproduction of granulocytes. It is defined by the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, resulting from a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 - t(9;22)(q34;q11.2) - which creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK539709/

question_text: Tumor that follows rule of 10 is-

These include the MEN-2A & MEN-2B syndromes, type I neurofibromatosis, von Hippel-Lindau syndrome & Sturge-Weber syndrome.  10% of pheochromocytomas are extra-adrenal, occurring in sites such as organ of Zuckerkandl & carotid body, where these chromaffin-negative tumors are usually called paragangliomas to distinguish them from pheochromocytomas.  10% of nonfamilial adrenal pheochromocytomas are bilateral; this figure may rise to 70% in cases that are associated with familial syndromes.  10% of adrenal pheochromocytomas are biologically malignant, although the associated hypertension represents a serious & potentially lethal complication of even "benign" tumors. 10% of adrenal pheochromocytomas arise in childhood, usually the familial subtypes, and with a strong male preponderance. question_text: You review a 55-year-old woman in the clinic. She has a thyroid mass, which was diagnosed as lymphoma on core biopsy. Which of the following is the best choice therapy in this case?
explanation:
• Radioiodine therapy is useful in management of differentiated thyroid cancer (papillary and follicular thyroid cancer). But it is not useful in lymphoma as the cells don't concentrate iodine.
  • Iodine 131 is a radioactive isotope of iodine (RAI) that is selectively concentrated in the thyroid tissue and metabolized by the same pathways as naturally occurring iodine.
  • This, together with its long half-life (8 days), allows it to deliver high doses of radiation to the thyroid gland (b-radiation) sufficient to destroy thyroid follicular cells.
  • So, 131I is used in the treatment of Grave's disease, toxic multi-nodular goiter and differentiated thyroid cancer.
  • External beam radiotherapy is used in the treatment of thyroid lymphoma, but not all tumours are responsive and treatment may only be effective for a short time.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 2952

question_text:
A 76-year-old woman with thyroid cancer comes to see you.
Which of the following has the worst prognosis in thyroid cancer?
option_a: Papillary carcinoma with lymph node metastases
explanation:
• Thyroid lymphoma represents only 5% of all thyroid malignancy. It is usually in women age 55-75 with chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis.
  • These may be positive serum antithyroglobulin or anti TPO antibodies.
  • The prognosis depends on the cell type and the extent of disease beyond the neck.
  • Primary thyroid cancer involving the C cells is medullary thyroid cancer which in 80% of cases is sporadic but in 20% of cases is familial Familial cases are associated with RET gene mutation
  • The other forms of thyroid cancer are of the follicular epithelium.
  • Papillary carcinoma (70% of thyroid malignancies) is slow growing and may be indolent for many years.
  • Follicular carcinoma (15% of thyroid malignancies) carries a prognosis dependent on its invasiveness.
  • Of all thyroid cancers, even those that have spread, anaplastic carcinoma (1% of thyroid cancers) carries the worst prognosis. It is very fast growing and invades the adjacent structures usually causing death by asphyxiation.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 2952

question_text: Cold agglutinin is -
explanation: Ans. is 'b' i.e., IgM Cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia This form of hemolytic anemia is caused by cold agglutinin IgM antibodies. Antibodies react with RBC at 0° to 4°C. Both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis may occur. IgM antibody bind to RBC and fix complement on RBC before complement mediated hemolysis occur. This transient reaction with IgM deposit C3b on RBC. C3b acts as an opsonin is that enhances the phagocytosis of RBCs in mononuclear phagocytic system of liver and spleen → extravascular hemolysis. However if IgM remains attached to RBC, sustained activation of complement results in formation of large amount of membrane - attack complex that destroys RBC directly --> Intravascular hemolysis. Causes of cold agglutinin immunohemolytic anemia : - Mycoplasma infection, I MN, CMV, Influenza, HIV, Malignant lymphoma

question_text: Which cytogenetic abnormality in CLL associated with good prognosis
explanation:
The presence of sole del(13)(q14.3) is associated with more indolent disease, prolonged survival, and good response to traditional therapies. Usually, this abnormality is not seen on banded karyotype analysis, and when present on karyotype, it indicates a larger deletion involving the retinoblastoma gene , which negates the favorable prognosis associated with this marker. Trisomy 12 has a more intermediate prognosis. The del(11)(q23.3) results in deletion of the ATM gene and is associated with bulky lymphadenopathy and aggressive disease in young patients, with inferior prognosis, and more rapid progression to symptomatic disease. The del(17)(p13.1) results in loss of one allele of the tumor suppressor TP53 and is associated with the poorest prognosis in CLL with rapid disease progression, poor response to traditional therapies, and shorter survival.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 107, Pg: 835

question_text:
A 39-year-old woman gives an eight month history of bloody diarrhoea. On average she has six bowel motions per day with associated urgency. She also reports weight loss of approximately 3 kg. On examination she is dehydrated and tachycardic. There is evidence of pallor and abdominal examination reveals left-sided tenderness.
Which of the following pathological features would you expect to find given the likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Chronic bloody diarrhoea in a young patient is very suggestive of a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis (UC).

The time course is too long for an infective cause and whilst Crohn's disease (CD) may cause a colitis, this is less frequent. CD often presents watery diarrhoea.

The predominant left sided symptoms (urgency and anatomical distribution of the tendency) should also point towards UC.

The answer here therefore is diffuse mucosal inflammation.

All the remaining options are histological features of Crohn's disease.

  • Transmural inflammation is seen in CD.
  • Sub serosal lymphoid aggregates are seen in CD

  • Upper endoscopy is generally required to make an accurate diagnosis.

Esophagitis in HIV:

  • Esophagitis in individuals with HIV may present with symptoms like odynophagia (painful swallowing) and retrosternal (behind the breastbone) pain.
  • Upper endoscopy (esophagogastroduodenoscopy or EGD) is often necessary to accurately diagnose the cause of esophagitis in HIV patients.
  • Possible causes of esophagitis in HIV include Candida, CMV (Cytomegalovirus), and HSV (Herpes Simplex Virus). Each of these infections can have distinct characteristics.
  • CMV infection typically results in a single large ulcer in the esophagus.
  • HSV infection is more commonly associated with multiple small ulcers in the esophagus.
  • Additionally, esophageal involvement in HIV can also be related to Kaposi's Sarcoma (KS) and lymphoma.
  • Sometimes, there may be large, painful esophageal ulcers of unclear origin, and these may respond to treatment with thalidomide.

Gastric Issues in HIV:

  • While achlorhydria (lack of stomach acid production) is a common problem in individuals with HIV, other gastric (stomach) problems are generally rare.
  • Neoplastic conditions involving the stomach in HIV-infected individuals can include Kaposi's Sarcoma (KS) and lymphoma.

question_text: Following are causes of hypokalemia. Which one of the four items listed does not cause hypokalemia?
explanation:
Hypokalemia may result from renal losses, gastrointestinal losses, or intracellular redistribution of K. Renal losses that result in hypokalemia include K-wasting diuretics, osmotic diuresis, glucocorticoid excess, mineralocorticoid excess, and leukemia. Gastrointestinal losses that result in hypokalemia include diarrhea, vomiting, nasogastric suction, and laxative abuse. Redistribution of K may occur, resulting in hypokalemia, in patients who have been administered insulin or glucose, in patients treated with beta-adrenergic stimulation, and in patients with alkalosis. Acidosis, on the other hand, causes hyperkalemia making answer B the choice that does not result in hypokalemia.

question_text: What is the diagnosis of a 50-year-old man who presents with symptoms of anemia, fever, and recurrent nosebleeds? The patient has hepatosplenomegaly and lab investigations indicate a hemoglobin level of 6g/dL, a total leukocyte count of 40,000/cu.mm with 10% blasts, and a platelet count of 12,000/cu.mm. Further investigation reveals the presence of t(8;21) in the blasts.
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation of pancytopenia (anemia, thrombocytopenia), hepatosplenomegaly, high white count with circulating blasts, and the specific cytogenetic abnormality t(8;21) is diagnostic for Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML). The t(8;21) translocation is a common and specific finding in a subtype of AML.

Explanation of other options:

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) (Option A): More common in children and is characterized by lymphoblasts, not myeloblasts. It is associated with different cytogenetic markers.

Preleukemia (Myelodysplastic Syndrome)(Option C): Involves dysplastic hematopoiesis and cytopenias but does not typically have a high blast count (>20%).

Aleukemic leukemia (Option D): A rare form where the white cell count is normal or low, which contradicts the high leukocyte count in this case.

Key Takeaways:

  • AML presents with signs of bone marrow failure (anemia, infection, bleeding) and organ infiltration.
  • Cytogenetic studies like t(8;21) are crucial for diagnosis, classification, and prognosis in AML.

question_text: A 60 year old man is investigated for weight loss and dyspepsia. Endoscopic examination reveals an ulcerated lesion in stomach.   2. Non cardio gastric adenocarcinoma
  3. Low grade gastric B cell MALT lymphoma

H Pylori provides protection against Reflux esophagitis and its sequelae like Barret esophagus and esophageal adenocarcinoma.

The diagnosis here is a gastric MALT (Mucosa Associated Lymphoid Tissue) tumour.

  • These are usually marginal zone B cell lymphomas associated an excellent prognosis.
  • MALT lymphoma is the third most common type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
  • MALT lymphomas are most commonly found in the gastrointestinal tract (stomach is the commonest). But they can be found in any extranodal site.

Low grade gastric MALT tumours are associated with Helicobacter Pylori infection and respond in over 80% of cases to helicobacter eradication.

A proportion of patients will not respond to eradication therapy alone and will go on to more conventional anti-lymphoma therapies such as cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, nucleoside analogues or radiotherapy.

question_text: Which of the following mutations is associated with the Philadelphia chromosome?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The Philadelphia chromosome is a cytogenetic abnormality caused by a reciprocal translocation between chromosome 9 and chromosome 22.
  • This translocation places the ABL oncogene from chromosome 9, which encodes a tyrosine kinase, next to the BCR (breakpoint cluster region) gene on chromosome 22.
  • The resulting BCR-ABL fusion gene produces a protein that activates signal transduction pathways, driving uncontrolled cell growth independent of normal external signals.
  • The Philadelphia chromosome is associated with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).

Explanation of other options:

Inversion (Option A): Inversion occurs when a segment of DNA breaks away from the chromosome, flips around, and reattaches in the reverse orientation. A mutation caused by inversion of the intron 22 sequence, which is present in about 40% of severe Hemophilia A cases.

Insertion (Option B): Insertion involves the addition of extra nucleotides into a DNA sequence, which can cause frameshift mutations. For example: Cri-du-chat syndrome is caused by a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5.

Deletion (Option D): Results in the loss of a segment of DNA from a chromosome.

question_text:
A 60-year-old man presents with fatigue, pallor, weight loss, and left hypochondrial heaviness. Splenomegaly is present.
Hemogram: Hb 10 gm/dl, WBC 165,000/cu.mm, Platelets 3 lakhs/mm2.
Peripheral smear: 15% metamyelocytes, 30% promyelocytes, 45% myeloblasts.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Marked leukocytosis with left-shifted myeloid precursors and splenomegaly point to CML, caused by BCR-ABL1 fusion gene (t(9;22), Philadelphia chromosome).

Pathophysiology:

BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase promotes uncontrolled proliferation and inhibits apoptosis.

Phases:

  • Chronic: Blasts <10%.
  • Accelerated: Blasts 10-19%, basophilia >20%.
  • Blast crisis: Blasts >20%, AML-like.

Investigations:

  • FISH/PCR for BCR-ABL1 (IOC).
  • NAP score: Decreased.
  • Bone marrow: Hypercellular with granulocytic proliferation.

Treatment:

  • Imatinib, Dasatinib, Nilotinib (TKIs, DOC).
  • HSCT: For resistant/blast crisis.

Explanation of Other Options:

Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (Option A): Characterized by lymphocytosis (increased lymphocytes) rather than myeloid precursors. Peripheral smear shows smudge cells and mature lymphocytes, not myeloblasts.

Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (Option C): Mainly involves lymphoblasts, not myeloid cells. More common in children, though it can also occur in adults.

Acute Myeloid Leukemia (Option D): Diagnosed when >20% blasts are present in the bone marrow or blood. In this case, 45% myeloblasts are seen only in the peripheral smear, making AML less likely. AML usually presents acutely with fever, bleeding, and pancytopenia, whereas CML has a chronic course.

question_text: A 50 years old male presented with fatigability for one year. Evaluation showed mild anemia, massive splenomegaly. Hb- 10gm%, ILC of 120 x 10(3), platelet 500 x 10(3), neutrophils 60, basophils 4, eosinophils 6, lymphocytes 15. Also seen were myeloblasts, myelocytes metamyelocytes and bands. M: E ratio 8:1. What is the most sensitive investigation?
explanation:
• The age, the symptoms and the presence of massive splenomegaly points towards a myeloproliferative disorder.
  • From the peripheral smear, we can see that there is an increase in neutrophils with a shift to left having band forms, myelocytes and metamyelocytes and an increase in myeloid erythroid ratio classical of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia.
  • The cytogenetic abnormality seen in 90% of patients with CML is the reciprocal translocation between chromosome 9 and 22.
  • This translocation can be identified by the technique of FISH and PCR.

Immunophenotyping is a process used to identify the cells based on the antigens on their surface. It cannot be used for identifying chromosomal anomalies.

FDG PET is the imaging technique used to identify areas of increased metabolism as in malignancy or infections. It can help us to identify the organ involved, but doesn't help in identifying the type of disease.

Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase measures the alkaline phosphatase in neutrophils.

  • Its value is high in leukemoid reaction, tissue damage, steroid use, OCP, aplastic anemia, hodgkin's lymphoma and Down syndrome.
  • It is elevated in myeloproliferative disorders, but is low in the chronic phase of CML. It is low in PNH and hereditary hypophosphatemia.

In CLL, ~60% of patients have IGHV that is ≥2% mutated from germline. This may indicate a more mature, postgerminal center progenitor, and is typically associated with a more indolent(silent/safe) disease course.

Conversely, ~40% of patients will have IGHV <2% mutated from germline, which is associated with more rapid progression of disease and short survival prior to the era of therapeutics that target BCR.

question_text: IGHV mutation in CLL is
explanation:
Immunoglobulin heavy chains undergo somatic hypermutation. In CLL, ~60% of patients have IGHV that is ≥2% mutated from germline. This may indicate a more mature, post germinal center progenitor, and is typically associated with a more indolent disease course. Conversely, ~40% of patients will have IGHV <2% mutated from germline, which is associated with more rapid progression of disease and short survival prior to the era of therapeutics that target BCR. Unfavorable biologic properties including enhanced telomerase activity, overexpression of activation-induced cytidine deaminase, increased nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) activity, high-risk genomic mutations (e.g., NOTCH1, SF3B1, TP53, ATM), and clonal evolution are also associated with IGHV unmutated disease.

question_text: Chemotherapeutic Agent of Choice for the treatment of CML is:
explanation: Answer is A (Imatinib): Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (Imatinib) are the chemotherapeutic agents for choice in the management of CML. Tyrosine Kinase inhibitors target the 'constitutively active tyrosine kinase' implicated in the pathogenesis of CML. Although they do not cure the disease, these agents are able to achieve long term control of CML in the majority of patients. Most recent texts (Including Harrisons) recommend Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (Imatinib) as the initial treatment of choice for newly diagnosed CML reserving Allogeneic Stem Cell Transplantation (SCT) for those who develop Imatinib Resistance.

question_text: A young woman reports recurrent headaches, easy bruising, and occasional visual disturbances. Laboratory tests show an elevated platelet count, with normal red and white blood cell counts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical manifestations indicate essential thrombocytosis; the key diagnostic finding is of elevated platelets with normal RBC and WBC counts.

Essential thrombocytosis

  • A myeloproliferative neoplasm characterised by an isolated elevation in platelet count.
  • This condition results from abnormal proliferation of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, leading to excessive platelet production.
  • Associated with JAK2 V617F mutation (50-60% of cases), CALR mutations (type 1 and 2) and MPL mutations.

Clinical Features and complications

  • Often asymptomatic
  • Thrombotic events (arterial > venous)
  • Erythromelalgia
  • Ocular migraines & visual disturbances
  • TIAs
  • Spontaneous bleeding & easy bruising
  • Complications include thrombosis, which is the major cause of morbidity, and hemorrhage, especially when platelet counts exceed 1 million/μL.
  • The disease may also progress to myelofibrosis, with a small risk of transformation to leukemia.

Diagnostic criteria

  • Platelet count >450,000/μL
  • Bone marrow showing megakaryocyte proliferation
  • Not meeting WHO criteria for other myeloid neoplasms
  • Presence of JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation

Treatment

  • Low-dose aspirin for thrombosis prevention
  • Hydroxyurea for high-risk patients
  • Anagrelide for cytoreduction
  • Plateletpheresis for severe cases

Explanation of other options:

Polycythemia Vera (Option B): Polycythemia vera presents with elevated levels of all three blood cell lines - RBCs, WBCs, and platelets. Patients typically present with ruddy complexion, pruritus, and thrombotic complications.

Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (Option C): Typically shows elevation in granulocytes and often an increase in platelets as well. The presence of normal WBC count makes CML an unlikely diagnosis, as it characteristically presents with marked leukocytosis.

Acute Myeloid Leukemia (Option D): Acute myeloid leukemia typically presents with abnormal levels of blood cells and can show varying counts of WBCs, RBCs, and platelets. The normal blood counts except for platelets make AML less likely, as it usually presents with cytopenias and blast cells in the peripheral blood.

question_text: Which microorganism causes cat scratch disease?
explanation:
Explanation:

Cat scratch disease (CSD) is an infection caused by Bartonella henselae, a Gram-negative, facultative intracellular bacterium. It is transmitted by the bite or scratch of cats (especially kittens) or via fleas carrying infected feces. In immunocompetent patients, it causes localized lymphadenopathy and fever, while in immunocompromised individuals, it can lead to bacillary angiomatosis, peliosis hepatis, and endocarditis.

  • Transmission: Primarily from cats; via scratches, bites, or fleas (Ctenocephalides felis).
  • Clinical presentations:
    • Cat scratch disease (immunocompetent): Papule/pustule at site, tender lymphadenopathy, fever, malaise.
    • Bacillary angiomatosis (immunocompromised): Vascular skin lesions resembling Kaposi sarcoma, systemic symptoms.
    • Peliosis hepatis: Blood-filled cavities in liver/spleen, hepatomegaly.
    • Endocarditis: Culture-negative, seen in immunocompromised patients.
    • Diagnosis: Serology (IgM/IgG via ELISA/IFA), PCR, Warthin-Starry silver stain, culture (difficult).
  • Treatment:
    • CSD: Often self-limiting. Severe → azithromycin or doxycycline.
    • Bacillary angiomatosis/peliosis: Doxycycline or erythromycin for months.
    • Endocarditis: Doxycycline + rifampin.

Explanation of other options:

B. quintana (Option B): Causes trench fever, spread by lice.

B. bacilliformis (Option C): Causes Carrion's disease, transmitted by sandflies.

Borrelia burgdorferi (Option D): Causes Lyme disease via tick bites.

Key Takeaways:

  • Bartonella henselae is the causative agent of cat scratch disease.
  • In immunocompromised hosts, the infection manifests as bacillary angiomatosis or peliosis hepatis.

question_text: HIV positive patients present with fever and non-productive cough and breathlessness. X-ray chest is normal. On work up LDH is elevated and CD4 count is less than 200. Which drug should be started in this case?
explanation:
The clinical scenario deals with Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia.

The risk of PCP is greatest among those who have experienced a previous bout of PCP and those who have CD4+ T-cell counts of <200.

Recurrent fever, night sweats, thrush, and unexplained weight loss also are associated with an increased incidence of PCP. For these reasons, it is strongly recommended that all patients with CD4+ T-cell counts<200 should receive PCP prophylaxis.

The standard treatment for PCP or disseminated pneumocystis is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX). Alternative treatments for mild to moderate PCP include dapsone/trimethoprim, clindamycin/primaquine, and atovaquone. IV pentamidine is the treatment of choice for severe disease in the patient unable to tolerate TMP-SMX. For patients with a Pao2 35 mmHg, adjunct glucocorticoid therapy should be used in addition to specific antimicrobials. Overall, treatment should be continued for 21 days and followed by secondary prophylaxis. Prophylaxis for PCP is indicated for any HIV-infected individual who has experienced a prior bout of PCP, any patient with a CD4+ T-cell count of <200 or <15%, any patient with unexplained fever of 2 weeks, and any patient with a recent history of oropharyngeal candidiasis. The preferred regimen for prophylaxis is TMP-SMX, one double-strength tablet daily. This regimen also provides protection against toxoplasmosis and some bacterial respiratory pathogens. For patients who cannot tolerate TMP-SMX, alternatives for prophylaxis include dapsone plus pyrimethamine plus leucovorin, aerosolized pentamidine administered by the Respirgard II nebulizer, and atovaquone. Primary or secondary prophylaxis for PCP can be discontinued in those patients treated with ART who maintain good suppression of HIV (200/μL) for at least 3 months.

Chest Xray findings:

Diffuse Bilateral Interstitial Infiltrates:

  • The most common finding is a widespread, symmetric, and diffuse pattern of interstitial infiltrates in both lungs.

question_text: A 36 year old man has HIV infection. Recently his CD4 count has dropped to 250 from 600 and viral load has dropped from 10,000 copies to 2000 copies /ml. He has now developed diarrhoea. Which one of the following is likely to cause diarrhea in a HIV positive patient?
explanation:
Common organisms such as entamoeba, salmonella, giardia, campylobacter, cryptosporidium, cyclospora, mycobacterium and also viral causes can cause diarrhea in HIV positive patients.

But in a patient where the CD 4 count has dropped rapidly, infection with opportunistic pathogens have to be considered.

Cryptosporidia, microsporidia, and Isospora belli are the most common opportunistic protozoa that infect the GI tract and cause diarrhea in HIV-infected patients.
