question_text: Spot diagnosis in HIV patient?
explanation:
Oral thrush, Aphthous ulcer, hairy cell leukemia and Kaposis's sarcoma are common oral lesions in HIV patients.

Oral thrush is seen as white, cheesy exudate, often on an erythematous mucosa in the posterior oropharynx. While most commonly seen on the soft palate, early lesions are often found along the gingival vestibule. The diagnosis is made by direct examination of a scraping for pseudohyphal elements.

Oral hairy leukoplakia presents as white, frondlike lesions, generally along the lateral borders of the tongue and sometimes on the adjacent buccal mucosa

Aphthous ulcers of the posterior oropharynx also are seen with regularity in patients with untreated HIV infection. The etiology is unknown

Oral Kaposi Sarcoma is seen as reddish purple nodular lesions which appear highly vascular.

So among the options, Kaposi Sarcoma is the best choice

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 202, Pg: 1569

question_text: Maternal HIV transmission to the fetus occurs Most commonly during?
explanation:
Maternal HIV transmission to the fetus occurs most commonly in the perinatal period.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 202, Pg: 1535

question_text: Which of the following opportunistic infections is most typical of HIV infection with a CD4 count less than 50 cells/&microL?
explanation:
Patients with HIV infection and low CD4 counts (<50 cells/μL) characteristically develop pneumocystis, toxoplasmosis, CMV retinitis, tuberculosis, cryptococcal meningitis, cryptosporidiosis, and disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex infection. Mucormycosis is typically seen in patients with neutropenia or diabetes mellitus and is rare in patients immunosuppressed because of HIV infection.

Nocardiosis can occur in patients with HIV infection, but is unusual.

BK virus causes disease in transplant recipients, with nephropathy seen in renal transplant patients. BK virus is most unusual in patients with HIV infection.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 202, Pg: 1563

question_text: Which of the following statements concerning the relationship of tuberculosis (TB) and HIV infection is correct.
option_a: Levels of plasma HIV RNA decrease in the setting of active TB.
option_b: TB usually develops only when the median CD4 count is 200/L.
option_c: Extra pulmonary disease is more common than pulmonary disease in the HIV-infected individual
option_d: Therapy for TB is the same in the HIV-infected patient as in the HIV-negative patient
explanation:
In the US, up to 5% of patients with AIDS have active TB infection, which is more commonly pulmonary than extra pulmonary. It is important to recognize and treat TB early in the course of disease in patients with HIV infection, since TB can increase the level of HIV RNA in the plasma.
Skin testing is helpful for predicting who is at risk for TB but is not helpful in the diagnosis of active infection. The epidemic of TB associated with HIV infection is probably the greatest health risk to the general public and the healthcare profession.

  • Though atypical mycobacterial infection occurs relatively late in HIV infection in patients with low CD4 counts, active typical TB may develop relatively early in the course of the disease.
  • Patients with relatively high CD4 T cell counts may exhibit typical pulmonary reactivation with the clinical syndrome of weight loss, fever, cough, and dyspnea and with a chest x-ray revealing apical cavitary disease.
  • In patients with lower CD4-+T cell counts, disseminated disease, including
    extrapulmonary manifestations are more common.
  • Fortunately, the treatment of active TB in an HIV patient can be quite successful, and the recommended therapy is generally the same as it would be in a patient who does not have HIV infection.
  • However, rifabutin should be substituted for rifampin in patients who are receiving the protease inhibitors or non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors because of adverse interactions.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 178 Pg: 1369-1379

question_text: A 50-year-old HIV patient presented with a painful lesion, as shown ?in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Kaposi sarcoma presents as violaceous lesions on the skin or mucosa, commonly seen in HIV-positive individuals due to HHV-8 infection.

  • The lesion shown in the image is a violaceous plaque located on the hard palate in an HIV-positive patient, which is highly suggestive of Kaposi sarcoma (KS).
  • KS is a vascular tumor associated with human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) and is classified as an AIDS-defining illness.
  • It typically involves the skin, oral mucosa, and internal organs like the lungs and GI tract.
  • Clinical stages:
    • Patch stage: Flat, pink or red macules.
    • Plaque stage: Raised purple or brown lesions.
    • Nodular stage: Firm, raised nodules that may ulcerate.
  • Variants of KS:
    • Classic KS: Older Mediterranean or Eastern European males.
    • Endemic KS: Seen in younger individuals in sub-Saharan Africa.
    • Transplant-associated KS: Occurs in patients on immunosuppressants.
    • AIDS-associated KS: Occurs in HIV/AIDS, especially with low CD4 counts.
  • Pathophysiology: HHV-8 infects endothelial cells, promoting angiogenesis and spindle cell proliferation.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Biopsy showing spindle cells, angiogenesis, and extravasated RBCs.
    • PCR or serology for HHV-8 may support the diagnosis.
  • Management:
    • Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is the cornerstone, as immune reconstitution leads to regression.
    • Chemotherapy (liposomal doxorubicin, paclitaxel) for extensive disease.
    • Radiotherapy or cryotherapy for localized lesions.

Explanation of other options:

Basal cell carcinoma (Option A): Typically presents as pearly nodules on sun-exposed skin, not as violaceous mucosal lesions.

Malignant melanoma (Option C): Presents as dark, irregular pigmented lesions, not characteristic violaceous plaques.

Squamous cell carcinoma (Option D): Can occur in the oral cavity but appears as ulcerated, keratotic growths, not violaceous patches.

Reference:

PubMed - 23679875

question_text:
A 76-year-old male is seen in the outpatients department. He reports weight loss over three months but his history is otherwise unremarkable. On examination his abdomen is soft with no palpable masses. A PR examination is normal. His blood tests show:
Hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL(12-16)
MCV 70 fL(80-96)
Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation for this patient?
option_b: CT scan of the abdomen and upper GI endoscopy
explanation:
This man has weight loss and an unexplained microcytic anaemia. The likely site of blood loss is from the gastrointestinal (GI) tract in absence of an alternative explanation.This may be due to an occult GI malignancy (age of 76 years) and therefore the initial investigations of choice are upper and lower GI endoscopy.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:322 Pg:2387

question_text:
A 45 year male presents with weight loss and watery diarrhea for several weeks.
Investigations reveal hypokalaemia. Which of the following would support a diagnosis of a VIPoma?
explanation:
VIPomas in adults are usually neuroendocrine islet cell tumors of the pancreas that produce high amounts of VIP. Other secreted hormones may include secreted gastrin and pancreatic polypeptide.

Achlorhydria (lack of acidity from the stomach) is classically associated with VIPoma. It can be diagnosed by measuring acid output from nasogastric contents (NG tube). Features of VIP syndrome include watery diarrhea, hypochlorhydria, hyperglycemia, hypercalcemia and flushing.

Hypoglycemia is associated with insulinoma

Pellagra a condition caused by niacin deficiency occurs in carcinoid syndrome

Migratory erythema associated with glucagonoma.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 84 Pg: 665

question_text:
A 78-year-old man presented with acute pain, pallor and absent pulses in his right leg. Investigations revealed an embolus in his femoral artery.
 What is the most likely source of this embolus?
explanation:
Ulceration of an atheromatous plaque of the abdominal aorta is the most common source of emboli in this situation.

Right ventricular thrombi would embolise to the lung.

The others are possible but less likely causes.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:274 pg:1921,1922

question_text: A 56-year-old male is admitted with vomiting and acute epigastric abdominal pain which radiates through to his back. Investigations confirm severe acute pancreatitis.Which of the following figures most accurately reflect the mortality associated with severe acute pancreatitis?
explanation:
Severity of acute Pancreatitis:

  1. Mild Acute Pancreatitis: no local complications or organ failure. Self limiting disease. Recovery in 3-7 days.
  2. Moderately Severe Acute Pancreatitis: Transient organ failure that resolves in < 48 hours. Or, local or systemic complications in the absence of organ failure.
  3. Severe Acute Pancreatitis: Persistent Organ failure that lasts > 48 hours involving one or more organs.

With single organ failure, the mortality is 3-10%

With multi organ failure( severe acute pancreatitis), the mortality is nearly 50%

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 348, Pg: 2661

question_text:
A 28-year-old woman presents to the Emergency department very agitated, complaining of abdominal pain. This has been her third attendance over the past six months, and each time there have been no significant findings. Her only medication of note is the oral contraceptive pill.
On this occasion her BP is elevated 155/90 mmHg, her pulse is 92, and her temperature is 37.8°C. Her abdomen is generally tender but soft, and she has active bowel sounds. She complains of lower limb weakness, and she appears to have 4/5 power weakness below the knee.Investigations show:
Hb 13.4 g/dl(13.5-18)
WCC 10.2 x 10^9/L (4-10)
PLT 194 x 10^9/L (150-400)
Na 132 mmol/l (134-143)
K 4.4 mmol/l (3.5-5)
Creatinine 1.1 mg/dl
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is associated with:

  • Hypertension
  • A mild increase in temperature
  • Non-specific abdominal pain

Patients feel normal between attacks, and the disease itself is due to accumulation of both porphobilinogen and amino-levulinic acid.

In general, drugs that lead to increased activity of the hepatic P450 system, such as phenobarbital, sulfonamides, oestrogens, and alcohol, are associated with increased risk of acute attacks.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 416, Pg: 3238

question_text:
A 34 year old lady presents with a long history of abdominal pain and diarrhoea. She also 
gives a history of recurrent mouth ulcers. Recently the pain has become more intense, she has begun to lose weight and has developed fever with night sweats and she also complains of a rash over her legs. On examination she is thin, she has clubbing and erythema nodosum. On examination of the abdomen a firm tender mass can be palpated in the right iliac fossa. In this patient, which of the following investigations is most appropriate?
explanation:
The clinical features in this patient points towards a diagnosis of Crohn's disease.

However, the features of increased pain, fever, sweats and a mass suggest the patient may have developed an abscess in the right iliac fossa.

Hence, imaging this area with CT scan to detect and treat the collection is the investigation of choice.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 326, Pg: 2477

question_text: A 31 year old gymnast has sudden onset vertigo and dizziness. On examination, there is horizontal nystagmus, with a full range of eye movements. Her speech is slurred. There is intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia which is asymmetrical. She has an ataxic gait. Which of the Following investigations would be most appropriate?
option_b: MRI and MRA of head and neck
explanation:
• The clinical picture is of an acute onset cerebellar syndrome, which suggests a vascular cause. This would involve the posterior (vertebrobasilar) circulation. If headache or neck pain were associated, a vertebral artery dissection would be most important to exclude. A Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) will help to diagnose dissection, stenosis or thrombosis.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 423, Pg: 3283

question_text: A 60-year-old man presents with pain in the lower back. The pain begins in the lower back and radiates to the lower abdomen. He has not been on any medications recently. Investigations reveal a normocytic normochromic anemia, raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Renal function is impaired. Ultrasound scan shows bilateral hydronephrosis. Which of the following investigations should be done?
explanation:
The presence of hydronephrosis points towards obstruction at the level of ureters on both sides. The cause is likely retroperitoneal fibrosis. It is also supported by the raised ESR and CRP. It is characterized by low back ache and lower extremity edema. It is often associated with IgG4 Disease. But IgG4 levels will be normal as the disease often presents in the fibrotic stage.

Ct abdomen will show inflammation around the aorta extending to the iliac vessels. CT PET will help differentiate between lymphoma and retroperitoneal fibrosis.

24 hour urine for creatine clearance may be used to asses the function of kidney, but it will not throw light to the diagnosis. 24 hour urine protein is also not useful. Intravenous urogram is used for diagnosing obstruction, usually intraluminal.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 368, Pg:2838.

question_text: A 52 year old man presents with lower back pains and lethargy. Investigations subsequently confirmed obstructive nephropathy and retroperitoneal fibrosis. His medication is reviewed on the ward round. Which medication is well known to cause retroperitoneal fibrosis?
explanation:
Retroperitoneal fibrosis is a disease featuring the proliferation of fibrous tissue in the retroperitoneum, the compartment of the body containing the kidneys, aorta, renal tract and various other structures. It may present with lower back pain, renal failure, hypertension, deep vein thrombosis and other obstructive symptoms.

It may have an autoimmune etiology. 1/3rd  cases are secondary to malignancy, medications, aortic aneurysm or certain infections.

Methyldopa, methysergide, amphetamines, beta blockers, cocaine and LSD are drugs which cause retroperitoneal fibrosis.

Azathioprine is used to treat the condition.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 319 Pg: 2375

question_text: A 32-year-old female presents with complaints of fatigue, paleness, and dizziness. Laboratory investigations reveal low serum iron levels and an increased total iron-binding capacity (TIBC). Based on these findings and the presence of a negative iron balance, which of the following findings is NOT consistent with her iron metabolism status?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ferritin levels typically decrease in iron deficiency as it reflects the depletion of iron stores.Bone marrow iron stores are absent when the serum ferritin level is <15 μg/L.

Reduced serum iron: In iron deficiency, serum iron levels decrease because the body's iron stores are depleted and not enough iron is available for normal function. (Option A Ruled Out)

Increased TIBC: TIBC increases as the body attempts to capture more iron from the diet due to the deficiency. (Option B Ruled Out)

Increased transferrin (Correct): Transferrin, the main protein in the blood that binds iron and transports it throughout the body, increases as part of the body's response to iron deficiency. This is often reflected as an increase in TIBC. (Option C Ruled Out)

  • Stages of Iron Deficiency:
    • Stage 1 - Negative Iron Balance: Demand or loss of iron exceeds absorption capabilities, often due to blood loss, pregnancy, growth spurts, or inadequate diet.
    • Stage 2 - Depletion of Iron Stores: As stores deplete, serum iron drops, TIBC and red cell protoporphyrin levels increase.
    • Stage 3 - Iron-Deficient Erythropoiesis: With continued depletion, hemoglobin synthesis becomes impaired, leading to the appearance of microcytic and hypochromic cells in peripheral blood.
  • Laboratory Findings:
    • Serum Iron: Decreases as stores are depleted.
    • Ferritin: Decreases reflecting depletion of iron stores; marrow iron is absent when ferritin is below 15 μg/L.
    • TIBC: Increases as the body tries to maximize iron uptake.
    • Transferrin Saturation: Drops below 20%, indicating impaired hemoglobin synthesis.
  • Clinical Features: Development of hypochromia and microcytosis as the deficiency progresses, eventually leading to observable changes in erythroid marrow activity and blood cell morphology with severe prolonged anemia.

Key Takeaways:

Iron deficiency anemia is characterized by reduced serum iron, increased TIBC, decreased ferritin, and low transferrin saturation. The most fundamental metabolic alteration is reduced serum iron.

question_text: A 48-year-old woman is undergoing investigations for secondary amenorrhoea and joint pains. Blood tests show her follicle-stimulating hormone level to be 40 IU/l (> 30 in postmenopausal women). What would be the best method for diagnosing osteoporosis in this patient?
explanation:
• This patient is most probably menopausal judging by her FSH level. All the options are non-invasive techniques for estimating skeletal mass or bone mineral density.
  • Dual energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is the 'gold standard' for diagnosing osteoporosis. A DXA scan provides a T-score reflecting fracture risk, which may influence treatment decisions.
  • T score of less than -2.5 obtained by DXA is labelled as osteoporosis while the value between -1 to -2.5 is termed osteopenia.
  • Fractures are readily detected by bone scintigraphy even if plain films are normal.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 3196

question_text:
A 58-year-old man from Thailand presented with abdominal pain and a mass in the right upper quadrant. He reported that he had been diagnosed with viral hepatitis several years previously. Investigations showed:
Serum alpha-fetoprotein 13,500 IU/L (< 10)
What is the most likely underlying viral infection?
explanation:
The patient has chronic viral hepatitis and presents with a hepatoma.

The underlying cause must be either hepatitis B virus (HBV) or hepatitis C virus (HCV).There is a higher prevalence of HBV in the Far East and since his country of origin is the only other detail that gives a clue to the cause of his hepatitis, the most likely viral agent is HBV.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 82, Pg: 643

question_text: A farmer presents with high-grade fever, rash, vomiting, retro-orbital pain, and myalgia for 5 days. Dengue hemorrhagic fever is suspected. Which of the following investigations is most appropriate for diagnosis at this stage?
option_d: Viral isolation of Aedes albopictus (C6/36) culture
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient presents after 5 days of fever onset, which means the viremic phase has subsided, and the antibody response (IgM) has begun.
  • Therefore, IgM ELISA is the preferred diagnostic test at this stage for confirming dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF).
  • Early-phase tests such as NS1 antigen and RT-PCR are most effective within the first 5 days of illness, whereas IgM ELISA becomes the test of choice after day 5.

question_text: Which of the following investigations is most likely to indicate that ovulation is imminent?
option_a: Follicle size of 20 mm on ultrasound scan
explanation:
• Sudden increase in luteinizing hormone (LH) -the LH surge - is of particular significance as it indicates that ovulation will occur about 24 hours after the LH peak.
  • Follicle size is usually around 22 mm prior to ovulation but an ultrasound scan gives no indication that ovulation is about to occur. An increase in basal body temperature and secretory changes in the endometrium occur after ovulation.
  • A positive Spinnbarkeit test is used to demonstrate oestrogenic activity on the cervical mucus. Elasticity of the cervical mucus is greatly enhanced prior to ovulation, but does not provide a clue as to when ovulation will occur.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 3031

question_text:
A 46 year old man presents with a 6 month history of severe indigestion. 3 years ago he had a duodenal ulcer seen on endoscopy.
Investigations reveal:
Fasting gastrin 160 mg/dL
Where is gastrin produced?
explanation:
Gastrin is produced by the G cells of gastric antrum. It stimulates parietal cells to produce hydrochloric acid. Its production is stimulated by neural reflex pathways and also by direct effect of digested peptides on the G cells.

Normal fasting gastrin levels are usually < 150mg/dL. Usually all gastrinomas have a fasting gastrin level > 150-200mg/dL

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 324, Pg: 2453

question_text:
A 27-year-old shop worker is referred with a three month history of recurrent episodes of disorientation and confusion. Her friend has found her wandering around the house on several occasions, apparently with no idea of where she is or how she got there. Her mood has been very low, with frequent emotional outbursts, and she has considered leaving her job because of problems with working the computer and managing customers' queries. Her friend feels her condition is significantly worsening.
Physical examination is normal, apart from recurrent, asymetrical, jerks in all four limbs.
Which of the following investigations is likely to be most useful in reaching a diagnosis?
explanation:
• This kind of rapid cognitive decline in a young person with myoclonus is strongly suggestive of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD).
  • A definitive diagnosis of any form of CJD requires pathological examination of brain tissue, which is usually only done post-mortem. During life, investigations are undertaken for two reasons: to exclude other possible diagnoses, and to support the diagnosis of CJD. Supportive investigations are EEG, CSF examination and MRI.
  • The EEG in sporadic CJD may show significant abnormalities involving deep brain areas such as the thalami. The normal rhythms are gradually lost. Initially the changes are diffuse, and non-specific, developing into generalised bi- or triphasic periodic sharp wave complexes with a frequency of 1-2 per second. High voltage sharp waves may be synchronous with myoclonic jerks. In an appropriate clinical context, this EEG pattern is strongly suggestive of a diagnosis of CJD.
  • Neither CSF examination nor MRI are options here, but both can also give supportive information.
  • The CSF typically contains no inflammatory cells, but the total protein content may be raised. Analysis for brain specific proteins, particularly 14-3-3, is supportive in the right clinical context.
  • In a proportion of cases, abnormalities of signal in the anterior basal ganglia (caudate/putamen, and sometimes the cortex) can be seen on MRI, which can also support the diagnosis.
  • Chest x ray and liver function tests may help to exclude other diagnoses, but do not give supportive information for CJD.
  • Visual evoked potentials may be altered in CJD, but no specific pattern has yet been identified to support the diagnosis.
  • CT head generally demonstrates brain atrophy in CJD, but this is not a specific finding and is therefore less useful than an EEG.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 438, Pg: 3420

20th edition Chapter:430 Page number:3152-3153

question_text:
A 27-year-old woman presented with a history of sudden onset right-sided weakness and dysphasia lasting 8 hours. She had returned to India from US 2 days previously. There was no significant past medical history and physical examination was normal. Chest X-ray, ECG and a CT head scan were all normal. 
Which one of the following investigations is most likely to reveal the underlying cause of this episode?
explanation:
The history here suggests a lower limb deep vein thrombosis with peripheral embolus through a patent foramen ovale, leading to a left sided cerebrovascular event.

This is termed the paradoxical embolus - so-called because a thromboembolus arising from the venous circulation can end up in the systemic circulation.

Transoesophageal echocardiography is the investigation of choice to investigate for a patent foramen ovale, although transthoracic echocardiography with contrast may be an alternative.

Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:273 pg:1913

explanation: Thromboelastography can be used for guiding intra operative transfusion. But it cant be employed in other disorders of bleeding and thrombosis. It has some role in venom induced coagulopathy

question_text: SARS-CoV-2 is believed to transmit primarily via
explanation:
Respiratory droplets: between persons in proximity when the droplets make direct contact with mucous membrane

Airborne transmission: May occur. But over long distances is unlikely.

Fomite transmission: Possible but not dominant mode of transmission.

question_text: Biosafety level of SARS COV-
explanation:
Biosafety levels (BSL) are used to identify the protective measures needed in a laboratory setting to protect workers, the environment, and the public. The levels are defined in Biosafety in Biomedical Laboratories (the BMBL). BSL-3 laboratories are used to study infectious agents or toxins that may be transmitted through the air and cause potentially lethal infections. Researchers perform all experiments in a biosafety cabinet. BSL-3 laboratories are designed to be easily decontaminated

Cultures of SARS-CoV-2 should be handled in a biosafety level 3 (BSL-3) laboratory using BSL practices

Inoculation of animals with infectious wild-type SARS CoV-2 should be conducted in an animal biosafety level 3 (ABSL-3) facility using absl-3 practices and respiratory protection.

Let us see the various biosafety levels

question_text: Which of the following is not an evidence-based measure for preventing the transmission of COVID-19?
explanation:
Explanation:

While several proven public health measures including vaccination, masking, and respiratory hygiene significantly reduce the transmission of COVID-19, ivermectin has not been shown to be effective for either prevention or treatment of the disease.

Initial small-scale studies suggested a possible antiviral effect, but subsequent large randomized trials and meta-analyses failed to confirm any clear clinical benefit. Consequently, major health authorities such as the WHO, CDC, and NIH do not recommend ivermectin for COVID-19 prophylaxis or therapy outside of approved clinical trials.

Measures to Prevent the Spread of COVID-19:

  • Cough Etiquette (Option A ruled out) Always cover your mouth and nose with a tissue or your elbow when coughing or sneezing. Dispose of tissues immediately.
  • Wear Masks (Option B ruled out)
  • Practice Physical Distancing
  • Wash Hands Regularly
  • Use Hand Sanitizer
  • Avoid Touching Face
  • Get Vaccinated (Option D ruled out)
  • Follow Local Guidelines
  • Avoid Large Gatherings
  • Monitor Symptoms and Get Tested

question_text: SARS-CoV-2 is
explanation:
SARS-CoV-2 is the cause of a respiratory disease called COVID-19. The virus is a member of lineage B of the Betacoronavirus genus that not only includes the highly pathogenic viruses SARS-CoV-1 (which caused a smaller epidemic in 2002-2003) and MERS-CoV (a lineage C virus that caused small epidemics in 2012, 2015, and 2018), but also contains the lineage A common cold viruses CoV-OC43 and CoV-HKU1 and MERS-CoV. These are enveloped, positive-sense RNA viruses encoded by a viral RNA genome that is quite large, a single linear RNA segment that encodes four structural proteins, designated the S (spike), E (envelope), M (membrane), and N (nucleocapsid) proteins, and a large polyprotein that is cleaved into 16 nonstructural proteins in infected cells.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition page Ch: 199 Pg 1507

question_text: In patients affected by COVID-19, which of the following patterns is frequently observed in chest CT scans?
explanation:
Explanation:

Bilateral, peripheral, and basal-predominant Ground Glass Opacities (GGOs) are the most common and characteristic early finding on chest CT in patients with COVID-19 pneumonia. GGOs appear as hazy areas of increased lung attenuation that do not obscure the underlying bronchial and vascular markings.

CT- chest of COVID-19 patient shows widespread faint ground glass opacity upper lung lobe as well as reticular shadowing bilaterally in the image below.

Explanation of other options:

Interlobular septal thickening and Crazy paving pattern (Option A and D): This pattern (GGO + interlobular septal thickening) can be seen in COVID-19 but is less common and typically appears later in the disease course. It is more classically associated with conditions like Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis.

Air bronchograms (Option B): Can be seen within areas of consolidation in COVID-19 but are not the primary or most frequent pattern.

Key Takeaways:

  • The classic CT finding in COVID-19 pneumonia is bilateral, peripheral ground-glass opacities.
  • This pattern reflects the underlying alveolar damage and inflammation.

question_text: Remdesivir's mechanism of action is
option_a: Inhibits the RNA dependent RNA polymerase
explanation: Remdesivir inhibits RNA dependent RNA polymerase of SARS and MERS CoV.

question_text: A 75-year-old man died because of a cardiac arrest in the intensive care unit. The treating doctor believed that he was responsible for the patient's death despite knowing that the patient had a poor prognosis. Which is the most likely cognitive distortion?
explanation:
• This refers to relating external events to oneself when there is no reason to do so.
  • All events that can be brought into consciousness are associated with a sense of personal possession, although this is not usually in the forefront of consciousness.
  • This ‘I’ quality has been called personalisation: and may be disturbed in psychological disorders.
  • There are two aspects to the sense of self-activity/personalisation; the sense of existence and the awareness of the performance of one’s actions.
  • The individual blames him or herself for the consequences of others’ actions.
  • In this scenario, the treating doctor is personalising the death of an elderly patient who had a sudden cardiac arrest and a poor prognosis.

Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, eleventh edition, chapter 28, page no. 875

question_text: A 45-year-old married man was referred for deaddiction; he reported that he currently used cocaine, intranasally by snorting, 3-5 days a week and that this pattern has been continuing for almost 5 years. On average, he consumes a total of 1-2 grams of cocaine weekly, at work in his office or in the bathroom. He is prone to develop all of the following long-term complications due to his addictive habit except:
explanation:
Complications of long-term use of cocaine:

  1. Nasal ulceration and perforation
  2. Neurological complications like acute dystonia, tics, migraine like headache
  3. Cerebrovascular: Non-haemorrhagic cerebral infarctions(Subarachnoid/Intraparenchymal/Intraventricular) due to vasoconstriction
  4. Seizures
  5. Cardiac: Myocardial infarction, arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy
  6. Increased risk of HIV AIDS and hepatitis B/C for intravenous use of cocaine(and not for intranasal use)

Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter number 20, Stimulant-related disorders, Page number 677.

question_text: Which of the following is not seen in cocaine intoxication?
explanation:
Cocaine intoxication is known to stimulate the central nervous system and cause various physiological effects. The symptoms typically seen during cocaine intoxication include:

  • Hyperthermia: Cocaine use can increase body temperature due to its stimulant effects on the central nervous system.
  • Agitation: Cocaine is a stimulant, which can lead to agitation, restlessness, and hyperactivity.
  • Myocardial infarction: Cocaine use can cause vasoconstriction, which increases the risk of myocardial infarction (heart attack), especially in individuals with preexisting cardiovascular disease.

Why Bradycardia is Incorrect:

  • Bradycardia (slow heart rate) is not typically seen in cocaine intoxication. Instead, tachycardia (rapid heart rate) is common. Cocaine stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, leading to an increase in heart rate and blood pressure.

Key Takeaways:

  • Cocaine intoxication often leads to tachycardia, agitation, hyperthermia, and myocardial infarction due to its stimulant effects.
  • Bradycardia is not typically a feature of cocaine intoxication; instead, it is associated with conditions like opioid toxicity or vagal stimulation.

question_text: A year after her husband died due to myocardial infarction, the wife again started exhibiting symptoms like feeling depressed, guilty, lonely and was not able to sleep. She developed these symptoms exactly on the same day that her husband died a year ago. This is termed as:
explanation:
• When the trigger for an acute grief reaction is a special occasion, such as a holiday or birthday, the rekindled grief is called an anniversary reaction.
  • It is not unusual for anniversary reactions to occur each year on the same day the person died or, in some cases, when the bereaved individual becomes the same age the deceased person was at the time of death.
  • Although these anniversary reactions tend to become relatively mild and brief over time, they can be experienced as the reliving of one's original grief and prevail for hours or days.

Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, Chapter 34 End-of-life issues, Page number 1355.

question_text: A 33-year-old divorced man has the chief complaint of 'I' m going to have a heart attack like my father. He explains that his father died of a myocardial infarction at 45 years of age. He is convinced that he is experiencing angina attacks consisting of nervousness, sweating, shortness of breath, palpitations, flushing and numbness in his hands, each lasting for several minutes. He is anxious about having these symptoms and despite negative results from a cardiology workup, remains certain that he will suffer a heart attack. His behaviour and lifestyle have not been otherwise affected. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• The most likely diagnosis for this man is panic disorder.
  • He displays characteristic features of panic attacks, such as recurrent episodes of anxiety associated with physical symptoms.
  • These episodes are spontaneous and he worries about the consequences of having an additional attack, namely, a myocardial infarction.
  • However, he does not avoid places and his behaviour is otherwise unaffected, as in agoraphobia(Option A).

Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 9.2, Panic disorder, Page no. 393.
